I remember when I first got this game, I was happy about it because I was thinking it would be much better than the first Raw game which bombed in all aspects, but unfortunately it didn't do much better than the first Raw.I'll give props for the graphics as the graphics were very nice and a huge improvement from the first Raw. The graphics were more realistic and looked how 3D models should look. Entrances were great as well. There was no commentary in the game and the announcers were Howard Finkel and a lady who was supposed to be Lillian Garcia but sounded nothing like her.The gameplay can be a little bumpy at times and hard to reverse the CPU. One annoying thing about the gameplay is that if there are more than 4 superstars in the ring, the game becomes ridiculously slow and frustrating as a result. A good example of this would be the Royal Rumble Match. After about 5 superstars enter the ring, the game becomes slow and it's almost like you're playing the game in slow motion. Very very irritating to play matches with more than 4 superstars, which is why I try to avoid playing Battle Royals and the Royal Rumble match as much as possible.There are plenty of superstars to pick from on the roster as pretty much every superstar and diva from the Ruthless Aggression Era is on here. Goldberg, Undertaker, Brock Lesnar, Edge, Kurt Angle, Rey Mysterio, Chris Benoit, Triple H, Kane, The Rock, Stone Cold Steve Austin, Shawn Michaels, Stacy Keibler, Scott Steiner, Trish Stratus, Matt Hardy, Chris Nowinski, Rikishi, and even Nidia, and so many moreThe main thing that bothers me so much about this game is the Season Mode. It's completely random and unrealistic on more levels than 1. For example, why is Jazz fighting Brock Lesnar for the WWE Championship in the main event of a PPV??? And more importantly why is Jazz winning the title and showing up as WWE Champion?? Other random things include being attacked by superstars who aren't even feuding with you. Like if I'm playing as Edge and I'm suddenly attacked in my locker room by Eddie Guerrero, who I haven't even feuded with. Or if I'm playing as Lita and out of nowhere Stacy Keibler runs in my locker room and knocks me out. It just makes no sense. It also irritates me that you can't wrestle in one match in Season Mode without there being an interference. Whenever you're involved in a match, one of your enemies will run to the ring and you think they're going to attack you.....but they end up attacking your opponent. WTF?? This happens in every match you have, unless you get lucky enough to have a Steel Cage or Hell In A Cell match.A cool feature consists of backstage interactions in this season mode. You can do things like encourage superstars to take out any diva or superstar on the roster, regardless of whether or not you're feuding with them, steal clothes from another superstar/divas' bag (if you do this enough times, successfully, you'll be able to unlock their titantron for you to watch in the Theater section of the main menu), try to attack a superstar in their locker room, call someone out, set a trap for a superstar, interfere in a match, rest, and many more. Each of those tasks will either succeed or fail. If you succeed at attacking a superstar or diva in their locker room or calling them out, your reputation and points go up. If you fail, they go down.You can also choose your referee for matches in Exhibition Mode. You can choose between normal (Earl Hebner), slow (Nick Patrick), or fast (Charles Robinson). If you don't want the match to take all day then DON'T pick Nick Patrick as the referee. How slow he counts is absolutely ridiculous. He takes about 5 second pauses between each count, giving your opponent enough time to kick out, regardless of how much damage you've done to them.Another bother I have with this game is the CPU. Beware that 99% of the time when you fight against the CPU, once they pin you, they won't stop. Meaning that if you get pinned by them and you kick out, they'll pin you again immediately before you even get a chance to get up. This will go on and on until you get tired of pressing buttons constantly and you lose. It's almost like the CPU is cheating to beat you which really pisses me off. The sad part is that there's no way to really reverse the pins, meaning that there's no stopping how constant they pin you.My favorite thing about this game is probably the Raw Theater. This is similar to the Theater section in Smackdown Just Bring It and Shut Your Mouth but instead of playing a variety of videos for you to watch, they only give you every playable character's titantron/theme song. As I mentioned, the way to unlock the superstar's titantrons/themes is by successfully stealing their clothes (I think 5 or 10 times) in season mode. After you've done that, go to the Theater, find the superstar's titantron that you stole clothes from and enjoy. Unfortunately, titantrons are all they showcase. I think other videos would've been a nice touchOverall: Slight improvements from the first Raw but not very much. Anyone who gives this game a 4 or 5 stars, must not have played any better wrestling games. A little known fact is that WWE Raw 2, was originally going to be called WWF Raw 2 with a roster and story mode based off of late 2001 and early 2002. Unfortunately after WWF transitioned to WWE in May 2002, they were forced to change it to Raw 2 and the game was kept in production longer for editing. By the time the game was finished it was 2003, so the game received a complete makeover with different graphics and a different roster. It's disappointing really because WWF Raw 2 seemed like it was going to be a better game x1000 than WWE Raw 2. In fact, I think there's still a trailer laying around on Youtube on what WWF Raw 2 was going to be like. I guess THQ got the picture that most fans were not happy with Raw and Raw 2, which would probably explain why this was the last Raw game made. Unfortunately for the short-lived Raw series, it received a less than decent burial. THQ would get it right in 2004 with their Day of Reckoning Series for the Gamecube

(First of all, don't you dare buy this game here on Amazon or eBay for some ridiculous, jacked-up price. Head over to GOG[dot]com and buy a DRM-free version for about $10.)Okay, on to the review. This is a great game. I just discovered it here in 2014 as I was waiting for AoW3 (which I haven't bought yet). AoW: SM is really a masterpiece of turn-based, role-playing fantasy gaming. It does have a few flaws, but overall it is probably the best turn-based strategy game I've played since Master of Orion (which is also excellent).Gameplay: AoW:SM is focused on building an empire and exploring/conquering a map, while making your wizard more powerful as a spell caster. You get to choose your wizard at the beginning of each match, along with your race (there are 15!). Each wizard can specialize in 6 different areas of magic, as well as be a bit of a hybrid. You can also specify the size of the map, how many levels it will have (that is surface, underground, and Shadow World), and even generate random maps. Sadly and somewhat inexplicably, you cannot choose the AI wizards or races that you compete against in a match. They are randomly chosen on random maps, or preset on fixed scenario maps. The gameplay itself is based on turns, with you doing actions such as moving troops, researching spells, fighting, and so forth each day (or turn). Fights can either be auto-resolved or fought manually, which means that you go to a zoomed-in version of the map and fight your opponent. This is usually where spells come into play. Overall, the combat is done well and can be intense.  The AI is pretty decent and can even surprise you on occasion.  There is a lengthy single-player campaign that comes with the game. I found it a mixed bag. On the one hand, it is a good tutorial for learning the game, and there are some interesting maps. However, the difficulty of the campaign is very uneven, with some easy maps that are just set-piece battles and some crazy hard ones that you'll have to restart over and over again due to overpowered AI opponents. By the second half of the campaign, missions are so tedious and difficult (even on the lower difficulty settings) that only the most hard-core players are likely to stick with it, without cheating.  Thankfully, there are a number of stand-alone scenarios that come with the game that are better than the campaign, and you can play random maps. I personally would recommend fiddling with the map editor that comes with the game.  You can build your own maps, create new wizards and heroes, change unit stats, and do other things to your heart's content. Overall, it's just a well-done game that takes advantage of the modding possibilities of the PC.Graphics & Audio: The game looks decent enough, considering that it's over 10 years old. Spell effects can be somewhat impressive, but don't expect a screen resolution higher than 1280x1024. Still, the graphics are all serviceable. The audio is quite good, especially the music. There are not a lot of voices in-game (as opposed to in the pre-mission introductions), but the sound effects are immersive enough.Bottom line: Superb game that really delivers a rich, diverse gaming experience for a turn-based, fantasy game. It has some good role-playing elements--your units and heroes level up--that make you care about your progress. The flaws are mostly minor, largely having to do with the lackluster campaign that gets painfully difficult over time. Otherwise, a highly rewarding game.Pros:+Great concept and execution+Customization options+Roleplaying and leveling up+Strong city-building mechanics+Vast array of races, spells, wizards, etc.+Modding possibilitiesCons:-Mediocre campaign-Random-map generator tends to spam mountains-Can't select AI opponents on random maps

Okay, most of my reviews are for games that are just pure crap or way overrated.  But having heard that this was one of the worst games of all time I had to try it.  I looked at it like renting a low budget movie knowing what I was getting into, and was pleasantly surprised!THE BAD:  Graphics, sound, voice acting, jumping mechanics (why do game makers have such a difficult time with this?), no final boss fight, some moves are just impossible to pull off, no dodge system (which is a real problem when people throw grenades randomly) and there was a glitch where the game wouldn't allow me to proceed to the next checkpoint- so I had to restart the level.This is a very low budget, bare bones kind of game.  Clearly extremely rushed and not well thought out.THE GOOD:  Face paced, good music, movie photos, a variety of enemies, outfits, and fight moves, the characters switch frequently and they all have their own moves and animations, very linear (which I like), and it had a lot of humor.  You CANNOT take this game- or the movies for that matter- seriously.  If you try to then you're missing the point entirely.  All you do is 3D brawl from beginning to end with the exception of pressing the A button at specific times or climbing a ladder.There are only 6 levels in the game, but they do get progressively harder.  The end was very abrupt and not very satisfying since there was no final boss, but at least there was a cut scene.  I had fun with it.  There's punching, kicking, weapons, combos, and lots of moves I couldn't pull off, but other than that the controls were good.I say it's a fun rent or really cheap buy if you're not expecting much and know what you're getting in to.  I had low expectations and had a great time with it.Don't overlook this one, but don't over think it either.

This is a fantasy RPG game that defies time and technology. It's story, voice acting, gameplay, and depth it's parts far exceeds any game that you have played today. Whether it's Modern Warfare 3, Black Ops 1-2, Halo 1-4, Mass Effect 1-3, Uncharted 1-3, Dragon Age, Skyrim, etc, Baldur's Gate 2 and its expansion remains top notch amongst them all.You couldn't ask for a better storyline and group of insanely memorable characters. The gameplay is easy to learn and harder to master. There is always something to do, and you really feel that you are part of this epic and dangerous fantasy world. The story draws you in and gives you many concrete goals to meet. You can choose not to follow them, though. The world is big enough for you to feel that you are part of something greater. The interface is manageable, though somewhat dated by today's quality of life standards. You will still need to pick up your spoils one by one, unless you have an appropriate mod through a third party website.Your character is at the forefront of an encroaching doom, but you are not always treated to such dire circumstances. You participate in a play, you fall into romance (or choose not to), you exchange witty (and not-so-witty) banter with friends and villains alike. However, when the time comes for you and your party to unleash the full might of your sword, spells, arrows or god--you will enjoy a depth of gameplay that you never thought possible in such an "oldie".To write this game off because it's old would be a BIG mistake. You would be missing out on one of the, if not THE greatest RPG the world has wrought. Don't miss out on playing this game. You will not regret it.

I loved DOTC for the NES, and this one expounds on it.  It's similar enough to appeal to fans of the older versions, yet different enough that it's not the same game.  The battles retain the appearance of the original with representations of units, but instead of just giving your troops an overall strategy like "Hold Your Ground" or "Outflank", you pick the unit you want to send and individual attacks for that unit.  It's more like a board game.  It's definitely strategy-light, but it's fun, and that's what's important.The swordfighting on castle raids has been considerably cleaned up.  It feel like fencing now, with looking for patterns in your opponent's swings, blocking or avoiding them, and counterattacking.  Archery raids are now possible (don't do them, though.  The control is TERRIBLE).  If you're a competent jouster, you now get a round to fortify your land winnings before whichever lord you won them from takes them back.  And there's the very well acted Robin Hood story line running throughout.  It's always the same, but it spices things up quite a bit.A huge added annoyance is the sea power of Prince John; he can now attack any coastal territory in England, instantly, with his ships.  You can circumvent this advantage by cutting off his advance early in the game, which is fine, but it forces you to play the game a specific way, cutting into your strategic options.  I still break this game out every couple years, though, so I can't bring myself to take a star away.  Perhaps they'll fix it in the next version?

If you've played any of the Prince of Persia games, you kind of have a general idea what this one is.  It's got some combat elements, but the majority is puzzle solving.  If you can get past the fact there's no voice acting, the main character generally just stands there without talking himself, and has this s-eating grin on his face all the time, the game is pretty fun.The star of the show is Sphinx who can jump, double-jump (eventually), has a weapon, gear, etc. to use.  You run around a series of "worlds" or "areas" and try to find things, do fetch quests, or fight monsters.  The controls could be a little tighter in regards to combat and the camera will fight you on occasion, but it's all still pretty good.  The sleeper star of the show though in my opinion is the mummy, King Tut.  The main reason I liked him is that he is dead so he's pretty much indestructible.  In fact, the primary puzzles he solves often involve him being set on fire, electrocuted, smashed, sliced up, etc. to trigger various things.  The puzzles are smaller, more localized, and more straight forward, but also generally lack the ability to save much during them which can be frustrating.  He also can't attack anything, but enjoys a measure of stealth.My main gripes with the game are inconsistent save statue (save point) placement, necessitating long periods between being able to save and some truly inexplicable level design.  The first one is a problem if you have, you know, a life and can't play a couple hours straight.  If you pick up on the puzzle quickly, then you might be OK, but otherwise you'll be really annoyed having to stop, start over if you get interrupted.  The second is a bit more serious for a puzzle game.  The elements they use are inconsistent and very arbitrary for a given puzzle.  Take the mummy being on fire, sometimes the fire lasts for X seconds, sometimes it's infinite, sometimes it's Y seconds long; it all has to do with what the puzzle requires rather than any "physics" system.  Without being too specific so I don't give a spoiler, there's one bit where you should be able to stand on a cage and jump over a fence to beat a trap, however for no reason at all there is an invisible wall that stops you; it would have been trivial to make the wall higher, but they didn't bother.  There's another, which is actually where I broke down and got a guide, where you have to get a key for a door and it involves hitting lamps...which have never been used for that at any point prior and make a chest appear out of thin air you can't possibly know would be there.  It's just not as tight as it could have been in my opinion.  I've played the first two Prince of Persia games and never quite felt the same level of "wtf?!?" I did with this game.Still, it's a game that will give you quite a few hours of enjoyment.  I'd just suggest you give the puzzles a try yourself, until the point they really start to tick you off, then just get a guide.  Otherwise, there's a decent chance you'll rage quit and not come back.

When the original PC-exclusive version of Far Cry, developed by Crytek (who went on to create the equally revolutionary "Crysis" series) and published by Ubisoft, was first released in 2004, it was hailed as a one-of-a-kind visionary masterpiece, which still holds up even today.  It offers the pitch-perfect blend of stealth, intense action, gritty realism, and creepy sci-fi that is able to hook anybody.  While it may not be an official open-world sandbox game like the later Far Cry sequels, the size and scope of the game is massive, allowing you to explore and exploit every opportunity while still keeping you focused on your objectives.  Some aspects of it may seem dated today, like the character models and voice acting, but it still manages to stay fresh and entertaining.The story of Far Cry centers around Jack Carver, a retired Navy veteran who now runs a freelance boat charter company in the South Pacific.  While caught in a storm at sea, a rocket destroys his boat, forcing him to seek refuge in a beached cargo ship.  Inside, Jack discovers a radio, and makes contact with someone named Doyle, who helps him survive the numerous mercenaries scattered across the islands.  In his travels, Jack discovers that a mad doctor, Krieger, is conducting genetic modification experiments, creating ugly hybrid creatures called "Trigens."  The mercenaries, led by Lieutanent Crowe, are there to ensure Krieger's research is not leaked to the outside world.Like I said, this game excels at allowing many different ways to play it.  Since you don't have regenerating health, you must replenish it through health packs and gain extra protection from bulletproof vests.  Furthermore, since these collectables aren't extremely plentiful, stealth is strongly emphasized.  You can crouch and go prone to reduce both your noise and visibility.  Your machete allows you to conserve ammo and make silent, one-hit kills, while the suppressed MP5 can take out a group of distant mercenaries with headshots without alerting them to your exact position.  You have an infinite supply of rocks to use for luring enemies into vulnerable positions, and you can even swim underwater to avoid detection.  Additionally, you have a special binocular that is able to track enemy movement and pick up their conversations, to allow for easier strategy planning.  When it's time to go loud, there is a healthy variety of other powerful weapons to use, including pistols, sub-machine guns, assault rifles, automatic shotguns, sniper rifles, and rocket launchers.  You can even take control of various land and water vehicles for added protection, faster travel, and massive firepower.  Unfortunetly, you only have four weapon slots, so you must make strategic decisions with your loadout to be as diverse and deadly as possible.On the hardest difficulty setting, Far Cry proves itself more than a match for experienced players.  The mercenaries you face are very accurate, dish out heavy damage, and work together in groups to suppress and flank you.  Successfully overcoming them requires a mixture of stealth, heavy use of cover, ammo scavenging, use of medpacks and body armor, and utilizing the right weapon for the right situations.  Fortunetely, ammo type is classified according to weapon class, not a specific weapon.  This means if you have a very powerful assault rifle with grenade launcher and scope attachments, like the OICW, you able to use ammo from the M4, which doesn't have any of these attachments.  The Trigens, on the other hand, are brutal monsters.  They're able to absorb and deal massive amounts of damage, and can be equipped with overpowering weapons like heavy grenade launchers.  You'll have to deal with them from a very far distance or use cover for protection while you slowly whittle away their health.  The drastic difference in these two types of enemies means you'll have to switch gameplay styles on the fly, as you'll often encounter both types in the same level.The technical aspects of Far Cry are still marvelous to behold, even today.  Powered by Crytek's signature "CryEngine," the graphics are absolutely gorgeous and immersive, showcasing sunny sandy beaches, dense mountain rainforests, dark messy underground research labs, and water so pristine and smooth, you'll immediately want to drink it.  The advanced physics, powered by the Havok physics engine, give real weight and interaction with environmental objects, and are well used on the enemies to provide killer ragdoll death animations, especially when they're caught in an explosion or you run them over with a vehicle.  Some issues do arise that reveal the game's age, like jerky animations, occasionly stiff controls, and unengaging voice acting, but luckily they don't take away from the enjoyment.Far Cry hits that pitch-perfect spot.  It's not as restrictive, unforgiving, or overwhelming as Far Cry 2, but it's also not as easy, dumbed-down, or unchallenging as Far Cry 3.  To this day, it remains one of my favorite PC-exclusive games ever, and it single-handedly made me re-evaluate my perception on PC gaming.

So whether you want to play as Stacy Keibler trying to rip off Lita's clothes or Torrie Wilson trying to rip off Trish Stratus' clothes, you're bound to have fun with it.Gameplay wasn't as smooth but still enjoyable. Reversing is still easy to do but it gets really frustrating when your opponent reverses half the moves you try to do. It happens and if you play it long enough, it'll happen to you tooThe 3D model graphics improved greatly and many of the entrances were on par. The best thing about these graphics is that history was made because for the first time ever, there was BLOOD. That's right! You could now take extreme to the next level by busting your opponent open during a match, meaning this game was also the debut of the First Blood Match. I really shouldn't say that this was the first game to feature blood as both WWF Warzone and WWF Attitude featured blood, but it was nowhere near the level of blood for Here Comes The Pain. In fact, it can't even be touched, comparing to the little blood droplets in Warzone and Attitude.The roster was fairly big. New superstars making their game debut included Victoria, Scott Steiner, Ultimo Dragon, Batista, Sean O Haire, Rodney Mack, Eric Bischoff, and more. At the height of the list was Goldberg. In addition to the superstars and divas, they also threw in legends to the roster as well. Legends involved in the game include Hillbilly Jim, George Steel, Iron Sheik, Roddy Piper, Old School Undertaker, Iron Shiek, LOD, Sgt. Slaughter, Nikolai Volkoff, and Jimmy Snuka. Interestingly enough, there's no entrance music for these legends.Season Mode was another plus to the game. The season was cut back to 1 year rather than 2 like Shut Your Mouth. Just like previous Smackdown games, the stories in Season Mode portray a lot of the storylines that happened on WWF TV. A few of these include a car storyline where your rival traps you in your car, lifts you up in a forklift and drops you in the parking lot. Very similar to what Stone Cold did to Triple H at the 2000 Survivor Series. A battle with a boss whether it be Vince McMahon or Eric Bischoff, Royal Rumble 2000 esque story where you and the remaining opponent fall out of the ring at the same time and the opponent claims your feet hit the floor first. One of my favorite stories in this game is where you earn a diva as your manager and a sick, perverted superstar will come along saying she wants a piece of her "pie". It'll lead to a match between your manager and the pervert wrestler. If he wins, he wins your manager and you're forced to watch him drag her away from your very eyes. If she wins, you either get kissed or slapped, depending upon how you treated her leading up to the match.Another thing I love about season mode is the stories that happen backstage. You can no longer travel backstage but you can see if any superstars are in certain rooms backstage. You'll encounter many different superstars backstage throughout. Depending on who it is and what you say, you'll either gain or lose superstar points, cheap shot them, get knocked out, or start a fight. There's also a feature where after certain matches you have the option of taunting, attacking, or respecting your opponent. If you attack them you'll either succeed or fail. If you succeed you'll see your wrestler giving your opponent a post-match beat down. If you lose, your opponent will fight back, knock you out and stomp the heck out of you.The backstage areas in the game for you to fight in during Hardcore Matches were majorly improved with many more interactive backstage things to do and use. In the trainers room you can throw your opponent into a hot shower, while in the parking lot you can drive a motorcycle and drag your opponent or climb a truck and throw your opponent off. This would be the last game that you'd be able to travel backstage during matches.Overall: 3 new match types, blood, Goldberg, a great season mode, and decent gameplay? That makes for a great A+ game and perhaps the best WWE game to be released so far! This game was so great it became one of Playstation 2's Greatest Hits and for great reason! Ignore all the people who gave this game 2 stars or less. They clearly don't know what a good wrestling game is. But this was a great end to the Smackdown series as the series would be rebooted which is where the Smackdown vs Raw series began. But that's a different review for a different time

Man, it's such a shame to see a once-fondly remembered icon fall deeply into the underwater abyss of washed-up nuisances. Spongebob Squarepants was a fun and lighthearted cartoon during its first few seasons and movie, but after the big screen appearance, the show tumbled downhill faster than a barefoot jackrabbit on a hot greasy griddle in the middle of August.Fortunately, this in no way changes how one would see the yellow sponge's earlier triumphant adventures, and some of those were immortalized into awesome video games like Battle for Bikini Bottom. This 3D platforming adventure has you play as Spongebob, Patrick, or Sandy Cheeks as they travel across familiar locales such as, well, Bikini Bottom, the beachy Goo Lagoon, the Mermalair, and even Rock Bottom (Gotta love that teasing bus)!Unlike newer Spongebob games, Battle for Bikini Bottom is incredibly well-structured and fully-fledged out, featuring worlds and designs that could give Mario a run for his money at times. In fact, the game takes cues from Super Mario 64 as Spongebob and co. set out to find Golden Spatulas (This game's Stars) in the large environments. And by large, I do mean LARGE. There is so much explorable territory, yet the locales always provide memorable set pieces and challenges for you to conquer.There's so much detail in this game it's easy to see the developers poured their hearts into it. Even the trademark humor from Spongebob's glory days is present and very well accounted for, resulting in plenty of legitimate laughs!With the amount of variety and fun the game can offer, this is a game that you can absolutely love even if you're not a Spongebob fan.

Being a child of the 80s, I love it when these arcade compilations come out. It's a lot of fun to go back and play these old games with your adult brain and unlimited quarters. You can see just how good you can get, and see how your play compares to back in the day. It's also great to see which games have stood the test of time. It's fun to try out the rarer games that you never even saw back then, but what we really want to do is go back and play our old favorites. It's all about the nostalgia.First thing I did was play Spyhunter and Paperboy like a dog. Boy those two are total classics. Really work well with the GameCube controller too, though you will want to tweak the controller setup. Setting the c-stick to the Spyhunter gear shift, now that's what I'm talking about. Then it was good old Defender and Marble Maddness. Those two have also aged really well. And it's great to play Marble Madness without that damn ball pinching my hands. You have to be an old timer to understand that. Defender is still too damn hard and repetitive for me.I really like the GameCube's control stick for these old games too. The precision and tightness of it will give you a real edge. I tried out all the games, but only really stayed with a few of them. Spider-Man 2: The Game, released in 2004 for the PS2 and XBOX, is definitely a great Spider-Man game. On virtually every "best Spider-Man games of all time" lists, you're bound to see this one somewhere near, or at, the top. While I do think this game was extremely revolutionary for its time, and is still good fun even to this day, I don't think this one quite lives up to the reputation nostalgic fans have given it over the years.I remember playing this back when it released, and the best thing about this game, by far, is the open ended New York City you get to use as Spidey's playground. It's awesome. You have all kinds of moves and tricks at your disposal for traversing the city's skyline, and the sense of speed, sheer variety of motion, sense of momentum, and the visuals for the city itself still hold up wonderfully. Lighted skyscraper windows and buildings as far as the eye can see are still impressive, though the draw distance isn't amazing. Thankfully, the developers hid this flaw to the best of their abilities. When I first played this, I would get so caught up in just exploring the city as Spidey, that I would put off doing missions for as long as possible, and honestly, that's probably the best way to play Spider-Man 2.Graphically, the game just passes as OK. Other than the city itself looking awesome for its time, the character models are all pretty weak. Something about Spider-Man seems off, especially around his head and eyes, and none of the other character models fare much better. It's a shame, as the dynamic lighting on these models looks great. It's just that the models themselves are less than stellar.The game revolves around you partaking in story missions that loosely follow the movie's plot, and the game does a respectable job. The missions themselves are varied and usually interesting, if a bit too easy at times, and in between the main missions, you partake in side missions. From stopping road raging drivers to thwarting off thieves firing at armored cars, the side missions work well, and this is a good thing, since it's essential to do these to progress to the story missions.This is what's known as padding. A vain attempt at lengthening the game by using shallow mechanics and gameplay sections over and over in place of interesting gameplay. The game can be beaten in a measly 6 hours, even without rushing through it. Without the inclusion of the mandatory side missions, this is probably a 3 hour game, at best. Luckily, you'll have so much fun traversing New York and stopping crimes with the relatively good and extensive combat system, that you won't mind much.Some missions do have huge difficulty spikes, however. Particularly one involving some mech suits, and some early Mysterio missions. Which is welcome, though, as most of the game is rather easy. It's actually pretty uneven, when looking at it objectively.The voice work is serviceable and the soundtrack is outstanding. However, the sound effects, particularly those of combat, get far too repetitive. Speaking of which, when it comes to the game's combat, even with an extensive combo list, it also gets repetitive. For later fights in the game, you'll find yourself web blasting enemies since they dodge or block literally anything else, then wail on them for a while, occasionally delivering a pile driver (which absolutely rules) to put them down, rinse and repeat. Again, it's not a bad combat system, it's just repetitive.The boss fights are uneven. The final boss fight of the game is great, and so is the second one with Shocker, but literally every other boss fight just lacks polish to feel well thought out, and the game's bland presentation while in interior sections doesn't help much. The controls were clearly made for swinging around a huge city, and when placed indoors, the movement just doesn't feel right, for some reason.All of this being said, I do think this is a great Spider-Man game. However, I don't think it's the best Spider-Man game of all time like most would have you believe. The sequel to this game, Ultimate Spider-Man, improved on absolutely everything this game had to offer. The combat was better, the boss fights were more memorable and intelligently designed, the art style was, and still is, incredible, the writing is superior, the voice acting was top notch, so on and so forth. I found myself enjoying it far more than I did Spider-Man 2.By all means, this is a great Spidey game, it's just not the perfect, supreme being that most nostalgia colored glasses fans would have you believe. Even games like Shattered Dimensions could be considered far more enjoyable than this, and I think if you want to play a free-roaming Spider-Man game of this style, I absolutely can't recommend Ultimate Spider-Man for PS2 enough. It took what was in this game, polished it, and built upon it to a great degree, and it shows.Spider-Man 2 may be a great game, but it's definitely not the best Spider-Man game of all time. I'd be willing to put Maximum Carnage, Ultimate Spider-Man, Web of Shadows, and Shattered Dimensions above this game any day. Don't get me wrong, though. Spider-Man 2 is absolutely enjoyable as a game. Its lack of polish, shoddy character models, and just passable voice acting, mixed with repetitive combat and far too easy missions padded by repetitive, combat based side missions, make this a passable, yet definitely above average and hugely influential game. I'd be willing to say it's great, even, if solely just for it's awesome web swinging mechanics. It's definitely not the best Spider-Man game of all time, though, and I can't stress that enough. There are better Spidey games out there, and I encourage you to play them.Play it. Enjoy it. Love it, if you want to. Just don't buy into the hype, or you might find yourself sorely disappointed with this one.

Out of every Call Of Duty game ever created, the first one stands out above all the rest, for one reason only: It doesn't have regenerating health.  Now, I know the entire public most likely believes that all COD games were made with regenerating health, but that's why this first game will always be the best.  It requires real strategy, tactics, and skill just to stay alive.  You have to stay in cover at all times, always observe the environment, and only cross open ground after you're sure you've killed everyone.  You also have to conserve all health packs in the environment, only picking them up when you're finally about to die.  For the ultimate mashochist, the hardest difficulty, "Veteran," completely removes all health packs and won't even register any checkpoints if you happen to drop below 50% health, not to mention the fact that all enemies are super-accurate and deal massive amounts of damage in no time flat.  I honestly thought that "Ghosts" would go back to this mechanic, given the title name's implied emphasis on stealth, but it didn't.  COD has become so blinded by its own success that it keeps spitting out basically the same old format year after year and refuses to try anything different.  That's why this first game will always be the best ever.COD was developed by Infinity Ward, which at the time was a brand new development company that was started by the same team who was responsible for the mega-hit "Medal Of Honor: Allied Assault."  Published by Activision, COD feels like a more polished, more diverse, and deadlier version of MOHAA.  Where MOHAA focused on only one perspective, the Americans vs. the Germans, COD adds Great Britain and Russia into the mix.  Of course, this means that you can also use each side's weapons to your advantage, some of which are even better than what the Germans have.  You can only carry two guns at a time, so it helps to have a short-range and a long-range weapon to maximize your effectiveness.  A sniper rifle is invaluable when it comes to wide-open areas with little cover, and a sub-machine gun is excellent for clearing out tight, enclosed areas with multiple enemies.

I'm not sure why, but this is one of the most addicting games ever made. I think it's the strange presentation and progression of your quest, along with the simple, straightforward gameplay. The cutscenes can be pretty weird, I don't know any other way to say it than this game is VERY Japanese. The translations are all pretty off, but it gives the game a unique character. The races are typically one on one battles through the highways of Japan, with occasional boss races that can sometimes hold multiple opponents either at once or in a chain for an added challenge. Originally intended to be the third and last installment of the "Broken Sword" series, "The Sleeping Dragon" came to both PC, X-Box, and Playstation 2. The series deviated from it's roots by going from the animated 2D point and click style to a full 3D interactive adventure game.Set a few years after "The Smoking Mirror", strange weather events and natural disasters are occurring all across the world with no apparent cause. Meanwhile patent lawyer George Stobbart is flying to the Congo to meet with a Dr. Cholmondeley to discuss a new source of renewable energy when his plane crashes, stranding him in the Jungle. At the same time in Paris, journalist Nico Collard is framed for the murder of a computer analyst on the cusp of uncovering an international conspiracy. It's once again up to George and Nico to solve the mystery and save the planet from an ancient evil.Unlike previous games in the series, you control the characters along a 3D plane and interact with the environment. While it's an unfortunate departure from the lovingly painted backdrops of the first two games, it  the environments are still well designed and the controls are quite smooth. In terms of graphics, they are alright. The cartoony style is pretty appealing to look through any surfaces are fairly featureless and a few of the character models look rather grotesque. What the game lacks in graphics it makes up for in writing. The series trademark humor and good writing return. This along with a really great and atmospheric soundtrack make you interested in seeing more.The game is good. Unfortunately it is, to me, the weakest of the original games. I felt that the 3D gameplay was a little basic and many of the puzzles weren't as memorable as the last two adventures. That leaves one last thing to look at though. How are the load times this time around? Well, fortunately, the game only loads between large environments, so you'll feel the wait was worth it each time, however they do still drag quite a bit. If you've come this far into the series then I recommend this game. Despite it's shortcomings It's still a good Broken Sword game and a pretty solid adventure game to boot.

The first Splinter Cell game basically established a new blueprint in the stealth action genre all on its own; nevertheless, it did have some issues, mostly that the game was simply just too easy even on the hardest difficulty setting.  The AI was so dumb that you could continuously lure them towards their unconscious comrades and knock everyone out with no alarms being raised at all.  Also, on the few parts that had no alarms, you could easily go around popping everyone with headshots without breaking a sweat.  The sequel, titled "Pandora Tomorrow," thankfully rectifies these problems.  If an enemy spots a downed comrade, unconscious or dead, an alarm is automatically raised, and all the other enemies reinforce themselves with flak jackets and bulletproof helmets.  If three alarms are raised, the mission is over.  This forces you to be much more strategic and plan out how exactly you'll eliminate enemies without alerting anyone else.

I've always been a huge Mortal Kombat fans so I picked this up solely because it contains arcade ports of Mortal Kombat 2 & 3. These are perfect arcade ports, and you can even adjust the difficulty and controller setup in both. Adjusting the difficulty is a big deal because the default setting are just brutal in arcade mode. They look crisp and clean, play well, couldn't be happier.But most of the rest of the games are lackluster. I think the problem is these games come from a lost era in arcade games. The arcade fad had died down at this point in history, so most of these games feel like experimental dead ends. You get a real feel of an industry trying to find it's legs again. The exceptions being Hard Drivin' and Primal Rage. This was my first opportunity to really dig into Primal Rage, an old fighting game featuring dinosaurs and giant apes. Boy, this game has some odd controls. The moves and combos are just plain weird. So I never really mastered the game, but I had a blast beating the game and seeing all the finishing moves. Hard Drivin' was one of the first 3D racing games and has aged very well. I spent a lot of time on that one.Those were the only games I could really get into. I played Rampage World Tour a little, but it didn't have a save feature so you would have to beat the entire game in one sitting. And that would pretty much take an entire day. So I put that down after a while. Timber was mildly amusing. A game about chopping down trees. Surprisingly, it's not too bad.I still go back and play the Mortal Kombats every now then so I will keep this game until my PS2 breaks. For a Mortal Kombat fan, this is a must buy. Set in 1992, in the main storyline of GRAND THEFT AUTO: SAN ANDREAS, you play as Carl Johnson. Carl left his home of Los Santos (loosely based on Los Angeles) and moved to Liberty City five years earlier. He receives a phone call from his brother, "Sweet", informing him of his mother's murder. After arriving in Los Santos, Carl is picked up by Officer Tenpenny, a corrupt cop. Tenpenny has recently murdered another cop and frames Carl for the murder and blackmails him into working for him. Eventually Carl is cleared, but Sweet is arrested and Carl spends much of the rest of the game completing various jobs and mission in San Fierro (San Francisco) and Las Venturas (Las Vegas) before ultimately returning to Los Santos.GRAND THEFT AUTO: SAN ANDREAS is a massive game. There are miles and miles and miles of ground between one place and another. Sometimes it can take several minutes just to get from one area to another. In the beginning this is fun. However, as you progress in the game it becomes frustrating. The game only automatically saves at the end or beginning of a mission and you can't try to manually save your game during the middle of a mission. So, there are sometimes missions that take nearly 30 minutes to complete and if you die, you have to start all over again.Make no mistake, this is an adult game. Drugs and violence are critical elements in the game. Foul language is a regular part of the character's dialogue. There's also a few missions that require some sexual activities.In terms of story and gameplay, GRAND THEFT AUTO: SAN ANDREAS offers a great deal. You can steal a cop car and perform cop missions. Enter a fire truck and you can do fire department mission. Take an ambulance and you can perform rescue missions. You get to drive a tank, fly a jet, and use a jet pack. You can also steal a pimpmobile and work as a pimp. Carl starts and ends gang wars and takes over a mafia casino in Las Venturas. Then there are the cars he steals to get around. You can spend a couple of months just exploring the terrain and doing side missions as you work your way through the main plot.One thing I was impressed about was the game's music. There are several different radio stations in the vehicles you drive and they play different music that's not just in a constant loop.You can change the channel and hear different songs or you can shut the whole radio off. It makes for a more realistic feel.The biggest drawback of the game is the lack of save points. When completing a mission it's either do or die.Overall, GRAND THEFT AUTO: SAN ANDREAS is an addictive game. It's adult content makes it a game not suitable for children or adults who are offended by such content. However, it's not difficult to see why GRAND THEFT AUTO: SAN ANDREAS is one of PlayStation 2's Greatest Hits.

To avoid reading a long review, let me just sum it up: S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is a game for those that enjoy immersive and very atmospheric games. And ones that aren't nearly as easy as most.To begin in more detail, the best part of the game is without a doubt, the atmosphere. Some of the more impressive aspects and moments of the game are so because of the game's great environment. Not only does the game play the part well through its look, it also has great sound design and music to compliment the gritty feel. On certain parts of the game you'll have to explore things like vaults and underground tunnels, which are kind of creepy.. A common comparison to make would be Fallout, but I assure you this game's atmosphere is much better in that sense. Just the sound design alone and the creepy 'What happened here..' feel that places in this game give make it worth it alone.Another thing that makes this game special, the brutal nature. It's not as difficult as even older games, but it certainly offers a challenge. The shooting mechanics have a peeking/cover system that make things more interesting to spice it up. Along this, other challenges the game gives is radiation. Be careful! If your level is too high, you will die in seconds. Even if you barely have any, you will slowly die -- just like you would in real life. Maybe this difficulty can be annoying, but it certainly makes for a more realistic and thus immersive feel.Also, exploring the world is a fun part. Though it's open world, keep in mind it's by no means as open as other high budget games. Most areas in the game will make you cross them to pass the storyline. There are a few other areas like small buildings and things like that that are optional, but they're limited -- so optional exploration isn't that big of a focus, but I don't mind because the world is so interesting to see and discover. Side quests, though not that interesting nor compelling will offer you places to visit and tasks to perform for things like money or supplies. This gives more of a reason to explore the world.Which brings up my biggest and maybe only beef with this game: The side quests. They're confusing, not in objective but in the way they're made. They're also buggy - objectives will stay even after finishing the quests, quests will randomly show up, their objective locations are sometimes different from where they should be.. and there's a 24 hour limit to side quests. While the time/day cycle is longer than most games and is more than enough for the objective, side quests get really repetitive and aren't very worthwhile for the most part. Also, some of them are really glitched. I'm really upset that I can't join any faction because the side quests associating to joining them are broken and unbeatable. Seriously, on one quest as soon as I accept I fail it. Instead of it saying 'Quest added,' as soon as I accept it says 'Quest failed' and there's no way to change this as multiple attempts have proved. I am still not very happy about this. While glitches are 'part of the package' in open world games they're still slightly upsetting.Alongside the excellent yet a little flawed singleplayer, there's a pretty standard multiplayer. There's some fun to be had here, but being an older game not many people play anymore and most servers are in places like Europe, so if you're in the U.S. like me your high ping over long distance connection will give you a hard time.Overall, very worth it. Atmospheric and brutal, yet very interesting to play. 9/10 due to some bugs. If can forgive a game for being rough around the edges for a highly immersive, atmospheric experience that's story-driven- S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is for you.

Rest in peace Pandemic, they made a lot of good games before they were gutted by EA. Mercenaries Playground of Destruction was one of them and is one of the most satisfying open-world sandbox games ever made. For me it falls under the same category that Saint's Row and Prototype fall under. Lack of story is no biggie because its packed to the brim with content and wanton destruction. The title "Playground of Destruction" really fits the game well since it seems just about every building can be leveled with enough explosives. So the underlying synopsis is as, General Song the military dictator of the un-Democratic People's Republic of Korea is exposed for selling nuclear weapons illegally. As the UN and South Korea move into oust him from power he goes underground with his cabinet and precious nukes. The North Korean military is waging a tenacious guerrilla war against the Allies and time is running out. So bounties are placed on General Song and his men to hasten their capture. Now ExOps, a private military contractor sends in one of their agents to cash in on the war.So at the start you are given a choice of several agents to play as. You have Chris Jacobs the American, Jennifer Mui the Brit, and Mattias Nilsson a Swedish-BA. The game says that they all have different strengths and weaknesses but in reality they don't make much of a difference. So what you really end up choosing is skin and dialogue. After you got your agent your dropped off in war torn North Korea and now begins the hunt for the "Deck of 52". The bounties are split up by card numbers and suits and you capture them (dead or alive) till you eventually get up to the man himself. To do this you can track down the smaller bounties on your own or gain intelligence from the various factions in Korea. Aside from the Allies; there are the South Koreans, the Chinese, and the Russian Mafia. You can work with these factions who in turn toss a fat bounty at you and information on others in hiding so as long as you do their bidding. Supporting them also opens up their resources to you, support the South Koreans you get their air support, support the Chinese you get artillery support and armor, the Russians Mob gives you small arms and contraband vehicles etc etc. However at times they can work against each other and you may end up making enemies of one faction in the process.The missions they toss at you are pretty typical in regards to sandbox games. Go there blow that building up, go here and take that guy out and so on. Though its not really the missions that you should come for but the destruction. Virtually every vehicle can be hijacked and it helps give you an edge. If a North Korean tank is rushing to you why not just hijack it and use it against them? Thats possible and more. You can slap C4 on a car and drive it into the checkpoint and detonate it in the process. If you are stuck in the middle of nowhere call in your Mafia comrades to pick you up with a captured Blackhawk helicopter. Thats another thing that makes this game really enjoyable is the "Merchants of Menace" site attached to your character's PDA. With it you can call in air strikes, supplies, or vehicles which are promptly delivered. Since the site is ran by the Russian Mafia its best to stay on their good side for discounts if you plan to use it frequently. Be careful with the M&M; app though because you may end up burning through all your money fast.This game is over 8 years old but still looks good. Dust rises up from explosions, missiles leave behind lines of exhaust, sunlight glistens off surfaces, and destroyed vehicles shower fiery debris. Battles are large scale and you'll often find two factions fighting hashing it out complete with tanks, helicopters and infantry charging at each other. If you use heavy types of air strikes like carpet bombing or fuel air bombs what was once a vibrant armor base is leveled flat into charred ruins. Looking back its quite amazing what they were able to pull of visually despite having dated hardware. So in the end the game was fun, and it's still fun. The game-play itself if very satisfying and rewards adventuring. Difficulty can definitely spike in certain missions but with some imagination most missions in this game are doable. Overall, great game and worth getting a used copy of.

GP Legend is a fantastic entry in the F-Zero franchise. There's tons of racers, hours of gameplay and vehicle testing in the games four single player modes and a forked narrative story between 8 F-Zero racers that is a good introduction to the GP Legend television series. The artwork is unique comic book style mixed with animation and it works really well bringing across personalities of the characters, vehicles, courses and the amazing soundtrack. Though there are five laps per race, the racing goes by fast as each lap may take under thirty seconds. While it's signature to earn a boost after the first lap that increases speed at the cost of the machine's health, this game is more technical in that boosting and acceleration need to be done strategically, not just by holding down the a button and boosting when you have health. You can also earn a boost at the race countdown but each machine has a different set time on the countdown and if you time it wrong, the machine will misfire. There's also lots of jumps and with machines going about 700-900 mph on skinny, winding courses, there's danger lurking around every corner. You also need to tilt the machine up in order to make a smooth landing. Although the sensation of racing thirty racers right next to your machine doesn't feel quite the same as it does in F-Zero X or GX, the courses are more narrow so it's easier to control vehicles like this. The AI is also really smart. There's just over thirty characters to choose from the majority of whom are familiar faces from the older titles. GP Legend gets an A++ because it's perfect and then some. Rock on Nintendo.

It makes what could be a great experience a good one, and a good experience a fair one.For example, when I was opening the first 4 ages in Relto in the base game, I saw the link to Eder Gira and thought, "I remember hating this Age. The quality of Halo 2 the game aside, I direct this review at the quality of of the Limited Collector's Edition as a package for the game.The case itself is a durable metal snap case with a minimalist design featuring the logo and 'Limited Collector's Edition' on the front and a grayscale Master Chief on the back.  This case will surely survive the occasional beatings a lot better than a regular DVD case, but be warned that the outer metal casing is thin and prone to dents.  It is therefor wise to keep it in the provided plastic sheath that superimposes the feature list and legal information on the front and back.The one star off is purely indicative of some of the content present on the second disc's Making Of featurette which is needless and frustratingly distracting from the point of the mini-documentary.  That said, the second disc is a healthy collection of Behind-The-Scenes clips and montages showing the numerous stages of development, from voice-actors in the studio to their early E3 demo.  The second disc is competant as a whole, but nothing standout.Included with the LCE ('Limited Collector's Edition') is a small 4 page pamphlet that highlights some textual exerpts from various characters from the game world.  It serves a little bit of flavor, but nothing more as it does little to expand on the overall plot of Halo.Personally, my favorite inclusion with this LCE is the tweaked instruction manual.  Whereas in the general retail copy of Halo 2, the manual featured Master Chief on the front, the LCE's manual features a random Sangheili Elite.  More than that though, while the manual is mostly identical, all of the flavor text in the original release that instructs the reader from the perspective of the UNSC is changed to reflect the perspective of the Covenant which perfectly mirrors the two sides of the story in Halo 2 where you play as both Master Chief and The Arbiter.  It's the little things like how the pages are purple instead of orange, the control map says 'Active Camo' instead of 'Flashlight', and the opening plot summary changes the noble Master Chief standing straight, standard issue Battle Rifle armed at the ready, to a very different image which features a darker Master Chief highlighted by a red glow and apparently lurking around with a rocket launcher.  The change in flavor text extends to the weapon & vehicle section which features Covenant tech first before insultingly listing off the "primitive implements of war".  I leave this review with a snippet from the Covenant's description of the Magnum:"Almost laughably weak in most circumstances; however, Human pistol fires metallic projectiles which can be dangerous when fired very accurately.  Often used as last resort by desparate Humans and one of their least threatening devices."

That's a controversial opinion, I know. But Resident Evil 4 is remarkable for trying to retain the panicked, limited-ammunition gameplay, the puzzle-solving and sweeping locations of classic Resident Evil while utilizing graphics still amazing nearly ten years after the game's release and an interface that's instinctive and easy to master. It was a survival horror game that didn't compromise it's mission to entertain and enthrall to sell it's horror or plot.It is a game that every modern third-person shooter and survival horror game looks up to. That crappy 'Cold Fear' game, Dead Space, even the Last of Us. An entire genre of over-the-shoulder survival games were created by Resident Evil 4. And though the Gamecube version sadly was never updated to get all the nice unlocks, it still has the best graphics and the most intuitive controls out of any version. it was designed to fit the Gamecube controller perfectly.Resident Evil 4 has a chapter-based campaign system. You can save at any typewriter and go back to play later on, but there's no chapter selection system. A 'mercenaries' mode is unlocked after beating the campaign, where you fight against the clock to rack up points and unlocks.Resident Evil 4 took a fresh start and avoided convoluted Resident Evil plot. What you'll find here is a characterization-centric arch about Leon S. Kennedy, who has changed from rookie cop in Resident Evil 2 to government agent and badass. He's in search of the President's daughter, Ashley Graham. A character or two make a cameo from older titles - and some show up in later games like the Dark Side Chronicles and RE5/6. But the influence of older titles is summarized in the opening cutscene. Raccoon City got wiped off the planet. Everyone thought the zombie menace was gone.When control is handled over to you as Leon, there's no aggravating Call of Duty level where a gruff sergeant yells at you to sprint over, jump, dive, shoot, use your iron sights. The game gives you some optional manuals and a MGS-style radio conversation, but the magic of Resident Evil 4's introduction is a silent tutorial.Your police escorts tell you to do the work yourself. Leon steps out into a foggy backroad, where crows stare down at him from the branches of withered trees. In the distance, a dilapidated, but inhabitable farmhouse sits, door cracked open. It's quiet aside from the rush of water from the nearby river. It's tranquil, but also unsettling.What you start with as Leon is a good indication of the nature of the game. His custom handgun, two spare loads of ammo and a full health restore. You have an attache case with a grid-based storage system that does away with the silly eight-slot system. A shotgun takes up as much space as it should, as will a grenade, a pistol or ammunition. The game isn't going to leave you to hang on general principal, but it's not going to hold your hand. If you cannot carry some ammo or health item, you have to leave it behind. It's reality.Everything in your first encounter is left to discovery. Things escalate quickly, and the isolation of the creepy European countryside sets in quick. Everything wants to kill you, but they're no shambling corpses. They look like living villagers doing their normal work, tending to crops and animals. When they spot you, the details start to show that indicate a much darker situation than first expected.Corpses are impaled on giant hooks, buildings are boarded up like they're prepared for a war. But you have the tools to fight back too. The first time you aim your pistol, a laser beam illuminates the target and you can see the gentle shake to Leon's aim. When you fire, there's a gravity not found in other Resident Evil titles. A shot to the leg staggers or trips an opponent, a hit to the face may stagger and blind if it doesn't outright kill. You can blow off locks, shoot through thin wooden doors to hit enemies behind them.You're outnumbered and cut off from support, but you can do almost anything to survive - push bookshelves in front of doors, shoot from behind barricades, crash out through windows. A well timed kick can floor several attackers and buy you room to escape, but don't stay put for too long in any one place, or your attackers might resort to throwing axes, molotov cocktails and sticks of dynamite to flush you out.No, these aren't zombies. They look and act human. You wonder why they want to kill you so badly. The beautiful graphics really help sell the mood of the game, from sleepy countryside shrouded with thick fog, to abandoned castles, mines and militia hideouts. There will never be something like your first Resident Evil 4 playthrough, I can almost guarantee.Resident Evil 4 stands out from its sequels because of the sheer passion that it was made with as a video game. Sure, some villains are incredibly hammy and the dialogue is cheesy as can be at times. Sure, items can spew from deceased enemies. The progression is meticulous, new enemies are introduced just when you think you can handle anything, there's multiple paths through the same basic area and treasures are hidden throughout. You find your rare allies, like the mysterious merchant with the inventory to start a small war. There's so much detail in the game. Every surface reacts differently when shot, enemies talk to one another when they spot you. You can shoot fish from a pond and eat them for a health restoration, and some treasures can be ruined if you recovery them improperly. At times there's a level of strategy in collecting and holding onto treasures and items that rivals a RPG.Resident Evil 4 is one of the games that comes to mind when a Quick-Time Event is mentioned. It uses them quite well to add to the urgency of grappling with an enemy, and to break up cutscenes. They're not overused and they certainly aren't instant kills against enemies, a place where the sequels fail entirely. Combat in general is highly seamless and fluid, as well as it is unforgiving. You can eventually accrue an arsenal that is hopelessly overkill for most encounters, but limited ammo will keep your murderous urges restrained well into the finale of the game.You will have a partner at times, but they don't ease the burden of combat and the feeling of isolation is never truly broken.It's a fairly long game, and your first playthrough will take about twenty hours. You unlock a new difficult mode and a set of costumes when you finish the campaign, as well as a minigame called 'Mercenaries.' A reference to a small game in Resident Evil 3, you take series classic characters like HUNK or Albert Wesker and dish out the pain against the clock as techno blares and new enemies join the fray at a frantic pace. There's a good deal of strategy involved in building the perfect combo, and every character has a unique ability and specialization - HUNK can break necks instantly if he uses his SMG or flashbang grenades but is not optimized to fight bosses, while Wesker's hand-to-hand attacks are almost always lethal and his varied arsenal can deal serious damage to miniobosses. The levels are largely taken from the campaign and unfortunately there's no retro levels, but in general it's an enjoyable treat after the unforgettable campaign has ended.But really, Resident Evil 4 has to be played. Don't read a wikipedia article, watch a lets play or any of that stuff. Just play and enjoy.

Let me begin by saying Resident Evil is my favorite series. I've played RE1, RE2, RE3, RE:CV, RE0, RE:REMAKE and RE4.  I'm a huge fan of survival horror and though I really enjoyed RE4 and consider it the best shooter I've ever played I don't think it should have been a Resident Evil game. It has too little in common with the series survival horror roots. Now I'm not saying it's a bad game.  Quite the contrary, it's an outstanding game.  Just not a good Resident Evil game. I feel it deserves to have its own series not related to Resident Evil. Now with that explained let me say if you've lived under a rock the last ten years and have yet to play it do so immediately.  It's an outstanding game that has a ton of replay value.  I've replayed it half a dozen times and each time is a blast. The graphics still look great too. If you're an old school Resident Evil fan you'll find very little creepy atmosphere. The only thing held over from the older games is the herbs and first aid sprays and of course Leon. Everything else is completely different.  No zombies, lickers or tryrants.  It is faster paced with a continuous stream of enemies from start to finish. You have access to a massive arsenal of weapons and each can be upgraded for a price.  There's no item box but rather a backpack to carry all your items. No need to be conservative either since there's plenty of health and ammo. The game even adjusts to how you play so if you're having a difficult time in one area the game adjusts to make it easier.  You can save as many times as you like too. There's no limit.  As I said there's very little of the old school Resident Evil here. This game was made to be fun and it is.

When Big Rigs was in development the naysayers told us that no game could possibly justify its unprecedented one billion dollar budget. They told us it was foolish to have a team of seven hundred of the finest game developers to collaborate on a single project. “Too many cooks spoil the broth” they said. Friends, if you are one of the few people who hasn’t already lost a job or ruined a personal relationship for the thousands of hours spent playing BROTRR, it is time to see why they were proven so wrong. Never, before or since, has a game been perfect on every level.The graphics: Big Rigs is the reason people even discuss what kind of video card they use. Nvidia and AMD were founded in order to create a video card that could run the game playably with detail on maximum. Even in 2014 they haven’t been able to reproduce the stunning almost painterly experience of Big Rigs. It’s easy to forget you are playing a game and not watching a summer blockbuster.The gameplay: This game is fun in its purest form. This game has been often called “the ultimate methadone” as drug addicts will immediately drop their vices in favor of playing as much Big Rigs as possible. 53% of divorce cases in 2004 cited neglect from spouses spending all available free time playing Big Rigs. Play at your own risk.The legacy: There simply wouldn’t be a video game market if not for the staggering success of Big Rigs: Over The Road Racing. In 2002 video game publishers were collapsing, video arcades were closing their doors for good, console sales were at an all-time low. Video games were going the way of disc…. Why I am I wasting my time writing a review when I could be playing right now?!

There was a weird time during the ps2/xbox/gamecube generation of gaming. At some point in that generation's lifecycle, the idea of having nudity in games was starting to catch on and people were accepting it as okay. I recalled several interesting titles that centered around nudity including the Playboy Mansion game, Leisure Suit Larry, and BMX XXX. What separated Guy Game from all the others was that not only was the sole focus on the game was to show nudity, but also the fact that it used real life people (while the other games mentioned certainly had real life video the game had 3d models most of the time). The Guy Game's other unique trait was that none of the exposed women were actually professional actresses. They were recruited during a Spring Break session and what you saw were actual college students possibly drunk and decided to participate in this game spontaneously. Think of it as Spring Break Girls Gone Wild-style but as a video game. There were paid actresses and actors in the video game, but they played a very small role in the overall game.The concept behind the Guy Game was that you answer questions, and you watched college-aged girls answer the question. If the women got the answer wrong, they have to flash before the audience. The idea was that as you progress in the game, you get to slowly get rid of a censor bar and seeing the raw nudity of these women.Guy Game was aimed at the college students. When the game was released, I too was in college and thought the game most certainly applied to my age group. The game centered around the idea that you answer trivia questions. The game initially featured a sprite that covered the important parts of exposed women. As you answered trivia questions the sprites that covered the nudity began to go away. You got 20 sets of questions, and each set contained at least three women (sometimes a set may feature two women competing in place of a single player).Personally I liked the game. The questions were similar to what a college student might be asked on a intro level test. There are some really silly questions like how many letters are in the alphabet. Remember this game is aimed at drunk college kids who are playing in their dorm. Once you finish a set, you can replay the set seeing full nudity without having to remove the filter. You can choose random questions and they relate to sports and other categories. These rate from easy to okay. I would say the questions were similar to what you might find in a sports bar that has a electronic trivia game that you can play as you wait for your meal.Now the problem with this game is that you getting the questions right didn't really matter. During a set, you are asked questions, and immediately after the question they play a video of the women about to answer the question. At that time you have to either guess if they get it right or choose which answer you think they might give. Getting these right made a gauge go up that slowly removed the filtered that covered the nudity. If the girls get the question wrong, they have to flash themselves in the first part of the set. On the second part of the set, the girls are always wrong. So in the 20 set you get, and the at least three women in each set, you might not see them flash during the first half but you are guaranteed to see each girls in a set flash at least twice. In some sets that occur while in other sets you might see them flash at most 4 times for 4 questions.Now granted I liked the Guy Game. I thought it was funny at best. There were some hilarious moments and I think I had a good laugh while playing the game. A lot of critics out there stated that the game was solely focused on seeing nudity. While this might have been true in certain regards, I felt the game was suppose to be a comedy and was suppose to be enjoyed and laughed at used as a mature trivia game that you played with other college aged peers. Now granted most of us who enjoyed the Guy Game are a lot older now, the game is still somewhat funny being played.The Guy Game was wrong in so many level. For starters, no other game featured actual nude women and the makers took a bold step in trending in that direction. Those of you who followed the history of this game would know that the Guy Game backfired. I believe the studio that made the Guy Game was a start up and this was their first and last title. There were several things wrong about this game. Firstly, the way they recruited these women to flash themselves was simply by going to a Spring Break party and going around asking women to play in this game. It's no doubt that most of these women aged about the same as the players who played it. I can't imagine that this was a good choice especially considering that their faces and body were shown in full light and no doubt recognizing someone who was in the Guy Game would be awkward and humiliating. I don't think this is unique too considering that immediately after the release of this game. one of the women featured in the game tried to sue the company. The woman claimed that she was 17 during the time of the game. She proved this with her birth certificate and a judge immediately ordered Microsoft and Sony to stop selling this game. Amazingly the game still sold in stores during this period but no new copies were being made. As the court case went into play, the Guy Game maker proved that the woman tricked them into saying she was 18 and the judge simply dismissed the case and no other action was taken. Even though the maker of Guy Game won the case, it certainly caused them to go bankrupt. They made a last ditch effort on releasing a DVD of the game I believe called "Game Over for Guy Game" or something to that effect. In the end, the company lost and the game was a complete failure. I can't imagine any other company would want to venture into the full motion video concept of nudity after this disaster.I had to buy the Guy Game again mainly because I lost my other copy. This game is truly a unique title to add to your ps2 collection and the big thing is that the supply of this game is slowly fading so it's becoming rare. The PS2/Xbox era featured a lot of unique games and this is one of them you have to add to your collection. It might not have been a awesome game, but it certainly had its place in history.

"Snake Eater" is the third game in the "MGS" series, but the first game chronologically in the timeline, and takes place during the Cold War in 1964, where "Naked Snake" is tasked with stopping a nuclear-equipped tank in the jungles of the USSR. It's important to note that this is not the same Snake from the previous 2 games. If you're familiar with the mythology then you no doubt already know who he is. The story this time isn't quite as serious, and actually has a "James Bond" kind of opening credit sequence. There are still harrowing moments, as when Snake gets captured. Three characters in particular besides Snake are allowed an unusual amount of depth: young Ocelot, who later becomes one of the series' main villains and here first develops his obsession with revolvers; Eva, a seductress and spy whose loyalties aren't altogether clear; and The Boss, the legendary female soldier and former mentor of Naked Snake. What's new to "Snake Eater" are the systems that maintain Snake's health, which include eating food scavenged from within the environment (snakes for example) and curing yourself after taking damage (like removing a bullet with a knife and then applying the appropriate medical treatment). Also new is the ability to change camouflage on the fly to better blend in and help avoid being spotted by enemy patrols. These are great additions. I enjoyed "Snake Eater" more than "Sons of Liberty." The boss battles are better and more numerous (the best of which is the sniper The End), and the story never falters. Is it as great as the first game? Maybe not, but then few games are.--- 5 STARS ---
