After 4 years of the Smackdown! series, THQ took the next step and rebooted the series into a new series dubbed, Smackdown vs Raw. With their Day of Reckoning series doing great with sales over on the Gamecube, I guess they felt the need to reboot the game and make it similar to the Day of Reckoning game.The controls for the game didn't really change much, as they were the same as previous games. This was the first game to feature on par, double duty commentary. On Raw, J.R and Jerry Lawler call the action in the ring and over on Smackdown, Michael Cole and Tazz make their commentary return for the first time since Smackdown Just Bring It. Cole and Tazz's commentary was MUCH better this time around.The Backstage Brawl debuted as a new match type. You had the option of choosing to fight either backstage or in the parking lot. Because this new match type was available, they took out the ability to be able to travel backstage in Hardcore matches. Dumb idea if you ask me. Players enjoyed the ability to be able to roam around wherever they wanted in Hardcore Matches and now they were limited and could only choose between backstage and the parking lot.There was a new meter feature added to the game as for the first time ever you could choose to have the wrestler you play as fight as a clean, neutral or dirty wrestler. If you fought as a clean wrestler, you were given a blue meter, if you fought as a dirty wrestler, you were given a red meter. And if you fought as a neutral wrestler, you were given no meter. If you fought as a clean wrestler, taunting and high flying moves from the turnbuckle fill your meter. If you fought dirty, eye pokes, removing the turnbuckle padding, and hitting your opponent with weapons fill your meter. Once the meter is filled, a movement of the right analog initiates the meter for 30 seconds. If you're a clean wrestler, you're given the ability to reverse any move your opponent tries to do to you for 20 seconds. If you're dirty, you can low blow your opponent constantly for 20 seconds. Once the 20 seconds is up, the meter us emptied and you start over.Another meter added to the game was the chop/spank meter. If you try to knife edge chop your opponent against the turnbuckle during a match, a meter will come up that will involve you trying to stop the arrow in the shaded spot. The same pertains to bra & panties matches when you try to spank your opponent. If you get the timing correct and manage to stop the arrow in the shaded area, you can chop/spank them 2 more times but it must be timed correctly each time. If you miss the shaded area, you lose the battle and only get in 1 chop/spank. This was a rather frustrating feature to the game that I rarely succeed at. To this day, I still have trouble trying to succeed in all 3. In addition to the in-match mini games, there were also pre-match mini games that were chosen at random for each match. In the pre-match mini game, you'll either engage in a test of strength battle, a stare down, and a shoving battle.The roster was very poor as many superstars and divas that were in the WWE in 2004 were absent from the game for some reason. The 2 most notable ones being Brock Lesnar and Goldberg, who would've been perfect to represent the Smackdown vs Raw theme. Others missing from the game include Jamie Noble, Eugene, The Basham Brothers, the APA (JBL is in but Farrooq is not), Lita, Scott Steiner, Nidia, Rikishi, Miss Jackie, Gail Kim, Kenzo Suzuki, Billy Gunn, Test, and more. The only 3 superstars new to the game were Rene Dupree, Garrison Cade, and Mark Jindrak. Overall, I was very disappointed at the large amount of superstars and divas missing. Lita definitely came as a surprise, considering she had been back the ring since September 2003 and this game was released in November 2004. But above all else, fans were very disappointed to know that Lesnar and Goldberg were not involved in this game.Legends were also part of this game that included people like Bret Hart, Old School The Rock, Masked Kane, Andre the Giant, Legion of Doom, Mankind, Jimmy Snuka, and moreSeason Mode was good for the most part. All of the storylines were original and not tv rip-offs which made it much more enjoyable. The most remarkable note about this season mode was that it was the first time ever in WWF/WWE game history that superstars had voice overs. That was a big plus for this game. The superstar you play as throughout the season, doesn't have a voice over however. Why half-ass the voice overs? Why not make your character have a voice over as well?? Some of the awesome storylines you'll be involved in throughout the year are trying to take a diva from her abusive boyfriend and make her your manager, fighting against or aligning with Vince McMahon, winning the heart of Stacy Keibler, fighting off an invasion from Raw or Smackdown, and more. Every choice you make throughout the season will determine whether you're a face or heel, who your allies and enemies are, and what titles you qualify to challenge for. The only bone I have to pick with season mode is the unrealism in the stories. For example, if I'm on Smackdown, I shouldn't see Undertaker jumping me from behind with a steel chair and then running away when someone comes to my rescue. Same goes for people like Kane over on Raw.Other new features in the game are Challenge Mode, Create A Championship, and Online. Challenge Mode involved a series of challenges that would involve you fighting different superstars and legends in different matches. Create A Championship allowed players to create their own championship for the first time ever. And Online Mode allowed players to play with other people from around the world for the very first time. Online would become a very popular mode and is still featured in WWE games to this dayOverall: This was just an okay game to kick off the Smackdown vs Raw series. They hyped the game to the maximum with numerous commercials. I remember back when this game was about to come out, they'd show the commercial at least 6 or 7 times during Raw. The commercial featured, Smackdown's Torrie Wilson and Raw's Stacy Keibler fighting and arguing with each other. In the trailer of the game, we see Smackdown's John Cena and Raw's Randy Orton going face to face. Unfortunately the game didn't live up to a lot of its hype. The roster was poor, a few unrealistic aspects in Season Mode, and the frustrating in-game mini match spank/chop battles rob this game of its 2 stars to make this a 5 star game. Smackdown vs Raw comes in at a 3/5 stars from me

I always found it odd that the second game didn't do better than the firstViewtiful Joe - Gamecube. I think the concept of Viewtiful Joe never really caught on. It can be hard to convince gamers that a sidescroller with a Power Rangers wannabe could be this awesome. When you explain to them how revolutionary the speed up, slow down, and other effects are, you just get blank stares. I think what also didn't help it was the game is just so damn hard. Both 1 & 2 will humiliate gamers in easy/kids mode. But make no mistake, the this is a unique and fantastic series with top of the line graphics and gameplay.This time around, you get to play as Joe and/or his girlfriend Sylvia. You will see a lot of old bosses as well as some new ones. There's a lot more vehicles you can use this time around, and all are just a pure joy to use. Then there's Sylvia. I ended up liking her more than old Joe. She has her own powers and most importantly a gun. This gives her great distance attacks, something about that just feels so right in this game.You may have skipped this one because you heard it was just more of the same. And it definitely is that. But it's bigger, more fun, and generally even better crafted than the first. Just like the first, story is engaging but doesn't take itself too seriously, and that's it's charm. The gameplay is more varied thanks to Sylvia and all those new vehicles. It's a longer and better game. And keep in mind that the first game was pretty much perfect and you get how high praise that is.Bottom line, this is one of the best games you will ever play if you give it a chance. And I would actually recommend that you play this one first then go back and play the first if you liked it. It's just more bang for your buck, and the story is explained at the start of the game and is so simple that you won't feel like you are not getting things. So if you played the first and liked it, buy this. If you haven't played the first, buy this. Any self respecting gamer should not miss out on this series. I would also STRONGLY recommend that you put the game on easy/kids mode. The adult/hard difficulty will make it almost impossible to beat for the first time player. Pretty important. And play the GameCube version if you can, as the game was designed for the GameCube controller, and you can tell the difference.

this is the second time i've played this game. i bought it soon after it first came out in 2005, however playing it again nearly a decade later, i didn't remember much of the game at all. the last zelda game i played before this was the newest zelda, 'a link between worlds' and i must say that this game (and other zelda games from this era) was far more fun. i played 'link's awakening' and 'oracle of ages' last year and i now strongly feel that zelda really hit its stride in the GBC/GBA era.this game in particular has its own unique and imaginative gameplay. a large portion of the game centers around the ability to shrink down to 'minish'-cule size, in order to achieve things in the field that regular-sized link can't do. this aspect of the gameplay is intergrated into puzzle-solving and even sometimes a boss fight. the sword you use in this game, the sacred sword (not the master sword) has the ability to charge up and produce multiple clones of link, depending on its levels of strength as the game progresses. this is also another aspect of the game that is deeply integrated into puzzle-solving and boss fights. it can be a lot of fun but also very challenging because the link clones all disappear if one of them are hurt.lastly, a fairly large aspect of the game is collecting kinstone pieces and fusing them together with random people, puzzles, etc. a kinstone piece looks like a half of a coin with a tri-force on it. the coins are cut in a number of unique patterns and colors. fusing kinstone pieces can reveal secrets in the game or can sometimes be necessary to advance.other than that. it's a pretty standard zelda game. fairly short, even with the sidequests, so if you think most zelda games are long, this one may be more up your alley. as far as items go, you have the standard zelda inventory: shield, bombs, arrows, boomerang, lantern. some perennial favorites from past zelda's like roc's cape and the pegasus boots, along with some new items that i will leave to you to discover on your own.

I never should have played the original or this updated version of the most overrated Mario title Nintendo ever released.  The praise this game STILL receives in this day and age, not necessarily for its gameplay but mainly for its influence mind you, is staggering... and sickening.  Super Mario 64 never impressed me at all in the N64 days nearly 18 years ago when I was supposed to swallow the enormous popularity but intelligently never did, and it certainly doesn't impress me now.  Nintendo had a perfect opportunity to finally make this overrated lackluster game into something truly special from a gameplay perspective but they failed to do so.  They could have finally corrected a wrong that's been annoying me for the better part of two decades.You can play as not only Mario but also Luigi, Yoshi and Wario each with their own unique abilities.  You have to search for and pick up their caps scattered throughout the levels, often times worn by the enemies meaning you have to take out the enemies to obtain them.  These are nice additions admittedly and I honestly don't even need to tell you what these abilities are- you already know since they haven't changed in years.  Luigi jumps high?  No way!  Wario's powerful?  Get out of town!  Yoshi spits eggs?  I doubt that!  Yeah, you get the idea.  There's a few other things this game adds that's totally unnecessary such as gigantic-sized Mario that can smash anything in sight for a few seconds, an overused cheap gimmick that would soon explode in eye candy redundancy when the New Super Mario Bros. games would release, and those irritating rabbit chasing games which appeared quite often in the Galaxy series.  The one mistake the Galaxy series made was including so many rabbing chasing obstacles and... Super Mario 64 for the DS gives us more of those than we can honestly handle.  Chasing rabbits is stupid!  The worst part is that there's an extended rabbit grabbing mission both inside and outside the castle when you get close to the end of the game that takes up a good 10 minutes of playtime and it's absolutely terrible.  The bloated floating Mario power-up is kind of cool though.The most unusual and annoying aspect of this game that totally perplexes me is that the levels *still* feel needlessly overlarge.  Nintendo had a ripe opportunity here to fill in all these dreadfully empty and boring areas with tons of goodies to make them feel complete.  I mean why not fill in the empty areas?  Instead Nintendo left these stages the way they are more or less.  They wanted to preserve the game the way most people like it which was of course a bad idea.  Of course the even BIGGER insult is that Nintendo added a few new levels that feel incomplete and outdated just like the regular levels!  Why Nintendo, why?  Why match basic, unfocused blocky-shaped level design with MORE basic, unfocused blocky-shaped level design?  Instead of fixing the outdated-ness of the presentation of the game, Nintendo just throws in a few more simplistically created areas and calls it a day.  Talk about a slap in the face for those of us expecting something more appealing visually.Another really big problem is that in order to grab all 150 stars, we have to go through the same levels AGAIN AND AGAIN!  Talk about repetition at its absolute worse, and going through the same areas over and over will only end up making me want to replay this game even less.  And by less I of course mean never again.  Knowing that the game is STILL intentionally made to force gamers go through the same areas yet again just to obtain another golden star is really pathetic.  Create Mario games either the Super Mario Bros. 3 way where you only have to go through a stage one time before moving on, or the Yoshi's Island way where if you successfully collect everything your first time and 100% a level, you won't have to return to the same stages anymore.  Don't MAKE us go through areas we already completed time and time again for one simple little golden star where the "adventure" getting to it is hardly ever rewarding, challenging or lengthy enough to make an impression anyway.The controls are horrible once again, this time persevering a d-pad instead of a big clunky N64 controller (both ideas fail to work right).  The music is absolutely terrible beyond comprehension.  Having to constantly rearrange camera angles is incredibly outdated and annoying.  Super Mario Galaxy proved that switching camera angles is no longer necessary.  It's WAY too happy which is no doubt deliberate on the part of Nintendo for the entire purpose of rubbing more salt in the wound.  Seriously Nintendo, it's possible to make happy music without the irritating obnoxiousness that only ends up distracting what's clearly already a really lame and outdated game overall.  No need to make the experience even worse with music that makes you want to tear the skin off your body.  An example of quality happy music is the stuff we hear throughout World 1 of Super Mario Bros. 3.  Remember the joyful and innocent music in that game?  The music was tame and never frantically irritating.  In Super Mario 64 DS however, the music's like a hayride from the county fair to the downtown post office that rides on an endless loop in the most annoying way imaginable.  Super Mario Bros. 3 is just one of several examples I could name that shows the way music SHOULD be for a platformer that often times requires concentration to succeed.  At least the remixed soothing water music now with techno-ish beats is decent.  If any other themes have been remixed I can't tell.And we have 30 more stars to collect bringing the total to 150 this time around, which means an extra hour or so to collect everything the game has to offer.  I would mention several other features that drag down this supposed "classic" but I already touched upon those subjects in my review for the Nintendo 64 version of Super Mario 64 so there's no need to repeat myself here.  The cuteness factor of certain areas is enough to make me puke though.  I don't mind the occasional childish graphics and objectives, but Super Mario 64 takes the childish aspects to really pathetic depths that feels more intended for babies instead of kids.  Take the penguin race level with the penguins and snowmen for example.  *throws up*  Not something grown men who grew up during the 80's when Mario was fresh, challenging, fast-paced and arcade-like would ever admit to enjoying without blushing.  And what DOES Mario say at the beginning of each level?  "Let's tickle!"  "Miss Pickle!" "Popsicle!"  There's like a million things he could be saying there.  I was informed he's saying "Let's a-go" but I absolutely can't make out those words at all.  I had this same trouble with the N64 version since it's the same exact line lazily copied into this game.Just skip Super Mario 64 DS.  I absolutely loathe this game.  The only reason I gave it another chance is because I thought Nintendo radically changed the game and morphed it into something entirely different by ditching all the old, outdated and tiresome ideas that never worked in the first place and yet only existed in the late 90's because Nintendo was riding the 3D wave and needed something cutting edge on the market.  It's no longer 1996, though.  My how I was wrong on all counts to give this game a second chance on the DS.  The two worst levels have remained which only adds to my anger.  The level where you have to tediously and accurately jump across a series of rotating poles above the water collecting coins, and the rainbow-colored carpet ride which is essentially an auto-scrolling level when you think about it.At least the ghost house is pretty cool.  A piano snapping and chasing me around the room is pretty fun, as is punching enemies and knocking them out for coins.  But uh... coins.  That brings me to another subject and another annoyance.  Absolutely the biggest thing Nintendo should have clearly changed is the "collect 100 coins for a star" levels.  This means for several minutes I'm forced to thoroughly explore mediocre levels JUST to obtain enough coins for a star.  A sickening, dreadful, terribly unsatisfying concept if there ever was one.  You'd have to be the most delusional person on the planet to enjoy collecting 100 coins while absorbing these unspectacular levels.  I'm done with this review.  Between gamers believing this game is actually a classic and the little enjoyment I get out of it despite relentlessly giving it more chances, I just can't handle it anymore.

Super Mario 64 was the biggest milestone in 3D gaming.  There were 3D games prior to this one, but this one brought something new to the table: genius level design, responsive controls, a real adventure to follow, and most importantly: fun.  But that was in 1996.  How does it hold up now re-released on the DS?For starters, it improves on everything from the original Mario 64.  It is still tons of fun to play, and has 30 new stars that weren't in the original Mario 64.  It also has new playable characters, each with different abilities, strengths, and weaknesses, along with a new multiplayer mode. This game packs in a ton of new content for fans and veterans of the original, without removing anything from the game we all know and love.The one slight downside is controls.  It is obviously a lot weirder and less effective to control a character in 3D space with a D-Pad rather than a joystick.  However, if you play it on a 3DS which actually HAS  joystick, it is flawless.I can recommend this game to either kids, or hardcore players alike.  It is bright and colorful, but has very challenging levels and will take a lot of time to accomplish all 120 stars.

...is surprisingly the best one.  Super Mario 64 DS, the first Mario game to appear on Nintendo DS.Plot- Mario, Wario and Luigi go to Toadstool's/Peach's (the name 'Peach' was first introduced in this game) Castle for a promised cake. They go in the tower, but they never return. Lakitu sees Yoshi sleeping on to of the Castle, and informs him about the matter, and that he'll be recording Yoshi throughout the journey to find the capped men. But, he finds that, in order to progress in the castle, he needs a number of Power Stars, corresponding to a number on the doors. There's 150 in all. 120 Stars in paintings, and 30 secrets. He finds paintings, which, after he jumps into them, uncover worlds that each have 7 Stars. He finds paintings of Mario, Wario, and Luigi, which means that the characters are trapped in them. Yoshi saves them all! But, what about the cake? WHAT ABOUT PEACH? Bowser seems to have Peachnapped her again. So, together, you progress further and further until you reach Bowser's final lair. Finally, Mario defeats him and Peach is free again!Graphics-the best you will ever find on DS.Sound-the themes are great, but Player Character voices sound slighly compressed.Controls-the +Control Pad isn't annoying as you may think. I have played TONS of Mario games. I got a Wii for X-mas in 2012, and a 3DS in December 2013. I never had the original DS, but the 3DS can play DS and DSi games. I've heard great reviews for this AND the original N64 game. Super Mario 64 is often said to be the best Mario game ever. I played the N64 version first on the Wii. The game was somewhat fun, but the horrible controls and the terrible movement of Mario & camera angles made it 1-star. I heard this game had new stars & characters, so I got it. Plus, because it was a game released in 2004, (ten yrs. old), the camera angles and graphics would be better than the game on the N64 (1996). I was wrong by a long shot.First, the "New characters" thing is stupid. It's a pain in the butt to have to switch from Yoshi to Mario and back to Yoshi for some stars. The "pick up a Wario hat and you're now Wario!" thing is lame because make one error, and you gotta start the whole level over again. I did not like this new feature at all. It's one area that the horrible N64 version is superior to the terrible DS version.Second, the graphics are a nightmare. The graphics look worse than on an N64! They bother my eyes, and you'll keep dying because you can't see where your going or where the goomba chasing you went! Three seconds later, he hits you and you have to grab a coin to restore it. Easy, right? Wait! I can't tell where the coin is! OK, I'm exaggerating a bit, but not by too much.Third, the controls are very confusing. The "Touch screen" thing is a fail. You have to drag your finger while looking at both screens at the same time!  If you are playing this on the old DS, your other option is the control pad. I never did good with control pads except on the Wii, so they might not be too bad. I'm glad I had a 3DS with the thumb-stick which is OK, I guess. But why "B" to jump? "A" is a much better fit for this! They used "Y" for sprint(good) and "A" for punch(bad). The controls overall are a complete mess that is not necessary.Third, the sound is horrible. That annoying music! Poor sound quality! That stupid sound Mario makes when he punches! These are all in here.Overall, Super Mario 64 DS is on par with Super Mario 64(N64), which both suck. Super Mario 64 is not how 3-D platforming should be done. For the price of 30 US dollars, this is not worth it. Rent it before buying it. It's not worth one cent to me. If you're looking for a 3D Mario game on the go, buy Super Mario 3D Land, with charming graphics, nice music, and good controls & gameplay. If you want a list of Mario games in order, here it is:Best:1. Super Mario Galaxy 2 (Wii)2. Super Paper Mario (Wii)3. Super Mario Galaxy (Wii)4. Super Mario 3D Land (3DS)5. Paper Mario (N64)Worst:1. Super Mario 64/Super Mario 64 DS (N64, DS)2. Super Mario Bros. 2 (NES)3. Super Mario World  (SNES)4. Super Mario Bros. 3  (NES)5. Super Mario Sunshine (GCN)Overall, for this, buy the far superior Super Mario Galaxy 2. I've got to say I really like this stand. Simple yet effective. At first, the design flaw that allowed the PS2 to wobble from side to side was a concern. Being of above average intelligence, I was able to solve the problem in two or three minutes by taking four half inch wide four inch long, adhesive backed "trim to fit" felt pads normally used for padding or cushioning furniture drawers and doors, lamp bases and wood curio boxes, so they won't scratch furniture. I trimmed the pads to fit around the circular center-well section of the base where the set screw is placed, and so they matched the circular shape of the base. The pads run underneath the side of the PS2 that is held in place by the set screw. Once tightened securely the PS2 no longer wobbled at all. The pads also act as a vibration buffer between the table and the PS2.I hope this helps all you People who were wondering how to make your PS2 stop flopping from side to side. When it comes to underrated video game gems 1998's Brave Fencer Musashi was easily the odd man out when it came to the various games Squaresoft released during the PS1 era. Yeah, I know a lot people just bought the game just gain access to the Final Fantasy VIII demo and pretty much threw Brave Fencer aside - at their loss - but I'm sorry, there is just no way Samurai Legend can even come close to that game. In all honesty I hadn't touched this one in over a decade and its really easy to see why....The game starts off well enough but soon every problem you can think off comes out of the woodwork. The world that Musashi is thrown into this game is simply nowhere near as engrossing as the first game because there simply isn't any humor in this game. Now, I'd expect some to point out the humor in the first game was "lame" because it revolved a lot around silly puns but at least the game was able to take that resource and make it its own -  at least in my case. Additionally, I'd also expect some to say that the humor should have been scaled back as Musashi is older in this game... but without it the game literally has NOTHING to fall back on.Once you look beyond the change in tone things just get bleaker. The game's adversaries (the members of the Grandrake corporation) are far from interesting, normal enemies constantly re-spawn (seriously, why can't they stay dead until I reenter a room?), bosses have an absorbent amount of HP and don't really have very big openings for attack, you CONSTANTLY have to adjust the camera to even see your attackers (don't even get me started this when it comes to bosses) and the development team couldn't even bother to give bosses health meters? I just don't get this... NONE of these problems exist in the first game so what's the deal?Seriously, there is a reason this game costs next to nothing these days and I had to replay it to remind me of why a) the first game is the vastly superior creation and b) how far Squaresoft fell after the merger with Enix. Not even the game's music and art style can save it. While I'm probably (obviously) biased I'd suggest picking up Brave Fencer on the PlayStation over this. Yeah, it's much more expensive but at least that game had some actual soul. All Samurai Legend offers is a lot of promises it can't even come close to fulfilling.

Games like Civilization and Master of Orion 2 suffer from end-game complexity--they're fun while your civilization is small, but in order to do well, you need to have a large civilization, and as a result, you're playing for the "reward" of the game getting too complex to be fun. Further, such games have turns of variable length--sometimes nothing happens for many turns, and then you discover a tech and change what you're building, and that one turn takes a long time. HOMM3 suffers from neither of these problems, which makes it a fantastic game for hotseat multiplayer. Your few heroes have a set number of movement points each turn, so each turn you will do something interesting but not too long; and rather than having your empire grow in size, in HOMM3 your heroes grow in strength. It lacks the strategic complexity of Civ and MOO2, but it has enough to be engaging.

This is my first time with Square's "Saga" line of RPGs. I don't know to much about them other than it's a series where you can play through the game with multiple characters. All I know other than that is that I loved this game.Here's how it works. You start a game by selecting which character you want to be with a choice of eight. Then there's a short little intro giving you an idea who the character is. Then you are basically turned lose to do whatever you want. The town and locations you can go to is initially limited but quickly expands to a spider web of places to go and things to do. And this is where this game really shines. There are so many choices of places to go and side quests that it's almost overwhelming at times. You will inevitably stumble onto the game's main quest and continue to dip into it every now and then until you eventually beat the game for that character. After that, pick another character and start another. It sounds tedious but what you have to understand is that each character starts in a different town and develops his own personalized story as they go. And through each play through you get a better insight into the story. All the monsters adjust themselves to you level so it doesn't really matter where you start. Bosses don't adjust themselves so they become the gatekeepers to the main story progression.If all that sounds very different from your normal RPG experience, that's because it is. I loved it but some gamers find it hard to bear. I'm not sure if you will like it. It depends how much repetition bugs you. Or whether or not you like a normal RPG experience rather than a bit of a sim hybrid, of which this game feels more like the latter.Options of more towns and things to do is partly dependent on who you choose to be in your party. And there are a ton of potential party members. Mostly you meet them in bars. Some are the eight playable characters, others have there own little side stories, some are just generic characters you use for muscle. You and every party member has certain weapons and classes they can use to power-up magic and techniques. And those magic and techniques combine in battle to create some really strong attacks. I really enjoyed the battle mechanics.Music is good and graphics are pretty sweet. Everything has a bit of a relaxed watercolor feel to it. Almost everything is voice acted, and there is a ton of talking in this game. But more than anything, I loved the sense of freedom this game gave me. I was always obsessed with figuring out some side quest or how to get to some secret location. And what I really liked was the length of the game. I only played through with five characters but the game stayed in my system for months. I think this turned out to be the longest game I ever played. Around 200 hours, at least. But I really took my time as I tend to do with RPGs. And while you have 8 character to play the game with, I highly doubt you will use them all. You will mostly likely pick out a few of them and play until you finally feel too burnt out to continue. And that's fine. But whatever you do, please don't play through it once with one character. That totally defeats the purpose of the game and only gives you a slice of what this game has to offer.My only complaint that when you do finally quit playing, you are pretty done with it. Time to sell it on Amazon because you won't be going back to a world you completely played out. So I'm taking a star off for that. But it was a great game while it lasted and a ton of play for your buck. Four stars.

This being my favorite game, I was surprised to see mixed reviews on it. But I think I figured it out. The is a very old school RPG. The story is thin. The random battles are numerous. I could see how modern gamers could get the sense that they aren't getting anywhere. But if you grew up on the SNES or Genesis rather that the Playstation or Playstation 2, this game feels natural to you. This is just the way games used to be. It doesn't have 30 minute long cutscenes or long conversations that people now expect as a reward for their playing for 15 minutes. What it does have is solid gameplay, drop dead gorgeous graphics and excellent music. Add a massive and lush world to explore and you have what us old school gamers would consider to be a perfect game.And in my view this is a perfect game. Let me just start with the graphics. The phrase "jaw dropping" comes to mind. Unlike most RPGs that are rather lazy here, the world is fully 3D. Meaning you can walk under a tree and look up and see the branches. You look in the distance and see a mountain, a tree, a beach. Not just a 2D representation of everything. It may sound like a small thing, but I prefer RPGs in total 3D. It adds so much to the realism, the earthy feel of the game. And it's nice to be able to see a massive world like this and decide where you want to explore, rather than just follow a cookie cutter path the programmer decides you must follow. And what a beautiful world it is to explore. The nice thing about cell shading is that if you do it right, you create timeless graphics. And that's exactly what you have here. Sly Cooper is about the only thing I have seen that comes close. Cell shading was a perfect for Dragon Quest. If you've played past Dragon Quest games you know they always had a flat, cartoony look to them. So it was just the perfect fit. And where it really shines is with the monsters. They just look so cool. And the bosses, man. The design, look, and feel really makes them simply stunning.Gameplay is pretty straight forward, attacks and magic. If you've played past Dragon Quest games you know they are famous for the excellent jobs system. That's gone this time, replaced by a weapons system. Each character has a variety of weapon types they can use. Picking the a certain weapon type meshes with your character and allows them to grow and learn moves consistent with that weapon. This actually adds to the replay value of the game as it's best to stick with a certain weapon for the entire game. I know this was a big reason for me playing the game twice.As with every great RPG, this one has it's crack like addictive features that keep you playing for an insane number of hours. For Dragon Quest the big one is the alchemy pot. Oh that evil little alchemy pot. When out in the field you can mix various weapons, items, armor and other things is this pot to make new and sometimes very powerful weapons and armor. You can find recipes in the game to make various items, but many have to be found with experimentation and the internet. My only gripe about this game is that they were too tight with the recipes, my guess in an attempt to sell more strategy guides. The other addiction is the monster hunting. Get some strong ones and you can summon them in battle, making you infinitely stronger. And you can also fight them in a monster arena.And there's just a thousand cool little things about this game. Changing you armor actually changes your how you are dressed. This is particularly cool when dressing up Jessica, the mega-hot redhead in your party. There's a secret casino to gamble in. There's even a new town and area to explore after you beat the game.This has been a long and gushing review so let me just sum it all up by saying that after finishing the game after 100+ hours, I left it in the system and played another game for 100+ hours. I've never done anything like that before. I know the story is simple for an RPG, save the princess and save the world from a bad guy. That's about it. But I never played games for the story. I played them to have an engaging interactive experience where I get to decide what happens next. And I still don't really want a long drawn out story that you get the feeling they made up as they went along. Maybe I just want to explore and maybe save the princess while I'm at it. Maybe I just want to play a game. And this game gave me that in the most perfect fashion I've ever seen. An easy 5 stars. Heck, I think I'll have it buried with me.

My son and I have played the first three R&C; games to death for many years, and I only recently became aware of this one.I think the description is a bit misleading.  Yes, this is "arena combat", but it's not really that simple.  The premise is that Ratchet is a contestant on a game show where you battle bots and, ultimately, boss battles with other star gladiators.When you enter a level  you generally battle in small areas then there are platforming elements where you move on to other parts of the level.  It doesn't really feel like you're trapped in an arena for the entire game.It's a quick game, maybe 8-10 hours or so.  My son has played through the game much more than I have so I can't recall how long the full story mode takes.  But the good part of this, and what my son loves, is that the weapons continue to upgrade if you continue with the same game save and restart at the beginning.  So your character and weapons continue to improve, which greatly enhances the replay value.  To my mind it's long enough, and it's not an issue at all.You can also play splitscreen multiplayer, either against each other in various standard game types, or co-op through the story mode.  The only complaint is that it gets hard to see what's going on.  That may be my aging eyes, but I think my son has the same issue to a lesser extent.Still, a fun game.  The R&C; games are top-notch, and easily some of the best on the PS2.  One of our favorite series of all time, and this is a welcome addition to the series, though overall it doesn't quite have what it takes for a full five stars.

The first Call Of Duty game, exclusively for the PC, was a strategic, realistic game that was immensely challenging and enjoyable.  However, the hardest difficulty, Veteran, took things a little too far.  The health pickups were completely gone, meaning any damage received was permanent.  Also, checkpoints wouldn't activate if your health was below 50%.  Combine this with enemies that were extremely accurate and did massive damage, and Veteran mode could be infuriating.  Luckily, its sequel, COD 2, introduces elements that make the game more balanced and fair, while still retaining a realistic, strategic atmosphere.  As a result, to this day, it remains one of the best WWII games ever created.Developed by Infinity Ward and published by Activision, the biggest change to COD 2 is in its health system.  Instead of finding medkits to heal yourself, you have a regenerating health system that automatically heals you completely if you don't take any further damage.  Now this was all the way back in late 2005, when the seventh-generation was just beginning.  Regeneration, at the time, was completely revolutionary, and everyone embraced the fact that they didn't have to focus solely on avoiding damage or hunting for healthpacks.  This system allows you to take greater risks and experiment with a wider range of tactics, while still being able to recover if you do mess up.The core gameplay in COD 2 remains the same as the first.  You play as three different soldiers in three separate campaigns: American, British, and Russian, all of whom are fighting the Nazis at different places and times.  All four sides have their own unique set of weapons, some that are essentially carbon copies of each other, and others that can be vastly superior.  Since you're only allowed to carry two weapons at a time, the key to progressing through the camapign is to pick a loadout suitable for short and long-range combat while also enhancing your movement speed.

Coming out all the way back in 2005, Call of Duty 2 is by no means new; the graphics seem almost foreign compared to today's wonders (Last of Us, this is not), but CoD 2 is still a great, great game. Anyone who has played any of the other games in the franchise should already know this game's incredibly easy control layout, giving your soldier the ability to chose from three types of stances, aim down the sights of your rifle, throw grenades, and swap weapons with ease. After playing with Killzone's mess of a control scheme, CoD's control layout is a welcome breath of fresh air.Back before multiplayer was expected to carry an entire franchise, game developers actually had to put a little more effort into their campaigns, and it is truly shown in CoD 2's case. Spanning across three military expeditions, you'll play as a freshly recruited Russian soldier sent to defend his homeland, a British foot soldier, command tanks, and (my favorite) star as an American private sent to fight on D-Day. The story is enjoyable, and the battles are varied enough to keep this action-packed, lengthy campaign exciting. The game also offers a multiplayer, but this is not CoD2's strong point. Seekers of a multiplayer experience should look elsewhere for WW2 action.Anyone looking to see how CoD started to transform the first person shooter should definitely pick up this classic, especially at the current price.

Sonic Gems contains 3 main Sonic games:Sonic CDSonic RSonic the FightersThere are also 6 Sonic Game Gear games:Sonic 2Sonic SpinballSonic Triple TroubleSonic Drift 2Tail's Sky PatrolTail's AdventureThere are also 2 unlockable games:VectormanVectorman 2Vectorman 1 & 2 are fun and are some of the best Genesis games there is. It is a shame that Vectorman died off so early because he had great potential.The Game Gear games are more of a curiosity. It is widely known that most Game Gear games are inferior to the Sega console games, but it was still interesting to see and play the obscure Sonic games. They aren't terribly bad either. They have their own unique feel to them and are fun for handheld games, but they don't feel like Sonic games.Sonic CD is a classic and is one of the most highly rated Sonic game, but it is a little confusing since it involves time travel. If you run in a direction long enough without stopping, you will go to either the future or past. Sometimes it is not intentional and I really don't see any difference in the gameplay, only the background.Sonic the Fighters is a strange game to say the least. It has bad controls for a fighting game but for what it is, it is a fun kind of bad. I enjoyed fighting my way through the game. There is a technique I found which let me beat everyone easily even on the hardest difficulty. It has it's flaws but it is fun to play as joke.Sonic R was I game I had as a kid and the main reason I bought this game. The controls are crazy. It is very difficult to maneuver. The turning always makes the character drift and to turn around you have to stop and turn slowly or do a U-turn like a car even though only one character is driving a car. You may think that the programmers messed up big time, but I believe it was intentional. The CPU's also seem to have the same problem controlling themselves as the player. The point of the race is not to see who is the fastest or who found the quickest path, but it is who can control themselves the best and make the least mistakes. Once you get the hang of the controls, playing against the CPU's is too easy. There are many short cuts which the computers don't even know about. If you're gonna race, race multiplayer.Sonic R was easily my favorite game in the collection. It is so unique compared to other racers. You can collect 5 Sonic coins to unlock other characters if you get 1st with all the coins. There are also 7 chaos emeralds to collect to unlock a certain super-powered hedgehog. There are also rings on the track and items ranging from a water barrier to a speed boost. There are gates which require different amounts of rings to open. They may lead to a short-cut or a chaos emerald. There are other modes to play as well. Time trials in normal mode and reverse mode which makes you race in the track backwards. There is also a balloon mode which has 5 balloons hidden throughout the track. My favorite mode though is tag mode. It is tag with the Sonic characters. I love to choose the slowest character and try to tag the fastest character. It is hard but fun.

I've already reviewed the Wii version of this game which I consider to be greatly inferior and falsely advertised as being superior to the GameCube version; so there's no need for me to repeat what I've already stated about the atrocious Wii Mote and Nunchuk controls. This version of the game has flawless controls thanks to the GameCube controller which some players regard as the best video game controller ever made. So I'm happy to finally review the GameCube version of this game. With that said, Twilight Princess is nowhere near a perfect game. This game has many, many glaring flaws which aren't as evident in previous Zelda titles. The most obvious being its complete lack of challenge.I can easily say this was without a doubt the easiest Zelda game when it was released and today it still remains the easiest Zelda game I've ever played, never played Skyward Sword nor do I want to. The enemies are pathetic. They pose absolutely no danger and no threat to Link whatsoever, especially the bosses which can easily be defeated the first time playing and without the loss of more than 5 hearts at most. The enemies found in Hyrule field are the most laughable and weak overworld enemies in video game history. They don't fight back and literally wait for you to kill them. Every single Zelda title before this game had challenging enemies and players were always in danger of losing hearts when in the presence of even a weak bat. In this game, the enemies don't fight back; you can kill scores of them with ease. Most of the enemies, after they've been attacked, are stunned for a few seconds giving you a great deal of time to finish them off. Bosses can easily be defeated with a minimal loss of hearts and figuring out their weaknesses has never been simpler than in this game since most of them have very obvious and cliched weak points such as the ever present eyeball and tail.A good scenario to use for comparison would be, imagine you were in a fight, the person you are fighting would delay each hit he makes by a few seconds giving you time to completely thrash him. Each time you hit him (and you can hit him multiple times rapidly), he pauses for a few seconds giving you even more time and an even greater advantage to completely annihilate him. That's exactly what playing Twilight Princess feels like, the enemies don't fight back and their speed can never ever compare to the speed of the player. If that doesn't make the game easy enough, you also have a shield. This shield doesn't have its own button and while using L to target an enemy, the shield is automatically drawn and remains present at all times during a fight; completely eliminating any possibility of the player ever taking a single hit in this entire game. Even flaming bats and fire arrows here bounce off the shield on your back. There's zero challenge whatsoever in this game. What you can do, is equip the wooden shield let it burn, and play through the game without a shield. This adds some challenge to the game and works for the most part. However, if I'm not mistaken, there may be some cut scenes which automatically equip a Hylian shield and you may have to buy another wooden shield, let it burn, and return to where you just were in order to play through the rest of the game with no shield. Just to add some challenge.As I played through the game, I kept waiting and waiting for the moment to come when I would finally face a challenging enemy worthy of my skills, but it never came. When playing through the Cave of Ordeals, I fought all the same enemies I faced in the rest of the game. Even the final enemies, the Darknuts were not difficult at all especially since I had the shield protecting me against 100% of their attacks. All you need to do is knock off their removable armor, hit them once and they become stunned allowing you to hit them continuously until they block you. After they've blocked you, manage to hit them again, repeat the process, and they're finished. There was no challenge anywhere in this game; the battle with Zant is so disappointing. And afterwards you enter Zelda's castle to experience the easiest Ganondorf battle in Zelda history and unfortunately a lot of this battle requires use of the wolf, instead of the sword like any other Zelda game. Why couldn't there have been an epic sword battle between Link and Ganondorf, two swords just like the teaser that eventually lead to WindWaker showed? Why instead did they have to come up with this ridiculous overdrawn ending fight? It's so childish. It's a complete disgrace to the battle from Ocarina of Time. Even the first time playing you'll take minimal damage. No enemy in this game is difficult; some of them can be annoying and tedious but not hard to beat.Years back I discovered some websites which contained Action Replay codes for this game. Some of these codes could be used to multiply the amount of health the enemies had. I used these particular codes thinking they would add some challenge to the game, but instead they only made battles much more annoying as now the enemies required way more hits to die and since they would never hit me back anyway, I was basically wasting time fighting a defenseless enemy that simply had more health than it originally would. Another code I tried was one that increased the damage dealt to Link when he would get hit by an enemy. This didn't make the game any more fun either, because now when I would occasionally get hit, I'd usually only be able to survive one more hit before dying and having to start all over. The game simply cannot be manipulated using codes to gain any positive results. The lack of challenge in this game is a programming issue on the part of the developers that intentionally made it easy for casual gamers and kids to play. Codes won't solve this mess.Another major let down was the false advertising from the game's trailers showing Link fighting hordes of Moblins that rode large wild boars. This event never happens in the game; instead you fight a mini boss riding a wild boar. The fight is very annoying because he can keep knocking you off your horse into Lake Hylia and afterwards (after losing a heart) you'll magically reappear on your horse ready for another attempt. It's really easy to win this fight because all you really have to do is charge a spin attack and you can hit this enemy each round. It's also very, very easy to lose this fight if you use any method other than the cheap shot spin attack. You know, like if you actually wanted to do a jousting battle with this guy, you'd lose each time so don't get your hopes up. You absolutely have to use a cheap spin attack to win even though it's physically impossible to do one in real life while riding horseback. Don't try to make this game feel realistic, you're wasting your time. Aside from this one fight, there's only 3 Moblins riding wild boars in one single part of Hyrule field and once you've defeated them they only re-spawn after you've left the screen. So no, there is no massive battle with an army of Moblins that ever happens in this easy game. That's called false advertising, why make a trailer of a beta when the official release will have such drastic changes?The wolf quests are unbelievably stupid and uninspired. As a wolf you go around sniffing out electric insects (from the ground or hiding in jars) which you kill to retrieve tear drops used to fill up a weird grape vine looking thing (that holds tear drops) given to you by a guardian light creature (based on one of the animals in the game) in any one of the fountains within each region of the game that uses the tear drops to restore light and remove the Twilight from that area. It's annoying and can take a very long time.I don't understand the game's use of Twilight creatures and how this could have possibly been considered fun. When you're in an area in the Twilight realm, suddenly this strange flying saucer looking thing appears in the sky and drops 3-4 alien looking monsters down to fight you. This is actually a portal from the game's Twilight realm and the aliens are Twilight monsters that must be KO'd simultaneously or else the last one alive will make a horrible shrieking noise that revives the fallen ones. You don't have to KO them all in one go, you just have to make sure that at least 2 are alive when you make your final hit killing both of them in one shot using Midna's targeting technique to target multiple enemies. They take one heart away each time they hit you and you can easily die if you're not careful. That doesn't make it challenging however, just annoying because you can't really tell when these enemies are going to make an attack. It's not clear because the graphics are convoluted in the Twilight realm and their attacks come suddenly.Some people actually have the audacity to compare the boring, tedious wolf quests to the sailing in Wind Waker which was actually fun, challenging, exciting, unique, had loads of treasures and new things for you to discover, and it was fun charting the many different islands in the game. The wolf quests on the other hand are simply used as filler material because the developers didn't want to take the time to develop something interesting and fun to do; so they have you waste time on boring bug killing/tear drop collecting quests like this. There weren't many mini games or extras in this game anyway even though the reviewers on IGN and Game Trailers said there was. Once you've beaten it, it's over and it's better to start over rather than run around Hyrule seeing all the same things you've already completed. I guess that's true about every game but this one in particular is very boring to play a save file you've already completed.You have two options for fishing in this game; one is using this mini rod you get in Ordon village. It's really easy to use and you can find either bee larva or worms to use as bait making the fish guaranteed catches. The camera view however is very awkward and you only know when you have a bite if this floating spike attached to the rod starts bobbing down into the water. At which point you simply pull the C Stick down until the fish is caught. The other option for fishing is the fishing pond which has been made more difficult than it was in Ocarina of Time, but that's okay. There's nothing wrong with some added challenge. After all the game needs to have a challenging aspect in it somewhere right? Might as well be here. For one thing, you use an assortment of different lures, each with its own unique technique for drawing in fish. Sometimes it can take forever to get the fish to come to you but that's kind of how it is in real life. If you're willing to pay the extra 100 rupees, you can have a "lovely assistant" sit in the boat with you. She doesn't do anything other than advise you on what spots are the best to fish in and she doesn't allow you to use a sinking lure in her presence, but it's nice to have the company of an attractive female rather than being alone. (Why doesn't Link ever have a girlfriend in these games? Why doesn't he ever kiss Zelda? Is Link, you know? I mean he does wear a skirt and in this game in particular, Link looks very effeminate? Way more than in previous Zelda games.) When the fish bite, it's not as simple as in Ocarina of Time where you hold the A and R buttons and pull down on the rod with the control stick. In this game, on screen indicators appear telling you which way to push or pull the rod. If the fish jumps push up on the C Stick, when it's in the water pull down, when it's close enough to you grab the fishing line with A to pull the fish out of the water. It's more realistic and challenging than Ocarina of Time and I actually kind of enjoyed this part of the game.With all that said, the game isn't all bad. The graphics are beautiful and the music in many places is serene and relaxing, except of course for the disgusting music for The City in The Sky. That song is so ugly and it never ever stops. It plays through both the inside and the outside of the temple, starting immediately after being shot from the cannon and landing in the water. It has annoying moans from these weird, creepy, hideous chicken like creatures that have human faces (Ooccas). The game is decent at best. I don't really like the whole Japanese aspect, the way female characters behave really frigid and repressed, and the way the other NPCs act is really strange and foreign to me. They make weird noises like "wwwwwwoooooohhhhhh", things that neither I nor anybody from the West could possibly understand or relate with.There are some annoying elements added to this game that weren't necessary and didn't appear in any other Zelda game before it. When you collect a rupee, if that rupee is any color other than green (worth 1 rupee), you will always get an annoying descriptive message about the type of rupee you just collected, similar to what happens when opening a treasure chest. It's completely unnecessary because we already know the amount the rupee contains based on its color due to our knowledge of previous Zelda games where this never occurred before. This means that every single time you turn off the game, the next time you turn it on the game is programmed to automatically display this annoying message once after collecting any non-green rupee (worth 1 rupee). There's no need for them to interrupt the gameplay like this, it's ridiculous and slows you down immensely. There actually is an Action Replay code to turn this message off and I always had this code enabled after discovering it. Hell yeah! Not only that, but after playing Wind Waker, you'll be deeply disappointed to find that the largest wallet in this game only allows you to carry a maximum of 1,000 rupees. Wind Waker's largest wallet allowed you to carry 5,000 rupees and that game was older. So there's no excuse especially since there are so many rupees in this game. Rupees are everywhere in this game, you need a bigger wallet. If you've reached an amount close to the maximum that your wallet holds, opening treasure chests with rupees will cause Link to put the rupees back in the chest. That's kind of annoying, especially since you're likely to never go back to that chest anyway. Just another example of them trying to fix something that wasn't broken.Chickens in this game will no longer attack you in swarms for stabbing at them, instead if you hit a chicken enough times you can actually take control of it for a few seconds. This serves no purpose and they spent time changing a feature that really didn't matter to begin with. Instead now it's the goats who will ram right into you as retaliation for you attacking them. I guess Nintendo's always tried to discourage animal abuse in their video games, except Pokémon.In conclusion, this game is somewhat descent, but nowhere near as good as previous Zelda titles. Including WindWaker, which was far better. It's not a must have by any means and not very memorable. There was way too much anticipation for this game in the months preceding its release; I and many other long time Zelda fans expected much better than what we got. This game should've been released way earlier than December 2006. Nintendo could've easily made this game one of the first 50 GameCube launch titles but instead it was the very last game to be released for the console. Not to mention, we had to wait until a month after the release of the Wii version to finally play this on our GameCubes, even though they initially told us both versions would be released that same month of November. It wasn't that special when it came out and although the graphics and sound are quite good, it should've and easily could've been one of the first games to be released for the GameCube.

This particular Tomb Raider story finds Lara Croft jumping around Peruvian mountaintops, cliffs and ravines -- swinging from her trademarked horizontal poles and grappling ropes, and shooting it out with many, many soldiers.  The gunplay is much easier than that found in TR 2013 (Indeed, the gunplay in ANY TR game prior to the 2013 release is easy), but the grappling was a bit "glitchy," although it worked.Two of the most difficult battles I have played in the TR series are found here -- one in Japan -- and the very last one in the game, the battle with "The Amanda Beast."  This last battle was the most difficult battle in all of the TR games, including Lara's battle with the ONI WARRIOR GIANT (and company!) in TR 2013.  The very long motorcycle battle and lightning-fast episode in the Khazakstan section was tiring, if only because it went on and on and on.The graphics and voice-overs were excellent and Lara's costumes were, to say the least, fetching.Some complain that this version of TOMB RAIDER was too short!  What do they want?  There were several subdivided localesof interest here:  Peru, Bolivia, Ghana, Japan, Khazakstan, Nepal, Croft Manor, and finally, more Bolivia, and, except for Croft Manor, the player spends considerable time in all of the other locales, including the final area (And don't go telling me that you killed the AMANDA BEAST in 5 minutes, because I won't believe you!).And so, because of the sheer excitement involved with Lara's dangerous adventures in all of these beautiful countries, replete with Buddhist monasteries, ice caves, shelves, slides, and mountains, not to mention Japanese skyscrapers, fast-moving railroad trains, and man-eating tigers, leopards, and snow leopards, I gave this beautiful game 5 stars because it deserves it!  And IT IS NOT SHORT!  I could see NO DIFFERENCE in length between this game and TR UNDERWORLD, or between this game and TR 2013.

Vampires and Cowboys, who would've thought? Apparently someone did and that was High Moon Studios. So Darkwatch takes place in Arizona 1876, Jericho a lone riding outlaw is about to get out of his life for good and its only one last train robbery away. Thats until shenanigans happen. That last train by chance belonged to a secret organization, the Darkwatch, who are vampire hunters. Also this train that Jericho just hijacked also carries a powerful vampire lord who he senselessly set free. Now Arizona is overrun with the undead. Towns and Indian villages are wiped out by legions of the damned. And Jericho is stricken with vampirism with all it's perks and downsides. So now the adventure begins after joining the Darkwatch, now Jericho is out to kill the vampire lord and try to fix everything. Aiding him is the ghost of a cowgirl and a deadly Native American seductress.Essentially it feels a lot like Halo. You carry only two weapons at a time, you have another health bar that regenerates on top of the one that doesn't, you can toss grenades without switching weapons, and it has some segments with a vehicle that while it worked for Halo they feel shoehorned in this one and don't handle as well. Since Jericho is a vampire he can also jump higher, absorbs blood, and can unlock abilities throughout the game. Which brings up the morality meter. You've got two of them and which ever one you fill up with bad deeds or good ones you can unlock a new ability to give you an edge in combat. Good deeds are essentially things like setting souls free and healing the wounded. While bad deeds usually involve snacking on whomever comes up to you looking for help. Bad deeds can be entertaining but seeing Jericho gnaw on the neck of some poor lass can loose it's novelty. Whichever side you choose, both skill trees seem to balance out quite well. These abilities work pretty good in terrible situations like the ability to be impervious to damage for a small amount of time to more elaborate things like temporarily having your enemies fight each other.Enemies pretty much follow your usual FPS format from the time. You've got your canon fodder enemies who's only purpose is to be taken down effortlessly. Then you have your superpower bullet magnet enemies who require clips of ammo before they finally kill over. A lot of attention was paid to design and I couldn't help but admire how nice (in a monster lovers view) the enemies looked even the canon fodder ones. Action can become quite fun if not hectic as you jump above the shootout firing at enemies and use your powers. Level design though can leave much to be desired and feels claustrophobic. Just about all of them look the same. Canyons is what you'll see most of the time with a few gray colored towns and mine shafts sprinkled in. There are parts with platforming which is always a pain to do in FPS games. While Jericho's vampire double jump is a nice touch in combat its pretty bad for this type of game play. Once in midair he just seems to kind of glide and you'll never really be certain where you'll land.Visually the game is actually pretty nice looking if you can get over the linear level design. Enemies look awesome, the horror punk western imagery is very nice, sound effects are top notch with guns blaring loudly and the call of vampires nerve racking. It was fun, and in the end that's all you should look for in old cult classics like this. Darkwatch wasn't a bad game, it was actually good and I'd definitely prefer it over most the AAA FPS games that are piling onto shelves now. It still has it's issues though and what it has done other games have done better. Still with it's western-horror imagery and vampire mechanics to game-play I doubt you'd find another game like it.

When the Nintendo Wii first came out, it was so popular that for the first few months you would be hard pressed to find a single one on any store shelf anywhere. As of January 2014 over 100 million units have been sold worldwide. That's almost 1 Wii per every 3 people in the US. Why was the Wii so popular? The answer is simple. The Wii appeals to everyone. Most of all, the Wii appeals to families. Their entire marketing scheme was based around the fact that the Wii is fun for the whole family and easy to use by all. Some of the ads even had grandma's playing the game console!The biggest negative point, and my only con, of this console was that it was being released in the HD era but not in HD, right before the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360, both of which ran games in HD while the PS3 even had a Blu-ray drive. Therefore, the consoles resolution and frame rate would not be able to exceed 480p and 60 fps and it plays neither Blu-Rays nor DVDs but does offer video streaming services such as Netflix. Perhaps the Wii's best and most appealing feature is it's motion sensing technology. Being able to use the Wii remote as a baseball bat or tennis racket gives you a feeling that you are actually IN the game, no other console offered anything like this at the time. Nintendo's evolution from the standard candy bar style controller from the NES and SNES days to the Nintendo 64 and Gamecube controllers took a step back to the simpler build and it worked perfectly. This design allows games to be played on the Wii remote by pointing the remote at the screen, or simply turning it sideways. There is also several accessories that can be used in conjunction with the Wii remote such as the nunchuck, which has a separate analog stick and can be held in one hand while the remote is held in the other, and even a Classic Controller, which much resembles that of the Super Nintendo.The console is quite easy to set up, the sound the Wii produces is decent but it is certainly feels like it is held back by it's lack of High-definition support. The user interface is incredibly easy to use, all you do is point and click, similar to using a computer and mouse.The Wii offered lots of Nintendo's great, classic gaming characters in fun games but it felt like something was missing. It wasn't until the Wii U was released that it became apparent that what was missing was the upgrade in resolution. The best thing about the original Wii by far was that it opened the door for family gaming, easily allowing anyone to pick up a remote and join in on a game.

Project Revolution. That was the title given to the Wii before "Wii" was revealed to a mocking world. But it would leave other consoles of that generation in the dust sales-wise (though I love my PS3 to death). The controls would be considered revolutionary, but we all know that when the console released they weren't exactly what we thought they'd be. The MotionPlus rectified the issue, but few games of merit utilized the feature.Upon release, it was seen as a party machine, a new form of the karaoke machine, if you will. Many members of my extended family had one, and plenty of friends had one too. My first experiences with the Wii as a gaming machine rather than a party machine were from a roommate's loaner. Because the Wii was backwards compatible with GCN discs, I got to play the NES Zelda and Ocarina of Time to completion for the first time (thanks to the Collector's Edition). Galaxy was the first title on the Wii I played in full, and it took my breath away. I was hooked.Of course, like many, I was confused as all heck when I found out the remote didn't generate 1:1 accuracy, especially when I played the Wii version of Twilight Princess for the first time, but I got on just fine. In fact, most of the games I played I ended up using another controller, like the GameCube or Classic Controller (and Pro when it was released). Only for games that required it, like both Galaxys, did I use the remote and nunchuk combination.At that time, I was a senior in undergrad, and the years prior I never let my gaming interfere with my education. But the Wii and DS destroyed that rule. After graduation, because I couldn't get a full-time job right away, I had to settle and wait for a while before buying my own console. It's funny, though, as I already owned Twilight Princess (Wii version) and Brawl for quite some time.Finally, my sister realized she wanted to get one too and we split the cost in July of 2008. This was when the Wii, over a year after its release, was still pretty popular and hard to find. We had to call our local Target almost every morning for two weeks before we landed one. I was eager to get one as I never really owned a Nintendo console as a kid, having only a hand-me-down NES which rarely worked. I was impatient to play all the Ninty games I missed out on.It's a fantastic system with a buffet of a library able to satiate any gamer's fancy. The gamer like me? There's Zelda, Metroid, and even the "kiddy" games like Mario. It's because of the Wii and its backward-capabilities that I'm a huge Mario/Nintendo fan, and Zelda has become one of my favorite game series--alongside Final Fantasy (pre-XII). Also, when I purchased it, I still lived at home and my kid sister and I had a blast playing games together. In fact, she's currently borrowing it right now and plays hours on end of Mario Kart and Wii Sports.One would think that with the Wii U available it may be a bit hard to sell the Wii, but that'd be wrong. The Wii is still priced competitively, and is probably the biggest bang for your buck if you want to play first-party titles. I have a setup of the Wii and PS3 and couldn't be happier.Of course, even from its launch, the Wii isn't known for its powerful graphics. Blame the hardware limitations; even if you get component cables it won't look that much better. In fact, on a flat screen LED or LCD TV it looks actually *worse* with component cables because there's so much jaggedness. I remember plugging in component cables for the first time on my new (at the time) Toshiba LCD and was appalled when playing New Super Mario Bros. Wii. I had upgraded my tube from an old 32" CRT Zenith and the Wii looked better on that with composite cables. But you always can go the way of the Dolphin.So, in 2014, is getting the Wii worth it? It depends; how caught up are you with Nintendo games? Sure, you can get a Wii U, but there aren't as many games on it as there are on the Wii if you get just the older, cheaper console, especially if you get the older GCN-compatible model. I invested heavily in peripherals, so that made my gaming experience much more enjoyable and competitive.I used the white GameCube controller and WaveBird for Brawl and Mario Kart, as well of course for any GameCube titles. For the Virtual Console I used primarily the Classic Controller and its variant the Pro, and I imported the Club Nintendo of Japan Super Famicom controller for the Wii. For fighting games and arcade titles that used a digital signal rather than analog (e.g., Tatsunoko vs. Capcom), I used Hori's arcade stick. So my experience may or may not differ from yours.Even today I think it's worth getting. There's at least ten solid titles for any kind of gamer. Sure, there aren't many M-rated games on the platform, but that's not why I got it. I consider myself a gamer whose sole intention is to enjoy every and all kinds of games available; I'm not a fanboy of any brand, and am open to try any games from the `70s and `80s to today. That's why I got a Nintendo console: to play all the games available on it that I missed in the years they were released. I can enjoy arcade and NES titles as well as the limited number of N64 emulated classics (I say "emulated" because it's not the same thing as playing on the good ol' N64). I have a 3DS now and play that more often than the Wii, but I still have a number of games I haven't completed to which I plan on returning; once those are out of the way, the Wii U will be my next purchase.Thus ends my review. I guess this isn't as much a review as it is a catalog of my experiences with the console the past half-decade, but I couldn't write it any other way.

As the reviewer below me has stated, the downloadable version of this game has no Starforce DRM protection, so feel free to get it if you had concerns in the past about it affecting your computer.I originally bought this game for my Xbox in 2006 and decided to get it again for my PC for nostalgia's-sake.  I can see how it was revolutionary at the time with the lack of onscreen prompts such as ammunition counts and a health bar, using only visual and audio cues to get your bearings.  Playing as the King himself was an added bonus and his levels occupy about a third of the game.Unfortunately, by today's standards, the game has not aged very well. There are 39 chapters in the game, and they last anywhere from 2-20 minutes.  Some don't even involve any gameplay.  Just walking from one point to another.  The Kong levels are the highlight, and there aren't enough of them.  It's fun to bash T-Rexes or giant worms, though the camera can be a problem as it's sometimes fixed which sometimes makes you lose perspective while in combat.For those that have Windows 7 and above, try running the game in compatibility mode under the operating system of Windows XP and you should be able to play the game.  After messing with the graphics options through my graphics card, I was able to play the game with hardly any graphical hiccups.For nostalgia's sake, this game came through for me.  If you can get past the dated mechanics and visuals, there is a decent to good game here.

i picked this game up about five years ago as i was checking out what the DS had to offer. i got to about mission 20 when the slow climb of progress i was making through this game ground to a halt. i began noticing also that single levels were consuming entire days and decided it was best to put this game aside for a while...five years later, a friend of mine is starting to get into DS games since they're so cheap now and i decided to give this another shot. it took me a week or so but i was finally able to beat the game's remaining eight missions. i'm glad i gave this game another shot and will most likely check out the other advance wars titles for the DS or maybe even GBA. here's some of my main impressions of the game:countless options! and i don't mean just what type of armed forces you use, which could be anything from soldier to aircraft carrier (and everything in between). but also commanding officers, COs, that each have their own unique strengths and weaknesses that you can develop. this theme has major pros and cons of course. having tons of options is certainly entertaining. "do i use a neotank or a megatank to destroy this lowly enemy reconnaissance unit?" but having too many options can also be paralyzing. "should i recruit more soldiers first or just start off with a rocket launcher?" the game grades you on a myriad of criterion, one of which being speed, so developing a long and slowly unfolding strategy on the battlefield may not always be an option.going back to the COs, by the time you're well into the game, you'll be commanding a couple or sometimes even three armies at once. luckily the game has no shortage of commanding officers. it seemed like every one of the earlier missions, i kept recruiting a new one. and eventually i found some that just kinda popped up on my roster. each one has their own strengths and weaknesses which is cool. they'll even try to hint if you made a good choice from the dialogue preempting the battle. the downside is that there are so many playable characters, that you're spread too thin and have to focus on a smaller pool to develop talent. otherwise you end up with a large group of mediocre COs, instead of 5 or 6 nicely ranked ones.the second theme i want to touch on is this games difficulty. the battles can be tough to get an S rank, due to the time issue. but also, the tide of the battle can very easily turn and change a decisive victory into a nail-bitter. each step in the battle execution is important and i had to sometimes replay entire levels and tweak placement, attacks, etc; in order to get S ranks.lastly, despite being difficult and sometimes having too many options for its own good, this game is tons of fun. it is often ranked highly on lists of 'best ds games of all time'. most other strategy RPGs like fire emblem or final fantasy tactics do not have the modern day story-line setting of the advance wars series, which i find to be refreshing. if you have an open mind about gaming, it's worth checking out, even in 2014. the 3DS would be wise to add an advance wars title to its catalog.
