I bought this game because it was $5 at my game store. I had heard that the 3D Castlevania games suck so I was a bit worried. I checked the amazon ps2 ratings for the game when I got home and was even more worried. Many people did not like the game or said it was mediocre. I put the game in my Xbox and then started it. I noticed the graphics were fair, but not that impressive. The controls felt pretty nice as well. I had no problems with the camera either, other than the inverted turning controls. I went into the Castle and noticed it was set up like a corridor, with walls shielding the left and right. At first I was afraid the game would be linear. Linear games are good, but they tend to be short and I was looking for a more open game. I got to a point where I saw two paths. I took the path on the right and it only went to a couple of rooms and then to a locked door. I went the other direction and it was a straight foreward path. I then played about 20 minutes and got to the end of the path on the left. I found an item in a treasure chest that I brought back to the locked door on the right path. I used the item and the door opened, accessing me to a new area. I actually liked backtracking because it gave the game a metroidvania feel. I continued down the new area and found a point where there were 3 paths to choose from. I chose one path and noticed it wouldn't end. I thought there was one main path and that the other rooms lead to small rooms with a special item or something. I backtracked to the point where the 3 paths were and tried another path. This path wouldn't end either. I then tried the third path and that wouldn't end. I took the 2nd path and ventured forward. The path just kept going and going. I got to a point where there were 2 paths to choose from when I was on the third path for a while. I kept having to choose between multiple paths, where to go. The one path I took lead me to other paths and eventually a boss fight. I haven't even explored the first and third path from beginning of the game that much. That means those three paths would all keep going and breaking up into new paths and then break up into even more paths. After I took the boss down that I got to from the 2nd path in thr beginning, yet another passage opened up. I finally realized what the game is at this point. It's a 3D metroidvania game! I always thought that metroidvania was only for 2D games, but this game pulls it off and does a damn good job of it too. This game is metroidvania to the core. It has lots of paths and routes to take and it has lots of backtracking to older areas, to access new areas or chests with an aquired item. For that reason, I am absolutely loving this game. This game and Metroid Prime prove that metroidvania works with 3D games too. It really is quite innovative. Other than those awesome aspects, the combat is hack and slash gameplay with simple button combos. It works well and combat is pretty fast. The level design is pretty much just paths with a skin over them, but it never really bothered me. At new areas, the skin would have a different them and it kept the game from looking boring or repetive. The enemies are a little repetive and are reused a bit too often, but in many areas there are new enemies to face. Overall the enemies are pretty varied and they all look awesome with their supernatural themes. The story so far is pretty good. It seems like a revenge story, but that's ok. The story is good enough to keep you interested and get you through the game. The music is fantastic and just very catchy. It changes enough that songs don't become repetitive. There are a pretty descent amount of songs overall and they all sound great. Combat is on the easy side, but that's perfectly fine with me because it means I can actually beat the game. (I have enough hard games that I can't beat). Save points are frequent and enemies go down pretty easily. The game is also an RPG, in that you level up and craft items. It also takes a note out of the Shin Megami Tensei games by giving you familiars to summon. Familiars are like the demons in SMT games, or like Pokemon, There are many demons to collect, use, and level up. They are a nice addition to the game because they help you out immensely and add variety to the gameplay. The voice acting in this game is, like everything else, very good. The characters are believable and pretty engaging. Hectar himself is a good character and he is pretty likeable. The only small flaw I had with this game was it's plain level design. There is no platforming at all here. It's just paths on level ground. This really isn't a big deal though, because the game is a lot of fun, and exploring is fun and rewarding. The other small issue I have is the story is a little underwhelming, but it's still good enough to keep me going and keep my interest. The game will take about 15-18 hours to complete, according to www.howlongtobeat.com so it's not that long, but it's not ridiculously short like some other games are. I would have liked the game to be 20-40 hours, but it's not that big of a deal. Overall I bought this game not expecting much and I was pleasantly surprised by it. It just absolutely surpassed my expectations and blew me away. It's a fantastic 3D metroidvania Castlevania, and as a fan of Symphony of the Night for ps1 and Portrait of Ruin for DS, I can say that this a great Castlevania game, even though it's 3D. 3D Castlevania does work, and this game shows that in spades. It's dirt cheap right now and severely underrated and overhated for no reason. It's far better than Castlevania 64 and definitely one of the, if not the best, 3D Castlevania game ever made. I'd even say it's one of my favorite Castlevania games of all time, out of all the games, This game is a gem and it should not be passed up. Get this and also get Castlevania Legacy of Darkness on n64. Nobody bought it because Castlevania 64 was a dissapointment. Legacy of Darkness, it's sequel, is actually excellent and much better than Castlevania 64. It too is one of the best 3D Castlevania games. Sadly that game sold poorly, and is now in demand because people started realizing how great the game is. It now goes for $35. Curse of Darkness is only $5 so get it while it's cheap. I just can't believe how great this game turned out to be.

Your health does not regenerate in any way, meaning that you'll have to manually search for health packs to heal yourself from enemy damage.  If you get surrounded by lots of enemies, you'll most likely die, as they do loads of damage and are extremely accurate, especially on the hardest difficulty.  This game is for those who actually want a challenge, and who desire a WWII shooter that truly breaks the mold.

If you are a longtime gamer like myself, then you were probably exposed to certain franchises like Super Mario Bros, The Legend Of Zelda, or Metroid.  But the real meat here is the Mega Man series.  One sequel and spinoff after another, Capcom drew zillions of fans to play each title for nonstop hours.I love that the Mega Man X series is included in one package.  It's Mega Man X through X3 for the Super NES, plus X4 through X6 which was originally released on the PlayStation.  And not to worry, people -- the atrocious controls that you saw on Mega Man Anniversary Collection have been corrected here.  The fire/jump buttons are EXACTLY where they are supposed to be!!I haven't beaten all 6 games yet.  However, I will briefly talk about the series.  The overall storyline has to do with Mavericks, a brand new ally named Zero, and a brand new headache by the name of Sigma.  (No Dr. Wily here, folks!)  And just like Mega Man 1 through 6, you will select 8 bosses to battle in non-linear fashion.  But that's not before starting the "prologue" stage and fighting a mini-boss.  So after you've creamed each robot boss, you will have to go through 4 more stages before facing that dishonorable, love-to-hate Sigma!  And yes, he is MUCH more difficult than Dr. Wily!  :)With Mega Man X4 through X6, the graphics, soundtrack and background schemes were vastly changed, thanks to the PlayStation.  And each stage is divided into 2 sections, so players certainly won't get bored anytime soon!However, what deeply saddens me is that Mega Man X7 and X8 were gravely omitted from this set.  I truly wish that the designers had included both titles -- even if that meant using a second bonus disc to cram all that content inside!  But oh well, I'll take what I can get.  It is up to me to get a PlayStation of my own if I want to burst through X7 and X8 ha ha.  Now, please be sure to check out the other Mega Man series -- Mega Man Zero, Mega Man Battle Network, Mega Man Star Force, and Mega Man ZX -- it's all too numerous to mention!

I LOVE this game. It is so fun. I have seen many poor reviews based on the fact that it is not like the PC game... They ARE completely different, but Sims 2 for PS2 has a story line unlike the PC version where you are free to do basically whatever you want. In the Sims 2 for PS2 you will find yourself progressing to new exciting areas with different objects, and more sims you can interact with. It is a lot of fun, but I would NOT recommend this to anyone looking for a game identical to the PC version. If you love adventure games, then this is definitely a game for you. I am a sims fanatic, and I also love this game despite the many differences between this game and the PC game.You create a sim(the options are almost endless, and you can unlock more by completing certain tasks inside of the game.) Your sim will live with different room mates from time to time, and you will have goals and objectives that you will need to complete to get to a new location. If you wish to do so, you can stay in a certain home if you wish, but you won't be able to unlock new locations or progress through the story. Each house has its own problem or purpose for having you there, and some locations are more challenging than others. You will always be able to travel back and forth between houses at any point in the game. You will find yourself in the country side, a cliff side retreat, a cruise boat, and even a movie set. The controllers you use are the analog stick and the x, square, circle, and triangle button. However this can be changed by hitting the select button.Some similarities with this game and the PC game is that you get to create a sim with a bunch of different options. You will also get to interact with other sims, get married, and have jobs. In free play, you will be able to have a family and I have not experimented much with free play so I am not sure if you can actually have children or how big the capacity is for the family.Some differences include not being able to get pregnant. You also are only able to use 1 sim in story mode unless you have more than 1 person playing the game with you(however you will be able to play as different sims depending on the location you are at.) The controls are also different, but again you can always change this. There aren't any expansions packs of course either. And you will not be able to go to "community lots". All of the lots in this game are residential. You also can not take pictures/videos and send them to your computer. Custom content does not work with this game but again that should be obvious.This game has a lot of replay value. I have never been able to defeat it because it takes SO long, but I always find myself wanting to start over and I never feel like I am playing the same game twice.

Smackdown vs Raw 2006 was the second installment in the Smackdown vs Raw series and probably the best one of the entire Smackdown vs Raw series for a number of reasonsWe'll start with graphics first. There's not much to complain about with the superstar graphics. The muscles and skin tone were on par as were the attires for. The hair for some of the superstars looks a little funky but it's completely forgivable.2 new match types debuted with the first being the Buried Alive Match. Really it should've been called a Casket Match instead of Buried Alive because all this match consists of is you trying to stuff your opponent into a casket, close the lid, and have a loader pour a fair amount of dirt over the casket. No graves or anything like that.The second new match is the Fulfill Your Fantasy match, replacing the Bra & Panties match. This match is much more fun than the Bra & Panties match as there're more things you can do in the match. First, you can choose between 3 different attires for the divas to wear of either a schoolgirl outfit, a nurse, or a French maid. The ring is decked out with a large fluffy bed in the middle of it, beside 2 chairs holding pillows. There are 3 humiliating ways to defeat your diva opponent: spanking, ripping off her clothes, or knocking her out with a pillow. There's a meter in the match that must be filled to win the match. So say Joy Giovanni spanks Michelle McCool or Stacy spanks Trish. Each spank given will fill the meter with a great portion. The same goes for pillow strikes and ripping off their clothes. There's a post-match cutscene for which way you win. If you win via pillow strikes, a cutscene is shown of you knocking your opponent out with a pillow. If you win by spanking, your player is shown putting the loser over her knee and and spanking her with a paddle. Great and fun match to play. Unfortunately this was the only game it was in. This was also the last game to feature in diva based matchBackstage Brawls were updated as well and split into 3 different ares. You could fight either backstage, in a bar, or in the parking lot. All 3 areas are fun to play in and feature tons of interactive features. In the bar, you can make a pool player shoot a ball into your opponent's head. In the backstage area, you can steal a soda from a backstage worker, slam them through a table or even hit them with weapons! This was a really great update that made the match more enjoyable to play, unlike the previous year'sSeason Mode was also a fun one to play in. Better than Smackdown vs Raws and the character you play as, gets a voice-over! If you choose to go on Smackdown for the season, you'll spend the year trying to solve the mystery of who ran down Smackdown GM, Teddy Long in the parking garage. Depending on what superstar you play as, there are 2 routes the ending of that story takes. In the middle of it all, you'll go on a Legends Tour, try to free Torrie Wilson from the evil clutches of JBL and his cabinet, and even do battle with The Undertaker who's been controlled by Eddie Guerrero. If you decide to fight on Raw, you'll form a friendship with Shelton Benjamin to take out Triple H and Ric Flair, go on a Legends Tour, win titles only to have Eric Bischoff take them from you and vacate them, and so much more! There are plenty of different stories you can play throughout the year with a great dose of added realism and it'll all end with you fighting for the company's top prize at Wrestlemania 21. LOVE this Season Mode!In addition to Season Mode there was also the new General Manager Mode that puts you in charge. Take the role of either Raw GM or Smackdown GM, form your roster, and run the show starting at Backlash and ending at Wrestlemania! GM Mode is not only about fun but about responsibilities as well. For 1 whole year you must fight to keep a well-balanced crowd and your audience entertained as you'll be battling with the opposing brand. You must balance your budget, book matches responsively, and keep your superstars happy. If a superstar becomes unhappy with you due to either being left off the show or something, they'll let you know. If a superstar gets minorly injured, it's best to keep them out of action before they become severely injured and are forced to be out of action. As mentioned, it's best to balance your budget because you'll have to renew your superstar's contracts as they expire. The last thing you want is to end up with a show of only 5 or 6 superstars. Throughout the week, you'll receive emails from J.R. to guide you through the year, the income salary, the ratings number, and more. To add drama to the mode, you can start rivalries between 2 superstars, send a superstar to the other show to cause trouble, and slander the opposing show. The show with the most popularity at the end of the season, wins a GM of the Year Trophy. Great mode that teaches the player fun and responsibilityThe roster was decently sized. Superstars and divas making their debuts included Orlando Jordan, Joy Giovanni, Muhammad Hassan, Michelle McCool, Carlito, Paul London, Sylvan Grenier, Christy Hemme, Eugene and others. There were also a fair amount of legends in the game as well. All 3 faces of Hulk Hogan were in the game (80s, NWO, and Modern), Andre the Giant, British Bulldog, Stone Cold Steve Austin, Mankind, The Rock, Bret Hart, Masked Kane, Junkyard Dog, and Ted Dibiase.3 other new features in the game were the sleeper hold system, the possum pin, and the stamina system. How the sleeper hold system works is, once your opponent's head turns yellow, lock them in a sleeper hold (sitting or standing will do) where they will pass out in the hold. Once locked into the hold, the CPU or human opponent will have three attempts to escape the submission hold or perform a reversal in a desperate attempt to turn the tables on the attacker. If the player should fail to escape from the hold before the referee reaches a final count of three, the match will be lost by KO. The possum pin works by storing a finisher. If you've been beat down enough, when your superstar goes to attack you, press the L1 and L2 buttons to initiate the possum pin where you'll surprise them with a roll up. The stamina system involves the amount of energy you and your opponent have. If you run too much, you'll lose stamina. If during a match, both you and your opponent run out of energy, you'll both fall to the mat, where the referee will start a count. You both have to the count of 10 to get back up or the match goes to a DrawOverall: Sorry for the long review, but this game was too great to not go into every nook and cranny about it. This is definitely one overlooked gem that deserves more attention than it received, and while I loved Tales of the Abyss, this game has some very neat quirks of its own. This game has Dreamcast style visuals, which I actually completely welcome, because I grew up with the Dreamcast, in fact, that was I was introduced to RPGs, as my first one was pretty much Evolution, and I also played the PS2 port of Grandia II. If you want a game that lifts you off of the real world, it will be this one! The soundtrack of this game fits with its perspective locations and is beautiful. Grinding is great in this game as it does not take that long to level up, and the in-battle controls do not take that long to grasp, and the story is very entertaining with events that naturally correspond with the storyline. This game easily has some of the most beautiful fantasy environments I have ever seen, and the characters are completely full with personality, and they change quite a bit throughout the course of the game. I'd wager that probably one of the complaints of this game that I could see that others may have could be the combat style. I personally don't mind the Soul Caliber style combat, it is just different, and it certainly does not subtract from the overall gaming experience. With that being said, I highly recommend this to anyone who is looking for a decent PS2 RPG!

While not the most comfortable Game Boy for an adult to hold, the SP AGS-101 (brighter back screen) is probably the best all-around Game Boy. While I prefer the DS for GBA games, the SP is able to play most, if not all, games from the Game Boy to the Color to the Advance, all on an amazingly bright screen.The Micro is another great alterative for GBA games, but sadly those play GBA games only, no GB or GBC fun to be had.That said, I guess it would be best for me to start off with what I don't like about the brighter GBA SP.For one, like I mentioned, it's not very comfortable to hold if you're an adult. I've even gotten a grip for it, but, while it does make it far more comfortable to hold, the grip has an awful lock-on mechanism that scratches the GBA every time I want to remove it. Not a big bother for me, as I changed the housing of my SP anyway (a mixture of black and cobalt, if anyone's interested).Without the grip, my hands become cramped as my palms try to rest against the sides of the Game Boy while my fingers are arched uncomfortably to the proximally close buttons. This isn't such a big issue with other models like the DMG or the original Advance, or even the DS if you're playing GBA games on it, since they're a bit bigger and allow your palms and unused fingers more room to grip the machine.I'm not a fan of the buttons either. Because they're recessed, they don't protrude out as much for thumbs to find them easily. When I changed the housing of mine, I actually thought I messed up and put the motherboard on too loosely, thus having the buttons recessed even more. So I retightened the motherboard and tried again and realized the buttons were the same. I found out that's how they were, and wondered why they didn't bug me before. But they do now, especially now that I've played excessively with older Game Boys and with my DS and 3DS (the 3DS XL has the best d-pad, in my opinion).So because they're recessed, they don't travel far to trigger, which is something I don't like. It's not a bad thing; it's just my preference. They're kind of "squishy," if that makes sense.The shoulder buttons are fine.The sound is decent. To use headphones you'd have to get an adapter, and sometimes you can hear a buzzing sound.In terms of Game Boy gaming quality, you can't get any better. There are clones that come near with the dimensions of Game Boys and Game Boy Colors, but nothing beats original Nintendo hardware. Granted, the SP isn't made out of Nintendium, but it's great in its own right, and possibly the best unmodded Game Boy, not to mention the penultimate model to carry the GB name.Like I said, out of playability it's the best Game Boy without any modification. Of course, you can get the original GBA modded with a backlit screen, and I'd probably say that would be best. There are some people who've modded original DMGs with backlit screens, and some even with shoulder buttons, but those seem to be much more work than what it's worth.Function-wise it's not the best design for bigger hands, but that's to be expected. The clamshell is a wonderful design choice from Nintendo that makes the portable gaming device even more compact and helps protect the screen and buttons, something we haven't seen since some of the Game & Watch games.Should this be in your handheld collection? Absolutely. Be sure to get the AGS-101 model, and then you can gut it and put on a custom shell at your leisure. I love the way mine looks, and I sometimes take it out of the case just to admire it.

Prey starts out looking like it's going to be a normal FPS where aliens invade Earth and start harvesting people.  Been there, done that, I know.  Fortunately, it quickly becomes a very unique story with great gameplay additions that make it different enough to really enjoy it.  It's a bit hard to explain why it's different but if you love these types of games you owe it to yourself to check it out.  It does have a pretty dark story with plenty of bad language and some partial nudity so I wouldn't recommend this for kids.  Hints the Mature rating.  The graphics are decent, especially for 2006 standards.  It's about like Doom 3.  I believe the developers even used the Doom 3 engine.  The gameplay is smooth and I had no issues with framerate or screen tearing.  You can save pretty much anywhere and it also autosaves.  The length of the game is about what you'd expect from this type of game so figure it'll just take a lazy weekend to finish it.  It moves quick and doesn't ever bore you with unnecessary cutscenes, etc.  Even the few missions where you learn a little bit about your Indian heritage, and so on, don't last long or drag.  Overall, I highly recommend this for any Sci-Fi/Horror FPS fans.

You have your visibility meter, your sound meter, your night and thermal-vision goggles, and the more organized set-up of cutscenes and levels. "Super Princess Peach" is a fairly traditional 2D platformer while also being quite unique. It's side-scrolling, each world has its own theme (snow, etc.), levels are divided into several sections, and it has the feel one expects from a "Super Mario" game. What's unique is Princess Peach herself. As far as I know this is her first solo adventure away from bros. Mario and Luigi (requiring her rescue for a change). Peach has a number of interesting abilities at her disposal. She can access four different "emotions" at any time: joy, gloom, rage and calm. Using Joy allows her to turn into a cyclone or fly, while gloom makes her cry uncontrollably, creating interesting puzzles around the use of water. Using an emotion drains the "mood bar" that can later be refilled. Peach also has a trusty side-kick in the form of Perry, a talking yellow umbrella that she uses as a weapon, and who suffers from some decidedly strange dreams after each boss encounter. Who's this mysterious figure occupying his dreams? Why does an umbrella dream at all? Who knows. Perry also gives Peach the ability to glide after jumps, reminding me a bit of "Yoshi's Island." Peach's use of emotions might have seemed odd in any other game, but here they add a kind of charm that fits well with everything else. I found "Super Princess Peach" overall to be surprisingly enjoyable.--- 4 STARS ---

Just to clear up confusion, this title is actually a graphically upgraded combination of two separate games that previously came out for the original Xbox: "Far Cry Instincts" and "Far Cry Instincts: Evolution."  Both of those titles were created in response to the first official Far Cry being PC-only, so that console gamers could have a similar experience.  Both of them have been combined here onto one disc under the title "Far Cry Instincts: Predator," and for someone who has never played the previous two games, this is obviously the best option.  The downside is that the FCI camapign must be completed first before the Evolution campaign can be unlocked.  However, it offers loads of fun content, and is well worth the money spent.FCIP is not a direct port of the original PC-exclusive version.  Rather, it is more of a re-imagining, with some elements that have been changed, added, or excluded, but the overall feel of the original is still there.  For instance, rather than having a blade take up one weapon slot in the original, FCIP has a permanent blade that you can use at any time to perform stealth kills and melee attacks with, which frees you up to experiment with better weapons.  Also, in contrast to the MP5 being the only suppressed weapon in the original, FCIP has suppressed pistols and sniper rifles for short and long range respectively.  Finally, unlike the original, FCIP allows you to dual-wield many weapons, which definitely helps for providing extended firepower during intense, tight firefights.  Sadly, though, FCIP is more linear than the original, and the overall quality of FCIP's graphics doesn't quite measure up to the original's vast, clear draw distances.The biggest difference, however, is FCIP's introduction of feral powers.  Early on in the game, you actually get injected with the mutagen serum that Dr. Krieger was testing on the Trigens, and you acquire a whole mess of animalistic powers, ranging from an instant-kill melee attack, to running extremely fast, jumping massive distances, tracking enemies using their scent, and even regenerating health.  It's by far the one feature that elevates FCIP far above the original.  It honestly never gets old running and jumping through the environments at blinding speeds, tracking enemies and then sending them flying with one massive punch.  It almost makes using normal weapons completely obsolete.  You have an adrenaline meter that decreases every time you use an ability.  It regenerates over time, but you can gain boosts by eating MRIs, killing enemies, or taking damage.  This combination of normal and supernatural abilities is extremely similar to the original Xbox game "Breakdown," and the mechanics work pretty much the same way.The hardest difficulty in FCIP is much easier overall than the original, mostly thanks to your feral ability to regenerate health.  However, for the first three levels of the game, you're a completely normal person, so stealth is obviously much more valuable.  To this end, you're able to perform silent kills with your knife, throw rocks to distract enemies, crouch and go prone to hide in the dense vegetation, rig whipping tree branch traps, and use suppressed weapons.  The only way to acquire health and added protection during this time is to find and pick up medkits and bulletproof vests, which can be in pretty short supply.  There's also many vehicles you can drive to travel much faster and avoid unnecessary combat.  At the start of the fourth level, from then on, things only become easier.  It's too bad the original PC version didn't incorporate this element, as that would've been the icing on the cake of an already amazing game.  There's one catch, however: you don't gain all the feral abilities at once.  They're slowly given to you as you progress further through the game.  This means that you still have to be sneaky and strategic to avoid being overpowered.  It adds a nicely scaled challenge without making the game too easy.The graphics of FCIP, like I said earlier, have been improved from the original Xbox versions, but don't quite match the overall quality of the PC version.  Still, FCIP boasts a large number of diverse environments, from bright sandy beaches, to thick overgrown jungles, to underground research labs and even inside a glowing volcano.  The physics still have the same level of high interactivity that the PC version had, the best part of which is sending mercenaries flying and flipping through the air with your powerful feral punch.  The voice acting is actually better than the PC version and doesn't sound quite as detached or cheesy.  Also, the environmental ambience is perfect, from the water breaking against the beach, to the leaves rustling in the jungle, to various animal noises all around.The "Evolution" part of FCIP is basically just an expansion pack, as it plays exactly the same as FCI, complete with all your feral powers from the part, and doesn't last nearly as long.  The only difference is that the graphics are slightly better, and the levels feel more open-ended overall.  However, this time, you face warriors that have the same feral powers as you, which levels the playing field and makes battles tougher and more strategic than fighting normal mercenaries.Overall, I have to say that I still prefer the original Far Cry on PC over FCIP.  However, FCIP is a hugely enjoyable title with basically two separate games in one package.  It stays true to the spirit and inspiration of the PC version, but at the same time sports enough unique differences about it to make it worth the time.

Sony and Media.Vision’s Wild Arms franchise isn’t as popular as say, Final Fantasy, although it nonetheless received a decent following outside Japan to the point where the first and second entries on the original PlayStation saw foreign release, alongside the third for the PlayStation 2. Afterward, Sony’s North American branch, which handled the localization of the first three games (although they partnered with Squaresoft to translate the third), seemed to give up on the series to the point where another company, Agetec, localized the remake of the original game, Wild Arms Alter Code: F. Fortunately for non-Japanese gamers, a new localization company, XSEED, arose, and handled the translation of the fourth game, Wild Arms 4, which makes several significant changes from its predecessors and provides an experience on par with them.When starting a new game, the player can import data from Alter Code: F for bonuses such as increased starting levels, additional money, additional items, additional badges, bonus treasure chests, bonus weapon abilities, and so forth. Despite this capability, the fourth installment bears no connection to F story-wise and takes place in a different Filgaia, and the overall setting of the game is different from previous entries, which bore steampunk and western elements, changed to a milieu almost purely steampunk, with occasional snippets of modern technology. The story itself isn’t anything spectacular, focusing on four adolescents that term themselves “children” despite being beyond childhood (and a kind of conflict taking place between “adults” and “children” throughout the game, and focuses on the aftermath of a great war. The villains don’t have a whole lot of depth, and one of the plot twists towards the end is a tad predictable, although the story is not without its redeeming aspects, such as commentary on the nature of war and good versus evil.Wild Arms 4 was one of XSEED’s first localization efforts, alongside Shadow Hearts: From the New World, and it shows. Grammatical errors such as a misuse of “it’s” abound, alongside awkward and sometimes loaded battle dialogue on part of both the player’s characters and the enemies, but the script generally contains a higher-than-average level of polish.The fourth installment, moving on, does well in the gameplay department, with the most significant change being that all battles take place on a grid of seven hexagons, and the starting positions of the player’s four characters, not to mention those of the enemies, are randomized, an initial strike against the battle system since victory sometimes depends on luck (especially versus the final bosses) and initial positions. The player’s characters and the enemies take turns depending upon agility, and execute their commands immediately after input much akin to other RPGs such as Final Fantasy X, a turn order meter mercifully showing character and enemy turn order for several turns and not running out of icons like the turn order meters in the Xenosaga trilogy.When one of the player’s characters reaches their turn, they have a number of options available to them, including attacking an adjacent hexagon’s enemies with their equipped weapon (with protagonist Jude Maverick equipped with an ARM that can run out of bullets and can reach the far hexagon from his initial position), defending (which reloads Jude’s bullets), moving to an adjacent hexagon (with Jude able to acquire a Personal Skill increasing his movement range) or out of the grid to escape from battle (which costs the player some money), using items, using a Force Point-consuming ability (with the Force Points gauge that builds up to a maximum of a hundred points shared by all characters unlike in prior series entries), or using an MP-consuming skill.Victory by the player may cause a treasure chest to appear in a random hexagon, although a character must be in the hexagon where it appears in order to obtain the item, or else the player will miss out on it, another negative random element of the battle system. All living characters also acquire experience for occasional level-ups and some money; those characters that died during battle and stay dead afterward, while they recover all their HP as other characters do between battles, experience a drop in maximum HP that consumable Nectars can rectify, alongside touching a Break Point, which is, to say, a save point, that also recovers consumed MP, and where the player may occasionally be able to fight a special battle to gain the ability to turn random encounters on and off in the current dungeon.If all the player’s characters die in a battle, the player has the option of restarting the battle or returning to the title screen to load a previous save. The option to respawn at the point prior to the encounter might have been nice as well, especially with regards to boss fights, since they typically follow long stretches without save opportunities. The final battles in the main storyline are also somewhat dependent upon luck, though mercifully, battles tend to end quickly in either the player or the enemy’s favor, the former especially if the player exploits enemy weaknesses, which the player can view anytime during one of their characters’ turns. In the end, the battle system is solid in spite of some occasional annoying random elements.The aforementioned poor placement of save points is one of the biggest strikes against the fourth installment’s control scheme, a step down from the third game and Alter Code: F, where special consumable Gimel Coins allowed players to record their progress anywhere, and save opportunities can be very far apart. In spite of no in-game dungeon maps, a feature that titles from prior console generations such as The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past had, dungeons aren’t terribly troublesome, and in fact have some okay puzzles, though some may or may not drive players to use a guide. The menus and shopping are easy, as well, although the developers could have certainly given the stingy save system a once-over.The soundtrack is perhaps the fourth entry’s strongest suit in spite of the reduced role of typical series composer Michiko Naruke, with a nice variety of tracks that always fit the mood, along with some occasional remixes of the main vocal theme song. The voice acting, though, is hit-or-miss, attributable especially in battle due to the sometimes laughable battle quotes, but otherwise, the game is fairly pleasant to the ears.The graphics look good as well, having a style that’s neither fully realistic nor cartoony, in spite of some bland textures and pixilation on the scenery when viewed close-up, and many cutscenes use static character art to narrate the storyline instead of the actual character models.Finally, the fourth game lasts about twenty hours, with an epilogue mode enhancing replay value and possibly pushing playing time even higher.Overall, Wild Arms 4 is for the most part a solid title that hits many of the right notes while leaving some room for improvement. The story isn’t much of a draw, and the translation could have used more polish, but the gameplay is mostly solid, in spite of poorly-spaced save opportunities, the aurals are pleasing, and the visuals look nice. Despite its shortcomings, the fourth installment demonstrated that an RPG franchise can evolve in a positive fashion, and its sequel would follow the same route with hexagon grid-based battles.

Let me first say that if you are an Harvest Moon orAnimal Crossingfan, this game is a must buy. The first thing you notice about this game is that it looks more like Animal Crossing than Harvest Moon. The camera is a top down view of houses, characters and trees that looks almost identical to Animal Crossing. The only big difference is the characters you interact with are human rather than animal. As far as gameplay, the social interaction feels more like Animal Crossing than Harvest Moon. But this is still a Harvest Moon game at it's core. Growing crops, raising livestock, and getting married is really what this game is all about. And the game operates in game time, not real world time like Animal Crossing.You start your game by being given a choice of where you want to locate your house, by the beach, on the river, or the center of town. On the river being the wisest choice because of the fertile soil, but each route has it's benefits. Now it's all about making money. At first you mostly forage for food and things to sell, at least until you get some crops or livestock going. The game operates on daily and monthly cycles. Meaning you wake up in the morning, then it progresses to day, then night. And different things happen at different times of day. Also months and seasons pass, again different things happen in different months and seasons. So it's always a changing world you interact with. Daylight hours and your energy are scarce, so you will have to careful plan your days and be sure you can get as much done as possible for each season. And there are holidays which typically are an excuse to play a mini-game.Social interaction typically comes in the form of talking to people and hunting down items they want. You can choose to be male or female and that choice will determine if you are able to marry boys or girls. You can only marry the opposite sex with the exception of an androgynous character named Jamie. Jamie seems to be neither male nor female but something of a magical character to which those labels don't apply. And you cannot marry right away but have to earn that right in terms of social interaction and physical wealth.What I really loved about this game what the freedom to do whatever you want. You can do some farming, work in mines, fish, forage, cook, decorate your house, upgrade your house and farm, ride your horse, or just be social. Game progression comes in the form of musical notes that you get as a reward for excelling in certain activities. Say you catch a certain number of certain types of fish, boom, musical note. Cook a number of different meals and you get a note. Get a bunch of notes and you beat the game. Though I should mention that you can actually beat the game twice. Once when you get a certain number of notes, another time when you get them all.Though simplistic, the social aspect of the game is a lot of fun. Getting married and having a kid is a lot of fun. My wife seems easy to please. I just give her a piece of cheese every once in a while and she's happy. If only real marriage were that easy.It all adds up to an immensely fun experience. I find my favorite games are the ones that just leave me alone and let me play, and this game does that perfectly. Five stars.Note: Also on the WiiHarvest Moon: Magical Melody

This game Has. It. All.If by "IT ALL" you mean "all there is to talk and make-believe about on the subject of an alternate history of World War II where a small Dutch political party composed of naval officers in charge of Dutch vessels gets its hands on some super-weapons and takes over from there, attempting to outgun the Japanese, the Germans, the United Kingdom, and the United States."You play the part of a breakaway faction of Dutch naval officers (not surprising considering that the Netherlands has a long history of mercantile seafaring) who are on the run from a crazed political organization of your fellow Dutchmen who have taken it upon themselves to interrupt World War II and take over the world using some Sci-Fi weaponry the likes of which the world has not seen.The game puts you in command of the firing position of a boatload of heavy artillery guns, torpedo launchers, machine guns, mine laying, giant gatling guns, missile systems, hi-angle guns, rocket launchers, and a whole slew of other anti-ship, anti-aircraft, and anti-submarine weapons. And that's not all you have on board. Your ship also features various grades of sonar and radar systems, firefighting and bilge pumping systems, electronic targeting and electronic jamming, bow thrusters, airplane catapults, helicopter launch pads, and a whole lot more. And you get to design it all.In painstaking detail, you launch yourself headfirst into a world of Computer Aided Design. Yes, the game features a very rudimentary, arcade-style computer aided design where your ship is represented as a blueprint and you pick up and move weapons and structures around the graphed-out plane in both top-down and side views. You are forced not only to account for the horizontal area required by (for example) large guns and their barrels, but also the depth of the ammunition storage located beneath the guns and other systems and structures you place on board. All of which have to accomodate the engine and propulsion systems which you also hand-pick and place according to your whim in the same blueprint with a graphing paper-like resolution. All of which has to fit within not only the hull's physical length, breadth, and depth, but also the hull's weight limits and somehow provide the right balance of speed and power, range and damage, capability and supply of firepower needed for the upcoming brutal mission -- or missions, when the story forces you to go through numerous battles without a chance to stop at the floating dock and berth for a change of design. Even the thickness of armor plating and the various steering and electronic guidance systems you install add to the overall tonnage.Every little detail is taken into consideration. Guns are available for various sizes of munition and various naval caliber-length barrels. Some guns that are standard in WW2 for each nation are included as well as guns that only a Sci-Fi "alternate history" geek could love. They even throw in an old-school, classic naval ball-cannon as a secret item to be found somewhere in the game. That's just a quaint little objet d'art by the time you are hewing through miles of coastline built up with military installations and peppered with battery turrets. Yes, that's right, you of course shell the living hell out of coastline installations and even lighthouses in your amazing quest to prove that this thing you've spent countless hours researching and designing is literally the incarnation of some titan born of Poseidon and Athena, the only incarnation fit and right to take on the gross and horrifying other titans born of some less noble, not so good intentioned Gods. It's seriously that good of a game.Oh, and did I mention research? You will spend even further countless hours poring over the games enormous, unfathomable research trees. Research trees so large that the game included a system within the system for you to shrink the data presented in each node of the tree so that it's easier to traverse and just look at and ponder. That also speaks to the game's involved design and attention not only to detail but to the actuality of things like readout readiness: you can shrink the humongous research trees down to just little tiny blips on the screen (using your L2 button) and they still carry obvious meaning. A lot of love was put into the game's presentation of various readouts, interfaces, gauges and controls so that they feel natural just like you would carry a high expectation of if you were the engineer in charge of designing naval ships that you were also going to be in command of. No wonder the game designers picked the Dutch as the heros and villains of this game's alternate World War II naval battles.The choice of location will not disappoint, either. The game begins in the Pacific and your first big arrow points from Japan straight down to Hawaii. Yes, your choice of various hulls that you can research and add to your design system do include cruisers (CA), carriers (CV), battleships (BB), and battlecarriers (BC). And, yes, those ship classes are capable of hosting between one and one bazillion airplanes of the entire imaginable range of capabilities (from post-WWI prop biplanes to Space Age stealth bombers), but no, there is no replay of Pearl Harbor, here. I haven't played even a quarter of the way through the game, but so far, the preliminaries are the respectable post-modern (post-bomb) fare we've come to expect from Japanese pop culture, enrenched in the same playful ribbing and social criticism we've come to expect from Japanese anime.Everything about the game glorifies maritime engineering, strategy, honor, and ultimately destruction. Massive destruction on a massive scale. The battles you will get into are no joke. You will frequently get your ass handed to you, and with the complex coastlines and placements you have to contend with there's no supreme "right way" through a given mission. You could spend even, again, more countless hours running through "practice" runs of earlier missions to store up enough credits to buy the research you need to build advanced ships early on and bully your way through, sure. But at the other end of the spectrum, if you just tried to speed run your way through it you would be in for an almost insurmountably difficult game. There's some balance in there and the game happily offers you every extreme of gaming experience.When I play it, I get the really uneasy feeling that I'm playing the sort of simulator game that old, retired war buffs have been soaking into since the early 90's. Worringly, the amount of time this game can require of you in terms of studying, designing, training, and playing, can require so much time that it could easily turn into an alternate lifestyle. You could force yourself into an early retirement if you're not careful. It is that sedentary, and that addictive. If somebody told you that one day you'd be addicted to sitting there doing CAD on imaginary ships, whether you'd laugh or nod in sagely agreement, this game is for you both, old retired people and twitch-reflex gamers alike.

If you have even an inkling of interest in playing this game, let me point out from the start that the designers most likely had this as purely an iPad/touch screen game in mind, because it took me a good ten minutes to figure out that I had to HOLD DOWN THE MOUSE BUTTON to move my line of sight. This isn't noted anywhere in the interface notes--though it does point out what the symbols (which YOU CAN'T SEE if you don't know how to MOVE) are--and the budget packaging gives no manual, presumably because it's all so ***obvious*** that it needs no mention. BOO.The rest of the game is bland at best, and the first "episode" made me nauseated from the game's quirk of centering then moving to the next section with a fade transition, which was aggravated with how apparently the main character can't just walk in a straight line down a hall; he slips slightly to the left or right as he goes. There are more than a few places where the game is needlessly long/tedious--for instance, traversing the thick jungle of the third "episode" after navigating it even once (I ended up having to do it five times!)--and the decryption puzzles were made miserably difficult because Hunt could not hold up the reference material to the object he was trying to translate, so after the first such "puzzle" I just consulted a walkthrough so I could get through it already.To get back to the subject, apparently there are twelve or so games Hunt is looking for, but by the third episode he's only found two. Are they at least fun games? Eh... not really. Both are "capturing" games, and they have the same problem as chess, when it gets down to each player having only a few pieces left, it ends up being a stalemate of moving pieces back and forth between safe zones until one player takes a chance. At least once you win, you get to play them "offline" without having to play the main game.On the whole, I guess it's worth the budget price, but definitely disappointing that, unless you know what "A Collection of 3 Complete Adventures" means, there's no indication that this is only a partial narrative. Since I had recently watched a cancelled TV show with a similar "epic" narrative that never concluded, I would have preferred going in to know that the disc content ends on a cliffhanger. At least I didn't spend a lot, but definitely no fond memories... except I guess the beach of Madagascar was pretty.

Some games are total crap. Some games are great. Some are mediocre. Rampage is....entertaining. I guess that essentially makes it a good game. We buy games to be entertained. But we also expect a certain level of art. Well, this is no work of art. You bash buildings. The end.But that is all the Rampage series have ever been about. So you have to hand to Midway for staying true to the series. And it's still fun to mindlessly bash buildings with no real point to it.But I guess that's a slight exaggeration. The game does in fact have a story. It even has an ending, though I think it only lasts about 10 seconds. And you can play with up to 4 friends, which makes it a social and competitive experience. But most of us will spend 90% of our time bashing building by ourselves, with the occasional friend picking up the controller.There are various modes and challenges. And it is mildly fun to bash specific cities all over the world, like Vegas. But for me this game was all about unlocking various monsters. You start the game with a slim selection of monsters. As you go through the game in various modes, all sorts of monsters are unlocked. Some as a reward for various challenges. Some are just randomly found. Some can only be unlocked in two player mode. And different monsters have different strengths and weaknesses. So it encourages a certain amount of experimentation, which is great. I became absorbed in the hunt for the perfect monster. And they look pretty cool too. My favorite being the uber secret giant squid.With all it's flaws, I still had a blast with this game. But I had to take off a star because I just felt it could had been great with just a little more effort. The simple retro-graphics are fine with me. And I'm good with simple gameplay. But it could have used a little more polish. Having said all that, this is a game I would highly recommend just because it's so much raw fun. But I would try to pay as little as you can, if you know what I'm saying. Oh, and you get a few classic Rampage games to boot. That's a nice bonus. Four stars.

Dynasty Warriors is one of my favorite franchises playing it all the way since Dynasty Warriors 4. The Empires spin-offs have always been better in my opinion, and this game is no exception.For the graphics, there is nothing special about them. The character models are decent for an early 360 game, but everything else is lacking. The draw distance is especially a problem since you can't see any soldiers that are only a few feet away from you.There are over 40 characters in this game, each with their own unique fighting style. You have all around characters such as Zhao Yun as well as overpowering bad asses such as Lu Bu. The voice acting for each character is better than past titles, but nothing noteworthy or special about it.As with all Dynasty Warriors titles, the heart of the game lies in its gameplay. Similar to other titles of the series, your goal is to hack and slash your way to victory, However, victory lies in connecting your main camp to your opponents. This can be done by taking over bases as well as defeating officers along the way. Even though this is seen as repetitive, it has allot of strategy since there are multiple routes you can take on the battlefield.The main mode is Empire mode, which has you picking a ruler and guiding your army to take over all of China. It is broken up into two phases. The strategic mode is where you enact various policies such as replenishing the troops in your army, forging alliances, creating tactics, etc. Having this really feels like you're in control and are able to forge your own destiny however you would like to. You also have to think about each choice you make as it costs resources (a.k.a. gold).Overall, this is a great experience. There is allot of strategy and depth when it comes to the Empire mode. As always, the best way to play this game is with a friend. It is even more fun when you are conquering China together as a team. My only complaints are the draw distance and the somewhat sluggish feel compared to the newer titles. However, I'd certainly recommend this to Dynasty Warriors fans as well as fans of tactical gameplay.

There is something for everyone in this game. Space trading, space combat, ground combat, planet exploration with probes, and even text based quests. The controls are logical and very easy to manage even during combat that you can have in turn base or RTS mode as you wish. The main quest is challenging but quite achievable. You can also pick the type of side missions that you like and totally avoid a type you don't like without any consequence. There are few if any games that gives the player so much freedom.There are some frustrations like the speed at which your ship and equipment deteriorate and the very high cost of ships and equipment. Combat in black holes is also often too difficult because your ship is very hard to control there but you can always altogether avoid it except if you intend to defeat the Dominators. But even with this considered, I loved this game and highly recommend it. Stay away from the Steam "sequel" to this game. It's an absolute ripoff.

Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Hyperstone Heist has a lot to live up to. With both the amazing arcade game and SNES port, Turtles in Time, Hyperstone Heist has big shoes to fill. Thankfully, Konami didn't go for a direct port here, as they knew the Genesis lacked the sprite scaling and Mode 7 capabilities for the port to be faithful. Instead, we get a new, original game in the Turtles beat 'em up series, and it's easily one of the best, even managing to surpass awesome games like Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Arcade Game and The Manhattan Project.It may sound like blasphemy, but I also believe The Hyperstone Heist manages to be a superior gaming experience to Turtles in Time, in some areas. The difficulty of the game is heightened, and we're left with a more rewarding, more challenging experience. While the color palette of the Genesis is technically inferior to the SNES, you really wouldn't know it by playing this. Colors appear much brighter and more contrasted than the already wonderful looking SNES arcade port, and overall, I prefer the visual style used here. It's not about how many colors you have at your disposal. It's what you do with them, and Hyperstone Heist is a great example of this sentiment.Like I mentioned, the gameplay here feels a bit more challenging. Enemies seem more ready to fight than they did in either the Arcade or SNES games. They simply do a lot less standing around, and a lot more fighting, particularly if you're playing on hard mode. It also seems the differences in the Turtles themselves were tweaked, allowing for a more balanced experience. It could just be the Genesis itself being responsible for the game feeling this way, but the gameplay as a whole feels much faster-paced here than it does in Turtles in Time. Especially if you're playing as Raphael, the fastest character in the game. It simply runs smoother, with no slowdown anywhere to be seen.There aren't as many levels here as there are in Turtles in Time, but thankfully, Konami opted to include longer levels to balance this out. The levels play out of amalgamations of levels found in the classic '89 arcade game as well as Turtles in Time. They're intelligently designed, with the game's pace in mind at all times, and nothing ever overstays its welcome despite these levels being longer in comparison to the SNES game. It's a shame we don't get the awesome Mode 7 levels, and I miss being able to throw enemies into the screen. Hyperstone Heist certainly isn't as much of a special effects powerhouse as Turtles in Time is, but I believe it's the smoother playing and better balanced game of the two.The boss fights are also more challenging than those found in Turtles in Time, with most characters using patterns that are similar to the '89 arcade game. This is welcome, as after playing both Hyperstone Heist and Turtles in Time for years now, Hyperstone is the game I keep coming back to. The difficulty presented just hits a sweet spot. Not too easy, not too hard. That's not to say that once you manage to play this game to the best of your abilities you won't be able to play through it without losing just a few lives, because you absolutely can. Even on hard mode. It's not what I would call a "hard" game, by any means, but it's definitely more challenging than the game it draws inspiration from, and it trades off the dynamic level diversity for dynamic enemy and boss encounters.The music here is also outstanding. Much like the rest of the game, the music here runs faster than what we hear in the arcade game or the SNES version, and lacks any and all of the distorted, tinny sound the Genesis is known for. The melodies come through clear, the bass sounds full, the treble sounds bright, and there's some great stereo separation throughout. It sounds wonderful. The voice samples don't fare as well, however. In comparison to the SNES game, there aren't as many of them, and the ones that are here don't sound as clear. I can't stress enough how awesome of a soundtrack this game has, though, and I vastly prefer it over the reverb-y, compressed sound of the SNES game.All in all, Hyperstone Heist is an awesome game, and easily my favorite beat 'em up on the Genesis. The animations are slick and smooth, the music is outstanding, and the game as whole runs peppier than its arcade or SNES counterparts. It manages to differentiate itself enough from both, and as a standalone title, it has a lot going for it. As a more challenging experience that runs smoother, with longer levels and boss fights that rely on patterns more than they do mashing a button to win, The Hyperstone Heist is an incredible game that deserves so much more than to be written off as a Turtles in Time knock-off. Both are amazing games, and Turtles fans shouldn't pass up on either one.

"Hitman: Blood Money," developed by IO Interactive and published by Eidos, marks the official seventh-generation debut of the series.  In many ways, it is a major improvement over the previous three games in the series.  However, it doesn't really feel like a true seventh-gen title; instead, it plays more like a high-end sixth-gen title with slightly better graphics.  This isn't necessarily a bad thing, however; it's just that if you expected something absolutely revolutionary and mind-blowing, you may be slightly disappointed.HBM adds some new touches that make for a more exciting experience and are also crucial to completing the game on the highest difficulty, Pro.  You're able to take human shields for protection to help you clear out an area.  You can switch from 3rd-person to 1st-person view for more accurate targeting.  You can hide in special locations like closets and boxes, where you can also store dead bodies.  Most importantly, however, you're able to use disguises to gain access to certain areas without drawing anyone's suspicion.  At the end of each level, you'll receive a newspaper article that's been written about your exploits and takes into account your weapon accuracy, the discreetness of your kills, how often you were exposed, and how many witness were left alive.  It's very entertaining and empowering to read about how much you're a "Silent Assassin" that everyone is absolutely terrified of.The first level is the most linear of the entire game, but it acts as a tutorial that covers every aspect that's included in the game, so I guess it can be forgiven.  You taught how to silently kill with your fiber wire, how to hide bodies and yourself, how to use human shields for extra protection, how to use disguises to gain access to restricted areas, how to use a sniper rifle, and how to make kills look like "accidents."  It's extremely diverse and then gives you free reign on how you wish to complete the missions for the rest of the game.The production values of HBM are a definite mixed bag.  The Xbox 360 version obviously looks better than the other versions, being the most advanced system.  Agent 47 looks really badass and animates very well, too.  There's some awesome blood splattering when you shoot an enemy, and their death physics are funny and entertaining.  However, overall, it's not as polished as a true exclusive seventh-gen title.  Other characters' animations can get incredibly stiff, jerky, and robotic at certain points.  They can also be incredibly stupid, not bothering to seek cover when you're using a human shield and instead just strafing awkwardly out in the open.  The aiming is also hit-or-miss, as sometimes you'll think you'll score a definite headshot, but it misses the target anyway.While it has definite strong points, HBM, at it's core, feels like just another sixth-gen Hitman title, even the Xbox 360 version.  It's still enjoyable, but it's not a completely mind-blowing masterpiece.  To add on to the missed potential, it would take more than six full years for a new Hitman game to be officially released.  Nevertheless, HBM is a really good game that makes you feel like you're an extremely lethal assassin who kills without a trace and strikes paralyzing fear into the general populaton.  For that, it's all worth it.

"Guns of the Patriots" is over-the-top, ludicrous, with a labyrinthine story that's often hard to penetrate - and it's also some kind of a masterpiece. Taking place in the "not too distant future" sometime after the events of "Sons of Liberty," war has now engulfed much of the world. Many sections of the game (Middle East, South America) have you negotiating through warzones where two factions are engaged in battle. A later section has you returning to Shadow Moses, the nuclear weapons facility you infiltrated in the first game. As Old Snake, who is Solid Snake suffering from some kind of accelerated aging, you can either sneak by and avoid conflict or choose to aid the rebels against the PMCs. Playing stealthily is more rewarding than runnin' and gunnin', and it's possible to beat the game without killing anyone, even the bosses, whose stamina bar can be depleted instead. I especially like the boss fights with the "Beauty and the Beast Unit," which includes Laughing Octopus, who attacks with long tentacles while blending in with the environment, and Crying Wolf, who's fought in a snowy blizzard reminiscent of Sniper Wolf. The two best gameplay additions are the OctoCamo, a high tech adaptive camouflage that takes the appearance of whatever it comes in contact with - helpful when sneaking, and a new over-the-shoulder view for aiming. There's also a neat system for collecting equipment on the battlefield, earning points, and then using those points to purchase weapons and ammo. I thought the first "MGS" was a singularly perfect experience whose only criticism is that it's limited by older hardware. "MGS4" by comparison is not perfect. The only FF I played was FF7, 8, and 10. That was 10 years ago. When FF13 came out, I hesitated because I heard of bad things like how it was very linear and that they messed up the whole battle and leveling system. How I was wrong... For the first few hours of playing FF13, I quickly realized that it plays out like a movie. Everything you do is in one direction. There was no puzzle and hardly any maze to slow you down. You only side-missions are to kill a certain enemy mob for rewards. Overall, this is not necessarily a bad thing because I realized how all the older FF games had frustrating, pointless puzzles with little guidance. The old FF games were torture. If you missed read a dialog, you ended up running around town and the world map aimlessly, and not knowing where the next objective was. In FF13, there was always a map and guide arrow. On the down side, I wish that there was at least a world map in FF13 to run around in lol. Grand Pulse is the closest thing to a world map, but it is really just a bigger area with monsters to hunt, very visually stunning though. The leveling up system, Crystarium, is like the Sphere system from FF10, except a whole lot less confusion. Although, I still like the FF7 Materia system better.The most important thing in an FF series is the battle system. Despite some other reviews, the battle system is very easy to understand. Most of the time, I just use the auto-attack. Once you figure out how to effectively use the Paradigm shift, there is nothing else useful to learn.You can upgrade your weapons instead of finding better ones, which is stupid. Let be honest, you want to open up a chest and find a better, bigger, more bad-a** looking gunblade instead of upgrading the same weapon which looks the same at every level.The summons were pointless, and since you only control one character in battle, only one summon can be cast. If you want to cast another summon, you have to build up the TP points from battling and switch to controlling another character if you want a different summon. Generally, summons were only good for rejuvenating the party, and building up the stag gauge while staying alive. Summoning was kind of a hassle, I beat the last boss without needing to summon. The other abilities were kind of pointless too, like Quake which didn't do much damage. I didn't summon that much because I was trying to save the TP points for harder battles, which I ended up not summoning at all.For most of the game, I complaint about the hard difficulty compared to older FF games. Well, there is a reason. When you die, you are no longer thrown back to the Intro screen and forced to reload the save file. I'm suprise it took them so long to fix this dumb problem. Instead you just reset right back to the point before you enter the battle. Since you can see the enemy, you can also avoid battles. This is so much better than those annoy random battles in the old FF games. Also, Gils are very hard to find, but that's ok because everytime you enter a battle, you have full HP and no "diseases". There is no need to refresh your party with sleep and tents at save points, none of that non-sense in FF13. And thankfully there is a save-point every 15ish minute you play, and all the cut-scenese can be skipped, even summons. All this makes the game a hell lot less annoying to play.Too beat ANY enemy, all you need to know is when to use the Paradigm shift to buff, heal, stagger, and inflict. Sadly, the rest is auto-attack. I do miss those legacy spells like Ultima which only the boss can cast in FF13. On the other hand, the battle system lets you chain combos, like Thunder, Fire, Blizzard in one attack, which is pretty cool. Sometimes I wonder why they couldn't let you control all three character if all you going to do is hit the auto-attack most of the time. The actual fighting is far better than any FF game before it. You can throw Monsters into the air while the other characters cast different spells on them. Your party members are constantly jumping, flipping, and moving around the area. Weapons enchanting spells look really cool like a slash of fire, lighting, or ice. The FF13 battle system is a good modern approach to the old FF games which is outdated, old and boring compared to modern games. I say, it is a better battle system compared to older FF games, but then it could have been much better.The story-telling is another important aspect in FF. FF13 is extremely confusing. They use weird and unconventional  names like L'cie, Fal'cie, Pulse, Focus, Cocoon, Orphan, etc. On top of that, they don't clearly define what the name actually mean, where they came from, and what their purpose is. In FF7 when they say the Shinra corporation develops Mako-power, you know exactly what they are talking about. After I beat FF13, I had to find a Youtube video to explain the whole story. The overall story, when I understood it, was just okay. FF13 story is not as good as FF7 though, but at least the ending in FF13 was intense and the CGI was topnotch. There are also a lot of text data in FF13 that explains everything from the spells and abilities, to the story itself, but who has time to sit down and read all that.FF13-2 and Lightning Return was already released and reviewed when I beat FF13. I played a bit of FF13-2, and watched reviews of Lightning Returns. Sadly, the 13 series seems to be going down the drain. When I play FF13-2 and watch the review for Lightning Returns, they look like beta versions of FF13 =/I recommend FF13, but it is really pushing for that 5-star since. 5-stars because I am an old FF fan, and FF13 is not all that bad. Despite the flaws, you still should appricate the limitless artwork, CGI, music, and sound-track that they put together. Unfortunately, I will probably skip the other two follow up games in the 13 series due to the degraded game quality, and continue playing where I last left off in The Last of Us which I have been putting on hold because of FF13.

First I just want to say that this is not meant to be the most accurate review that can be found on Amazon. This review is only meant to encourage people to try this game and to try it the right way. I've been a follower of Square games ever since the original Final Fantasy. I've also followed Enix since Dragon Warrior (Quest). The two companies have since merged and it's a decision that makes sense at least from my point of view. Both companies have been putting out high quality RPGs for well over two decades. It wasn't a hard decision for me to at the very least give this game a chance. I just had to make the time because in today's gaming industry there are more selections than ever and not really enough time to try everything, especially if you commit to an RPG. I think I spent an entire summer trying to master Final Fantasy X. It just depends on how busy a person is I guess. I'm assuming that anyone looking to try this game has played the previous installments. Is the story as good as previous Final Fantasy's? Well, I can't really answer that because I'm only a couple hours into it. So you may be asking yourself why I'm writing this review already. I'll tell you why. I'm playing this game on a 120 inch screen with a DLP projector that converts 2D into 3D. The difference is outstanding! I mean, I compared just a little bit of this game in 2D and in 3D and all I can say is if you haven't tried it yet you should wait until you can give it the "theatrical experience" because it is much much better in 3D on a big screen then just standard 2D on a t.v. The world absolutely comes to life in 3D and really makes the game that much better. I really do think it's the only way to experience it. Perhaps Square-Enix intended this because there is a brightness adjustment in the menu and I don't think any other Final Fantasy games had one. Anyone scratching their head about that statement should know that when you convert a game from 2D into 3D you usually have to turn the brightness up a few notches to compensate for the 3D glasses because they are slightly tinted. Anyways, so far the story is decent enough to keep me interested. Square-Enix have never disappointed with stories(at least the ones I've played) so I'm optimistic about the long run. I've heard about some of the complaints about this game and all I can think is it's not going to matter on a 120 inch screen in 3D. I'm not talking about an expensive upgrade either, you probably just need your own living room and maybe a little over $1000 to upgrade. I'll never go back to t.v. and this really is one of those games that feels right at home on a big screen because it really is like playing a movie. The only other thing I can add information wise about this game is the battle system seems a little overwhelming at first but starts to become comfortable with practice. That and the level up system is a lot like the sphere grid from Final Fantasy X. Hope this helps anyone looking into getting this game and sorry if it sounds like I'm trying to promote DLP projectors or gloating about mine or something but it really does merit a mention because of the big difference it makes.
