I've played about half of the Dragon Quest games now and this one is second only to DQVIII.There is one thing I have to gripe about (aside from the typical JRPG end boss) is the class system.  At some point you choose classes.  Your character level and class level are separate.  Classes will level up depending on how many battles you fight, not XP.  Problem is the game won't tell you when you're awarded points or not and when the game deems your character level too high for an area, you won't get any points toward your class level at all.  This can cause a problem that snowballs on you if you decide to grind in order to beat a tough boss.  My only advice would be to avoid grinding once you gain classes, up until the last boss.  Then you can grind away.  Go nuts.

Very simply, I came across and bought this one at the time locally, because compared to the others available, the kit for the Midnight Blue one also included a soft case and the large pen stylus that the others lacked. Overall, I've been very impressed, especially in the homebrew aspect. And the Midnight Blue was my most desired color to choose from the versions available.The DSi XL manages to have what looks like a lacquered clear-coat finish... one that gives it a nice, soft gloss on its top when closed, but also protects the outside very well from scuffs and scratches. The bottom of the handheld has a kind of grit feel that is somehow not rubbery, but also seems to be a non-slip grip of sorts, allowing the rather large handheld to feel good in your hands.The big draw with a DSi XL is in the "XL" part - namely, the larger screens. Even though they retain the same technical resolution as the regular DSi, it doesn't overly distort or blur the image. If anything, I find playing compatible games on this one sharper than they are on even a 3DS (regular or XL). The nice and clicky buttons also are very snappy. And the larger screens does a lot more than I initially gave credit for to improve the ability to take pictures with the front or rear-facing camera. I would even say that this is probably one reason why many regular flipnote users or those using the drawing apps/games on the handheld preferred the XL model, because the larger screen enabled better precision.One interesting thing of Note: Yes, I do homebrew with the handheld, as I am wont to do. While the system isn't expected to be able to TELL what it is I am running (after all, it's not like the 3DS in that regard that retains an activity log), this may very well be the best handheld for DS(i) mode homebrew for one reason, and one very good reason. As an example, let us mention nesDS, a very popular and exceptional NES emulator to run on a Nintendo DS. A standard DS, DSi, or 3DS renders the running game pretty much identically, and relatively sharp, as one would expect with an emulator running some kind of smoothing. Yes, on the DSi XL in particular, it somehow introduces *scanlines*. I don't know how, but as a result of this behavior, emulation on the DSi XL is somehow even MORE accurate visually, because now it feels like I'm playing these old-school games on the kind of display they were meant to be run on - a big ol' CRT TV. In the palms of my hands. This is especially impressive and palpable when emulating Turbografx16/PCEngine games especially, and it looks fantastic. If anything, I am really sad that the recent releases of virtual console titles to the nintendo eShop aren't made as DSi-ware, in part because I would have loved to see them in their super-sharp, scanline-y glory on this thing. At least the homebrew is covering that gap pretty dang nicely.If you can get one at a good price, it definitely doesn't hurt to add it in your group of systems. Paired up with a good and strong flash cart for homebrew, and you have a gorgeous device to do the job.

Simply put... this is one of the greatest video games of all time. And for less than $20, every wii u owner who has not experienced the arkham series needs to own a copy.I have never played the 360 or PS3 version but the seeming advantages of the wii u version are significant. The gamepad is AWESOME. The developers really tried to use it in a variety of useful ways (scanning crime scenes, controlling a remote control batarang, hacking computer systems). Probably the most useful way is that you can easily access the game map at any time without pausing the game and change between gadgets at the tap of a button.I usually played on the TV because I wanted the game on the big screen and enjoyed the above features, but I also played a few times just on the gamepad and it really came in handy. The game looked great, no glitches and the TV was free for others to use.What makes this game special is you FEEL LIKE BATMAN. My previous experience (and I know this is dating myself) was with Batman Returns for Super Nintendo and Batman Brave and the Bold for Wii. Both had a few redeeming qualities, but you were basically mindlessly beating up bad guys. Arkham City embraces the true heart of batman as a detective. You find clues that guide you through the story and in almost every situation you have to think through, "okay, with the gadgets I have how can I get through this?" In most situations the bad guys have guns and batman never does. You're always over matched... except because you're batman you're never truly overmatched. It's an AMAZING feeling.The plot is excellent (think good batman cartoon TV movie, although definitely with PG-13 content FYI), it's understandably underdeveloped in some areas but still excellent for a video game. And there is a LOT of REPLAY value. I'm not one to replay games, but I just finished and I only have 36% complete. What makes it fun is that you can restart the game with all your gadgets and you can choose between different popular batman costumes. Whereas the first time you were learning the ropes, now you can just execute. There are also tons of side stories and also different character stories (Catwoman, Harley Quinn, and Robin).The only negative is the game is a bit older... but that shouldn't stop anyone from buying the game if they haven't experienced Arkham City before.

The first thing you need to know before getting this game is that if you expect it to be anything like SOTN or the GBA/DS Castlevania games, you'll be severely dissapointed.  Mirror of Fate is classic NES/SNES action with a few small RPG elements thrown in for good measure.If you want to get a more direct comparison, this game is basically a 2D-perspective version of God of War.  The fighting style, down to the QTE-boss-kills, the puzzles, even the mash-button-to-open-chests-and-get-upgrades system is here.  If I didn't know about the older Castlevania games I'd say it's a blatant rip-off, but instead I realized that God of War owes a lot to Castlevania.The second thing you need to know is that this game is dark.  Literally, really dark.  As in, impossible-to-play-in-daylight dark.  But that's fine, because it's best to play this game in the darkness, to get sucked into its world.If those two things are of no consequence to you, or you actually find them appealing, then this is a game you should play.  The gameplay is fun, the art style is magnific, the story is classic and the content is extensive.  That being said, there are a few cons that might turn players off.First, as I mentioned, if you prefer the Metroidvania style, you're bound to be dissapointed.  While you can backtrack in this game, it's still more in line with the classic titles.  The map, instead of being one big comprehensive page is divided in zones, making it kinda useless, except for one thing that makes it too useful: a red arrow that constantly points you where you need to go, which cheapens the experience.In fact, that's the main gripe I have with the game: it's too easy.  Yes, enemies are strong, and offer a variety of attacks, but when you lose you return almost to the same place.  This is specially jarring in boss battles, in which if you lose you'll return in the middle of the battle, and the boss doesn't get his energy back.  That reduces the challenge quite a bit, and you have to resort to certain puzzles to find some challenge in the game.Another thing, but this might be a matter of personal preference, is that you don't feel your attacks have power.  In the previous games (most of them, anyway), when you struck and killed an enemy, you FELT it.  Your attacks had "oomph".  There was good audiovisual feedback that your attack was strong, no matter how much damage you actually dealt.  Here, you feel as if you're hitting your enemies with a big straw.One more thing to mention, and this is not necessarily a bad point, is the style of the cutscenes.  Characters move, talk and their faces change expression, but their lips never move.  This is obviously a stylistic choice, and, as I said, it's not really a bad thing, I just think it's strange.Still, it's a good game, I just hope the next one addresses the difficulty issue.

Nike+ was something I would not have believed existed. I bought a 360 and a Kinect specifically for Dance Central strictly in order to workout, as getting to a gym while being a single dad is only slightly harder than getting to Mars. But Gamestop had a spare copy of this, and thank holy heavens they did. I almost gave up on Xbox entirely with the XBone debacle, but I'm glad I held out.The workouts are brutally direct. You're run through a coursework of various exercises that are varied, effective, and will quickly leave you rung out on the floor if you're not used to a workout. But they're just short enough (20-30 minutes unless you ask for more) to know that you can make it through, pending heart attack be damned. And the exercises are so unique you won't ever feel like you're just being a metronome for a pushup counter. Also included are some interactive games that're actually enjoyable.There are quite a few nits. There's no pause, meaning unless you're on an exercise that has reps, which will go on forever, theres no way to stop in the middle. I'm not even talking about collapsing and begging for respite when you can barely stand. I feel like they needed to include a verbal command like "Xbox, real life problem!" that you can scream when, for example, your baby start shrieking in the next room, or the phone rings, or you desperately need a bathroom break. The Kinect range means you do have to have a 12' by 12' room almost set aside for nothing but working out. I lucked on by having a bunch of furniture that I can pick up and move in a few moments. You're badgered constantly to buy new "workout mixes" every time you turn the program on. Some of the menus are hard to navigate and the profile data is hidden somewhere I can't find(I accidentally selected "female" instead of "male" and there seems to be no way to correct this).Overall, between the cost of the Xbox, the Kinect, and Nike+, I would advocate everyone buy the whole package just for this. At just under $250, this is the cost of a 6 month gym memebership that you have on call basically forever. And hey, you've got an Xbox that you can fish more stuff out of the Gamestop bargain bin until they're phased completely out. And while you need an online account to do the nike fuel thing (I still haven't explored that aspect) this isn't one of those infruiating setups where you have to have Gold to make it work.

The Good: Fun and fast paced action, fun multiplayer modes, lots of customization, looks great, Declassified Missions add fun challengeThe Bad: Horrible story, extremely linear, very short, lack of maps, lack of new contentGears of War is the Xbox 360's best series and one of the best of this generation. It introduced cinematic gameplay in a gritty post apocalyptic world with revolutionary gun play and cover system. Judgement proves that all series run out of steam. It's the worst Gears game, but not terrible. People Can Fly (of Painkiller fame) took the driver's seat thanks to their successful collaboration with Epic during the development of Bulletstorm. Judgement isn't anything like the previous games in a bad way. It's dragged down by balance issues, linearity, and a poor story.Let's start with the story. It takes place years before Delta Squad was formed and Baird was a Lieutenant. He's accompanied by UIR Paduk, Sofia Hendrick, and Augustus Cole. They are arrested and are being held in a trial in the middle of a battlefield by Colonel Loomis. You play their flashbacks as testimonies. Honestly the story never goes anywhere and there's nothing gripping about it. You just play as each character in short 30-45 minute chapters. Once you catch up to the present moment you play one more chapter and that's it. Nothing interesting at all. Even the bonus chapter called Aftermath is pretty lame. It takes place after Gears of War 3, but all you're doing is finding a boat to get out to sea. There's nothing revealing to the overall story.Challenge and pacing takes a back seat as well. Judgement is all about the kill count and tactical combat takes a back seat. All the enemies health have been dialed back a lot so you can run around pumping them with lead. It got so bad that 5-6 enemies will pile up on you or an ally. This would never happen in previous Gears games. I honestly rarely used cover and just went around blasting enemies with the Gnasher. The game is broken up into sections with score totals at the end. The only awesome thing about Judgement that impressed me were the Declassified missions. These are giant red gear logos on the wall at the beginning of each section that make the game a bit more challenging. Ranging from time limits, to certain weapons, more enemies, more defenses etc. These also increase your star rating which are used to unlock items and achievements.Half way through the game it starts getting extremely repetitive. I honestly almost hated the game, but the action itself kept me hooked because it was faster paced than previous games and a bit more exciting. There really isn't much new added to this game either. There's one new enemy that acts like a mini Berserker. Once you shoot it it will grow bigger and only head shots will kill it. There are a few new weapons, but they are UIR weapons. The Booshka is a grenade launcher, the Markza is a sniper rifle with a fast firing rate. There's also another rifle that is nearly as deadly as a Longshot but fires 4 rounds before a reload. I wanted more content, honestly even the levels were generic and boring. It's the same hallways and battlefields over and over. The overall game is just really disappointing.Once you finish the campaign there's really no reason to go back unless you really want all the stars and find the hidden COG tags, or to play co-op. The multiplayer is probably the best out of all the Gears games, but is lacking content. There aren't many maps, and Horde mode is absent, but there's a substitute mode called Survival and Overrun. Survival pits a Gears team against AI controlled Locust, and Overrun lets players control the Locusts. This mode is intense and another small step in the evolution of the Gears multiplayer suite. The classic modes are back and feel as solid as ever, but the lack of maps may bore players quicker than previous games.Overall, Judgement is a huge disappointment. The campaign is generic, short, and almost boring, the tactical side of Gears is taken away for running and gunning. Multiplayer suffers from a lack of maps, but at least there's a lot of customization stuff to unlock for your characters. You now get rewarded for all those kills and ribbons you earn in the from of Prizeboxes. The graphics look great and push the 360 to its limits, but the console is seriously aged and it shows. Judgement is  fun weekend rental or bargain purchase, at this point Gears of War needs a reboot to keep from going under.

I remember when this game was still in development there was a big article in the Official XBOX Magazine, at the time it was simply titled XCOM - a first person shooter and it looked awesome.  Then the XCOM fanboys started whining and complaining about how it was too different from the previous turn based strategy xcom games, blah blah blah.  Sadly, 2K listened to all the fanboys' pitiful sobbing and switched from 1st person to 3rd person, slapped on a squad based system with a tactical interface almost identical to the one used in the Mass Effect games, along with the cover system, dialog system, squad member upgrades, and pretty much everything else from ME.  So what I'm sensing as I play this game is that 2K heard all the moaning, got scared they might have a flop on their hands, and in a last-minute panic made some major changes, slapped on a bunch of features that were a hit in a different game assuming it might make this game appeal to a wider audience, or at least keep the game from completely tanking.  What we get in the end is what feels like a 3/4 finished game that was rushed thru QA testing.  Dialog is stiff, often doesn't match the facial animations and some of the cutscenes feel like segments have been cut out.  The cover system is difficult to manage, "unsticking" yourself from cover is harder than it should be and when you're getting flanked it'll get you killed pretty fast.  Another complaint - it's too easy to swap your weapon with one laying on the ground without even realizing you've done it.  They should have made made it so you "tap" the X button to reload and "hold" the X button to swap weapons, open doors, etc..  Also the story is pretty weak and is poorly told - again, most likely because of last minute cuts.  Anyway, I just want to send out a big "THANK YOU" to all you pouty-faced fanboys for ruining what could have been a great game.  What's even more baffling is well before this game was released they gave you the turn based game you wanted (Enemy Unknown) yet The Bureau still came out as a half-a$$ed, generic, clunky game that is full of stuff that's already been done.

First of all, the biggest flaw with this game is not that it is using the XCOM name and producing a non-strategic shooter.  The biggest problem with The Bureau is its incessant need to force you to do BORING things.  Walk through static environments that have no purpose and no interactive features.  Retrace your steps just to talk to someone AGAIN, like those horrible old RPG's.  Then, it gets WORSE--the people have mostly NOTHING to say, nothing interesting to say, or just engage you in TIME-WASTING conversations.  When you finally do get into the fighting, the game is as linear and paint-by-numbers as you can get.  No freedom.  No multiple routes through an encounter.The cover system is hit-or-miss (Pun intended).  Sometimes it feels like your controller is broken when you try to maneuver Agent Carter.  Sometimes the camera angle is horrible and you get shot from mystery angles or just cannot see your foes, the battlefield, your allies.Half the voice actors are good, half are laughably bad.  And that is sort of the theme with this game: half is good, half is horribly bad.The game play is otherwise fun.  Most of the time.  It's a basic 3rd person squad shooter.  You can order your men around, using a few specific class skills in each encounter that, once used, require time to be used again.  The soldiers follow your orders, but often get killed anyway.The aliens are very cool to look at, and they have some unpredictable moves that will surprise you.  You fight some fun enemies, even though the idea that you can take them down with bullets is laughable.  For example, you fight an alien dropship.  With rifles.  And win.  Let's be honest: with those materials, the aliens should not have gotten through our atmosphere let alone through a battle with 1960's Earthling weapons.Overall it's OK.  Nothing novel, except the aliens.  Story is drab.  Lots of wasted time.  Lots of missed opportunities and lack of freedom during game play.  But when you do play, it is fun.  Not Gears of War fun.  Not Hitman: Absolution fun.  Not XCOM: EU or XCOM: EW fun.  Definitely not.  But mindless, pass-the-time fun.

This game is an interesting concept, and something that really hasn't been done before.  The whole game is basically a GTA sort of concept, but in reverse.  However, just because you like GTA games, does not mean you will like this.  Instead of being able to do whatever you want, and wreak havoc on the world, this game closely monitors and prevents the player from doing things that it does not want.  Let me say, I did not buy this game expecting it to be a GTA, nor do I play game like this immaturely.  In GTa, you hijack cars, in LA Noire you politely ask the occupants to leave.  In GTA you are a hoodlum outside of the law, in LA Noire you are a policeman/detective.  In GTA you can, at any time whip out a rocket launcher and blow people up, and get police called after you, in LA Noire, you cannot access your firearm unless the story mission automatically pulls it out for you, or lets you access it, and you can slam into police cars and nothing happens since you, yourself are a detective.  Furthermore, if you are looking for another game to cause havoc in, this isn't it.  Partly because you cannot access your weapons unless told to do so, but also if you hit a pedestrian with a vehicle, you will lose ratings upon completing the mission, and in some cases, if you hit a few pedestrians, you will fail the mission and have to restart.  See where I am going?  So if you are buying this game for someone who acts immature with these types of games, and just wants a GTA to just run people over, hit other drivers, and blow people up, this game is not that in any way.  Basically, it is a GTA for responsible, more mature players.However, while the concept interested me, as I never have had a game where you need to determine if someone is lying or not, and then prove to them why they are lying, find clues and such, I was pretty let down upon actually playing it.  This game is very difficult to play ,and therefore is not very enjoyable.  I do not know how you are expected to play this game correctly without a walkthrough.  Sometimes, there are even items around a crime scene that do not have anything to do with the crime!  In many cases, when interviewing a suspect, you need to select why they are lying, but your selections although make sense, are not the correct choice.  Or even, having to remember every little detail about the entire mission, and remembering who told you what and why, in order to succeed in investigations or interrogations, and this is very frustrating and not very enjoyable.  Halfway through the game, I used a walkthrough just to be able to find all the clues, go where I needed to go in order, and know when an individual was lying or not, and how to prove it.  And car chases?  forget about it - speeding through tight alleyways and around corners is impossible without slamming into other cars, buildings, or hitting pedestrians.  It isn't even fair sometimes.Very difficult game to play, very tedious, and rather inappropriate.  I am in my 20's, and seeing naked women lying on the ground covered in blood made me a little uncomfortable too, so this is a game I would definitely not recommend buying for those below the M rating.  And even getting achievements can be frustrating, as there were times, such as getting a fleeing suspect to stop with a warning shot, that I had the opportunity to get the achievement, but I was not allowed to have my gun out.  Very frustrating game, and I do not believe it is possible to do well without cheating.

"SAW: The Video Game" was not a perfect game by any means, but it was still well made and had some elements to it that could potentially be redone and enhanced in a sequel.  However, that sequel, "SAW II: Flesh & Blood," completely ruined everything that was great about the first game.  On the surface, both games may look exactly the same, but dig deeper, and you'll find that they're as different as night and day.  If you're a SAW fanatic, just play the first game and pretend this one doesn't exist.Developed by Zombie Studios and published by Konami, the sequel charges out of the gate with a prologue level as Campbell, a drug addict who has a son.  The very first thing he must do is get free of a Venus Fly Trap by cutting open his face to remove a key that's been implanted below his eye.  As the level draws to a close, Campbell is revealed to have a form of cancer that is terminal, and must make a choice: save himself, or commit suicide in order to save the life of a complete stranger, who's roughly the same age as his son.  Suddenly, the game transitions to the official primary character, Michael Tapp, the son of Detective David Tapp from the first game.  He must investigate his father's death, deal with Jigsaw, and bring a circle of corrupt drug-dealing cops to justice.In the beginning, the game shows a whole lot of potential.  The screen is completely free of any kind of HUD or other information, and your health is measured by a nifty heart-rate monitor mechanic.  When health drops low enough, it starts flashing and beeping, which is the cue to find a health syringe to heal yourself.  Some of the puzzles are also unique and actually require you to use your brain to solve them, an element which is sorely lacking in gaming today.  The graphics, powered by the Unreal Engine, are also pretty good as well, with almost all the surroundings having a dirty, dilapidated, and disgusting appearence that fits the film franchise's atmosphere perfectly.Unfortunetly, everything soon goes on a major downhill slide with no hope for redemption.  One unforgiveable flaw is the pervasiveness of Quick-Time Events in every action sequence.  Whether your dodging an environmental trap or engaging in combat with an enemy, you have to perform QTEs almost every time.  It takes all of the skill and suspense out of everything because pretty much nothing will hurt you without letting you know about it beforehand.  When the most dangerous things you'll encounter are broken glass and acid on the floor, everything's completely messed up beyond repair.  At least the first game provided you with several admittedly creative and cool ways to dispatch your enemies, from setting up traps to brawling with melee weapons.The other serious flaws are in the story and characters.  The prologue section with Campbell was decent, but the rest of the game as Michael reveals that none of the choices you make in the game really matter at all.  The primary characters that you have to save from traps pretty much all end up getting killed later on, either by your hand or someone else's.  What's the point of even saving them if they're just going to end up dying anyway!?  Also, there are two endings to the game, both of which are dictated by whether Campbell lives or dies at the end of the prologue section.  Neither one is concrete or satisfying.  The "Blood" ending ends with both Campbell and Michael dying, and the "Flesh" ending ends with a really poorly-done cliffhanger, where Michael is presented with two options to choose from, then the game just cuts out without even giving the player a chance to choose which one they want.  To add insult to injury, if you want to see both endings, you have to play through the entire game TWO times, instead of just accessing a checkpoint like in the first game!The control system and gameplay mechanics in F&B; has also been completely downgraded and trashed from the first game.  Before, you could run just by pushing the left analog stick forward all the way.  Now, you can only walk, and have to hold down the RB button before you can move at the exact same running speed.  In the first game, you crossed narrow platforms with no problems by using the left thumbstick to move forward and the right thumbstick to keep your balance.  Now, you have to alternate between pulling the Left and Right triggers while using the left thumbstick to slowly inch your way forward, which takes an eternity.  In the first game, David Tapp was knocked out by Pighead and fitted with the shotgun collar, which he was unable to remove.  Here, Michael Tapp sees a shotgun vest and voluntarily puts it on BECAUSE IT HAS A FLASHLIGHT STRAPPED TO THE HOLSTER!  That's one of the absolute dumbest things I've ever seen.  It just emphasizes the cold hard truth that you cannot pick up any alternative light sources in this game, unlike in the first title.This is, without a doubt, one of the worst sequels ever created.  It makes me have much, much greater respect for the first game.  It completely baffles me how both games are from the same developer!  Take my advice: do not play F&B.;  You may think it's alright at first, but once you get far enough in, it's too late.  So, when Jigsaw asks if you want to play a game, you know which one to pick.

This is an above average MMO and it's free now. You don't have to buy the game or pay a subscription fee. Buying the game will get you some kind of Founder status and some miscellaneous freebies for whatever that's worth but you don't have to. Download the game for free and if you like it enough to keep playing it buy some stuff from the cash shop.It seems to me that based on all the freebies I got just for creating an account, actually buying the game isn't really a good investment. I think you get a couple mounts you can either use or sell, some potions and I think some XP boosters but I got all that too, just for downloading the game and creating the account. I got only 1 mount which is a very good mount that I could use at level 1 and even if you didn't get this the game gives you another as a quest reward at level 11. Sure, you can sell the mount(s) for an insane amount of game currency but will you need that much currency so soon that you won't have ample time to earn it? No, you won't nor will you need those XP boosters or any potions you may get. You level like a rocket in this game, get a "care package" of pots or a weapon every 5 levels or so and way overpowered weapons are routinely given to you for free at all stages of the game, via a system of finding the appropriate number of "relic pieces" (monster drops) that makes said OP weapon materialize in your inventory. As for potions, I have used almost none in this game yet and the ones I have used have all been either during a big solo boss fight or just as a convenience because I didn't feel like waiting for the regen.The leveling in this game, in my opinion, is entirely too fast and I don't understand why developers are making games this way. I've been playing this game for about two weeks and I'm 8 levels away from the cap already! Anything but the most trivial investment in your gear before reaching the cap is a near complete waste because especially pre-40 you can conceivably go thru 2 complete gear sets in no more than a day, if you play that hard. Even if you don't, you're still going to fly thru the levels.So, I say get the game for free and support it via cash shop purchases if you like it.Regarding the game itself, I mostly like it. The fighting mechanic is good, although at higher levels it does begin substituting a fair amount of cheapness in lieu of properly designing the mobs to become exponentially more challenging. They DO become more of a challenge but it isn't all due to design. Examples would be multi-cast attacks only hitting the target once, shield blocking animations working but failing to block frontal attacks, knockback attacks knocking enemies behind instead of in front of you and failed hit detection; i.e., your attack goes right thru the mob while causing no damage. Perhaps some of this is due to poor programming (like hit detection) but the issues of the shield blocking and the backwards knockback is something that I definitely did not experience until later levels and yes, I watch for this type of stuff in every game I play.Also regarding the combat system, while I like the way it plays some classes fair better with it than others. I haven't played every class in the game but I have played 5 of them (Lancer, Sorcerer, Warrior, Slayer, Berserker) which ought to be enough to form a reliable opinion. Classes like the Lancer are very tight and intuitive while others like the Slayer and Warrior often come off clumsy and you find yourself missing a lot of attacks while rooted in place, flailing about with your weapon(s) at a target that has long since moved out of your hit reticle due to an overly long casting time and the fact that once you key the attack you cannot readjust your direction. The problem here is usually the casting time, not so much the rooting, however, there are times when you CAN adjust your direction to follow the target before you attack but all too frequently the direction of the attack does not follow suit.The casting time also creates an additional problem that has a lot to do with an inconsistency in the programming. This isn't going to be easy to explain but I'll try to as best I can. Tera has attack chains. They're pretty good chains too and you can even swap around different attacks to customize them but you have to be careful because certain chains apply a casting time negation to the follow-up attack that you can lose if you replace it with the wrong one. The problem is that the transition from one attack into another sometimes takes so long (due to casting and recovery animation) that the attack is wasted because your target simply moves out of the hit reticle, interrupts the attack or recovers from his condition (let's say, stun) before the stupid animation gets finished and the chain actually goes off. This problem is compounded by the inconsistency in how long it takes to transition from one attack to another (sometimes it's very fast and other times you may as well have keyed them as completely separate attacks) and when exactly the chain prompt appears on your screen. For some chains the prompt for the second attack will appear immediately upon initiating the first attack, while for some other chains there will be a pause of up to 3 seconds before the prompt appears which renders this chain basically useless. There is also an inconsistency with the amount of time the prompt is visible and thus usable. The default time is 4 seconds but I have seen the prompt routinely disappear in as little as 1-2 seconds for no reason at all.These things aren't game-breakers but they do take away from fluidity of the combat when they happen (and they happen rather frequently)and for a game that makes a big deal about it's combat system these things are pretty inexcusable and should have been polished out a long time ago.You'll find one or two other issues with the combat system as well and while the specifics have more than a few rough edges, it's a good system on the whole.And because nothing in the world is perfect let me file one more additional complaint: the movement speed handicap aka "combat movement speed". Basically, you have one movement speed out of combat that slows to about half that when you are IN combat. This, to me, is simply an AI cheat (because this handicap is applied only to the player and not the AI enemy) and the pinnacle of idiotic game mechanics only employed by lazy developers. The fanboys like to call it a "debuff" but this is incorrect. A debuff implies that your speed was artificially higher due to a bonus stat (buff) applied to you somehow that was removed by an enemy's skill or an environmental factor, hence the prefix "de" attached to "buff". This is not the case, therefore the so-called combat movement speed is a handicap, plain and simple. If one were too fanboyish to call it what it is - a handicap, the proper alternative term would be "nerf".People like to argue the proper usage of "debuff" all day long but it really doesn't matter. Anyone that ever took (and passed) a 5th grade English class understands what the "de" prefix means and why we use it in the first place. And no, kiddies, the fact that you've been using this word improperly for so long doesn't make any difference. A player is not DEbuffed unless they first had a buff to BE debuffed. After you learn this please also stop using the non-words "dat", "doe" and "meh". They make anyone that uses them sound like idiots.Anyway....The graphics are great and the maps are varied and beautiful. My only complaint here woud be too much time spent on snow maps but that's just a preference issue. Tera has some unique map designs and mobs to go with them. Mobs like the circus-like Jack in the Box jester/vampire and witches, etc. styled in the same manner. That's only one example but you get the idea and most of the mobs are equally well-designed. Of course, there's the obligatory wolves, pigs and panthers but those are just filler mobs and not worth mentioning beyond that point.The dungeons are okay. Nothing spectacular and they're designed for group play because thankfully Tera designed it's classes so that each class is unique and important unlike, say, Guild Wars 2 where everybody is essentially the same with the only difference being skill animations and armour type. I hate Guild Wars 2! Don't even get me started!Never done any crafting or PvP in this game so I can't say anything about that. This is my PvE game. When I want to PvP or spend insane sums of money to craft something nobody wants to buy I play Aion.Now, for you parents thinking of getting this for your kids or letting them play it, you may want to read this part. This game is M-rated and very heavy on exposed female flesh. For me it's fine but I'm 40 years old. Just know that it's there in massive amounts.Also, this game has to have the worst, most profane and juvenile community I have ever experienced. Hardly one sentence is spoken that isn't laced with a cussword, usually beginning with the letter F. It's atrocious and the community is my biggest gripe with this game. Never before have I seen such unchecked poor behavior in an online game and I have no idea what I'm going to do when my blocklist of foulmouthed 14 year olds is full, which is fast about to happen. I haven't found anywhere in the chat or general game options any sort of profanity filter either so I guess the only option is to stay in a tab that the entire community isn't using.The fanboys and the degenerates that act this way will say that it isn't any different than any other MMO but this is a lie. Not even Guild Wars 2 is this bad and judging by the Tera player community I'd say it's well on it's way to replacing that game as the Romper Room of MMOs. Why it's this way and why Enmasse doesn't do anything to police it, since these people apparently don't have the either the decency or the self-awareness to police themselves is beyond me but this is the way it is.In the end, the game itself is pretty good minus a few technical quirks that should have been ironed out long before now and the apathetic attitude concerning a very, very large portion of the players that make the chat seem like a live-taping of The Jerry Springer Show or perhaps a typical day in any classroom of the modern day public "school" system.

It might be possible to run-and-gun your way through DEHR but to do so would be to miss the point of the game. DEHR is all about stealth, hacking, persuasion, and cautious combat. And it does all this very well. There’s also a fully realised story that has much more depth than most games. It’s also worth noting the soundtrack, which is very atmospheric throughout (and somewhat redolent of Blade Runner at times). The visuals are a mixed bag, however, with impressive environments but often disappointing character models and animation. And the colour palette is rather muted and bland. The worst aspect of the game, however, is the inventory, which is bafflingly annoying: it rather pointlessly forces you to shuffle things around in order to fit all the items in. I really don’t see the point of this as it adds nothing to the game. There is also no real variation in the environments visited during the game; it’s basically one urban landscape after another. These may seem like minor criticisms but when combined they were enough to dampen my enjoyment a little. But having said all that DEHR does what it sets out to do so well that I can forgive it’s few flaws.

I almost gave up on the game.  I was annoyed and ticked and the hacking minigame you have to do a few hundred times was tedious and got on my nerves.  I died repeatedly and was cursing it.  Then...I got to the China level.  It's not that the game improved drastically there, it's that I finally got some upgrades.  After that, smooth sailing.The reason the hacking mechanics are so annoying at first is that it's literally a large measure of pure chance when you're first starting out.  You have to first get up to a skill level to hack level 2 through 5 security systems, but you'll also want to invest in stealth so the random chance of getting caught diminishes and probably fortifying skills so you can protect yourself when the counter attack (the trace) starts up.  You can play the game with minimal hacking skills, but it's more suited to playing with high skills and you'll be rewarded with more bits of the story.  Oh, you can also hack robots and turrets which are sadly fairly limited in number, but are still fun.  I got enhanced strength and at one point carried my "little buddy" around an entire level just plopping him down and letting the turret kill all the enemies.  Yeah it was cheap; yeah it was stupid; it was still highly amusing to be able to.Combat is really well done with a nice cover system that helps the stealth mechanic.  You can also get up close enough to trigger a melee attack that can kill someone outright (don't try it on a boss though) and can be upgraded to kill two at a time, which is danged handy.  You also have access to a nice little Typhoon system which lets you trigger explosives near enemies and if upgraded far enough will even kill robots.Short version, this game is a stealthy one where you can't take too much damage even if you're fully upgraded.  You instead have to rely much on stealth, a hacking mini-game that's based largely on luck, and you have an interesting storyline as you uncover a plot.  The ending you have several choices, though none of them are all that big of a deal.  If you want to see all of them, just save before you make your final choice.  Don't worry, the game tells you when that is.

This game is the latest in a long line of Star Ocean games. Fortunately, you don't need to play any of the older games to understand this one (I've never played the older ones, and I was able to follow the story fine). The game is a turn-based RPG with a few twists.The game takes place in a sci-fi setting, after earth has been ruined by World War III. You are part of a crew tasked with exploring other planets in order to find a suitable new home for humanity to colonize. So there is plenty of sci-fi elements in the game, like starships, travelling between several planets, and advanced weaponry. On the other hand, several of the planets you explore are quite primitive or even completely wild. So the game mixes sci-fi with some more traditional RPG settings, like jungles and little villages.The combat is turn-based, in a manner of speaking. You can freely move your characters around the combat field when you enter a battle. You can attack with one button and then use combos or magical abilities that you have mapped to other buttons. I say it is turn based because there is some delay between your movements. For example, after a combo of attacks, your character can't immediately enter another. It takes a moment, which usually allows an enemy to recover. So while your movement and attacks are fairly free, there is a certain rhythm to combat that can't be interrupted. There are no random battles in the game, as you can see all the enemies moving around on the map. This lets you avoid fights, if you want to.The game has great graphics. Everything is bright and colorful. There is excellent detail in environments, enemies, and character designs. The game has a much more round, anime-inspired look than a game like Final Fantasy XIII, which had more realistic character designs. Still, I enjoy these stylized graphics just as much. They give the characters a cheerful demeanor. The game's environments are enormous. Each planet has several huge areas to explore, sometimes with several dungeons that can be just as large. There is plenty of reason to explore every inch, as you can find treasures and resources. Resources are used to craft items in the game.The game's sound is pretty good. I wouldn't say that there are a lot of stand-out songs, but none of them are bad. They serve their purpose well enough, setting the tone and giving you something pleasant to listen to. But I doubt that many people will remember a lot of the music. The character voices are good enough, too. Some lines of dialogue are delivered a bit awkwardly, though I feel that this was more of an issue with translation. Certain things the characters say just don't sound like something a native English speaker would ever piece together.Overall, I greatly recommend this game to all fans of RPGs. With a neat sci-fi story, massive environments to explore, and a challenging battle system, there is plenty to dig into here. Be aware that parts of the game can actually be very difficult, although you can choose your difficulty setting to make it easier.

I don't move the headphones around much while wearing them, so that is definitely not the problem and the material is comfortable, though it should have been slick or silky smooth instead of a mesh over foam material. Stylistically, this Tomb Raider Trilogy is very different from Tomb Raider 2013, the latest installment of the Tomb Raider video game series.  Tomb Raider 2013 is a facinating game. It is a complete reboot of the series.  It is realistic, brutal, and bloody while the games in this Tomb Raider Trilogy are essentially platform games with fairly simple puzzles and cartoonish gun plays.  The Trilogy consists of three games: Legend, Anniversary, and Underworld.  They are vintage Tomb Raider games with upgraded graphics.  They look great. They entertain the players without the blood and gore violence that keeps some of them awake at night.  The price of nineteen dollars for three games is unbeatable. However, they are not for players who are looking to extend their experience of Tomb Raider 2013.

This PS3 exclusive release packages the first three Tomb Raider games released after the franchise was taken over by Crystal Dynamics.  When I played them on PS2, I was amazed at the increase in quality and richness in the in-game graphics.  When I played them again on the PS3, I was again amazed at the next jump in good graphics.  Unlike other previous generation console ports which have reportedly suffered glitches in sound or gameplay at the expense of higher def graphics, this release preserves the gaming experience precisely and adds that richer touch of realism.  Gameplay for Legend and Anniversary is fluid and identical to the PS2 versions, but Underworld is far superior.  Because TR: U was created for the PS3 and later ported for PS2 (as the console was still in phase-out mode), it lacked a great deal of content—there were very few enemies and many of the puzzles were oversimplified or completely omitted.  I remember being able to tell it was a port because I constantly ran into objects or items that I could tell should be interactive (as they looked different than the background in terms of texture and dimensionality) but were not.  Playing the PS3 version gave me the full experience and I didn’t feel cheated.  Plus I got 3 games for a fraction of what I paid for them originally on the PS2.  This is must have for true TR fans to relive the glory days of Lara Croft!

As a street fighter fan since the original Street Fighter II, I've owned Street Fighter games spanning from the 5th to the 7th generation, even Pocket Fighter and Puzzle Fighter. Street Fighter IV was good, but Super Street Fighter IV Arcade Edition blows the original out of the water with so many new characters that it would take countless hours of gaming to master them all.Currently, I'm only focusing on multiplayer (logged in 50+ hours as of this review) because I didn't bother to play the story mode much seeing that the cpu cheats on harder difficulty. The multiplayer is great, swtiching between SSFIVAE and SSFIV is smooth and quisk, and there's hardly any lag for most games in your region and sometimes elsewhere like Japan, Brazil, Britain, etc. Sadly, noone plays Tournament or Team matches, most players are on Ranked and Endless matches. The ranked matches usually match you against people around your skill level, but there are a few times when you face people that have 4 or 5 times more player points than you, even if you set your parameters to search for people of the same skill. But, I guess it works overall, plus, it's always a nice feeling to beat someone that has much more points than you!All in all, all the characters in this version play differently, even the shoto characters have their own unique characteristics. Some characters feel very cheap, like Seth and Bison, but they are boss characters so it's understandable I guess. But the rest of the characters are very fun to play and test out online. The online community is for the most part, very friendly, there are some players who will constantly taunt you if you are doing bad in a match, but that's your own fault (and if that player is Dan, it's expected). Not many people use voice chat, but endless battle and ranked battles are the closest feeling of fighting your friends (and strangers) on an arcade cabinet.Can't wait for Ultra to be released!

...I like it. It doesn't hold a candle to Dark Souls (I'm not even sure why Dark Souls keeps coming up in the conversation), but it's a relaxing adventure which holds little interest beyond a first playthrough for non-trophy-hunters.Dragon's Dogma concerns the adventures of a nameless character (called the Arisen), as he battles to win back his physical heart from a nameless dragon (called, apparently, the Dragon). I have no idea what the dogma of this dragon is. Most likely, a developer/localization team just thought the word "dogma" sounded cool.The game is a 3rd person affair. You have the choice of 3 initial classes, but this later extends to 9 (6 pure classes, and 3 hybrid classes, assuming my memory serves me). You can pretty much switch classes at will. In fact, this is key to creating the best possible character, stat-wise, in the game, but nothing in the game actually tells you this, and truthfully, it's not that important. You also have helper characters, called Pawns. One pawn is your creation, and you have pretty good control over him/her. For example, you can choose his/her class (although I think pawns only have access to 6 classes). In addition, you are allowed to hire 2 more pawns, of which you have little control. Basically, these pawns fill in the gaps for your party. If you have a friend who has played the game, you can hire that pawn for free. This causes severe balancing issues in the game - I advise against it, unless you are looking for a quick path to platinum. You can also send your pawn out for hire. As s/he progresses, she will learn abilities against particular enemies, and knowledge about particular quests, even if you've never seen these enemies/quests before, which is helpful.Battle is...frenetic. Enemies will swarm you, and your pawns will often do much of the work (particularly on an initial playthrough). Later, you will encounter huge, boss-like enemies that are more readily dispatched with special tactics. It's quite fun, but it can be difficult, particularly if you stray off the road and run into an enemy you are not prepared for.The story is laughably stupid. It's not terrible. It's just...stupid. However, you'll probably lose interest, unless you're a fanboy-in-the-making.The single biggest problem in the game is the difficulty of movement in the overworld. While there is a teleport feature, it's horrible. You have access to a very limited number of gate-type stones (I think you have one, in fact, for most of the game), and the warp stones necessary to utilize them also cost money. If you play through a few times, you see why the developers did this. The game is very short if you have warp speed between towns. I think I beat the whole thing in around 7 hours without really trying, and under 5 when I was trying.There are some bonuses as well. I particularly liked the online dragon. If you play him offline, he's a relatively tough enemy who gives you good loot after defeating him. If you fight him while playing online, he is a holy terror who will likely rip you to shreds unless you have gone through serious preparation. The loot he drops in his online form is awesome (including special armor and masks off legendary heroes such as Beowulf and St. George). I beat him twice myself, which I why I know of those two particular masks.However, outside of this, there is little reason to play the game past an initial playthrough. Unlike Dark Souls, whose New Game + is a great experience, there is absolutely no change in the enemies level or power. You will cut through everything the game has to offer, and if you use your money to purchase gate-type stones (I think they were called "Rift Stones"), you will blow through subsequent playthroughs in record time.For twenty bucks, though, it's not a bad game. I think its "sequel" Dark Arisen was a free game on PS+. Happy gaming!

This game is AWESOME. There really is just no other way to describe it. It's one of those games where it was just so obvious that eventually SOMEbody had to make it, and I'm glad it was Capcom because they do action games right.The story, which isn't terribly long or important, is about your character commanding human-like 'pawns' while you journey to destroy the dragon that stole your heart. ...wait, it's not what it sounds like, I mean it LITERALLY steals your heart. Just up and eats it. After you kill the dragon, much about the world your character lives in is revealed, and the game gets harder.Anyway, story aside, you run around in this game and kill tons of mythical beasts and monsters using a myriad of different character classes, each with its own move sets and skill trees, and you can change classes at basically any inn.Accompanying you are the aforementioned pawns, which are npc's that you share with people online. The cool thing about the pawns is that each one remembers the strategies required to kill certain monsters as they experience them, sharing them with the people online. It's pretty cool to go up against an enormous monster and have one of your pawns shout where the weaknesses are....which brings me to the monsters of this game--they're magnificent. You'll fight chimeras and dragons and cyclopes and griffins and cockatrices, totaling in, I think, something like 80 different species of monsters. Some of them are absolutely colossal, and you actually get to grab onto them and climb around like a mountaineer, which is some of the most fun ever. Many of them are extremely tough, too.Anyway, while I greatly recommend this game, you may want to instead get the expansion, Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen, which adds a whole new continent to the game.

Battlefield follows a very Call of Duty pattern, swapping between Russian and American forces as various groups of soldiers attempt to avert a terrorist nuclear strike.The story is weak, which was a significant let down for me. The main villian has so little involvement, that when you finally see him, you expect him to offer you a grande no whip cappucino rather than be a threat. And theres no motivation thats every explored, so the whole story links together on the thought that some guy somewhere woke up one day and decided that it was a fine day to orchestrate a nuclear event.If you like looking down gunsights, you're already willing to buy this just for the new multiplayer experience, and thats fine. But for a fan of Spec Ops: the Line, which really tries to make the experience more emotional and visceral, you'll be grossly disappointed. You feel as connected to the characters in this as you would to sock puppets. Theres lots of POV moments that're entertaining and even startling, but even when "you" are being executed, you don't feel any regret or remorse or loss. Thats pretty sad considering. The Good: Fantastic combat and gameplay, the slicing engine is fun, graphics are amazing, great soundtrackThe Bad: Extremely short, generic tone throughout, confusing story, enemies repeat often, nothing to do outside of combatThe Metal Gear franchise hasn’t seen too many spin-offs. Acid being the last one. Revengeance puts you in the shoes of Raiden, a cyborg  fighting against other cyborgs for the greater good. The plot is supposed to hover around MGS4, but it’s boiled down to a confusing, and ultimately, uninteresting mess. There’s something going on about children’s brains being harvested for implants and people making money off of war. Raiden is the good guy trying to stop all this, but the game is so short and broken up so much that it’s hard to follow.What is great is all the action. Raiden responds wonderfully and has an array of flashy moves that would put most action adventure games to shame. As you progress through the game you can upgrade your life, fuel cells, weapons, and moves. The whole game pretty much revolves around a slicing engine. When you defeat an enemy enough you can slow down time and use the right analog stick to slice enemies up into ribbons. It’s pretty fun and never really gets old, but it’s sensitive and some times finicky. Boss fights will rely on this and lining up squares can cost you the entire battle if you aren’t quick enough.I honestly wish Platinum never put stealth sections in the game. This isn’t Solid Snake, I want to run around slicing things up. The enemy placement isn’t smart and laid out like a typical Metal Gear game. You get seen most of the time even if you try hard not to. One problem lies in the fact that there’s not much else to do. It’s just wave after wave of enemies and then a boss fight. It also doesn’t help that the game is ridiculously hard outside of easy mode. Even though it took me less than 6.5 hours to finish the game, it was broken up throughout a year of playing. I would spend hours on some areas just because of how hard the game can be. There’s no block button. Let me throw that out there right now. Instead you can dodge and parry which is extremely difficult to get down right. You can die in just a few hits and healing relies on slicing enemies at the right moment and getting there nano strands to fully heal. You must slice them before they hit the ground, this can be really tricky to master.The enemies also repeat often and the game is overly generic in tone. Sure the graphics are fantastic, the music is great, and the action is fast paced and looks amazing. However, the enemies are just generic soldiers and Geckos. The environments nearly all look the same and some boss fights even repeat. I appreciate the difficulty which forces you to master the combat system, but a larger variety of gamplay would have been nice.So the final question is this: Is Revengeance the be all-end all of the action adventure genre? Not likely. Sure it’s up there with some of the better games combat wise, but everything else just falls a bit flat.

Since its release, early adopters of the PlayStation Move have been looking for new experiences tailored to mature and core audiences. The Fight: Lights Out is Sony's first real attempt to cater the PS Move towards these markets by providing violent and gritty bare-knuckle boxing action. Is this game a contender? Or is it destined to take a beating?Starting with a fairly robust character-creation mode, the game immediately follows into a series of unintentionally-hilarious video tutorials hosted by none other than 'Machete himself', actor Danny Trejo. These videos manage to perfectly set the tone for everything else to come -- but not in a good way. From the gritty urban setting to an angry Trejo speaking as if he is passing a kidney stone, the game fails to muster any kind of edginess. It tries to be so tough, but watching Trejo teach you how to fight in an aggressively over-the-top way while waving hot pink and baby blue-lit PS Move controllers, makes it completely impossible to take seriously. The tutorial ends up being much more of a gut-buster than the fighting could ever hope to be. You'll be down for the count, but probably because you're rolling with laughter.After undertaking a laborious calibration process (which happens before every single fight), Trejo will take you step-by-step through all of the basics you will need to learn in order to handle yourself in a fight. These include moving your fighter, ducking and weaving, blocking and throwing punches. These are all fairly self-explanatory, aside from the need to press buttons for certain actions that really shouldn't need buttons. You'd think that blocking would be as simple as holding your dukes up towards your face, but many times we would lose calibration and would have to hold the O button on the PS Move to calibrate the fighter in the right direction again. This can feel extremely unnatural and it'll take some time to get used to pressing it before you think about throwing your hands up.Throwing punches seems like something that'd work quite naturally with the PS Move controller. Unfortunately, this isn't the case. No matter how hard and fast you throw your punches, your on-screen counterpart moves with the speed and precision of a blindfolded senior citizen trying to whack a piñata. I kept finding that while some of the time my punches would hit their target, I'd also have a frustrating amount of my punches go way off the mark. It also doesn't help that even when your punches do connect, they are weak and ineffectual.Moving your fighter involves holding down the Move button and tilting one of your Move controllers either to the sides or forward (Trejo's deadly serious demonstration of how this works is sensational). As the game requires you to stand in the same spot for the entirety of the fight, moving around at all will cause the camera to misplace you, making your punches even more inaccurate than they already are. Add to this the fact that most of opponents keep just walking backwards, or other classic fighting tactics, such as constantly walking around you in a circle and you will be spending much of the fight not punching with one hand because you're holding your controller forward in an effort to catch up.

I love Portal. The universe is both very unique and interesting, but also has lots of small detail and secrets.A continuation to the original Portal, but improved in literally every aspect. The graphics are much better, environments much more detailed, and there's many more new puzzles and tools to use. If you felt the original Portal lacked character, story, or wit, Portal 2 gives you a huge portion of all of those. There's a story that holds together the whole game, not just simple puzzles. Because of this, huge portions of the game are just getting from point A to point B, but the environments and contributions to the back stories these locations give are a treat on their own! These each make room for character development and revealing things that will make you question the entire story in the game.If you are wondering if it will be full of puzzles and chambers to complete, there's a healthy dose of both these and just wandering around, discovering more and more secrets of Aperture. The puzzles do feel a little less difficult than the original, but there's many more interesting ones that for the most part make up for this.It's much longer, and lasts around 10 hours if you rush through it, but I urge you not to do so; this game is riddled with Easter eggs left and right; each connect to very interesting and hard to decipher back stories, or even into the Half-Life universe! I have many theories about the origin of the character or even the whole company due to the various clues the game gives you. I won't reveal any, but I'll just tell you this; check every little writing or seemingly meaningless little script that's given to you; or even yet, go beyond- check behind walls, scout your environment and see if there's anything of interest. Excellent game with amazing hidden stories that change your whole view of the game's universe and storyline.

Portal 2 improves on the original Portal in every regard, and has been expanded into a full size game this time around.For those unfamiliar with Portal, it was released by Valve as something of an experiment as part of the Orange Box package (alongside Half Life 2 and Team Fortress 2), and was so successful that it was rereleased as a standalone title (Portal: Still Alive). In both the original and Portal 2, gameplay involves navigating test chambers using the titular Portal Gun to open portals in the environment while solving physics-based challenges to reach the exit. This simple concept is steadily broadened through new hazards (toxic sludge, turrets, lasers, and more) and other features that increasingly challenge the player to think in progressively more creative ways to reach the goal.The diversity of challenges has been improved with new environmental feature and hazards being combined with features from the first game to diversify the experience. Graphical improvements are present everywhere, and the sound design has been expanded and refined as well over the first title. Controls remain tight, and some remapping has made for a more fluid and ergonomic layout that improves the experience. For the most part, puzzles and challenge ramp up in difficulty and complexity at a steady and reasonably rate, keeping the gameplay fresh. My only real gripe came from some of the later puzzles necessitating standing in very specific and often obscure locations to spot a wall to place a portal on, as in many cases these were not in intuitive locations and quite hard to spot. While the first game did have a basic (yet intriguing) story that moved the game along, Portal 2 expands greatly upon this with an actual cast of amusingly defective characters that never cease to amuse throughout, though the plot is greatly enhanced if you have played the first game.The biggest addition to the package is the cooperative game. Not only does this allow you and a friend to experience Portal gameplay side by side, it moreover goes beyond what the single player of Portal 2 and the original game present. Having two players and four portals allows for even more diverse and challenging scenarios, and your teamwork abilities will be amply challenged (not a game to play with that friend who likes team-killing/trolling therefore). Not to mention the ample choice of expressions and interactions the co-op bots can carry out with one another never get old.Overall then, for a game that will challenge your brain as much as your reflexes and control, Portal 2 provides a challenge to all three, whether you are playing alone or with a friend, and is worth every penny spent.

This game comes with a lot of baggage.  If it were released as a different franchise, I think people wouldn't be nearly so critical of it.  It's a solid game.  Whether or not it appeals to you is another question.  It's a Duke game.  I am perplexed at how many popular franchises have rabid fans because of the "story".  Most shooters don't rely on story much at all and the in-game plot is always lacking for me, regardless of the game.Duke Forever is really no exception.  There is a basic plot within which you plod along from level to level, solving puzzles and defeating bosses.  The graphics are fine.  I didn't notice any real horrible problems with the engine.  The only thing I really had a problem with was Duke's animations.  You don't notice it unless you're checking yourself out in a mirror, but they consciously decided to have Duke's animations mimic the stiff sprite animations from Duke3D.  I'm sure this was on purpose and intended to be a joke/homage, but...I just don't think it plays.  This would annoy me during multiplayer.Other than all of that, the game is replete with references to how awesome the franchise is.  That's part of the charm of the game.  If you're a Duke fan - you really shouldn't pass this up, there's nothing wrong with the game.  If you like shooters in general, I think it's worth checking out as well.

Its not often you come across a game that is fun to play, challenging without being ridiculous, and not so long it seems to go on and on forever. Batman Arkham City is one of those great games where the mix is mystery, darkness, difficulty, and less is more are all combined to make for a winner.I actually had heard of Batman Arkham City a few times since its release. I ignored it as I assumed it to be another boring Batman game. A gift card this past Christmas had me at my local game store and I decided to give it a try. I was not disappointed. Batman Arkham City can be a smaller game if you do not download the Catwoman extras which affords you several levels that are worked in as you play the regular levels of the game. If you choose not to, or cannot download the Catwoman levels, its no big deal, the game will not suffer because of it. I had no means to connect so I played the basic game.Batman Arkham City as has been explained takes place in a section of Gotham that has been sealed off and all criminals set loose within its borders. But be they as it may, these criminals always seem to find a way to wreak havoc of some sort, and Batman gets into the mix. The basic overall story in a nutshell is this. Batman must enter Arkham City to make a rescue and the Joker infects him with a deadly virus and he must get the antidote or he will die. In this pursuit he will have to deal with the like of Joker of course, and also a few other favorites such as Penguin, and Mr Freeze.The whole game is a big puzzle. You must learn how to travel from one end of Arkham to the other. You'll be doing this a lot. You'll also need to learn how to take out enemies, both passive and armed. There are plenty of level up's along the way that apply to Batman's abilities, suit, and the tools he has to work with. As you progress you will gain access to a few advanced weapons. You start out with a very basic arsenal. I liked the idea of realistic basic weapons instead of loading him up with ridiculous weapons you would not see Batman have. Getting into areas of buildings is always a challenge. You have to find the entrances, but getting to them alive is easier said than done. You have to be stealth, and you need to think about your moves and what skills you have available to you.Enemies can be very deadly at times, but none are impossible to defeat with some thinking and learning to use and apply different skills. Use of the Detective Mode is a must to get through the game and help with your ability to apply stealth as you can see your enemies before they see you and you can know which are passive and which are armed. Detective Mode also is your key to finding your goal or your way to that goal. Use it often. Bosses are difficult without being so hard it became frustrating.Travel is either on foot, which can lead to lots of fights as the streets are full of thugs and murderers. Or you can use the roof tops by jumping to gliding. Some areas such as the industrial area are more difficult to get to and require the ability to fly and grapple to get there. Once you get the hang of it, you can travel from one end of the city to the other in a few minutes by gliding and grappling.Puzzles were not overly difficult which was perfect for me, I do not like to waste too much time solving puzzles. There are hints in the game for your benefit in solving a puzzle. Challenges can be well, challenging. Some are easier than others. I found the Gliding sequences in Ra's Al Ghul to be quite frustrating as the gliding and diving doesn't exactly work very well. But it is possible, if I made it anyone can make it!There are side missions of course, and you can choose to play them as they become available, or wait until the end and go back and play them. I chose to play them after I completed the game. That way I had my skills up, and knew how to do most of the things required to get through the missions. One mission is a series of missions based on how many Riddler trophy's you found. SO you may no be able to complete all of that mission depending on how many of those trophy's you picked up. You can go back and collect them if you want, they appear on the map as question marks. Some are just sitting ready to be picked up, others involve some action to get to them.In the end I really enjoyed this game. It was not overly difficult, the stealth game play was fun, and the open world allowed me to pick and choose what I wanted to do at any given time. I'm going to go pick up Asylum and see what the original game was like, I'm hoping it will be as much of a blast as Arkham City.

The Good: Captures the Cold War atmosphere, fun tactical combat, deep character customizationThe Bad: Every battle starts to feel the same, nothing in between to break it up, story is muddled, squad perma-death is frustratingXCOM: Enemy Unknown was one of the best RTS games to come out in years. It had tightly coordinated tactical gameplay that packed a punch and kept you on your toes. The Bureau kind of keeps this idea while bringing you into the dice rolled battles first hand so you can control them. The game takes place after the Cold War where agent William Carter is tasked with helping save the entire planet from an alien invasion. That is one hefty mission, but you have squad mates to bring alongside with you.XCOM is a third person cover based tactical shooter. It pretty much feels like a zoomed in more detailed Enemy Unknown. You will encounter some of the same enemies and the art style is even the same. You can snap into cove and order your squad to do things like lift and enemy up, heal, revive, throw out traps like mines, sharpshoot and enemy etc. You can queue these up while time slows down and watch it all unfold. It's a very powerful tool in this game and can get you out in a pinch. The shooting itself is mediocre. Weapons never feel all that powerful and somehow just feel off. Ammo runs out constantly and you can end up weaponless a lot of the times in a hot firefight. At least the level are well laid out enough for you to find adequate cover and plan your attack.There's really not much else to the game outside of shooting. You move from fight to fight pressing switches or finding intel. The game is a bit on the cinematic side and the opening sequence is pretty awesome. Once your back at HQ you can walk around and talk to people, start side missions, and upgrade your squad and loadout. You get the same death penalty as in Enemy Unknown. A completely leveled up squad member can be lost in battle if you don't revive them in time, however the revive time is way to quick to pass. It's not enough time for someone to go across a battleground and save someone. This becomes frustrating since leveling up takes so long. When you do choose squad members you can choose from Snipers, close combat, medics, and various other classes. This mainly just determines their skill tree.I also found it annoying that weapons are slow to unlock. 25% through the game I only found a few weapons and two alien weapons. There's various other blueprints or tech you can find to turn into other things, but it's not as deep as Enemy Unknown. What's here is solid fun, but it gets repetitive and boring quickly. Every battle turns out the same, you get the occasional boss fight but it just gets so monotonous where there would be more substance. The game looks pretty good on PC, but looks very dated on consoles. It's nothing special, but the attention to detail on the Cold War era atmosphere is pretty awesome and engaging.As it stands, The Bureau is a solid shooter that takes the tactical RTS gameplay and puts you in the driver's seat. The atmosphere is well captured and the skill tree system makes battles easier, but the frustration of perma-loss when a squad member dies is excruciating. The overall combat can get dull and repetitive early on with nothing in between.
