But it sure bothered me.20:53 The Bureau: XCOM Declassified Dev CommentaryIf the alien-invasion plot could keep its act together for the course of its roughly 15-hour campaign and work as a stand-alone alternate universe, I'd be totally willing to ignore that admittedly nit picky continuity issue. Alas, despite one really good idea that cleverly toys with the way we experience games through characters, it completely falls apart. The way main character Agent William Carter reacts to a major revelation is pretty much the exact opposite of what a sane person would probably do in that situation. It's to the point where I have to wonder if a bug might caused the wrong dialogue option to be selected. This isn’t the only inexplicable moment in this baffling story, but it's the most spectacularly weird.What does work, at a basic level at least, is The Bureau’s tactical combat. Like Mass Effect and Brothers in Arms, each mission against the alien invaders is a linearThe Bureau: XCOM DeclassifiedAUGUST 20, 2013The battle of humans against an invading alien force erupts in The Bureau: XCOM Declassified, a new story and unique gameplay experience set inside one of gaming's most storied and beloved franchises.→ MUCH MOREDAN STAPLETON SAYSMore tactful tacticsSpec Ops: The LineBrothers in Arms: Hell's HighwayMass Effect 3 series of encounters where you and the enemy take cover and open fire, then try to maneuver to flank the other team or drive them from cover using grenades and special abilities. Most of those come from the two lightly customizable XCOM agents that accompany Carter on every mission, and each of the four agent classes has a set that unlocks as they level up in combat. They’re mostly useful: abilities like the Sniper’s critical shot and holographic distraction and the Engineer’s deployable turret and land mines can combine into some satisfyingly lethal crossfires and traps.Squaddies are ordered around using a well-done UI, which allows you to easily set waypoints for your squaddies in the super-slowmo Combat Focus mode (somewhat reminiscent of Fallout 3’s VATS), which you can enable at any time. Its biggest aggravation is in how it sometimes refuses to let you throw a weapon without a walkable path to the landing point, but otherwise it’s a very capable tool.In the other corner is a new alien race called the Zujari, a bland race that fights exactly like humans with advanced technology. Their minions – classic XCOM aliens like impish, mouthless sectoids, lumbering mutons, swift silacoid blobs, and flying drones – all have much more character. With several varieties of Zujari, though, the enemy diversity is respectable, and manages to keep fights from going stale too quickly.01:32The Bureau: XCOM Declassified - Battle Focus TrailerHere's where it all falls apart: The concept of squaddie permadeath (borrowed from X-COM: UFO Defense and Enemy Unknown), simply doesn’t work properly in a game with one character that must live. Any situation where a fight went so badly that I wasn’t able to reach a downed squaddie before his bleedout timer expired was so bad I was probably doomed anyway. And when Carter dies, he and any dead squaddies are revived at the checkpoint to try again. It's a bizarre system that punishes partial failure more severely than total failure.Of course, that’s all rendered nearly moot by a revival system that you have to consciously avoid exploiting. Even while they're being pounded on by a huge muton, your two agents can constantly revive each other in an absurd seesaw dance of perpetual near-death. Between those two goofy systems, I lost only two men on my Veteran difficulty playthrough.12:05The Evolution of The Bureau: XCOM DeclassifiedBetween missions you return to base to wander around and converse with other XCOM agents and scientists. The base is large, yet there’s not much to do there other than a couple of simple puzzles. The only thing you need to do there is equip your squad, another key idea borrowed from classic X-COM that’s reduced to pointless busywork by an infinite supply of clearly superior weaponry and a lack of a research mechanic (despite franchise tradition and an entire section of the XCOM base labeled as research labs).Captured alien weapons aren't anything special, either. They have some flashy effects, but they're simply more powerful red- or green-glowing variations of ballistic firearms, and none stands out as the slightest bit distinctive. Even the Blaster Launcher is nothing but a green rocket launcher.I can give the Bureau credit for its 1960s setting, which looks pretty good thanks to fine detail in both the base and the towns and rural farms you’re sent out to liberate. A farm mission stands out as particularly atmospheric, with battles playing out from behind tractors and bales of hay, leading to an unexpected hidden area. Scattered notes and voice recordings from civilians succumbing to an alien virus give it a touch of real creepiness. Characters' faces aren't bad, though not particularly well lip-synced to their mostly wooden voice acting. It's commendable that conversations can play out in dramatically different ways based on early conversation choices, such as whether you play good cop or bad cop in an interrogation. I can’t say I have any desire to replay The Bureau, though.

Let's get right down to it: Far Cry 3 is a LOT of fun to play.  They did a great job in creating this large world (island) for you to explore, enemy AI wasn't spectacular but decent, and the wildlife was unpredictable...where did that komodo dragon come from?!  The combat works very well, and the weapons all feel very satisfying.  There is also a very good "stealth" system, and the close-combat kills are a lot of fun to pull off.The pacing of the story worked well enough, and there were some truly cinematic action setpieces.  There's a kind of RPG-lite leveling system in place that allows you to unlock various upgrades and abilities, and I really liked the way it was designed.  They tried to give the player as much freedom as they could to play the game your way, and tailor your upgrades along the same path.The game isn't without its flaws, however.  The voice-acting was very good, with moments of real talent, but that wasn't due to the writing.  The story and writing through most of the game were nothing special, but then at the very end the writers tried to pull a sudden 180 and make it seem deep and thought-provoking.  Instead it came across as "too little, too late".  Throughout most of the game, I definitely wasn't playing it for the story.Technically speaking, I didn't really encounter any major bugs or glitches with the single-player experience.  I can't say the same for the co-op mode, however, which was riddled with glitches and poor programming.  During a match I would see an enemy spawn out of thin air just a few feet in front of me...on a regular basis.  The "difficulty" felt wildly imbalanced.  I did try the PvP multiplayer as well, and let me first say that I am mediocre when it comes to multiplayer FPS games like this.  With that said, it just felt very generic to me and didn't do anything particularly well or different.  Overall both of the multiplayer types, competitive and co-op, just felt tacked-on, rushed, and completely unnecessary.Bottom line: a great game, a throwaway story, and a multiplayer that some might enjoy but doesn't set itself apart from any of the other FPS multiplayer games available.

Crisis is a great Sci-Fi adventure where you're armed with a nano-suit and an arsenal of weapons.  You must use brute force, stealth, and your wits, to save the Earth from enemies, both extra-terrestrial and domestic.Story: 8/10This is more than a basic, "There are the bad guys, now go kill them" story.  Crysis 3 also takes a look into humanity and self-sacrifice.  You play as Prophet and your mission is to exterminate enemy forces who have set up a militarized zone as well as any alien stragglers left behind from the last game.  Unfortunately, the story is small in scope and there are only a handful of characters.  The story is told mostly in cutscenes and unfortunately, many of the scenes are over-acted.Gameplay: 9/10The gameplay is very tactical and it allows the Player to take on the missions (and optional side missions) any way they choose.  You find generic upgrades in the world and apply those to your nano-suit.  Less powerful upgrades cost 1 to unlock, while the more powerful ones cost 3.  You can have 4 upgrades equipped at any time.  You can also store 3 Sets of 4 Upgrades from your Pause menu and access them with the push of a button.  The upgrades range from Increased Armor, Powerful Melee, Faster Shooting, Faster Running, Longer Stealth, etc...  So, you can use these to customize your play style.  The perks that you use will also evolve and give you additional stat bonuses.  So, if you have an armor perk and you take lots of damage, the armor will evolve to provide increased protection.  If you want to sneak in and ambush enemies, you can use 4 stealth / speed perks.  If you want to charge into battle, you can use health and armor perks.  Complete your missions the way that you want to complete them!Prophet also has an arsenal of weapons: Grenades, Charges, Rockets, Sniper Rifles, Assault Rifles, Short Range Weapons, and a Bow that you can use while in Stealth mode.  You can also hack automated enemy defenses like gun turrets and mine fields and turn them on your enemies.Levels: 8/10The levels are large and offer multiple ways to complete them.  So, you may need to sneak into an enemy base and sabotage 3 power sources.  Start with Stealth and turn the enemy automated guns and mines on your enemies.  Then hide in the shadows... or out in the open with your stealth camouflage and pick off some guards with your bow.  When the enemy forces have been weakened, swap in your Assault Perks and charge them head on to finish them off.  How you accomplish the missions is up to you.Graphics: 10/10There are city levels, alien levels, jungle levels, and enemy base levels.  The lighting, the cloth effects, the special effects, enemies, animations, all look awesome!Sound: 9/10The sound effects are OK.  The SFX punctuate the action and the background music is atmospheric.  But the acting could be better.Maturity: TeenI know the game says M, but this is just a sci-fi war game.  There is some swearing and some blood, but no gore or anything gruesome.  It's no worse than any war movie or cop drama.Replay Value: 9/10The main campaign is only 7 missions long and you can finish it in 6 or 7 hours in the default setting.  You can probably finish it much faster if you don't use stealth.  There are 4 difficulty levels.  In addition to the Single Player Campaign is Vs Multiplayer.  There a many modes to choose from: Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Defend / Assault areas, Capture the Flag.  As you play multiplayer, you can gain XP and level up / customize your character.Overall: 8.5/10Crysis 3 is a great looking, fun FPS, that rewards strategic thinking.  Every mission gives you multiple ways to complete it and you can customize your character to suit your style of play.  Crysis 3 is also really cheap right now at $15.  It's a great deal!

Making over one billion (with a B!) dollars in the first week of its release, Grand Theft Auto 5 is one of the best selling video games, ever. With a title like that, it has to be good, right?Well, good is an understatement.The folks at Rockstar had the courage to have GTA5 star *three* deep and realistic characters, each with their own personalities and interesting quirks. Michael is a middle age bank robber with a long and complicated history outrunning the law. Trevor is a meth-head psychopath who has a desire to decimate anyone who gets in his way. Finally, Franklin is a gangster recruited by Michael to help them with his own backstory and opinions on things. I still haven't decided who my favorite character is, and that is a very, very good thing. Each character feels deep, and even though you wouldn't do any of the things they do in the game in person (I hope), you can't help but actually care for each person. These are some of the best antiheroes ever created, and the trouble they get themselves into is incredibly interesting to play through and watch.Gameplay is MUCH more varied than GTA4.  Instead of the "drive here, kill this, get this" formula there are plenty of clever side missions. If missions aren't your thing, the classic free roaming crime playground is still here on a HUGE map. When you aren't busy with the game's LONG story (which, amazingly, never feels repetitive), you can play tennis, golf or even scuba dive. Upgrading cars and buying properties is still here, but both are more detailed than previous titles.What might be the biggest new feature is Grand Theft Auto Online. In this mode, the huge world of Los Santos opens up to you and 15 friends (or random players) for exploration, racing and death matches. Unfortunately, most of the online content feels unfinished and half-baked. While there is plenty to spend money on, earning it is EXTREMELY difficult.  This has led to lots of people digging for exploits. Only tiny amounts of money can be made from completing missions or robbing small stores.  Sadly this feels like a cheap excuse for Rockstar to say "But you can rob stores for money!"  In addition GTA Online is full of glitches, some of which are harmless and funny, while others break the game.  Exploits that spawn money and change elements harm the experience.While the online content still needs some work, it doesn't detract from the single player's incredible tale and I give GTA5's single player 5 stars for being perfect in all respects and for improving on the previous titles in the series.

In previous GTA games, replaying the story mode could be a drag, but with this one you can be in a different place at any given time for most missions for the end of it. Not to mention most missions allow you to pick out your own crew which also helps with more variety every time. AND, some missions you can switch between your characters making for even more variations for every time you go through it.Second, the online. The online had a bumpy start and I still think Rockstar could have been better prepared, knowing this was going to be the release of the decade, yet failed to be ready for the millions of online users that flooded the servers and crashed them to hell. But they eventually got it up and going and gave everyone a bunch of cash as an apology which was cool. After various patches and little fixes to stop cheaters the online can be fun and frustrating all at once. The new missions that get released as you rank up are cool, and they put out more stuff every now and again, all for free which is cool too, yet I think we are all waiting for the Heist missions to start. I wish there were also more Survival missions as well.The only problem I see with online is that you are at the mercy of other players. You can either all have fun with each other or just pointlessly kill one another, which gets pretty old pretty fast. There is the occasional lag as well as with any online game but at least its nowhere near as bad as Halo. (which will be a thing of the past with the new game ;)Its also a light-year ahead of what GTA4 online was all about too. That fact you can actually get on and do more than just screw around is really cool.One thing I wish they would completely get rid of is having a bounty put on you for stealing a random AI car. Its old and annoying and rather dumb.As far as any issues with the game itself, its hard to find any. The only thing I wish they could have done was do away with the giant mountain in the top of the map and maybe create either Las Vegas or San Fransisco like they did in GTA SA. Rockstar is proud to say its the biggest map they've ever had, and while that is true, only about 30% of the map is of any use. Especially online, you rarely see someone leave the city. Unless they are at the Sandy Shores airport or stealing a jet from the Military base, theres not much to do on the north part of the map at all. Its kind of a bummer. Hell you cant even go to the snowy part of the map unless you find the glitch. I also have not had much encouragement to go play "water" missions. Such as go underwater and stuff. Once you see it, you've kinda seen it all.That reminds me of another thing I really dont like. You cant actually go into either the prison or the military base at all without getting shot to s***. Unless you are on story mode and have the invincible cheat turned on, you are screwed. Even then, the cops will still be trying their best to kill you. Highly annoying. Thats a good 10% of the map right there that we cant even use.So for having the biggest map in any game ever, just know that about 70% of it is a complete bore or useless.I personally would to have loved to see how they could have incorporated either a Las Vegas or San Fransisco like they did in GTA SA like I said before. That could have really been awesome. But who knows what the future holds for GTA games down the road. I hope they decide to go back and do Miami again, and hopefully do San Fransisco too.Other than all that, some honorable mentions are, the new weapon wheel selector and assortment of weapons, variety of cars and ways you can customize each of them, owning property again, overall insanity.Not so honorable mentions are, Map size (most of it useless), music/radio selection, crashing your car and having it explode on impact, bounties for stealing random cars in online.No matter the flaws, it is still one of the best games I have ever played. Besides all the violence, the game is fun as hell and worth it. I just hope that down the road they go back and do a few of the other places we love too. Mainly the other two cities from GTA SA and GTA VC

Alright, in the first few moments of this game, you are treated to a theme song by the heavy, witness an action packed train wreck, and meet pandora's most famous robot. Borderlands 2 is an action packed, super violent, long, hilarious, and just downright screwed up first person shooter/RPG. Known for its large amount of weaponry and addictive co op gameplay. The story centers around one to four (depending on how many players you have.) "vault hunters" as they are called, trying to thwart the maniacal schemings of one of the greatest villains of all time, handsome jack. Jack, who is the CEO of the intergalactic corporation, Hyperion, is trying to awaken a great evil hidden on pandora for millions of years. The overall story, while stereotypical, is one of the smartest I've ever seen. With an unbelievable blend of serious, thought provoking  questions, to goofy, tung in cheek, blow the bad guys head off comedy. Jack however, is just one of the many eccentric characters you'll meet on your journey. Such as the cold hearted arms dealer Marcus, or the super sexy bartender mad moxxi, or the iconic redneck mechanic scooter. There are also a lot of playable characters as well. Four original characters, and two add on characters. There's Axton the versatile commando, maya the phase walking siren, Salvador, the badass gunzerker, and zer0 the mysterious space ninja assassin. (See what I mean about tung in cheek?) each class has their own special abilities like in the first game, such as zeros' ability to become invisible and increase damage. Their are also plenty of nostalgic throwbacks to the first game, so prepare to reminisce. The graphics are great. Classic cel shaded borderlands. I would recommend installing it to your hard drive though, because there can be a lot of texture issues. The sound is great. Everything from a psycho midget screaming about his face gravy, to hearing scooter exclaim "catch a ride!". Voice acting from the main cast is great as well with daemon Clarke getting a VGX award for handsome jack. The gameplay is great. Smooth as silk for anyone who has played a FPS before. Also looting has never been as fun with the wide variety of weapons you can find on your adventure. Though the violence takes a step down from the last game, (you can't completely blow peoples heads off.) it's still way over the top. But it's animated so it's not that bad. There's also some sexual reference if that bothers you. I would recommend it for 15+. So we have a great story, fun characters, great co op, great acting, and just overall fun. If that sounds like a fun time, then you'll really enjoy Borderlands 2!Story: 10/10Handsome Jack became CEO of the Hyperion Corporation and took credit for everything good that happened in Borderlands 1. He declared himself dictator of Pandora, and remodeled the city after his own ego. As you and your fellow Vault Hunters enter Pandora, Jack tries to blow you up.  Throughout the game he constantly insults you!  He's more full of douchebaggery than the entire cast of Archer. You must take down Jack and restore 'relative' order to Pandora. On your mission, you'll meet all sorts of 'Violently Psychotic Redneck-Type Characters'; and they're hilarious.Gameplay: 9/10Go to town, get some quests, head out into the wastes, and kill stuff. Then, get the loot, sell it, get better weapons, upgrade your character and kill more stuff. Play solo or with friends!The shooting mechanics are similar to Call of Duty where one trigger zooms, and the other fires. Your characters get special attacks and stat upgrades that are upgradeable through a skill tree. You can also carry very customizable grenades. You'll fight through hordes of enemies, sub-bosses, and some pretty powerful main bosses. The AI is pretty straightforward. Enemies will charge at you, some take cover and shoot, and some have powerful abilities.If your HP reach zero, you don't die immediately. Instead, you fall to the ground. If you can kill any enemy before you bleed out (via timer) you are revived with some shields and some health. Or a party member can aid you, so you don't have to die, respawn, and lamely run back to the battle in shame.Upgrades and Loot: 10/10Borderlands is famous for its weaponry. There are different weapon types: Pistol, Submachine Gun, Shotgun, Rifle, Sniper Rifle, and Rocket Launchers. They all have randomly generated stats and special perks: Damage, Accuracy, Fire Rate, Reload Time, Magazine Size, Special Damage Type, Damage per second, and chance for that special damage type to affect enemies. (Fire guns make the enemies catch fire.)There are different types of guns best suited for the types of enemies that you face. Electric guns are great against shields, Fire is especially good against flesh, Corrosive is great against armor, and explosive hurts every enemy type.Grenades and Shields also have a ton of statistics and perks. Grenade modifications include the way they are deployed, their damage, their explosive radius, and damage type. Shields have a damage absorb, a delay to recharge, and a speed in which it recharges as well as extra perks like damage reflect, absorb ammo, Max Health Increase...The beauty of this system, is that you'll always have pretty good guns for any given situation, but you'll always want better guns. So, if you have a super awesome rare shotgun with corrosive damage, you will own all enemy robots at close range. But if you have to engage enemy snipers or rocket troops, you'll be at a disadvantage. If you pick up a sniper rifle with fire damage, you'll do much better. As you progress to the harder areas of the game, even your favorite gun will need to be swapped out for something better.You start the game, with 2 quick swap gun slots and a backpack so you can carry more guns. Throughout the game, you can upgrade up to 4 gun slots by leveling up.Borderlands 2 also features a special currency that allows you increase the Maximum amount of Ammo that you can carry for each gun and the amount of items in your backpack. This currency is extremely valuable and you appreciate it when you find it.There are two types of vehicles in the game, too. You can spawn 2 at a time and teleport directly to them. Vehicle combat is kind of fun, but definitely takes a back seat to the running and gunning.Graphics: 9/10Who needs Assassin's Creed Graphics, when you've got style? Borderlands 2 isn't the best looking game, but it has style. It looks like a graphic novel come to life. Because the game doesn't take itself seriously and it's really fun, the graphics help create a fun environment.Sound: 10/10The voice acting, battle effects, and soundtrack are all GREAT!Maturity: MThis is like an ultra-violent graphic novel with sick humor. It's not for kids. It's perfect for older teens, though.Replay Value: 10/10The game has 4 Playable Characters, it's Single Player or Co-Op, and it will take 30-50 hours to finish, depending on how many side quests that you do. Once you finish, you unlock a New Game+ mode where you can play it again on a tougher difficulty, but keep your current weapons and continue leveling up. Borderlands 2 is selling for $10-$20 right now and that's a great deal!Overall: 10/10If you just want to have a great time shooting bad guys, upgrading your character, and laughing at twisted jokes, then this is the game for you! The shooting does get a bit repetitive after a while, but it's easy to forgive the game when a slain enemy drops a powerful weapon that rounds out your arsenal. You'll get at least 30 hours of fun for less than a dollar an hour!

AC3 had some big shoes to fill after the knockout the Ezio trilogy was, and that's what people seem to hate most about it: it wasn't another game about Ezio. It's not a perfect game, but most of its issues stem from growing pains as the series transitions to a new control scheme, the addition of naval combat, a revision of the Assassin recruiting-and-summoning system and a new protagonist in Connor.The most condemning faults of the game can be found in glitches that, while not game-breaking, are still largely noticeable, mostly with visual cues. If you transition areas too suddenly, textures fail to render promptly and correctly, often requiring an additional moment of time to load. There was another instance where a visual effect meant to immerse the player lingered beyond the mission it had been intended for, which was only fixed by resetting the game.The ending is also a point of contention. The quality of the 'final boss' of each AC game has decreased from the first, to the point where AC3 doesn't even bother trying; Connor's story comes to an abrupt ending, which is very disappointing.Still, the game is much better than cynics will lead you to believe. If you're still in doubt, buy the game used from an Amazon vendor; you get the double bonus of not spending full price on a game, and not feeding money to a sexist-revisionist company like Ubisoft.

Assassin's Creed has become well known in the gaming scene for its large, detailed open worlds with simple-yet-addictive button mashing gameplay. The familiar white hood returns again, this time during the American Revolutionary War. But is this year's entry in the series as memorable as previous ones?AC 3 stars Connor, a Native American who seeks revenge on the people who have destroyed his home, while also starring Desmond Miles in the present/future. I never was a big fan of Desmond's story; I always felt it was there to "pull you out" of the meat of the game. It is better than previous games (more action based, less rambling) and has some decent twists and turns, but Connor's story is significantly less memorable than Ezio's and Altier's of the previous games. While Ezio was witty, clever, and charming, and Altier was serious but likable, Connor's dialogue is flat and boring. And with a few exceptions involving Connor's tribe being destroyed, he does little to pull the player into the game's large and incredibly detailed world (which is awesome to both play in and look at). That being said, I'm a huge fan of the game's time period, and it put a smile on my face seeing Connor interact with some of the war's significant leaders and soldiers alike.The game's signature block-then-strike gameplay returns, and it flows better than previous games, allowing you to tackle multiple attacking foes at once. The incredibly gory takedowns also return, but are MUCH more varied, and are a treat to watch. This makes the repetitive gameplay seem less so, even if most of the weapons feel the same with different animations. The naval battles in this game are better than most FULL PIRATE games (to the point they made the fourth game into one). Anyone who buys this game and skips these are SERIOUSLY missing out, because they are probably my favorite part of the game. Other side quests involve finding random chests in the woods (boring), a deep hunting system (very fun!), and building up a small town to earn you more money later on (missed opportunity here, I felt it was shallow and a chore to do). There are a LOT of things to do in this game when the main story is done putting you to sleep. The multiplayer returns from previous games, with a few new game modes to change it up. Most of these work, and it is a fun distraction from the game's lengthy single player campaign.Fans of the series have probably bought this one, but for people looking for a fun, open world to mess around with, Assassin's Creed 3 is a good game.

First, AC3 feels least like Assassin’s Creed game. From the overly specific full synchronization mission objectives to the walk-between-cutscenes missions, the player is stripped of the sandbox style of play. The game forces you to play a predetermined style, which rids of the fun. In fact, the entire game plays out like you are more of a soldier than an Assassin.Connor is the least strong of the AC characters and I actually found him quite annoying. The game is rather shallow in that it does not delve at all into the Creed or Brotherhood, but only that it exists and is there to stop the Templars.The game lacks any polish. First, the game suffers from poor mechanics. Fluidity and consistency are the biggest problems. While there is the random ledge grabbing and haphazard horse controls, the combat is the biggest misstep. I use to love the combat, but in AC3 it is tiresome. The counters work like half the time. The gunplay ruins any flow. I died so many cheap deaths because of the odd mechanics. Second, there are more glitches in bugs in this game than in any other game I’ve played, which is sad for a blockbuster franchise like AC.Next, the extras do not tie into the game whatsoever. I completed the game without doing any extras. I did not find them fun and rather unnecessary unlike previous installments where I did everything. They were not explained well. Also, I did not see weapon upgrades or costume upgrades.Other serious complaints are the rather terrible fast-travel between zones, strange menu design, and the insanely long 4 hour tutorial at the beginning of the game.The Assassin’s Creed franchise is one of my favorites and AC2 is one of my favorite games of all time. I found so much disappointment and squandered potential with AC3.

The original "Sniper: Ghost Warrior" was a decent game, but it suffered from numerous design issues that ultimately decreased its quality and enjoyment.  Also, the "sniper" and "ghost" aspects were ignored in some places, in favor of run-n-gun assault rifle sections.  However, the second game lives up to its title in every way, and is heads and shoulders above the first in terms of production quality.  It almost doesn't seem like a sequel in the same series, but rather a completely different game altogether.Developed and published by City Interactive, SGW2 moves away from the singular tropical country of Isle Trueno from the first game and takes on a much more daring and adventurous format.  Spanning exotic locations like the Phillipines, Bosnia, and different countries and even different time periods, the overall story is centered around a rogue American soldier and his Eastern European terrorist friends attempting to sell an extremely powerful bio-weapon to the highest bidder.  As elite sniper Cole Anderson, your job is to save the world one hollowed-out noggin and slit throat at a time.The first thing you notice about this game is just how amazing everything looks and controls.  Where the first game was powered by the Chrome Engine 4, this game is powered by Crytek's CryEngine 3, and the difference is massive.  The graphics are extremely amazing and beautiful, and the controls and animations are smooth and incredibly realistic.  Also, in the first game where you were allowed to exchange your sniper rifle for an assault rifle, you only have 3 weapons in SGW2: a sniper rifle, a silenced pistol, and a non-throwable combat knife.  This emphasizes that it's a pure sniping game all the way through and nothing else.However, the best thing that's been changed is the stealth system.  In the first game, a meter would fill up as an enemy was about to spot you, but you had no idea who exactly it was.  Also, there was several sections where alerting any enemy automatically resulted in mission failure.  All those mistakes have been eliminated in SGW2.  As the meter fills up, it indicates the exact direction of who is about to spot you, so you can safely duck back behind solid cover.  And if enemies spot you, the mission doesn't automatically end; you're able to shoot it out with them and possibly win.Playing this game on Hard difficulty is the only way to truly appreciate just how much better it is.  The lower settings hightlight the enemies in red, place marks over their heads, and even show where exactly the bullet will land when adjusted for distance, wind, heartrate, and gravity.  On Hard, all of that is eliminated.  You have to manually keep track of enemies, as well as judging for yourself where exactly the bullet will land based on the above factors.  Not to mention that enemies have better accuracy, can deal much more damage, and have heightened awareness and reaction times.

Far Cry 3 is a first person shooter set in a vast open world on an island in the Pacific Ocean. Basically while on a vacation trip you (Jason Brody) and your friends decide to go sky diving. They land on the island whose inhabitants vary from normal villagers, wild animals, and a bunch of pirates led by Vaas (he's the guy on the game's cover) who take you captive and hold you for ransom. His plans are to get ransom money from your parents and then sell you to slavery. But you, with help from your brother, escape and now the real fun begins as you travel the island in search of your friends. Eventually you meet up with the group who opposes Vaas and the pirates they are known as the Rakyat's. Upon leveling up and completing missions you earn different tattoos which in turn give you different abilities which are focused around stealth takedowns, assault takedowns, and long range takedowns. An example would be say there's two enemies and you sneak up on the first and silently kill him with your knife then you throw the knife into the second enemy.Along the way you will meet allies and many enemies. The story is pretty deep and each character is well developed in my opinion. It is very interesting to see Jason's transformation over the course of the game. There will be plenty of twists and turns in the story and it will probably take you around 20 hours to complete. I think the vast amount of wild life is really cool just to name a few there's alligators, leopards, wild boars and there's even sharks. Along with the wildlife there is a lot of different weapons to use one which will become a favorite is probably the bow and arrow. While playing the campaign there will be optional objectives to do such as finding collectables, killing certain members of the pirates, hunting specific animals and doing Rakyat Trials.Additionally to the single player main campaign there is also a side campaign which can be done in co-op and it is much shorter missions focused around a different group of people. And there is also online multiplayer although it doesn't compare to any of the blockbuster games that come out now it is still enjoyable for a while.I would highly recommend this game purely for the main campaign. Although I find little replay value in it, it is still a lot of fun. If you can rent it or grab it for less than $20 I don't think you'll regret it. My overall review would be 4.5/5 stars.

Too many sandbox games are bad for your health - probably. At one time they were new to the industry, an exciting and new formula in the first days of GTA, the formula of which has seeped into the ingredients of today’s gaming blockbusters. This broke barriers in terms of how restricted video games were with their “levels” and sequential structure. Around the mid-2000’s, sandbox was no longer intriguing, and had the potential to bore players to death by permitting aimless wandering with no direction of the character or storyline.Far Cry 2 actually had many gamers highly annoyed at some of its features, which are no longer an issue. The world actually feels like its breathing, pumping blood around its tropical veins – whereas the former was a body on the brink of death. A huge part of the atmosphere stems from the addition of animals and their AI, which is at its best convincing not only as to suspend disbelief but also to occupy the player during the many treks over the map. Hunting animals allows materials to be created to carry more ammo or objects. Leaves can also be combined from plants which enhance the players ability for a short while (more specifically, by injecting syringes into your veins). The player can paraglide off mountains which overlook harsh seas while the sun sets in the distance. Crops can be set on fire and the terrain burns to ashes. It’s all atmospheric, engrossing stuff.The storyline is not the best, but perfectly acceptable. As a twenty-something male, you go on holiday with a bunch of almost-alcoholic friends who end up being kidnapped by modern-day Pirates Of The Caribbean enthusiasts. Escaping their grasp, the campaign consists of finding your friends who are located somewhere within the two large islands. Your character goes from being nothing to a full-force fighting machine by the end with the aid of an XP system which allows perks to be activated to change how the game plays. The game is addictive though, and allows you to gain all the perks before long. Even with all the perks and upgrades, the difficulty level never promotes you to a god, which is important as to make the game sustain its challenges.As expected, the campaign has several different mission types, which for a sandbox game didn’t seem unreasonable or predictable in any shape or form. The missions are completely relevant to the storyline which chugs along nicely. It’s also hugely eventful without reverting to “EXPlOsIoNS!!!” Drugs play a part of the game and allow the player to hallucinate in some cut-scenes, and some playable areas too – this is intriguing and improves the pacing of the story from stark seriousness to the plain weird and exciting.Outposts are back in Far Cry 3, and play heavy relevance to ranking up of your character, as without performing them using a certain method, new abilities can’t be unlocked. Stealth is encouraged, although definitely harder to perfect than using the guns blazing approach. Enemies can be marked by sighting them with your camera, at which point you can view them through walls. They can be influenced by throwing rocks, where they can be silently melee killed– although doing this anywhere near conscious enemies fails as their bodies can’t be disposed of once they fall. Alarms can be called unless you cleverly disable them first which ensues in havoc. Once you unlock silenced weapons, stealth does become easier but many players will choose to take the messy route at least after the stealth perks are unlocked.The selection of weapons is impressive. New guns can be unlocked by collecting “hidden” items such as Relics and Letters Of The Lost scattered around the map. That this is completely optional does provide rewards for players who wish to experience all of the game. Achievements are perfectly laid out and players are enticed into completing all the activities by experiencing all the optional features. There are hunting quests, hitman quests, as well as other trials that break up the main story.Visually, the graphics are something else, definitely the best we have seen this generation. Very reminiscent of 2007’s Crysis. This was a game which tested PC’s to their limit and honestly – the first title I’ve ever played where the graphics completely made the game. FC3 does this also with sights which can and will make your jaw drop over its stunning beauty. It’s expertly done, and makes the game great to look at all times. How FC3 does this with minimal load times and slow down, is incredible. The fetching landscape consists of tropical terrain, with a classic colour pallet - lush green, sky blue and sandy yellow. It’s definitely nice to look at not just for this but the fact the textures are highly detailed and the effects are fetching.The campaign lasted me a good twenty hours, which is rare nowadays – I even rushed through several parts to grab some achievements. To complete all the side-quests and extra activities (which are optional), you could probably squeeze a good thirty-five hours out of Far Cry 3.Overall, this is a title which has been overlooked by many, but captivated me with a surprisingly fresh campaign, incredible graphics and addictive XP system which consumed many of my hours. Well worth a buy.

There is an indescribable exhilaration that comes with being let loose on a tropical island armed with a locker full of weapons to fight pirates, skin tigers, and ride ATVs off a cliff into shark infested waters.  Far Cry 3 successfully delivers its promise of an open world sandbox of tropical mayhem while also delivering a memorable, at times even thought-provoking story with a strong backing in classical themes of survival and madness.  This was my first Far Cry game and I must say it leaves a lasting impression.The plot of Far Cry 3 feels very much like a contemporary version of Heart of Darkness with the protagonist journeying deeper and deeper into madness, encountering increasingly mad characters and situations the further he goes.  Of course the standout character is the game's antagonist, and poster child Vaas, who captures the protagonist and his friends with the intent of selling them into slavery.  Motion capture performer and voice actor Michael Mando really knocks it out of the park portraying this mentally unstable pirate, making for one of the most memorable video game characters of the last decade.I'm not a game critic, so I can't speak much of the gameplay other than to say it works and is a lot of fun.  Far Cry 3 combines the best elements of the FPS genre, open world sandbox gameplay with the exploration of Tomb Raider, and the level progression of an RPG.  The graphics are impressive for the Xbox 360, and I never encountered any game breaking glitches or bugs.If you're looking for a fun single-player FPS experience that offers freedom, open world exploration, and an interesting plot full of memorable character you definitely should give Far Cry 3 a play.P.S.: If you enjoy 1980s sci-fi action films the downloadable game "Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon" is worth checking out.

The Good: Fantastic graphics and sound, tight and balanced gun play, new enemies are fun, lots of fun new weapons, meaty multiplayer suiteThe Bad: Confusing story, campaign is repetitive and unbalanced, feels too similar to other HalosThe Halo series is probably one of the most repetitive and unchanging series I have ever played. The first 3 were pretty good and Reach and ODST made me fall asleep. With Bungie out of the picture and 343 Industries into the captain’s chair I figured Halo may have some great new changes. I was half right. The single player campaign is pretty fun and is as tough as nails. The new weapons are awesome to shoot and there’s new enemies for once that are different. The story is convoluted and confusing, but hardcore fans may be able to follow it okay.The mechanics are pretty much the same as previous Halo games. There’s no iron sights, the game is fast paced with high jumping and fast sprinting. There’s still no cover system which is a shame and the game is damn hard. I felt the story was a bit random and the environments felt the same way. One minute I’m shooting the same tired Covenant then these machine type aliens, then mutated Covenant, then regular Covenant. There was some vehicle sections and I was riding a giant vehicle. The game just felt all over the place, but it was fun at least.The story is really confusing and never makes much sense. Something about Cortana being infected and a giant being called the Didact trying to destroy everything. It’s nothing fancy or sophisticated but you can’t expect much from an FPS. At least the game just feels tighter and a bit more heavy feeling and less floaty than other Halos. I felt the weapons had weight to them and the sheer variety had me switching them up all the time for different situations. I did find that there were repetitive scenarios through the whole game like jump into stations to hit a button at the top and running back down to get to the next one. This scenario repeated often through the whole game and felt archaic and overly simple.While the structured campaign felt old and tired the multiplayer is still the best part of Halo. The constantly updated match types makes you come back for more all the time. The game feels faster paced and just more fluid and balanced than any previous Halo game. Customization is deep for your avatar, there are many levels to climb, and the unlocks are sweet and rewarding. After you beat the Halo campaign just once I doubt you will ever go back because of how forgettable and repetitive it feels. I honestly think at this point Halo should just continue as a multiplayer only game and maybe jump on board with PC.The few little tweaks here and there help the game just become more balanced overall. The lack of duel wielding makes the game feel more raw and “hardcore”, various adjustments in damage from each weapon and the increased damage for melee attacks is nice. I also love how great the game looks. This is the best looking Xbox 360 game out and the voice acting and animations are so life like. However, the Xbox 360 doesn’t have the processing power as the PS3 so you won’t see The Last of Us quality textures and lighting effects. There are some ugly textures in Halo 4 and it really showed some times. Surprisingly there wasn’t any slow down or glitches that plagued other Halo games.Overall, Halo 4 is a great final opus for the 360 but isn’t the revolutionary new Halo like everyone thought. The campaign is repetitive, extremely difficult, and confusing, the story is so-so, but the multiplayer is where the meat of the game is at.

So, I bought this game back in November of 2012 (for $4.99, if memory serves), and finally just got around to giving it the chance I'd meant to give it since then (I have a tendency of doing this; I'll download a dozen games at once, and some inevitably get shelved for a while, if not forever).  Well, I can safely say that, being a huge sci-fi fan who gravitates toward first-person shooters (there ain't no "stealth" here...and thank God for that...), while I wish I hadn't waited this long to play the game (its second birthday was yesterday), I'm glad I finally did.  Why?  While nothing revolutionary, it's pretty darn cool as a gaming experience.  Let's dive in, shall we?For those who don't know, the game takes place in 2069, in New York, Los Angeles, as well as a man-made paradise in the middle of the North Atlantic (a la "Elysium").  Not a post-apocalyptic rendition of the future, per se, but a "Blade Runner"-esque rendition; a post-modernistic vision of ridiculously bright neon, mile-high skyscrapers, and division of "wealth" to the extreme, where the wealthy are indicated by bionic implants (namely chips that permit super-human mental functioning).  It's very, very cool, and frankly, I can't imagine any fan of sci-fi not being impressed by it.  The game also "looks" amazing, in spite of the game requiring very little GPU power; with two 670s, I'm able to render the game at 4K (downsampled to 1080p), easily maintaining 60fps at all times (all settings maxed).  The game's art is extremely impressive, made all the better by nifty lighting effects, etc., that really help to add to the atmosphere of the environment that you're in.  (Some complained of the "bloom" utilized here, but for me, it adds to the experience, given how colorful and bright the environments are.)Second, the weapon selection, somehow, is fairly inventive and unique; you'll have the standard shotgun, CQB subs, assault rifles, rocket launchers, flamethrowers, etc., but much more interestingly, a "gauss" gun whose bullets steer toward enemies you've locked onto (it can't hit something three feet in front of you if you're not locked on), a rifle that shoots through any and all walls (provided you're in "bullet-time" mode, which this game handles better than most), a laser (to the extreme) that instantly blasts through shielded enemies, etc.  Gunplay is very satisfying, and handled as well or better than most shooters on the market (it's reminiscent of Chronicles of Riddick; no surprise, given that they're both Starbreeze creations).Third, there are three "breach" abilities that permit the player to effectively disrupt or take control of enemies; they include "suicide," where an enemy will self-detonate, taking any enemies within proximity with him, "backfire," which causes the enemy's weapon to explode, knocking said enemy to the ground (causing a stun effect, as well as to reduce "hit points"), and persuade, which causes an enemy to turn on his fellow soldiers (when all enemies are dead, the affected soldier will commit suicide).  These truly do add to strategy, and I only wish that more "breach" modes had been made available; hopefully, we'll see more in a a sequel.Finally, the game is of good length; there are twenty "milestones" that comprise chapters (by fifteen, I figured each of the next would be the last; all-in-all, around an eight-hour campaign), and there are numerous old-school "boss fights" strewn throughout for good measure.  Further, there is a co-op mode (that I can't comment on), which presumably extends replayability that much more.In summary, if you're a fan of sci-fi in the vein of Blade Runner (and who isn't), as well as first-person shooters, this game is for you!

I put off playing these games for years for various reasons.  I'm glad I did, because I greatly enjoyed marathoning them in one go recently.  I had a hard time getting into the first game, primarily because of the clunky controls and baffling UI design.  I almost gave up on it several times, but it was slowly endearing itself to me.  By the time I got to the end of the first game, I was pretty well hooked.  By the time I got to the end of the second game, I was devoted.  At the end of the third game, I was holding back tears.The writing in these games is top notch.  I cared for each member of my crew like they were real friends and family.  I felt responsible for their safety and when I would occasionally let them down, it devastated me.  I can't imagine what kind of emotional wreck I'd have been if I'd failed to protect Liara or Tali.  It would have broken me.What I'm getting at is that the writers have done an incredible job giving the player a real emotional attachment to the story, the characters, and the world.  Even if the freedom of choice in the games is often illusory, it still feels like your decisions have real weight to them.  I often sat thinking about the wider implications of my choices for minutes before nervously committing myself.  Most of the time, it's easy to tell what choices will have the desired outcome, but that isn't always the case, and when this game decides to hit you with consequences, it usually means something heartbreaking.  But that just makes your triumphs all the more sweet.That's where the 5 stars go.  The writing.. and also the superb soundtrack.If I were judging these games for their combat alone, they would score pretty low.  I think the combat in Mass Effect 1 is some of the worst I've ever seen.  It's vastly improved in the sequels and is almost really fun at times, but it's very rough and unpolished, with terrible controls (on keyboard and mouse, anyway) and often extremely frustrating.Regardless of this, and many other frustrating elements of the games, they're absolutely worth playing.  It's one of those things where I feel like I'm somehow a better person for having experienced it.And now let's talk about the DLC.  The story DLC for the second and third games are all essential to me.  They're not all necessarily worth what they're charging for them, but I wouldn't want to play without them.  There are many key pieces of story contained in them, and many essential crew interactions involved in them that I have to recommend getting them.  You'll miss out on whole crew members/squadmates if you don't have them and I can't really imagine how some of those gaps would otherwise be filled.  I say they're mandatory.  You can skip the weapon packs, though.  You won't need them.

When first hearing about the Ouya, I thought it would be awesome, to have a micro console compete with the big boys. With cool retro games, neat android set up, and the fact most or all games are free to try, for $100 it was a no brainer for me.Now I own both PS4 and Xbox One, so my two stars is not because I tried to compare it to those dudes, this review is solely judging the Ouya and Ouya alone.Packaging-------Box came in great shape, neat looking colors and material, very stream line and modern and definitely conjures the curiosity of any techie. The controller and system are the first thing you see and just those two alone. Very neat and clean, the system itself can't no bigger than  a softball. Underneath all that in  a separate compartment is the manual, which basically tells you to just plug it in and nothing else, a decent hdmi cable and the power.Controller-------The controller is pretty sharp looking, button placement is decent, very heavy nod to the xbox. There is tons of plastic covering on the controller that'll take a bit to take it all off the nooks and crannys. Referring to what I said about the manual, there is no info on how to install the batteries that are included. I just happened to remember from a YouTube  unboxing that you had to take the top gray plates on the left and right side of the controller off, which just pops and snaps, then install both batteries on each side.The middle "U" button turns on the a Ouya system when it's in sleep mode, and very easy to sync. One thing I didn't know is the middle area of the controller also serves as a mouse pad which you'll see a cursor spring up when you start running your finger along it.The top of the of the controller has two bumpers and two triggers, I've yet to see any game utilize all, but it's pretty neat for a small system.System-------After the initial boot, you'll be asked to create an account which will require a linked credit card. Then you're in. It will probably come in with a free demo and then the rest is up to you.You'll have choices to discover, make (more for developers, but some third party apps you can put here as well) then of course system options and settings.The discover section is like any App Store, google play, etc. You can check out top rated, new, trending etc. The list go on forever, the search function isn't that great, but you can get deeper in there and go by genre.For the most part, the simpler games run pretty flawless but it can get into major drag with the more heavy graphical games. See pro / cons belowThere are some cool streaming apps, no Netflix or prime, but you can use XMBC or Plex to stream your personal stuff which is a neat feature.Now for the breakdownPros------The concept of what they want to achieve is a huge proGreat looking little consoleController is pretty decent for this price point.Clean interfaceFast set upTons of gamesCons-------The system itself so far as specs slacks, with the older tegra, this system is already coming in brand new with a "last year" vibe and specsLots of games drop on frame rate drastically, choppiness and sluggish throughoutThe controller itself will have weird and awkward delays and not sync once you get past only 9 feet away, which is pretty standard for most couch to TV.My controller, I can't speak for everyone else, the left stick was squeaking bad and catching, like it needed W40 and to be re-screwed. I troubleshooted it myself and tried some things, but it kept on.The games with exception of a few seem like an afterthought for the ouya with heavy focus for the cell phone.And maybe just personal opinion, but the power cord being so high on the back makes it hard to keep cords stream lined and out of sight.Wifi is really slow to download. If you got a game over 500mb, even with a decent network, expect to be waiting a bit.The system could have been great, I think a lot of people that backed them on kick starter and have been following like myself, are pretty upset with how this console turned out. The OUYA gets a whole lot of bad press, and I honestly don't know why. Maybe it's the unrealistic expectations of the early adopters. Maybe it's the deluge of promises from OUYA that it would cause a tidal wave of disruption to a stagnant gaming industry. Maybe it's an unimpressed, jaded gaming press that doesn't care unless your hardware has the latest GPU installed. Maybe it has something to do with how thus far, OUYA's marketing has basically alienated the mainstream gamer with a "we don't need you" mantra when the fact is, in order to sell enough units, they really do need them. Regardless of what it is, I find myself liking OUYA's little gaming box, even if it does have a lot of rough edges. I like rough edges.To be fair, the OUYA has had its issues. The controller lag made a lot of games unplayable (this has largely been taken care of thanks to tons of software updates), the lack of native streaming apps for Netflix and Hulu make it a hard sell as a streaming box for most people (no matter how well XBMC works), wireless performance has been horrid for some (though I've oddly had no issues with my release-day unit), 8GB just simply isn't enough storage for most users (this has been remedied, again through software updates, although the external storage features are still in open beta) and a lot of the games people want to play just aren't on the platform (though that's a selling point for some it seems). Whether these are negatives for you will really depend on what you're looking for, but if nothing else, it shows that the OUYA team is committed to resolving issues, as the little box is a whole lot more stable now than it was from day one.Streaming is a mixed bag on the OUYA. My personal experience with XBMC (XBox Media Center for the uninitiated, which these days has very little to actually do with the XBox) streaming via TVersity has been a positive one, as it's largely been able to playback most everything that I've thrown at it. Some files have required me to re-rip/re-encode them, but that's an issue on any box. The lack of native apps for Netflix and Hulu remains an issue and one of the most glaring ones available for the platform. If those were available, the OUYA would be an easy sell as an Apple TV or Roku alternative, but without them, XBMC alone just isn't enough. You can sideload apps for those services, as I've done, but the touchscreen interfaces those Android apps were designed for just doesn't make for a great experience with the OUYA's controller. Sideloading is also something the average consumer just isn't going to want to have to do. If someone wants to go out and buy a media box for their HDTV, they want something that's going to work right out of the box. They're not going to want to have to jump through the hoops that sideloading demands.OUYA is kind of difficult to wholeheartedly recommend as a gaming box as well, not because I don't like the gaming experience (I do), but because a lot of the "indie" games available for it just aren't that great. I love the platform for some of the obscure indie (and even free) titles that are available (Bombsquad, Maldita Castilla, Donkey Me and Amazing Frog! come to mind), but a lot of other standout OUYA titles are also available on other platforms (Sine Mora, Saturday Morning RPG, TowerFall, Final Fantasy III, 100 Rogues, The Cave, etc.). That OUYA has released a platform where anyone can make a console game with minimal financial overhead and a streamlined means of releasing titles on their marketplace is great and a boon for indie developers getting their feet wet on console development, but having them continue development for OUYA after that might prove difficult given the comparatively small customer base (something you need to sell more OUYA boxes to improve).All that said, and as negative as it might sound, for $99, the OUYA is still kind of hard to resist. It might not be the best at accomplishing any one function, but a small $99 box that will stream media, play games, provide a stable development platform to indie developers and give customers the ability to sideload any number of Android apps to it is still going to provide a whole lot of entertainment (and learning) to a whole lot of people. Whether or not that number of people is ultimately large enough to continue OUYA's "disruption" of the gaming industry remains to be seen, but I'm hoping that they'll be able to carve out as much of a niche in the current generation as they can so that they can ultimately stick around for some time to come. As long as they're part of the game (a sometimes cutthroat industry that's scene once-great console makers like Atari and Sega fall to the wayside), they'll have a chance to make those dreams of disruption a reality.

For all of its promise, the Ouya falls victim to design missteps, poor performance, and a critical lack of compelling content. With the potential to improve, the product as it exists today misses the mark.The system is also marred by a number of technical issues. Under the hood, the Ouya has 1GB of RAM, 8GB of local storage, and runs on Nvidia's Tegra 3 processor -- a generation behind the latest model, the Tegra 4. While more than capable of running 2D platformers and even some more taxing 3D titles like Shadowgun at 720p or 1080p, performance is completely inconsistent. Some games run smoothly, others start to get choppy during action sequences and firefights. The system even struggles to handle the load of the primary UI at times, freezing up or producing a noticeable delay while scrolling.And then there's the controller.The Ouya's take on a traditional gamepad is an impressive effort, but has some glaring performance and ergonomic issues. The design has dense rounded grips that blend into a flat base with squarish corners. While the 4-way d-pad, action buttons, and analogs feel good, there is often noticeable delay between commands and on-screen actions. Some games perform better than others, but the Ouya can't compete with the precision of higher end game systems. Whereas the Xbox 360 gamepad or DualShock 3 have shoulder buttons that conform to your index fingers, the Ouya's are wide with hard edges. Subsequently, I  felt my fingers strugling to make fast taps.Like the DualShock 4, the Ouya features an integrated trackpad, but there are few apps or games that make use of it. While a centered Ouya button will take you back to the dashboard, the controller lacks a pause button or any dedicated method for bringing up contextual menus. As a result, game developers have been left to assign the role to one of the action buttons, but there's no standardized assignment. In some cases it's the O button, in others, it's the A. The complete lack of a dedicated button or established alternative seems like an absurd oversight. Better coordination with developers could resolve the problem, but for now, it ruins the user experience.Overall if the price drops It wouldn't be a bad pick up

First things first; if you want to play multiplayer, you need an online pass, which is $10. So add $10 to the price tag you see here on Amazon that's so attractive (should be around $5 now) and think about that. You can just buy the single- or multi-player campaigns for PSN separately for about that. So if you absolutely don't think you care about one mode or the other, might as well just download this puppy on the PSN. Just sayin'. Online passes, yo. They were a thing.So a significant portion of Starhawk isn't available right off the bat. What DO you get here in this package? Unfortunately, not much. And what's here is really uneven. Starhawk is a 3rd person shooter who's uniqueness hinges on the titular (incredibly cool & well-realized) Starhawk, a transforming star fighter in the vein of Robotech's Veritech/Macross' Valkyrie fighters. Which would be totally original on PS3, if it weren't for all the other excellent shooters with transforming robot-planes in them, like Transformers: Fall of Cybertron or A.C.E.-R (Japan import). I mean, there's no region lock on the PS3, so you can grab all sorts of great mecha shooters on the platform from Japan. Transformers FoC though? That is the one that absolutely kills Starhawk for me. I'll get to that later...So what we have here is a solid 3rd person shooter with an interesting aesthetic; this bizarre 70/30 space western (70% dusty western mining story, 30% space opera). There's no cover system, but who cares - that's worn out at this point anyway. It's solid. There's not really any interesting weaponry - you got your pistol, your machine gun, your rocket launcher, your shotgun, etc. Starhawk differentiates itself by borrowing the "drop structures and items from the sky" mechanic seen in other games like The Outfit or Section 8: Prejudice. It's done... okay, here. Your AI companions are boneheads though, so don't expect them to always take advantage of what you're dropping. And don't expect to always have the energy you need to actually build cool stuff the first time you go through missions. Heck, don't even expect to have many options here - the campaign acts a tutorial, so to make sure you know what each unit does, you can only build the 3 or 4 things each level wants you to use. Lame. By the time it finally opens up, the campaign is literally over - it's VERY short. Build & Battle could've been amazing, but everything is too dumb - it seems the developers were far too eager to get to multiplayer and ignore coding good Artificial Intelligence. It's insane that an action RTS from the early 00's like Battlezone, Urban Assault or Uprising had more interesting "build structures and lead AI friends into battle" mechanics than a game from today. It's a real shame.Anyway, the rest of the campaign? What are the coolest parts? The parts with the Starhawk, of course. Unfortunately they're few and far between; the emphasis is clearly on the ground-based action, which is pretty forgettable. It's standard modern shooter stuff; you can drop a few turrets and walls, but otherwise, it's like a dumb Halo. Move to the next point with dumb AI buddies, defend something, ride in a hover bike or Warthog (called the "Razorback" here... y'know, another word for Warthog? Very clever) to the next point, repeat.The thing is, while mostly standard, the Starhawk elevates the campaign so much when it appears! So the few times they DO get it right, it's exhilarating. It's genuinely amazing how it changes the level designs - you'll find yourself flying around these orbital platforms engaged in intense dogfights (fans of Microsoft's similarly-overlooked Crimson Skies will feel right at home), then land at any point, hop out of the Hawk and you realize these tiny platforms (when viewed from the sky) are fully designed gamespaces that accommodate on-foot battles, complete with a detailed, atmospheric interiors. Then you're pushed back out into space to find another Hawk, and take off once again! It absolutely sucks that THESE moments are the ones they DIDN'T focus on, because these moments are one-of-a-kind and by far the best parts of the game. They're some of the best parts of ANY GAME this generation! That's why Starhawk is so disappointing though; because there are a few moments that show off what this COULD'VE been if the focus had been shifted away from boilerplate 3rd person shooting and dumb, repetitive multiplayer modes, and focused back towards what makes this title unique and memorable. There's a little bit of that here, which just highlights how much worse the rest of the package is.Unlike Transformers Fall of Cybertron - I said I'd get back to that! See, I put off buying Starhawk for a long time because I owned that title already. It's a game with a brilliant, memorable single player campaign and super fun, fully featured multiplayer suite that DOESN'T require an online pass. The on-ground combat is better thanks to more interesting weapons, better mechanics (you can switch if you're aiming over the left or right shoulder in Transformers - you can't in Starhawk here), and the fact that every character in TF doubles as their own transportation. Every multiplayer level also lets you play with a flying character if you want to - something you can't do in all of Starhawk's multiplayer levels (at least going by the "Explore" options). While zooming around as Starscream or whatever isn't as exhilarating as it is screaming around in a Hawk, and feels very different (Starhawk's flying model is MUCH BETTER; Transformers' is much simpler), it's more than good enough. It's such a better package if you're looking for cool transforming robot plane battles and a great 3rd person shooter experience with fantastic multiplayer; I cannot recommend this game when THAT one exists.When I want multiplayer, I will just fire up Transformers. I'd suggest renting this. Starhawk can be AMAZING though; it's just that those moments are too few and far between. If you love multiplayer though? Who knows; it's probably going to be better for you - until, like I said, the servers go offline and/or the community dies. Then you're sitting on a disc that's incredibly light on content.If Lightbox is listening, you should've coded some AI bots, you goons. Let people set up games and just play by themselves in these levels with these vehicles and mechanics. That addition would've added potentially thousands of hours of fun to this package. But because there's no thought at all given to giving solo players anything to do besides wander throughout empty multiplayer levels (seriously?), the multiplayer component is honestly just useless for some people like me who won't buy the online pass. And it's useless for EVERYBODY ELSE eventually, when servers get shut down. What's left is 2-4 hours of a campaign that's just plain disappointing. For the record, I hated the Black & White generation. It had enough pitfalls that really made the game unenjoyable for me and after playing every generation of Pokemon it looked like it would end there. A strong lack of variety in the Pokemon, combined with a very uninspired generation of Pokemon and a somewhat rehashed story from Diamond and Pearl made those games a big letdown from HeartGold and SoulSilver before it. You can easily see a stark contrast in quality and enthusiasm between the two games.Then this game came out and fixed a lot of that. What made this game fun again?- A stronger mix of Pokemon.The game has a much larger mix of Pokemon across all previous generations and while you won't find everything here, it at least gives you a ton of options and doesn't pigeonhole you into using this or that Pokemon because it's the only one available. This was a common issue when I played Black and I'm glad they fixed this right up. Also this game gives you essentially two starter Pokemon with a choice of the Kanto starters a little ways into the game, which opens up even more options for you.- Quality of life improvementsFor years it was either your Running Shoes or your bike, with the bike being too fast, crashing into everything so it was almost faster just to run there instead. This game adds Roller Skates which is a nice medium ground to that; faster than running but not so fast you crash into everything all the time. Exp Share changed from a held item to a general Key Item and affects every Pokemon in your party. This was a gamebreaker for me since in the past you didn't get this thing until much later in the game and only one Pokemon benefited at a time. Makes leveling faster and less monotonous than before. Wonder Trade and GTS off the bat gives you even more Pokemon options than you already have within the game.- Non-worthless side gamesFinally they added ways to interact with your Pokemon that actually has tangible rewards in the game. Pokemon-Amie lets you feed and play with them and gain actual benefits in the game, such as avoiding random attacks, EXP boosts and more. Super Training allows you to do special training with your Pokemon via mini-games that improve their stats.- Fairy, the anti-Dragon.A new type of Pokemon, Fairy, was added and a lot of older Pokemon like Clefairy and Togepi were changed to be included into this type. Someone at Game Freak or Pokemon International finally had enough of Dragons crushing everything so they made a group that was just meant to stop them cold.With all this said the game isn't perfect. 3D battling aside the graphics are only marginally better. The story is pretty much yet another redressed rehash of the previous games. I also found the end-game a bit lacking...no roaming Legendaries or much of any Legendaries at all to catch outside the ones from the current generation. The current generation of Pokemon is only about half as big as the previous generations, which may be way they included so many Pokemon from the past. The game also desperately needs to draw from previous DS games if you want to have any hope of completing the Pokedex.Still, despite these things they are trending up again. They made the game fun again and this is a fine addition to the franchise.

Ah, it's Pokemon! The mere mention of the word evokes feelings of nostalgia in me. If the reader is unfamiliar with the series, it's a type of RPG in which you play a little boy that wants to these catch and train creatures called Pokemon. You train your Pokemon by battling them against other people who have Pokemon, and throughout the course of the game, you collect eight badges and go on to battle the Elite Four, the greatest Pokemon trainers of them all.Pokemon Y is another game like what I just described. If you're looking for an innovative storyline or something, look elsewhere. That's not really what Pokemon is about. It's a game that's built around customization. There are many different types of Pokemon, and you can form your 'party' with any Pokemon you choose. Each individual Pokemon has the ability to learn different types of moves. The player is encouraged to build his or her party in whatever manner they see fit to try and win the game. I think that's why Pokemon is so successful. The customization is great in these games, and Pokemon Y is no exception.Despite that level of customization, Pokemon Y is just a little too linear in terms of where you can go and such. The pathway to the next town is always blocked off until you beat a certain Gym, talk to a certain person, or something like that. Since Pokemon lets you make plenty of choices throughout the game, it's really not as big of a deal as it might be in some other games. However, I'm still not a fan of NPCs popping up to block my path for no apparent reason.Also, you now have this item called "Experience Share' which shares the experience needed to level your Pokemon with all the Pokemon in your party. I turned it off from the start since I'd heard that using it makes your Pokemon too strong. Presumably because of that decision, I approached the end of the game with under-leveled Pokemon. It's actually really challenging if you choose to play it that way.An important thing to mention is just how complicated this game can be. Physical and Special attacks aren't as clearly delineated as they used to be. For example, I had a Tentacruel with a Poison-type attack. In old school Pokemon, Poison attacks were physical and relied upon a given Pokemon's Attack stat. However, it appears that some 'physical' attacks now rely upon Special Attack stats. Then, you've got O-Powers and training stat bags. I don't claim to understand what is going on there. I think the stat bags improve your gains somehow and that the O-Powers are temporary. Back during Generation 1, I had Pokemon down to a science, but I don't really know how a lot of things work in Y. It would an interesting thing to study for younger players who probably have more time to analyze it all than I do. ;)I should add you don't really need to understand all of the specifics to win the game.Finally, you should know that the multiplayer options seem really good for Pokemon X and Y. Since TM moves can be taught to an infinite number of Pokemon now, you can try out a variety of different Pokemon and strategies with impunity. That's a luxury that didn't exist in the older games. You have to love that! It's true that these 'Mega Evolutions' tend to steal the show in multiplayer battles, but I think that's forgivable when you consider the larger experience.So, yeah, Pokemon Y is a really good, really complex, 3DS game. Get it!
