The Classic Controller isn't utilized for any of its "good" games and is mostly used with the virtual console games, not that the Classic Controller didn't suck as well because it did and the GameCube controller was far superior and felt far more comfortable in my hands. The Wii classic controller is really small, has awkward placement of its buttons, is extremely light and feels like it was made from very cheap plastic with no rumble feature, the trigger buttons are awkward, the joysticks are weak and can easily break, and the DPad is stiff and gets stuck during gameplay. The Wii Classic Controller is complete garbage compared to the amazing Nintendo GameCube controller that came out years and years before it.If you have played The Legend of Zelda Twilight Princess on the GameCube, than do not buy a Nintendo Wii and play the Wii version of that game. The Wii controls for Twilight Princess absolutely destroyed a somewhat decent Zelda title. In the Wii version of Twilight Princess you have to keep a floating fairy that corresponds to the position of the Wii Mote with the TV and Sensor Bar, dead center in the middle of the screen or else Link will walk off in another direction and you'll constantly fall off annoying ledges and it will slow you down and reduce the quality of your game play significantly. It'll also make your wrist tired from having to keep it constantly aimed at the center of the screen. I AM APPALLED BY THE AUDACITY, OF THOSE ADVERTISERS ON GAME TRAILERS AND IGN, WHO LIED OUT OF THEIR TEETH ABOUT THE NINTENDO Wii. They made the Wii appear to be something that it was the complete opposite of. They advertised Twilight Princess and made statements about how wonderful the Wii Mote controls are and how good it feels to swing a sword around. LIES! You don't swing a sword around in Twilight Princess, you flick your wrist around and Link moves the sword in correspondence to a predetermined set of directions. The sword doesn't move in the direction you aim it in, it goes in the directions the game aims it in, which is the same exact predetermined set of directions. Using the shield is also annoying because you have to punch with the Nunchuk and it doesn't always work unlike the GameCube version where you press the R button to hit with the shield. Fishing becomes much more needlessly challenging and horseback riding is much worse all because of the Wii Mote and Nunchuk controls. Fishing doesn't feel like fishing at all, despite the lies of the advertisers on IGN and Game Trailers. All you're doing is reeling in the lure by rotating the Nunchuk in a circular motion with the annoying cord of the Nunchuk, I preferred the control stick and A button from the GameCube version. Horse back riding was also destroyed by the Wii Mote and Nunchuk since you have to keep the on screen fairy dead center in the middle of the screen or else the horse will move in another direction slowing you down and running you into obstacles and cliffs. Same thing when controlling the wolf.Super Smash Bros. Brawl is another major disappointment and without a doubt the worst addition to what was a decent fighting game series. Brawl is awful, especially when compared to the original Smash Bros. for the N64; and when compared to Smash Bros. Melee for the GameCube, Brawl is complete garbage. I recently got Brawl and was playing it on my recently purchased Wii U (which is another garbage console but I'm not here to review the Wii U). I had to pay $20 for a Mayflash Nintendo GameCube to Wii U controller adapter (which is another piece of garbage as well) just to play Brawl with "decent" controls because I was playing it with the Wii Mote earlier before this adapter arrived. It's so unbelievably boring and I completely refuse to play through the subspace emissary, all you do is side scroll fighting weird creepy enemies that look like dolls stitched together from old throw pillows (Primid). The adventure mode in melee was much better and much cooler. There's new characters in the game that are completely obscure and uninspired. All the problems that existed in Melee are back tenfold in this game like the clone characters (Ganondorf, Captain Falcon, Fox, Falco, Wolf, etc). Melee's Link was much cooler since his design was based on the Ocarina of Time Link, Brawl's Link is based on the very effeminate and wimpy looking Twilight Princess Link. The graphics hurt my eyes and I'm playing on a Plasma Screen 40 inch Samsung with the Wii U HDMI cable. The way Brawl plays just feels sluggish and slow. It feels like the frame rate has been downgraded immensely and slowed down from Melee. There's no fun factor in Brawl, I've technically only played it for 1 day and I'm ready to sell my Wii U and everything that came with it. I thought for sure this would be the one decent playable Wii game, but it's just as bad as all the others and I won't sit through this abomination. Brawl is virtually unplayable, especially if you've experienced Melee or the original Smash Bros.; Brawl is a disgrace to the series.I was lied to about the Nintendo Wii and no one told me how terrible it really was, otherwise I would have never bought it. All the so called "good" games on the Wii turned out to be complete failures because of the awful Wii Mote and Nunchuk controls. When playing New Super Mario Bros. and Metroid Other M, the control is even worse than in other Wii games. You don't use the Wii Mote and Nunchuk, you use the Wii Mote flipped on it's side. Having just finished the game, I have to say I was satisfied. A couple of caveats for me: I only paid $10 for the game, I have the benefit of all the most recent patches that apparently fixed a lot of the issues, and I am a casual fan of the Alien(s) franchise, from the movies to the old AVP on PC (still need to try the newer one on consoles).Is this a AAA title? Some parts yes, some no. Was it fun? Actually it was, and I don't think Gearbox deserves ALL the hate they have received for this title.Pros--Atmosphere: A number of times I stopped moving and took it all in because of a well placed lighting effect, a large set piece like the giant gunner, or when storming up a hill while a giant ship took off from the planet. The game itself has some great graphics, textures, and environments. Sure, some are reused or modified, but you get the "look" of the series pretty down pat.-Teammates: I sincerely believe you aren't the main character and that O'Neal's story is what you are actually facilitating in the game. He's loud, brash, carries a giant gun, and has tattoos--easy to write off as "Marine #5." He also experiences a unique loss that he cannot prevent, deals with suicidal ideation, and has two situations where he holds lives in his hands and you get to see how that plays out. Not the most unique plot, but still neat to see the interactions and have a buddy to back you up. I also liked having a team of fire squads, especially at the end when you storm the enemy army's encampments and facilities. That's a lot of fun.-Weapons Customization: You earn XP each level that you can transfer into your weapons, adding silencers, scopes, lasers, more ammo, or alternate fire modes. This gives you some progression as you move forward and lets you choose your style of play to some degree. Also, finding the Legendary Weapons in the game is a nice touch, both from an atmosphere perspective and as an Easter Egg one.Cons--Length: Not a lengthy single player game by any means.-Polish: Many small things, such as enemy AI, clipping errors, some of the FMVs, a few confusing level designs, and the abrupt stops between levels take it down a notch. This game needed just a little longer to clean up some minor issues that make the developer look a bit amateur (which we all know is far from the case). I expect this from a new studio, not someone who has been doing this for over a decade.Final Thoughts:I am about to delve into the multiplayer to see how it stacks up, but as a single player bargain bin purchase I would recommend this to fans of shooters with a few hours to kill. I feel bad for folks who paid full price for this one, as they are disappointed. But I had some fun with it, so don't be so quick to dismiss it due to it's rocky presentation to the gaming community.

This review may be late and thus somewhat unnecessary, but I wanted to make up for the fact I had to give Dark of the Moon such a low score.First, if you're not used to shooters where you're being attacked from multiple directions, don't be afraid to play on 'Easy' your first time through. Also, be aware that you will have access to 4 weapons at any one time, 2 in robot mode and 2 in vehicle mode, although Bruticus and Grimlock control a bit differently from the rest. You can also buy power-ups for all of your weapons throughout the game, whenever you come to a Teletraan store.While you can't choose from a small roster of characters in each of the levels like the previous game, each level is custom made for the robot you are controlling at the time. Throughout the game, you'll play as Bumblebee, Optimus Prime, Cliffjumper (who's really just a clone of Bumblebee), Jazz, Vortex, Swindle, Bruticus, Soundwave, Megatron, Starscream, Grimlock, Jetfire, and temporarily as Swoop. Backgrounds are beautifully done for what is now a last generation game, and levels are craftfully made. There is always an indicator pointing to the direction you need to go so most of the time you shouldn't be too lost. There are some crevices where your character can get physically stuck in the game, but a lot of times you can transform or use a 'boost' power to 'unstick' your robot. Unfortunately, I came across a couple of places where the game froze up on me, but it could be the fault of my console, although I bought it in 2009 after most of the 'Red Ring' incidents.The best features of the Cybertron games is how respectful there are to the original G1 Transformers, which means you won't see any Michael Bay influences here. But understand even with G1, you had two continuities: the comic and the TV series, which often gave different backgrounds to characters such as the Dinobots. The Cybertron games just try to take or make the best from each of these sources. Most voices sound spot on- such as Perceptor, Grimlock, and Jazz, while some voices just don't fit the character, such as Cliffjumper.Metroplex is a sight to behold, although you never really get to control him directly. But then you never got to control Omega Supreme or Trypticon from War for Cybertron, so it may have been too hard to figure out a way to implement control of such large characters in the game. Playing as Grimlock is loads of fun though, as you work up his fury to transform him into his powerful T-Rex mode. Another fun touch is that at the end of levels, you are often required to race out of the area before time expires. I hope to see further efforts from High Moon, as the latest Rise of the Dark Spark game from another developer is getting pretty bad reviews.

The original Fate was the PG version of DIABLO: cartoonish graphics, simplified quests, very limited gore and a cute child/hero running, fighting (and fishing!) in armor. The dungeons were endlessly random, the beasts well deserving their fate and the weapons and trinkets imaginative (and surprisingly expensive!). Overall, very fun to play!Its first sequel, Fate: Undiscovered Realms, offered more of the same in a second set of dungeons. And  the second sequel improves little beyond offering yet another set.Very few things are new in this standalone incarnation. True, you can now choose amongst four races (Human, Shadow Elf, Half-Orc and Cogger). The best one is still Human, a true Jack-of-all-trades: Elves are agile but have a very hard time defending themselves; Orcs are clumsy tanks, strong but with low dexterity; whereas Coggers are strong geeks but with no magical abilities.There are new armor sets, new weapons and spells and new pets. On the other hand, I could discern no change in the graphics and sounds compared to the previous installments.Finally, the two previous dungeons each get twenty extra levels to explore and plunder. This is a steal because for the price I remember paying for the first game you now get both the original game and its first expansion. On the other hand, you may find exploring all three dungeons and completing one run-and-fetch quest after another a bit tedious. Nevertheless, it is still good casual fun.RECOMMENDED.

This is a unique action/strategy game in a growing genre of "tower defense hybrids".  Dungeon Defenders breaks the tower defense gametype out of its typical mold, and I have enjoyed it a lot.Unlike other TD-type games, the maps in Dungeon Defenders aren't set up on a grid.  In other words, you can place your defenses anywhere, as long as there's enough room for the defense.  Also, you'll be able to roam around the level, repairing or upgrading defenses, collecting resources from fallen enemies, and even attacking the enemies yourself.I tried the demo over a year ago on PSN, didn't like it, and quickly forgot about it.  The demo does a very poor job of explaining basic game mechanics, and instead just drops you into a level with very little instruction.  It helps to spend a few minutes looking at some basic information online, and you'll be up and playing in no time.  The maps are very well-designed and get fiendishly challenging.  The game comes with four playable classes, and each one plays totally different.  The developers did a great job designing the classes and their different traps and defenses.There are some RPG elements as well.  You can level your character up, and put points into a variety of stats, depending on whether you want a character focused more on dealing direct damage, or one who is focused more on the traps themselves.  The leveling process can feel a little slow at times...it's a gradual but steady increase in your abilities.  With that said, I never felt like I was "grinding" for experience.  I have over 100 hours logged so far, and it's still just as much fun to play, even when my friends aren't available online.If it does start to feel "stale", there is a lot of content here to try out.  In additional to the main campaign levels, which can be played on four different difficulty levels, each of these levels can also be played in a "survival" mode so you can see how long you can last.  You can also enable a "strategy" mode where you rely entirely on your defenses...no attacking allowed!  Furthermore, there is a full set of separate challenge levels with a decent variety of challenge types and difficulties.  And lastly, if you're playing the PC version you'll also have access to a vast array of player-created content to sample.Of the various TD and "hybrid" games that I've tried so far -- Sanctum 1 and 2, Orcs Must Die 1 and 2, Tower Wars, etc -- this one is my favorite.

Since acquiring the Spider-Man license, Activision took a quantum leap in Spidey games with 2000's Spider-Man. That was, unfortunately, followed up by a couple mediocre games until they cranked it up to 11 with 2004's Spider-Man 2. Every game since has tried to duplicate or emulate everything that made that game so enjoyable to varying degrees of success.Amazing Spider-Man is the latest in that lineage, taking place not during but rather immediately following the film of the same name. Of course, they can't help but play up the first movie's plotline somewhat during the course of the game. Returning are all the familiar random crimes: stop a mugging, race someone to the hospital, end a car chase, police shootout, but this time they appear after certain points in the game rather than randomly. Also back are the photo missions, extended past assignments to also including elements within various levels to unlock concept art. Then you also have the racing challenges (with Bruce Campbell making a return to host those) and city collectibles in the form of some 700 comic pages that appear to spawn randomly as you collect others around the city.Differences from previous games include "Web-Rush Mode," a controlled any-direction zip-line which allows the player to slow down time long enough to select a point for Spidey to quickly move to or to strike an enemy. Each level has several items to collect, building up experience points to unlock and fill character upgrades. Coinciding with that are tech upgrades, unlocked by completing secret Osborn Lab missions. Also, rather than the typical comic cover gallery, collecting a certain number of comic pages unlocks a COMPLETE comic book that you can view in the Extras.A welcome surprise was the quick inclusion of alternate costumes. No sooner do you start the game that you receive the Sam Raimi Spider-Man movie costume, allowing you to switch out of that awful new movie one. Instead of all the regular alternate costumes that populate Spidey games, all-new ones from the last few years of Spidey comics are included: Spider-Man 3 Black costume (and an ASM version), Future Foundation, new Scarlet Spider, Big Time from Dan Slott's run, vigilante and a cross-species Spidey variant. There's even a way to unlock a 50th Anniversary party hat which sports the Spidey 50th logo that adorned the comic covers of that year.As expected, the graphics are top notch and the city looks gorgeous with its various times of day and states, depending where you are on the story missions. However, quite a few NYC landmarks are noticeably absent from the city unlike the previous free-roaming entries. The camera also proves to be quite an issue, particularly when trying to wall-crawl, move up buildings or during particular fights. Another problem is that the automation on a lot of movements and commands takes away some of the challenge and player control over the game. The web-swing has been simplified and its physics engine removed, boss fights require a lot of button pushing, and you're even prompted quite often on where to go and how many times. Despite an interesting story, the dialogue tends to run a bit on the painful side.Overall, it's a fun game and a step in the right direction as far as Spidey games go. It's not without its glitches, but it has enough going for it to keep you wanting to play it to completion.

After hearing about/watching its gameplay, with elements like mashing the square button until your fingers hurt (more on that later) and leaning the six axis controller to dodge punches, I was skeptical. However, I had also heard the story of the game is fantastic, and I picked it up at my local retailer.What I got was an immersive and exciting story mixed with dark adult content. The game jumps between four protagonists, ranging from a father who can't seem to have anything go right to an FBI agent sent to discover the truth behind the main villain of the game, the "Origami Killer". The story is long, detailed, and really makes you start to question what makes us human (corruption, guilt, revenge, and hatred are the big motifs here), all accompanied by a great soundtrack and plenty of twists and turns to keep the action going, once it DOES start going.While the writing and voice acting are superb, the rest of the game feels somewhat outdated; some of the animation is spot on, but basic tasks such as walking or picking things up look and feel choppy. Normally I wouldn't mention this, but in a game that relies entirely on its presentation and animation, it makes me feel a little less forgiving. The quick reaction events are usually fine, but the parts of the game that use the six axis feature of the PS3 controller got on my nerves because they force you to sit up straight when I'd rather get in a much more comfortable position. The continuous mashing of buttons does take a toll on your wrist and thumbs.  So make sure to play this one in bursts. I can't speak for the motion controls included as I do not own a PS Move, but they are there if you chose to use them.So, what you get is a great story mixed with some "meh" animation and controls. However, everything Heavy Rain gets right outweighs the things it doesn't, and the story definitely makes it worth your time and money.

I have yet to play all of the Soul Calibur games, but being a fan of Soul Calibur IV, I was pretty exited to get this game. To be fair, I didn't buy it at release and I knew what to expect due to the various reviews and what people said about it. There were many mixed feelings about this game, but overall this is a very good game without some flaws.The first thing you will notice playing this game are the amazing graphics. Bar none, there is not a better looking fighting game than this game right here. I was stunned by the amazing visuals, the smooth animations, and the vivid environments.The next thing you will notice is a change in roster. The old favorites such as Sigfried, Nightmare, Mitsurgi, Ivy, and a few others do return. However for some of the ones who don't, there are new characters that replace them. Unfortunately for the others, there isn't anyone who appears in this game nor has someone to replace their style (Why? I'm not entirely sure). The characters are pretty well balanced, but some of them (especially Z.W.E.I.) are seriously outclassed by others.The combat engine is still amazing and remains to be one of the most accessible fighters on the market. However, there has been a few changes that appeals more towards the mainstream audience rather than hardcore fighting fans. Each character's movelist has been stripped, forcing you to use and see the same moves constantly. Still, there's allot of strategy in the game with the new Soul Gauge meter that you can use to perform Brave Edge (makes your normal attacks stronger) or a Critical Edge (which is basically a super move). Guard Impacts remain, but have been toned down as it drains your meter the more you use it. Offensive play is certainly encouraged while defensive play is punished. I prefer this since it prevents people (especially online) to continuously guard attacks without any repercussions.Now for the modes. Offline mode features a story mode which focuses on Phyrra and Patrokolos who are the children of Sophitia. Both are pretty unlikable characters and the story took me about two hours to complete. The cutscenes are beautifully done, but the storyboards seem out of place. The story is also rushed and pretty bad, so after you beat it you most likely won't play it again. Offline also includes an arcade mode with NO intros or endings to ANY of the characters, but it does feature various routes that you can choose from. There is a Legendary Souls mode, which is basically a very difficult and cheap arcade mode. Quick battle makes you face a bunch of created fighters around the world, and this mode is pretty worthwhile in my opinion. The training mode is pretty detailed offering many options to practice with.The offline content leaves something to be desired, but thankfully the online mode is a blast to play. There are many features included in online along with a very superb netcode. In my experiences, I haven't experienced any delay or bad connections as everything was very smooth. You can set up rivals, watch and download replays, meet new players, set up tournaments, and a bunch of other features. This is certainly where a majority of the effort went to.The character creation is also very superb as it has been expanded on in this release. There is much more to customize, and creating your own fighter certainly has it's own appeal. Your character will mimic one of the other characters, but it is still an incredible feature. You are also given the ability to customize the current roster to your liking.Bottom line, this is a very good game. While the offline content is a bit lacking, I had fun with this title. It might not be as good as the previous Soul Calibur games, but in all honesty it is still worth a purchase especially since the price has now dropped. I don't dance.  At all.  Well, I might do a sidestep, and even snap my fingers quietly if a song REALLY moves me.  But coordination to pull off even basic moves?  None.As I burn through the Kinect catalog, I'm running out of titles that get me up and moving.  I tried Dance Central when there was nothing else at the store that caught my eye.  That was fun, but a little too strict in judging my moves, and a lot of starting and stopping.  I then tried Just Dance 4 based on reviews, and hated it -- more specifically, hated most of the songs, as well as the rapid fire moves that I wasn't given time to learn (don't hate on me if you're a fan of JD.  I'm 45 years old and still stuck in the 80's as far as musical tastes.)I slowly drifted towards the Zumba games.  Since I don't live in a cave, I've heard of Zumba's massive popularity, and decided to dip my toe in with Fitness Rush, and can report I am very, very happy with it.  Even though my girlfriend said I looked like a dancing bear (she's right.  I have zero grace, as stated).I don't know any of the songs on it, but there are very few truly obnoxious ones, unlike Just Dance 4.  But what I love most about it is the repetition, which gives me a chance to learn the moves, HALLELUJAH.  I unfortunately get tripped up constantly by which side I should be moving (and don't get me started on legs and arms moving at the same time), but the game doesn't seem to mind if I get the side wrong.  For that matter, it gives you love even if you're barely moving at all, which is unfortunate, but of course you're only cheating yourself if you don't.Love is in the form of either winning stars or "ecstasy" (bright splashes of lights and different camera angles), but I just did a new song with new moves, and I'm sure I didn't successfully hit a single one, and I think I still pulled off four stars.  Everyone gets a medal (but at least I'm moving and sweating, and that's all that ultimately matters).If you, like me, are a non-dancer, you can probably skip the "tutorial" section as you'll have almost no memory of any of it once the music starts, and you'll pick everything up as you go easily enough.There's a nice mix of low, medium and high intensity songs, though I do wish you could sort by intensity.  I've been doing the short classes.  Mid length classes are twice as long, so I'm terrified to know what a long class is.  But just tonight I discovered the "custom class" feature, which is fantastic (again, would be better if we could sort the songs).  This will let me work up slowly to 10 songs, and also create different playlists to avoid boredom.  There's a nice quick break between songs, just enough for a quick sip or two of water, so you don't lose your momentum but can catch your breath.I don't know if I'll ever not look like a dancing bear, but I'm having fun and getting some great aerobic exercise in my own living room.  What more can you ask from a video game?

I'm one of those gamers who have mixed feelings about ME3. It was probably the best game of the series throughout. The combat was improved, the controls were pretty fluid, and the graphics were a notch higher than that of the other games. The moral choices were even harder to make and the galaxy flight was much improved from ME2 (no more refueling every time you want to visit a new star in the local cluster). Ultimately, you feel like you are making choices that will affect the ending of the universe for better or for worse.--------------Spoilers Below--------------Regardless of your choices, the endings are exactly the same. When I had to choose between the Geth and the Quarians, it kind of tugged at my heart. Can my choice alone really doom an entire race to extinction? When Legion says he was wrong in trusting the organics, it made me feel even worse after allowing the Quarians to win the battle. So in the end, why don't we get any closure on what ultimately happens to the Quarians? Why are all of my choices throughtout the game just thrown out the window in favor of an ending that never really has anything to do with the series?After getting to the Citadel, the creepy little boy that is destroyed by the Reapers at the beginning of ME3 and haunts you throughout the game is there, in AI form. That makes absolutely no sense. Are the Reapers reading Shepard's mind and taking a form Shep recognizes? If they can read Shep's mind, why weren't they able to before this scene.Then we get the few choices for an ending. Let the Reaper's win, and Shepard dies... Uh okay. Let the humans win, and Shepard dies. Well that's kind of anticlimatic. Synthesize the races, but none of Shepard's friends will ever recognize her (isn't this what the Reapers had been doing since the first game anyways).I understand BioWare/EA can't make an ending for every single decision you make in the series, they would have to make 1000 different endings. I'm all for an ending where Shepard dies, we all knew Shep would eventually die. But at least give me some closure to the ending. No matter which ending you choose, you see almost the exact same cutscene. All of Shepard's friends crash land on another planet. What happens to them? Are they stranded there forever? Are they found by the others? Let me know something! I have a lot of imagination, but I didn't sink almost 200 hours into the series to decide what happens to them myself. It's worse than those movies you go pay $10 for and they just have a sudden ending and you don't really understand what happened, and you sit there watching the credits for 5 minutes trying to piece it all together.Yes I feel entitled to a better ending than this, but who wouldn't when they've spent a lot of time and money on a game that just has no closure?

"New Vegas" is a sequel to Fallout 3; itself a sequel to two prior games.  In a nutshell America turns into a sort of future retro 1950's  that erupts into a nuclear war about 2075.  Two hundred years later the survivors come out of the fallout shelters into the new world.In Fallout 3 you started out from a shelter (called a Vault); in "New Vegas" you begin in the outside world, as a courier who is gravely wounded and enters the game as someone with no memory trying to find an identity.Along the way you can make choices, ally with factions, obtain sidekicks, and so on. There is no one way to play the game, nor good or bad choices.  Developers have tried to shy away from having "good and evil" character sets for something more realistic.  In "Mass effect," for example, you can be a Paragon (virtuous but unyielding) or a Renegade (self adsorbed but doing what has to be done).  In "New Vegas" (and the prior Fallout games) you have a negative or positive karma, but it's applied to how certain factions view you, and to please one often ticks off another.It's something developers try to do is make a sequel that is bigger and better than the original. Well they did that, but it may also be the game's downfall. My time on completing it with most quests discovered and siding with one faction was 51 hours, almost twice what it was Fallout 3.  To have tried to see how different faction choices played out would easily added another 20 hours.  Overall I spent a few weeks on it, but looking back I honestly can't say I enjoyed it.  The problems I had with the game are best run off as list:A future where the economy runs on bottle caps (?) and despite 200 years of post apocalypse environment computers are still up and running; a 2075 computer looks an awful lot like 1980.  This was also in Fallout 3.If anything too many quests and complexity.  To get one thing done you have to see someone who gives you three quests, and in turn someone else on one of those quests give you more, and so on.  There is a LOT of searching and looking around, and the pointer telling you where to go is really only good for a general heading in the wasteland.  Many of the vaults and casinos are literally mazes to find your way around in.  This also results in things like you enter a room, surprise someone and get into a fight and kill them, then get a message you failed a quest you were never on as it depends on some decisions you made a few quests ago.Navigating the wasteland can be difficult as you try to get to one place by climbing a ridge and run into a mysterious invisible block as they don't want you getting over it. A lot of "boss" characters have the HHF (Huge Hitpoint Factor) where it takes multiple hits with a grenade launcher or a sniper rifle to take them down, despite looking like any other character in the game.As with Fallout 3 everything has a vague cartoony look and the color palette is a dull somber shading of browns, tans, greens, greys, and so on.  I realize this is a wasteland but still a depressing landscape makes a depressing game.Really?  Follow ons to the Roman Legions and Mongol hordes?The characters are nothing more than general roles (leader, follower, medic, seller, comic, etc.) with a repertoire of canned lines.  That essentially is most video game characters but in many you identify with them as if a from a book or movie, they seem real even if they aren't.  Here it just all runs together.  It doesn't help that so many canned lines are repeated over and over.The ending, however is what finally soured me on the game.  Without giving it away it's a slideshow of about 25 or so vignettes; with from 4 to 6 variations depending on how you played each major part of the game.  Some may never be present if you missed  that set of quests.  Therefore there is no "cutscene" at the ending, and easily a few hundred variations.  Some turn out the way you expected, many were "well if I'd known *that* I would never have played it that way."Basically I entered a confused and uncertain mess, expended an enormous amount of effort, and left the place an even more uncertain mess.  Call it "real" or too much like reality, it felt more like a performance review than ending a game.If you want to see a story done right that is involving, colorful, and still a large world to play in with a surprise ending, look at "Bioshock Infinite."  As it is I doubt I'll play this one again.

Gripe number two is for whatever reason they have defaulted to random events like errors to add "difficulty" in this iteration of the game. While they are certainly present in the console game, they are few and far between and honestly do feel random and more importantly seldom, in the vita version they are used for difficulty. Are you doing to well? or is the difficulty high? then be ready to enjoy multiple throws right over your baseman's heads, and be ready for your fielders to forget how to close their gloves. If you're pitching the odds are no better while your professional pitcher fails time and time again to get his fastball anywhere near the strike box. The result is a game that feels like its cheating you, rather than beating you. My last major gripe with this game is overly small strikebox, this isn't a TV and that screen isn't that big, they could have easily used a little more space and made the strikebox a little bigger, instead you're stuck trying to watch a pixel speeding at you to determine if you should swing or not.Problems aside, the game is playable, and even enjoyable if you don't have your heart set on winning or doing well, which is more up to the occurrence of random events than to your own skill. A game most will immediately look at and call mediocre. In some ways I agree. The story is bad and there are some things that make absolutely no sense. Characters aren't very likable and the villains are pretty lame.The stealth aspect is still there though. If you've played the first game on PS2 or any of the Tenchu games then you know what to expect. Sneak up on enemies in various ways and kill them. It works and it works pretty well. You're given (or you can create) all kinds of tools with which to aid you on missions which are admittedly very short.There are a myriad of stealth kills, however, due to the fast paced nature of the game you'll be seeing the same one or two kill animations often. Others you tend to have to go out of your way to create specific scenarios to witness the other kills. Tools are a blessing and a curse. It's interesting enough to play around with them, but if you so choose, you can make the game a cakewalk by creating bombs that one shot everything.There are also things from the first game that have been omitted in this one. There is no level editor for one thing. Neither in the form of a level editor mode nor the Garden you got in the first game. Also unlike the first game, you have no reason to try and manipulate the warlords to keep the ongoing power struggle to a stalemate. There is no hidden true ending based on how you deal with them. Instead, endings are based on choices you make at certain points during the story. These are incredibly finite and the endings themselves are lackluster at best. There are also maps that have been taken out. This wouldn't be an issue if there were new maps. Sadly there is only one. Some of the old levels do have some additions though.The DLC itself is nothing to write home about either. In fact it throws the stealth aspect out the window and wants you to fight enemies head on that kill you in two or three hits. This wouldn't be nearly as bad as it is if the combat system wasn't so clunky.Story related things aside, there is fun to be had in this game if you're a stealth fan. It doesn't try anything overly complex, the short missions seem to work for handheld purposes, and I personally love the art direction. There are a number of unlockables raging from several skins to recipes you can find to make new items. If you're willing to try everything this game has to offer, replayability is moderately high.

This game is developed by Acquire the same one's who did the original Tenchu games beginning on the Playstation 1.If you are familiar with Tenchu then this is basically what it is.For those unfamiliar, its basically a 3rd person Ninja stealth game where the gameplay involves a lot of sneaking and stealth kills. This game also includes mixing components to create items to help you on your missions.The game is laid out like this:A mission screen is displayed where you can pick an assortment of side missions and a main mission. Most are categorized as Thievery, Robbery, Assassination, Obliteration, Kidnapping and so forth. Each mission is associated with a clan. Performing missions for a certain clan will gain you favor with that clan and diminish other clans in the process. The goal of the game is to play the main missions as well as supporting a clan (or clans) or your choice, doing side missions to further level up your character and farm items.The game plays remarkably the same as all those old Tenchu games which can make it fun but it's hindered by one huge flaw: the controls.The controls in the game in my opinion (and I'm a veteran gamer) require a lot of getting used to. Practice and playing the game frequently will definitely help but even then you will probably still be frustrated at the control system.Moving and sneaking and performing stealth kills are not really the problem. The main problem is controlling the camera and melee combat (which you will be forced to do at some point). The camera is incredibly slow to turn and melee combat is only possible if you hold the left trigger down to lock onto an enemy otherwise you will constantly swing into thin air and it is very difficult turning the camera around on your own to face an attacker. So left trigger hold, moving with the left stick, trying to pull off attacks and move at the same time is very clumsy.Thankfully enemies (and bosses) can be cheaply killed by throwing them\pushing them from a high ledge or over a cliff saving you the torment of melee combat.Overall its an OKAY game that could have been much better if the controls were handled properly. As it is I can recommend it to Tenchu fans but nobody else.

Look, The Witcher 2 is not a bad game, per se, but it misses too many notes in its own genre for my liking. I heard a lot of good things about the Witcher 2 but was not able to try it out since I lacked a pc for gaming. After the Enhanced version came out on the Xbox 360 was available I was finally able to play through it. Personally I think a lot of the praise for it is pretty well deserved. The game play was very challenging, but satisfying. The story is good with great lore and characters to back it up. The visuals were beautiful, making the fantasy world very immersing.You take on the role of Geralt a witcher. The witchers are supernatural warriors with cat-like eyes who hunt monsters and break curses, for a price. Luckily there is no shortage of monsters so work for the witchers never seems to run out. The main story line continues off the first game, (which I haven't tried so I had to tediously read through walls of text to get a basic understanding of the overall setting). Geralt a career monster hunter is dragged along by a king as a glorified body guard. After the king is assassinated Geralt finds himself being blamed for the murder of the king and sets off on a journey to find the real assassin. Though that little bit only scratches the surface of the overall story. The medieval setting feels very true to history. The nobility are pompous and prone to betrayal. The peasantry is bigoted and superstitious. Wars are fought brutally with soldiers behaving more like bandits. While there is a moral choice aspect to the game its not as clear cut as other games like Mass Effect. Good and bad are blurred, and choices you make whether moral or amoral can come back to haunt you. In the end you just have to go with what satisfies you most. Example (Spoilers): In one part of the game you are given the choice to helping a ruthless guerilla fighter by setting him loose, which only seemed fair given that not long before hand he had done your character a favor. Without thinking much of it I let them go. Suddenly when I returned to the settlement that I had been based in for that part of the story you suddenly bare witness to a horrific massacre of innocent people with the release of the terrorist leader being the justification. Unpredictable and yet very realistic. No fairy tale endings in this story.The game play is very challenging, and if you tackle it on the hardest difficulty like I did, it can be downright infuriating on certain parts. Combat especially can be very difficult and unforgiving if not prepared for properly. You'll find yourself dodging and blocking more often than swinging your sword around relentlessly like Kratos. Sometimes it seems pretty straightforward, you use the steel sword on humanoid enemies like bandits, then you use your silver sword on monsters like the undead. Otherwise some strategy is required which sometimes turns into plain trial and error. You have your run of the mill level system as well with various branches that offer their own advantages. Like a branch for combat for more melee damage and better sword combos. An alchemy branch for better potion making skills for medicines or traps. As well as a magic one for better spells. While the difficulty can make some cringe I was pretty satisfied with it. After all fighting werewolves and draugrs shouldn't be a walk in the park. The only tip I can throw in is the Quen sign is extremely helpful when taking on groups.There are a few mini games on the side like dice games and pit fighting, but they are ridiculously easy when compared to the game play of the main plot. In the it was good game and I can't wait for the third release.In summary,The good-A good story and characters, like the moral choice system and different plot-lines you can follow.-Cool over worlds, gives a very authentic medieval feel.-Great graphics, character models look good and so do the monsters, environments are beautiful and life like.-Challenging game playThe bad-Somewhat confusing UI, did without grenades and traps for awhile because I couldn't figure out how to equip them.-Auto save system is bad, so you should save manually often.-Difficulty can become ridiculous in some parts.

I just completed this game last night and am now afforded the ability to browse the reviews on here (I'm a stickler for no spoilers) and formulate my own opinion.I got this game for one main reason - it was billed as an RPG that allows you to make choices that either majorly or moderately affect the world you are in and the story of the main game.  To a certain degree, this was true - but that fact sinks to a watery grave when diluted with the game's other problems.Graphically, the game isn't exactly spectacular - but this is being said in the afterglow of next-gen consoles and I do own an XBox One, so.....perhaps my view is muddied somewhat.  The cutscene graphics are fairly poor, and funnily enough in-game graphics are quite good (comparatively).  But - I can overlook subpar graphics for a great game.Now, I will start with the good:If you were looking for an RPG, then you have definitely come to the right shop!  I have missed RPG-ishness ever since finishing Skyrim (which is a game with its own issues), and it was really nice to be able to step into a fantasy world again.You are indeed able to make decisions at key points in the game - mostly through a 'persuasion' system in dialogue options.  I like how Geralt casts some witchcraft to 'persuade' people, too - it sets him apart from the other characters.The world is huge and varied, although I do get the impression that you are only shown a tiny sliver of it.But now, unfortunately, for the bad:Player connection to the playable character of Geralt is seriously impeded by the brick wall of lore you are expected to consume, process, understand and form your own feelings about.  The game does NOT ease you into the world whatsoever.  While ME2 did a great job of introducing the player to the world all over again (as Shepard had been basically resurrected), this game does NOT.  In missing the opportunity to enkindle a basic interest in the world at large in its players, The Witcher 2 has one, initial, major fatal flaw:  it failed to make me care.  In a decision-based RPG, that is VERY bad news.  I felt that I was basically a non-sentient floating through the game's books and maps and cities, being TOLD about all these other places, people and wars - but that I had absolutely NO reason to worry about any of it, or care.The map system.  The map system is one of the main technical reasons that I did not achieve a fuller understanding of the game world and story.  I literally missed 90% of the side quests (some of which with significant stories and/or characters in them) because I was not able to follow the quest markers effectively.  You can only have one quest marker at a time on your map, meaning you have to manually choose which quest to go after.  Unfortunately, this in turn means that you may stumble into another quest (or advance the storyline) just by attempting to transition from whatever area you are in to the marked quest area.  This is very unfortunate.  Not only that, but the quest markers seemed to me to be HIGHLY unreliable, unpredictable and - at times - completely incomprehensible.  I spent literally HOURS attempting to find two guys to armwrestle in the dwarven city (Vergen, was it?).  The quest marker showed their location, at which I was standing, but they weren't there.  I went under ground, scoured the city, looked for secret doors, stumbled through catacombs (all the time initiating and completing other missions by accident), did EVERYTHING I could think of to find these guys to armwrestle - to no avail.  I can only assume that it was some kind of glitch - but unfortunately it ensured that after that point in the game, I paid almost no attention to *ANY* side quests and did not go after any of them, because I knew I could not rely on my map or the quest markers.  Major flaw and one that makes the player feel like they are bashing their head against a brick wall.Adult material inclusion.  I welcome adult language, situations and sex/love in a game.  It makes me care, and it makes me want to succeed in a game.  I wholeheartedly encourage the use of them in all games.  However, even I was left with a bad taste in my mouth after my pummeling by The Witcher 2's profanity, sex and unbridled objectification of women.  To make matters worse (and I don't know if this is just the way I played the game or not), but I was totally unable to actually form a romantic relationship with anyone in the game.  I mean - apart from Triss, who is just sort of the cookie-cutter 'girlfriend' - but even then there was no culmination of our relationship, or after Geralt saved her.....nothing. Well wow - here's a game aspect that is under developed and under used.  You cannot drink potions in battle - I repeat, you cannot drink potions in battle!!  So basically, you have to remember to 'meditate' before you ANTICIPATE there MAY be someone to fight soon, and drink your potions.  This is a terribly convoluted way to treat something that is supposed to be one of the Witcher's main methods.  Hmmm.So, yeah.  The rest of my review really just sums up how I feel about the plot and game story in general.  It's pretty unfollowable and mediocre.  It definitely has its shining points, but they are few and far between.  I had heard the hype about this game and was really looking forward to playing it and seeing what it was like.  In reality - I'm exhausted and very happy that I've finally finished it (well - I say finally....but minus the unfollowable, unfindable side quests it only takes about <20hrs to complete all three Acts).  The ending of the game came very suddenly and anticlimactically, and because I was playing on easy difficulty, battling the dragon (Was that Saskia?  I have no idea.....) was just a little side thing to do to get you to the credits.There was an epilogue with lots of troop movements, people I didn't know, and places I didn't recognize with armies moving through them.  No idea what that was about.

The short version, if you are a die hard South Park fan and love video games and have been hoping for the ultimate South Park video game to emerge - hope no further that moment has arrived. Buy this game.The slightly longer version.South Park for almost 20 years has been a consistent purveyor of pop culture since it first aired. Offering up a dose of comedy via cardboard cut out cartoon characters that have found a way to tackle every issue imaginable in a funny and sometimes perverse way without overreaching it's boundaries of leaning one way or another to poke fun at both sides.Since that time there have been many video games that have tried to capture the essence of the show to allow fans another way to connect, and each one has failed miserably being nothing more then a cheap nod to the show we've come to love. Until now.South Park: The Stick of Truth has managed to pull off the miracle of presenting a game so rich in South Park lore that at times you will forget you are playing a game and truly feel like you are part of an episode which is exactly what Trey and Matt had wanted from the get go. Every aspect of the games artistic design screams classic South Park and there is not one point in the game where you are taken out of that experience. It's the little things that matter.The amount of nods to past episodes is going to please even the most die hard fan and will still provide hours of entertainment to anyone who is just along for the ride to watch someone else play the game for the sheer comedy value it provides.Gameplay wise this is a standard meat and potatoes turned based RPG game on the surface that allows you to rank up your character and last about 14 hours give or take. The most pointed reference I can give you as to how this plays out are two games - Earthbound and Paper Mario. If you were to combine those two games but make it all based in a South Park universe I think that pretty much hits as close to the mark as you are going to get as to how it all works.There are four classes to choose to from you can be a Fighter, a Mage, a Thief, or a Jew. The latter providing some additional comedy jabs from Cartman for obvious reasons if you are a fan of the show.For those who are looking for a long deep RPG though you may want to look elsewhere and know what you are getting here. South Park: The Stick of Truth never tries to extend it's hand past the point of being what it was intended to be - a light RPG geared towards a hardcore fan base of the show knowing that not everyone who plays games plays RPGs but also trying to carefully balance itself for those who are hardcore gamers that will get some occasional laughs at it's nod to the genre.It is simply a great ride that provides hours and hours of entertainment for anyone who has been a life long fan of the show by doing exactly what it was set out to do, entertain you and make you double over in laughter by providing the ultimate South Park experience.Excellent job Matt, Trey and the entire Ubisoft team for finally giving the fan service we deserve and doing it right! Thank you.

I usually steer well clear of any video game that's a spin-off from a TV show or movie. They're almost always terrible. I'm delighted to say that this is an exception.The game's central conceit is that you're a new kid in South Park, playing a LARP game with Cartman and the other kids, trying to make friends. This sets things up for a spot-on pastiche of the Final Fantasy games and the Elder Scrolls series, not to mention D&D;, with the creaky game mechanics and lack of realism in many RPGs lovingly mocked for laughs.State of the art console graphics are used to reproduce the juddery animation and crudely cut construction paper look of the TV show. Combined with the extensive voiceover work, the end result is exactly like an interactive free-roaming episode of South Park.Of course, the downside to reproducing creaky RPG mechanics is that the gameplay can get as tiresome as a second-rate turn-based RPG. I did find that the combat started to get tiresome around level 5 or 6, but I persevered and found that things got amusing again once I had leveled up some more and found more weapons.There are a few technical rough edges here and there. Twice I've ended up with the game wedging itself into a situation where I couldn't continue, thanks to bugs in the code; fortunately, the autosave meant I could restart and continue without losing much progress. The other major issue is that when you move to a new area, if you move too quickly and the game needs to scroll, the frame rate can drop to what would be an unacceptable rate in any other game. Fortunately, since South Park's look is jerky to start with, it's no big deal.Oh, it's also funny.So in spite of the minor flaws, I'm going to give this one five stars, because it's everything I wanted from a South Park game.

There is likely something in this game you'll find offensive.  I have a high tolerance, but I know Al Gore, and his South Park version is one of the sub-missions for ManBearPig. That tough to do.There is an avalanche of offensive material in the game, from Nazis, government conspiracies, abortion clinics, girl power, social media, LARPing, zombies, aliens, the homeless, gays, and more.The gameplay is particularly nice -- battles are turn-based, with each side taking turns whacking each other. All the 200 or battles so battles I fought seemed different, and most had ample dialog and new material.  I've played well over 150 rpgs on PC, PS1/2/3/4, DS, DS3D, Apple Apps, Sega, Android Aps, and Wii. If you've seen some of the behind-the-scenes videos for the game, Trey and Matt had a huge stack of scripts they read through, perhaps 5000 pages of dialog.I wouldn't trust Cartman for anything, and I liked the powers of Butters and Jimmy Valmer (crippled bard) better -- but I eventually gravitated to have Cartman as my main partner in battles. In this hilarious, (and hard-M rated), epic RPG from the creators of South Park, you take on the role of the New Kid. Your mission - make friends, and save South Park doing it. Picking up around the time of the Black Friday Trilogy, the New Kid arrives in town to find himself amidst the neighborhood children's imaginary battle between Cartman's faction of Humans and Kyle's faction of Elves. Like any classic episode, what begins as a childish game turns into a fight for survival as the kids battle against the absurdity of the world around them. And from the beginning, the game is unmistakably a hilariously filthy product of Matt Stone and Trey Parker.You begin by choosing a class for your New Kid - Warrior, Mage, Thief... or Jew. Arm yourself with weapons ranging from simple knives, to Dodgeballs, to the Canadian Halberd (a hockey stick), and even sex toys. Recruit and befriend all the regular characters of South Park, and some classic special guests like Mr. Hankey,Terrence and Philip, Crab People, Jesus, and Al Gore. Battle local Gingers, Visitor Aliens, Zombie Cows, and Nazi Hobos. Collect Chinpokomon dolls hidden throughout town as a side game. Travel to exotic locales like the Visitor Spaceship, the lost woods, and 8-bit Canada.Gameplay can be fairly easy, but you are encouraged to save often because an untimely death can set you back hours. Battles are the classic, turn-based, RPG style (the game makes fun of this on occasion), with an element of timing, and some environmental impact. Sneak up on an enemy to strike first, or better yet, use the environment around you to stun or knock them out before the battle begins. Customize your weapons with elemental power ups to get an edge in battle. Travel with a companion to use their special abilities (like Jimmy's Bard powers, or Butters's healing and Professor Chaos attacks). Collect EP to level your character and choose from various Power Ups and Abilities. Progressing through the game will grant you special tools and power ups that will allow you to reach areas that were inaccessible before. Explore everywhere, and talk to everyone, as there are plenty of surprises.The real reason to play the game, however, is for the obscenely hilarious story. The difficulty of the game can be adjusted at any time, so if you are just looking forward to "watching" you can set it to its easiest setting and go thought the motions for the sake of enjoying the story, or crank it back up for a challenge. The humor of this game is filthy one moment, dark the next, and self-deprecating next. There is no question that this game should absolutely be rated M. It is not for kids! Forget about the adult language and the cartoon violence, its the situations in which the New Kid finds himself that are M-worthy, raunchy, gross, graphic and explicit. But that said, I have never in my life laughed so hard playing a video game.

For any fan of South Park this game is a must! The game has the same writing and art style as the series, and the gameplay is very approachable while remaining deep and fun.So first of all, this game is hilarious... you will laugh out loud... and this is a very difficult feat for any video game to accomplish. Matt and Trey have managed to capture the same humor that exists in the show. Furthermore, the gameplay looks identical to an episode of South Park. In fact, it is the best adaptation from a tv show to a game that I have ever seen. A huge accomplish by Ubisoft and Matt and Trey. As for the game play, it's an RPG. This means get ready to explore every box in your room: you'll find items that improve your character, items that serve as easter eggs from past episodes, and items that will just make you laugh.You follow a fairly linear story with some freedom in what you do (pokemon comparable) . The fighting is resolved in a turn-based fashion where you attack with your party then your opponent attacks you... (imagine Pokemon, or more accurately Mario and Luigi Superstar Saga (or paper mario)) except there is a built in timing element that enables you to hit harder and even block. There is strategy in what attack you choose as an effective blow depends not only on the opponent, but also his defensive stance and you're ability to press "A" at the perfect time. HP and PP bars are displayed as well as hit damage, so you feel rewarded for well-timed hits and are easily able to calculate what you need to for your next attack.That's the game! You level up your custom character in the world of South Park as a war for the stick of truth escalates into a bigger and bigger battle. The game is riddled with South Park comedy, and the gameplay is done so to be engaging to gamers and approachable for non-gamers alike. I highly recommend this to any South Park fan. For anyone who hasn't seen South Park, this is a great stepping stone into that world. And for those who don't like South Park, although the gameplay is very well done, this game is very close to the show in all its forms and if that's not for you, you should stay away.

(This is for the PC version of the game.)I can't remember the last time I had genuine laugh-out-loud moments when playing a video game, but in South Park: The Stick of Truth, there were lots and lots of them. (I'm an older gamer. When I arrived in Canada on a particular quest-line, I nearly ruined my keyboard with a massive spit-take.)If you're a South Park fan and know the show even reasonably well, you'll 'get' so many of the in-jokes. Don't believe me? Just go open Cartman's bedroom closet. There are even characters I never expected to see again. I think the best thing I can say about SP:TSoT is what others have noted: It's almost -exactly- like you're a character inside an extended South Park series episode.Now, as for the critical game-play review:Okay, if you're a hardcore gamer looking for a South Park version of Call of Duty, this game ain't it. Combat is turn-based, more of a strategy thing than having to be especially fast in anything other than mashing certain keys or buttons when prompted to do so. Many of the situational challenges are puzzle-based, in that you'll do better if you can figure out what to shoot or fart at in order to achieve a desired effect or thin a crowd of enemies from a bunch to just one or two (or none).The game itself practically screams 'meta' much of the time, in the way characters in the game remark about you as the New Kid being involved with the other kids' Live Action Role Play (LARP) game. If you stand around too long, your current buddy will often crack wise about you wasting time, that there's a game to be played so let's get on with it.Who is this game not for? The easily offended or grossed out. Those who can't take a joke. Anybody who finds South Park itself mildly offensive -- because it's like they took South Park and amped everything to 11. There's an extended scene involving an abortion clinic, 'kay? And scatological crudity everywhere.Controller vs. Keyboard: I played my first go (Mage class) using a keyboard, and most of the second (Jew) that way, too. The other day, I finally acquired an Xbox 360 controller for my PC and discovered it was way, way, WAY easier with the controller. There are some combinations that I'm not even sure are possible using the keyboard, but which were trivial as soon as I tried the game controller instead, especially some of the magic (fart-based) attacks. Inventory management is a tad more clumsy, but the difference in simply being able to sprint when I wanted was worth the trade-off.Classes: I've tried three so far, and personally I've found them all fun -- Mage, Jew, and Thief (the first two of those all the way to the end of the game). Haven't tried Warrior yet. All can be a little dicey to start with, but around level 10 start becoming powerful. Whatever you play, look to put your Skill points into abilities and acquire weapons that are (1) good against a single target and (2) have some kind of area-of-effect attack as well. You'll face both powerful bosses and crowds of enemies and it's always a good idea to have something to deal with both. In other words, don't specialize 100% in one or the other.Perks: These are bonuses you collect as you acquire certain numbers of South Park friends. Be sure to stick to perks that apply to your class and what you do. (For instance, don't bother taking bleed perks if you throw fireballs.)Duration: I'm one of those folks who like to explore everything, find everything, and collect achievements. Based on this, and having gotten myself rather lost in the sewers of South Park one evening, I'd say my first play-through was close to 30-40 hours total. But again: I really take my time and didn't skip any conversations. The second time, I skipped some of the longer stuff and I'd say I agree with what others have reported, that if you really barrel through, this is about a 20 hour game.Replayability: Well, no spoilers, but there's really only one semi-serious plot choice regarding the choice of a particular side to support. A choice which before long actually ends up not mattering all that much. Based on that, I'd say the replay factor of this game depends on whether you want to try a different class.Helpful non-spoiler hints:- Goth Dance: If using a keyboard, use the arrow keys. Because WASD is so conformist. Same applies to when using Jimmy's song abilities.- Some paths and climbing ladders aren't always obvious. If not sure, move in that direction and keep moving and there's a good chance the hanging wires or a shadowy ladder you can't even see will actually take you to a new area.- Some locations and objects are not accessible until the story progresses and you acquire certain abilities. Don't go nuts trying to reach a bag on a roof before the means to get up there presents itself.- Speed potions are your friend. Use them.- When selecting a potion for use, you can use them on yourself or on your buddy. The same applies for your buddy. Which means technically, in each turn of combat, a single character could quaff two potions. Useful when you're trying to maintain your health, power, and/or power-ups.Oh, and to answer a common question: No, you can't start the game with a girl character. But just as Kenny found a way around that particular restriction, there comes a point where you can too, if you want. Sort of.Anyway, I had a great time playing and I'm hoping they consider a DLC or a sequel at some point.

Since I'm not usually a fan of RPGs, I would've turned my nose up at this game...except that it's South Park. I'm not a die-hard fan, and haven't watched an episode in years, but I still love the style of humor the show represents. Apparently, though, this game was in developer hell, but I don't know the whole story about that. Also, despite several major release date delays the game came out, finally, and is near perfection. There is literally only one thing I don't like about it, and it is VERY minor. That minor thing is that when you loot bodies and sometimes boxes and chests, sometimes you get caught on one plane. What I mean by that is, you can only move up and down or left and right, but not both. Most often you can't move left or right. The simple solution to this is to hold one direction (snicker snicker) and then just let go of the stick completely and then you can move freely again. Now THAT'S minor.The game itself feels kind of short, about 13 hours + for me to do everything that i could find, including all quests. The creative team behind the game did a great job of thinking about how to maintain an RPG world inside the already-existent South Park world, i.e. using houses and basements as dungeons or as the Giggling Donkey tavern.Thankfully the two creators of the TV show wrote the script so that, as they said in many interviews, they could create the illusion that this game was really just another episode. And boy does it feel like one. All the best obscenities are used with perfection, all the appropriate racism, potty jokes, fart jokes, (I mean...the magic your character learns is different types of farts!) character belittlement, and gay jokes that we've come to love and laugh at in South Park. Those guys at South Park Studios were pushing the envelope before Family Guy and perhaps much further.The gameplay itself is very polished. Again, I'm not much for RPGs, but they really simplified the RPG concept into just maintaining Perks (additional abilities that are permanently brought into each battle) and Abilities (standard things like magic and special weapon attacks, done, of course, South Park Style). In this game, they have the enemies set up in columns and rows so that other enemies are sometimes stacked above/below or in front of/behind other enemies. Certain attacks affect the whole field, while others only do columns or rows. Having not encountered this before, I thought it to be ingenious. I must reiterate again that I am not a regular RPG gamer so this may not be novel, and may, in fact, be quite old. It is, though, new to me.The missions are usually pretty funny and the sex scene (yep, they did just do that) is hilarious! This was probably the best feature of this game. The humor. Throughout the entire game I was kept laughing and not just little chortles, but real belly laughs. It makes me wish there was more comedy in games. The Uncharted series has some good dialogue/banter, but it isn't as continuous as this game's laugh bucket was.Overall this is my favorite game of the year (so far) and it will be hard to overthrow based on how amazing it is. This is the second game I have beat and then gone back and replayed immediately after finishing it (the other being The Last of Us) because it was so good. If you don't like offensive JOKES then you won't like this. If you are unfamiliar with South Park and it's humor, but appreciate offensive JOKES and what could be juvenile or risque humor, then you'll do fine. There are a lot of references to many things that happened in the television show, but one doesn't need to rent/buy all 15+ South Park seasons to catch up in order to enjoy this game. Seriously one of the best games I have ever played, hands down. You need to play this!

South Park: The Stick of Truth is a fantastic game. In a world where the only decent licensed games are the occasional Batman game, (minus Arkham Origins,) I wasn’t expecting much. The hilarious source material plus a Paper Mario-like RPG makes for an all around great game. While it may be short for an RPG, or maybe even a normal game, it has lots of other stuff to do after the credits roll, including trophy/achievement support. It’s definitely a wacky game, with levels ranging from a spaceship, to a Taco Bell/military base, plus some others that I’m not sure I’m allowed to post here. It is definitely the funniest game I’ve ever played, being far more hilarious than Portal 2 and to a lesser extent, Borderlands 2. There are funny Skyrim references all over the place. The story is actually a good one, and makes for some funny scenes. I love how everything changes so much once you enter Canada. The only gripes I have with the game are the power wheel and QTE’s. The power selection wheel, (or whatever it’s called), is tough to control sometimes, and every once in a while I found myself selecting the wrong power by accident. The QTE’s are awful in this game. I had lots of trouble with the battle where you fight Cartman or Kyle, as there was an extremely difficult button-mashing prompt that took a long time to complete. The abortion mini-game (which you have to do twice in the game) explains itself very poorly and has difficult QTE’s yet again, and I failed it over and over. ok, first off if you've ever seen the show 'South Park' then I'm sure you're fully aware that political correctness and niceties are non-existent - and the video game stays true to form! Nothing like a television show that parodies everything from Easter, to world dictators, to celebrities and beyond, parodying RPG gaming itself. It makes fun of RPGing and other gaming elements like you'd imagine South Park would.The more of a fan you are of South Park, the more of a fan you will be of the game and the more you will enjoy its elements. The game references tons of moments from the television show over the years. I haven't kept up with the series in a few years now. Not that I don't enjoy the show and watch it from time to time but I have an 8-year old son now and this show or this game are not for 8-year olds, much less 14-year olds.... or anybody who is offended at all.. about anything... no matter how remote or innocent.It's a lot of fun exploring South Park and controlling the characters and the story and writing are genuine, original and unique. Finally, a South Park game worth writing a review about!Over the years, South Park has had some really shady offerings outside the show itself. The Stick of Truth has been in development for years, and Obsidian has taken the time to cram as much of the sleepy little Colorado town's life as they could into it. And it shows.For RPG diehards, there will be very little challenge here. The battles are simple, items and cash are plentiful, and the game's map clearly marks all your objectives and tells you how to complete quests. The game itself, however, is cleverly and faithfully recreated to make you feel like you're in a very long episode of South Park. All of the voice work was done by Trey and Matt, so it's all 100% authentic.You start out as a mute "new kid" who is sent out (rather forcefully) by your parents to make new friends. I spent as much time as I could in my house, opening drawers, picking up money, finding Health Potions (cheesy poofs), until my dad came running into the kitchen, yelling at me, "It wasn't a request, it was a command!" The first kid you come across is your next door neighbor. After saving him from one of the enemy drow elves, he introduces himself as Butters the Merciful, a holy paladin in service to the Wizard King. He becomes your first friend, which you can verify by bringing up the game's Facebook menu. Butters brings you to Cartman the Wizard King where you introduce yourself for the first time. I type in my name, expecting it to appear somewhere in conformation. Cartman looks at me and says, "Your name is Douchebag?" No... That's not what I typed. I navigate to No and Cartman repeats, "Are you SURE you want your name to be Douchebag?" No! I hit it again, and Cartman says, "Very well, Douchebag! Now select your class!" In the Stick of Truth, your class determines your abilities. Will you be a fighter with the ability to beat the snot out of people with a baseball bat (like the heroes of old), a mage who can burn their opponents with mystical fireworks, a theif who can sneak up behind their enemies for massive stunning damage, or a Jew with the Sling of David that can hurl stones at unsuspecting enemies? This doubles as a checkpoint for the squeamish. If Cartman satirizing the Jewish faith or peoples offends you, turn off your system now and sell the game for what you can. It only gets more over the top and potentially offensive from here.Everything you do behind the scenes in The Stick of Truth (much like everything you do in real life, right?) is done on Facebook. This includes inventory management, friend requests, quests and the map of South Park. While its presentation is cute for a minute, navigation is clumsy and it feels like it takes too long to access the information you need. This is a minor drawback, however. On the front page, minor story updates can be seen on your wall, and depending on what part of the story you're on and how many friends you have, there are some hilarious things to be seen there.Combat is where things turn a little stale. It's you and one of your buddies against the enemies. So far I've faced drow elves, meth heads, bully girls and one surly security guard. When its your turn to attack, you select your weapon and the enemy and a well timed button press can increase your damage. Defense is handled with the same buttons, but a perfect defense doesn't completely negate damage. It isn't too pressing, because your HP and PP are restored completely at the end of battle.REVIEW UPDATE -- After completing The Stick of Truth in less than 2 days, I've had a lot to mull over in this review. As fun and unabashedly offensive as this game is, there are some pretty dramatic flaws holding it back that might have been solved with another delay. There are some instances, particularly in the first set of tutorial battles where events are supposed to queue up in the middle of the fight and simply don't. The only fix is to reload an earlier checkpoint.Speaking of checkpoints, that is the only way to save games. The pause menu has a Save Game function, but when you press it you are informed that all saving your game does is make a copy of your last checkpoint in a different location. Useless. The only redemption here is that checkpoints are almost literally on every screen, so you'll never have to backtrack very far.These flaws, in addition to the slow menus, low replay value and a sloppy inventory, really hold back The Stick of Truth from being a good RPG. As a definitive South Park experience, however, it is flawless. References and direct voice samples flow from hundreds of South Park episodes over the years, the game sends zings at celebrities throughout including Kim Kardashian and Morgan Freeman, and Kenny dies more frequently and greusomely than any other party member.
Nothing says South Park like a summon of Mr. Slave doing naughty things. South universe at it's finest! Lol.Love it!
