Anyone who knows me knows how much I love the Souls games.  My review of the original Dark Souls was a ranting, sprawling mess so I'm going to try to keep this one as short as possible.  This is an extremely impressive addition to the already incredible Souls series.  When Dark Souls II was initially announced to be in development there were a lot of concerns that the game would be dumbed down and less difficult.  These fears were only further enhanced when it was announced that the original director of the Souls games, Hidetaka Miyazaki, would be stepping down.  I am pleased to say that this is not the case at all.  In fact, if anything this game may be harder than the original Dark Souls at some points.  Some of the bosses are downright brutal and the enemy AI has been improved significantly.  The combat also seems much weightier but all and all this game plays and feels just like its predecessor.  It still has the wonderful level design, dark and brooding atmosphere, sense of exploration, and fantastic enemy placement that its predecessors had.  When I started playing this game my experience with the original Dark Souls (and Demons Souls) made me believe that I would be able to catch on really quickly.  Boy did Dark Souls II shove my hubris down my throat.  While I beat the original countless times I felt like I had to relearn everything again when I started playing this game.  Shielding takes longer, the timing for parrying is different, the enemies recover quicker, etc.  Essentially the way I played Dark Souls was useless to me here.  So while this game does feel and play a lot like the previous Souls games it also doesn't ride its predecessors success at all and has quite a few gameplay quirks and a ton of new creative difficulty to give you that suffering that hurts so good.  My only complaint is that a couple of the bosses feel like they were ripped them out of the last game.  Hell one of the bosses is a straight copy of one of the bosses from the original Dark Souls (I'M LOOKING AT YOU BLUE CATHEDRAL!).  I would've loved to see purely original bosses but it is a very minor complaint from me and overall this is a truly fantastic game that has completely captivated me like few games can.  I highly recommend it and I honestly believe that the Souls series is now the best current franchise in video games at least amongst RPGs.  Seriously if you love a challenge and/or enjoyed what the other games had to offer, BUY THIS GAME!!! NOW! Oops I said I was gonna make this short.  I guess I failed again haha!

I have played both of the previous Souls games and Demon's Souls is one of my top 3 favorite games of all time. I have hundreds of hours and many fond memories poured into it. So needless to say I was really anticipating this game, to the point of having it pre-ordered since January 2013. After playing a good 6 hours into the game I can say it was well worth the wait.Dark Souls 2 is a nice mix of both Demon's Souls and the first Dark Souls. The open world format, bonfires, and estes flasks make a return to this game from Dark Souls, while the healing options, leveling up and dying is a throw-back to Demon's Souls. Another thing that hasn't changed from either of the previous games is the brutal difficulty and I must say, this sequel takes that difficulty and runs full out with it.Yes, this game is HARD, but that is expected with any Souls game. DS2 has made things more difficult by lumping more enemies together. So instead of fighting 1 or 2 enemies at a time, you are typically fighting 3 or 4 enemies. This can make things really challenging. The game also hides enemy ambushes around every corner so you learn really quick to take corners carefully or with a shield thrown up for any surprise attacks. However, if you don't have any stamina to withstand an attack to your shield you are stunned for a few seconds, which can mean a quick death. The game also seems slower to react between attacking and then trying to roll away. My O button is taking a pounding with me trying to quickly get away from an incoming attack. One of the big changes from either of the previous games is enemies stop re-spawning after a time. This can make the game easier if you were having a hard time in an area previously, but can be annoying if you are wishing to farm an area.As I have been saying, DS2 is hard so you WILL die. When you die you become Hollow. The more times you die the lower your health goes down until it bottoms out at 50% of your health. This is like Demon's Souls, but instead of immediately loosing  your health this is a gradual process. Also similar to Demon's Souls is a ring that acts like the cling ring. This enables your health to bottom out at 75% instead of 50%. I suggest getting this ring ASAP or you will have a much harder time. When you are Hollow you have the ability to become human again which is done by consuming human effigies. This will make you human and restore you to full health, but be stingy with them as they are rare early in the game. You can also become human by being summoned as a white phantom. This seems very hit and miss. Sometimes you are restored to human on the first summon, other times it takes multiple times. It also doesn't seem to require the death of a boss to accomplish this. I don't know if this is a server issue or if there is some other factor that contributes to becoming human but right now it seems random. I hope this is something they fix.Summoning works very much the same as the previous games. You put down your sign and you are summoned. There are 2 different types of summoning soapstones. You have the regular White Soapstone and the Small White Soapstone. The SWS can only be used in certain areas and has a short time-limit on its use. I summoned someone with this and he lasted through 2 enemies before being returned back to his world. So I suggest just sticking with the regular WS. There is also a ring you can get that can make match-making with friends easier. I haven't tried this yet but one reason I loved Demon's Souls so much was being able to play with my sister. We were never able to play with each other in Dark Souls due to that games poor match-making so I am thrilled we will be able to play with each other again. I have not yet been invaded or invaded anyone myself so I cannot comment on that online aspect of the game.As for the world, it does keep the open world quality found in Dark Souls. You have a main village that acts as a central hub and from there you have paths that branch off, getting larger and larger. Within the village you have the Emerald Herald who is like DeS Maiden In Black. She is responsible for leveling you up and who upgrades your Estus flasks. Instead of starting with 5 Estus flasks like in DS you only start with 1. You can still upgrade how many uses you get by collecting estus shards that are found around the world. You can thankfully get 2 shards pretty early in the game. You can also upgrade how much HP it will regenerate. Along with the Estus flasks you also have lifegems that can be dropped by enemies and are also scattered around the world. They are a 1 time use which will gradually restore your health.Since the world is more open and doesn't interconnect as fluidly as Dark Souls, you are able to fast travel to any previous bonfire you have been to. This has been especially helpful since you can only level up through the Herald. Like in the previous game the bonfire will heal you, restore your estus flasks, give you access to an item box and restore the areas enemies.Despite how hard this game is and how many times you will die like a b*tch, this game is still a blast. It is brutal but when you get past that enemy or boss you were struggling on there is this intense satisfaction of `I did it!' I highly suggest this game to anyone who has played and liked any of the previous Souls games. It has taken some of the best from the previous games and put them together in this wonderful addition to the Soul's family. This game is definitely not for everyone, but if you have the patience and will, you will be rewarded with an amazing experience and a deep sense of satisfaction.

Welcome to the land of Drangleic; a place being persistently eaten away at by the curse of the undead. Here, most everything is a twisted abomination that has long sense lost it's life and sanity. To disturb these creatures is to tempt their wrath, for the undead are always in search of souls to feed their hunger. The ones that are lucid, and friendly enough to aide you, are all likewise numb and accepting of their own fate; resigning themselves to rot away in peace as they watch a dream-like sunset that never ends on the coast of purgatory.It ain't no candy crush, baby. This is Dark Souls.There are two types of people I figure will be interested in DS2...players of the first two Souls games, and people who want to jump on the bandwagon after hearing about the hype from the other games.For the former, all I can say is that I recommend DS2 whole heartedly. If you liked the other Souls games, you'll probably like this.To the latter, just remember what you're getting yourself into. DS2 is most definitely challenging, but if you love the feeling of toppling great adversity, then you might like this. The combat is tight, the atmosphere is excellent, and every death is your own damn fault in one way or another.DS2 may very well be the game that keeps the 360 / PS3 multiplayer scene alive for a few years.

Sequel to the widely acclaimed Dark Souls and finale to the "Souls" trilogy, Dark Souls 2 puts sword and shield (or sorcery, or hammer, or axe...) into your hands once again in hopes that you can triumph death and despair in this RPG by FromSoftware. Bigger, meaner, and more epic than either of its predecessors Dark Souls 2 represents a stunning achievement in design and execution. It welcomes new players with a friendlier tutorial and improved mechanics, but veterans of the Souls series need not be worried. Dark Souls 2 is brutal and challenging, testing you every step of the way with tough bosses and overwhelming odds. But Dark Souls 2 is also beautiful and stunning, featuring a world that is well worth exploring every nook and cranny, from dark and dead pits to harrowing civilizations long lost in time above the clouds. Dark Souls 2 is nothing short of a masterpiece, through and through.Story, Presentation, and World – 10/10/10 – 10The story of Dark Souls 2 is a fantastical tale of kingdoms lost in time, ruled by monsters and hostile forces ready to challenge the player. Similar to the previous games, Dark Souls 2 is a mildly minimalistic game in terms of delivering information; the player must explore and discover most of the world himself or herself. It’s an impressive story and world, with a staggering amount of thought behind its deep lore and characters. It’s a world filled with mystery, where the player’s imagination is key to understanding and connecting the loose ties between characters and their place in Drangleic. And I’m sure the ending will be something discussed by Souls fans for years to come.Dark Souls 2 also features a significant upgrade in presentation values. Things are cleaner, nuanced elements in character building are more clear and menus are designed with a greater emphasis on ease of use. It’s all still very much like the previous games, just refined and improved to perfection.Graphics and Art Direction – 9/10 – 9.5The world of Drangleic is an epic land ripe for exploration. Half of this experience, though, is the staggeringly huge variety of places you’ll visit while on your quest. Decrepit crypts, castles in the sky, and even the garbage bin of Drangleic itself, the art direction for Dark Souls 2 continues the FromSoftware’s creative trend in developing horrendous creatures and placing them in a fascinating world. There are tons of unique bosses and enemies out for your hollow head, and each and every one is animated with a certain professionalism only a Japanese studio could produce. Along with these disturbing denizens of Drangleic, the places you’ll visit are equally impressive; not simply because of their design but also the character, increased color pallet and pure imagination every new area brings. To say that Dark Souls 2’s art direction is great would be a crime; it is simply stunning, and is one of a kind.Graphically, Dark Souls 2 is superior to its predecessors in many ways. You’ll be happy to know that the game runs at a steady 30 FPS throughout (PS3) to 60 FPS (360 version is more consistently smoother, PS3 does hit 60 FPS in enclosed and small areas) and technically performs without a hitch. The big improvement here is the animations, which have benefited immensely from being motion captured. Elements of your character react with realism, and enemies feel lifelike and move like they should. The improved lighting engine creates a surprising sense of immersion (although is not the lighting engine we were advertised last year), and the improved physics engine is icing on the cake (character’s armor, such as loincloths and hoods flow in the wind and react realistically). Grainy textures and anti-aliasing problems do occur more often than I would’ve like to see (and are simply limitations of the Xbox 360 and PS3). The dumbed down lighting engine is a disappointment as well as the grainy textures and various visual hiccups, making a next gen version of Dark Souls 2 all the more tantalizing.Gameplay and Design – 10/10 – 10Where as Demon’s Souls introduced us to the impossibly challenging difficulty the series is known for and Dark Souls improved the online and flow of combat, Dark Souls 2 has perfected what the series is known for. Tight and claustrophobic combat headlines the game, while rewarding exploration, online PvP, summoning and aiding other players are all improved. Dark Souls 2 continues the trend of “endless tactics” with the numerous amount of weapons, which all feel distinct and fun to use. Everything has been improved, refined, and polished. The classic gameplay is still as challenging as ever, too. Fears of Dark Souls 2 dumbing down the difficulty and level of challenge have gone completely unwarranted. If anything, this may be the most challenging of all the Souls games, but also the most fair. Yes, you’ll die, get punished because of it, and lose your souls (which can be retrieved within the next life) and your human status, if you’re human. But Dark Souls 2, unlike its previous entries, clearly explains the effects of items, materials, and penalties. You die because you’re unfamiliar with a boss, area, or unique enemy tactic. You only come back stronger, more aware of the dangers you will face and more capable to tackle them quicker with more precision. Of the 245 times I died through my play-through, I rarely felt cheated. Only a few times (fighting optional bosses and online PvP) did I feel this way.In terms of design, Dark Souls 2 is built with the player in mind. Beginning the adventure is tough, as is every video game. Healing items are rare in the beginning, and the Estus Flask only offers a swig at first. But as you explore this hostile and beautiful world, you’ll be rewarded with new and better armors, lifegems, status ailment healers, new weapons and sometimes the rare shards to improve the Estus Flask. Exploration doesn’t get more rewarding than this. Dark Souls 2 also offers a huge collection of memorable boss battles; everything from quick thinking to pure dodging skill is required throughout the many, many bosses that stand in your way. And you will take them all out, I believe in you! Dark Souls 2 is rewarding every step of the way; from it’s improved, tighter combat, intricate level design and unique character building this is an RPG that sacrifices nothing it’s famous for, but rather embraces its flaws and only improves upon them.Sound Design and Soundtrack – 9/10 – 9.5Dark Souls 2 will immerse you in more ways than one, and that’s mainly because of it’s subtle sound design. Some say the best sound design is one that you don’t even notice; Dark Souls 2 is accomplished in this aspect. Swords will clash and spells will be cast, and they all sound great. The ambience while exploring each area really shines brightly as well. From creepy distant cackles to hollow and decrepit crypts, everything sounds as it should. Voice acting, a small part of all the Souls games, has been improved and expanded here and it is all delivered very well.Dark Souls 2 features, hands down, the best score for any of the Souls games. Each boss fight has it’s own unique theme, memorable and musical enough to listen to outside the game. The tragic and intense orchestration and score really highlights each boss fight, making each an assault on the senses and emotions (and the emotional depth of the soundtrack itself is stunning). And don’t worry, the classic finale aria is beautiful and thoroughly composed with a purpose. Mr. Motoi Sakruaba, take a bow.Lasting Appeal – 10Unlike previous Souls games, once the credits roll there is still more to do. An altered new game plus allows people to continue to explore past the credits which is excellent for those who want to continue their adventure and clear optional areas. The game does have the classic new game plus, though, in which you do less damage while enemies do more. There are multiple new challenges that await players in new game plus, all of which require new tactics and skills. Aside from that, players can re-spec their characters to try different builds, join and work through multiple covenants, beat optional bosses and work your way through PvP. Dark Souls 2 offers a lot to do post-credits.Final Score - 10/10Dark Souls 2 took me just about 52 hours to complete (final time - 51:50) and I died 245 times. Oddly enough, though, every minute within this world was incredible. Drangleic is a gorgeous and oddly inviting world to explore, and your adventure will take you to the far corners of this hostile place, fighting off monsters and battling players along the way. It was an immensely satisfying and enjoyable game, and most of all it felt incredibly fair the entire way through. It is not only one of the best games I have ever played, but it gives reasons for video games to exist. Only in video games can you receive the same sense of exploration and discovery that Dark Souls 2 offers, and that’s why it’s such a grand masterpiece and a testament to video games as a medium.(average = 9.8, rounding to 10 based on 20 point scale)

My review title really says everything I want to say about this game.Dark Souls II is amazing. But because it's not the 10/10 game that Demon's Souls and Dark Souls were, it's hard not to be a tad bit disappointed.Why isn't it on the level of its two forefathers? It's hard to say. Hidetaka Miyazaki wasn't at the helm of this game, like he was with the previous two games in the series. But honestly, my thoughts are that the reason is because Dark Souls II tried too hard to be a mix of its predecessors. While in theory this isn't a bad idea, I think the game ended up tripping over itself a bit at times. The game features an inter-connected world marked by bonfires serving as checkpoints, just like Dark Souls did. Yet it also brings back the concept of a "hub", a separate area where the player goes to level up, visit blacksmiths & vendors, interact with NPC's, and most importantly, fast travel anywhere, just like Demon's Souls did. So where as the world of Dark Souls felt like a brilliant, cohesive whole (which it was), Dark Souls II's world never feels that way. And at the same time, Dark Souls II's individual areas never feel quite as distinct and brilliantly designed the way Demon's Souls did. Part of this may have to do with the designers' desire to make this game more Demon's Souls-esque than Dark Souls was, but ultimately, it's the level design itself that is to blame. The level design is fantastic still, with some incredibly memorable locations. But it never really reaches the heights of the previous games, which is a shame.With that said, there is no denying that Dark Souls II is a still a wonderful game. If Demon's Souls and Dark Souls didn't exist, this game would be revolutionary. In fact, despite my 4 star rating, this game is still better than almost anything else out there. It's sure to be considered in any worthwhile Game of the Year conversation for 2014. It even does some things significantly better than previous entries in the Souls series. Most notably, it accomplishes the absolutely incredible feat of becoming a much more transparent, accessible game, while at the same time not losing an ounce of the depth, challenge, and high levels of player satisfaction that the series has been known for. Esoteric game mechanics like the covenants (which are still present, but much easier to understand and utilize), world tendencies, and navigation are a thing of the past. Dark Souls II is approachable and easy to get into, yet as difficult as ever to master. In this reviewer's opinion, the leveling system overhaul in Dark Souls II has been an extremely positive change for the series, allowing for greater player flexibility without the need to level grind, and adding consequences for those who do choose to grind. And most notably, the multiplayer features are much richer, easier to use, and much more fun in general. Multiplayer in the Souls series has always been arguably the most innovative around, offering a game within a game for those who choose to take part in it. Dark Souls II does the best job of this yet.And like I mentioned earlier, this is still a Souls game. Meaning you're going to have some of the most immersive, intense, and satisfying gameplay available anywhere. Perhaps Dark Souls II's level & world design aren't as masterful as Dark Souls'. Perhaps its enemies and bosses aren't as memorable as Demon's Souls'. That's irrelevant. Dark Souls II is a must-play game no matter what. And the best news is, that despite it perhaps not being quite as perfect as its predecessors, this is still the best place for a newcomer to the series to start. It does a fantastic job of easing the player into its world and allowing them to figure out what's going on without holding the player's hand. For that alone, this game deserves to be commended. And Dark Souls II continues to solidify what so many of us already know....that this Souls series, from developers extraordinaire From Software, is the best thing to happen to video games in a very, very long time.

The Souls series are among the most challenging and rewarding of modern gaming and its latest offering serves as a perfect balance between the mechanics and concepts of Demons Souls and Dark Souls, with a sprinkling of new feature aimed to make the game more approachable to mainstream gamers.Namco Bandai has made quite an effort in getting the word out to the mainstream gaming and while some Souls fans were a bit worried about “accessibility” the game is more than a worthy successor to the original Dark Souls. Some of the changes, like a clearer tutorial section which explains the controls and various game mechanics , and the ability to warp from bonfires from the start are a welcome addition…the fact that leveling is only available from a specific NPC is not such a good idea, since the constant warping affects the flow of the game. One new mechanic is good for the game balance but bad for the old school RPG gamer is limited respawns which force you to keep on moving forward and limit level grinding.The combat is slower and more brutal, and it (not so gently) forces you to adapt to several mechanics  like dodging, rolling, jumping and using the environments to your advantage to stay alive; this is not a game for the button mashing fans of God of War, only careful planning and balancing will let you succeed here.The graphics are not so hot anymore, which is understandable for a game running on 8 year old console tech, but the gameplay is a challenging and sweet as ever.If you are a Souls fan you won’t be disappointed and if you have never tried the Souls series don’t listen to all the “it’s so hard” comments; it is challenging but at the same time really rewarding when you manage to beat it and you won’t be disappointed

EDIT 4/15/14: I have updated this review from 5 Stars to 4 Stars.  I picked up Demon's Souls again and was reminded how flat and washed out the graphics are.  I give the developers 5 stars in terms of gameplay, but the game really does look like something several years old.  The game also feels more patch-work in its level design as though it was rushed and does not have the polish of past games.The fact that I struggled as much as I did to write this review is a reflection of my entire experience with the game.  I have no reservations in giving Dark Souls 2 Four Stars.  If I had the opportunity to break it down further, I would give it 8 out of 10, as there has never been a "perfect" Souls game.  And, that's really what this all about isn't it?The Souls series of games, and Dark Souls 2 in particular, are imperfect in more ways than I can possibly count.  But, as is often times said, when we see someone or something as imperfect, it is a reflection of our limitations, not theirs.  If that is the case, why do so many people relish this Action RPG?  Because there are so many aspects of Dark Souls 2 and so much has already been written, I make some assumptions that you have an idea of what the game is about from existing commentary or other reviews.REGARDING GAME MECHANICSGame mechanics are extremely simple, and at first glance, feel very un-evolved compared to games of the current/past generation (PS3/Xbox 360).  You try to kill opponents either with spells and ranged attacks such as arrows, or you get in close and bash them with a weapon like a sword.  For melee combat, there are few, if any, combo moves or special/trick button assignments other than the infamous Back Stab.  This is not a Batman/Arkham or God of War style of action game.  For casters, the majority of spells are ranged attacks, but there are additional options such as Hexes/Miracles that might change your style of play.  Greater complexity and options: Spell Casters.  Greater focus on button mashing and quick movement (early game): Melee Combat. If you choose to be a melee combatant, your style of play will not evolve as much in the course of the game as would that of a caster.  But, there are DEFINITE nuances that play a more significant role mid to late game, especially when you start to talk about gear and its effects on combat.  How does this possibly work out as a good thing?Especially in the early game, you focus far more on what is occurring on-screen and in the moment than any game I have played before.  You become distinctly aware of your environment.  As you play, you will become aware of such things as how long it takes you to round a corner or reach the top of the stairs.  You will know exactly how many steps into a room will trigger a mob.  You will learn where you can roll and back up.  You will learn attack patterns of each enemy you encounter.  By being simplistic and unrefined, combat in Dark Souls 2 is actually more visceral and exciting than most any other game I have played.  Oh, and, you will learn to die.REGARDING DEATHDying has a more significant impact on Dark Souls 2 than other Souls games.  When you die, you are undead.  You become a warrior zombie and begin the process they describe as Hollowing.  Each time you die after, you lose a bit of your total available health down to a minimum of 50% of your maximum.  This is similar to being undead in Demon's souls as that put you at 50% upon death.  The game does do you a favor that most mobs disappear after a dozen or so plays through an area.  This does not include bosses.  Additionally, this is a very double edged sword.  There are some early areas of the game that allow for some minimal soul farming.  Once the mobs go away, they are gone for good.  I do not add much to Vigor stat (Health) anyway as (to me) it only makes a difference if you will die after 2 hits or 3 depending on the enemy.  Basically, try to block or not get hit is my strategy.  SPOILER: Minor spoiler that there is a treasure in the game called a Ring of Binding that cuts that boosts the minimum Health from 50% to 75%.  Again, just try not to die. REGARDING LEVEL DESIGNThis is probably the one game aspect where I can accept someone rating down on the game.  First, the levels are in no way inferior to previous Souls games.  However, they are stylistically copied and do not feel as large.  Both Demon's Souls (even with its hub) and Dark Souls gave a much greater sense of depth.  So far in Dark Souls 2, I feel much more like I am traveling from the beginning to the end of each level.  I don't quite feel that sense of exploration as I had in past Souls games.  Like Demon's Souls, Dark Souls 2 has a somewhat centralized hub, but even beyond that, from the start of the game, you can teleport between bonfires once discovered.  I loved how in the original Dark Souls the levels, especially the early ones, overlaid one another.  When you reached certain boss fights or completed levels, you were rewarded with short cuts.  I liked how you could look off of cliffs or towers and such at numerous points in Demon's and Dark Souls and see areas you had already gone or were going to.  I really miss that sense of scale as it is missing in the Dark Souls 2.  Each level feels more self-contained and is the one thing I would strongly advise the designers to improve upon in any future Souls game.  I have come across several "elevators" of such that just take you to another floor or chamber within the same level/zone and I thought afterwards, "What's the point?"  They could have simply had a door.REGARDING DIFFICULTYNot like World of Warcraft.  This is actually the best comparison I can possibly give, as World of Warcraft, and several other games, subscribe to a game difficulty mechanic that I find completely unrealistic.  If you have ever played World of Warcraft, you know you begin in a starting zone that is "simple," but at level 1 or 5, it is very easy to die fighting one of the enemies in the area.  Jump ahead a couple of months, and your level 60 character can enter the same zone, and have 10 creatures run up and attack and take ZERO damage.  Additionally, a low level character cannot survive in higher level zones.  This is not the case in this or any Souls game.  Anyone can kill you.  Granted, higher armor ratings and such will make a difference, but there are places where 4-5 relatively weak creatures can rush you and make players weep.  Monsters do get harder as you progress, but earlier stages cannot be taken for granted.  You cannot just rush through an area to get somewhere in most circumstances as the mobs will follow you.  Such a "herd" will make very short work of you. . .I know.  You will hear many people describe the Difficulty of Dark Souls 2 as cheap and sometimes even say unfair.  9 times out of 10, once you die from falling off a cliff, hopefully you learn your lesson the first or second or third time.  And, if you find it impossible to get past an area, but thousands of others have made it, maybe it's not the game.REGARDING HINTSI love Blood Stains.  That is the single best hint system ever devised in a game.  Click a blood stain, and you can see how someone died, just like other Souls games.  With that said, the single biggest cause of death is easily falling.  Although the camera is better and less a hindrance than in Dark Souls, they made it MUCH easier to fall in the game.  I can't rate that is a con as it was obviously an intentional design choice and does impact your style of play.  There are some non-combat oriented platforming sections where you have take running leaps to reach a location.  I died several times, even after what I thought was a patient, well-timed and executed move.  It is mighty frustrating at times and was not so annoying in past games.The other style of hints are the notes left by other players on the ground.  Most of the time they mention enemy locations or placement of secret doors or traps.  It's a nice touch, and has been around in previous games.REGARDING EVERYTHING ELSEThere are some differences from previous Souls games, but for the most part, it is the same style.  You could easily confuse Dark Souls 2 for Dark Souls or Demon's Souls at first glance.  You create a character from a number of different classes that establishes your initial style of combat.  And, really, there are only two. . .caster/ranged and melee.  Stats really just establish a baseline from which to grow, and very easy to start as either a caster or melee combatant and transform or merge into either the later or former based on how you began.  I am currently playing as a Sorcerer with enough strength to manage a shield and sword.  That is just my style of play.  But, there are a few other things I will mention.Adaptability is a new stat, and I am finding it has some interesting impact on the game.  For that matter, there are other new primary and secondary stats that have significant impact on the game and there are whole articles on the subject (Google it).Related to the platforming reference I made earlier, some of the level design will drive you nuts.  There are places where a stone doesn't go above your character's ankle, and you cannot climb over it.  There is no true environmental interaction.  In a sense, the level designers built a giant frame for you to move around, and then overlaid it with textures.  Sometimes those textures just do not make sense.  You can climb up and down ladders but not a 2 foot high block of stone.The graphics are good/ok.  They work for the game, and do not appear to have frame rate issues like in Dark Souls Blight Town.  As mentioned earlier, sense of depth and distance is missing from the game.Story. . .what story?  This Souls game actually attempts to tell a story, but it still is not made clear.  But, to me, that is part of the beauty of a Souls game.  It does a fantastic job of making you feel alone and lost and not knowing where you are going next.  This will obviously frustrate people.  SPOILER: Very early in the game you can go down a path and come across a knight and a couple of monsters and door with a switch blocked by a statue.  I spent an hour there and moved on as I could not figure out what to do next.  I eventually Googled and found out you cannot access early in the game.  This would not have been so frustrating if the level design was more open.  However, it seemed like I was meant to go to this place, but no indication of if I "could" get through.  I came across this in other areas where rooms and locations seemed to be more than they were, or I at least hoped they were.  There is a balance between a story that guides you and a that provides setting.  Most of the story in Dark Souls 2 is there for setting and not to guide you until later in the game.  Game story as lore.  That's just the way Souls games roll.On being invaded by other characters.  It has only happened a few times and I beat them all except one.  It does not ruin the game and adds an element of surprise.  Related to this topic are Covenants.  Online play is a whole other article/review.  Google it.SPOILER: Some of the bosses are the same or nearly the same as in Dark Souls.  Many of the enemies fight in the same manner as in Dark Souls.  There is not a lot that is new in terms of how they fight.  Not a good or bad comment.  . .just be aware that is more of the same with some variations at time.REGARDING ADDICTIONOverall, I am really enjoying this game.  I like some of the game mechanics, less graphic glitches than previous Souls games.  I miss the sense of scale and openness of past games though.  Although I have a lot games both on PS3 and PC, only a few series of games stick out in my mind, and I continue to come back to again and again to play:  Grand Theft Auto, Uncharted, Civilization, Batman, anything Bioshock, The Last of Us, and. . .the Souls games.  Dark Souls 2 is no exception.  Each one of the game series I mention does at least one thing if not more better than anyone else or at least nears the best.  For me, Dark Souls 2, and the other Souls games, connect with me on a level to where I think about it when I am not playing.  I might go to bed thinking about lore or how to get past a Boss.  Heck, I have gotten up to go boot the PS3 to try just one more time. . .several times.  And, I have come to the conclusion that this is only possible because the game is so imperfect.  I have to think about where I am constantly and am 10 times more aware of what is going on in a Souls game than any other game I mention.  My connection to my character is more real.  I know that as I move my analog stick I control my own destiny.  Nobody is telling me a story.  I am writing one as I go, and each time I boot the game, I prepare to die again. . .5 Stars, 9 out of 10.NOTE: This review is based on digital download of game from PSN.  That option is not available on Amazon at the time of this review that I know of (yet).

In 2011, the original Dark Souls hit store shelves with the slogan, "Prepare to Die." It was an unapologetic challenge and a masterpiece. One that spawned an enormous cult following. Nearly three years later fans still talk about Dark Souls. Fans of Dark Souls don't just like the game. They love it. They're passionate about it. To this day I'm still thrilled, awed and challenged by Dark Souls. Needless to say a sequel to Dark Souls has very high expectations. It's especially daunting because the original is such a huge cult classic--one that didn't need too many major refinements to begin with. Dark Souls II is definitely familiar to anyone who played the original or who played Demon's Souls. But it also has some surprises.You play as an undead who is seeking to break the curse upon you before you go hollow. That is the story of Dark Souls II in a nutshell, but the story of Dark Souls isn't comprised to just a basic plot alone. The world you'll enter has a lot of diverse characters, lore and a lot of storytelling through more than just dialog to get you to understand what's going on. It certainly has more dialog to help you along than the first game, but the emphasis here is still on exploring your surroundings, meeting a diverse cast of characters and the lore of the land in and of itself. That's not to say the story is somehow bad or put under the bus. It is only to say that the approach to storytelling here is not like every other game out there.As with the first one you'll begin by choosing a class and selecting a gift. Each class comes with their own set of levels and skills at first. A sorcerer, for example, begins with a little bit of magic and a boost in intelligence while a warrior begins with a boost in strength and will be able to wield better melee weapons at the start. As with the first, however, no class is restricted in any way. A sorcerer can still use swords and a warrior can still use magic. You may, however, find your stats growing differently as they start off with higher stats in certain attributes than others. There are a couple of new classes added to the mix. The swordsman, who is able to wield two swords at a time with ease. And the explorer who has some slightly more balanced stats but the real benefit is that they start off with more items than any other class. You can customize your character to look anyway you want and you have a lot of options to choose from.Once all this is done, Dark Souls II becomes incredibly familiar with anyone who has played either Souls game before it. You've got a life gauge and you've got a stamina gauge. Each swing of your weapon drains your stamina. When depleted you can no longer attack until it replenishes. Your stamina also effects how long you can hold your guard against an enemies attacks with a shield. Combat in Dark Souls II is just as meticulous as it's ever been. Those who enjoyed the original Dark Souls, though, may have an edge up if only because some moments take a very similar approach. What is slightly different, however, is that the AI of your enemies has increased. Enemies no longer stand around watching as their allies fall to your blade. They are more willing to jump in and attack you while you're in the midst of combat. While this happened in the original, it was often easier to lure enemies away from each others and divide them. This doesn't happen as frequently in Dark Souls II. Combat also flows faster and smoother. The strategic element is still there to a large degree. You still have to be careful with your stamina and utilize dodge rolls and backsteps.That being said, it's quite surprising that Dark Souls II doesn't quite throw you in the same way the original does. One of the hallmarks of the first Dark Souls was that it established itself as not being a very handholding type of game from the get go. Dark Souls II's tutorial area allows for more exploration and throws some relatively weak enemies at you early on. Where as the first one plunged you into a boss fight within the first five minutes, Dark Souls II takes a bit more care to let you get acquainted first. This isn't to say that Dark Souls II holds your hand. In fact, it is better described as a false sense of security. There are markers and messages telling you the controls while also presenting you with an obstacle or objective to try and apply what it is you've just learned. But it isn't as quick to throw you into a boss battle. For the enthusiast this might suggest Dark Souls II is easier than the first one, but in truth it's not long before it actually start really punishing you.Dark Souls is a game where dying is an integral part of the experience and where learning from your deaths is also integral. And make no mistake, you will die. You will die a lot. You'll fight bosses and perish a couple of times before learning their patterns and learning how to defend against their attacks and dodge them. But the sense of accomplishment when you finally do overcome a boss is quite exhilarating. Dark Souls II is one of the few games where the sense of accomplishment is the reward. You are, however, rewarded in more than just a sense of accomplishment. Usually either with better weapons, rare items or a multitude of souls which you can use to increase the attributes of your characters, or buy some much needed weapons, armor and items. . Also make no mistake that Dark Souls II expects you to really work for those rewards. To get to a rare item or a chest often takes a lot of work. Sometimes taking some daring risk or getting past unusually powerful enemies to do so. Dark Souls II is no hand holding experience by any means and it hammers this in several times.Death is going to happen. When you die you will lose all your souls. When you respawn from a bonfire you have a chance to get them back by running to place where you died and retrieving those souls. Of course, what killed you is usually still lurking around as well. The penalty for death is slightly more harsh than the first game, however. Each time you die now, your maximum health will also decrease. And this stacks until you are at fifty percent health. The only way to cure it is by burning an effigy, which is a fairly rare item to come by. Considering how many times you'll perish, this is an invaluable item. The game also makes another couple of tweaks. In the first Dark Souls you could keep respawning enemies and killing them to your hearts content to grind for souls. Dark Souls II takes a different approach. Eventually the enemies in the area will stop respawning, cutting off your ability to farm for souls or grind. While this seems strange at first, you do have an item that allows you to revive every enemy in the area (including bosses) and they'll all be more powerful when you do.Dark Souls II still has a good deal of covenants to join, items to collect and deadly traps in store. Exploring the world is both a fascinating and frightening experience. It is a game where death can (literally) lurk around the next corner. As I said, you will die a lot. Gamers easily frustrated will find this is not the game for them by any means. Dark Souls II isn't always unfair about death, but you will approach several moments where you'll have to die first before you can succeed. You might stumble upon a trap that'll kill you, or find yourself encountering an enemy you weren't prepared for who will massacre you. For the purist of Dark Souls, this is the name of the game. This is what you've come to expect. For those who ignore the warnings that you'll lose your souls over and over again (or who constantly ignore the "Prepare to Die," slogan) this game is a rude awakening. It can be frustrating. Especially when you lose everything you've worked so hard to obtain, but Dark Souls II is still a rewarding experience.One of the most rewarding aspects of Dark Souls was always the online community. Throughout the experience you'd find people who would leave messages. Some were quite helpful like warning you of a fall or a tough enemy ahead. Others were deceitful, such as tricking you into jumping off a ledge when you shouldn't have or leading you to your doom in other ways. This returns in Dark Souls II. And like before, you can rank them. A lot of the time they're helpful. Other times they can be deceptive. That being said, the community serves as a nice guide at times. Often you'll learn when new dangers are around the corner or when great rewards await. The community works for and against you, however. Soon you'll find yourself being invaded by other players. One of the other new additions to Dark Souls II is being able to use an item to make the enemies in the area notice the person invading you. This seems small, but it adds a nice layer into the experience. Dark Souls has always had a unique online experience and it continues here. You'll be invaded and you'll be able to summon an ally to help you fight off tough bosses. You can also touch bloodstains to see the final moments of another characters death.Whenever you need a rest or need to level up or shop for wares, Dark Souls II provides you a hub area that is a lot more similar to the Nexus in Demon's Souls. It slowly becomes populated with more people who can be both your friend or your ally. Some of the NPCs carry valuable items and you can attack them at any time, although they're no slouches. They'll come back at you. But once you kill them they're gone. While some carry rare items others are necessary for you to go through your adventure.There are also plenty of covenants abound. You can join some that add layers to the online experience. Some covenants have an emphasis on helping other players while others put an emphasis on invading them. Most of them will be, from the outset, indistinguishable from the first game, but there's a little extra layer here. There's a lot more emphasis on the online experience here. In particular, a covenant that will summon someone to your aid any time you get invaded is rather nice.Graphically speaking, Dark Souls II looks really good. The rag doll physics aren't present here anymore. There are also fewer dips in the framerate. Every now and then there is still a hiccup but the game runs smoothly. Likewise, the game sounds magnificent. The sound effects are good, but the music score is just as haunting as it can be. There is certainly a wider range of music here than in the previous game. It's a good looking and sounding game. That's not to say some issues don't get in the way. When listening to other characters speak there are some strange pauses. The dialog and voice acting itself is quite good, but sometimes the game has to load the next line of dialog.Dark Souls II is a huge experience. The world is enormous in all sorts of ways. There is plenty to explore, lots of characters to meet and plenty of enemies to kill and be killed by. Dark Souls II is a good game and great for those who want a challenge. It can feel unfair in its approach to difficulty sometimes. Dark Souls II doesn't hold your hand in any way, shape or form. When you explore the game will throw just about anything and everything at you without ever preparing you for what is to come next. This makes the game exciting and exhilarating, but it can also be dreadful. Players who simply rush into any situation expecting to be triumphant will be knocked down a few pegs. Dark Souls II is hard, but not for the wrong reasons. A lot of the time when you die you'll feel it is through your own doing or missteps as opposed to the game itself. The game also expects you to learn from those deaths, however. Obviously this means that Dark Souls II is not going to be a game for everyone. But it's difficulty is meticulously well designed. If you accept that several deaths are inevitable going in, Dark Souls II is apt to be a fun experience.

Dark Souls II is the sequel to Dark Souls, which is the spiritual successor to Demon's Souls. Both of the aforementioned games were masterpieces in my opinion, so I had high expectations for Dark Souls II. Fortunately, those expectations have been met. What exactly were my expectations? I wanted a game that is challenging but fair, a beautiful world that you can explore freely (more or less), and a story line that makes one yearn for more...NOTE: This is review is mostly spoiler free! I do talk a little bit about some of the differences between Dark Souls II and it's predecessor below. If you played the game for a few hours, chances are these will not be spoilers at all. I also have a warning below.NOTE #2: I have a big update at the bottom!! I have not changed this review except for my update at the bottom, which I would recommend reading first.CHALLENGING===========If there is one thing Dark Souls [NB: when I just say Dark Souls I really mean all three games in the series] is known for, it's the challenge. This challenge, is what makes the game. Sure, the game is aurally and visually beautiful, but a major reason for this is the difficulty. For example, as you try to progress through the game, you come across a number of monsters that quickly attack and make short work of you. Eventually, you figure out how to deal with them, only to be sniped by an archer. Then, you try again and once you get past the archer you find there are even more enemies and they make short work of you! By your sixth try (or more) you finally defeat them, and then you realize just how beautiful are the ancient ruins around you! While the game is very challenging, it is also very fair. If an enemy looks like it can kill you in one or two hits, it can. Also, there really are no "simple" enemies. If you let your guard down and become shall we say a bit "overconfident", you may very well find yourself defeated by "weak" foes despite the fact that they are not nearly as difficult as more heavily armoured enemies.DIFFERENT THAN DARK SOULS I==========================Dark Souls II is incredibly similar to Dark Souls I in many ways. If you played the first game, you will immediately be familiar with the controls. However, I find that a running leap is harder in Dark Souls II than the previous game. In fact, my first death [note that your "first death" in Dark Souls is like your first kiss on a date] was not jumping properly. There are however a few other differences. In fact, I would say that Dark Souls II is in a number of ways a blend of Demon's Souls and Dark Souls. For example[WARNING: possibly a few minor spoilers below]***You do not level up at the bonfires.***Your flask, as you will find out, is not nearly as powerful as in Dark Souls I.***You can now warp between bonfires from the start!***Overall, the plot is more defined than in Dark Souls I. In fact, you speak to quite a few people at the start of your adventure.***Some enemies will STOP spawning after you kill them a number of times! This was done to prevent "easy" soul farming!***Fewer classes to choose from during character creation. Not that classes really matter, UNLESS you are one of those players that want to complete the game on Soul Level 1, in which case I think you are in for an amazing challenge![END of possible spoilers]For the most part the game really is a slightly tweaked version of Dark Souls I, but that is exactly what I wanted. FromSoftware said that the "tweaks" were mostly done to make the game even more challenging, and I believe it. Thus far, this definitely appears to be the most challenging of the three games.SINGLE PLAYER=============I played through both Demon's Souls and Dark Souls I offline. I did briefly try the online gameplay, and while I think it is very original and clever, I also thought it detracted from the atmosphere. We all play games for different reasons, the reason I play Dark Souls is for the atmosphere and story. The challenge is a huge part of the atmosphere, and also gives the atmosphere this sense of loneliness, dread, gloom, and at the same time hope and beauty. I realize many players probably enjoy "invading" other players and fighting them. At the same time other players may enjoy "hunting" those that invade other players, as well as helping players with "difficult" boss battles. I respect other people's opinion, but I enjoy playing through games such as Dark Souls on my own. This way, I feel that I can truly breath-in everything the world has to offer. Of course, this makes some of the boss battles incredibly challenging, but again, in Dark Souls ANYTHING can be overcome with skill and patience.VISUALLY and AURALLY===================The music is melancholy, beautiful, eerie, and reminiscent of Dark Souls I. The visuals are much like the music, in that they depict the end days of what was once a great civilization, but now is mere ruins. Overall, the atmosphere is more lonely than in Dark Souls I (believe it or not) and yet just as majestic. The detail on everything (from a basic sword to a giant statue) is superb. The sound effects are also superb. In fact, the sound effects are not just for show but also very important. For example: if you're in a tunnel and you hear "strange" sounds, you can be fairly sure that something ominous is nearby! Again, the atmosphere of the game is breathtaking. When I look around this terrible and yet beautiful world, I almost wish I was there, and if that's not the sign of a great game I'm not sure what is!"BLACK ARMOR" EDITION?=====================If you pre-ordered the game, your "normal" game was automatically "upgraded" to the "Black Armor" edition. This edition includes:->A beautiful steel book that houses the game.->A soundtrack CD (hurray, an actual CD!) with the beautiful music from the game!->A dowloadable code (DLC) for "early access" to special weapons.While the first two are very welcome... who in their right minds came up with this terrible idea for this DLC?! I enjoy Dark Souls because of the challenge, finding powerful weapons right at the start of the game may not "break" the game, but it will undoubtedly ruin much of the enjoyment, at least it would do so for me. Thus, the DLC will not get used! That said, I do certainly think this Black Armor Edition is well worth the hefty $60 price tag.PRO========++Beautiful game both aurally and visually. The atmosphere is so vivid, at times it may just be tangible!++Very difficult, but fair game. This is the most challenging of the three games in the series thus far.++Expect to spend lots of time on this game! This will be a long, beautiful, and challenging game!++"Black Armor" edition includes a wonderful steelbook, as well as the soundtrack on a CD!++ADDICTIVE: this game should have a warning label.CON========--NO manual! I know many games are doing it, but if you're going to pay $60 for a game, it would be nice to have a printed manual!--DLC: the good news is you don't have to use it of course, but I see no purpose in this asinine DLC. I would have liked to have seen something "unique", but not something that would give me an "early advantage" in the game.--ADDICTIVE! I realize I also have this under "pro", and the truth is it is a double-edged sword! It is SO addictive, you may let things slide that you should not! You have been warned.BOTTOM LINES: If you played Dark Souls I and loved it, you probably already have this game. If you have NOT played Dark Souls I nor Demon's Souls, then I strongly suggest you try one of those (I would recommend Dark Souls I)  BEFORE purchasing Dark Souls II. Currently, Dark Souls II is $60. I believe the "Black Armor" edition is worth every penny! However, I am also sure that the price of the "standard edition" (just the normal game) of Dark Souls II will come down. Thus, if you just want to play the game but would rather not spend $60, in a few months this will almost certainly become a "Greatest Hits" release at half the price. While I rarely pay full price for games these days, I think Dark Souls II is certainly worth the price. Not only are you getting an amazing game, but you're also telling FromSoftware that you love this! Here's wishing everyone happy gaming and let us hope in a few years we will see Dark Souls 3!EDIT: After having completed the game and spent more time on Dark Souls II than I would like to admit, I will say that this game is definitely a must for fans of Dark Souls. However, it does not measure up to the original Dark Souls, nor even to Demon's Souls. Again, I speak from the single-player perspective (if you enjoy PvP than Dark Souls II is the best of the bunch). The main problem, which can not be fixed with any update, is that the world simply is not fluid. Although you can walk from one end to the other, everything feels like separate pieces. In the original Dark Souls, anywhere you went felt like it was a natural and majestic part of the world. In Dark Souls II, there are some beautiful places but everything feels like a mini-game. Walking from one section to another feels disjointed. In the original Dark Souls you could easily get lost, but everything made sense. The Darkroot Garden connected to the basin and the castle. Yes, that is logical. In Dark Souls II there are castles, and crypts, a dragon aerie, and much more. However, it's as if the designers said "This is a great idea!" but then had no idea how to connect it with anything else and so just decided to drop it somewhere in the game haphazardly. The original Dark Souls had numerous short-cuts to be found, doors to be opened, keys that played a major role. In Dark Souls II, I just go from area to area and clear out the enemies. Another flaw, albeit not as bad as the game design, is that there are far too many enemies that are nothing more than a knight with a sword. Some are giant, some are small, some have shields, some do not, some are bosses, most are not, but they're all over the place! Although Dark Souls II had some epic battles, I felt that most of the boss designs were uninspired. For example, in the original Dark Souls you come across two gargoyles you must beat! In Dark Souls II you must beat 5 of them! Why? It seems like the designers were more into "Oh, this will be REALLY hard!" Rather than "This will be fun and unique, as well as challenging". Also, in the original Dark Souls I grew attached to the few characters found in the world. Some had tragic ends, some happy, it depended on how I interacted. In Dark Souls II there are quite a few characters, but I did not see them much nor does it appear like I could influence their outcome. As in Dark Souls, I can kill any NPC. However, they then come back as ghosts. So did I really kill any of them? I guess it really does not matter if I kill them or not! That in essence is one of the major problems with Dark Souls II. Many things that used to matter, simply do not. It doesn't matter if I rest at this bonfire, because I can teleport anywhere I want at any time. It does not matter if I accidentally kill someone, because I can resurrect their ghosts which in essence is the same as having them around. Despite my complaints, this is still a "good" game, just not a masterpiece. I don't think it's fair to summarize anything in just one number, but if I had to give a score, my final score would be 80/100.

Disclaimer: These are my impressions after 8 hours of play, and I'll be sure to update as I progress through the game.[April 10, 2014: I have completed the game twice and updated at the bottom.]Dark Souls II isn't your standard direct sequel, and as many people have noticed the game takes quite a bit from its spiritual predecessor Demon's Souls, maybe ever more than it does from the first Dark Souls. I was pleased with this for the most part, the small health penalty on death is a fitting punishment without being quite as extreme as going straight to half like Soul Form a la Demon's Souls. I'll elaborate on the less successful changes later on, but for now I'll focus on more of the positives.Starting from the beginning, character creation is what I see as an important aspect of Dark Souls, and although it hasn't been vastly improved as I had hoped, progress has been made. Face models are more believable, and there are a few more options, notably the addition of facial hair and two options for muscularity.Regarding combat, the AI definitely jumped out at me as a vast improvement. Enemies can be found patrolling areas, defending better against backstabs, and being more defensive in general. When I baited a group of enemies by climbing up a ladder to take them one-on-one, I was shocked when they simply gathered around the bottom of the ladder in a circle with their shields up, lying in wait for me instead. Enemies are more formidable in other ways, too--shields are difficult to break, firebombs are more accurate and powerful and enemies stagger you more easily (although this may change later due to the fact that one can now acquire poise without armor). Some of the traps and ambushes I encountered in the beginning of the game surpassed Dark Souls and Demon's Souls in deviousness. Backstabs have been altered as well to remove invincibility as well as being harder to perform, and as such are no longer as much of a "crutch" to be used when faced with an overwhelming group of enemies.The game isn't perfect, of course. One of the most major Demon's Souls influences is the return to an open world connected by warping, rather than the interconnected World of Dark Souls traversed mainly by walking. My problem with this was that it felt like Dark Souls II can use the ability to warp instantly as an excuse for lazy map design, as no area I've come across yet is mapped out as ingeniously as the first areas of Dark Souls, namely the Undead Burg and Undead Parish. One of my favorite experiences in Dark Souls was returning to Firelink Shrine after nearly giving up in the vast, unforgiving Blighttown. Had I been able to warp to safety when cursed or running out of purple moss, this victory would have rung hollow.The Emerald Herald, a throwback to Demon's Souls' Maiden in Black was another change I wasn't quite happy with. In Demon's Souls, the Nexus was clearly established as the only true safe haven in the game, where you would return to store weapons and level up. The Firelink Shrine of Dark Souls was similar to this, but Bonfires were in actuality closer to what one would call a home--a place to level up, repair weapons and manage items. In Dark Souls II, I don't feel like there's a clear base of operations. One returns to bonfires to heal, but can't use them to level up, instead traveling to Majula to meet with the Emerald Herald. All this feels like is an extra loading screen, and doesn't serve much of a purpose except to hinder the establishment of a clear base in the game. One doesn't need to travel to a bonfire to restore humanity like in Dark Souls either, as human effigies can be consumed anywhere, similarly to the Stones of Ephermal Eyes of Demon's Souls.My most major concern with the game before it game out was the world and lore. Despite the game's ties with Demon's Souls, I knew the atmosphere and rich detail of Boletaria would be hard to match, and the initial previews of Dark Souls II left me unsure. I feel a bit better after my short experience so far--the new armor is far from generic fantasy, and from what I've seen of them and the weapons, there's a lot of uniqueness and eccentricity that I loved in Demon's Souls. It's still hard to say at this point, but I have faith that the experience of Dark Souls II will be satisfying.The last detail I have to add, which isn't particularly positive or negative, is my thoughts on the difficulty. Surprisingly, from my experience with the game so far it's possible that Dark Souls II is even more difficult than the first--something you can probably thank the smarter AI mentioned previously and less exploitable backstabs. I have no comment on whether the bosses are harder as I've only fought the first one, which was fairly easy but in no way an accurate indicator of things to come--though I'm excited to find out.[UPDATE]After finishing the game twice there are several more positives and negatives I've noticed with the game.Fortunately, the end areas of the game aren't rushed like they were in Dark Souls I, meaning the quality of the game is pretty consistent.Dark Souls II also seems even more open-ended then the first game. The path I took on my second playthrough was completely different than my first, and the path only becomes more linear when approaching Drangleic Castle, one of the final areas. This seems to be the opposite of the first game, where the start of the game was somewhat linear with the latter half of the game branching out completely.One of my biggest complaints is with the balancing of the covenants. The Brotherhood of Blood, successor to the Darkwraith covenant, is absolute s***. There is no reason to join it. The final rank requires about 500 successful invasions and rewards you with basically nothing. In addition, acquiring cracked red eye orbs is much more difficult, compounding this. There is no reason to join BoB over the Blue Sentinels if you want to invade.Soul Memory is another annoying and controversial decision. You're restricted on all online cooperation based on the total amount of souls acquired throughout the game. This is obviously meant to combat twinking, but instead leads to being forced to bothersomely count your souls throughout the entire game to avoid having online play become a barren experience. According to Namco's website, you need to be within about 50,000 souls of another player to connect. Did you lose twice that much dying before your bloodstain? That sucks. You'll have to deal with a tendency to be underleveled compared to to other players unless you want to restart your character.Also, the final boss and climax. I don't want to spoil anything, but you get railroaded into a single predictable and uninteresting ending after the game deludes you into thinking you have a choice in the matter.I don't feel like the game deserves a different score overall.

(this is more geared to people thinking of starting out the series than veteran players)Dark Souls has a well-deserved reputation as a brutally difficult game.  Despite dying untold times in Demon's Souls, Dark Souls and now Dark Souls 2, I found it a thoroughly rewarding game, if you are patient and are willing to invest time and effort to play it.  Yes, you may die 20-30 times against one boss, but what a rush when you've finally offed her.  And, sometimes, you'll walk in and just nuke another boss the first time around, which is also a big boost.But, make no mistake, it is a hard game to play.  Many low reviews because it's too hard.  Run into a room all guns blazing, not paying close attention to your enemies' style?  You'll die.  Expect your videogames to hold your hand?  You'll HATE this game.On the other hand, it is gorgeous, highly replayable, full of clever traps and unique enemies.  The control mechanism feels just right for a console controller as well.  Very well-balanced as a RPG.  Like playing a tank?  You can.  A wizard, ditto, slightly easier class to play with as well.  And a sneaky assassin is also highly doable.  In fact, the level system makes it possible to evolve your character in tons of different directions.Now, one thing to understand about Souls is that these are highly, highly, tactical, _thinking_ games.  Yes, many foes can kill you with one shot.  You never have strong enough armor or powerful enough weapons.  But... the starting layout is _always_ the same.  So you have to gradually learn how to bring an enemy down.  Sometimes it's a vulnerability of theirs, sometimes it's something with the terrain that you just get in an "ha ha" moment.  Sometimes it is a glitch you can use to your advantage (they feel cheap at first, but you learn to appreciate small favors from this game).  Most often it's closely observing your enemies' scripted attack patterns.You can get plenty of help from YouTube or the wiki sites.  But, at the end of the day, you're the person who has to make it work.You may even have to change your fighting style.  Fighting the Ruin Sentinels boss, I kept on dying using my light-armor assassin&wizard; kit, as I couldn't maneuver on the narrow starting ledge.  Heck the first 3 times I died without even seeing who had hit me.  So I took up the heaviest, most stagger-proof armor I had, and slugged it out - no luck.  Finally, I resorted to a tactic many veterans will recognize - I ditched all my armor to max my speed.  Went into battle with loincloth & shield and just focused on not getting too greedy, keeping my distance, gradually wearing them down.  Sword on the ledge, spells on the ground.Bit about myself.  Been playing games for 25+ years, love turn-based wargames and RPGs.  Civ2, Steel Panthers, Shogun.  Prior to Souls, Baldur's Gate would have been my fave RPG with Fallout a close second.  Skyrim?  Nice, but too sprawling and way too forgiving.  Used to be a big Quake 2 & 3 fan, love the raw speed and aggression they require.  I am picky too:  Call of Duty 2 on PS3?  Played 3 hours before ditching it, hated the auto-heal feature.Point is, you don't have to be a top-reflexed teenager to enjoy Souls, though it helps.  But you will have to work at this game and there is no substitute for using your brains.p.s.  Sitting on the fence as a Souls newbie?  Pick up Dark Souls I for a lot less, game mechanics and quality are substantially the same and the wiki hints @ Dark Souls wikidot are much more complete.p.p.s.  (for veterans)I didn't mind most of the changes, except that low Agility seems to make your PS3 controller react like molasses.  As it not clearly explained what that ability is for, you may get frustrated until you figure out that you need to improve it.Enemies that eventually stop respawning?  A good thing, IMHO, it means that you are not constantly cutting your way through by now thoroughly overclassed enemies.  It also means less loot.Graphics are good enough, but not a huge improvement on Dark Souls 1.Dying and gradual HP loss?  I found the Ring of Clinging early on, so I have had no problems whatsoever.  I realize that it would be different if I had not found it.Curses are too lenient now.  The 50% HP loss used to be a major problem, now I am not sure what they do to penalize you.Some brilliant additions, in a "OMG this is hard" way.  Thinking of the bandits in the whiteout fog level, for example.

Let me start by saying that DSII is awesome but very hard, and most people won't enjoy this game for it's screeching difficulty. If you disliked Dark Souls you most likely won't enjoy Dark Souls II since they are so similar, but if you did enjoy Dark Souls then you know what you're in for - and all is well. DSII is familiar in a way DS vets will understand (controls, mechanics, UI mostly the same), with enough new material and variation to keep things fresh.A few great changes: you can warp from any bonfire to any other bonfire you've already discovered, basic fast-travel is fine and unlocked at the beginning of the game, afetr all the world is huge so you'll need the help getting around; secondly, DSII holds a solid 30fps at all times even when there are a dozen things happening on screen at once (remember how awful Blighttown was in Dark Souls?); thirdly, DSII has an updated game engine and visually it's an obvious step above DS, the lighting is especially enhanced and really makes for some fun exploring - especially when monsters come sneaking out of the shadows! You're also able to light torches at bonfires now which helps you explore extra dark areas, it's a very cool feature.Souls `vets will find just as much difficulty as DS offered and new players may find the game a bit strenuous. Players who explore, persist, and learn from their deaths will find great reward in the new challenges DSII offers - especially those players who explore each nook and cranny in the world. The stakes have never been higher in DS, with each death your total life will be reduced, and while a rare human effigy will restore this, it makes each venture into the unknown a tad overwhelming (which is kinda the point, amirite?).Multiplayer is monstrously improved this time, connections are smoother, and joining another player is much easier - the best part, if you summon another player you get an immediate response whether or not it was a success, thank goodness! It wasn't as hard for me to buddy up with a phantom in the first few hours and we had a jolly good time breaking faces. There are new covenants this time around, each offers a different take on multiplayer, but I won't spoil those here.New-Game+ is here as always but now you can choose when to begin, very nice if you're holding off for late game PvP. Over all it's a really dang fun and a worthy successor to Dark Souls, definitely a must buy for me.One thing is for certain though, DSII is not watered down. You're going to have your butt handed to you on a silver platter, a lot.Prepare to die, over and over and over again.

First off, I'm a casual gamer. I liked rpg style games, but I'm kind of sick of the fantasy rpg's. If you are sick of the fantasy story lines then buy this game. The investigation missions are very challenging and sometimes I had to look up the cheat and I never felt bad because I would have never figured it out. I have friends that have played all the missions with no help at all though. So it's doable. I would say this game generally attracts and keeps the more mature players playing. Most of the cabal that I have joined are mothers, fathers and well into 30s and 40s of age. This is a good thing though. It makes the chat channels less cluttered with children being immature. The leveling system is different. You don't level. You get experience, but they get you your stat and ability points. Stat points will get you into better gear, and ability points will get you new abilities.I saw a bunch of reviews where people said that the game doesn't give any instructions on how to play. This is entirely not true. Most of the missions have a quest helper tool that will even show you where you need to go. The NPCs on the game will send you on missions that will get you to the next NPC areas as well.And here is the cool thing about missions. There isn't so many boring fetch quests that plague most MMOs. You know like, "Go kill 10 bears and 15 hides." There are some missions like that, but they are not common place in this game. These are the green colored quests and the completionist in me tried to do them all while playing through, but I found myself just doing the main story missions with the cut scenes because they are so much more fun to play!There are instances in this game and different difficulties. Normal, Elite, and Nightmare. You will notice that the instances do not have very many mobs in between bosses. Some of them have 0 trash mobs. I was a little bit dissapointed with that, until I got to fight the bosses on Elite and Nightmare difficulties as they become challenging with boss mechanics that you have to be mindful of, attacks that need to be impaired. Needless to say tanking in this game is by far the most challenging. The instances do follow the trilogy of a dps, tank and healer roles but you dont have to stick with that role completely. I have builds where I am a leech healer, so I dps and am the main healer. I have a tank/dps build where I am super squishy, but deal pretty respectful dps compared to the actual dps. As a dps you can do raw damage, sometimes you need to help the tank impair boss attacks that will wipe the whole party.
