The Last of Us had instantly made Naughty Dog one of the greatest and most respected video game developers in the world. Ever since the first Crash Bandicoot game was released back in 1996, they haven’t had one bad game yet in their name. The Last of Us is no exception, it is simply a masterpiece.The player takes control of Joel who is living in a post-apocalyptic United States in the year 2033. He then has to escort a young girl by the name of Ellie to a resistance group called the ‘Fireflies’ who they believe may be the key to finding a cure for the infection that has ravaged the world. The player must defend themselves against zombie-like creatures infected by a mutated strain of the Cordyceps fungus. Apart from zombies; you also have to fight against armed hostile humans such as bandits and cannibals.The game uses a third person perspective similar to games like Resident Evil 4. You control Joel while Ellie is controlled by the AI. The combat is very well detailed and feels fluent and perfectly responsive. There is gun fighting, melee combat and a cover system that works perfectly. There are two ways to eliminate your targets, you can go smart by quietly sneaking up to enemies by choking them or stabbing them in the neck. The other tactic is to go loud and dumb by using your scarce ammo against them. The choice is yours, but sometimes you’ll have no choice to use either one of these tactics. The most innovative feature is you can find out where enemies are by hearing their sound. Since there’s no way for an actual TV to pinpoint the exact direction of where sound is coming from within the game, The Last of Us made an ingenious idea because in real life, you’d be able to tell which direction a footstep or voices are coming from.As you proceed with the game, you receive more weapons and items. Items include things from simple pistols, to more advanced weapons such as a bolt action rifle, shotguns, bows, flamethrowers and assault rifles. You can also use melee weapons that you can find throughout the environment such as metal pipes, planks, baseball bats, machetes and hatchets. These however will break after repeated use so it’s wise to use them sparingly. You can also pick up empty bottles and bricks off the ground and throw them which can be used to distract enemies so you can sneak by them, plan a sneak attack or they can be used as a simple melee weapon. This game requires both skill and brains.You also have a crafting system. You can create items by combining various other items you find along your journey. These ranges from first aid kits, Molotov cocktails, nail bombs and smoke bombs. You can even attach scissors to melee weapons to make them more powerful, but they won’t last forever. The idea is to plan each move carefully. Another thing about the crafting system is that using the system is based on real time, meaning that the game does not pause while crafting. So plan your decisions well or you leave yourself vulnerable to enemy attack.The player is also able to collect toolboxes and parts to help upgrade their weapons which again is similar to Resident Evil 4.Things you can improve are the number of weapons you can carry without going into your backpack to change them, the weapons fire rate, clip capacity, power, range and you can reduce the recoil. You also find training manuals along the way to increase your weapons even more so. These improvements include the durability of knives, the radius of Molotov’s and Nail Bombs and so on. You also find pills and plants along the journey which increase your maximum health, crafting speed, healing speed and so on.There are periods in the game where there is no fighting when everything is calm and the player can engage in conversations with other friendly characters. You can discuss the current situation with Ellie and she can even tell jokes.This game also has a bit of strategy in it where you’ll need to give Ellie boosts up to platforms you can’t reach. Ellie will then unlock doors from the other side, drop down ladders and so on. Unfortunately Ellie can’t swim so in order to get her across the water; you’ll need to find floatable planks to get her across.The story is also very well detailed and emotional. I won’t spoil anything though, you’ll have to play the game yourself if you want to know more about it. I will say Ellie is an awesome character. She isn’t like Ashley from Resident Evil 4 who couldn’t defend herself. Ellie is eventually given a gun and is very good at defending herself, even against big enemies and grown adults. She is just awesome.Is there anything I don’t like about it? Well there is this one glitch (which I’m not sure if it’s been addressed yet) when you are running from a tank, the camera just moves out of control making that part of the game unplayable. Fortunately if you die, the camera is fixed. I also don’t like that this game isn’t as scary as other horror games like Silent Hill or Resident Evil. My biggest complaint is that you have checkpoints in the game which doesn’t make the game challenging or scary. In the original Resident Evil on PlayStation, if you die, you have to start over from where you last saved. But you were limited to how many times you can save so it made you more cautious when playing the game. But in The Last of Us, you aren’t really that cautious because the consequences of dying aren’t severe. My final complaint is the game doesn’t come with an instruction manual. It only comes with an online pass code that can only be used once and two Naughty Dog stickers. But some people claim that they didn’t receive stickers with their game, but I did though, I even put one of the stickers on the back of my laptop. The manual is built in the game itself, but the downside is that you have to leave the game completely and select the manual from the PS3 main menu. I hate games that do that, people who don’t make instruction manuals are just frickin’ lazy and slackers.In conclusion, The Last of Us isn’t that scary, but it has awesome gameplay elements and a deep storyline that is well worthy of praise. I can honestly say that The Last of Us is the greatest PlayStation 3 exclusive I have ever played. This is a must play for any gamer, especially fans of survival horror which the current generation was lacking. The Last of Us is probably the greatest survival horror game of the seventh generation of video games and this will go down as a classic as more new consoles are released.FINAL RATING: 10 OUT OF 10

It's much more than that. The Last of Us cannot be called survival horror. It's about survival. It's about people. It's not a perfect game, but you'll never forget it. It might not end up the national archives. Not everyone liked it. But you need to try it. It's built with numerous references to a very many movies, it's built to cater to those who hunger for realism or a greater challenge in gaming. But it isn't necessary, because at core it's a game about people.And if you ignore the rest of my review, don't ever watch a playthrough or read a plot synopsis. Your FIRST playthrough is something you will never, ever get back. So you have to do it yourself.I think my original review was far too wordy, so I'll try to be brief, and detailed.I think this game is very much worth it's full price, which makes it doubly worth it at a discounted price. Just be careful to get the online pass with the game, so you don't have to pay for that separately like I did. You unlock multiplayer after finishing the campaign. The Season Pass DLC costs $20, gives you a roughly two-hour campaign in 'Left Behind,' boosters for multiplayer, a documentary on how the game was made and the soundtrack, and a yet to be released mutltiplayer DLC. It even has Facebook connectivity - done so in a less-annoying-way than most, I might add. Good value.The DLC, 'Left Behind' focuses on two plots occurring around the story. I'd suggest you play it after the main game. I played both the campaign and the DLC on 'Hard.' You can unlock a Survivor difficulty after that. While the game feels very different at high difficulty, you need not be intimidated to only play it on Hard. This game should be played by neophyte and hardcore gamers alike.Unlike a few other titles in the survival-horror genre, the multiplayer is a seamless fit with the campaign and the game wouldn't be complete without it. You can see my full review of the multiplayer here: http://www.amazon.com/review/R2CDYWK4110BKD/ref=cm_cr_rdp_permLast of Us is a heck of a campaign experience. You might be in tears by the end of it, you might be upset. The only way to know is to try. My first playthrough took 16 hours. It has four difficulties and bonuses after you finish it. There is a basic director sort of influence which changes the game and the supply drops depending on how much difficulty you're having. The game basically melds itself to your playstyle and skill, meaning just about anyone can pick up the game.It is incredibly violent. The violence is usually understandable, but it is not for the weak of stomach. You kill a whole lot of living, breathing people as well as infected.In Minecraft or Day Z, people chat about the crazy random things that they were involved in. These games have players make their own stories. Then you have more linear storytelling, where every player experiences the same rough story. Resident Evil games, a majority of survival horror, many FPS games, also many JRPGs - parts where some dialogue seems incredibly corny, or when a fan-favorite character dies in Final Fantasy VII.The Last of Us is a little bit of both. The campaign will always have the same ending (no multiple endings here) and you'll do the same basic things, but different difficulties present different challenges, and you may play the game differently in every playthrough. There's plenty to discuss with friends, both in who dies, who cries, what happens, or spontaneous events like a zombie surprising you, running out of ammo right before a big gunfight and so forth. The game is designed well, in short.Joel, the man on the cover has seen many terrible things and has been forced to do some bad things himself. He might seem to come off as the typical bearded action hero, but the realism here comes from his flaws. The ending for Last of Us is known to be controversial. In fact, his demeanor and decisions the entire game are. He will do what many players won't do. But you never stop and go 'What? Why!" because the game is consistent and convincing with who he and everyone else in the game is like. It's his small attempts at changing as he meets other people that are so interesting.And that's why it hurts you so much to see the things that happen to these characters. I can't go too much in depth with the campaign, for fear of taking away with it. At core, I feel that it's about healing. There's a lot of thought put into the campaign about how hard it is to survive, even if you are as good at it as the main characters. Some of the early game plot elements are pretty predictable but... if they're not, I can't exactly spoil them for you either.If I had to guess, you fight for about 65-70% of active game time in various ways. At core, you collect resources, craft items, upgrade weapons, enhance skills by taking care of your character and finding training manuals, while exploring a very varied terrain that's sampled from all across America. You fight as many people as infected. There's never a time where an item begins to feel redundant. Every bit of equipment you carry has a purpose. Weapons feel punchy and have a definite weight to them. Enemies react to the firepower and tactics you employ. Every tactic has its effects.There isn't environmental destruction, but you can explore almost everything and there's few invisible walls. It's almost like a Parkour game. You can slide into cover, vault over low obstacles, climb into high windows, kick doors open, shove furniture over to block people, take huge jumps from rooftop to rooftop. It is not a game with waist-high walls. Almost everything can be bypassed in someway.I have to draw an early comparison to Resident Evil 4. The levels were designed to allow you to go through the same basic area in a variety of ways, using exploding barrels, breakable windows, conserving ammo and funneling crowds. This is something broadly absent from it's sequels, but Last of Us embraces the same idea. You go from the same basic point to the next in every playthrough, the methods involved are left up to you. The game has its intensive peaks and thoughtful lows, when you have a lot of time to think about the events in passing.Your characters will actively talk to each other and there's a load of optional conversations that you can miss entirely if you're not careful. Each one adds a bit to your character's very well-fleshed out backstory. A certain pair appear for maybe an hour or two, tops, but I found myself empathizing with them and wondering how many others like them were still out there. The characters make SENSE, unlike many other shooters I had to slog through.In that respect, every element of the game fits together in a way that few games can really compare to. The music is always thematically consistent, while making use of every symphonic and acoustic tool the composer can get his hands on, with an overall western feel that reflects your traveling across the US. It's complex, emotional music that doesn't rely on bass drops or screaming to convey an idea. Character animation is seamless - you pat walls as you sneak around, characters have more idle animations than hours of staring could uncover. There's detail in everything from applying a bandage to the specific area you got shot, rather than a stock animation, to how leaves rustle when you push through them, to how your character shields their eyes when they emerge in a sunny area from darkness.I could boot up this game just to watch the environment lightly bob in the breeze as nature has overgrown urban sprawls, as much as could log on to thrash people online. It's a thoughtful game.Any complaint directed at the game would mostly concern online game balance, and again, the ending and the general linearity of some decisions. A good number of people just dislike why the characters make the decisions they did. I do also agree that sometimes you can't use brute force in some linear stealth spots, or use stealth in places intended to force heavy gunfights. It seems like the game doesn't want to let you find a way around things with less killing.The thing is though, playing again I realized that in many areas, I could pass by enemies. But it was because I knew the exit points. You can't just know who not to kill and who to pass in a real disaster. There's a definite theme relevant to surviving real-life disasters and I didn't find it overly heavy-handed. If anything, the game does its best to inform you of a heavy cost involved in any tragedy.There's so much to say, but it's easiest just to state the game deserves a fair chance, alright?
Without a doubt, the greatest game I've played in my entire life, and I don't think any game will ever top the experience I had playing The Last of Us.

Examples include ridiculous traffic sign placements, something I take seriously here in the real world. The Last Story is a fun game and a good game for the JRPG lover. However, there really isn't anything about it that stands out. As always my reviews will be split between story, gameplay, and characters with story having the most weight.Story: 6/10So the story is good enough to keep you interested but really that's about all you can say about it. It's a good story but nothing that is just going to blow your socks off. It really fealt like I was playing an old FF like FF 3 or 4 with updated graphics and gameplay. This is one area that I think the japanese writers have been surpassed by the western writers. The stories in JRPGs have just become lack luster and the Last Story is a perfect example of this. Don't get me wrong. The story was interesting and well written but overall just kind of bleh.You play as a mercenary trying to make a life for himself and his friends until one day you meet a beautiful girl on the run from the soldiers. You find out that she isn't just any girl but (stop me if you've heard this a million times) a PRINCESS. Woah didn't see that coming did you? But she's being married off by her evil uncle the count. One day you receive a special power and only you can stop the coming destruction....yeah yeah it's been done before. And this game's story is well done...but how many times are we going to rescue the land and the princess people. It was nice how they added a little sci fi in the story (not spoiling anything) which spiced it up a bit. Thus the 6/10 and not a 5.Another complaint is that the story is tooooo predictable. They pretty much slap you in the face over and over about who is going to be the surprise (if you can call it that) boss and who is behind all the evilness. I thought in this decade we had gotten past this kind of foreshadowing. Apparently not. Oh well. Like I said it's a story that was well written and still interesting enough to get you through but one that was overly predictable and one that has been done a million times over. With JRPGs that have great stories like Xenoblade and the FF13 series...there really is no excuse.  6/10Gameplay: 8.5/10Now here is the really charming part about this game. As unoriginal the story is the gameplay is not. A completely new system. Very much team and tactics oriented. Just a really fun system. The developers really came up with something fun that I have not seen before. You basically have two types of players, warriors and mages. And each play off each other to use different and unique tactics to win the fight. You can pause the game and issue commands based off of how much stamina you have. Mages can cast spells that leave a magic circle on the ground. Warriors can then use these circles to cast spells of their own like causing physical damage, healing the party, debuffing an enemy, or buffing the party. Each character learns a special skill. Warriors it's usually some sort of new attack, and mages it's a spell of some sort. Each player will also learn a "Limit Break" if you will that you have to build up spirit points to use.There is a ton of loot. And loot upgrading. You can collect weapons and armor and upgrade them with money at first and then special materials you gain along the way. You are constantly updating your gear which is always fun to me. And as you upgrade you can visually see the differences in the armor/weapon which is a very nice touch.  More RPG's should do this.Now for the bad. CAMERA ANGLES...oh geez. Seriously? We are still having camera angle issues in video games these days. Nothing more infuriating than being in a big fight and not being able to turn the camera around. Sure there is a button that turns you around automatically...but when you do that and you still can't position the camera correctly...it get's pretty maddening real quick.The only other negative are the sidequests. There aren't that many really...but at least there are some (here's looking at you FF13). But really the sidequests are really ridiculous time sucks like "Go catch 3 frogs" or "I have hidden 10 coins in this city go look for them". And the sidequests give you little more than junk usually. Pretty much a waste of time. The arena was a nice touch but not enough to pull this part up. Overall though the gameplay is truly the best part of this game. 8.5/10Characters 5.5/10The characters are probably the worst part of this game, with a few shining exemptions. First the good.Ok. Lowell and Syrenne are the best characters in this game by far. Maybe some of the best supporting characters I have played in quite some time. They have more personality than your general RPG side characters and more personality and human nature than the rest of your party. Truly funny and truly gems among rocks in the characters of this gameNow for the rest. They are once again, your generic 1990's RPG characters. The main character plays the stoic warrior with little to say. The damsel in distress plays the shy girl with not much to say. Then you have some supporting characters that have daddy issues and another that was raised in the forest but still..doesn't have much to say. Then one more that plays the stoic warrior again.  The enemies offer little in personality as well.Overall the characters are just dull. They belong in an old 1980's or 1990's JRPG. I like the thought of capturing the nostalgia of the old days but one thing about the old days is...well it's old and we are looking for something with the same charm but a little more interesting. 5.5/10Overall 7/10All in all this is an average game with some really fun and unique gameplay. If it wasn't for the gameplay it would be a solid 5 or 6 maybe. The story is interesting but completely unoriginal and predictable. The gameplay is truly fun and unique while the characters are just dull and usual except for a couple more interesting additions. Overall this game should be played by huge fans of JRPG's but will fail to interest those that are just casual fans. Without the lush history like a Final Fantasy or a huge adventure with a completely unique story like Xenoblade, The Last Story comes off as a quaint charming game that really just screams mediocrity.

First let me start off with a rant.The United States is currently plagued with mindless games with no meaningful story.  The most popular games of our age are mindless FPSes.  This breaks free from that tradition.  As others have reviewed, this game is a visual novel.  There are two aspects to this game.  Story Parts, which progress the story, and puzzle rooms, which you must solve a complex puzzle in a room to advance.  I love these games as they force a player to develop longer attention spans to pay attention to and follow the story over a long period.Pros:- Fantastic Soundtrack with tracks I'll still listen to.- Good Animation/3D effects.- The story is good, but I do feel it's a bit confusing at some points (ESPECIALLY at the End).  I followed it closely and didn't even see it coming.- Good characters--you'll recognize some from the prequel 999.- The game has a BRANCHING storyline.  Meaning when you get one ending, you need not replay the whole game, but you can rewind back to where you broke off.  This is a HUGE IMPROVEMENT over 999 which forced you to replay the whole darn game.Cons:- As mentioned earlier, the story is fantastic but does get confusing.  Ending is very confusing but manageable.- Some puzzles are just bad and don't make sense in my opinion.  I feel like they could have used more development.  For the most part, 90% of the puzzles are fine, it's just those 10% that are like WHA?- Short Memo pad.  You get 2 memo pads in game to track important notes--we need more.Overall, I'd recommend this game easily.  I got it for $20 bucks on the Nintendo eShop.  That's a no brainer,

VLR contains a lot of UI improvements from 999: the greatest of which is a built in flowchart that lets you see how your decisions are affecting the paths you take and what ending you'll arrive at (the chart will just have a mystery block at places and paths you haven't gotten to yet so no worries about spoilers). This is a godsend as their are more than 20 different endings in the game (as apposed to the 6 in 999) and you don't have to worry about accidentally getting the same ending twice as you can see where you are on the flowchart. You are also able to "jump" around to places all over the flowchart, so there is no need to start from the very beginning of the game each time you complete an ending.Another great addition is the much higher level of difficulty that the puzzles in VLR achieve. One of the few things that I disliked about 999 is that the puzzles were often incredibly easy, making them a little boring. VLR has fixed that with puzzles that raise the bar much higher and actually require some thought (although they can range from very easy to ones so difficult that you might have to switch to Easy Mode or look them up in a guide).The game also gives you a memo for writing things down, an archive feature that allows you retain more items used for puzzles or key events that happen on different paths, a PASS feature that retains the password for puzzle rooms you've already completed, and a secrets folder that keeps background information of various supplementary knowledge mentioned in the game (if you can unlock it by getting Secret Safe passwords).With so many improvements it was hard to see such a downgrade in terms of the characters, setting, and story. I don't hold 999 on a pedestal but when comparing the two, VLR has almost none of the atmosphere and great characters that made the original game so fantastic. Clover (as well as a few more characters from 999) returns--for example--, but she has now been flanderized as a ditzy airhead. But I think the story was the most disappointing. Without any spoilers: The ride you take throughout the game is actually very enjoyable. The ending however, becomes {opinion} a huge clusterf--ck that, while technically making sense, is just extremely stupid and relies on one big cop-out after another. The plot also does not get resolved; having been saved for the 3rd Zero Escape game.Of course I wouldn't give 3 stars just for a disappointing story (not with the gameplay and puzzles being improved so much). The main reason for the rating is that the 3DS version still seems to contain very serious bugs that still have not been patched since release. Thankfully I only managed to fun into a small bug once that just froze my game in a puzzle room. There exists, however, a very big save bug that might completely wipe your save randomly if you save in either the PEC room or the Crew Quarters (where my game froze). Because of this, I just avoided saving during puzzle sections all together. It was annoying but worth it to avoid losing a 40 hour save file. Even with the save bug, the game still appears very playable, but seeing how it is highly unlikely that Chunsoft is ever going to release a patch, I would have to recommend getting the Vita version (bug-free) perhaps.

Look, I've played some mediocre games in my day. And if a game has some redeeming qualities, I'm not above hacking my way through the unpolished parts to get to them. Two Worlds II, for example, was a little rough around the edges. But I enjoyed it nonetheless, and spent upwards of 40 hours fighting my way through to the end.Risen 2 takes the term "unpolished" to a whole new level. To the point where I'm only an hour in, and I'm ready to throw in the towel. Let me count the ways that this game is absolutely atrocious (so far)...1) The title screen for this game -- which, as near as I can determine, is set sometime around the 1600s -- features an image of a foreboding skull, along with a spinning CD (with a message about autosaving). Excellent art direction so far, fellas. You couldn't have changed that CD icon to something more period-appropriate? A treasure chest perhaps?2) All of the text in this game -- from the intro sequence to the character names to every bit of text in the menu -- is all in caps for no reason whatsoever. And it's italicized. And I'm pretty sure it's Times New Roman. It's almost as if no one who developed this game knows anything about design, because it's an eyesore.3) Despite being set in a tropical pirate setting, the graphics are dull and muddy.4) The voice acting is awful, as though the seemingly-disinterested actors were thinking to themselves the entire time, "I'm getting paid in cash for this, right?"5) While locked in a tense duel with some sand crabs or something at the start of the game, the camera inexplicably rotated 180 degrees, so that all I could see was the main character, flailing wildly with his sword. The creatures I was supposed to be fighting were located somewhere out of the frame.6) The cutscenes not only feature choppy graphics that look like they're from 2002, but also textures that appear and disappear randomly, clunky dialogue and a general sense that whoever "directed" these scenes has never actually interacted with another human.7) I have no idea where I'm supposed to be going, because the map is utterly useless. I managed to figure out how to get out of the outpost by simply talking to everyone, but now that I've hopped a ship and ended up in some other town, I foresee being completely lost at all times.In my short time with Risen 2, I can confidently say that it's the worst PS3 game I've ever played. I know that making games is not an easy task, but this is just an unfinished mess of a game that never should've been released. Because I'm a glutton for punishment, I'll continue chipping away at it for a bit, just to see if there are any redeeming qualities, and I'll update this review accordingly if this game grows on me at all. But for the time being, this is just an absolute trainwreck.

This is not a game worthy of perfect scores but I probably should have gave it 5 stars on here because that stands for 'I love it' and I do.  I just didn't want to be misleading and make people think that it was up there with other action RPGs like Fallout or Dragon Age 2, which do deserve near perfect scores.Despite the lack of perfection, it is still a really fun game.  All of the key action RPG elements that I enjoy are there.  There are obvious flaws in graphics and frame rate but that hasn't stopped me from being glued to my PS3 for hours on end playing it.  People have complained about the difficulty so I started playing it on 'easy' and have had no problems what-so-ever.The map system isn't as troubling as others have made it out to be either.  I thought it was easy to find the map or find out which person has a map and buy it.  It'd be one thing if the mass of all the islands were together but each island is small enough on its own to be easily travelled and searched with or without a map.  People just need to learn to use their memory skills and quit expecting games to always show them the way.The fighting in this game has also been under fire but I remember the first time I played Dragon Age.  I thought it was awful but I still enjoyed the game enough to hang in there and was completely glad that I did.  I don't expect every game to have fighting that is extremely fluid and I know that some developers just don't focus on that as much as others.The soundtrack is good as far as the music but some of the creature and character sounds were obviously skipped over in production.  For example, you can fight and kill a group of creatures and the sound of said creatures will still linger as if they were still around and alive.  Once again, not something that stopped me from enjoying the game.A couple of the biggest pluses that don't have to do with in-game play are the saving feature and fast travel.  You can save anywhere, anytime.  I always love that.  You can fast travel from any 'found' and marked location on an island and it only takes about a second to get there.  No long loading screens!  That's a huge plus for me.  I should also mention that the submenu is well designed and doesn't require all of your attention but is fun to go through and use.There's tons of things to do, items to find, skills to upgrade, etc.  If you are a fan of action RPGs and don't expect a perfect 10, you will probably enjoy this game.  It's cheap enough now that you won't feel robbed by it's flaws.  I got it as a gift but I would've paid up to $40 for it, although you can always find it for less than $25. Maybe 3.5 stars.So I finished this game...finally. I enjoyed it more than the first which I never finished. It seemed like it had everything there for a good game but it was just boring after a while. I played on easy since I read that was a better option to enjoy the game with less frustration. I won't cover combat, it is what it is. Simple and shallow like everything else in the game.+Some character development. Even with the gamma turned on max brightness and playing in a dark room, I could barely see with the pathetic torch.-Chests and lockpicking. The mini-game for picking locks got a little old after a while. I know developers try to come up with clever new ways to present the lock picking skills in games but it was just old after a while. And there were no consequences to failure. You only need one pick in the whole game and if your skill is high enough, you get to try their little mechanic as many times as it takes to "win". Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty"Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty" didn't quite end up as people expected. The opening section takes place on a Tanker being infiltrated by Solid Snake, who's on a mission to get evidence of a new Metal Gear. This acts as a 1-2 hour prologue to the main part of the game, which takes place on the "Big Shell," a huge oil rig-looking structure with multiple connecting platforms and pathways. Despite the cover promptly displaying Snake's mug, what players got instead during this section was Raiden, a less gruff, less battle-weary, very "green" rookie soldier with distinct long white hair. I dug him. One of the things I like about Raiden is how he's introduced. At the beginning of the "Big Shell" mission you aren't sure who he is. Is he a clone of the Big Boss? Is he a re-imagining of Solid Snake? In proper "MGS" fashion, the answers only slowly reveal themselves all the way up until the closing credits. The big upgrades to gameplay over the previous game include a first-person perspective for aiming, along with useful maneuvers like hanging off the edges of structures to avoid detection, etc. There's also a fun dog tag collecting sub game where you can hold up/threaten enemies into dropping their tags that then unlock items if you collect enough. This game hinges on its story, and it's mostly thrilling all the way through, despite an ending that goes a bit off the rails. "Sons of Liberty" doesn't reach the greatness of the first game. That's not to say it isn't entertaining as hell.Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater"Snake Eater" is the third game in the "MGS" series, but the first game chronologically in the timeline, and takes place during the Cold War in 1964, where "Naked Snake" is tasked with stopping a nuclear-equipped tank in the jungles of the USSR. It's important to note that this is not the same Snake from the previous 2 games. If you're familiar with the mythology then you no doubt already know who he is. The story this time isn't quite as serious, and actually has a "James Bond" inspired opening credit sequence. There are still harrowing moments, as when Snake gets captured by Volgin, etc. Three characters in particular besides Snake are allowed an unusual amount of depth: young Ocelot, who later becomes one of the series' main villains and here first develops his obsession with revolvers; Eva, a seductress and spy whose loyalties aren't altogether clear; and The Boss, the legendary female soldier and former mentor of Naked Snake. What's new to "Snake Eater" are the systems that maintain Snake's health, which include eating food scavenged from within the environment (snakes for example) and curing yourself after taking damage (like removing a bullet with a knife and then applying the appropriate medical treatment). Also new is the ability to change camouflage on the fly to better blend in and help avoid being spotted by enemy patrols. These are great additions. I enjoyed "Snake Eater" more than "Sons of Liberty." The boss battles are better and more numerous (the best of which is the sniper The End), and the story never falters. Is it as great as the first game? Maybe not, but then few games are.Vita version:This Vita collection includes the "Substance" version of "MGS2" (including: Boss Survival, Casting Theater, 300 VR missions, and 200 alternate missions) and the "Subsistance" version of "MGS3" (including: "Metal Gear" and "Metal Gear 2," skill challenge missions, side story missions, and a new user-controlled camera). "MGS3" on Vita looks and runs much better than its 3DS counterpart but doesn't include the ability to crouch-walk as on 3DS. The analog controls work mostly well but can be a bit finicky here and there when extreme precision is needed. The only real omission is an upgraded "MGS: Peace Walker," which is included with the console version of this collection. When all is said and done, this is one of the must-have Vita releases.--- 5 STARS ---

The crime with the "Epic Mickey" games is that it's a cool idea. You get to control Mickey Mouse and wield a magical paintbrush that's able to paint in sections of the cartoonish levels or thin them out. It's fun experimenting with how the mechanic works. Painting and thinning everything around you, trying to find all the secret paths and collectibles, or just plain wanting to see what happens as you mess with the world keeps you interested. The idea of tying morality to your use of the brush is interesting as well, with thinning (green) being evil and painting (blue) being good. And who doesn't want to play a 3D platformer where you get to explore environments based on classic Disney films and theme park rides? What's not so good is that the world as a whole is a complicated, confusing mess to navigate through. Every time you jump into a projector, warping from one area to another, you have to suffer through tediously boring side-scrolling segments. They aren't fun and serve no real purpose. Why not just cut them completely? Other annoyances manifest when attempting side-quests. The objectives are often too obscure and lack helpful detail and description. The map on the menu screen only shows the current area and isn't all that helpful anyways. Then there's the clumsy AI of your NPC partner Oswald. Still, playing as Mickey and with that brush and in these environments does have its charm.--- 3 STARS ---

I'm a completest when it comes to games like this.  I didn't even come close to completing it.  After finishing the game proper I continued to play and try to accomplish the different tasks but I lost interest, especially as you can't complete certain tasks unless you play through the game more than once or complete them within a certain time limit.  I suppose this is supposed to enhance the replay value but for me it enhanced my frustration.The game's visuals are great and the story this time around follows a musical plot line wherein the Mad Doctor has been reformed...or has he?  He guilts Oswald into helping him save Wasteland from being irrevocably ripped apart by what turn out to be his machinations and Mickey is brought in to help.  You can play through solo as Mickey, with Oswald doing assigned tasks (frustratingly he often doesn't easily go to them), or you can play with a partner with one person playing as Mickey and one as Oswald.  This would be the preferred way of playing if you and your partner have the ability to be patient with each other (spouses beware), but the frustrating camera though slightly improved over the first game isn't improved enough and too often your views will be hampered by the splitting of the screen.Another element that helped the first game out was its throwback charm and channeling of Disneyland's Magic Kingdom.  This game keeps some of the same areas, especially the Mean Street hubs, but changes much and so the charm is lost.  Places like Bog Hollow are interesting but just don't drum up the nostalgia like the first game was able to do (something that perhaps only some older gamers who had been to Disneyland back in the 70's & 80's were able to appreciate anyway).  There are an abundance of side quests with the most enjoyable I found being the one where you were taking hidden pictures of Mickey and Oswald, pics that had to be discovered by dissolving areas and changing landscapes.  For those people who enjoy fetch quests in their games there is a lot to enjoy as long as they don't mind endlessly exploring returned to areas.  Unfortunately for me my tolerance waned.If there was an Epic Mickey 3 I would pick it up on sale in hope of being able to again experience Disney park nostalgia not hampered by a bad camera and with the ability to play as a variety of characters in solo mode.  My hope would be balanced by lowered expectations.*Note: I bought this game for my wife who had enjoyed the first Epic Mickey, as well as myself.  She didn't get far into the game before giving up finding some elements too difficult and/or frustrating and then when we started to play through together...well, like I said, you need to have patience with your partner.

This is the germ of a truly great game.  It's old school almost 16-bit level game play, which is great.  I miss a lot of the old simplistic ones you could pick up and basically just play and have a good time.  Plot?  Who needs a plot?  You're an Army dude and there are zombies.  You can find a Russian and a German officer and they'll join up with you to save their own skin too.  It's really nice once you have them, since they add firepower and give you an extra "life" since if you die you can take over one of them; you can also switch between them anytime you have them along.So what were the problems?  Well, first off the game has no real tutorial.  It's an annoying trend and IMHO that's just a lazy developer.  You're creating a unique world of your own imagination.  You need to provide a basic framework to the people who are visiting or they'll end up getting frustrated more than is necessary.  The game needlessly wastes your time trying to figure out what makes you survive by trial and error.  There is also the frame rate.  I have a core i7 running 3+GH and I got massive slowdown at full screen from time to time.  The engine that runs it needs a significant amount of polish.  This can also leave you frustrated.  Still, considering the price, it's not a deal breaker.So the verdict?  The game is quite a bit of fun and if you can find it on any kind of sale I'd say go for it.  Watch some videos online to see how the basics go and just figure that if you do end up rage quitting, you're at least not out much.

Addictive fun is how I would describe this game. I have finished the Act 1 and I thoroughly enjoyed it. In fact, it has made me impatient to finish the other acts.POSITIVES:*Real-time action (I hate turn-based games)*Dubbed in English: Most of the dialogue is dubbed in English. Japanese dub is also available.*Open-world: You select an area you wish to go to from a world-map and those areas are open for exploration. You can re-visit the areas as many times as you like.*Easy gameplay: The Gigacals and different attacks may seem complicated but it was very easy to understand once I started playing and in fact added to the variety of combat, making it fun.*Fun characters: The characters are very interesting and unlike do-gooder angsty heroes, you get to play for a truly wicked witch. Wait till you see what Lia, excuse me, Metalia does to an enemy of hers at the end of Act 1; it'll make you shudder!*Very interesting story: I was very intrigued by the story and made me want to learn more. There's a mystery as to who Metalia really is.*Adjustable difficulty: I am playing at Normal difficulty and had no difficulty defeating enemies. You can lower/increase the difficulty level at any time in the game without any penalty.NEGATIVES:*Graphics quality not up to par: This game does not take full advantage of the PS3's graphics capabilities. The graphics quality is not bad but it looks like a PS2 game rather than a PS3 game. However, the gameplay was so much fun that this minor flaw was overlooked.*Some cut scenes are 2-D stills: I don't mind 2-D scenes but I wish that they had fully animated the cut-scenes instead of using stills.I wish Japan would make more real-time action JRPGs like this (instead of churning out turn-based Final fantasy sequels all the time). Open-world action games like this and Dragon's Dogma are a step in the right direction, in my humble opinion. Japan seems to be realizing this as Final Fantasy: Lightning Returns and Final Fantasy XV are both open-world real-time action games.

The Witch and the Hundred Knight is a rather niche game in an already niche genre so the game will not be for everyone but once some time is put into the game it can become fun and interesting.  The tutorial for the game starts off extremely slow and uninteresting so I would recommend playing through at least the first few chapters before you completely pan the game is trash.PlotThe Witch and the Hundred Knight revolves around the Swamp Witch, Metallia, who's goal is to cover the world in swamp before she dies.  Instead of playing as Metallia you play as her magical familiar, The Hundred Knight, who's goal is to travel through the world destroying magical spires to spread swamp magic.  The story starts off very crude in the actions that Metallia does and how she speaks which can be off putting at first.  The story didn't start becoming interesting for me until a few chapters into the game.  By the end of the game my opinion of the story turned around quite a bit but was never anything that I would call spectacular.MusicIf you have played any of the games from Nippon Ichi Software(NIS) already you will recognize most of the music from The Witch and the Hundred Knight.  Some of it is really good but quite a bit of it can become extremely repetitive.  Luckily most of the music that plays on maps while you are controlling the Hundred Knight is decent.Game playMost of the actual game play is done while exploring maps as the Hundred Knight hunting down the magic spires.  The Witch and the Hundred Knight is a top down isometric action RPG similar to games like Diablo but much more simple.  The Hundred Knight can equip up to five weapons that are used to attack enemies which have either the property of Slash, Blunt, or Magic damage.  Each enemy is weak against a specific type of attack and strong against the others.  Because of this you need to make sure to have at least one of each type of attack equipped so you can always deal damage without having to go back and forth between the menus switching what type of weapons you are using.  The main issue in this is that two thirds of your attacks will be usually dealing little to no damage against enemies.  Attacks and running are controlled by the use of a stamina gauge which needs to be watched so you don't run completely out.  If you run out then you will have to wait a few seconds for stamina to start regenerating.  Battles are overall fairly simple but is what I usually found to be the most entertaining portions of the game.My main con in the game play of the game was that there is a severe difficulty spike late in the game which required me to level quite a bit to get past which took a while.Overall I found Witch and the Hundred Knight to be an entertaining game but none of the portions of the game ever became anything spectacular to make it anything above average.  I'd recommend the game if you are already a fan of the games that NIS comes out with or are a fan of niche RPGs.

This game is bloody awful right out of the gate. The tutorial is WAY longer than it needs to be, and it's excruciatingly boring. I literally fell asleep twice, and it was the middle of the day! (And no, I don't normally fall asleep while playing video games, especially when I'm not tired.) The character of the witch is not funny; she's just abusive. You might think this will eventually develop into some kind of sick humor, but no, she's just an all-around jerk for as long as you will know her.Likewise, once you get out of the tutorial, you are probably hoping the game finally gets interesting, right?  No. You are just in for more disappointment. And tedium. And wishing you were doing something else. If you haven't paid your taxes yet, this game is boring enough to make you want to do that, just for some thrills.Combat is absurdly basic. The designers should be embarrassed at how little they've done to spice this up, seeing as it's all you really have to entertain yourself when you're not being berated by the horrible witch. Yes, there are story elements, and choices, and an extremely artificial-feeling timer element, and some other halfhearted attempts to dress us this nightmare, but in the end it's all very transparent and insulting.Seriously, every step of this journey, you'll feel like the designers are taunting you, saying, "Hee hee hee! We got your 50 bucks, sucker! And there's nothing you can do about it!" If you're into that sort of thing (and i know some people are), more power to you. Otherwise, I would steer well clear of this pathetic piece of trash.I fully admit that I did not play past Chapter 1. I was not having any fun, so sue me for not wasting more time on this game just so I could write a "more informed" review. Sarcasm quotes there because I feel like a better game would have made me WANT to play more, and the fact that I did not want to is enough information to form (and express) my negative opinion. If you want a more detailed negative review, feel free to google the opinions of the dozens of paid critics who also hated this unbearable garbage.

So, I purchased and downloaded this game straight from the PSN, and here's the deal: the mixed feelings -and poor reviews this game got- are very valid, unfortunately.Here's my analysis and list of CONS: the game mechanics and controls so far are not bad, but nothing great. However, even though this game is a 3D game, it's still a top down mostly. The camera can only go so low (it feels like older RPG games' view). The protagonist here is a "not-so-heroic" looking character (Hundred Knight) who CANNOT even talk.If you think the pokemons are cool with their 2-3 word vocabulary, then you'll probably like this one too.If just like myself you think the Witch looks cool, then here's the "bad news": in this game, (so far at least) you/we are the bad guys.In other words, if you want this game because you think you'll get to play as a cool witch, guess again: you play as her minion, and she herself is the mastermind and an evil character (this is not a spoiler, as you find this out very very early on in the game).The storytelling is done the same way many NIS games are done: simple scenes where you see characters on both sides of the screen talking, and that's it. There are some animated scenes, but the animation quality, even there, is very poor (early first playstation games poor).There is a 'time limit' type of mechanic which forces the player to move quickly while inside a level. There are ways to extend how much 'time' you have left, but even that is not clearly and straightforwardly explained. That's all I've noticed so far.The PROS: the Witch is hot, the game mechanics are pretty simple, there are some funny moments here and there, the 2d art looks neat.Overall, this game is not necessarily that addicting or great. I've cleared a few chapters ever since I started playing and I put it down to go back to older games I have on my PS3, so, yeah. A good piece of advice would be to wait for a small price drop.The ugly truth is that it's not worth the $50 you'd want to pay for some other games out there right now.

The Good: Dozens of amazing songs, simple yet fun rhythm mechanic, RPG elements are nicely implemented, lots of content, various modes that extend gameplayThe Bad: Opening and ending themes are boring to play, gameplay consists of only 3 different tap types, gears towards mainly Final Fantasy fans, later Final Fantasy songs aren’t as great as older onesFinal Fantasy has had some strange off shoots like Chocobo Racing, Kingdom Hearts, and the TBS Tactics. A rhythm game is probably the only genre Final Fatnasy hasn’t touched and it’s one that the game belongs in. Final Fantasy is full of some of the best video game music ever created. While later titles aren’t exactly up to par, there are plenty of songs here that fans will love across all 13 core titles.The basic gameplay is broken up into 3 stages that are randomized. BMS is Battle Music Stage. Usually one song from each game is picked that was used in a battle, usually a major boss fight. Your four characters stand in front of bars similar to a horizontal Guitar Hero. The entire game consists of only 3 tap types. Hold, tap, and slides. The speed and combination of these 3 can make things really difficult on the Ultra mode but the standard mode is just way too easy even for beginners. EMS or Event Music Stage is a song picked during some sort of popular or well known cut scene and the said scene plays in the background to the music. It’s great seeing Rinoa and Squall waltz in Final Fantasy VIII or watching Aerith’s death scene in Final Fantasy VII. The game is mixed up a bit where the ring you tap flies around the screen as you follow it to complete the required taps. The final stage, FMS or Field Music Stage, has your leader character walking down a re-rendered field from each game collecting chests and the field music from each game accompanies it. This stage consists of one bar that you can move up and down to follow waves. There’s a third boring stage where you tap a crystal in the center of the screen as bubbles fly into it, these are for the opening and ending themes in the main mode which are as boring as ever.This may sound simple, but the other half is leveling up your cute chibi FF characters and equipping items and weapons to last through the harder difficulties. Characters with higher HP won’t die as easy (meaning you can mess up more) and this includes their armor (they won’t take as much damage when you do mess up). Characters with higher luck in field stages will find more items. This is a unique twist on the rhythm genre and helps push it forward in a way that’s never really been done. Thanks to the many extras such as fully rendered trading cards and DLC there’s a lot to be had in this package. If you like the lesser known songs in these games the Dark Notes mode will help you here. You can acquire new songs vita StreetPass or battling friends in multiplayer for the highest score. These are all set to the hardest difficulty so practice is needed.With such a content heavy rhythm game is begs the question as to who this title is for. Rhythm game fans will appreciate the mechanics and use of the touch screen, but may not care for the orchestra and chiptune heavy music. Final Fantasy nuts may love this game but not really like the fast paced rhythm action. It’s something that can appeal to anyone who even hates RPGs, but the Final Fantasy only music may turn Rock Band and Guitar Hero fans away. Despite who this game is made for, whoever picks it up will enjoy a simple yet rich game full of detail, content, and attention to detail that hasn’t been seen since the earlier days of Final Fantasy.

It's a decent enough rhythm game.  The limited music selection is where things start to go south.  You see... when most gamers say, "I love Final Fantasy music", what they really mean is, "I love Final Fantasy IV, VI, VII, and IX music".  So when Theatrhythm presents an equal amount of music from ALL the games, there's going to be trouble in the lifestream.  Each game only has about 3 measly tracks (there are a handful of bonus tracks too).  At first I thought Square was just planning to soak me with DLC but there really isn't anything to download either.  (Maybe the upcoming Curtain Call will remedy this.)  For now Theatrhythm has very little content.  Which ties into my other gripe about this game, it takes FOREVER to unlock extras.  50 hours in and I've gotten about 50% completion.  This game doesn't have nearly enough content to justify that.  By the time you 100% this game, the mere mention of One Winged Angel will make you vomit.

As a fan of both music/rhythm games and Final Fantasy, I definitely had high expectations for this game. The mechanics, look and feel of the game are incredible, and a lot of the arrangements of the songs added a pretty nice level of depth, especially for the older games. The "battle system" was interesting, although it's basically just for show, especially if you're good at the game.Unfortunately, while the game was definitely engaging while I was playing it, I wasn't drawn in. There was never an excitement to play the game. This game is best suited for those times when you have 15-20 minutes to kill. It's a good nostalgia trip, and the game loves to literally remind you - on more than one occasion the word nostalgia was actually used.Overall, playing the game isn't an enveloping experience, but it doesn't need or try to be.

When we think of rhythm games, we don't often imagine the possibility of mixing in other genres. Square Enix, a company far more competent at innovation than most give it credit for, has brought RPG elements to a rhythm game, and I think the latter genre is the better for it. Yes, it has familiar characters - which often seems to be a source of consternation among those who are tired of Final Fantasy. But the gameplay is solid. The tapping is fun. The songs are memorable.It does get a bit repetitive after a while, but I'm awarding five stars to Square Enix's credit for trying out a new approach. I hope to see them dabble in and shake up more genres in a similar way.

I was just reading through Game Informer's preview of the upcoming Arkham Knight that will be released only on the PS4 and I'm glad that they released a final PS3 version of Arkham Origins, for this generation of systems before leaving it entirely behind.If you like me, have played Arkham Asylum and were completely shocked at how awesome the game was, from dialogue, to fight sequences, to how great all the gadgets and equipment works then this game is a great extension of the Arkham Asylum engine created by Rocksteady. Your not stuck inside a prison this time spending each moment trying to escape, but face plenty new enemies from the Batman DC universe and are able to fly around in a new environment and map that is pretty humongous. You've got a checklist of clues to follow on how to fix the city, which is closed off from the public as an evil doctor feels Batman poses a threat to the community.There's plenty of hours of gameplay and I didn't want the game to end so I continued to solve all the riddler puzzles and play side-quests and challenge maps to get every extra minute of gameplay, flying through hoops to glide farther, upgrading equipment, etc. but the real fun is playing the missions. Batman on the SNES was probably one of the worst videogames ever created and Superman on the N64 was not much better, but it looks like Rocksteady is able to bring the tough, ruthless, and troubled Batman character portrayed in the movies to life in this game.You can even play as Catwoman, Nightwing, and Robin in the games as DLC (downloadable content), but only Catwoman is able to roam the streets of Arkham City and even gets a few missions herself to add to the story, thankfully. Robin and Nightwing DLC is a little-bit extra money and I decided to pass on getting it because they only are playable in challenge maps and don't have any quests of their own. I would have loved to play 5-10 missions with each of those characters in the game, but their play is restricted to beating up thugs.I probably won't be getting next-gen PS4 anytime soon, as I'm not too hardcore of a gamer, but I'll be watching gameplay and trailers on youtube and might check out Arkham Origins.5/5

This is my third review and completed adventure in this series.First, I'd like to start by dividing my review into two factions.1) The game itself2) My personal detective work.* PART 1 *PLOT: Set in a Bavarian castle in Germany, I was excited about seeing the traditions and festivals that is within the culture. Can I attend an Oktoberfest?! [No, sadly this takes place in March]. I did get to explore the confines of the castle, but the courtyard residents would not offer to talk to me which was a huge downer.  Reason being, a monster was on the loose and I had to find out if this whole thing was real or a setup.INITIAL SCORE: 82CHARACTERS: Lukas was interesting at first with his pranks, but once I ruled him out as significant to the plot, I basically ignored him [except to play the Monster game with him]. Anja was a real go-getter and I admired her spirit, although this love entanglement with Markus [the castle owner] led to some speculation as to what her "stake in the game" entailed.  I commend Karl greatly if only for his designing of a "Magic; The Gathering" type card game called RAID that he was trying to finish and publish. I loved playing it with him. The table board game he had was cool too. The "monster" seemed too bland and I wondered why the castle iron gates were drawn up to allow it to wander the courtyard unabated; that seemed weird that an ancient threat was regarded with zero security measures. Renate rubbed me the wrong way as a crusty, old woman [not your own grandmother] would. I mean she was okay in general, its just I didn't enjoy any of her blathering.CUMUL SCORE: Even = 82SCORE/GRAPHICS: I liked the live violin, double bass, accordion, and tuba for the waltz's.  Many of the pieces relied on Germanic folk music for its' propensity.CUMUL SCORE: +1 = 83PUZZLES: Anything to do with the Raid games and the colored tile box was fun. The hexagon picture puzzle was very interesting as well. Balancing the items in the banquet hall room where Renate sat was a little frustrating, but I didn't mind overall.CUMUL SCORE: +1 = 84ENDING: This is the first game [of the three thus far] where I actually got to select who the culprit was. Obviously, I ruled Lukas out in the beginning and it was quite apparent he wasn't involved since he was exposed in the ornate hallway as a hoaxer while the actual monster was visible right outside the burg walls. Renate is too old to move around and Karl was accountable whenever the monster was active; whereas when I talked to Anja, she literally disappeared in  two seconds when I had my back to her! That's a strange game mechanic right there!  Most of the darker places of exploration seemed trite and not all together relegated to the story, so I never had that scary tension going.  The monster was clearly not authentic, unlike the possibilities of Ghost Of Thornton Hall where they had you believing she was real. I just felt the momentum was lacking the second half of the game. And why didn't Karl NOT get up from his desk and look for the lost Lukas? That is crazy neglect!CUMUL SCORE: - 2 = 82* PART 2 *I try to solve cases without any hints, walkthroughs, etc, even if it were totake weeks! Well, it took me a little over two months and I gave myself a DetectiveScore Of : 74My Strong Points: Solving the Puzzles pretty fast. I remembered quite a bit from the books and newspapers if proper recall was expected, but the time rarely called for it. I really got into the music puzzle.Weak Points: The fact you were caught red-handed in Karl's office constantly was not a great game device. I felt that a forewarning of a time pressure should have been made apparent beforehand [yes, it's always implied, but I didn't think I had to own up to it as part of the game.] That also goes for the culprit hitting Nancy in the head with a board a couple times. Yes, I was a victim of that and Nancy acted as if she was totally fine afterwards [before solving the final puzzle]. That was a huge turn of events that was taken rather lightly by the game designers.  So overall, I got caught up in several cheap deaths, but the puzzles never stumped me.OVERALL GAME SCORE: 74+82/2= 78 [C plus]

The Good: Fantastic production values, fun new passive abilities, interesting new locales, decent storyThe Bad: Combat is tweaked to nearly being broken, no interesting or memorable boss fights, poor pacing and balancing, so-so multiplayerGod of War was once Sony’s unstoppable power house that helped sell consoles and push them to their limits. While God of War was revolutionary for the time it is starting to show its teeth, and it’s never more apparent then in Ascension. While the game shines in production values the quality and content is seriously lacking compared to past games, even the smaller PSP ones.You play as the angry Spartan demi-god, Kratos, once again. This time you are playing through a prequel of the first game. Kratos is trying to free his bonds from Ares after swearing and giving up his life to defeat his enemy. He has to defeat the Furies along with his living prison Hechatonchires. The game starts out with an epic giant boss fight as usual and even a cinematic torture scene where you get to start beating down one of the Furies right off the bat. It starts out with a bang and quickly fizzles out once the combat system is introduced to you. Honestly, it’s nearly ruined. The combat engine has been tweaked so much that it just doesn’t flow like it used to. It’s now based on a momentum system where the more you hit without getting hit the more damage you do. I honestly hate this as it sets you back in difficult areas. What’s more is that the magic system has been screwed with too much and same goes for the upgrade system.I like the idea of having four different blades with elemental abilities but they don’t mean anything. Should my fire blades be strong against an ice enemy? Doesn’t seem so. Each sword is supposed to have one magic attack by they are acquired at certain upgrade levels which I really hate. The rage meter has been turned into a bar that slowly fills as you hit enemies. If you get hit it rapidly drops and your damage dealt is reduced along with your more powerful moves. The game is hard enough as it is with enemies wailing on you so your best moves are locked away until you can get enough hits in to “acquire them” temporarily. A horrible system that needs to go away in the next game.With that said, Ascension has the most cerebral puzzles in any God of War game which is a nice change. I had to actually think on nearly every puzzle and some completely stumped. Some new passive abilities is one where you can decay and heal objects. Another ability allows you to duplicate yourself to solve puzzles and do extra damage in combat. These are probably the only thing in the game that show an overall evolution.With that aside let’s talk about bosses. God of War is famous for its epic and memorable bosses that are larger than life. Ascension has the weakest bosses in the entire series. First off, there’s a lack of them. Most are small and about the size of regular enemies. The only exception are the beginning boss and the end boss. That’s nearly 7 hours in between with weak fights. The overall flow of the game just feels messed up and broken. I kept looking forward to amazing boss fights that blew me away, but I just kept getting regular fight after fight. This really brings the God of War experience down quite a bit. Ascension just feels like a basic bare bones God of War without all the memorable moments.Like I mentioned before, the production values are at least here. Ascension is probably one of the top five best looking PS3 games or even game of this generation of consoles. The game just looks freaking fantastic and will blow you away. However, you start to not care if there aren’t those amazing boss fights and fast fluid combat. Ascension is a step in the wrong direction for the series showing that tweaking something to the point of nearly breaking it isn’t the answer to innovation. Should Ascension have never been made at all? We certainly wouldn’t miss it if it completely disappeared, but what’s here is a decent game with some experimental multiplayer that will last for a few weeks and you will move on to the next game.

Excited about the Reboot, I tried the demo... and hated it.  I thought, what the hell is this crap?  Who is this emo punk calling himself Dante and why does the combat suck so bad?  These graphics are terrible, too.  The game looks like concept art SKETCHES!  After seeing DMC on many Top 10 Game Lists, I gave it a try at the incredible low price of $15.Story: 9/10This is an origin story for Dante.  He's not the cool super hero Dante from the first series who rides missiles like skateboards.  At this point, he's a young punk with an attitude, but he talks and acts like a real person.  Hung over after a night of clubbing, the story begins in Dante's trailer when a mysterious girl exposes him to a hell dimension full of demons.  On the adventure, Dante learns he has a brother, Virgil, and that he and Virgil are Nephilim, the spawn of angels and demons.  Dante and Virgil must team up to slay the demon who killed their parents, battling through an army of demonic minions along the way.  Although it does feel like a show on the WB, the longer you play it, the more you like the characters.Graphics: 8/10They're highly stylized, but I'm not too crazy about the style.  The environments are varied from streets, to office buildings, to hell dimensions, to ancient ruins.  This is not a great looking game, but the environments are very dynamic.  They explode, twist, expand, collapse, strech...  They couldn't just use standard texture maps with baked in lighting, so I'm cutting them some slack.  The characters are very well animated and the creatures look like old dolls left to rot in hell.  They're creepy looking, instead of just looking like your typical video game monster.Gameplay: 9/10The gameplay consists of:10% Easy Platform Jumping with generous checkpoints.  Use an Angel Whip to pull Dante toward a grapple point or a Devil Whip to pull the grapple point towards Dante.1% Puzzle, which is pretty easy.9% Exploration, where you should revisit old levels when you have new powers.  You may see a ledge but have no idea on how to get there, and later you get an ability that makes it accessible.80% Modular Combat.The combat lock is gone and pushing directions to trigger Dante's moves has been replaced with a modular system.  They new combat system works like this:Dante has 4 weapons equipped at all times:A Sword. (Y,B buttons)A Gun. (X button)An Angelic Weapon. (Hold LT+Y,B buttons)A Devil Weapon.  (Hold RT+Y,B buttons)There are multiple types of guns, angelic weapons, and devil weapons and you swap them by pushing the D-pad.  Up toggles your guns, Left toggles your Angel Weapons, and Right toggles your Demon weapons.The combos for each weapon are very simple and a pause in the button presses differentiates the moves.  So, Y, Y, Y, Y is one combo, where Y, Y, pause, Y,Y, is another.The controls are:  A = Jump, B = some kind of launch attack, X = shoot, and Y is a melee attack.Hold LT to equip your Angel Weapon.Hold RT to equip your Devil Weapon.The beauty of this system is that the combos are completely modular and you can switch between them on the fly.Start with your sword, Y,Y,Y, switch to your devil axe, B to send the enemy skyward, use your guns to shoot it and keep it airborne, use your angel whip to pull yourself up to the enemy, perform a Y,Y, pause Y, attack in the air, switch to your devil weapon for a smash him to the ground attack.  How you mix and match your sword, gun, Angel, and Devil weapons are up to you.  Transitioning between weapons is exceptionally smooth.Because Y is always attack, B is always launch, X is always shoot, and A is always jump, it is incredibly easy to learn the combos.Mixing and matching weapon attacks is where the game gets really fun.There are some color coded enemies that are only weak to a certain type of weapon.  Blue enemies are resistant to angelic weapons, while red enemies need to be slain by devil weapons.There's a pretty wide variety of enemies, too.Leveling Up: 8/10As you kill enemies or smash objects in the environment, you get orbs.  These are used to buy new moves for your weapons.  There is a TRY (Before you buy) Mode which enables you to try out all of the weapons and their attacks so you can pick the upgrade / combo that you really want.  This is GREAT!Levels: 9/10You can replay levels on any difficulty at any time, so if you want to go back to level 1 and farm orbs, you can.  If you want to try out the tougher levels on harder difficulties, you can do that, too.  The levels are varied and there's a good mix of combat, platform jumping, and boss fights.  There's also quite a bit of spiteful dialogue between Dante and the Demons to keep you motivated.At the end of each level, you are given a score based on your combat style (switching weapons and combos scores much higher than using the same move over and over), the hidden objects that you find, and the time it took to complete the level.  This isn't the type of game where your health regenerates, so you will need to purchase health items.  Each time you buy one, that item gets more expensive.Sound: 10/10The acting is very good, the music is great, and the combat SFX punctuate the action.Maturity: MThis is a super violent game with lots of swearing, adult themes, and partial nudity.Replay Value: 8/10The game is 20 levels long and it will take you about 12 hours to finish.  When you finish, there will still be a chunk of unlockable moves and stat boosts for Dante, so you're free to play on the harder difficulties.  The game also has increased difficulty levels where the enemy AI is different and everybody (including Dante) dies in 1 hit if you want a challenge.Overall: 9/10I didn't think I was going to like this game, but I really enjoyed it once I gave it a chance.  I like the new Dante and he gets better as the story progresses.  After a while, I enjoyed the modular combat once I unlocked my first Angel weapon and my first Devil weapon.  This is a really fun game if you like God of War style combat.  To fully enjoy it, you do need to let go of the old Devil May Cry games and understand that this is a reboot, and not a remake.Buy it if you love God of War style combat.Buy it if you love teen drama shows on the WB.Rent it if you have about 12 hours to blow through the game on default difficulty.Avoid it if you need the target lock + directional push attacks that the old Devil May Cry games had.Avoid it if you can't get over the red saturated art style.Avoid it if you love the old series and can't stand reboots.

I don't have a lot of history with the DMC series, having only played Devil May Cry 2 on the PS2 (I didn't fall in love, but it's my understanding that was the weakest of the the trilogy).  So, I went in without knowing much and that may affect one's enjoyment for better or worse.On its own, this is a wonderful game for anyone who enjoys melee combat.  Yes, you have firearms, but they serve primarily to buy you time as a baddie is charging up for an attack.  If you try to rely on even the most powerful firearms to get through the game, you're in for a challenge.The AI is lightning-fast, but fortunately so is your control.  The control you have over this character is pretty tight and you can easily switch weapons, even assigning a new one in a slot, on the fly.  There were a couple of moments where I'd get a bit overwhelmed with the options (to the point where I would forget how to fire a gun LOL), but that was more my fault than that of the game.  The only problem I encountered is with the camera.  There would be times I would want to turn around and go after a green pod for health, but the camera would disagree with me and try to stay focused on my nemesis.I thought the story was pretty good, but again, I don't know anything of Devil May Cry lore.  I found the protagonists likable and the bad guys deliciously evil.I liked the use of the pull systems as well.  You can use cables to either hoist yourself in the air or drag foes to you (or, if you're so inclined, to pull yourself up to airborne enemies).  The moments where you had to focus on traversing using these cables were nice breaks in the fighting.The variety of enemies is also quite nice.  Every breed has its own method and weakness.  I appreciated that the game gave color clues as to what to do.  For example, if you see a red spot on an enemy, you'd use a "devil" weapon (an ax or gauntlets).  If you'd see blue, you'd use an "angel" weapon (a scythe or a set of glaives attached to cables).  When you'd see gold, whip out your trusty sword.  Again, firearms have very limited use.  But even the boss battles gave you some clues as to how to take them out, which I appreciate.  I hate it when a boss causes a huge spike in difficulty (some makes sense, but games tend to ratchet things up disproportionately when a boss comes along).Finally, I liked that the game didn't encourage you to ditch using old weapons as you got new ones.  You may have a new weapon, but you will run into parts late into the game where you have to rely on the old ones.  Heck, the sword I started the game with came in handy right up to the end.In short, this is a very fun game that will take about 8-10 hours to go through if you just want to see the story played out.
