(Preface - bought this game at Gamestop last weekend and my husband and I are now more than two thirds of the way through the campaign).Had this game released twenty years ago, it would have been hailed as one of the best games of its kind that would kick-start the Star Trek franchise off into a renaissance of popularity.Unfortunately, the game did not release in 1995; it released in 2013.  It released in the autumnal years of the XBox 360 and PS3, right on the cusp of next-gen consoles and in a time when new titles for current-gen consoles were looking stunning anyways (think Tomb Raider and Lightning Returns), and 1080p-Gate is in full swing on all the gaming sites.  As such, when it released, this game looking like nothing more than what it was:  A joke.Where to start?I have been playing two-person co-op split screen with my husband on this game, and I must say that it adds nothing to the experience as your field of view is squashed and you don't have the range of view that you would normally expect.  But this is only the start of my complaints about this horrible, glitch-plagued mess of a game.It feels, looks and plays like an episode of the Original Series of Star Trek - complete with cardboard props and bad voice acting.  Indeed, if that was the (almost clever) effect that the game devs were going for, they nailed it harder than anyone else could have.  The monsters look feeble and improbable, the NPCs are caricatures of themselves, and the scenery throughout all the game's levels is elementary at best - unfinished at worst.  The best thing I can say is that MOST surfaces DO have textures applied (unlike Aliens: Colonial Marines - think the unfinished, untextured black holes for air ducts), but that is the furthest I can go.  The details and textures on background and incidental props are basic and very rough.Game mechanics are abysmal.  The cover system is largely broken (think taking cover behind a box, then asking your character to break cover, and he remains on rails and crouch-walks away from the piece of cover until you re-double-click the crouch button).  Combat is acceptable but nothing amazing and quite boring, although when you walk up to an enemy to 'take it down' by pressing X it is very hit or miss to juxtapose yourself in the right position to get the 'take down' option.There is NO map - so good luck figuring out where you're supposed to go without having a walkthrough guide on your iPhone constantly at hand.  Adding to this topic, the layouts of levels remind me of Mass Effect 1's convoluted, circuitous areas on the Citadel, only more junked up with enemies, boxes and broken features/terrain.  Mission markers fly around the screen as you look for them, trying to figure out which location on the game's compass they are actually residing in.  Once you reach the mission marker location, you find out that they do not in fact mark the mission (and, by extension, an end to this tortuous game), but actually mark the exit from the current room you are in to continue LOOKING FOR the main mission.Difficulty seems completely off-the-wall - for god's sake don't attempt this game on anything but Easy.  And that in itself will require a disciplined memory every time you return to this game, because every time you switch it on and load up your game progress, you will have been reset to Medium difficulty again and will have to change it in the menu.  On anything but Easy, enemy turrets will annihilate you in 1.5 seconds, and space battles will be IMPOSSIBLE.Overall gameplay is frustrating, time-consuming and unrewarding.  We have literally spent HOURS of our lives trying to traverse the same levels, only to fall off platforms due to the jump-delay issue (controls are VERY laggy), die, and have to start all over again back at the last checkpoint.....which could be quite far back.  Oh - and the game doesn't give you any option to save at any point manually - so you are completely at the mercy of when and where the developers decided to put checkpoints.  Fell off a glitched platform and died?  Too bad - it's back to the start for you!Character interaction is pretty terrible.  Whereby the original Kirk and Spock played off each other quite well, the game's Kirk and Spock are a terrible duo of clashing personalities.  Spock sounds and acts like an android, while Kirk sounds and acts like an 18-year-old rogue tyrant.  The other backdrop of common Star Trek characters are pretty much just parodied fluff, although they could be worse I guess.So, all in all I really can't give this game anything above one star.  It's unfortunate, mainly because of the broader view of the fact that developers out there still seem to think it appropriate to create a game like this in this day and age.  Do yourself a favor and get Tomb Raider - or just replay Mass Effect 2.  This game is a waste of time in more ways than one.

i recently got around to taking the pikmin franchise out for a spin and was very pleasantly surprised by the first installment in the series. i want to eventually purchase a wii u and figured i needed to beat this game as well before attempting pikmin 3. my impressions are generally that there is a lot of give and take in this game compared to the original pikmin.the game-play has been expanded significantly. with the addition of a second leader, olimar can command one group of pikmin while his partner, louie leads another. it may be slow at first to get used to, but the levels seem larger in this game and as you gain access to all the areas in each level (by utilizing various different pikmin), this aspect of the game-play comes in handy.in addition to the original red-blue-yellow pikmin trifecta from the first game, this game introduces three new types of pikmin. purple pikmin, which are stocky, heavy and slow but have the strength of 10 regular pikmin. white pikmin, which are small, very quick and have x-ray vision that can see buried treasure. they are also resistant to poison and will poison most enemies that successfully eat it. finally, there's the addition of 'bulbmin' (bulborg pikmin), which are unfortunately only temporary. they white and purple pikmin also do not have 'onions' and can not reproduce by the usual harvesting means. you can only convert R/B/Y pikmin into P/W pikmin by means of the candy pop buds.they also re-tooled yellow pikmin to have electrical properties for the sake of conceptual symmetry to the elemental properties of the reds and blues. the levels have more of these elemental hazards that require you to divide up your pikmin by color to address the appropriate hazard. bulbmin are unique in that they can go through any hazard (they won't die in water, fire, poison, etc). finally, the game also adds the introduction of multi-level dungeon-style caves.all these expansions to the game-play make this game significantly more difficult than the original. one level of one of the more difficult caves, had about forty or so bulborbs in it! there were many moments in which i cursed openly at the pikmin predators. while all these additions from the first game sound great, i'm now coming to the game's main short-coming: the story.ok, so olimar finally returns home after rebuilding his spaceship only to find that the company he works for is bankrupt. his co-worker, louie, botched a delivery job, which left the company deeply in debt. the president decides to sell off company assets to pay the debt, but the only asset they have is olimar's ship, which gets immediately repo-ed (including the ship parts made by olimar's kids...) everyone's about to call it quits, when they notice olimar brought home a souvenir from the pikmin planet for his kids. a treasure-detecting ship immediately snatches it up, paying olimar and co. a modest sum. thus, the president decides to immediately send olimar and louie back to planet pikmin to retrieve more treasures and repay the debt.so yeah... they didn't even let olimar use the first toilet he's seen in a month or perhaps refill his prescription for his cholesterol medication, much less see his kids before sending him back into harm's way to bail out his boss. i like this game, but i feel like they could've come up with a better premise for returning olimar to planet pikmin. the first game had a time limit and a sense of urgency. there is no time limit in this game and even the days (which lasted roughly 13 mins in the first one) are now significantly longer. time is even suspended while you're in a cave. there's well over 200 treasures in this game to collect, so it can get rather repetitive.pros and cons aside, this game's new game-play features and harder challenge make this a great expansion on the first title. bring on pikmin 3 and let pikmin apartheid continue!

The Elder Scrolls Online (ESO) is a game which is trying to bridge two gaming genres - the immersive, single-player explorative role-playing game worlds of the previous Elder Scrolls (TES) titles (e.g., Daggerfall, Morrowind, Oblivion, Skyrim), on the one hand, and the massively-multiplayer online game world (MMORPG, or MMO), on the other.  In order to do so, the game was designed with certain compromises.  The issue is that, while there is some overlap, these two types of games are fundamentally different.  They attract different sets of players, generally, although, again, there is some overlap.  More fundamentally, both Elder Scrolls fans and MMO fans have pre-existing expectations for what an "Elder Scrolls game" should be like (for the first group of players) or what an "MMO" should be like (for the second group of players), and when the finished game doesn't contain X or Y features that either group "expects in an Elder Scrolls game" or "expects in an MMO", disappointment results - and this among BOTH sets of players.A few examples of this may be illustrative of the issue, and the conflicts that the game design creates in terms of these expectations.Elder Scrolls games are known for being immersive, open environment games where the player builds a heroic character in an unforgettable context.  They are very focused on free exploration, and encourage the player to wander around, discover things, and essentially do what the player wishes to do.  Stories and quests are present, but can be played or ignored as the player wishes without adversely impacting the game experience.  The essence of these games has been the sense of freedom, immersion, openness and exploration that they afford - as compared even to other single player role playing games.In designing ESO, attempts were made to give a sense of immersion.  One is the user interface, which is minimalist in Elder Scrolls games, and has remained so in ESO (to the immense consternation of many MMO fans - more on that below).  Attempts were also made to give a sense of exploration.  There are rewards for a player fully exploring any one of the game's zones - hidden treasure chests and skill-generating skyshards, lorebooks, and hidden quest areas.  Readable books are scattered throughout the game, as in the single player games, which provide stories and lore contexts.  However, most of this is less than satisfying for the typical TES fan.  The exploration feels weak for many of these fans, because it is constrained by level-based zones (unlike the more recent titles in the series) and MMO design mechanics such as invisible walls or terrain effects that act as such.  The sense of freedom is attenuated by the presence of levels, and quests matching levels that are done in a sequential order, more or less, following a path through the game ordained by the developer rather than the player - as is the case in most MMOs.  The sense of immersion feels broken because of the throngs of players everywhere, the constant chattering taking place and so on.  So, many of the TES fan element who are in the game are disappointed with many of the compromises made to render an Elder Scrolls game in an MMO setting, because these seem to go too far in breaking the immersive, open, explorative character of the single player games of the series.But, by contrast, for many of the MMO fans who are in the game, many of the things that give some or many of the TES fans pause are considered by the MMO fans as not going nearly far enough.  How is this so?  Consider the following:The immersive UI --- MMO fans, by and large, do not place a very high value on immersion.  The reason is that MMO games are generally not very immersive regardless of their design, due to the presence of huge amounts of players with non-immersive names, acting in non-immersive ways, and saying non-immersive things.  Immersion is more of a backdrop for many MMO fans - a backdrop against which the non-immersive interplay between the human players of the game forms the core of the massively multiplayer experience.  For many of these players, the immersive/minimalist UI is highly irritating, because while MMO fans don't place a high value on immersion, they place a high value on real time information, and want the UI to provide relevant information on a timely basis.  Information like location (i.e., a mini-map), information on buffs and debuffs impacting the player or their foes, information on damage given and received, information on the range of effects and abilities, information on the identity of other players (i.e., nameplates) and so on.  Some of these are available, now, as player-created interface add-ons, but many MMO fans expect much of this in the "stock" UI of any serious MMO, and the notion that they have been excluded for immersion purposes is precisely the kind of thing that seems "off" from a design perspective for the MMO fan type of player.The account vs. character concept --- ESO is designed in such a way as to tie together all of the characters created on one player's account in ways that are not common in other MMOs.  For example, the bank space - all of it - is shared in totality between all of the characters on a player's account - there is no "personal" bank space for any one character.  (This may sound harmless, but it is not - more on that below.)  Similarly, while a player can join up to 5 guilds (the reason explained below), these guilds are joined by every character on the account, and this cannot be changed - essentially the player joins the guilds and not a character.  What this essentially means is that "alt" or alternate characters are not really very separate from the rest of a player's characters.  If a player wants a "downtime alt" that is guildless, or an alt focused on PvP or PvE and in different guilds, or what have you, all of these characters will be in the same guilds, making this kind of play impossible.  This obviously is fine from a single player perspective, but in the MMO perspective, tying these together is not common, is unexpected by many MMO fan type players, and leads to other issues which I will describe next.The trading system --- MMO fans are accustomed to robust trading systems in their games.  Pretty much every significant MMO released since 2004 has had a clearinghouse type system (either using an auction or a simpler listing system) which allowed players to trade with other players.  Of course, this isn't a feature of single player games, and so the single player TES fan element isn't nearly as concerned about this as the MMO fan element is.  In ESO, trading is limited to trading guilds.  Each player can join up to 5 guilds, and these guilds can have up to 500 members.  This means that the total theoretical market, other than spamming general chat for customers, is 2500 players.  Players, mind you, and not characters, because the guild membership is tied to the players account - all characters belong to the same guilds.  Coming from a single player perspective, this is understandable, because trading is not really an element in a single player game, and the player simply pursues all of the things they want to do independently - including pursuing all crafts and so on, as is the case in the single player TES games.  In an MMO context, however, MMO fans expect to be able to trade easily with the vast world of players in the game - and not be limited to a maximum theoretical of 2500 plus chat spam.  It seems very likely that this design was also driven by the megaserver backbone of the game, which would create a massive market which could have implications on the overall supply of everything in the game, but needless to say this design decision is problematic at best to many of the MMO fans who are involved with the game currently.Bank/Storage system.  Similarly, the bank system in the game is also limited, and based on the player's account (i.e., completely shared by all characters).  This design, which appears intended to limit both the ability of players to craft all crafts at the same time comfortably as well as to place a soft supply cap on materials in the game world, annoys both sets of players for different reasons.  The TES fans, who are used to inventory limits from the single player games in the series, nevertheless are also used to homes and, barring that, modifications which can be used to greatly expand storage capacities fairly quickly in the games.  This cannot be done in ESO, for balance reasons, and this is leading to a great outcry, because many of the TES fans want to do all of the crafts themselves, as they would in a single-player game, and the system seems designed to frustrate that.  On the other hand, the MMO fans are used to limits on what they can do at once on any one character, as well as bank size limits, but are also used to being able to do another set of crafts on an alt character with the same freedom/limits as for the first - this is not the case in ESO, because the entire bank is shared.  So adding alt characters who are also doing crafts simply decreases the overall amount of bank space available - this is because the cap on storage is an account-based cap, not a character-based cap.  This design frustrates many of the MMO fans, because it removes many of the reasons they might want to play an alt character, or even several characters at once, making this much harder to achieve than is customary in MMOs, precisely because the cap is enforced at the account level, rather than the character level.Conclusion --- In all, ESO is a series of compromises that appeal to one or the other type of player more, in some cases coupled together with a few different ways of doing things that appeal to neither type of player very much.  It needs to be said that it was an extremely difficult assignment to take a game world that is associated with quintessentially solo, even lonely, gameplay in an extremely open, immersive world and translate that effectively into a game genre that is characterized by massively multiplayer gameplay and mechanics to ensure balance.  This is very hard to do.  I am not sure it could have been done any better by anyone else.  But, having said that, as we know, in all translations - even the very best - something is lost, both for the original speaker and the eventual hearer.  This is also the case with ESO.  The game plays kind of like an Elder Scrolls game, but not really.  The game is obviously an MMO, but misses elements of MMO design, in many cases in an effort to avoid making it even less like an Elder Scrolls game than it is.  In short, the compromises made in the design of this game undermine its ability to appeal fully to either the TES fan or the MMO fan and increase the likelihood that it will disappoint both types of gamer, albeit for different reasons in each case.  Again, I'm not sure that the game could have been produced any differently than it has been.  However, it does strike me that perhaps trying to render a quintessentially solo/lone, immersive, explorative type of game in a massively multiplayer setting is an extremely difficult thing to do very well, and that this difficulty underlies the issues of ESO at this time.

Elder Scrolls Online (ESO) is still firmly beta and was released far too early. Barring the glitchy in-game problems, the story is lackluster and the quests are way too short and easy. I will also point out that it costs anywhere between $13-16 a month for access to the online service in addition to the $60 you pay for the game. Though, you do get 30 days of service included (with a catch).Quests / StoriesWhile Skyrim felt epic in nearly every way and every story seemed to matter, ESO feels hollow and already been there, done that. In Skyrim, you always felt like every story did something to progress you towards the final ending. In ESO, the stories are short, random, haphazard and disconnected and don't seem to lead somewhere important. In short, don't go into ESO expecting the same experience as Skyrim.GameplayFrom Oblivion to Skyrim, some of the gameplay pieces were dumbed down and intentionally limited. The same is true from Skyrim to ESO. Features in Skyrim like pickpocketing are not in ESO (at least not yet). Additionally, it now costs stamina to crouch and sneak. In exchange for losing stamina, you no longer have to level up your sneak ability. Keep in mind, I did choose a character adept at sneak, but I still expected to level it up. You also don't level up other attributes by swimming or running like you did in Skyrim. The level up system has changed again in ESO, but not necessarily for the better.Veteran RanksAfter having finally reached Veteran Rank 2, I can honestly state the game is effectively over. The only territory you have open as VR is Craglorn and replaying faction quests in Cyrodiil, which is not very much. By the time you reach level 50 (aka Veteran Rank 1), your game is over. The main quest is complete and your character is locked into its health, magicka and stamina stats. The only way to augment your character from VR1 forward is to search for skyshards to finish skill points, to search for materials to improve or enchant your armor and weapons and, well, that's it. The stories are over and there's not much else to do. Oh, you can grind if you like, but you can only grind in VR dungeons and VR territories. You cannot grind in 1-50 territories. Though, you can finish up unfinished quests there, in most cases they are boringly easy. Basically, the Veteran Rank quests and dungeon crawls are all endgame content. Oh, leveling up from one Veteran Rank does yield special armor as a token, but you don't get anything else. But, expect it to take ages to level up to VR12 (max level at this point) as it takes nearly 500k experience to move from one VR to another. And, if your VR is less than 6-10, don't expect to get invited on looting parties in Craglorn or Cyrodiil much. On the other hand, questing solo in VR dungeons is near impossible. So expect to grind grind grind your way to VR10.Glitching, Crashing and EnvironmentsAs with another MMO named Defiance, ESO chose a somewhat similar MMO strategy with 'shards' falling from the sky reminiscent of Defiance's Arkfalls. As for environments, I've run into places where walls are missing from being rendered. Network player characters simply walk through one another rather than having any sort of collision. Getting on and off of a horse is stupidly unrealistic. Instead of actually housing your horse in a stable, you call it with a key and it appears out of thin air and you hop on. When you hop off, it also disappears into thin air. What's the point? Clearly, a step backwards for realism in this franchise. The horse running animation is easily one of the weakest in the game. When running, you feel like you're on a toy horse.The glitching and crashing have not improved in the 2 months since I started playing ESO. In fact, crashing is quite frequent. If I'm grinding in Craglorn, the ESO client crashes after every 8-10 wayshrine teleports in the middle of battle. The time it takes to restart the client, the whole party has moved onto to the next grind point and you're left well behind. Keep in mind that I'm on the Mac client, so it may be specific to the Mac. The PC client may be more stable.LootingMost chests are empty in the environment. When you do find something, it's 1 gold or a worthless food item that you don't need because health auto generates too quickly. Unless you've specifically killed (or helped in killing) an enemy, you don't get the choice of looting a body.  So, you'll find bodies laying around where you can do nothing.Graphics / HUDThe graphics quality are somewhat better than Skyrim (at least for character faces and environments). The character bodies are still a bit too blocky and are incorrect proportionally. Looking at a male character, you can't tell he's actually male (if you get my meaning) other than by them wearing male clothes and a muscular upper body. It's clear that Bethesda has no intention in treading into 'relationship' territory. The characters seem more like what you might see in early Second Life than what you'd see in a next gen game. Bethesda is clearly out of their element when it comes to producing realism. They just don't have artists capable of realism in characters, unlike the characters in Mass Effect, Infamous Second Son, Killzone Shadowfall or even Halo 4.  The graphics are somewhat better than Defiance, though.The mouth motion when talking is like a puppet opening and closing. There is no actual attempt at trying to make the lips appear to say actual words. This is another step backwards towards realism. I mean, you create these characters with seemingly realistic skin tone, but the mouth moves like Kermit the frog? You create environments that look amazingly realistic and then create a horse that runs like a mechanical windup toy?The HUD is standard for Skyrim with map screen, inventory screen, settings screen and main play screen with compass quest locator at the top. When necessary, the health, stamina and magicka bars are at the bottom. Chat is to the left bottom.OverallThe game is underwhelming and not currently worth the $15 a month online charge on top of the $59-$99 price tag of the game. The story setup is underwhelming. The voice actors are just not that great. Yes, I do realize Bethesda used Michael Gambon (or a very close soundalike) as one of the primary voice roles, but it was not a good choice. His voiceover work is inconsistent even between sentences in the same dialog. The environments are overly crowded with other network players. All of this just serves to clutter the environment in that you don't know which NPC you're supposed to interact with. Worse, most quest giving NPCs are crowded with players hovering there trying to do the same thing you're doing. There's entirely too much spam text chatter which can be turned off.In other words, ZeniMax's decision to create the Elder Scrolls as an MMO was not kind to this franchise. It just doesn't hold up well enough as an MMO the way that it is. For a light kind of RPG you might find online for free on Facebook or one of those other free MMO sites, it's probably okay. But, for top end heavy-weight questing game, ESO doesn't fulfill that need. ESO feels like we're back in the 90s trying to figure out how to make an MMO game work. ESO feels unpolished and unfinished. It needed at least another 1-2 years development effort and a rework of some very fundamental aspects of the game.  In fact, even as poor as Defiance's graphics were, the game hit a homerun in the questing and co-op pieces. Not so much with ESO. ESO's questing leaves a lot to be desired.Cyrodiil is one big game of Risk with limited questing available, but quests are specifically towards the campaign. The PVP elements were shoehorned in awkwardly and in a territory where PVE also exists. So, when you're just trying to finish quests without PVP, there are a bunch of gamers running around that area playing death match on would-be PVE gamers. As I said, awkward and frustrating. On top of this, the endgame Veteran Ranks don't really offer enough actual questing value just to keep people in the game. In fact, there is basically no questing after VR1. There is just a lot of looting and grinding.I'm hoping that by the time ESO reaches the console in December (moved out from July) that Bethesda will have a much better product to offer. If you're looking for a polished game, don't look here yet. Perhaps in time Bethesda can patch it to greatness. Though, I'm not confident that Bethesda can actually polish it more than it already is. Note that ZeniMax moved the game from July to December in an attempt to get the console networking issues resolved. Apparently, ZeniMax is trying to created a unified MMO world and will need to help from Sony and Microsoft to make this happen. Some gamers have also claimed the gamepad is the issue. However, I can definitively state that I've used a gamepad to play on the Mac the entire time. So, mapping of all of the most necessary keys to the gamepad is possible on the nextgen console controllers. The PS4 controller will likely have the easiest time playing ESO with the touchpad. The Xbox One's controller is barebones basic. Without a keyboard, Xbox One gamers may find the game more challenging to play with the limited keys available.Ratings out of 5 starsGameplay: 2 out of 5Graphics: 4 out of 5Voice Acting: 2 out of 5Quests: 3 out of 5Story: 1 out of 5Overall: 3 out of 5Recommendation: If you're a fan of the Elder Scrolls series questing, I'd strongly recommend waiting for the next non-MMO Elder Scrolls game.

Don't buy this game if you like having strictly defined classes or having dozens of abilities to choose from in any given fight.However, DO buy this game if you like both MMOs and the Elder Scrolls universe. Buy it if you appreciate stuff like lore, voice acting and storylines. Get it if you like to roam and explore, yet still want to run across most of the quests and events (i.e. they'll find you.) Buy it if you enjoy deep crafting systems or complex 3-sided siege-style PvP on a grand scale. Get the game if you want a unique looking character, with a unique skillset, with a mix of abilities that suit your playstyle (i.e. like a bow wielding mage than wears plate armor or a defensive tank-knight that can use a fire staff).

I had been on the fence about whether or not to try Elder Scrolls Online due to the mixed bag of reviews. By far the two biggest complaints I heard were the broken gameplay mechanics and the overpopulation of people. I figured the tide of people would have subsided by the time I joined up, and I didn't personally notice any of said gameplay mechanics in the beta, so when I saw ESO drop to half price here on Amazon, I jumped on it.This game is beautifully breathtaking. My first impressions were that this is graphically just like Skyrim, which is one of my favorite games of all time. If you don't like Skyrim's graphic style, you won't like this. It's pretty much identical. I was drawn in immediately by the ambiance and expertly crafted environments. The attention to detail in this game is far greater than any other MMO I've personally played. It feels like a real, living, breathing world. The world is also enormous. If you love exploration, you will love this. Special little rewards can be found by those that seek them out and explore every nook and cranny of an area. Also, just as with Skyrim, you can rummage through any container, sometimes finding junk, but sometimes also finding crafting materials and equipment to better your character.Regarding the issues with gameplay I read about, I've experienced none of them. Granted there's been quite a few patches since release and we're about 3 months past launch now, so I suspect if there were any such issues, they've all been ironed out because I found nothing wrong. I was concerned about the combat, because while it's very similar to traditional Elder Scrolls combat (identical to Skyrim, really) it's very different from any other MMO I've played. I heard from a friend who played the beta extensively that the combat is what ruined the game for him. I suppose it's really a personal preference, because I love the combat system.It's very different from standard MMO combat, but that also makes it very refreshing, and not in a "Oooh shiny!" way that gets old after a few days or weeks, but in a long lasting way that really makes the entire game more enjoyable for me. You actively have to swing your sword or fire your bow or activate your staff, while also actively blocking and dodging any incoming attacks. In addition to this, you have your standard hot key bar but with a twist. You're able to "slot" 6 abilities at any given time. It's very reminiscent of Guild Wars, but in a less restrictive way. You are free to pick and choose whatever 6 abilities you want at any time and you can level up many more to change up your playstyle. Say you want to be a magic DPS when you're solo, but swap to a healing role when you're partied up. Very simple to do by leveling the right abilities and swapping them at will.This skill system is where the game really shines, beyond all the flashy graphics and engaging combat. This system is, in my opinion, best compared to that of Rift. You get a skill tree for your chosen class (dragonknight, templar, sorceror, nightblade or templar) which consists of 3 "branches" off that tree. Each of those 3 branches contains numerous skills that you can put points into when you level up, thereby unlocking that skill and allowing you to level it up by using it, much like Skyrim. Some skills are active, some are passive. Then you have another skill tree for your weapon, armor, race, guild, world and craft, each with it's own set of branches and subsequent skills. You're free to pick and choose absolutely any combination that you could dream of. There are no limits.By carefully selecting your skills, you can craft your character to be exactly how you envision it. With MMO's becoming more and more mainstream, leveling up in said games has also become less interesting as you're heavily guided down a singular path in many of them. The skill system in ESO is like a breath of fresh air, coming from many many years of playing World of Warcraft and having my talents now spoon fed to me to ensure I don't make any mistakes. If you do make mistakes, you can also reset your skill points and start all over until you get your build just how you want it. It's a system that rewards critical thinking and planning, and it doesn't just look good on paper, it performs beautifully.There really are no downsides to ESO in my experience. Given that it's an MMO, you WILL run into other people, all the time, in fact. People are everywhere, which is what I was really looking forward to in ESO. In all my hundreds of hours playing Skyrim, I often thought to myself, this would be so much more fun if I could play with my friends. That's what ESO is, Skyrim with friends, new and old alike. The storytelling and immersion is just as superb as it was in Skyrim and it's predecessors. But as with any community, be it online or out your front door, there are bad apples in every bunch. There are jerks, there are spawn campers, there are immature people shouting in town. You will find that with ANY MMO, I promise. So far in ESO, the exposure to such things has been barely noticeable and by comparison, far better than WoW in general. I noticed ONE person camping a boss in one cave, but I got my kill in (which wasn't even required for the quest I was on) and went on my merry way. I saw nothing of these mobs of people hoarding bosses and killing them instantly after they spawned, but again, we're a few months past launch and the population has spread out across the levels rather than everyone being tightly packed into the same areas which is an issue with all brand new MMOs and their expansions.I could go on for ages about all the things I love about ESO, but suffice it to say, if you love Elder Scrolls (and Skyrim especially), you love MMO's and you're not going to cry that your immersion is ruined when a couple players charge into the crypts and rush that boss with you, you'll love ESO. Now that the price has dropped significantly, there's no reason not to at least try it for your free month and see how you like it!

This game takes some getting used to, but overall I'd say it has potential, but isn't worth a subscription.On the plus side, the quests aren't too terribly boring, the voice acting is quite good, the graphics are very good for an MMO, and once you get used to the oddities of the gearing system, you can appreciate how flexible your main character really is. The story eventually gets interesting enough to keep your attention (and there is a story, which is a rarity for many MMOs these days). The world is quite large and well-done, and you're not bogged down by a boring shooting gallery of trash mobs.On the downside, I was confused by how the classes blend together at first (you select a class but then can equip whatever you want, although it's best to equip a little of every type of ability/armor), but once you get used to it, I suppose the flexibility is liberating. I also didn't like how the game drops you in the middle of nowhere as an amnesiac with uncertain loyalties - I much prefer how most MMOs let you know who and what you're fighting for. The interface is very different from other MMOs (very RPG-like) and while there's a lot to explore, there aren't nearly enough quests to feel like you have the freedom to go where you want and do what you want. You're very much on rails.On the PvP side, there's one PvP zone and it's monstrously huge - so monstrously huge that it's impossible to get anywhere or do anything by yourself. I just don't like oversized WPvP - I prefer the instanced PvP of games like WoW that don't waste your time running everywhere and force you to group into artificial teams and battle against castles and NPCs.Overall, I'd say there's a lot of potential here, but it lacks a lot of polish and doesn't play as well for an MMO as it should. Even more than SWTOR, the game - with its amorphous class roles, separate stories and no obvious prompting to group for most of the content - plays better as a single player RPG than an MMO. Still, it's a lot of fun so far, but there's simply not enough content to warrant a subscription for this MMO. It should be a regular RPG with a co-op option, because it's a horrible failure as an MMO.

For those more comfortable with group adventuring maybe this wont be so bad but for me used to solo questing it was an act of frustration for sure.  And battling with 10000 other adventurers to try to complete your individual quest that everyone is doing at the same time is an issue for me as well.  Waiting for a boss or an item to respawn from all the other adventurers grabbing it, is not my idea of fun.Not as big a deal though but an annoyance was the voices of the characters tended to be some of the same voice actors with little variation in the sound of the character's voice.Don't get me wrong the scenery and design of the game is beautiful and well done and several of the quests were fun to do although sometimes repetitive. I actually initially enjoyed doing the beta tests and some of the early game but that quickly wore off and after seeing relatively little improvement in the bugs, it became more of a chore than fun.But the final straw for me was when a bug basically locked me out of my account and prevented me from basically doing anything and after several failed attempts at getting it fixed through customer service, I gave up, asked to delete my account and went back to solo adventuring games I can play without being online to do so.This game is ok overall but not without issues and maybe not quite the Elder Scrolls you know and love.  The bugs and game trolls really drove me out of the game in addition to being forced to join groups to complete certain quests.  Without these bugs and some improvements in gameplay and this game could be so much more.

I was in the beta for a little bit, one weekend, and had the game preordered so have had it since the beginning though decided not to have my membership renewed past the first month.  The game is alright, but it just wasn't really keeping my attention.I didn't encounter many bugs, and actually this was probably the smoothest MMO release I've participated in.  Actually got to play right away on release day, servers were behaving great and lag was minimal.  By comparison, WoW had a horribly laggy launch.  I have encountered a few quests that you just can't complete due to NPCs not appearing... after wasting some time with it I abandoned the quests and left the area.Questing is somewhat different in this game than most MMOs.  You generally don't go from town to town, accepting everything everyone has for you.  Going out and doing them, then coming back to turn them all in.  You pretty much go from area to area to perform one quest.  Each quest generally has a series of things that need to be done, you get more involved with the story of each quest this way.  Unfortunately though, the quests I was doing didn't seem to mix with each other nor the main story line.  The main story line progresses too slowly, where you're essentially told to wait a while.  Maybe 5 levels later you'll go back to do one more main story quest and it'll stop again.  The mages / fighters guild are also very slow to progress.  It's sort of annoying if your favorite things to do in the previous elder scrolls games was the guild quests.  Currently there is no thieves or dark brotherhood.The combat in this game is somewhat misleading coming from the single player elder scrolls games.  At first glance it looks almost the same, at second glance not so much.  It comes off as appearing appropriately live action, where you aim your attacks, but that is not the case.  You're locked on to whatever you are fighting, even if loosely.  Your arrows will hit your target even if you're not facing your target.  Taken, most mmos are like this, aside from Tera which shows that mmo combat can be done differently.  Even though several years ago when they announced that the combat was going to be more like traditional mmos due to latency concerns I was still hoping they would have changed their minds, especially after Tera online came out.  But they did not, it is what it is but it could have been better.  I generally prefer being either an archer or mage class, however with the lack of focus on aiming and keeping aim it's a bit dull.  Fortunately the game lets you essentially form your own fighting style, so it still has unique elements about it.PVP is pretty cool, extremely large scale, and only takes place is one zone.  If they opted not to make the game on one giant mega server they could have had dedicated PVP servers, allowing for certain types of PVP to occur elsewhere in the world.  Could make the dark brotherhood more exciting from a PVP perspective, but I don't feel the dark brotherhood will have any PVP aspects when it is implemented.  You will not be a sneaky assassin killing other players, it's all very zerg like which is unfortunate.  The large scale PVP zone is cool, but I was also imagining smaller 1v1 style PVP elsewhere.  Unfortunately also you can't even interact with members of the other factions except for in Cyrodiil.  Once you finally can go to the other 2/3rds for the world you exist in a different instance than the actual members of the faction are in, so you don't see each other.I never participated in the group instances so I cannot comment on them.Positives of the game:-Graphics and scenery are beautiful.  Environmental effects and sound effects are very nice.-The voice overs are nice-The quest layout is nice (fewer world quests to grind, each individually quest taking more commitment to complete)-The combat is nice when comparing to most other mmos, but not so when comparing it to the single player elder scrolls games.-Lots of character customization options  (Khajiit can have leopard spots, and other cat patterns.  A favorite addition.)-Nice leveling system / skill treesNegatives:-More like a MMO, significantly less like an elder scrolls game.  It's a MMORPG with an elder scrolls skin.  I feel they could have squeezed a little more of the elder scrolls experience in, but it's been overrun by MMO turf.-PVP experience has been short-sighted-combat not appropriately real time-main and guild quests have too few quests too far between to make them really interestingAnd on other notes, I don't like how they included a free mount with the imperial edition of the game.  And if you didn't get that edition your option is to wait a while and then spend your life's savings in game on a horse.  It's essentially paying real money for and in game hefty value.  It's silly.  I don't like the concept of buying game goods with real money regardless of who you're paying the money too, I see it as not fair.  I don't mind the other perks, but the mount perk of the imperial edition is a bit much.

I think my title pretty much says it all.  I knew this was going to be the case before it was released.  This is an MMO so Elder Scrolls fans shouldn't expect to be able to change the world in this game as much you can in the single player version (but I think MOST TES fans know this).  You can't kill that quest giver because the next guy needs him too.  It's been 2 months since release and I've decided to give up my subscription.Things I liked?The crafting system is pretty good and the food and potions were similar to what you would make in a TES game.  The ingredients were just as much of a pain to find as well (which is good in my opinion).  There are special crafting stations scatttered around where you can make gear with special stats if you are wearing 3+ pieces.The PVP was fun and I don't typically like PVP.  You can go solo if you want, but the idea behind the PVP zone (capturing keeps mainly) is more oriented for group PVP which I enjoy more.Books!  I don't mind going to every bookshelf in an attempt to level up a skill.  And it's one of those little things that make it feel like a TES game.  Same with lockpicking.  Chests spawn in random locations and you don't lose the lockpick when you use it.Things I didn't like?As others said, customer service and their maintenance of the game itself.  There was the bug that others here have listed where you fall through the world.  Customer Service's answer was that it was somehow my fault and I needed to turn my graphic settings down.Then there are still the bugged quests even after 2 months.  In the first month you received an email if you submitted a bug report, but in the past month I have gotten no indication that they have read them other than a week later (yes a week) the quest is no longer bugged.  For one bugged quest, I logged out nearby so I could complete it when I logged in and 3 days later it still wasn't fixed.  The 4th day I logged in to find that the event was no longer bugged, but the NPC to trigger it was.  This was why I decided to cancel my account actually.Bots are everywhere and this company doesn't seem to want to do anything about it.  Oh, that's not true- they nerfed the ability they are spamming when grinding.  Of course, this has nerfed it for those of us who aren't bots either.  If you report them, they will remove the bots account and then refund the botter's money so they can just go out, buy a new license and continue on with a new account.  Very generous of them.The questing is a lot more limited than it might appear at first.  Every quest giver has an arrow over their head and you are told when you complete all the quests in a zone.  I like talking to NPC's and I talk to every one I can and I have never gotten a quest from one that didn't have an arrow over their head.  The most that has happened is an area of the map has been revealed that I otherwise wouldn't have gotten without traveling there.  I was really hoping for some NPC's randomly giving out quests when you speak to them.  I heard that this was done in the early portion of the beta, but people didn't like having to actually work to find the quests so they started marking them.In the end, it wasn't the limited quests or massive amount of bots that made me unsub though - it was definitely the lame service that made me quit.  Your monthly fee is supposed to pay for people to make sure everything is working smoothly in-game and I just felt like I wasn't getting what I was paying for.  Blaming customers for bugs that should have been taken care of before release is crap.  Taking 4 days to a week to fix a glitched quest?  Pathetic.  There are games out there that are free to play that have better service than this!So why even give it 3 stars?  Because if it were free, then I would still play it.  Many people would still be playing it if it were free.

After playing it for the last 9 weeks, and getting to through the main story I think I can give it a more accurate review. Personally I liked it, it was a little slow at first, but the story line gets better as you go along. Also, very different from Skyrim in alot of ways, so that took a little getting use to. However it managed to keep me interested enough to want to play it daily ( 2-3 hours on average). They have managed to leave themselves a lot of room for ways to build onto the game. It will be interesting to see how they approach this in next few months with the large number of people getting to where they have completed the main story. I'm still playing it after completing the main story, but cant really say why without spoiling it for those not there yet.Graphics - Excellent graphics and I say that because I play it on Ultra settings. If you play it on anything lower or have a basic video card, yeah you'll think it just looks ok. But on Ultra with the right video card it is beautiful, down to the blades of grass, the water, the plants,  armor detail is very good. I have played on Medium and Low ( when forced to play on my laptops) and noticeable difference. The environment itself looks amazing. Some of the creatures, such as the Trolls, were a little disappointing in comparison to the ones in Skyrim. However, the faces, and bodies of the NPCs look really good.Gameplay - As you go along, things of course get harder. What I did like is that, when it came to some of the bosses it wasn't as simple as just hack and slash, you actually had to use other fighting techniques such as blocking and dodging and pay attention to what you were fighting, change up what you use. The hack and slash approach worked ok at lower levels and when just fighting the basic enemies. Someone mentioned the bow and arrow aiming, that part was a bit of a letdown in comparison to it on Skyrim. None of the precision aiming here.Group Play - Worked rather well, get with a good group can be a lot of fun. The pvp area is like a whole different game, but does require you get with a good group to really enjoy it.Storyline - Gets much better as it goes along. However, I found it slow getting into it for the first 10 levels. The side quests vary, some are simple mindless and some full blown storylines on their own. They do have a few puzzle like side quests, which I would of liked to have seen more of these type of quests.Character Development - Lots of options here, and many ways to build your character and it takes time. So many options you almost have to plan how you will develop your character prior to starting to get the best build as your leveling up and not waste skill points. There is a lot of grinding, so if not into that , might find that boring when it comes to crafting and building up skills, I happen to like that part.In conclusion, I'm happy with my experience with ESO. Not too happy about the price of game ( which is now down to a more reasonable price), and then paying the monthly fee, but I understand their is a cost to what they do. I'm hoping they can keep up on the long term play ability of the game.

Great job ZOS! 5/7/2014 We are now enjoying the game even more and we are role-paying and questing in peace.*From what I've read about some negative reviews is that some people complained that this game costs money, and you have to pay more for game subscription fees (this is the same for other popular MMO games and is normal for high quality online RPG/MMO)Also unless you have played this game up to at least level 15, where you will be able to switch ready weapon sets / combat abilities with a touch of a button in the middle of combat (PvP or PvE), you haven't really experienced your true combat potential.*I purchased two of the DIGITAL versions, one Imperial Edition for myself and one regular for my wife.  Having said that, my review is about the game and not the physical.  All versions of this game are the same regarding the gameplay and the world of Nirn.The beauty is in the details!  Even though a lot of players are previous fans of "The Elder Scrolls" lore and series of games, I believe newcomers will have the most fun in the world of Nirn because the lore about The Elder Scrolls and all things in Tamriel will be new to them!  That means some serious adventuring and fun.Playing tip:  If sometimes you need help in figuring things out in the game, there are so many websites dedicated to "The Elder Scrolls Online" with all the tips and tricks to make life in Tamriel easier.  But of course, you can always be a hard-core adventurer and figure out all things by yourself.When you enter this game, it feels, sounds, and looks like you are really in their world.The music mesmerizing and the graphics superb. Here it is, the next big entry in the MMORPG genre -- also the next big Elder Scrolls game.This almost needs 2 reviews. One for Elder Scrolls and one for an MMORPG...As an Elder Scrolls game, you have to ask yourself one thing: "Do I want to play an Elder Scrolls game with a bunch of other people?" If the answer is "yes, at all costs!", skip the rest of this review and click "buy". If the answer is "Yes!....wait, what costs?", then read on.The first cost, of course, is the actual monthly subscription fee. What this gets you is a multiplayer world and (we all hope) regular content updates included as part of the subscription. The other cost is a bit more subtle...how do you have an Elder Scrolls style world where everyone can go everywhere while still customizing all content to YOU? The answer is "you can't", or at any rate, they didn't make any new big innovations here. ESO is more linear than other Elder Scroll games, far more like other MMORPGs. When you are level 15 you need to be in an area that's appropriate for level 15. The game isn't totally linear -- it's not Half-Life 2, for example -- but it's no Daggerfall or Skyrim either. You need to move through the world as is appropriate for your level. Consequently this has the same problem as all PvE MMORPGs, which is that if you want to play with your friends, you need to work to stay in synch. If someone runs ahead and plays 8 hours of quests without you, you can't just log in the next day and join them where they are (not unless you want to die a lot because you're in an area too high level for you).So that's what being multiplayer does to Elder Scrolls. If that's acceptable to you, buy away. If you were looking for a single player experience, though, you may be disappointed.For people already familiar with MMORPGs (and may not be familiar with Elder Scrolls) probably the biggest surprise is going to be the combat system, which is, in my opinion, far more immersive and engaging than a lot of games. You are expected to actively swing your sword and actively block and actively dodge. This isn't WOW where you target something and eat nachos while mashing "Shadowbolt" over and over. You need to get involved. And it works surprisingly well. The lag seems to be invisible and the game's performance is actually amazing.I really mean that. I dunno who they hired to do their network code and graphics engine but they're not paying them enough. The game handles hundreds of players on screen in crisp, high resolution graphics and it is frankly better and more amazing than any other MMORPG I have ever played, and I've played most of them. From high end machines to low end, all of my friends and guildmates are amazed at how well this game runs and how good it looks.Character design is more akin to Elder Scrolls than regular MMORPG tropes too. Don't look for a "tank" or a "healer". Decide what role you want to play, decide which class looks like the most fun and then figure out how to build that class into that role. All classes can be any role, in their own way. I'm playing a Nightblade, which on the surface looks like a rogue, but I'm playing him as a tank. One of my friends is playing a Nightblade healer. It basically means we both have some decent abilities for burst damage and escape but I am very tanky and he is very healy and our character builds don't look much alike, despite being the same class. You could be a sorcerer tank or a dragonknight archer, etc. The class/role system is pretty wide open.PvP? Elder Scrolls offers probably the best PvP we've seen since DAOC. It follows the DAOC model, which is somewhat like the GW2 model but with some important differences:Most of the world is PvE but the 3 teams come together in the middle of the map. The middle zone is, we estimate, on the order of 15 times larger than GW2's "Eternal Battleground" (search YouTube for the travel time comparison video someone made), and that's the 3-team PvP area. There are keeps to fight over, PvE quest hubs (where enemies can and will gank you, but the XP is great if you can avoid getting murdered), "Elder Scrolls" to steal from enemy keeps, small public dungeons (where enemies can and will gank you), LOTS of open space to hunt in and, "coming soon", the Imperial City, which is a huge PvEvP area in the middle of the PvP map (not yet implemented, though you can SEE it...)Will this game have legs to go long term? I dunno. At worst, I think it'll be the next Rift -- alive and kicking for a year or two before the new wears off for everyone. I don't think it'll be another SWTOR -- which was closing servers due to lack of players less than a year after launch. Whether it's the new WOW, exploding onto the MMORPG scene and there to stay, remains to be seen. It may depend on how popular the PvP is (which sustained DAOC for years) and how well they can deliver new content.All things said, I'd vote "go ahead and get it". The only people I think will be unhappy are those who expected another Skyrim with an open world meant for soloing. This is not that.For me, it's fun. I dunno if it's long term ("Magic 8-ball says: "Ask Again Later") but it really has its moments and is not a flash in the pan.

The Elder Scrolls Online manages to be a unique and compelling game that bucks the conventions of traditional MMORPGs and brings a little of that Elder Scrolls flavor into the MMORPG scene.  But do not mislead yourself, it is NOT Skyrim 2.Essentially it is a fairly free form MMORPG that makes questing interesting and matter, gives great freedom of building your character, and on a more subtle level really makes the world feel satisfying.  The quests all make sense, areas don't feel the same, interesting little things are tucked around every corner, and the atmosphere and music cap it off.  The world just feels alive.Lets get down to business.Story: 10I'm not talking about huge jaw dropping story moments here.  The game manages to be consistently real and interesting throughout.  Each quest feels real and you don't get sent out on fetch 10 or kill 20 quests.  Instead they want you to do things like save crew members, stop rituals, find books of dark knowledge, stop mutinies, pray at shrines to pay respect to a mothers children, etc.Killing and item uses happens during these quests, but the focus is on accomplishing something and not just slogging through something to put more exp on your bar.  This is the first time in forever that I actually read quest text.SWTOR did well on story too, but it had great high points and then everything else sucked.  TESO is consistently good throughout.  TESO beats out every other MMORPG when it comes to consistently good story, hands down.Graphics: 10This has some of the best graphics of any MMORPG on the market.  Within it's genre it is top notch.  But this is not to be compared to skyrim, it's a multiplayer game with the capability of putting 500 people on screen at one time and still running smoothly, that would kill Skyrim.Also, people tend to think about MODDED skyrim.  Vanilla Skyrim and even DLC HD Skyrim is not near as impressive before you start adding all the custom mods to it.Atmosphere:  10Each area feels hand crafted.  I've been looking for areas that looks the same and have not yet found one.  Each area feels appropriate to itself and the quests in that area.  The music and the quests given strengthen this.  There are scenic views, shipwrecked coastlines, swamps, forests, beautiful cities, etc.I've been been playing MMORPG's a long time and without a doubt this is the best one I've played in regards to atmosphere.Gameplay: 8/10The game starts out a little slowly in the gameplay department and before you hit level 10-15 your combat is much less dynamic and interesting than it will be later.  So hang in there.  Once you make it past those level though:The gameplay is solid and fun, but it's not groundbreaking and it won't be the reason you stay in TESO.  Granted this is much much better in PVP, but even then it's just good and not heads and tails above other games like some of it's other aspects.The combat is complex enough to be challenging without overflowing you with buttons.  The character building is varied and doesn't seem to have "right" answers atm and dungeons have even been run with all DPS.  Speaking of, dungeon encounters are really fun :D.Dungeons: 10I'm not much of a raider.  I raid and do dungeons in every MMORPG a little bit but have never been drawn in before...till now.  I've raided in quite a few MMORPGs too.TESO dungeons however manage to be consistently entertaining and CHALLENGING.  A good clean run through might have 2 wipes in it, but it doesn't feel too punishing to wipe out here and there and in fact each boss gives you a soul gem (to revive with) so it's kind of expected.Boss mechanics are fun and challenging, the atmosphere in dungeons is amazing, the story of dungeons is solid, and the level design is great.PVP: 10PVP is amazing and is likely the closest thing to Dark Age of Camelot that has happened yet.  I would say it's very comparable to Guild Wars 2 PVP EXCEPT it's much deeper and more satisfying.  Losing battles in TESO MATTERS.  Rezzing is limited.  The map is HUGE.Combat is fast and frenetic but not as much so as Guild Wars 2, being slightly more strategic.  I wouldn't say it's perfect, there are still some tweaks that likely need to be made, but it's VERY good.Also, just watching a battle with siege weapons and spells firing back and forth is a spectacle to behold.UI: 8/10The games minimalistic UI is clean and immersive, staying out of the way to enhance you feeling part of the world.  If this does not appeal to you then you can turn on more UI in the options to get the information you crave.  If this still isn't enough for you then the game supports add-ons via LUA .But the game loses 2 points on UI for it's Guild Store system, which needs some work currently.Conclusion:Very very solid story based MMORPG that has a unique feel from there others and has well done PVP.  I highly recommend trying it out for yourself

Ok, I have waited a long while, and experienced much of this game, from Beta to today, and am finally writing a review. I have a love hate relationship with the Elder Scrolls games. They are wonderfully imaginative and open ended, but also riddled with bugs.This is not your typical MMO, you will not be constrained to any class restrictions, and they really did a fantastic job of letting you play any type of character how you want. Heavy armor mage tank, no problem. One can get really creative with how they approach the game.
