This game was somewhat disappointing and just the slightest bit frustrating, but at the same time it was still quite fun and altogether well made. The game's biggest issue to me was its story and narrative. You begin the story as Dracula defending his castle from an army of Brotherhood of Light soldiers and their giant Siege Titan. After completely destroying the army and coming face to face with his son Alucard, time jumps to the present day where Dracula has recently awoken from centuries of slumber and finds himself in Castlevania City, which has been built over the ruins of his old castle. His old enemy Zobek (still voiced by Patrick Stewart, thankfully) seeks him out and forms an alliance with him in order to kill the acolytes of their common enemy, Satan, in order to prevent his return to Earth. As interesting as the plot may sound, the accompanying narrative proves to be somewhat uninteresting with the game itself largely consisting of Dracula accomplishing lots of fetch quest missions like tracking down the acolytes, their servants, or special items. He will also be able to travel to the past through certain time portal altars and visit his castle in order to reacquire his old powers and other items important to his quest. The story is rather unclear and vague for quite some time with regards to explaining how and why Dracula is able to travel through time and why both old and new enemy creatures in his castle are even attacking him to begin with. Even the game's ending was surprisingly simple and straightforward, providing very little of a resolution to Dracula's cursed existence. To summarise, the story for Lords of Shadow 2 had its moments, but I felt it was largely a missed opportunity and think they could have done so much more with it. Fortunately, most of the other gameplay elements in Lords of Shadow 2 fare better than its story.The combat has actually improved a bit compared to the previous games. Dracula's main weapon is the Shadow Whip, which works pretty much the same as the Combat Crosses and other whip-like weapons in the earlier games, allowing Dracula to attack enemies with strong direct attacks or area attacks that hit multiple surrounding enemies. His two other weapons are the Void Sword and the Chaos Claws. Much like the use of Light and Shadow Magic in the previous games, these weapons run on magic meters and therefore can't be used indefinitely, making them more tactical abilities. The Void Sword drains health from enemies it strikes and transfers it to Dracula, and it can unleash ice attacks that freeze enemies in their tracks. The Chaos Claws can be used to burn through enemy shields and armor, and they're the strongest weapons in the game, although they also require you to get really up close and personal with enemies. Mastering the many different combos and abilities of all three weapons by using them repeatedly upgrades the weapons' strengths. The Void Sword and Chaos Claws are also needed in order to advance by using them to do such things like freezing waterfalls so they can be climbed and burning through chains to cause the platforms they're holding to drop down. Dracula has some secondary weapons/abilities to aid him further in his quest: Shadow Daggers to attack enemies from a distance, a Bat Swarm to disorient and distract enemies, and a Mist Form that allows him to phase through gates and avoid enemy attacks (these abilities can be combined with the Void Sword and Chaos Claws to unleash newer abilities and attacks). A large collection of special item relics add temporary buffs and abilities to Dracula: one temporarily increases his health limit and restores whatever health he may have previously lost, another unlocks all combos/attacks for his weapons for a limited time, and his most powerful relic allows him to transform into a dragon and obliterate all surrounding enemies. His last ability, the Demonic Wings, let Dracula double jump and are necessary to advance through the last quarter of the game, as well as in acquiring the majority of the game's collectibles.Dracula, being a vampire and all, can even grab weakened enemies and drain their blood to regenerate some health before ripping them apart. His standard physical abilities have also improved compared to when he was in his human form as Gabriel Belmont. He can jump from high ledges and land without suffering damage, he can climb along grapple points much more quickly and fluidly, he has a quicker dodge move, and he can sustain more damage than ever before. The previously mentioned collectibles largely consist of gems that increase Dracula's health and magic, and others unlock challenges that can be accessed in the Chupacabras' shop (where experience points can be used to purchase more gems and art work). The challenges consist of Dracula killing enemies while completing other tasks like not using his Void or Chaos powers, or killing a certain number of enemies in a set amount of time. Many of the collectibles require you having to revisit previous locations in order to get to them with the appropriate upgrades (mainly Mist Form and Demonic Wings), but the actual backtracking can be a bit of a challenge itself. Dracula's castle and the city are both very large areas made up of different wings/districts and it's easy to lose one's way. Dracula can use Map Rooms located in different areas of the castle and city to teleport to other Map Rooms and make backtracking less time consuming. Fortunately, aside from increasing Dracula's health and magic, the collectibles are all optional and finding them all doesn't unlock anything like secret cutscenes or bosses.The enemies Dracula faces provide consistent challenges, but largely because they are rather unbalanced. A number of enemies, even the weaker ones, are able to block many of Dracula's attacks; they also tend to spam unblockable charge attacks, which can be incredibly annoying. Due to this combination of many enemies always blocking and using unblockable attacks, as well as constantly swarming you, makes it rather difficult to pull off some of the more complicated and powerful attacks with the Void Sword and Chaos Claws. It's not impossible, but it does take a lot of work to find the right opening to use some specialized attacks. At times it feels like the game is pushing you to rely solely on using counterattacks to damage enemies. The different enemy types are less numerous compared to the ones in previous games, but that doesn't make them any less challenging. The returning monster enemies include skeletons, harpies, and vampires, and the rest are demons of the small, medium, and large variety. There are even soldiers in mechanical exoskeletons and mechs that can be irritating to fight in large numbers, and of course there are Dracula's previous allies, the soldiers, clerics, and paladins of the Brotherhood of Light. The bosses are the high points of the enemy encounters, with many of them providing tough but fair challenges. The final boss is also appropriately challenging, but far from impossible. Quick-time events make a return and are just as well executed as before.Replacing the puzzles from the previous games are the highly controversial stealth segments. In most cases, Dracula has to avoid being spotted by enemies and go into shadowy spots so he can transform into a rat, which in turn allows him to go through air vents and other small openings so he can reach normally inaccessible areas. He can also sneak up behind unaware enemies and possess them so he can unlock certain doors. I personally didn't hate these stealth segments and some of them took some time to figure out. HOWEVER...one specific stealth segment was incredibly frustrating. It involves Dracula sneaking through a garden maze and trying to reach the other end without being spotted by its guardian. If Dracula gets caught, the guardian will pierce him with his spear and instantly transport him to the beginning of the garden maze. Furthermore, stepping on any leaves, which are almost completely covering the floor, will give away Dracula's position and the guardian will be on him in seconds. I and many other gamers could have done without this horribly designed stealth segment, so those who haven't experienced it yet should prepare themselves. One general criticism about the stealth segments involves those cyborg enemies that Dracula always has to sneak past: I felt that Dracula should have been able to fight them directly at some point instead of having to always avoid them even towards the end of the game when he has become more powerful, it would have just made more sense.The DLC for Lords of Shadow 2, Revelations, lets you take the role of Alucard and experience what he was doing behind the scenes before Dracula awoke from his deep slumber. The entirety of Revelations, except the very ending, takes place in Dracula's castle in the past where Alucard must acquire and safeguard Dracula's Void and Chaos powers so his father can reach them himself in due time. Alucard explores new areas of the castle and fights pretty much the same Brotherhood soldiers, vampires, harpies, skeletons, and jailers that Dracula faces in the main game, with a couple of newer varations thrown in there. The final boss is the only truly new enemy, and not only is he appropriately challenging, he also shines some new light on Alucard's eventual role in the main game. Alucard has his own collection of weaponry and powers to deal with his enemies and advance through the castle. His sword, the Crissaegrim, is his main form of offense and has a decent array of combos and abilities for Alucard to utilize against his enemies. The Crissaegrim is forged from the shards of the ice sword Glaciem and the fire sword Igneas, granting it similar magic-based abilities as Dracula's Void Sword and Chaos Claws, namely draining health from enemies and freezing them (Glaciem) and burning through their defenses for greater damage (Igneas). Alucard's secondary abilities are crucial to advancing through the castle and solving the rather challenging puzzles that make a return from the previous games (no stealth segments this time for those of you who detested them in the main game). His abilities are the Bat Cloud, which lets Alucard transform himself into a cluster of bats and dash to distant grapple points in a flash; Timeless Vision, which lets Alucard temporarily rebuild specific ruined portions of the castle in order to reach new areas; and the ability for Alucard's spirit to leave his physical body in the form of a Spectral Wolf that can phase through gates and hazards, as well as jump greater distances to get to out of reach areas. Alucard can also make use of the same item relics as Dracula in the main game, except for the Talisman of the Dragon. Collectibles that increase Alucard's health and magic litter the castle and can be reached at the player's convenience, though some are tricky to find. Revelations was a pretty good DLC, if a bit on the short side.When all is said and done, Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 is not a bad game, but it's not a great game either, and it's definitely lacking compared to the first Lords of Shadow and especially Mirror of Fate (the best game in the series, in my opinion). While I still find the game to be good enough to earn 4 stars, it's on the lower end of the 4 star spectrum. If I were to grade this game on a 10 point scale, it would get a 7 or a 7.5. Some gamers might be kept busy by the unlockable challenges even after completing the main game, though I personally found many of the challenges to be too frustrating to bother with. Fans of the previous Lords of Shadow games might want to wait for the price to drop to the $30 range before getting this game, and the same pretty much goes for fans of adventure games or the hack and slash genre. Again, this is a pretty good game, it just doesn't excel at anything it does and isn't worth a full price purchase.

Castlevania is one of those iconic series in video games which saw its heyday in previous generations (with, generally speaking, the best game in the series being Castelvania: Symphony of the Night on PS1).  The first Castlevania:  LOS game did breath new, fresh air into this series.It is a shame then that, instead of building on the success of this game, that the developers tried to borrow from so many other successful games and turn this game into a middling, inconsistent frustration of a title.Don't get me wrong, when CLOS2 is good, it is GREAT.  Stunning looking vistas and areas.  Diverse combat, whether it's your main weapon (whip) or sub weapons which use magic (ala God of War).  In fact, this game might as well been the 5th GOW title, so much is cribbed from it.So well, where does this game fall apart?- MANDATORY stealth sections.  You're playing as a bad-a** Dracula, so why, exactly, do you need to SNEAK by enemies undetected, when you have all that firepower at your disposal?  Castlevania is NOT Splinter Cell or Thief.  It has ALWAYS been an action game, throughout all its titles.  Not only does it manage to break any flow in the game, but they are poorly executed.  In one section alone, I was stuck for THREE HOURS trying to figure out how to get by it.  That's both poor game design and poor choices.- I might be wrong, but I'm pretty sure in Transylvaina, you are not seeing robots, androids and the like.  What in the world are those things doing in a Castlevaina game?  Ghosts, zombies and other supernatural things, yes.  Data, KOS-MOS, type characters, no.- It's short.  Paying $60 for a game that will last you, on average, 10-15 hours, in this day in age, simply is not a smart investment.So I'm sorry, all the 5 stars reviews in the world should not convince you to spend $60 on this game.  I guess it will be up to you to decide who is right:  All those reviews, or the current 62 score the game has on Metacritic, from people who do video game reviews for a living.This game very much could have been one of the best Castlevaina's, especially with the combat.  But the uninspiring story, wonky stealth sections, and short length simply put this game in Simon's Quest territory:  Decent try, but simply not good enough.

For starters, I liked Lord of Shadows 2, but I didn't love it. There was nothing about the game that really annoyed me, but I was always waiting for that missing piece to "pull me in", as so to speak. I don't necessarily agree with all of the criticism that's been aimed at this game, but one overall point has been pretty much unanimous - it's not as good as the first LOS.Combat - I'll attempt to make an analogy here. How would you feel if you had a brand new sports car, but you weren't allowed to take it on the freeway to see what it could REALLY do? Well, that's how I feel about the combat in LOS 2. There are so many interesting combos and attacks to purchase, but don't expect to be able to use many of them. Unlike the last game, it's a free roaming camera, and I initially thought that was great. However, it'll be used against you. While engaging in battle, you better keep your head on a swivel! You'll be in mid combo, when all of the sudden, someone will come behind you and break up your combat attempt. The other issue is that most of the enemies are heavily armoured, or have some type of protective shield. You'll need to get very creative when attacking some of these enemies, and it gets pretty old. Here's my formula when judging combat: If I look forward to fighting bad guys, that means the combat is pretty fun. If I cringe at the sheer thought of having to fight a room full of enemies, that means there's a problem. With LOS 2, it was the latter. Like I said, you'll be presented with a boatload of fancy combos, but you won't be able to pull off most of them.Weaponry - I actually enjoyed the weapons, and I felt they were all completely different from each other. The main weapon is the blood whip, and Its formed from Dracula's own blood. There are two other weapons, created from ice and fire, respectively. The ice weapon (a sword) actually replenishes your health with every successful strike, and I think that's pretty neat. The fire weapon (chaos claws) can be used to penetrate armour, but the meter runs out much too quickly. There are a couple other secondary weapons, but I didn't use them for much of anything. I thought the weaponry was nice (if only the combat equaled the weapons).Enemies - Wow, maybe the first game set the standards too high? You know what, I'm going to start with a good aspect first. The boss battles were freaking phenomenal!!! Dare I say the boss fights were better than the first game, and that's saying a lot. During the last 2 or 3 hours or so of the game, I swear there were 5 or 6 boss battles, and they all felt like they were back to back (which is a good thing, by the way). I don't want to leave the impression that the non-boss bad guys were subpar, because they really weren't. It's just that the bar has been set so high, so I had unrealistic expectations I suppose. Many of them looked the same, and they were all kinda uninspiring. The boss battles are the meat and potatoes of LOS 2, trust me.Miscellaneous - Haha, I almost completed the review without addressing the most polarizing featuring of the game - The stealth missions. I'm in the minority here, I absolutely loved these! These were the closest thing to a puzzle that the game had to offer. Stealth missions probably made up less than 5% of the game, so they're not really that big of a deal. I enjoyed them because they were a fun change of pace. This is more of an open world game than it's predecessor, so there's definitely some exploration to be had. I really took my time, and I finished right at the 34 hour mark, very similar to LOS 1.I know my review may have had somewhat of a negative undertone to it, but I did enjoy my experience, for the most part. There are quite a few neat elements to the game. But I had to deduct a star because there was no it factor (and the difficult combat didn't help). Please understand this is the kind of game that takes a looooong time before it starts rolling. If you're patient and open to change, you'll definitely like this one. The problem being, when I pre-order a game, I expect to love it, not just like it. I refuse to give a 5 star rating to a game that lacks that all important 'it factor'. Dante's Inferno, you're up next!

As a long-standing (and very dedicated) fan of the Castlevania series - the reviews that preceded the release of this game did little to deter me from purchasing it. And if you're an avid fan as well, then I would say the same can probably be true for you.However if you're considering whether to buy this new or are just not the type of person to pickup a Castlevania game simply b/c there's a new one - then the following is for you.While the overall story arc is a continuation of the very awesome LOS, and the basic action oriented gameplay is the same...there are a couple of very real issues in this here sequel that keep it from being as good as the last one. And while I am usually hesitant to give any credence to the usually overly-thoughtout professional critiques of any game - this time they're generally right.The gameplay keeps with the basic GOW style that the first LOS established, but takes the "clone" aspect to the place where it's a straight up copy. If you played the latest entry in the GOW then you've played this. You can upgrade the three preset weapons you have via a basic skill tree from XP gained in combat. The new moves you get would be cool - if you could use any of them. I had this complaint with the first one as well, as both the enemy AI and the sheer amount of them this time around makes skilled combat almost impossible. You're going to be mashing the crap out of the primary attack button a lot more than you'd like.The "open world" also really isn't that open, but it's def a step up from the previous linear setup. It's NOT even close to Symphony of the Night. It's just a bunch of backtracking to get a life/magic bar gem or two, but at least there's a level of exploration.I've also heard folks complain about the way the game missed out on the opportunity to use a more "modern day" setting. And while usually those kinds of complaints are "nitpicking" in my opinion, in this case it's true. The backdrops/stage settings for this really do lack that Castlevania flair and are about as generic as possible. The original LOS nailed that. And while graphically there are some cool moments, you can't help but get bored with the types of things you've seen in everything from Resident Evil to GOW. If deserted alley ways with garbage cans, and overly complicated lava bridges are your thing...well then prepare to have your cup run over.And the "stealth" aspects are as bad as everybody says. In addition to making absolutely no sense (i.e. Dracula can take down a whole army of enemies…some of which are way bigger than he is but still needs to sneak around certain ones?) towards the end they get frustrating as all get out. It's also just another mechanic to get you to "do something," but serves no purpose.And outside of generic "pretty much everything" I think that's one of my biggest complaints about this game. Most of the time the mechanics are thrown in just to increase playtime. For instance, you'll sometimes have to switch between the current modern setting and "the past" via a series of portals that you stand on. Which would be fine if you didn't have to activate the portal and then walk over to somewhere else on screen, then walk through this weird dream phase and then walk out of it. It's well past the point in time in game development where should be able to just stand on the portal and be done with it. It's just padding.And this ties into the fact that for the first time ever you're playing Dracula in a Castlevania game…which should be awesome. But outside of the first few minutes - just isn't. Does the Prince of Darkness really have to climb up old beams to get somewhere? Really? I mean that makes for a great Uncharted/Tomb Raider mechanic…but here it's just silly.Now all that aside - the overall story is great (the execution leaves much to be desired) and it's not a "bad" action game pound for pound. But it's not special, and there's so much about the experience that's just too generic and/or contrived to make this worth it. I am really glad that there are Castlevania fans out there that are loving this game, but for me this is the literally definition of mediocre.And if you're trying to figure out if this game is worth it - honestly I could have given this a miss and been better off. If you're not die-hard Castlevania fan then there's nothing LOS2 has that will make it worth your time/money. Unless you've got an unlimited supply of both.

Let me start my review by saying I am a huge Castlevania fan, and I, like many, had high hopes for the sequel of the critically acclaimedCastlevania Lords of Shadow. This summarizes what I believe is the main problem of this sequel, the first one was so great and well written that we all expected something at least similar to the original. And this is where Mercury Steam failed to deliver.The following paragraphs may contain spoilers for the original Lords of Shadow, however, I am NOT including spoilers for Lords of Shadow 2.A lot of the criticism has gone to the stealth sections of the game, but the problems in Lords of Shadow 2 go beyond than that. The opening scene of the game (wisely selected to be the demo) shows you in an amazing sequence the vampiric powers Gabriel acquired at the end of Lords of Shadow. However, as the game starts in the present day (after a lengthy cut scene that resumes Lords of Shadow and Mirror of fate), you are immediately stripped of such powers and have to regain them... in your castle. Lords of Shadow 2 uses a quite silly plot device (if we could call it that) so you can travel from the present time to your castle, nothing of this is explained nor makes any sense. As the story progresses characters who died in the prior game reappear, but it is not explained how such thing would be possible, are they a vision? Are they ghosts? Are they memories? Who knows? But it sure helps having them around so they can conveniently explain what you have to do or where you have to go. Which leads me to another problem I have with the game, Gabriel is pretty much reduced to an errand boy who does not question or hesitate to follow orders, from anyone, even characters that, if you played the last game, you know should not be trusted.The infamous stealth sections aren't really that bad, but it is clear they are there to indulge whoever came up with them at the development stage. Imagine this scenario: you fight a boss on the top of a train with full use of your abilities, you defeat him and arrive to the next station, and then you have to turn into a rat to evade 3 security guards (fighting is not an option, the game forces you to stealth though these sections) Like this, there are many other similar situations in which the game forces you to do things that really don't make any sense, like hiding from a character in a library (otherwise you are killed on sight) only to fight that very same character in the next room as a boss battle. Bottom line, in an attempt to make the gameplay varied, they sacrificed having a consistent story told in LOS2.At a graphic level, LOS2 is also disappointing. There is a big difference between the design of the castle stages and the present day Castlevania City (that is what it's called) All the scenery in the castle is simply stunning, the amount of detail is noticeable, something that does not happen with the city settings, whatever may be the reason for this (perhaps the leaked information about a troubled development is true?), it does not help the game either. Something I am surprised no one has mentioned (at least on the reviews I checked) is how pixelated many sequences of the game are, especially towards the end, there are a couple boss battles that I honestly thought were pixelated on purpose as a homage to the NES games, but of course that was not the case. This problem is more noticeable in sequences with bright lights, but happens so often near the end of the game that is just too distracting.The game also offers an upgrade system that in my opinion, is not rewarding at all. Whatever upgrades you may buy, they are barely noticeable. I pretty much played through the whole game with the basic weapons and had no issues at all. The upgraded powers you acquire are similar to the first game in the sense that many of the items and upgrades you find throughout the story are only reachable when you acquire those new skills. I am not joking here, you acquire the full powers almost near the end of the game. Do they really want you to backtrack the whole game to find those upgrades when you are 3 bosses away from ending the game? You may want to try it if you want to replay those stages but you certainly don't need to, I didn't and was successfully able to defeat the last bosses without them.  How so? The battles in the game are unbalanced to a point beyond frustration. There are maps where enemies will be thrown at you that require a lot to do to kill them (like huge demons or the big mechas... yeah, Dracula fights mechas in this game), which is pretty much an impossible task to do when you have other big enemies attacking you. On the other hand, if you master the power to become mist, you can pretty much defeat any boss in this game if you time your powers right. The mist power makes Gabriel invincible when used, so you can literally stand in front of any enemy hitting them and turning into mist when they are about to hit you to prevent damage.In all honesty, I really wanted to like this game and I would lie if I said I did not enjoy playing some bits of it, but it is nowhere near as good as the first Lords of Shadow. If you like Castlevania games you will definitely want to play this one, my recommendation? Wait for a price drop (though it seems to be dropping price rapidly) otherwise, there may be better hack n' slash games out there for you to try, like the first Lords of Shadow or any game in the God of War saga.

(Forgive my gushing...)I will preface by saying that I found the original Lords of Shadow to be an unexpectedly good game. The reviews ranged from middling to outright hostile. Upon playing initially I thought it would turn out to be a mediocre God of War clone and didn't think much of the first few levels I played. But upon progressing the story and gameplay only got more captivating. By the time I had reached completion and it's grandiose twist ending some 20+ hours later I knew that I had just experienced a true modern classic.Mirror of Fate was the Nintendo DS follow up (later ported to HD) that detailed the Belmont clan's  subsequent struggles and eventual defeat of Dracula. It was meant to be the Act II of the series and was pretty decent in it's own right but not on the same technical or story level as the original. Fast forward four years and Mercury Steam has at long last brought us a proper conclusion to the LOS saga. And I am happy to say that it doesn't disappoint.LOS2 continues where MOF left off. Dracula awakens in a near future steam punk city built upon the ruins of his castle that the game dubs Castlevania City. Weakened and defeated, Lord Dracula is a pale remnant of his former self content to wallow in self loathing in an abandoned cathedral. Until a former member of his knightly brotherhood (in life) turned traitor, comes back to inform him that Satan and his minions are poised to once again take over and dominate the earth. Zobek, voiced by the indomitable Patrick Stewart, recruits Dracula by offering him the one thing that no one else can seemingly grant him... an end to his miserable immortal existence. What follows is a long drawn out battle between the forces of darkness and the Prince of Darkness himself Lord Dracula.First off it needs to be said that this game is visually stunning. The game engine has been completely revamped and improved to allow for full 3D camera control and somehow manages to keep it's high quality graphics running smoothly. I experienced no slow down or bugs in my 8+ hours of gameplay so far. Some rough textures here and there but that's about it. The soundtrack is top notch and beautifully orchestrated and the voice acting is still done by top tier actors who give performances worthy of any film production let alone video game. Gabriel/Dracula in particular is a haunted nuanced character whose regrets over the past really shine through without coming off as overly dramatic or campy.The combat while largely the same as last time around, is as fun as ever. It's focused and intense with a huge set of moves and skillsets that improve steadily as you play. Instead of the linear progression we had with the last game this one is a free roam sandbox style romp that actually encourages exploration of the striking and varied locales.The boss battles that I have experienced thus far have been nothing short of magnificent and the game is full of action set pieces and cut scenes that keep the pace flowing nicely. The art and level design is bar none the best I have seen in this cycle of consoles and you can really tell that the designers poured their hearts and souls into creating it.I don't understand the negativity that the so-called professional gaming sites out there have leveled towards this game. It's as if they don't know what to make of grandiose games that actually take the time to present a meaningful story. Yet they will lavish praise on every generic Call of Dutyesque shooter that comes their way. Paid industry trolls IMHO. No matter. Lords of Shadow 2 is a fantastic game and worthy conclusion to an epic storyline. It's also a wonderful swan song for this outgoing cycle of consoles that displays both technical and literary brilliance. To pass this one up would be denying yourself one of the best games of this generation.

I think it looks kind of Neo-Gothic, not unlike DMC or any of the games in that series.What you are getting is an incredibly well made brawler with amazing fight controls. That is the only reason this game is a 4 out of 5. After completing those segments of the game, the stealth sections of the map become open for both combat and exploration. This allows you to pour hours into finding every relic and collectible you can.

In the highly unlikely event that you're unaware, Nintendo makes these games about an Italian plumber named Mario. They usually involve running from left to right to save a Princess and things of that nature. New Super Mario Bros. 2 is another game like that. It's really fun. You should buy it.New Super Mario Bros. 2 might look like New Super Mario Bros. Wii, but make no mistake, it doesn't really play all that much like it. The graphics are a deception. When it comes to gameplay, NSMB2 is like a return to form, in many respects.One of the best features of Super Mario Bros. 3 and Super Mario World is Mario's ability to fly. Nintendo really nailed good gameplay in those games with the Super Leaf and Cape Feather, respectively. In New Super Mario Bros. 2, the Super Leaf makes a return, and it's GREAT. There's nothing quite like flying Mario high up into the air to look for hidden secrets.Another great improvement over the previous game would be the boss fights. These new boss fights are closer to being on par with Super Mario World than those in the Wii game were. The enemies have some pretty creative attacks, and often make use of the elements associated with their world (e.g. Wendy Koopa, boss of the water world, causes water to cover the screen and make Mario swim while he dodges her attacks.).NSMB2 is pretty easy, to me anyway. However, it would probably be a good challenge for someone who has never played a 2D Mario game. But that doesn't really matter, because there's much more to do in this game besides just saving the Princess. The game's main staying power comes from finding all of the Star Coins and secret ways out of the levels. Personally, I love doing that kind of stuff. Your mileage may vary.There's also a Coin Rush mode which involves trying to get as many coins as you can in three random levels. You can also purchase brand new DLC courses in this mode. Since the standard game has more than enough levels in it, the ability to purchase additional content feels quite welcome.In summation, NSMB2 feels sufficiently different from the previous NSMB game I'd played. I honestly believe that a lot of hate the game gets is related to its graphics. It's true that the NSMB2 could have used a new art style and some new music, but the gameplay is as good as it's ever been.

After 3 days of playing the game (bass guitar) quite a bit and just finishing my 2nd gig, I've learned that you can NOT learn to play well using this game alone. It's a reasonable tool and is fun, but don't count on this as your only educational source.Cons:1. It didn't teach me how to hold my hands well, the proper way to hold the guitar or sit with the guitar. Watching the videos helped some, but they didn't go over the proper way to pluck, or hold a fret, or where to hold a fret. It wasn't terrible, but it should be a lot better for a beginner. Thank you YouTube!2. The bass line changes every time I restart a song. I think it's trying to adjust my difficulty higher because it thinks I go 80% on the song (which is wrong). It's really aggravating! I want to play the song on the easiest level over and over until I do it well...and to do that I HAVE TO PRACTICE IT. Stop changing it.3. The Interface is so confusing. I've figured it out for the most part now, but it's not intuitive at all. It's slow to get to the things you want to do. Lots of button pushing on the controller and waiting.4. Why does the song disappear in Career mode just because I do ok on it? I need to practice it!5. There needs to be a quick restart for a song. I don't want to have to click X 5 times and re-tune just to play the same song again.6. Tune your bass. Tune it again, tune it again, every 3 minutes you have to tune it again. Ugh....7. Most of the songs are just not that good. They really need to include more classic rock and the riffs that everyone knows.Pros:1. Sometimes you can play a little while you're waiting for something to load. The amp is fired up for you.2. It's fun! Even with the frustrations I list above, it's still fun to try and get better at the songs.3. Multiplayer...though I haven't tried this yet.4.  Tuning: Though I don't like tuning every 3 minutes, the built in tuner is cool.5. Games: I've only played the duck game so far, but I can see these being very useful to find frets without looking for them.6. Techniques: These are cool and fun. If you're like me, you're a fan of fighter games.  This is not only a fighter game, but it's a Marvel fighter game.

Back in 2006, comic book fans were given the supposedly ultimate superhero experience in a game called Marvel: Ultimate Alliance. Though it was not perfect, the game gave us a good taste of what a superhero crossover could be. Even still, it lacked certain Marvel characters that would be fun to play as. Since playing this game, I have always hoped to finally play the truly ultimate Marvel experience. I am here to tell you now that Marvel’s The Avengers: Battle for Earth is unfortunately not that experience.Released for Wii U and Xbox 360, Battle for Earth is a game that attempts to bring the biggest Marvel superheroes together in a fighting game. Though this is a good concept, the game has very little depth and is little more than an expensive iPad game.The game has a story mode, but it is so uninteresting that it might as well have been left out. It is pretty much the story of how the Skrull try to take over the earth by disguising themselves as certain superheroes. The story is told through pictures that look like they came straight out of the comics. Though the story is probably interesting in the actual comics, the way it is carried out in the game is very uninteresting. It eventually got the point where I just skipped the cinematics due to its dullness.The gameplay is very basic. On the Wii U, it is played entirely with touch screen controls. You are given icons on the screen that activate certain attacks. Some of these attacks require you to match certain movements with the stylus. You can also slide the stylus across the screen to avoid attacks from your opponent.…That’s pretty much it.As stated earlier, the gameplay feels very much like an iPad game, except you have to pay $40 for it. There are different modes, such as story mode or tournament mode, but even these do not stray too far from each other. It really stinks too, considering that a fighting game with Marvel characters sounds like a really cool idea.You can unlock characters in the game. The game features about 20 different characters to play as. One would think that considering how simple the gameplay is, it would be easy to add as many different characters as possible. Sadly, the character roster does not expand far beyond the Avengers, Spider-Man, and some X-Men. Not only is this unfortunate, but some of the characters they chose seem inappropriate for a basic roster. Why would they have an obscure character like Spider-Woman when they could have had a more popular character like Mr. Fantastic or Deadpool*? Or villains like Venom who aren’t even related to the Avengers?I understand that Spider-Man and some of the X-men become Avengers in the comics eventually, but it still seems off that they stop there, especially since many more Marvel characters become Avengers, too. If they are going to limit their character roster, it might as well feature the most popular superheroes. Not characters that require more advanced comic book knowledge to know.There are some pluses to the game, particularly the fact that you can unlock costumes for certain characters. The Avengers movie costumes are a really nice touch to the game and almost make the rest of the mediocrity worth it. It is a shame, however, that some of these costumes have to be purchased instead of unlocked.The graphics are okay, although they are not exactly impressive. They feature a cel-shaded look to them which makes them look very much like a comic book. For some reason, however, they do not look nearly as interesting as other cel-shaded games like Sly Cooper or The Wind Waker. The cel-shaded look when mixed with more realistic-looking characters just does not seem that appealing.The sound really is not much better. In fact, it is worse. The voice acting in and of itself is not bad. However, when you hear the same lines a hundred times after a few fights, you start to really hate the acting. Seriously, if I hear the background voice say “Launcher!” one more time, I think I am going to explode.In the end, Marvel’s The Avengers: Battle for Earth is a half-baked game with little going on that is actually interesting. If this game was a $5-10 eShop (or Xbox Live) game, I might have actually recommended it. The gameplay, though very shallow, might actually entertain you for a few hours, and the character costumes are pretty neat extras. But as a $40 retail game, it is just not worth it. If you are looking for more games for your Wii U library, I could recommend several others that would be better for you. And for those who are looking for the true Marvel experience… go play Lego Marvel Superheroes.…No, seriously. Go play Lego Marvel. Now.Final Score: 6.6/10

I spent a lot of time ignoring missions and just doing my own thing until I got tired of it and got back on point. I'm not big on simulator games, but I have to imagine this portion of the game is rewarding to the type of person who digs those tycoon type of games.Of course in addition to all of that is the absolutely stunning naval battles.  Just like everyone else, I enjoyed every chance I could get to board my ship and start sinking the heck out of Redcoats.  And the quest for Captain Kidd's treasure just sweetened the naval deal.  Lots of fun to be had here, and it just makes the pirate based Assassin's Creed: Black Flag look that much more appealing.Graphics wise, I thought the game looked great.  I can't compare it to the other big boy consoles as I've never owned them, but for a Nintendo boy like myself, they were more than fine and better than we're used to.  I know there's been a bit of problem with glitches and whatnot, but what little weird glitches I ran into really didn't bother me too much. There was a floating bear here, a disappearing deer there, but nothing that really took away from my experience playing the game.A couple of things that may bug some people:  I don't know, maybe I'm not the expert gamer that some people are, but some of the stealthier missions come across as a little difficult because the bad guys seem to notice you no mater what you do.  That could just be player caused, but it seemed to happen a lot.  I ended up getting into huge group fights more often than not.Also, the beginning of the game rewards the patient.  It is several hours (or at least seems like it) before the game opens up.  Thankfully, this portion of the game is fun to play and it gets you used to the style of play the Assassin's games seem to be known for.  You also get to play as the swarthy Haytham, who is a much more fun character than Connor to spend time with.Of course I have to make a mention of off screen play with the Wii U Gamepad.  It seems some people find the Gamepad to be a useless add on, but I'm digging it for the simple things it does.  Having the map on the gamepad is a simple yet effective use of the controller.  And the off screen play is very cool for a guy like me with wife and kids.  Thanks to that one feature, it took me half the time completing the game being able to still play while the TV screen itself is dominated by Curious George and the X-Factor.All in all, a very pleasing experience.  It's a big game with a lot of stuff to do and keep you occupied.  I wish the rewards for some of these tasks were a little more hefty, but it was still fun to do.  The story is cool and the gameplay is simple enough for non-hardcore gamer and satisfying enough for everyone.  I really dug the game and if a lot of people are right and it's not as good as the second game in the series, I can't wait to play that one.

I've been playing Zombi U for the better part of a month since I got it for Christmas, and I must say I'm really not sure I'm playing the same game as many people who are giving it five stars.To begin, I am willing to give any game a chance, despite it's difficulties and shortcomings. To be fair, Zombi U has an entertaining premise, great atmosphere including the music and sound design, and a compelling story with the prepper being one of the best good guys you love to hate. BUT THIS GAME IS BROKEN!Never in my almost 40 years of electronic gaming have I experienced such a glaring collection of poor mechanics and programming. I'm not the best gamer but I'm persistent, and when I decide I'm going to conquer a game, I usually do, but Zombi U is too fractured to mend no matter how many times you start over. Poor positioning of controls, lack of configurability and a host of other issues is totally unforgivable.Anyone who has raged over this game must be thinking the same thing; "Is Ubisoft trying to punish gamers or give them a memorable challenge?" I'm starting to wonder, and keep in mind as you read this I'm not even playing in survivor mode yet!It's not easy to accept one's destiny to reincarnate over and over (at least your primary firearm retains it's upgrades), however I did, and was enjoying it for a little while, till it's shortcomings revealed themselves. I am quick to believe this game was just not ready for release, or they simply did not care in the end. Updates should have fixed some of the issues, but well into the game's second year of it's life cycle, the fact these issues are still finding their way into the experience is truly sad.Some of the more frustrating problems for me include the run button being L3. This works for other controllers but not the game pad, as L and LZ are right underneath it. If we had the option of switching to the Pro Controller it might be a different story, but this is a gamepad only game. To effectively run you have to remember to hold your index finger just underneath L so you don't accidentally hit LZ. And how about some kind of stamina meter? You can't run forever but it might be nice to know if you can run at all after you've exhausted yourself from a wave of undead.Another big problem I have is the timing required for Melee attacks with the stick. It's all about getting LZ and LR in sync and when you've just wasted precious seconds to switch from your depleted firearm, often you end up being Zombi food if you're being overwhelmed. This makes interaction with the game pad and actually PLAYING the game, glaringly counterproductive. This doesn't even include the fact that you cannot invert axis on the gamepad view as well. Some might not find this important considering targeting is done with the gamepad's gyroscope, but I think it should have been implemented to make switching between the two views less uncomfortable. In other words, not everybody is going to hold up the game pad to look around every time! I am one of those idiots from the old flight simulator days that believes when you pull back on a stick, you should look up, not down.Anyway, so you're dead, no big deal, right? WRONG. Because if you're in the final chapter of the game, and you happen to cash in one too many times, Zombi U has this wonderful way of setting you back by way of removing your shortcuts! This was what happened on my first play through, and why I decided to start completely over. I'm sorry however that I gave this game another chance because of what happened next: the game glitched out in one of the safe rooms in Buckingham Palace.Just before you get to the flaming scaffolds there is a small door in the wall with the key code written in blood. I had no problems with this room on my first play through, but on the second, once I got in there I literally could do nothing but move the outside camera around, or quit! Of course once you quit, all your progress is lost, so for the next 10 minutes I tried EVERYTHING! I moved the game pad every possible direction, I pushed every button, I went to the option screen, I switched over to Miiverse for help, I prayed to Baby Jesus Fetus, BUT I GOT NOWHERE! All I got was that stupid camera staring blindly at the door in which my current game was hidden on the other side. So I quit Zombi U.... for good.I've read many reviews of this game, and most gave it positive marks, which is why I'm wondering if I'm playing the same game they did? First assumptions would be that the poor quality of this game indicates that it was rushed to launch and they have no desire to fix it because people aren't buying it. Something else tells me that they just tightened up the game to make it challenging in lieu of content. That worked in the old 8 bit days when storage and memory limitations were part of the reason why games were so hard. But at least they didn't leave you at a dead end.Because of Zombi U, Ubisoft has lost me as a consumer of their products. Any future releases from them will be avoided, and I'm tempted to take note of the creators of this game as well, so as to know who's making the games I might be spending my hard earned money on, or not.Ultimately I really wanted to like this game, yet I can't say I've hated any other game as much as I do Zombi U.

The game that got me to purchase the first Playstation back in the day was "Resident Evil". My fiancee and I picked up a Wii U shortly after Christmas and we have had blast with it so far.  I am amazed at the prices Amazon is offering on some of the games and ZombiU was no exception.  At $23 this title is an absolute must have.This is the first title I have played on the Wii U that makes full use of the Gamepad functionality.  Whether scanning an area for items of interest, setting markers on your map, managing inventory, or blipping the radar, the Gamepad integration is natural and fun.  I am really impressed with this aspect of the gameplay.Aside from the Gamepad functions the game controls and plays like most other first person shooters, but most would be quick to point out that this game is a survival horror game - not your typical FPS.  I would tend to agree.  Having never played any of the Resident Evil series, this was my first foray into the survival horror genre and so far I like it.  There is very little music, and the dark atmospheres and sudden sound effects add to the spookiness.As several others have mentioned, your character becomes infected when you die and you must retrieve your equipment from your now zombie-fied character.  This is a really cool aspect of the game.  The game tracks your longest lifetime and your best survivor stats - death is inevitable in this game, and I was uncomfortable with this at first, being used to other shooters where tons of ammo, and a run & gun approach can get you far.  This game rewards patience and care, and even the most cautious players will lose a few survivors in the process.I have three complaints about this game that have cost it a fifth star. 1) The environments are so dark that if there is any glare in my den, it is impossible to discern anything on screen.  I understand this comes with the territory but it has lead to some frustrating deaths in the heat of the moment when trying to find doors and access points while running away.  2) The aiming is really flighty.  It can be adjusted in the options but as another reviewer mentioned, the ideal option would be the ability to adjust horizontal and vertical sensitivity independently.  One gets used to it, but again, in the heat of the moment ammo is too precious to be missing shots.  3) The graphics while certainly not bad are on par with the last gen's graphics.  I have been blown away by the smooth HD graphics on other games such as Super Mario 3D World and The Wonderful 101, but I feel like this title falls a little short of the mark here.  The graphics are adequate but they fail to really impress.Overall I would recommend this game for shooter fans at the standard retail price, but at Amazon's $20-25 price point I think this is a must-have for any mature Wii U player.

I I can't believe this game got such negative press reviews.  I'm not sure what game they were playing, but this certainly is a gem of a title.  This is survival horror in its truest form.  I love games like RE1, 2 and 3, Fatal Frame, Kuon, and Haunting Ground.  Unfortunately the survival horror genre doesn't really live up to its name anymore, containing run-and-gun action adventure shooters with maybe some atmosphere and creepy stuff thrown in.  ZombiU is a rare exception. It's not all that creepy, but it doesn't hold your hand and there are few second chances for each unlucky survivor.You wake up as a randomly generated survivor, with little background information (name and occupation only).  You could be male or female, and things like hair, features, and race are random.  ZombiU features perma-death.  Once your survivor dies, you wake up as a different survivor in the base holding only a gun, a few bullets, a flashlight and a cricket bat.  Key items and weapon upgrades are retained, but any weapons other than the basic handgun that the previous survivor was holding will have to be retrieved.  To get your gear back you must go back to where your previous survivor died and kill their zombie.  Each survivor can build up weapon skills, but these skills are not passed on when you die.  Each time you die you will receive a score which goes on the leaderboard.  Your score is based on weapon skills, number of kills, etc.  In story mode, your progress is retained, you just pick up with a different survivor.You can survive a few hits but one bite and you're dead (until you get the Virucide shot, which gives you one chance to stab a zombie before it bites you and instantly kill it).There is a metal container in the base where you can store some items that will remain there even if you die.  I like to leave found weapons, ammo, land mines and large medipacks there for when I really need them, since anything you carry has the potential for being permanently lost.You will not end up significantly stronger later on, and the game doesn't get easier.  You have to plan, conserve, and strategize.  Most enemies will not drop anything when you kill them.  Some might only drop one handgun round or a tiny health boost.  If you get overrun and have no way out or no ammo, you're probably dead.  If you have no patience, this game is not for you.  If you're one of those casual gamers who only plays shooters and sports games, chances are this will frustrate you very quickly.  If you're an old school survival horror fan, give it a try - you will probably love it!I only gave this 4 stars because amazon doesn't have a 4.5 option.  It's not a perfect game - though the gamepad works pretty well, it can be clunky at times.  The game doesn't pause when you loot, and sometimes trying desperately to swipe the gamepad to close the backpack (or BOB - Bug-Out Bag) doesn't work right (I found out you can solve this by moving the control stick backwards to close the BOB).  Sometimes you can't swing the cricket bat because you hit the button ever so slightly too early and the animation didn't fully reset, resulting in death.  However these are small complaints and can be worked around with some practice.  Sometimes zombies walking up angled planks or on the edge of things causes them to walk on air, but it doesn't happen often.  Don't let the critic reviews fool you - this is a wonderful game.  If you have a Wii U and love survival horror, don't miss ZombiU!

You won't find literary gold nor deep narrative here (only the shallowest post-Occupy references hint any kind of attempt), but you will get a solid survival horror experience. I did encounter a bug once (crouched to go through a crack in a wall, all controls disabled, and I had to re-load), but I didn't experience any of the serious game-breaking experiences described by others. I'm mostly interested in the game's willingness to learn from Demon's Souls and to apply some of its lessons to a classic survival horror environment. The lack of narrative depth is a serious handicap for a game that had the atmosphere and mechanics to deliver one (if we're already compulsively searching for survival gear, why not throw some bones?). Somewhere between The Last Of Us's narrative and this game's mechanics, there is a new standard waiting to be set. In my opinion, it's an all around better experience than Dead Island, too--that game didn't know what it wanted other than a big map and algorithmic mechanics.

"ZombiU" effectively captures exactly what survival horror fans crave: tension and scares. It's first-person, there are guns, but it's not a "shooter." Ammo and inventory space is limited. You start with a melee weapon and a pistol, with more weapons and upgrades collected along the way. The GamePad is used for sorting items and navigation, and also for scanning the environment similar to "Metroid Prime." What makes "ZombiU" special is the intense pacing and atmosphere it creates. Like the "Souls" games, patience is a virtue. Death looms around every corner. Zombies may be of the walking sort, but once they start at you, be ready. Slowly creeping your way through the dark halls, or tunnels, or streets with a flashlight that's slowly depleting in power and only three bullets left creates a sense of dread not found in other games. "ZombiU" does not feel like a launch game, but a game made by people passionate about creating a great horror title. The environments are dark and oppressive, the zombie encounters intense, and the GamePad use inventive. It's also genuinely scary. Here's to hoping for more Wii U titles of this quality, and for a "ZombiU 2."--- 5 STARS ---

Reason For Purchase:After it became to painful on my thumbs to play Soul Calibur III on my PS2 using the D-Pad, I eventually replaced the official PS2 controller for a Gamestop brand PS2 controller for it's much improved D-Pad and more confortable shoulder buttons.  Unfortunately that same controller design used with the PS2 would pass over onto the PS3 and nothing but the SIXAXIS function, Home Button, and wireless design were changed.  The horrible D-Pad and Shoulder Buttons were still intact.  I recently purchased BlazBlue: Chrono Phantasma for PS3 (the only system it released for) and having played the series so far on the ever reliable Xbox 360 controller, I expected issues.  And there were.  Moves I could pull off most of the time on the 360's concave Left Control Stick were beyond impractical to even attempt with the PS3's D-Pad or convex Left Control Stick, and if you've ever played Soul Calibur AND BlazBlue, you'd know that BlazBlue demands MUCH faster and more precise input with commands that more heavily use the Left Control Stick.  The PS3 controller was going to kill my hands.  So I bought this.Results:With no fiddling around, all I have to do is plug the adapter into the PS3 and the Xbox 360 controller into the adapter and after a second or two, BAM, light comes on and I'm playing BlazBlue like it was on Xbox 360.  No lag or discrepencies with any buttons, the Xbox Guide Button takes the place of the Playstation Home Button and the only sacrifice is that you can't use the controller to turn on the system.  Other than that...Xbox 360 Controllers work with BlazBlue on PS3.A simple unplug of the 360 controller and plugin of the Gamestop PS2 controller confirm the same thing.  Even though the controller has no Home Button, the adapter's own Home Button fulfills the same function.  Everything checks out.PS2 Controllers work with BlazBlue on PS3 (though the 360 is still better).Here's where it gets sticky though:  I tried the Mayflash Universal Adapter with Kingdom Hearts 1.5 HD Remix.My conclusion is:  PS2 Controllers work with KH1.5HD on PS3, Xbox 360 Controllers ALMOST work.Everything seems to work just fine, EXCEPT how the PS3 reads the control sticks.  Using the control sticks to move straight vertically or horizontally there are no problems, but as soon as you swing the camera around and try moving diagonally Sora immediately reverts to a walking pace even with the control stick tilted to it's max, this happens any time you try moving the control stick anywhere other than up, down, left, or right.  Unfortunately, this easily damns the 360 Controller as inferior to even a basic PS2 controller.So, in summary:  The Mayflash Universal Adapter makes using your PS2 Controller on your PS3 easy, but the Xbox 360 Controller may only work properly with certain PS3 games.  I have not tried the adapter with Xbox 360 or PC.

I had almost given up on reigniting the spark I felt for this series after Island of Happiness. The edit feature is a godsend for the series. The fact that I don't have to throw my crops into the collection bin, amazing. The art style is gorgeous and the 3D makes it pop. Honestly with most 3DS games, I end up playing with the feature turned off. Here, as with Ocarina, you really miss out on the quality of the graphics without it turned on. The depth of the gameplay, is terrific. You could spend your entire time just playing with the crops but there's so much more to do. As much as I want to punch that cowboy hobo mayor in the face every time he barges into my house, I really feel invested in his mission of revitalizing the town. There's more appeal for growing and expanding the town than I felt in Island of Happiness. Hunting down new blueprints, recipes, and music sheets is a terrific diversion. Sometimes though, the rewards from the Sprites for expanding the town are a bit underwhelming. The additional fact that they have to be unlocked in sequential order -- for instance I built the clinic before the cottage but I didn't get the clinic's music sheet unlocked until after I unlocked the sheet from the cottage -- is a tad annoying but not so much that it detracts from the game. Despite the slow start of the first month, you're constantly compelled to be doing something: foraging, fishing, flirting, building. This game is great.

First off, this is a budget title priced at $39.99, so it came out to $31.99 + tax for me at BB since I belong to Gamers Club ($13.xx after reward certs), and for its budget price I'm pretty happy with Enemy Front. It's a game that has stealth, run & gun, and some nice sniping mechanics, and you can use these whenever you want and aren't forced to do one over the other, so that makes this game offer some nice variety to enemy encounters that other first-person shooters don't have. In addition, environments are very large and open, allowing for experimentation.Enemy Front is also a WWII-era game, which there aren't many of these days. Instead of offering a lot of drab colors, this is a game full of brightly colored environments that are very pleasing to look at. That said, the graphics range from mediocre-good. Sometimes the game can look beautiful, but other times the game can look messy with poorly textured objects, pop-in, and other strange graphical glitches.Since I mentioned the graphical glitches above, let me go into further detail on that since I find it to be one of this game's biggest downfalls. To be quite frank, there are a lot of oddities with graphical glitches in this game. For example, I was in the top floor of a house, there was a fire on an object across the street, but if I moved to the window in the top floor of the house and got in the right position, the fire would actually be on the window frame of the house that I was standing in. This is just one of many graphical glitches I've noticed. There's also something always on the bottom of the game's UI that makes it look like burn-in on your TV.As for story, it's overall enjoyable, but voice acting can be cheesy at times.Another thing I noticed is that this game sometimes takes you from level to level, but it also sometimes has a hub world environment that allows you to choose between which mission to take on next. I know that this game went through development hell and this is likely the reasoning behind two different types of game design clashing together in Enemy Front.Overall, I do really enjoy the game and the choices it gives you on the battlefield, but I can't score it higher because of its unpolished nature.Do NOT buy this game for multiplayer. Whatever console you own, whether Wii U, PS3, 360, 3DS, Vita, PC, or even soon PS4 this game is excellent.  The team at Ubisoft has added to the already successful Rayman Origins game by taking all of the best elements and adding to that formula.  The musical end world stages play like a platforming Guitar Hero (or Rock Band) adventure.  The worlds are colorful and the music engaging.  It is great fun for one to four players.  I hate comparing it to the New Super Mario Brother games, because playing one without playing the other does both an injustice, but Rayman Legends uses some of the same four player mechanics.  When one player rushes through the level the others are pulled behind him in bubbles.  In Legends these players simply press a button (I believe the A button on most consoles) to be released, while Mario has you shake to catch up with that player who must pop your bubble.  The only problem with either formula is that it is assumed the fastest player knows what he is doing and so if he jumps in a pit or hits an enemy and dies, the level ends.  There isn't as much problem with characters bumping into each other, but it is still a problem.  That mentioned the game is challenging, fun, and has most (if not the entire game) of Rayman Origins inside unlockable by playing through levels in the game.  Time attack challenge levels are also VERY plentiful in this game by simply earning points from playing through the game.  I say the Wii U version of this game is best because that is the console it was designed for.  Some levels have you control a character with the touch screen or by motion control that really require the GamePad. Note: I am not a Call of Duty hater. The original WW2 games and the Black Ops series are some of my favorite games. I do not take the "Battlefield vs. Call of Duty" rivalry seriously.Call of Duty Modern Warfare 3 is a fun game, until you realize it lacks all innovation that the games are famous for, and that it's shoot, shoot, die, shoot some more, blow something up, shoot. Sure, all of them are like this, but it's especially obvious in MW3 (especially in it's multiplayer mode, more on that later).The story starts off where the MW2 left off; Captain Price carting Soap to safety, and the introduction of Yuri. The story has a decent amount of twists and turns, almost all of which are incredibly predictable over the 6 hour course of the game. The ending is an okay end to the Modern Warfare trilogy, but getting there involves a ridiculous amount of shooting brain dead AI. With the exception of 2-3 stealth missions and an AC-130 Gunship mission, you won't get far from the "here's an MP5, go kill a couple thousand people!" mechanic.The multiplayer of this game is what REALLY made me regret dishing $60, though. If you ever played Modern Warfare 2, you've already played this one. Infinity Ward got VERY lazy with this game, literally copying and pasting guns, emblems, attachments, titles, and equipment. One might argue that they fixed many of Modern Warfare 2's bugs (there were a LOT of them), but I honestly expect a lot more out of a sequel than things that should have been fixed in the first game. Infinity Ward added a few new toys to the toy box (a few "new" guns that feel the exact same as the others, a new kill-streak system that doesn't change the game at all), but that isn't nearly enough for me to recommend coughing up $60.Spec-Ops mode returns... Skip it. It's a few "bonus" missions that don't feel any different than the missions that I already played in the campaign (back to the "go kill a couple thousand people!" algorithm).I sold this game back to GameStop, and I don't regret it. Keep your money and go see a movie instead.

The Drake games are kind of like the best of Mission Impossible and Indiana Jones. Nathan Drake, treasure hunter/Terminator hybrid attempts to follow the path of his namesake Sir Francis Drake to find Ubar, the fabled "Atlantis of the Sands" finding a long buried plot and a sinister conspiracy behind its disappearance.Graphics and voice are superb as always. Naughty Dog almost has the crown on this, but I feel like they're barely edged out by Mass Effect and one or two other series, as dialogue can be lost in the wash of combat a little too easily.Gameplay is probably the best of the series, though U2 still has the best sequence by far with the train. Exploration and treasure hunting are still nice diversions without being impossible nit hunts, but some treasures have really odd reqs to reach.There's only one major nit that peels off star 5: The ocean of dispoable grunts. After 4 waves of enemies, you'd think there'd be some more exposition on why the opposition cares so much. In U2 they we're a mercenary unit under a tyrannical psycopath, but there's not a drive like that to fight through burning buildings and crashing planes when rational people would be running for exits or parachutes. Other nits are present. You can throw back greadnes (yay!) but they're on timers that sometimes allow the greande to still explode and kill you even when you're successful at throwing them back (boo!) Snipers have unlimited ammo, but when you loot their corpse they have, without fail, only a single spare clip remaining. Close combat has been revamped, but the AI apparently doesn't really care about friendly fire, as they'll pump you full of lead while trading punches with a guy. Again, how do you drive a group of guys to swiss cheese one of their own?MP is actually decent. There's leveling bonuses, but you won't feel like you're armed with a peashooter among RPG's when you are dumped repeatedly into levels with all level 45+'s to your 3.Overall, totally worth it. Great story, entertaining dialogue, great play sequences. Even with all the QTE's it still doesn't feel like press X to not die and more like you're in the cutscene, which is fantastically hard to do. Looking forward to the next one, though hopefully sans the zombie army.

After being thoroughly disappointed by the first Uncharted and thoroughly impressed by the second, I was prepared for pretty  Uncharted 3. What I got was far and away the best gameplay of the series, but a story that did not quite feel as epic as the second.The single best part of Uncharted 3 is the improvement to use of the platforming elements. The mantra of the first two games in this series may as well have been, "Why walk through a door when you can back-track 30 feet, drop down two levels to shimmy around the side of one building to climb up four stories to swing back down three levels just to get to the other side of said door?" It was annoying, time consuming, and greatly disrupted the flow of the game.  All of the platforming seems to have a purpose in Uncharted 3. It isn't just there because it can be. You also don't have the long, boring missions where it seems like all you do is jump, climb, and shimmy for 45 minutes. I can't stress enough how much I appreciate this change.The graphics are improved over the already impressive Uncharted 2, the weapon variety is greater, and they feel even slightly better than UC 2. The combat is improved and a bigger part of this game. This is both a good and a bad. When just fighting one person, it works pretty well. When fighting a larger group, it feels pretty ridiculous.  Think the combat system from the Arkham games, but instead of being Batman with his free flow combat, gadgets, and fighting animation variety, Drake has like 3 moves that you'll see over and over through the fight.While still solid, the story for UC 3 lacks the punch of UC 2. This could just be a matter of personal preference, but I never found myself as emotionally involved in this game as I did UC 2. The Sully-Nate origin story was interesting, but I didn't feel like it carried the middle of the game very well. Also, in UC 2, I thought I was near the end when I reached the mid-point, and I couldn't believe how much game I still ended up having left. With UC3, I couldn't believe it was over. I'm not sure if this is because the game was significantly shorter, paced that much better, or just moved so much quicker when you were not swinging around like a monkey all the time.Overall, I would call UC3 the most fun to play of the trilogy, but the story lacked the punch of UC 2. Had the UC2 story been paired with the UC 3 gameplay, this would have moved the game from great to near perfection.

This package contains That Game Company's three titles, and because each of them are unique in their own sense, I broke the package down to its bones.Fl0W:I don't have much to say about Fl0w, other than that it is the weakest of the three titles included in the bundle. In a nutshell, you glide around as a cell-like creature looking for blue orbs that make your organism bigger while dodging other organisms that are bigger than you. While the game offers multiple organisms for you to play as and it is definitely pretty to look at, the "gameplay" rapidly becomes stale as you realize all you are doing is tilting the controller one way or another. It's fun for an hour, but I wouldn't buy the package exclusively for "Fl0w".Flower:Flower is more of an interactive piece of art than an actual game; you "play" as a lone flower petal, looking to collect as many different types of flower petals while turning the desolate land around you into a flowing plain. TGC truly shows off their ability to mesmerize the player with solid visuals and great game physics. This short and sweet "adventure" lasts a little longer than Fl0w did for me, as there are multiple environments and flowers for you to play as. This is a nice distraction from the main piece of the package, which is...Journey:WOW. TGC really blew the gaming norm with Journey. Many might be turned away when I say that I completed Journey in a mere two hours; however, this allows players to play this masterpiece over and over again, finding every collectable and enjoying this experience of a game. You interact with your environment by flying/gliding through deserts, up waterfalls, and exploring mysterious ruins that are truly incredible to look at. The game also features something other games don't; throughout your odyssey, the game will incorporate other players into your game without any chat boxes or name tags, only revealing who your companions were after the game's credits. Journey is a masterpiece in ways that many wouldn't think of a traditional "game", with its stunning visuals and rememberable physics and gameplay.While I wouldn't buy this package if you've already purchased the games via the Playstation digital store, the bonus content are nice, and they sweeten the deal that much more. Included are interactive wallpapers for the Playstation menu, the game's astounding score, and other little pieces of swagger for your Playstation. Definitely pick up this package if you have yet to experience any of these titles.

It’s about as easy to describe the game Journey to someone as it is to describe Doctor Who.  You love it, you know why you love it, but to put it into words is nearly impossible.  While describing your love for Doctor Who may make you sound certifiably insane, trying to describe Journey makes it sound boring, which it is certainly far from. Yet, despite that potentiality, I will do my best to paint a more detailed picture as to why we still love it and will continue to love it for years to come.You’ve probably heard from so many mouths that Journey (crafted by thatgamecompany) is “touching” and “beautiful” to the point where it almost sounds cliche, but it’s true.  This game genuinely provides you with an experience unlike that which you could have with any other game.  I haven’t played it in nearly two years, and yet I can still remember precisely how I felt when I reached the end.This is going to sound cheesy, so prepare yourself, but you don’t play Journey to have fun, you play Journey to be moved and to be taken on a ride you’ve never been on before.  If you end up having fun anyway, then that’s great, but sitting down to play Journey is more like going to a museum of art, as opposed to strapping in for a day at the theme park.I don’t want to spoil the ending for you, but to sum up, it pretty much falls into the categories of: unforgettable, shocking, moving, touching, resonating, and sobering.  It will put a smile on your face moments after it makes you cry, and you will come to understand how you can bond on a deeper level with a real person whom you’ve never met.  And single player is not an option - well, at least at certain points.  You’ll understand why when you play.While you may delightfully frolic with your anonymous companion on your mission to get to the mountain (located at the end of what seems like the largest desert imaginable), you can do nothing more than jump or speak to each other in song, something that would, in reality, be more than sufficient, should we ever end up alone on such a quest - a quest that becomes more evident by the end of the game and will have you nodding in approval.Under any other circumstances, Journey would probably suck.  But it’s with those kid gloves with which thatgamecompany makes all of their games, including flOw (a subtle game of evolution) and Flower (where you control flower petals on the wind), that make their gaming experiences more of an interactive meditation than a traditional gaming session.  You play games like Call of Duty and God of War to release your aggression, but you pick up a thatgamecompany game to soothe your soul.The fact that Journey is an indie title makes it even more impressive that it was so memorable, though less surprising that it is as profound.  The visuals are breathtaking, particularly the glimmering pink sands, and the soft sounds are unlike any you’ve heard before in a video game.  Journey is the perfect example of why you don’t need a lot of glitz and glamour - sometimes less truly is more...so much more.
