Killzone Shadow Fall, the latest in the long running Killzone series from Guerilla Games, is being promoted as the showcase game for the new Playstation 4. For the most part, the game does a good job of introducing the capabilities of Sony’s new console. It checks off all of the requisite boxes on the first person shooter checklist, but it never really manages to achieve anything great.The story takes place many years after the previous three games, where after repelling a Helghast invasion of Vekta, the Vektans followed the Helgast to their home planet and basically ended up annihilating their planet. The Vektans, in a terrible act of judgement, decide to let the remaining Helgast come back to Vekta with them. The Helgast are given half the planet, allowed to militarize, and a giant wall is built between them. That, more or less, is the completely unbelievable setup to Shadow Fall: the Helgast are right on the other side of that wall and are plotting revenge.The story is told primarily through cutscenes that set up each mission and occasional radio messages sent to you during gameplay. There are also audio logs that you can find in the levels, but they tend to contain secondary information that is not very important. The audio logs play out of the new speaker on the Playstation controller. I found this to be rather obnoxious for a couple of reasons: the audio quality of this speaker is not great, you cannot adjust the volume of it from in-game, and it’s awkward to have audio come from my controller when I am using headphones for everything else.The narrative tries to add some moral ambiguity over who the “bad” guys really are, but it is hard to care when none of the characters are particularly likeable and everyone is in a bad in a situation of their own making.The actual shooting mechanics feel tight and responsive, and there is a good selection of weapons to use with some of them offering secondary fire modes. The highlight of the gameplay is a little hovering drone you have called the OWL. You can send it out to attack enemies and provide covering fire, deploy a one way shield in front of you that allows you to shoot out of it, and EMP strike an area disorienting enemies and removing shields. It also has an ability to deploy a zip line allowing you to reach areas you otherwise would not be able to, but this sees limited use in mostly pre-determined areas. It can also heal you if you die, given that it’s not currently recharging and that you have medical supplies available. You have to swipe in various directions on the touch pad to change which mode the OWL is in. It is a bit inconvenient as you have to take a hand off of a thumbstick to do what basically amounts to a button press. Hopefully developers will come up for more creative uses for the touch pad later on.Speaking of controls, the game only has two control layouts to pick from and both of them only swap what the triggers and shoulder buttons do. There is absolutely no way to change what the face buttons on the controller are assigned to. This seems sloppy, as it should be pretty trivial to allow remapping of buttons.It is a bit disappointing that you are required to hold on to your primary weapon at all times. Since you can only hold two weapons at a time, this really limits the number of loadout configurations you can have. Want to have a sniper rifle and a shotgun? Sorry, you have to hold on to that Assault rifle you started with that has no ammo left.The enemy AI is not particularly smart. They will run around corners into your line of fire one after another, decide to climb ladders in the middle of a gunfight, and don’t really make much of an effort to flank you or seem to work together in any meaningful way. The game tries to make up for this by either sending large amounts of them at you at once, or giving them energy shields that turn them into bullet sponges. It can make for frantic fights at times, but for the most part they are not particularly interesting opponents. Repetition also becomes a problem later in the game, as there is just not a lot of variety to what you fight. They do add some robots in towards the later stages, but they are used sparingly and don’t really do enough to keep the combat feeling fresh.The game has a fairly limited cover system that allows you to crouch behind cover, but it feels really unfinished.  There is no button to go into cover, but if you crouch behind cover of the right height you will automatically peak over when you aim down the sights. It is often hard to tell if the cover you are hiding behind is actually tall enough, and when you aim down sights you get anchored to that cover preventing you from moving. The cover also only works vertically, so you cannot take cover around corners or at doorways.What really kept me playing the game was the level design that included a number of cool setpiece moments. You are constantly on the move from one area to the next. Some of the more interesting highlights include a ship that is flying into the sun, where you can shoot out windows to burn enemies and melt parts of the ship, and a floating train yard where high speed trains are flying all around you as you jump from platform to platform.Killzone earns its highest marks in presentation. The graphics are undeniably better than last generation consoles, although anyone with a high end PC has been seeing graphics as good as this for a few years now. The biggest improvement is that is it actually rendering natively in 1080p at 60 frames per second. The game has a nice artistic style that unfortunately often goes overboard with the lens flare and reflective surfaces because apparently almost nothing on Vekta absorbs light. Texture quality and lighting is impressive, although the lighting is completely static. You cannot shoot out lights or otherwise effect the lighting in the environment. Characters are a bit mixed. In the pre-rendered cutscenes they look pretty great and are expressive. During actual gameplay they tend to look a bit stiff with faces that don’t move much and eyes that don’t blink. There also seems to be some issues with lip syncing at times as well. It is also worth noting that the graphics quality seems to have been turned down a bit for the multiplayer, perhaps to provide a more reliable framerate in the unpredictable online modes.A lot of people are going to be picking up Killzone for the multiplayer, and I am happy to say that I can recommend it for that without any reservations. Pretty much everything you need for a good multiplayer experience is here: fast matchmaking, unlocks and customizable loadouts, solid map design, lots of game modes, and the ability to customize to your satisfaction. When you set up a lobby you can determine everything from which weapons and abilities are allowed to which game modes pop up. The highlight of multiplayer is the Warzone mode, which consists of a variety of different game types that change during the match. For example, a match might start out as team deathmatch, change to a capture and hold mode, before finally switching to a defend and destroy mode. The side that completed the most objectives by the end wins.Overall, Killzone Shadow Fall is a by the numbers first person shooter whose main draw is its graphics and multiplayer. The single player is a mostly repetitive and forgettable experience that only occasionally reaches greatness during certain setpiece scenes, while its multiplayer offers enough depth to keep people playing for a while. As a launch title it does a decent job at introducing us to the new capabilities of the Playstation 4 and is worth picking up. A year from now though, Killzone Shadow Fall probably won’t be worth your time.

First off my opinions are those of a person that doesn't enjoy first person shooters that much, so if you are an FPS fan you can probably ignore my misgivings. Also I have not yet finished the game (I'd say I'm 1/3 through? tough to be sure). For those of you that aren't fans of FPS games I doubt this one will change your mind.I think the game play is just ok. So far this is pretty standard FPS style, the only thing to get in the missions are slightly different guns/weapons and a pretty small amount of other items (grenades or explosives for instance). Missions are basically to go kill stuff and not die.  There are some interesting features such as a little drone to help you (for example: attack/distract enemies), stim packs which let you basically go into slow motion and shoot people more effectively and you can climb in some pre-designated places the developers have chosen.I also haven't found it particularly friendly to multiple play styles.  Technically you can semi-stealth through some of the missions but I've found it to be more a function of luck rather than game design which allows you to choose the stealth style.  Much of the time you can eliminate several enemies with stealth but then there is a grouping which has to be brute forced (even after waiting for patrolling).So if you are looking for some reason to try out an FPS again to see if they have evolved, I wouldn't look to this game. It's just a slightly different flavor of FPS from the other options out there.  The story thus far has been semi interesting and that will probably be the only thing that compels me to finish this game. The graphics are also quite nice but if you look at the scenery too much your likely to get shot lol.  If you are an FPS fan this may be a great game, I personally have a tough time getting excited about them as in general strategy is much less important than the amount of ammo available for your weapon. There is no real character progression and so you reset on each mission.

I was highly surprised by how much fun I had in the first two inFAMOUS games. I have so much fun just smashing everything in sight - there are so many destructible objects in Seattle that you could spend a day just going around and finding more DUP stuff to destroy. Gameplay hasn't changed too much, except for the touchpad, which just feels like it was meant to be there.The story is intriguing. I'm going to keep it there to avoid spoilers, but the other characters are just as interesting in their own ways, and the plot isn't too easy to predict (but plays it safe and avoids too many twists). I have had an absolute blast with Second Son since I brought it home on launch day. I've beaten the Good Karma and Bad Karma route already, and platinumed the game, yet here I am working on my 3rd play of the game. I just don't get tired of it, the characters, the story, the gameplay, none of it!First off, the game is gorgeous. I remember thinking that a lot to myself as I saw trailers and stuff leading up to release, but somehow I just never really thought the game would look that good in action. The environment, the lighting, the character models, the effects, it all looks so polished and beautiful. Special note goes to the expressions the characters make throughout the game. The facial capture SuckerPunch employed payed off in a big way. Delsin and Reggie's faces reflect the tone of their conversations with others and you can actually SEE the feelings their voices and bodies are conveying because they actually reflect on their face in a way that looks natural. It really helps you connect with these characters in a big way.Second Son plays as well as it looks too, which is saying something. I won't spoil the powers for anyone, but I'll say this; Delsin does not flesh out his powers like Cole. Instead of mastering them all, Delsin is a textbook example of a "Jack of all trades, master of none". He beefs up the individual powers, but never truly takes them to their full potential like their Prime Conduits have. I happen to like this aspects in most cases, but I understand why many reviewers are complaining about this. Combat itself is fast and fluid; Delsin is constantly having to jump and dash around areas to fight like the inexperienced fragile kid he is. Unlike inFAMOUS 1&2, you won't be taking cover behind things often, most of the time the best thing to do is smoke dash through a vent and hide on a roof to get a quick breather, or re-charge your powers before dashing back into the fray to whale on some more D.U.P mooks while bouncing around between hits.The story takes a different path than the previous games, I won't spoil it, but it's more grounded in reality so to speak and closed off, instead of the big sci-fi-ish stories we got with Cole. Again, this is something I liked about Second Son. It was more about Delsin's personal, private journey on a much smaller overall scale, and I very much enjoyed the change of pace. I've got nothing but great things to say about the characters as well, especially Delsin and Reggie, but to not spoil it I won't say anything more.To address the "it's short" complaints, inFAMOUS 1&2's story modes are both beatable in about 8-ish hours if you forego the majority of the side missions and activities and stuck to the story missions. Second Son follows that same formula, so I personally don't agree with the reviewers who are rating it lower because of this. Each story path (Good and Bad) takes around 7-8 hours if you do minimal side quests. If you DO choose to do things like clear out the D.U.P from areas, collect all the blast shards, do the tagging, all of are required to reach completion, you'll rack up a lot more time in the game. I took my time doing all that in my first run and I believe it took me close to 16 hours to 100% that save. So, Second Son is not a very long game, but it's really not all that short either.To sum it up, Second Son blew me away in so many ways it's not funny. The only complaints I have, and they are relatively minor ones to me, is that some of the secondary characters weren't developed as well as they could have been, and at times it seemed as if some of the story got cut towards release. None of this significantly impacts the game, but it just feels as if maybe SP didn't quite get some aspects as polished as they'd planned to.

Although his motivation is to save his tribe, he attitude about it and how he gets there is different.Cut scenes are great with facial wrinkles and subtle but key eye movement. They aren't overblown, but important enough to create an interesting story.Game-play is mostly unchanged with a few key exceptions - three are three different power types, the first power type feels like a natural evolution of the electricity powers from the two games whereas the other two power types and the final power type as a reward for game completion feel different and unique. I don't want to spoil these new powers, but let me say that although they have the same power types (hovering, a quick move, a simple shot, a heavy shot, and a grenade), each power caters to a particular play style (shotgun, machine gun, sniper - balanced, fast, even faster), Mobility is no longer a problem (scaling the buildings is a thing of the past), combat is more challenging now that power is consumed even by firing "simple shots" of power. The AI is wise enough to take cover to draw you into combat, and just as nimble and mobile as you are. Fast travel is introduced.The graphics are great. I did notice frame-rate drops, but overall the game is consistent. I don't think that the graphics are better than Killzone, but the artistic quality of the game (the ascetic) is well done. It is a beautiful game.This is a must-have PlayStation 4 game. Why there isn't a multi-player component is surprising - there is much opportunity here for that.

Infamous Second Son is a beautifully crafted game that compliments the series, yet is also capable of standing on its own. The graphics are superb and the gameplay is full of action. This game does a wonderful job of showing off the potential of the PS4.You are Delson Rowe, younger brother of a newly elected sheriff. You accidentally siphon the powers of a so called "bio terrorist." This leads you and your brother to Seattle, Washington.In this contemporary Seattle, the Department of Unified Protection (DUP), led by a ruthless woman named Brooke Augustine, hunts bio terrorists. Augustine has powers of her own, and she has bestowed some of her powers unto the DUP troops under her command. DUP has militarized much of the city, and they run patrols as well. DUP's oppressive presence is evident in the attitudes of the people.Your goal is to stop the DUP and its powerful leader. First, though, you need to increase your powers, or you'll be no match for Augustine.Seattle is divided into districts. Each district has main story quests, along with many side activities. You gradually erode the DUP's presence in a district by doing all of the activities, then challenging the DUP in a district showdown, in which you must defeat a group or groups of DUP soldiers that are dispatched to your location.You will gain powers through main story quests. Other powers are purchased by collecting blast shards, which are also used to upgrade your powers.It's autumn, apparent from the colorful trees. The rain effects look great and don't hinder performance at all. I noticed no framerate issues regardless of all the action in the populated city. I did notice some infrequent texture tearing in the form of fallen enemies meshing together like a two-headed, four-armed and -legged mutant.You'll gain four classes of powers, not counting melee. The effects are stellar, and the visuals of Delson recharging his powers are literally the coolest thing I've seen in a game in decades.I would like to see more story implementation in the side activities. Much time is spent in combat, exploring, and doing side activities. It's easy to forget what the main mission is because it's so easy to get side tracked. Once you hit the main story icon, however, you quickly get back on track.The controls are excellent. The map and powers tree are easy to understand and navigate. This game looks and plays like a dream. The great thing about Infamous is that it warrants two play throughs---one as good and one as evil. Each has its own particular powers, and the story tilts to go with whichever side you choose. The world and your character no longer turn gray when playing evil. Now it's just Delson's clothes that change color. Of note, only the decal on Delson's default vest changes to represent his karma (good or evil). Decals on the bonus vests do not change.One thing I don't particularly care for is the requirement of creating a separate online account with a computer in order to experience the additional content in the game. This content is called "Paper Trail." It offers more things to do as content is periodically released. I think this should be downloadable from the PSN store, not require the player to log on to an account with their computer. I think this is a hassle. This is the only hang-up I have with the game.I highly recommend Infamous Second Son. It's a blast to play and the graphics are nothing short of awesome. If you're a fan of the series, you'll appreciate the improvements in Second Son. If you're new to the series, you're in for a treat.

I've played both the other inFAMOUS games on PS3 and enjoyed them quite a lot. They had their issues, and so does this one, but it's largely a fantastic game. Firstly, this game is absolutely gorgeous. I mean, drop-dead pretty. The character models, landscape, particle and lighting effects, all of it. It's just mind-blowingly pretty. Gameplay is good, similar to the other inFAMOUS titles but adding just enough to make it feel different and fresh. Combat is improved over previous titles allowing for a healthy mix of defensive and offensive abilities with each set of powers feeling unique. Except the very last power, which I won't spoil, but really feels like an afterthought.The characters are very well voice acted and Troy Baker does a great job putting voice to Delsin. The main character does feel a little bit shallow, though. I don't feel he has very much character progression until the very end of the game. The supporting characters are good enough, but are incredibly stereotyped. The bad guy is probably the most complex character in the game and isn't just evil for the sake of being evil. She has motivation and reason for doing what she does, her methods are just extreme.The game is pretty short and might be one of my largest complaints. It's still plenty long to enjoy, but once you beat the story and do all the side missions (which are all pretty uninspired) there isn't much left to do besides screw around in the city. I take that back, it's pretty fun to play with the Photo Mode, take screenshots, export them and make awesome desktop backgrounds. Otherwise the only replay-ability you'll get from this game is playing the other "side" of the karma path. This leads me to why I hate dichotomous moral-choice systems: you either have to be a Boy Scout or Hitler. There's no middle ground, no grey area. It's black or white. The game presents you with a handful of moral choices but ultimately what it comes down to is "Choose this to be evil or this one to be good" - Nothing that lets you make a choice that you truly feel is right or justified. I guess you could choose whatever you wanted but that'll just screw up your talent points because only certain talents are available for certain "ranks" of Karma. The bigger jerk you are the more powerful you get. You get the idea; in fact it's just like the other inFAMOUS titles.Overall though, my complaints are far outweighed by the sheer fun this game presents. It's ridiculously fun to run around the city as a flash of neon light, climb giant buildings and jump off or just search for all the collectibles. The main story leaves some to be desired but it's plenty engaging enough to pull you through the game and want to see what comes next. Hands-down it's the best PS4 game out right now, at least until The Last of Us Remastered drops.

I'm going to be honest, I got Infamous Second Son for my birthday recently, and although I was grateful, I was not particularly excited. I gave it a try though, and the first time I played it I ended up dropping 3 hours into the game!As a sceptic of this game, as a long time gamer and as someone who just beat the game last night I can confidently say that Infamous Second Son is phenomenal!GRAPHICSGraphics are truly next gen with highly detailed models and textures and excellent lighting. There are countless little details around the city that make the game truly immersive. Character models are also excellent, although not quite as good as some other games I've seen on PS3 (Last of Us, Beyond: Two Souls).GAMEPLAYIn terms of gameplay, character movement felt a little too fast and artificial at first, but once I got the hang of it that feeling went away. The game is really fun once you start gaining powers and learning how to use them. Mechanics are delightfully well thought out and make the game feel really unique and entertaining. The game also presents some interesting, and surprisingly non-gimicky ways of using the features of the Dualshock 4 controller.I have a couple of very minor gripes on the gameplay side, just keep in mind these are minor and don't detract from the overall greatness of this game. First, non-story activities in the game, such as collecting certain items, can feel just a little repetitive (although some of these items are optional). Overall, basic gameplay can be so varied, even within these activities, that it's still pretty fun. Also, you can't swim in this game. It's kind of annoying that you can scale a 20 story building with your bare hands, but as soon as you touch a body of water your character freezes and you have to press a button to "Go Back to Shore"STORYThe plot of the game felt compelling enough that I wanted to power through the game in 4 days to see how things developed. Characters are multidimensional, each with their own backstory. Emotional moments actually felt impactful and drove a connection with all the characters. Really well done.SUMMARYDo you have a PS4? Do you like playing single player games? If you answered "yes" to those questions then you should give this game a shot.

I wasn't expecting a lot from Second Son, as I'm not a huge fan of the franchise. I was never interested in the first Infamous, but I couldn't resist grabbing it when it hit $20 without being relegated to crummy Greatest Hits packaging; it had only been out for a few months. I liked it more than I expected I would... enough that I played through it twice, just to see the full range of both karma move sets. I was mildly excited when Infamous 2 came out, but I didn't like it as much as the original. It was basically more of the same in what I personally thought was a less appealing setting. Emprire City from the first game might have been a generic metropolis, but I guess I prefer that to a run down s*** hole armpit of a town like New Marais. Flood Town... difficult for me to believe anyone actually enjoyed running around in that dump. I appreciate the political commentary on Katrina, that doesn't mean I want to play a video game set there. Like many other Infamous fans, I didn't approve of the new and improved Cole redesign, turning him from a skinhead bad ass into a metrosexual pretty boy. Sucker Punch immediately pussed out and cowtowed to us whiners, ran back to the drawing board and whipped up a new "original formula" Cole instead. He looked so lame that I wondered if there was some spite behind it. He ended up looking like some kind of not-yet-fully-formed man-sized foetus. It was a perfect lesson in "be careful what you wish for," I really wish SP had stuck to their guns. I thought Infamous 2 was the definition of a tepid, phoned-in sequel. I finished it once with good karma, but I could only stomach about half of a second play through. It wasn't terrible, though... I can't say I regret playing through it the one time.So when Infamous SS was announced back in Feb 2013, I shrugged. It was clearly going to be a nice bit of PS4 eye candy, and I suppose I assumed I'd buy it at some point if only for that. Well, about a week before it came out, I read somewhere that Jamie Griesemer was the lead game play designer. *THAT* got my attention. Anyone who knows me knows that I'm a diehard Halo fan, specifically for the single player campaigns. And that's where Jamie made a name for himself as a game play designer. Suddenly SS had become a "must play on day 1" title for me. I spent the entire last weekend playing it and am now almost finished with my second play through. All I can say is that this is by far my favorite Infamous game. The game play is indeed great. It very much keeps to the spirit of the first two, but it's considerably expanded and much more polished. Easily the best city so far, both in terms of looks and being fun to explore and run around in. I don't really detect any of Griesemer's fingerprints specifically... it's just good fun to play. Some of the traditional franchise elements have been discarded, like "riding" along rails and lines throughout the city, but they've been traded in for major upgrades- e.g. light speed running up walls and across rooftops, or literally flying up and over them. Combat has been seriously tuned and tightened up compared to previous games. The graphics are at least as good as expected, if not better. The characters are likable, unless they're not supposed to be. Troy Baker's been getting on my nerves lately simply due to his sheer ubiquitousness... but I didn't mind him one bit in this game.The only downsides I can think of are that the game is relatively short compared to the first two. It took me at least two or three full days worth of playing to finish them, but SS took me just over one day. And it does fall into a rut similar to games like Assassins Creed 1, where you get to do the same small handful of mini-missions over and over and over as you clear out the separate sections of the city one by one. Repetitive or not, they're still fun for the most part... so I don't see this as a major gripe.Truly great game, nice to finally have another PS4 showcase to go along with Killzone Shadow Fall. I can't imagine any PS4 owner would want to pass on this game.

This game is incredible.  Simply put, this is THE game you want to have friends over to show off.More and more, we are seeing PS4 games where the concept graphics differ virtually none from the actual game.  Furthermore, one cannot discern between real-time and pre-rendered scenes; the graphical fidelity is always top-notch and consistent.At the outset, I would say, don't read a lot of reviews, watch videos, read walkthroughs, etc; as this game has numerous surprises, and it's way more fun when you get to experience the surprise for yourself.  Everything just *works*.  You're never left wondering how to do something or where to go, and it's so open-world, you can do anything in any order you wish.  Kudos to Sucker Punch and the game testers who made the gameplay FLAWLESS.  It wasn't so many years ago that even in an AAA title, it was difficult to make a character walk down stairs properly.  In this game, you can do EVERYTHING.  And all the side missions are interesting and have purpose, which is the way it should be.  They will gain you new knowledge, new abilities, and keep the story going, plus they are pure joy to do...  How can parkour and conduit powers ever get old?And the engine!  We've kept hearing the word "photorealism", but this game really gets there.  In the cutscenes (which are realtime, not pre-rendered) the facial (and body) animation is truly the most realistic that I have seen since LA Noir; a great game that was a bit ahead of its time and didn't get enough light (pardon the pun) shun on it.This game is EPIC.  It just keeps throwing new powers, new missions, new abilities, new plot elements, etc, at you, and never lets up.  Going for 100% is FUN, every second of it; but even then, you will want to re-play the game to play using the other Karma system.  This Karma system is great; it determines things that happen in the world, and your abilities, and even what the general public thinks of you.  It even becomes a challenge in itself; as if you get a "Karma Streak" you gain the ability to do an Orbital Drop, flying high in the air and then smashing down upon foes, leaving a large blast radius.  During a second play through as "evil"/"Infamous" Karma, the new powers, new missions, etc, all make for a very different play through, controls, scenes, dialogue, and all.On that note, without any spoilers, I recommend going the "good"/"Hero" Karma route during the first play through.  Then you will be inspired to try to the evil Karma play through, which is quite a bit harder (it goes against instinct to not rescue people, people dislike you, etc; it is like New Game Plus, in my opinion).  This is great, though, as there are special powers associated with each, and different story lines, so the game can be what you make it, equalling at least two games in one!  The second play through is really great, because everything is different, you get to see what you missed the first time around.  This harkens back to the days of old NES games when you had a "second quest" after finishing the first!  And at least two REAL ENDINGS, they don't mess around.  And if/when there's DLC in the future, I will definitely be picking that up.  Kudos, too, for NOT having the typical "micro transactions" and other gimmicks that some publishers have been sneaking into their games.  It's a massive, complete game, and the extra wait shows they really gave it a lot of polishing.  This game is like a magician that never runs out of magic tricks.  It is really quite an accomplishment.The game's AI is worth a mention, too...  Whatever rocket scientist came up with the enemy AI is a genius.  None of the old glitches fighting enemy AI are present in this game; enemies are incredibly intelligent and strategic.  They have to be!  Just think, when you have such a powerful protagonist, how do you make things challenging?  It's something they solved with great effort; it's perfection.  I'm also stunned at the pure amount of stuff going on at any time-citizens, traffic, street lights, not to mention all of the architecture, side quests, power ups, and a million other things.  It's a living, breathing, world, all in this game.  I predict quite a few studios will copy concepts invented for this game; it is innovation in its purest form.Nearly everything in the game's wonderfully crafted world (with creative liberties) of Seattle is destructible, climbable, malleable, intractable...  The sky is the limit.  Doing a "dash" (where you turn into particles and swirl through the air" is great for regaining health, but also lets you travel far-you can dash into air vents, and fly out of the tops of buildings!  Delsin sometimes exclaims, "Wooooohooo!!!", and that's pretty much the entire feeling of this game summed up into one word.  It's pure fun, gorgeous to look at (I've never used the screenshot/share function so much in any game).  There are more powers, but don't read up on them, experience the surprise for yourself!  It really keeps you guessing, which few games are able to do.If you're a fan of 90s culture, you'll love the homage to that era and its music, as well.Sucker Punch was one of the many dev studios flown out to Sony's Japanese studio to give input on what they wanted in an ideal console and controller, and it shows.  The controls are flat out perfect.  Really innovative and natural-feeling use of the touchpad on the PS4; I can't see gaming without it now.  The quick swipes, holds, two-finger holds, etc, all make perfect sense and never fail.  A lot of care was put into the crafting of this game, which has been in development since the inception of the PS4.  Did I mention, it was totally worth the wait?This game was well worth the wait, and even better than the hype.  Sony, with the PS4, has pretty much shut down the Xbone with this latest epic game.  Don't believe reviews you see on MS marketing websites.  This game is easily a 10/10!It's a great time to be a gamer, and PS4 is making that possible.  Kudos to Sony and Sucker Punch for creating such an epic and downright fun game.  Will be playing this one a looonnngg time.  I hope at some point, Sony will remaster, or at least port, the previous entries in the series, to be playable on PS4, as I'd be interested in those now, too (I somehow missed them before; this one is NOT to be missed)!  But firstly, I can't wait for DLC, sequels, etc!Sony has promised 20+ exclusives for the PS4 this year alone, and are delivering in spades.  I can't wait to see the coming titles.  Being able to get games now straight through PSN (and Amazon codes for PSN), straight to the PS4, is a huge plus; no waiting in traffic to have a game store asking you for personal info that will go straight to marketing callers, etc.Go with the limited edition of this game, since it's the same price but has added content.  Nothing major, but a few extras for the same price.  Either way, it is, as I mentioned, truly one of the greatest games ever made.Lastly, I highly recommend the SonyGold Wireless Stereo Headsetto go with the game.  This headset is excellent.  Once you use it, you'll never go back to TV speakers; you can hear so much more.  I've been using it for Killzone: Shadow Fall, Battlefield 4, and now InFAMOUS: Second Son.  The 7.1 surround sound (multiple speakers in each ear, and a mic for voice chat, plus noise canceling) actually really helps with gaming; as you can find items/players/etc by directional sound.  There is a headphone app, too, which allows you to load presets for mode 2 (there are 2 modes-normal mode and preset mode); Second Son already has its own preset available in the app, tuned specifically for the game.  Works great!!!  PS, if playing a multiplayer game like Killzone, hit the mute button on the side, and unmute when you need to talk (so others don't hear your background noise, etc; it's common courtesy).Game on!

This was my first inFamous game, and it's so good! The story begins brilliantly, and there are enough twists and turns in the story to keep it from being too repetitive. The combat is awesome! I don't know why people complain about it being "repetitive" or a "chore." As you progress through the story, you earn 3 main powers, and you can absorb any of the nearby, corresponding elements to fuel one of your three powers. Each power has a very unique feel to it, and I often find myself using specific powers for specific purposes (Smoke is the most well rounded and I feel most comfortable using it; Neon is the best for ground travel and has the best melee; Video is the best for flying travel and has the best shooting ability). Interestingly enough, you get a fourth power only at the very end of the story, and for an important reason, but you should probably play the first mission of the game to get a hint about that. There is also a fifth power that you get post-game (Paper), although I am fully satisfied with the three main powers, and the fourth power seems like the bonus. The story itself has a lot of feels. Some reviewers complained about the main character, Delsin Rowe, being irritating. However, I feel like he's actually a character I can really emotionally connect with. I like how you, the player, get better at using the powers as Delsin learns about them as well. Finally, another reason to get this game is due to excellent free roaming. It took me 6 days to complete the main story (only as the good side, mind you) but I can tell it will take me many weeks to get all the trophies and the one platinum trophy (for finishing the game 100%). It's a lot of post game content, but at the same time, it's not too much to tackle. I'm heading for the platinum trophy!

"Infamous" has always been a series that never quite stuck with me. Electricity powers were cool, and seeing the story unfold depending on my choices was neat, but a bland protagonist and a sort of pedantic narrative offset any enjoyment I could gain. Yet I had high hopes for this entry, given that it looked like the first "must-own" PS4-exclusive title after the disappointing "Killzone: Shadow Fall" and "Knack," and that despite my apprehensions about the franchise, Sucker Punch is still a very capable developer with a lot of talent under their wing. Perhaps they could deliver the exclusive that I'd been waiting for since launch day, one that could stand head and shoulders with the best Sony has offered in the past. Is the third time the charm for "Infamous: Second Son"?Yes and no. All of the pieces are here, that's for sure. The charming rogue protagonist, Delsin Rowe, is a Native American whose Washington reservation is barged into by a prison convoy escorting three Conduits (read: people with superpowers) to a maximum security facility. They, of course, break loose, Delsin absorbs one of their powers, and has his reservation assaulted by the ruthless antagonist, Brooke Augustine. With the help of his cop brother, Reggie, Delsin sets sights on Seattle to absorb more powers, stop Augustine's oppressive regime that has taken over the city, and use his new abilities to help his tribe recover.The story does so much right in a lot of regards. First off, it's genuinely refreshing to see Native American characters portrayed as, well, actual people, and not defined by worn tropes about spirits or hating "the white man," like we saw in last year's frankly poor "Beyond: Two Souls." Here, we see Delsin and Reggie as two brothers, and their tribe as a family; it's very respectful, and I admire it for not going down a more racist path. Furthermore, the characters themselves are generally likable, but perhaps none more so than the protagonist. Delsin is a remarkably likable protagonist, almost like a PG-13 version of Dante. His quips and witticisms are funny and delivered without a hint of irony, and on top of that, his trials and tribulations throughout the course of the game really make you feel for the guy. His realistic reactions to gaining powers and coping with the burden of being discriminated against by the general populace round him out, helping to avoid the pitfalls of having a character who's too stoic or too silly. The writers struck a perfect balance with this character, and I sincerely hope we see more of him in future entries.That being said, the rest of the writing could have used some serious work. The supporting cast is all over the place, with high points like straight man Reggie, and the delightfully evil Brooke, and serious low points like the walking cliche that is the gamer geek Eugene, or the manic pixie hobo girl that is Fetch. Characterization isn't the real problem here, though. No, what really sets "Second Son" back is its by-the-numbers, "us against them" plot. Despite some later twists and turns that genuinely surprised me, the story is unfortunately hamstrung by its usage of the same narrative ideas "X-Men" was touching on back in the 1960's. Not only that, but the supporting cast backstories come across as afterthoughts, tacked on to make the mostly ancillary cast seem more compelling. Ultimately, the story gets the job done, and there are some truly emotional moments during the climax, but it doesn't dig quite as deep as I'd like it to.Same goes for the moral choices players can make. Aside from the obvious (don't kill civilians, don't act like an all-around hooligan,) players are often given two choices during cutscenes, and the binary choices available are astoundingly black-and-white. There's no moral grey area, only "good" and "bad." There are even games with binary choices that still managed to make me think about things for a few minutes, but the choices here are so blatant, a child could tell you what's wrong and what's right. It makes it so that players either have to be playing as an intentional hero or intentional villain, with no moral wiggle room to speak of. Granted, it is nice that what choices you make have obvious impacts on the narrative, which is more than I can say for, say, a David Cage game. Still, a bit more ambiguity would have gone a long way here.Issue with the plot aside, let me stress how much fun this game is once the world opens up to you. I've played a lot of games with superpowers, as they've always been a guilty pleasure of mine. And while this might not be the best out there, at least in my opinion, it's definitely one of the most creative and consistently fun. Players are given three sets of powers for most of the game: smoke/fire, neon, and video. Each of these offer their own projectile capabilities, melee attacks of varying strengths, and other various attributes. For example, smoke lets you break yourself down into ashen soot and go through vents; neon allows you to run up walls and snipe enemies from a distance; video lets you sprout wings and, eventually, fly around the city to some extent. Players are, of course, given attacks that are similar to third person shooter weapons, such as pistols, rocket launchers, assault rifles, but with such unique twists that they never feel like mere stand-ins. Few games have given me as much joy as I felt gliding over a hundred feet above ground, sending enemies below flying with a constant barrage of pure television static.At the same time, though, "Second Son" plays it too safe too often for me to truly commend it for being original. The same gripes I've had about open-world superhero games for years reared their ugly head several times over the course of my time with this one. Finding awkward ways to exploit my powers to cheaply take cover from enemy fire, realizing that all of my enemies have similar powers and immediately feeling less powerful, nagging limits to otherwise cool abilities... the downsides here are immensely annoying, and it continues a trend of games that give you cool powers, then immediately start pounding you into submission with stronger enemies. I hesitate to bring up other games so much, but I can't help but be reminded of "Saints Row IV," and how downright satisfying the powers in that game were. While what's on display here is fun, and certainly interesting, I can't help but feel disappointed at the lack of innovation on display here. The game limits the player far too often for them to feel truly empowered, and with a game built around superpowers, that's a serious problem in my book.Still, where it counts, the gameplay is mostly solid. Players are given a large playground to mess around in, and one that has plenty of things to do in it. Aside from just tooling around by scaling buildings, or pulling ridiculous stunts off, you'll also get to participate in some truly engaging side missions. While a few of these are standard "find the collectible" or "fight a hoard of enemies," they take place in the midst of some great set pieces, and with cool powers that truly allow the players to navigate the environments in any way they see fit, even the most trivial parts of the game become ridiculously fun. That is to say, the goals themselves might not be that interesting, but if you're creative, you can turn the game into a hectic, creative and engaging time with a few flicks of the analog sticks.Lastly, the game makes pretty great use of the DualShock 4 touch pad, perhaps the best I've seen in a PS4 title thus far. It integrates the little gadget in a way that, while somewhat gimmicky, is nevertheless creative and seamless. Turning the controller sideways and shaking it to paint graffiti is cool, as using it to tear open fences, smash support pillars, or absorb energy. Other than that, there are some contextual moments where it's used to an impressive degree. For example, Delsin goes through a security checkpoint early on the game, and gets his hand scanned. The game prompts the player to place their finger on the pad, then keep it there as the game "scans" it; this prompts the controller to rumble and make noise. While, yes, this is a little goofy, I still found it a neat way to show off the latent potential for immersion that Sony's newest little gizmo has to offer.Graphically, though, there are barely any complaints to be made. The world Delsin inhabits is beautifully rendered, down to the very last detail. I only spotted the occasional jagged edge, and there were no real pop-ins to be seen for the most part. A colorful urban sprawl, Sucker Punch's dystopian Seattle maintains the atmosphere and scenery one would expect from Washington, yet offers enough interesting, futuristic technology to keep things fresh. Aside from the eye-catching scenery, the character models in "Second Son" are arguably some of the very best I've ever seen in a video game. The main characters speak, and their faces crinkle, their complexions change, their eyes bulge and narrow. For all of the pretensions of Quantic Dream's "emotional" graphics, I found the characters here to look and behave in a far more human fashion than anything that divisive studio has ever produced. Sure, there are some lazy textures here and there, like reflections on buildings that don't match what's actually behind them, or clothing on certain pedestrians, but that's really just nitpicking. This is a gorgeous game, hands-down, and given that we're already getting something of this caliber early on the PS4's life cycle, it makes very excited about the graphical capabilities of this system.Yes, "Infamous: Second Son" is a bit trite in the execution of its narrative, and yes, it has some serious issues with limiting the player's enjoyment of their powers in combat situations. Yet it's hard for me to discount the sheer amount of fun that can be had with this game, and the impressive amount of content offered for sixty bucks. This is a sleek-looking and fun experience with plenty to do, and an enjoyable cast of characters participating in a relatively fun plot. While I would hesitate to call this a "system seller," this is undeniably the best console-exclusive title of this generation so far, and one of the more intriguing superpower-fueled experiences on the market.Score: 8.5

I've played through the first two Infamous games, and I consider myself to be a moderate fan of the series. It's not one that I would say I'm obsessed about, but I am very satisfied with the series in general. The story has always proven to be interesting, and the characters are pretty well fleshed-out as well. I recently beat Infamous 2 in anticipation of Second Son, but to be honest the stories are so far apart that I don't really feel that it's necessary to have played the last two at all. Second Son is an excellent stand-alone game, and it's by far the best in the series.First thing's first, the game is just gorgeous! The graphics are incredibly detailed, and the color gamut is beautiful. Each power has a color palette of their own, and they are quite a sight to behold. Sucker Punch's rendition of Seattle is massive and very detailed. All in all this is just a pretty looking game.The gameplay is what you will expect from any Infamous game if you've played any of them. Easy to navigate, climbing is encouraged, and the combat system is fun and fluid.What I would say is the biggest departure from the first game is how the powers are handled where before you could switch between Thunder, Ice, or Fire in the fly, now you have full control of one power at a time. In order to switch back to another power you have to absorb energy from a fuel-source of that power. So go to a chimney to reactivate smoke, or go to a neon sign to reactivate neon, etc.The level up system is a bit more organized now as well, and finding blast shards (which are used as power up points essentially) is much easier than in the other two.Perhaps my favorite thing about Second Son is the main character. Delsin Rowe is a really cool character, it's easy to like the guy. I think this is mainly due to the fact that Troy Baker did a hell of a job voicing Delsin.All in all, I think it's a fair assumption to make that Infamous: Second Son is the first must-own exclusive for the PS4. I'm a huge Sony fan, and an avid Killzone fan, so I wish I could give this honor to Shadowfall, but the latest iteration of Killzone really did disappoint me in many ways. Infamous, on the other hand, impressed me immensely.

I picked this game up at the day it came out, and I beat it 1 week later. Mind you I didn't sit and play it for several hours a day but I thought it was a bit short. I will try to keep this game spoiler free for those who do not know much of the game.Presentation- I thought the idea for this game was great. It had a great concept of people who gained powers being called bio-terrorists or conduits. I loved the fact that there were pretty much two sides fighting each other. Conduits vs DUP. Pretty much the DUP is the military for taking care of conduits. Everybody is afraid of these bio-terrorists and the powerless people as well as governments/military treat them all like criminals. As a result the military tries to capture every conduit they spot and lock them up just for having spacial powers. This is pretty much the theme of the game for the most part. It kind of reminded me of a revolution.Story- Now honestly I thought the story was going to be really interesting and dark. But in the end I was a bit disappointed by the story. You play as Delsin Rowe who is kind of a delinquent and has a brother who is a cop. I think Delsin is a pretty likable character throughout the game and I liked how he responds to certain situations. The main antagonist is pretty cool too, she is the head of the DUP and she shows that she can be ruthless to get what she wants. She shows no mercy. All of the other characters however I think they could have fleshed them out more. These include Delsin's brother and other conduits who appear in the game. The beginning of the game shows lots of promises but by the time you are half way through the story it starts to go down hill. Once you gain a new power from a character, they have you do a few missions with that person and then the story seems to just toss them aside and forget they exist. They do appear again maybe towards the end but they need more  time for development. You only get maybe 3 missions for these conduits, which is pretty lacking. I thought the story was okay but I think it would've had much more potential.Graphics/Sound - The graphics for the game is probably the highest praise for me. The powers are gorgeous and are done so smoothly. The animations and is really well done too. The ways the powers are done in battle and they each have a nice theme to it. The open world cities are unbelievable good and very well designed. It actually looks like Seattle. There is another city as well but I will let you figure that out.  The voice acting and sound effects are also very good too. Not much else to say other than that.Gameplay- If you played the previous infamous games, then it will pretty much be the same here. The fighting and destruction are fun to always do. They transit very smoothly and I never had a problem with the gameplay. This is also probably it's strongest point in the game along with the graphics and sound. There are 4 different powers you get in the game and are very nicely themed. However I must say I only enjoyed the first two powers the most. The last two felt like the developers slapped it in the game and didn't have too much for a purpose compared to the first two powers. They are cool, but not needed except for the story. I think they could have either done more for them or left them out completely. There is also a leveling system that you can level up you powers by collecting blast shards. However I found the leveling system lacking especially compared to Infamous 2. In infamous 2 you selected whatever powers you wanted in the menu and you could change it up offering a nice variety. It is not like that in this game. While I do like the fact that there are different sources to pick whatever power you want, you can change anything in that desired power whether you wanted maybe a sniper like short of lots of fast shots.Lasting Appeal- I think this is probably one of the biggest thing I was disappointed with. There is not much to do believe it or not. The main story is actually pretty short, you could maybe beat it in about 8 hours or so. As far as side quests go, they were pretty lame and repetitive. You get sections throughout the city and that you need to clear of DUPs. Each area will have a percentage. There are about maybe 6 missions in each sections which ranges from spray painting a billboard/wall to freeing or killing people held in a cage for being suspected of being a conduit. These missions all repeat in all the areas and it gets really repetitive. By the time I was done clearing out the first city, I didn't bother with the side missions in the second city. They were boring, repetitive and not much fun. You also get to search for blast shards through the cities which are carried by drones that you have to shoot done. However I didn't like the fact that they were all able to be seen on the map once you cleared a satellite. It became less of exploring the city and more of fetching the blast shard. I feel that the exploration was not very good. The side missions and blast shards don't really seem to put you in unique places and it kinda gave me no desire to truly explore the city like the first two games did.Overall- I enjoyed the game, and I definitely think everyone should try it at least once for themselves. I was just a bit disappointed that it felt like it was lacking many things in this games compared to the previous Infamous games. I think the developers maybe focused a little too much on the graphics and while they could have focus a little more on other things. I say give it a shot and see if you like it or not. This game is great, but is does lack content. Thank you for taking your time to read my review. Let me know what you guys think, do you agree? Disagree? Ask me any questions that you may have.P.S. The patch that is supposedly to add 5 extra hours of gameplay, the developers seem to only add something new every week, so it's not like you are actually getting 5 hours of content right away. They release a small chunk each week.

If you've unfamiliar with inFamous, the concept is the coolest thing you could ask for in a game.  Every inFamous game is a sandbox with endless freedom, like GTA, but you've got super powers.  While other super hero games are limited to established abilities, whatever was introduced in their respective comics, inFamous gives you Cole MacGrath and now Delsin Rowe, characters with completely fresh powers that grow until the game's completion.inFamous 2, in my opinion was hands down, the best game for the PS3 and my personal favorite game of all time.  Suckerpunch provided the aforementioned concept, incredible voice acting, beautiful graphics, great story & characters, finely crafted cut scenes & well written dialogue and fun, fun, fun gameplay.  It's a 10.  So inFamous Second Son was anticipated with high standards to be met or surpassed.Upon first hearing Delsin talk, I said to myself, "Oh screw this guy."  I immediately missed Cole  But as the story progressed, he quickly grew on me.  There are definitely aspects to Delsin that make for a far more thrilling character to play.  As soon as you get your first power, taking into consideration this is a vast open world sandbox, graphics are absolutely stunning, comparable to Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes.  The fire effects, smoke, streets, lights and reflections, all just pop.  The variety of people occupying Seattle, however, felt lazy.  I saw the same faces over and over again, but I am guessing this was deliberately kept minimal to concentrating efforts where the pay off was obvious.  It just becomes noticeable when some of your missions involve looking for people.I'm big on great music in video games and the score in ISS felt at times like it was trying to be cool.  But generally it worked.  Just occasionally distracting.  Nothing beats inFamous 1's soundtrack in this franchise.When present, story, dialogue and cut scenes are just as solid as inFamous 2.  But these character moments are bare bones, mostly riding the book ends of the game, leaving you longing for much more in between.  The game wants you to care more for these characters than is warranted because they are simply not very involved in the journey.  To this issue, there is no real counterpart to keep you company and enjoy your growth with you like Zeke did for Cole in inFamous.  One very important element lacking in this installment which was present in previous was a sense of urgency, a constant driving force.  Particularly with inFamous 2, the stakes kept getting higher and throughout the entire game there was a looming danger.  inFamous Second Son however doesn't keep you aware of why you're playing.  What sends you on this mission to Seattle doesn't really come up again until the game is over.  The game sought to maintain the serious tone of inFamous, but Delsin doesn't really experience any down points or set-backs like Cole did.Despite the aforementioned shortcomings, inFamous Second Son has some really great surprises.  The previous installments had far more variety in terms of optional side missions and as a completionist, I found myself annoyed at the unforgivably identical side missions that filled each district.  The game plagiarized itself about 20 times.  There is a spray paint side mission in every district, sometimes more than one.  I have no idea why this is part of the game and made to feel important.  It may as well have been a cut scene you are awarded for watching, as that's how much you participate in the spray paint side missions.  They're not even missions.  They're just a hassle you have to do if you want to do everything.  And just when this was about to take it's toll on me, ISS hit me with something strong, near the mid-way point that rejuvenated my energy.  Then it does this again at the 75% mark and even up to the end.  That being said, the second half of the game is far more interesting than the first half.Regardless of your powers, upgrades and the area you are playing, what you you encounter most are the DUP: Depart of Unified Protection.  They all work for the big bad boss you meet at the beginning and know you are going to have to fight.  But what might have helped is if Sucker Punch gave this boss at least one or two mini bosses you had to face.  Instead, you deal with the same henchmen again and again.  And while they get progressively stronger, thusly more difficult and interesting to battle, it can't help but feel a bit redundant.  No other super bosses is pretty disappointing, knowing they did this better in previous installments.The most frustrating thing I learned only after the fact is that I probably shouldn't have been such a completionist until I beat the game, as you are given opportunities between story missions and even post-ending to finish up anything incomplete.  My advice if you haven't played it yet is to follow the story forward whenever the game will allow you in order for you, the player, to appreciate what you are given to play with.Just to be clear, the positive aspects of the game, which are huge and very fun, I can't really discuss, so as not to give away surprises.Summary:Despite the very annoying shortcomings (mainly because I had very high expectations),  ISS feels like a passable continuation.  I have no regrets about my purchase and still love it.  Sucker Punch produced the most beautiful game for the PS4.  It's very fun when you're not doing the uncreative side missions.  With each story mission, the game continues to elevate right up to the end, as it's predecessors do.  While the journey is not as well constructed as inFamous 2, Second Son is certainly the biggest inFamous game with the most options and choices for your main character.  I highly recommend it and still feel that it made the PS4 a worthwhile purchase.  I look forward to the next inFamous installment and will be pre-ordering that as well in whatever the collector's edition is available.  Currently, inFamous 2 still holds the champion title.

I'll start off by saying I LOVED the first two inFAMOUS games for the PS3. They were fantastic in every regard from the look to the gameplay. Getting a PS4, I was excited to play Second Son as I loved the previous games and could not wait for the next-gen inFAMOUS. I can say after about 20 hours of play time, this has to be one of the biggest disappointments I've had in a game. I'll start off with the good...- The environment is amazing. The game looks and feels alive. Every building you can climb up and there are many nooks and crannies to explore- The mo-cap and voice acting is top notch- The whole "bio-terrorist thing" is an interesting story ideaThat's about all I can say that is GOOD with the game. What makes up a game more than anything is the gameplay. It can be the prettiest game ever made but if the gameplay just isn't there, the game will sink as Second Son did.- The gameplay here is awful and difficult. There is no enemy variety whatsoever and the enemies that are in the game are relentless. There is no "dodging". You hide behind a structure or wall or you will be hit.- The smoke and neon powers are cool, but never really come to life. Never did I feel like I was this big bad "bio-terrorist" the game made you up to be. The combat in the game is some of the clunkiest I've ever seen in a game.- The neon powers are underwhelming. You can sprint up the sides of buildings and shoot colorful neon beams from your hands, but that's about it. There is too much of a pause between neon shots that by the time you get 2 or 3 off, the enemy has you down 70% health.- There is no variety in mission design at all. Each mission is a boring "go here, kill this guy" or an extremely irritating "search for the glowing spot in the environment to show you the way to the generator you have to destroy" mission.My biggest complaint with the game is that it's just not FUN to PLAY. It looks great and the mo-cap and voice acting are top tier. The gameplay just never reaches a point where you can say you're actually having fun. I stopped playing about halfway through because playing this game became dreadfully boring and repetitive I can't recommend this game to anyone. There are plenty of games FAR MORE worthy of your money. Pass on Second Son, you will not have fun.

I have beaten this game twice, and I can say with full conviction that this game is a solid title. It has a smooth frame rate, with very rarely any hiccups that I have noticed. This game looks phenomenal, using the power of the PS4 to make a great looking game that is extremely enticing and immersive. Being from Seattle, Sucker Punch nailed their home town into a video game format, and then some. Personally, I feel the love in their city by how much detail they placed into the city, how much detail they put into the citizens, the environment, and so on. Each power looks amazing as well; each has a distinct look, color scheme, and effect on the environment in the form of color, particles, and residue of power left over, ie. Karma moves aftermath. Each power also has a separate color scheme based on the morals you chosen throughout the game. The sound is easily my favorite part of the game, funny enough. I think the sound of a game can either break all immersion a game has tried so hard to make, or it can sink the player deeper into the world the creator has made. This game nails the sound and feel of the game's world; the soundtrack is extremely memorable and exciting, the powers in the game each have a specific sound that adds to the immersion of the game, with each creating a different impact upon the player (for me, each power left a different and specific impression thanks to the color, the sound, and the textures of them). But seriously, the OST for the game is so great, I probably will end up purchasing that just to hear the soundtrack while I walk around or jog. The story in the game is maybe the weakest part, but that isn't because I didn't connect to the characters or anything, but instead I (like many complaints) did not like the moral system in this game. Let me be clear: I loved Deslin, Fetch, Eugene, and Tommy. I love the overall story (I won't go into detail, play it or watch videos on it for they are worth it). The Moral system in this game felt too black and white, however. Too many times I wondered if there might have been opportunities to make a mission or two have multiple branches, with maybe how you choose to, overall, complete your mission be the determination of being evil or good (which in that is arbitrary sometimes as well). And to go a step further, I loved the ending to the game on both playthroughs, but I felt as if I was an Antihero on my evil playthrough, and not so much the evil villain like Cole could have been in previous games, especially Infamous 2. Infamous Second Son made me feel like Deslin was meant to be the good guy, but that might also be because of the canon they chose to follow (the good ending of Infamous 2). In any case, that is my only complaint, for the story and characters were actually fun and interesting, and the free DLC that has come out so far have been very helpful making the story to ISS really become fleshed out, especially Paper Trail. I hope there are more meta-online games like this in the future, not so much that we deserve the free DLC for I would pay for Festival of Blood like DLC any day of the week, but I think it would be awesome to set up a month and a half free DLC game for players centered on a power and to build the background on certain characters, especially Eugene and Fetch who I grew to like quite a lot yet felt there was room to learn even more of them. Lastly, the gameplay itself, which is quick and easy: it is fun. The game feels smooth, fun, exciting, and yet novel with each power. Each power feels different, acts different, and can and should be used differently in many different ways (ie. Neon is the one I use most because it packs a good punch, but it also is accurate and a long-range attack, with a powerful heavy attack and awesome karma attack, whereas Smoke is more of a in and out, powerful and fast attack plan that, when used right, can decimate the enemy easily and quickly.) Overall, this game is amazing, and I still play it a ton despite a Platinum that is easy to earn to be honest. One last criticism, however: once the game is beaten, there isn't a ton of stuff to do. Don't get me wrong, there are still lots of DUP people to beat and lots of side stuff to do, but the issue is that once all major side missions are done, such as the spray painting and whatnot, then there is even less to do. But from what I have seen of the Paper Trail DLC, I love what Sucker Punch is doing to support the game further, and I expect continued DLC along that path. Anyone with a PS4 should in the least play it, but I recommend purchasing this game easily, and anyone on the fence for a PS4 this should defiantly be on your radar as a reason to lean for PS4 (but to be fair, Titanfall is pretty awesome too).

As a big fan of the inFAMOUS franchise, I was really looking forward to Second Son. I still enjoyed it immensely, but the pointless boss fights, incoherent story, and outdated "morality" system made this game less than great.The boss fights are a prime example of why boss fights need to be eliminated from video games. At best, the boss fights are tedious and boring. There is no challenge other than take some hit points off, evade, recharge, take some hit point off, evade, recharge, ad nauseum. At worst, they are a lesson in how to control yourself from ragequitting, especially the final boss. The black and white (or in this this case red and blue) morality system is clichéd and outdated. Life is more than pure good or pure evil, and it's about time that inFAMOUS reflected that.The overall story itself is idiotic. I won't give way any major spoilers, but it's clear from the start of the game that the lead antagonist is a cruel, sadistic woman. The description of persecution from other conduits that you meet along the way (and what they had to go through) support that. Her justification at the end is mind-numbingly bad and does not properly explain her actions. I wish I could go into more, but the ending was nonsensical in the overall arc of the story and so many issues that you learn about during the game were never properly addressed or explained.  As such, you get no resolution of why many the things you learn about during the game actually happened, leading to a very unsatisfying ending. And unfortunately there is one particular point of drama in the game that I feel was thrown in just for the sake of adding drama, and the effect was rather hollow.That said, I still enjoyed the game overall. I've absolutely LOVED the Infamous series.  I received the first after the Sony data was compromised, as a free game from Sony.  I was instantly hooked, and it was perfect timing since the day after I finished it, Infamous 2 was released.  I had never heard of it prior to that, so it was a great "accidental" find.There were things in Infamous 2 that I loved and didn't like as much, mostly centered around the controls.  But this isn't an uncommon thing, just ask any Halo fan about how those games jumped back and forth and couldn't seem to settle on anything.I've played Infamous 1 and 2 so many times, both good and bad karma, and it's always been right up there with Halo for me as something that never seems to get old.  I was a bit uncertain about the new character though during the reveals and trailers leading up to the game's release.  But I was happy to find that I fell into the game without any problems, and the character change isn't an issue for me at all.  There are times when his "altruistic selfishness" is downright charming.Graphics are well done.  I've not had any issues with tearing or stutter or anything so far.  It's very visually appealing.And the powers are enjoyable as well, a nice change of pace from the electrical based Cole.  I do miss the ability to get little charges from so many sources that you could as Cole though, since with Delsin you're limited to burning things - i.e. cars on fire, or chimneys.  So there are fewer chances to charge up.,The shards are still present, and you collect them to upgrade your powers.  But I wish there was a little more clarity in the upgrade paths.  But I do like the menu for those upgrades, a nice flowchart tree branching powers off of the different core powers.However, some of the things with the controls I wish they had done differently.  For example, the "hover" bit is done by pressing the X button to jump and hold it.  But you really have to press it twice, once to jump, then a second time to turn on the hover.  I would have preferred a shoulder button for the hover since it would be a more natural and easy thing rather than always having to double tap it.  Also, having to click the touchpad to pull energy from the smoke - this is awkward, and anything that takes my thumbs off of the joysticks to me is a bad thing, since it impairs quick movements especially when you're in the middle of a fight and recharging.  I did some digging to see if there are alternative layouts for controls, but I couldn't find any.  But even though they can be annoying, just like any other video game franchise that swaps controls around between installments, you *DO* get used to these and they don't seriously impair gameplay.As expected though, even with my dislike of control choices, this game is a pure pleasure to play.  Cole seemed to be easier to control scaling up walls and such, in this one it sometime doesn't have Delsin "grab" things as well like window ledges and such, but that's a small complaint when you're leaping from the tops of buildings and see the incredibly well done graphics of the city spread out around and below you.  The story flows well, and as you progress, you start to get the side missions any Infamous fan is familiar with.  One different thing, as you take control of an area, it isn't suddenly just empty - there are "showdowns" you do in each district once it gets below a certain percentage of DUP control, where basically it's you vs. a bunch of them in a "final" battle for that area.  I really enjoy these as this is where some of the best fighting ends up getting done.Picking up other powers from other conduits is really slick, and a nice change.  By absorbing different power sources then you change between which conduit's powers you want to be using.  The only downside is some have things you love and things you don't, and you can't have all at once, so you can't pick between the best of each to make a single mix of the best things.  But that's to be expected, and it makes for a nice change of difficulty when you absorb another's, and haven't gotten all the powers unlocked yet.  Fortunately for me, my method of gameplay (inadvertently) makes this easier, since I clear all baddies from all areas before I go and do any of the boss fights or character changing missions. So by the time I've absorbed another conduit's powers, the areas are like 3% under UDP control, so I have little to worry about while finding more cores and such.All in all, it's definitely a worthy third installment of one of my favorite games, and if anyone has played the first or second, this one is a must have. First off, I played the first Infamous all the way through and thought it was a decent game at best that wore out its welcome far before the game's conclusion. The combat and parkour style traversal were tedious and melee was practically useless. Once I saw the trailer for this game, I remembered hearing good things about Infamous 2 and that it was an improvement over the first. So I gave the second one a try because it was free on PS Plus and found that it was more of the same and stopped playing after about 4 hours.Those experiences with the first two put a major damper on my expectations for Second Son but I am happy to say that Sucker Punch really knocked this one out of the park. My biggest gripes with the first two games actually became some of my favorite parts of this game. In the first game I would sometimes avoid enemies because of how ineffective my arsenal was to take them on. In this game I go out of my way to pick fights with stray DUP agents just to practice my tricks.The best part of the game is how deep and rewarding the different powers are (I won't spoil them here because if you don't know, it's fun to be surprised). Each power plays very differently, you have your basic melee and ranged attacks (which are actually quite varied), but beyond that the powers are very different and offer different advantages depending on the situation. You might enter a fight with one power but switch in the middle once you realize another power will be more advantageous. Every power has some variation of a dash move and the implementation of this couldn't be better. I've never had so much fun just running from one place to another; so much so that I rarely used fast travel points.The graphics in this game are stunning and make it reeeally hard to go back and play anything I missed on PS3. I highly recommend having photo mode on all the time because freezing the action and taking a peek around is very addicting. I've beaten the game on good karma and I'm not sure I'll be able to resist jumping right back in and playing the game through on the evil storyline.Which brings me to yet another improvement of this game over the others. The karma system is much more than just the big choices you make and the little side missions. Now it can come down to how you attack an enemy and in which way you decide to stop them. The big choices have also been taken up a notch because the bad karma choices are really evil this time around. It'll be very interesting to see how those choices play out.Overall, I cannot recommend this game enough. It's by far the best game I've played on the PS4 and probably the best game I've played this year.
