As an owner of both a current PS3 and a first gen 60 gig PS3 model, I have to say older is better. I miss the PS2 backwards compatibility as the four USB slots in the old version compared to the two in the current models. This Amazonbasics charger gives you the option for more USB plugs. So you can have four controls being charged at once. Perhaps an Eyetoy, two move controllers and a regular PS3 controller at once. There are a lot of plug in options for a PS3 and this accommodates all of them.Unfortunately, this charge hub isn't as good as it could be. First, the circular shape is very awkward. It neither stores nor looks right anywhere. It also doesn't help that this is large for a charge hub. Perhaps a square or rectangle would have been a better design. Second, the charge hub only works when plugged into the PS3 and then only when the PS3 is on, making it a bit odd to use. Finally. you have to plug the charge hub into the wall IN ADDITION to having it plugged into the PS3, which seemed a bit superfluous. Most chargers either let you charge directly from the system or just via a wall socket. To have to have the charge hub plugged into both makes it harder to use and less convenience than other options.The big positive though is how cheap this thing is. Sure you get what you pay for, but the price tag is extremely low compared to other options and this makes a decent, if oddly designed choice, for those who need for plug-ins for their PS3.

This Amazonbasics Controller Charge Hub for PS3 is basically a USB hub with four USB 2.0 sockets. The user can charge up to four PS3 control-devices simultaneously with it. The charge hub measures 3-15/16 inches across and 9/16 inch thick. It comes with two USB 2.0 Standard Type A to Mini-B cables, one measuring approximately 41-1/2 inches and the other 14 inches. It also comes with an AC adapter with 100-240V 50/60 Hz AC input and 5V DC output.Before ordering, Amazon shoppers should know this: To charge a controller, this PS3 charge hub must be plugged into one of the two USB sockets of the PS3 console with the console power ON. It will NOT work independently of the PS3 console. Amazon should have made this point clear on its webpage but didn't. Furthermore, the AC adapter for the hub must also be plugged in. The AC adapter powers the charger and the PS3 console monitors the state of charge of the controllers. When connected properly as instructed in the manual, a tiny blue light on top of the PS3 hub turns on and a red light on the PS3 controller flashes continuously.As a PS3 charger, this unit is quite basic. I find it annoying to have to turn on my PS3 console to charge the controller. There are smart chargers on the market that work independently of the PS3 console, but at a relatively higher price. For shoppers looking for an inexpensive entry-level multi-port charger, this Amazonbasics Controller Charge Hub is a good choice. See my notes below.Note 1: The webpage says, "Access for up to 5 total USB ports". It is a misleading statement. The user might think that he could charge up to 5 devices. There are four USB Type A ports for charging and one USB Mini-B port for connection to the PS3 console.Note 2: For an independent smart charger, check this out:Playstation 3 Energizer Power & Play Charging System.

What is this for?Exactly as the name states, it's a charging hub for PS3 accessories that can be charged via a USB connection.Why do I need this?This product offers the user the ability to charge up to four PS3 accessories at the same time. So if you need help in charging a controller or headset while playing, I guess this product would be quite useful....or is it?How hard is the setup process?Remedial and redundant is the best way to describe the setup process. You connect the charging hub to the PS3 and then you plug in the charging hub. Which for some odd reason you might suspect this gives you the ability to charge your wares while the PS3 is off, yeah, no.Can I use it as a standalone charger or does it need a PS3 all of the time?Which brings us to the horrid part of this product. I don't want to leave my PS3 on all the time to charge my controllers. It just seems to defy the whole purpose of a standalone charger. But here I am, staring at a charging hub that needs toCan I charge any USB device, like an iPad or iPhone?It will charge PS4 controllers, but I'm worried about the underpowered ability of the charging hub to use it for charging it repeatedly. For Apple products, let me just say...no. Anything else, don't even bother, as the power output of this thing is tantamount to a Pop Rock.Does this product provide value to me?Simple answer, no. I give this product two stars because I reserve one star reviews for products that don't work. The fact that I had to keep my PS3 on the whole time was the death knell in this poorly thought product. Also, let's be honest here, who wants to have a Medusa of cords in their living room or gaming room? I plugged in four accessories, took a look at the Indiana Jones snake pit of wires I had, and I could just hear my fiance complain about how it looks in my head. What I wanted from this product was the ability to plug in this hub, be able to charge 4 USB powered items, and live in a land of cupcakes and Unicorn laughter. Sadly, I will be disappointed yet again. I will say this, if you need a charging unit that can charge multiple items and can work as a standalone unit, try out the PS3 Move Quad Dock Pro by dreamGEAR.

The Amazonbasics Controller Charge Hub for PS3 sounds like a good idea, but the execution leaves a lot to be desired. Not only does the hub need to be plugged into an AC outlet, if you're planning on using it to charge your PS3 Controllers, etc., you need to also plug it into the PS3, and the PS3 must be powered on. The hub also only includes 2 USB cables, 1 of which is needed to connect the hub to the PS3. So if you're charging/using more than 1 device, you will need to supply your own USB cables.The Amazonbasics Controller Charge Hub for PS3 does do what it is intended to do and is very inexpensive. The way it does it though, isn't really worth the hassle to me.

Here are the pros and cons of this charger as I see them.Pros:*Officially licensed, with a nice PS logo on the top and a matte black that matches the PS3.*Four ports and all cables included.* Value priced.Cons:*Power cord is relatively short.*Does not charge controllers when PS3 is off.*Relatively large.Summary:If you a USB hub for your PS3 and miss the old Fat (60GB/20GB) units 4 USB ports and want something that looks like Sony made it AND have the shelf space for this AND that shelf isn't too far away from a power outlet then this unit could be for you.  For me though, I mainly needed something that would charge my DS3s when the PS3 was off and this unit doesn't do that which is my biggest complaint with this unit.

The Amazonbasics Controller Charge Hub for PS3 is apparently just a regular, powered 4-port USB 2.0 hub with the PlayStation branding on it. It does require a PS3 connected and powered on in order to charge a controller. DualShock 3 and Move controllers require some type of data transfer between a PS3 and itself before accepting charging from the USB connection. The Charge Hub, like a standard USB hub, doesn't do any of this itself and instead relies on a connected PS3 to do that.The supplied AC adapter powers the hub so that it has enough power to charge multiple controllers simultaneously from a single USB port on the PS3. The adapter supplies about 2A at 5VDC, so you may not be able to charge a high powered mobile devices in addition to controllers at the same time.The Charge Hub comes in a frustration-free box and includes:- 4-port USB 2.0 hub (with a fifth mini-port for connecting to PS3)- AC adapter- 14" USB 2.0 type A to mini B cable- 42" USB 2.0 type A to mini B cableIf you don't mind leaving your PS3 on while charging your DualShock 3, Move motion and navigation controllers, the Charge Hub is a good, cheap choice to have. Otherwise, you may want to consider another charger that is designed to charge the controllers independently without a PS3.

This charge hub is underpowered which causes unnecessary hassles.The charger needs to be plugged into an outlet AND a PS3 USB port in order to charge Dualshocks or Move controllers (I tested both). There are plenty of 3rd-party chargers that work fine plugged into an outlet only. I suspect the reason this Amazonbasics charger needs dual plug-in is because it is a low-voltage charger that needs the extra juice from the PS3.Other observations:-When the PS3 is off, the controllers do not charge. This can be a big inconvenience.-It does not power any PS3 device (Dualshock, Move, Eye) when plugged into only an outlet OR only a PS3 USB port.-When plugged into an outlet and a generic 2.1 amp USB charger, the controllers do not charge.The output listed on the AC adapter is 2.0 amps. Divide this among the 4 USB ports and you are only getting 500ma per port which is very weak these days.If you plan on buying this as a generic USB hub to charge non-PS3 devices like phones, tablets, etc., it does work for this purpose as a low-voltage charger only. When I plugged in my Kindle, it gave me a low-voltage charger notification (this means it will take a much longer time to charge compared to a better powered charger). Thus it is not ideally suited to be a universal charging hub.Note: Two usb to mini-USB cables are included and 1 of them needs to be plugged into your PS3. So if you want to charge more than 1 device, you will need to supply the necessary cable.The bottom-line is this charger works but it utilizes a PS3 USB port and is generally underpowered. Nothing will charge when the PS3 is off which is a major negative.Instead of this charging hub, I would recommend getting one of the dozens of charging stations (search Amazon for "ps3 charging station") that works via outlet only thus independent of PS3 status.

I will start off with saying that I don't have many add-ons for my PS3; just a standard controller. But, I have always wanted something to charge that controller without having to have my PS3 powered up. Most were more expensive than I was willing to pay, so when I saw this item, I thought I would give it a shot. The first thing I noticed, when plugging the device into the wall, was that there was nothing to indicate that it was recieving power. Just to make sure that it wasn't a problem with the outlet, I changed the device to another outlet that had been used with other electronics. I plugged in the device, but still received no indication that the controller was getting powered. I left the item overnight, and returned in the morning; when I powered up the PS3, it still told me my controller needed a charge.So, there are two definite negatives with this device:It doesn't have any way of letting you know your controllers are getting charged.It feels pretty flimsy, so it could have easily have been damanged in shippment.I don't feel like I can recommend this device; for now, I will keep charging using my PS3 fully powered.

Will this device charge your PS3 accessories? Yes. Would I recommend it? Absolutely not in most cases.The one use I would recommend this for is if you constantly have three or four players locally and have USB charge cables for all of them, because this only charges while the PS3 is actually on (*not* just in standby mode). For most people, this is just inconvenient; the point of a charger is to charge the controller when you are not using it so it's fully charged when you're ready to play. You'll also need a free outlet near your PS3 because this requires both an A/C connection to a power outlet and a USB connection to the PS3.I should also note that the plug is one that "hangs down" from the outlet (think the charger plug from early-2000s cell phones), so you'll need to plug it in the bottom outlet if plugging it directly into the wall or an in-line surge protectorThat being said, for the relative expense, it's very well built (just like all the other AmazonBasics products I've had over the years) and the circular shape mitigates cord entanglement somewhat. It's strictly the odd design choices (only charging while the console is on despite having an oversize power plug) that limit its appeal.

Like others have reported, this hub will NOT charge the controllers UNLESS it's plugged into the console AND the console is powered on.That said, I already have independent chargers for all my controllers so I don't have much use for this for that reason although the product description uses this as its main selling feature.What I DO find it useful for, however, is for playing Rock Band 3.  When Sony released the slim model for the PS3, they made the unfortunate design decision to take 2 of the 4 USB ports away.  This hub, however, works fine to plug in 4 Rock Band peripherals into leaving the additional USB port open to plug the keyboard in, etc.So while it does have its minuses as a charging alternative (despite having a separate AC adapter), it works great as a hub.  However, many PS3 users may not have use for it since very few games require more than 2 USB ports to begin with.  Depending on your usage, this may or may not work well for you.

Most of the other reviews have detailed what makes this hub a success and a diasppointment.  Yes, you can charge multiple controllers, but the PS3 has to be on??  Gimme a break.  The point of charging a wireless controller is so you don't have to charge it when you're playing.  The way this hub is configured, you'll never be able to do that on a consistent basis.  Sure, it's only 7 dollars, but even for that price this is a hassle to use.  First time I've ever said this about an Amazonbasics product, but this device is a definite fail.
I got this to streamline the cords from my PS3 and it works great.  It hooks up via the charging cable and charges the controllers quickly and all at once.

This nifty device includes two cables (one short, one long) for controllers and a power adapter.The instructions recommend plugging the hub to the adapter with a USB from your PS3, then you get to work charging various devices like the Eye or a Vita. The hub can simultaneously charge four PS3 devices.After the hub connects to a PS3, the charging begins as normal. It's pretty awesome.

I was very disappointed in this charge hub.  I was looking to bypass purchasing an expensive charger and utilize this with all the extra USB cables we have.  What I did not realize was that it will not work without it being plugged into a wall outlet AND the PS3 that is powered ON.  I wanted to use this to charge controllers without having the PS3 on.  The only thing I can think of that will make this at all useful for me is on the rare occasion when I have 4 dead controllers/Moves/Eyes then I could charge them all at once. Then at least it is better than only having the two outlets built into the system.For those who don't mind having their PS3 on, and have a handy wall outlet, this might be an inexpensive alternative for you, but it was not what I was looking for at all.

PROS:+ Can charge 4 devices at onceCONS:- Will not charge devices when PS3 power is off- Power cord ends in a "box" instead of a NEMA connector plug- Power cord for the unit is only 3.5 feet longI used to have a PS3 "fatty" with the 4 USB ports. Due to my gaming habits, 60 GB wasn't enough storage, so I upgraded to a 250 GB slim. The only drawback was a loss of 2 USB ports.I figured I'd give this a chance because I wanted to find a low-cost alternative to charge my PS Move controllers and my Dualshock controllers. Unfortunately, the low cost gave me high aggravation.To start, this hub only works if you have a cord connected to a free USB port on the Playstation 3 _AND_ a connected power supply.If you have your Playstation 3 next to a power outlet, this won't be a problem...but in my case, the cord is 43 inches long and it's too short to reach the top of my 49-inch high entertainment center. Plus, the plug is an I.T.E power supply which means it ends in a box instead of a standard 2-prong plug.**I've uploaded a picture to the Customer Image Gallery for you**I had to use an extension cord just to connect the power supply!Once I did this, the hub worked fine. It worked on my Dualshock controllers, my PS3 headset, and my Move controllers.If this hub had a cord the length of the one included in thePlayStation Move Charging Station(which is 103 inches, just over 8.5 feet), I would have easily given this 5 stars...but the short plug ruins the convenience of the product.Spend a few extra bucks, there are plenty of charging stations out there which don't require connection to the PS3 and a power supply at the same time. I'd recommend passing on this one.

I finally got time to write a review for this game but there is so much content in this game that I find myself being pulled away to continue playing rather than write a review. 5+ months later, I can finally sit down and write something about Disgaea D2. Please note there IS spoilers abound in this review mainly concerning characters (but I honestly thought it was obvious) and it's a long detailed review.Disgaea D2 decides to go back to the original cast after fans demanding that Laharl and his vassals become the main characters again. This was already hinted in the post game of Disgaea 4 where Laharl clearly states that he’s going to be the main character after Valvatorez. Sure enough, we get a trailer announcement that the next Disgaea game is a direct sequel to the original game.The story is very simple but does seem to jump around from time to time (but never actually creating plot holes). 10 years after the events of the first game, the Netherworld and Celestia have a pact with each other. The first arc starts with Laharl still trying to get the other demons to recognize him as the Overlord (and the reason why no one has apparently recognized him is that he never made himself known…despite the fact he made that huge challenge in the first game where he destroyed everyone that wanted his position as Overlord but demons must have short memory loss.) However there are a trio of demons that go by Krichevskoy Group who refuse to acknowledge Laharl as the Overlord and that his father was the better one and that they knew Laharl’s father better than him therefore they deserve to rule. This despite the fact they resort to cowardly tactics and/or understand the heart that Krichevskoy had. This technically lasts for three chapters before the plot moves on to something more noteworthy that was foreshadowed in the opening and the beginning of the first chapter. You get a filler chapter with the infamous gender bender of Laharl-chan (that really does nothing to move the plot along unless you count character development because the chapter is treated as comedy and while brought up multiple times by the NPCs, its not brought up again) before the plot shifts to the Yuale flowers that are covering the Netherworld. Demons think angels are trying to invade the Netherworld and the relationship between the two races are getting thin again so Laharl and co have to do all in their power to find out what is causing the change in the Netherworld.In all honestly, there are no real plot twists in the actual story. Like the game and content given out before the game was released likes to say stuff like “Is Sicily really Laharl’s little sister?” Or “What is Xenolith’s connection to Etna?” You just have to look at the character and say otherwise. Speaking of characters though, this game does justice for Laharl and co. After much flanderization in games after the first one, the group manages to go back to post character development of the first game allowing the viewer to see that “Yes the first game did matter. Laharl did not go back to being the card carrying villain. Yes Laharl was always a brat but the other games tend to make him a bigger jerk for comedy purposes. The same went for Etna and Flonne as they weren’t as obsessed with being flat chested in the first game as later games would like you believe (lets not talk about how Etna’s segment post game of Disgaea 4 dragged out her flat chest and her desire for a bigger chest). Flonne also while the original love freak, it was not used to the extremes again shown as Disgaea 4 (then again they are at their worse in Disgaea 4 in terms of one of their major character tics being used for comedy purposes). This game tones it down for the most part or uses it for the most important situations at hand (when Flonne goes Magical Girl, that's all she talks about for the most part but hey, it's a parody of the Mahou Shoujo genre).Anyways, the three characters that the game tried to push are newcomers Sicily, Xenolith and Barbara who apparently replace the space crew (Gordon, Jennifer and Thursday) as major characters. This is odd given the role of the human characters but the plot noticeably avoids mentioning the human world and just focuses on the problems with angels and demons. Despite promoting them, Sicily is the only one that is a main character while Barbara only shows up when its convenient for her without adding much besides a difficult boss and a huge annoyance with her personality. As for Xenolith…he obviously plays a huge role in the game…SPOILERS HERE. Scroll past unless you already know about the plot twist!Sicily is Laharl’s little sister. The anime played this plot before and showed that it was a lie and I bet the creators did the same thing to make players have a similar mindset. No one believes Sicily when she says that she’s Laharl’s little sister…except Xenolith ironically. Gameplay wise actually shows that she has some similarities such as having Angelic Fist to Blazing Fist and her affinity for spears despite the fact that she’s a magic oriented character (and the King is known for using spears as his main weapon). I won’t say how this is possible but its what a lot of fans expected (and the only logical reason without making a plot hole of the first game). Personality wise, she fits the little sister trope while having a personality of her own and having her own insecurities like how she’s an angel instead of a demon making it hard to prove that she is the little sister.Xenolith is Etna’s older brother and serves as the anti villain of the game. And I state anti-villain because Xenolith’s actions are incredibly sympathetic…except for how he goes about doing it (and even then the reason why he’s doing it becomes justified when you actually hear his side of the story). And Xenolith being the older brother to Etna does not contradict anything if you recall that Etna has no memories and that either she didn’t all of her memories back or she can’t remember that far back. We sadly don’t know about Xenolith’s character given he’s described as a person who only speaks when spoken to and even then its straight to the point without wanting anyone to get too close. And Xenolith is the hardest main boss in the franchise (harder than the boss of the first game).SPOILERS END HERE.Barbara is just a wasted character in comparison as she is used to introduce the female knight that works identical to the heavy knight except…female. The sea angel is a monster class introduced too and the angel class finally split into two male and female angels that have different abilities instead of letting the angel class being female with a few exceptions.But beside the characters and the story, everything else has improved immensely that is already covered by other reviewers. The most noticeable examples are that items are divided into three categories now: common, rare and legendary so you don’t have to worry about the number on it anymore when obtaining said item. The item shop always has the same weapons and will constantly add when you pass bills for stronger weapons. This makes things easy to collect all the items in the game (but you need to go into the item world or level the item up to get the rare or legendary version of the item). The item pocket also allows you to carry 999 items at all times.The Dark Assembly is easier now where there is always someone behind you that acts as a Legendary Assembly. They tend to be able to influence whether a bill passes or not and even if it's a character you have, don’t be surprised if they screw you over and say no. You can beat the demons up if they refuse to pass a bill or do the new option of bribing the assembly with money (and you need a lot of it for them to pass). This should have been in the first game given that NPCs tend to joke about this. The item assembly is also in the item world now and can be accessed at any time as long as you have the money to pay to enter the item assembly instead of having to go ten floors and asking for the demons to pass a bill that might not pass because you pay with a lot of mana instead. Additionally Innocent characters can now be placed in a storehouse instead of having to put the innocent in a weapon and forget where you put it. If you go over the limit of how much an innocent can have then it simply starts a new set of innocent to stack up.Now that the system goes back to the weapon mastery and master/apprentice, mana is easier to maintain and keep in contrast to Disgaea 3/4. The master/apprentice system actually allows for a weapon mastery rank to go up depending on the character like if Flonne is the apprentice to Sicily, her staff goes from A to S (with the highest being SS). Alas even with this boost, some characters can only go up to C at most even if you reincarnate them and they are best at said weapon. You can have one character have multiple apprentices and can learn every skill and magic in the game without the need of having to have the exact amount of skill to learn a move from a sword or gain a certain level.Class changing is easier now because you don’t have to reincarnate to unlock the class. You get the class by leveling up the common unit and then transferring to the next class until you lock all six tiers. Additionally monster classes are unlocked once you defeat them (while with the human classes, you have to complete a certain chapter because even if you fight archers in the item world, you can’t use them until after chapter 4). Capturing enemies are easy because its based on the level of said characters and you can only capture an enemy if you have the class.The best feature I feel that is added is the cheat shop. Despite its name, this allows you to change how you want the game to play. You want to earn more EXP rather than balancing the money and mana you get during battle out? You can change it so where EXP is rampart and the other areas are non-existent. You want a smaller item world to get to the anchor instead of a random medium size item world? You can do that too! The best part though is in the item world; you can get rid of geo blocks effect. This makes things a whole lot easier unless you want to earn double the amount of EXP if an enemy is on that space.We’re almost done. In battle, the throw command was changed so you can throw in any direction rather than just north, south, east or west. This saves a lot of time and makes throwing missions easier. In battle, characters can have two evilities (everyone starts with one) and can only get a second one if they max out a relationship with another character. Yes this game has relationship values that boosts stats and allows for more opportunities of a combo attack or a team attack. The relationship value is important to get some endings of the game and while its best to have high relationship values, lowering them allows you to get a rare innocent that makes soloing maps easier. Relationship values show in the base when you talk to characters. They gain a point if you speak to them, work together in battle and give them items if they show up in the dark/item assembly. If they have a master/apprentice, they get more points together. The easiest way honestly to build the relationship up is to stack a tower and just kill all the enemies. I think what I like about the relationship value is that each character says something to someone when they speak and it changes depending on how high the value is. At the highest value, you can get adorable conversations that bring out more about the character. But lets say you maxed out Laharl and Etna’s relationship value. Etna is less snarky the higher the relationship value (plus post game, she brings up how she intends to leave the castle to go train leading directly to the events of Disgaea 2). My favorites ones are with characters from the other Disgaea games or outside of the franchise that have conversations. Most of the DLC characters have conversations with each other such as Adell and Rozalin (god they have the best relationship value dialogue that confirms that they a great couple). Surprisingly Axel actually talks to Alex from Makai Kingdom despite the fact they have never interacted in any of the game prior (but the dialogue implies that they know who each other are and seem to be very close. Insert fan theories here.) And of course the Fenrich/Valvatorez/Artina triangle is still present (luckily due to the fact that Artina is time traveling from Disgaea 4 and how Valvatorez and Fenrich are seen before the events of Disgaea 4, Fenrich won’t be ripping Artina’s head off).My final score for this game is 95/100. The few nitpicks I had was that all the DLC characters have a trophy. You don’t need the DLC to get the universal trophy in the game. HOWEVER, on the PS3, the thing will not show up as 100 percent if you do not purchase the DLC. There are at least 17 DLC characters (Rasberyl is free and Fuka and Desco come in a package). The fact that many of the DLC characters were pushed back a date (I’m looking at you Gig) created more annoyance. Finally there are glitches that freeze the game. I’m pretty sure with the recent update that the game doesn’t glitch anymore but I wasn’t happy when post game I was going to beat Barbara and the game froze because I shot a geo block and the geo effect crashed the game (no data was lost though and this is the only time it ever happened). Finally, by giving Asagi the chance to be the main character (since you can use anyone at the base) it kind of defeated the purpose of the joke that she can’t be the main character but if she gets a game soon then the joke is coming to an end anyway.

When the original Disgaea came out in 2003 on the Playstation 2, it stood out because it was just so... different.  A complete satire of the genre.  Instead of saving the world, your goal was to conquer it.  There were exaggerated stat values, damage values and just all around absurd systems in play.  Over the years Disgaea has maintained a cult status among SRPG players.  But more than a decade later it's hard for Disgaea to have the same impact outside of its fanbase.  It's a good game, to be sure, but Disgaea is no where near as groundbreaking or original as it used to be.  Some things here feel like a by the books inclusion without taking too many steps forward to help Disgaea evolve.  There isn't much that separates D2 from Disgaea 4, for instance.D2 is a direct sequel to the first game and focuses on Laharl, Etna and Flonne.  Laharl is the overlord of the underworld, but what he's soon finding out is that not everyone is actually okay with him being in charge and ruling the world.  A resistance that preferred Laharl's father sets out to challenge him.  More than that, a few interesting things are happening in the underworld that are just all around strange.  From flowers suddenly blooming to Laharl spending a short period of time as a woman.  What exactly is going on in the underworld?  And who is responsible for all this turmoil?D2 Disgaea pretty much sticks to a lot of the same tried and true conventions of other Disgaea games.  The story is carried out in skits where portraits of characters face other portraits.  It's peppered with the same voice acting you've always known and the same type of humor.  It's a Disgaea game through and through.  It also utilizes a lot of familiar tunes you've heard in just about every Disgaea game.In terms of gameplay it's about the same.  You can explore Laharl's castle, but you'll always have to select an episode to progress the story along by going through various episodes.  Battling is about the same as you remember.  You'll begin each battle by sending out your characters through the base panel.  You can have up to ten characters sent out at a time.  Your characters have their own weapons and skills they can utilize.  More than that, the characters also each have what's called an "evility" that may help them out.  Some have evilities that'll boost the stats of the characters around them.  Others make it so they take less damage from elemental attacks.  It's an interesting system, but it isn't just for show.  Your enemies also have evilities and you can bet that some maps are designed for you to keep it in mind.  On one map, for instance, I faced off against knights who got a 20% increase in stats for each enemy that defeated.  By the time I got to them I had to plan very carefully how to go about the situation.And generally speaking, this is what is very nice about Disgaea.  These are not handholding games.  Once you get past the tutorial stages, Disgaea doesn't insist on guiding you through each map.  This is because every battle isn't just about making sure you are strong enough to defeat each enemy.  Thanks to the returning Geo System many battles are treated like a puzzle.  One where not only do the enemies matter, but so does the terrain.For those unfamiliar with the Geo System, every map has titles that are colored as well as the normal scenery.  On some titles rest a Geo Symbol.  They can have various different characteristics.  One may give you 50% more EXP and another might grant you an additional attack.  Not all of them work for you.  Sometimes you might find an Enemy Boost Geo Symbol.  Whatever the case, when a Geo Symbol is on a colored title then EVERY tile of that Color grants that buff or debuff.  So if an Attack+1 Geo Symbol is sitting on a red tile, then all red tiles are affected.  Any character standing on a red tile is affected as well.  Meaning that when they attack, they will attack twice.  It's a good system, but the game utilizes it more to impact your strategy and provide another obstacle.  It's very rare that the Geo Symbols are present with the task of aiding you.  That's not to say you won't find moments like this.  As a result there are also plenty of maps the game has that are specifically there for grinding up your level or getting more currency.The Geo Symbols, however, can be destroyed.  Any time they are, they will change the color of the panel to correspond with the geo symbol you have destroyed.  But only if it isn't the same color as the tile.  Thus, destroying a red geo symbol on a blue tile will then turn all the blue titles red.  If, however, you destroy a red geo symbol on a red tile nothing will happen.  If any geo symbols are on the same color and they get destroyed because of another one's destruction then you'll chain them together.  It may seem like there is little point to destroying geo symbols and getting chains.  But there is.  Every map also has a bonus gauge that fills up to nine levels.  Destroying Geo symbols and creating chains is the fastest way to do this.  The more full your bonus gauge is, the greater your bonus.  And the bonus can range from rare items to additional experience.Disgaea has never been a game that holds your hand.  In fact, it's by far one of the least hand holding SRPGs out there.  Once you're past the tutorial that is it.  More than that, the difficulty curve increases quite drastically.  Disgaea is not a game that one can simply power through.  You will find yourself having to stop and grind.  This is not an SRPG you simply rush through.  Luckily the game has various means of helping you grind.  None of more use than the item world.A staple in Disgaea since the very first game, the item world allows you to enter any item in your inventory and level it up.  This makes your weapons and armor more powerful.  It raises the potency of your healing items etc.  Mostly, however, it's actually just a good way to grind.  Each item is at least thirty floors deep.  If it is a rare variant of the item or a legendary variant, however, you can go deeper than thirty levels.  You can go down sixty for rare items or one hundred for legendary.  Each floor is randomly generated and may be covered with various geo panels and symbols at random.  The goal is to either fight your way through each map, or find the exit.  Along the way you'll also find a lot of different random bonus rooms.  Some that sell rare and legendary items.  Some that might just be filled with chests.  Others that might contain monsters set to challenge you.  Either way, the item world has a lot of variety to it and will keep you on your toes.  Obviously the more powerful the item, the more powerful the enemies are in there.Each item also has residents that can be used to make certain stats grow faster than usual.  It's interesting to play around with all of this stuff and see what you get.There's more to Disgaea, however.  You can also go into the Dark Assembly and pass laws.  These laws will impact certain aspects of the game itself.  At one point you might find the enemies aren't strong enough and make them stronger.  Later on this opens up additional maps for you.  But you'll also need the Dark Assembly to make more characters for you, reincarnate other characters (where a certain percentage of their stats carry over) and to access some neat little tricks such as the infamous Prinny Day.  All that being said, there is a new type of shop introduced into D2: Disgaea called the cheat shop where you can, quite literally, tweak with the game system to your desire.  You have the option to increase the amount of experience you obtain for defeating enemies for instance.  You can also make enemies stronger, select to turn off geo panels and symbols in the item world or leave everything as it is.  The game WILL encourage you to use this quite a bit.  The further you get in the game the more options are available and the more you're allowed to tweak the system.For those new to Disgaea all of this can feel overwhelming and incredibly complex.  Some of it is.  For the returning player, however, this is pretty basic DIsgaea stuff.  And that may be the only real problem with D2.  It's a good game, but it's so familiar that Disgaea doesn't really do anything that really stand out the way it used to.  This is hardly a bad thing in the long run, but it certainly doesn't make for the same ground breaking success Disgaea was a decade ago.  It hasn't quite become stale yet, but it doesn't feel like it wants to be anything different either.  The humor and the heart are there for sure.  No doubt, gameplay wise, it may be one of the strongest Disgaea's out there.  But I still can't help but note that it doesn't do enough to separate itself from the games before it.  It has a few things but not quite enough.A lot of the sprites are pretty much the same as before.  There's a nice distinct anime look to them, but many of them are just higher resolution sprites that you've already seen since the very first Disgaea game.  There aren't too many new or unique designs as it is.  Like so much of the gameplay a lot of the graphics and sprites you've already seen before.  Some of the animations for spells and skills are different, but chances are you'll tire of seeing them over and over again and simply toggle the animations off.Disgaea is still as strong as ever.  But here's to hoping there's more of a spin put onto the formula the next time around.  The series as a whole still manages to offer a lot that other SRPGs do not and for that I'm grateful.  That being said, if you are a Disgaea fan there's no reason not to pick this up.  Small gripes aside, Disgaea fans should really enjoy this.

I've been a fan of Assassin's Creed since the release of the first game. So it's been pretty interesting to see how far the series has come. In the end it's become one of those games that I can only judge on game play alone, and with that it has pretty much delivered. At this point, to be honest, I think only the most diehard fans of the series still care about the overall story. I pretty much lost interest with the third one. Still as disappointing as that game was it hasn't made me toss the series aside as a whole since it had it's moments. Since I got this on the Wii U I can say its not that different from the other versions. Visually its superior to the PS3 and Xbox 360 versions. Game-play wise the only difference I noticed is that the tablet is given map duty which does clear up the UI a bit. You can even play on the tablet which doesn't take away much since it looks really good on it.So from the 13 Colonies we now end up the Golden Age of Pirates. Taking on the role of Connor's grandfather, a Welsh privateer named Edward Kenway. Something I appreciated about this game in particular was Kenway who seems to be a much better character than Connor was. Since this one is based in a time period not to far behind from the third game there are many game-play aspects that are pretty similar. You've got your signature daggers, your pistols, smoke bombs, etc etc what only seems different inventory wise is that he duel wields his swords and a dart gun you get later on. Though despite that the combat feels a lot smoother than it did in the third game. Another thing that is different is architecture. This Golden Age of Pirates has a lot more to offer in regards to climbing and jumping off from than Colonial America did. Everything on land is pretty much a debugged version of the third with a few goodies added in like side missions.Probably the strongest part of the game play though is sea faring. The best part of the third game was brought back and beefed up.  I can't really recall how many hours I spent sailing the Jackdaw (name of Edward's ship) around. All I can say is that it was a lot. As soon as I was given the ability to free roam over the whole map, I completely dropped out of the story all together. Instead I went on to raid British convoys at sea, destroying Spanish forts, obsessively tracking down every bit of treasure I could find, even going out into a rowboat and hunting sharks. Finally I had sunken every legendary ship, destroyed every fort, treasury was overflowing, and had nearly driven the large sea fauna to extinction that I begrudgingly went back to the main story.Then thats where it kind of fell off. If there is one thing that really bugged me about the main story game-play it was the "tailing missions". These bits of game-play have been in the series since the first game but it seems as though Ubisoft has done little to improve them. In fact it feels as though they have gotten worse. Step out of the circle you lose, get seen by a single guard you lose. Also as stated earlier the main storyline (aside from Edward's) is just not very interesting. Especially when we see Edward slowly turn into another dogmatic assassin. It got the point where I only did main missions to unlock new toys to play with and as soon as I got them I'd disappear into the ocean again. Though like in the third you are interrupted by the world outside the animus though it's no where near as annoying as the Desmond missions.Overall the game was very fun. You can sink a lot of hours into the side missions and mini games alone without having to go back to the main story which while better than the thirds still leaves a lot to be desired. If you want to play a nice open world game that you can invest quite a bit of time into, this is one you can sink your teeth into. The naval game-play is awesome and I was happy to see this brought back. In the end I'd recommend it.The Good-Game-play, there is a lot you can do and battles at sea are very fun and entertaining-A lot of room for customization regard weapons, your ship, and other things-Visuals, graphics are great from the very lifelike port cities to the open sea-Runs great on the Wii U, and the tablet goes pretty well with itThe Bad-While Edward's story is pretty fun, the main story overall is kind of bland and (personally) I lost interest in it a long time ago

I'm 50 hours into AC4, and the game is STILL fun. I've completed the campaign, explored every location, collected all Mayan artifacts, chests, bottled messages, animus fragments, manuscripts, etc. I've also completed all Assassin contracts, naval contracts, naval fort challenges, crafting challenges, etc. But there's STILL more to do, and most importantly - I'm still having a blast! This is, quite simply, the greatest open world I've ever seen in a game, and it's a joy to behold and explore. I typically don't enjoy open world type games too much, but this one is just about perfect, enhanced with intelligent "fast travel" options (not just for major locations, but for locations within other locations!), clearly marked objectives, and a beautifl ship that is magnificent to pilot across the open waters.Though the combat (both on foot and aboard the Jackdaw) is fun and intuitive, my favorite parts of this game is the exploration. It's such a joy to sail across the Carribean, diving through sunken ships, searching for loot while attempting to avoid the notice of the circling Great White sharks... or slinking through a smuggler's cove, attempting to relieve the pirates of their stolen goods... or finding a new island with hidden secrets and interesting wildlife.There is so much detail AND content packed into AC4, it's astonishing... it's clearly a labor of love, and one of the few games where you can actually see why it required hundreds of developers, programmers, and artists. It's so much fun, and such a beauty to behold, I still look forward to my trips into the animus, and I'm hoping for my content, in addition to the Freedom Cry DLC (I have not tried the multiplayer yet). When I'm playing AC4, I can almost feel the sea breeze against my face, the salt on my lips, and the spray of water against my skin... it's one of the best games I've ever experienced.

What a fantastic game Ubi ended up with here. ACIII was a good game in my opinion. But, it was held down in some ways by featuring a lackluster antagonist in Conner when compared to his predecessor in Ezio. ACIV rectifies that greatly with Edward. Edward is fun to play as, has a great personality, and fits his role perfectly. One of the biggest pluses is that the naval battles (one of the highest points of ACIII) are back in Black Flag and even more plentiful. The Wii U specifically, once again, has the advantages of the Gamepad. Always having a full map readily available, not having to go into a separate menu, is a big plus for me. Also, like in ACIII, I enjoy watching the cutscenes on the Gamepad when they happen then looking back to the TV for gameplay. Visually, it's a step up from the X360/PS3 versions, but not as good at smaller details like PS4/XBO in areas like water effects and plants.Of course one of the biggest things in this game's favor is...You get to be a pirate! It's almost baffling to see that no other big AAA games have really gone down this road before. It is so much fun just taking a break at times and sailing the ocean. Listening to your crew singing their shanties is so much fun. Then, being able to customize your ship is a huge win. Obviously, the more you progress the better you can make your ship, thus the bigger the battles you can get into and get bigger loot and more equipment for upgrades and such. One complaint I will give about the game, and this is just me, is that they went with the first person perspective during the "present day" sections. Getting rid of the character to identify with during those sections like you had previously with Desmond. Not a big deal, just something I wasn't a fan of. But, other than that, it's really nothing I came across that I find I can complain about.Overall, this is a fantastic game. Even though, I enjoy all the games in this series, this is the best installment since ACII, which is my favorite of the entire series. But, now that i've finished this, ACII may be knocked to second place. If you're a fan of Assassin's Creed this is a game you should absolutely pick up. If you've ever wanted to live out the life of a pirate in a big open world environment you should absolutely pick this up. Great job by Ubisoft....Now if they can just give us that Assassin's Creed game set in Japan we'll be all set :-)

A note about personal bias:  I like pirates.  My favorite attraction at Disneyland has always been "Pirates of The Caribbean", and "The Curse of The Black Pearl" is on my list of Top 20 movies of all time.  That said:"Assassin's Creed IV:  Black Flag" STILL lived up to expectations.I put in between 50-60 hours on this game, and they were nearly all Worthy.  Is it a perfect game?  No, of course not, no game is, and I'll list some Cons below (as well as some Pros), but first, let me hit on what I consider to be the 3 major pillars of gaming:1.  Story:  For me, this is usually the weakest, and least important, aspect of most video games.  But despite the sci-fi wraparound element Ubisoft insists on flogging to death with their Assassin's Creed franchise, the actual pirate portion of the story was pretty decent, hitting most of the classic pirate tropes you'd want to experience.  And fortunately, this pirate portion comprises well over 90% of the total story, so it gets an overall thumbs up.2.  Gameplay:  Mostly good, and sometimes great.  The good is standard stealth and combat mechanics.  Some have complained that combat is too easy (Counter + Kill + Chain), but I enjoy feeling powerful - and if you want to challenge yourself, just choose not to counter-kill or drop any smoke bombs.  The great continues to be the ship battles, well expanded from their introductory success in Assassin's Creed 3.  You earn upgrades for your ship as you continue to play and, again, it makes you feel like you're genuinely earning Lord of The Seas status.3.  Immersion:  This is the biggest reason I personally play video games:  To inhabit a wholly created world, whether it be historic, contemporary, fantasy, or sci-fi.  And here, "Black Flag" delivers in a big way.  There are major ports to explore (Havana, Nassau, and Kingston), and each has a different art design.  There are also unmarked islands and inlets to discover and, again, each is a little different - some are misty, some are covered with Mayan ruins, some are built on stilts.  And then there's all the ocean between them, filled with ships to sink (or board), wrecks to dive, and sea life to hunt (with a fun harpooning mini-game).  And you can run, climb, or parkour over almost all of it in a most satisfying way.  Like previous Assassin's Creed titles, the environment is really (for me) the biggest star of the show.Now, onto the promised Pros and Cons:Pros:- Beautiful, varied, pirate-y (?) scenery.- Good balance of Main and Side missions.- Plenty of activities (hunting, crafting, naval contracts, assassin's contracts, looting) and collectibles (treasure maps/chests, animus fragments, seas shanties) to keep you busy.- Sense of exploration and discovery.- Overall fun feel.Cons:- The sci-fi "Animus" wraparound.  I hated being taken out of the pirate story without warning and being forced to complete some tedious mini-mission in contemporary times.  Further, while the detailed rendering of the 18th century Caribbean was beautiful, the sequences back at "Abstergo" looked like they were leftover from a PS2 generation game.- Not all the gameplay was great, or even good.  Some of it was downright irritating.  Case in point:  Follow missions.  Where you have to stealthily follow a couple guys for a while and eavesdrop on their conversation - i.e., 10 minutes of walking around trying to avoid detection - which is an AUTO FAIL - just to listen to an exposition dump.  And there were A LOT of these.- The requisite number of bugs and glitches although, I must say, for an "Assassin's Creed" game, there might have been actually FEWER of these than usual!However, at the end of the day, the important point is, the Pros FAR outweigh the Cons in "Black Flag".So belay yer delay, matey, and unfurl all sheets to the wind for one of the best games of theYARRRRR![Couldn't resist.]

First I would like to say that while I have played and enjoyed the assassins creed games I have never been amazed by them in the way that some people have been, however that changed entirely with this game. There were so many things that I loved and a few things that I really hated as well.After turning on the game and starting to play, the first thing that hit me was how beautiful the world was. You can certainly tell that the creators spent a great deal of time making sure the world looked flat out incredible. It was a nice breath of fresh air from so many other games where the worlds looked alright but not really stunning by any means. I also liked the huge amount of collectibles incorporated in this game, not just in the cities but also on random islands in the middle of the ocean. It added many extra hours of exploring and game play onto the game as well as quite a bit more satisfaction having collected every treasure chest, animus piece, floating bottle, and treasure map. Which brings me to another thing that I thought was really creative; the use of treasure maps. Throughout the world, you have the opportunity to find treasure maps that give you a picture and a set of coordinates. You then have to sail to the coordinates and based on the picture, find and dig up a treasure usually containing a plan to upgrade your ship or a couple thousand reales. Just like the collectibles, it just added a couple more hours of exploring and greater satisfaction having found them all. (some of which are exceptionally hard to find)The game play itself is also very satisfying. One thing I was worried about prior to this game coming out was how important the pirate theme would end up being. I wasn't sure if it was only a minimal part of the story, however I can tell you that the pirate theme is a major part of the story. not just a gimmick by ubisoft. You are actually able to upgrade your pirate ship to be more powerful, then attack other ships to gain supplies. You are also able to form your own entire fleet of ships to trade with various colonies to gain extra money. This kept my attention for a very long time.Overall the movements seemed very lifelike and I found it pretty easy to fight. One thing that I have never been a fan of in the assassins creed games, is the universal action button. I always found it to be tricky to use in certain situations, such as when you are trying to chase a target or avoid being detected and this game is no different. the universal action button, while a good thought in theory and 95% of the time, the other 5% of the time can be a real pain.The main story was slightly more involved than previous AC games, however not as much as I would like to have seen in this game. In all honesty, I probably only spent 15-20 hours on the main story which helped to explain alot of the backstory of the Kenways. However in this game you are never actually an assassin or templar, you are simply a pirate who happened to stumble upon the legend of the observatory. Towards the end you start working with the assassins, however that is one of the last parts of the game. In that regard I would have liked it to be more like the prior assassins creed games but I was still captivated by the idea of being a pirate so it did not matter much to me.The last thing that I wanted to talk about was the game play app that is available for apple and android products. I was worried that this might be a small failure on ubisofts part because it is such a new concept in the gaming world, however I was proven wrong yet again! I downloaded the app and had it open on my ipad while I was playing which made it so much easier to see where you are in conjunction with whatever it is that you are heading towards. It also made it extremely easy to find treasure without having to open up the map every time you needed to look at the picture again. The best thing about it (in my opinion) is that you are able to control your fleet from the app. So even when you are not able to play the game, you can still open up the app on your ipad, iphone, or android phone and you will still be able to send your ships to trade and keep making money which is a huge plus in my mind.Overall, this is by far my favorite assassins creed game to date, the stunningly beautiful world coupled with the massive amounts of collectibles and normal gameplay, you will be entertained for weeks. the only things I would say need to be better would be the universal action button as well as a more immersive storyline however Overall, I think this is a 5 star game.

I am fully aware that I'm about the un-cool-ify this game but it is completely awesome.  I write this review from a non-traditional perspective -- I am woman, I am over 40, and I love video games. Plus, my doctoral dissertation had to do with the Caribbean in the early 1500s, and I happen to be a Caribbean woman, so I think I have a unique background to bring to this review.Briefly, I admire the attention to detail. The layout of the lands and especially the building structures was a good reflection of that era, so feel assured that you are walking through what is probably a very good representation of the Caribbean islands at the time.  The only thing with which I may have an issue are the accents; slavery was still going on so the accents for the African descent people would have been more African than Jamaican, for example.  Nevertheless, since the game takes place in Jamaica and has African descent characters, it makes sense for game purposes to show them with "modern day" accents.Unlike the traditional gamer who probably sits down with his chips and Mountain Dew for hours of gaming, I sat with my ginger tea and toast for hours.  At first I ignored a lot of the missions; I spent hours traveling all over to take money from chests, song sheets, viewpoints and other articles.  I didn't pick-pocket or accept any assassination missions.  But then I saw the weaponry I could get with more money!  I started stealing -- but only from men in rich attire.  Not for anything having to do with race, but only because the people of poor attire wouldn't have made much of a difference. I also started to accept assassination contracts as they are not all that difficult. I speak Spanish, so I would stop and listen to the people on the street in their sinful conversations, and sometimes get cursed out if I were caught pick-pocketing a man of means.I have trouble guiding my ship at sea and moving quickly to catch people, but I am thoroughly enjoying this game! It's really like participating in a movie as the plot unfolds before you -- if you follow the story line.  This is my first AC game so I really do not get why he "returns" to that modern day office and what all that is about, but I haven't found it to be a hindrance yet.  If you're a mom thinking about getting it for your kids, do it but set up a profile for yourself and play alone! It's fun!

Terrible Assassin's Creed game.First let me say that I love the AC series. Played the first game and loved it, then followed Ezio's journey towards its tearful end. Then AC3 came out and I hated it so much I traded it in. I was very reluctant to buy Black Flag even after reading the reviews because I just wasn't sure if I wanted to continue with the series as it has problems that really annoy me. However, after a while of not having any games to play I decided to bite the bullet and buy the game.The Good:Kenway is a strong male lead.The Pirate theme is very exciting.Sailing your own ship and naval battlesInteresting side characters.The Bad:The Templar enemies weren't interesting, they were very forgettable.The Assassins were dull and served no real purpose.The present day storyline still sucksThis story follows Edward Kenway, a poor man who dreamed of making a better life for him and his wife and set off as a Privateer in the Caribbean despite the strain his choice was causing his marriage. After being stranded on a island after an attack on the ship he was on he comes across an assassin. After asking to work together the Assassin opens fire on him and Edward kills him. after reading his letter about meeting some men in Havana with promises of a reward Kenway decides to take the assassin's gear and pretends to be the man so he could collect. Turns out the meeting was with a group of Templars and thus throwing Edward into a world of Assassins, Templars, First civ stuff and so on. However, if you're expecting Edward to just become an assassin right away you're mistaken. Actually he isn't an assassin at all, even though he has all the skills of one. You're pretty much playing a character who is technically on the outside. His actions caused harm to a lot of people including the assassins and just wants to make amends. Kenway spends much of the game living as a pirate and therefore the game focuses heavily on pirate tasks, like robbing ships, looting booty, and so forth. This game is essentially a pirate game through and through. It feels more like adding the assassins were just a nod to the AC series more than it being an actual continuation of the story and order.Once again the series tries to follow the same formula of "Protag must find X item that belonged to First Civ before the Templars do." and honestly that formula is beyond tired. Seriously, how many items and pieces of eden et al did these people leave behind? However, despite that, the game was very good and exciting and I enjoyed Kenway and even the story. My issue with the story however, is that it is extremely short, so short to the point where when I returned to the Animus after being forced out i was expecting to continue the story only to find that it was the freaking ending. The only reason why the game is long is if you focus on ship upgrades, making money using the fleet management system which works in real time, or if you are a completionist. Mind you, I enjoyed upgrading my ship et al but it seems to me as though these side missions are considered a part of the story as well and because of that the actual story is short.  We see Kenway's journey and how the Creed changed him but right at that moment the story is cut short. I understand that Kenway's story as an assassin is covered in a  novel, but I don't want to buy a freaking novel just to finish up a protagonist's storyline. It should be in the freaking game I'm paying for. That was a huge disappointment. The ending was bittersweet and yes it connects to AC3 but it felt lacking to me and I guess that has to do with me not reading up on Kenway's story in the novel et al which is stupid.Also the ending felt so disjointed because you're thrown out the Animus for a "let's wrap up the present time story" cut scene then when you return to the Animus to continue the story (after finding out that Kenway needed to go after another guy) the story freaking ends! Honestly, I've reached a point of not giving two craps about Juno, first Civ, or anything involving the present day events. It's so obvious by now that the Animus is just a gimmick, a good premise gone downhill with shoddy and halfa**ed execution.I'm tired of these silly reasons why someone needs to be put into the animus. I just want the animus to go away. No, hacking stupid computers is not fun. I honestly believe that the series would have been much better if they simply showed the historical storyline all the way through without any mention of an animus or showing present day crap, then at the end of the series (if there is one) let us in on that. Anything would have been better then this disjointed present day/historical storyline. I feel that the present day story is interfering at this point.  Before I wanted Desmond and his crew to fix the order, for him to use everything he learned from Altair and Ezio and fight Abstergo. But that fell flat. So I wish they would just get rid of it. I honestly have no faith that Ubisoft will deliver on that front. I bet that the next game will give us yet another reason why Juno can't escape the internet (or where ever the heck she is) and we will be given another pointless present day protag and now with the possibilities of looking into dna that isn't even your own will give us even more faceless, nameless present day protags.I know it sounds like I hate the series, I don't, I love it, but I have to admit that certain elements are very disappointing to me. Overall, I think that Black Flag redeemed AC3, it is a fun game to play and all the characters in the historical storyline are very moving and I was sad to see it end. The song "Parting Glass" by Anne Bonny truly captured my feelings and it was very tearful. But the game didn't redeem the series in a massive way for me because I cringe just thinking of their stupid present day "storyline".  If I focus solely on the past story then I would say the game did a great job even if the story was cut short. I do look forward to the next installment but I'm no longer the fan who would buy the games at release.A star was taken away due to AC's present day storyline and its interference with the historical one.

I'll admit, I've never played any of the previous Assassin's Creed games. After about 12 hours gameplay on Black Flag, I realized I've been missing out on a great gaming series. I never really knew what to think of the game prior to getting this, so my review may not be as reliable as a seasoned Assassin's Creed player. I'm hoping people will pardon a beginner's opinion, though.The game story and graphics really made me feel I was in the realm of the Colonial West Indies. The level of detail put into the history of the Colonial West Indies is incredible. The game has many different areas to explore and side-missions to accomplish. I think the characters are well-developed and very believable. There has been very little cliched dialogue. I'd be hard-pressed to say this game is boring. The covert-styled fighting can be repetitive, and the AI for enemies and civilians has been a hoot. However, the covert operations are pretty intense and make up for the rather dim enemies I've encountered. When you get into a fight, you'll often be confronted by multiple enemies. The great thing about combat in this game is the number of different ways to dispatch foes.I've had a pretty easy time learning the controls. I think the ship controls are probably more tedious to remember, but I suppose this is just related to switching between controlling characters and ships. So, there may be initial confusion for other people who have never played this game before, but hints are available throughout the game. Moreover, an in-game user guide is also available and explains how to control the character and other assorted interfaces, particularly your pirate ship.Overall, the gameplay is nothing short of majestic. You couldn't hope for a more immersive game. If you are like me and enjoy games like Red Dead Redemption or open-world Final Fantasy games, you'll love Assassin's Creed Black Flag (and I'm sure the previous Assassin's Creed games). I decided to learn more about the series. I watched gameplay of the previous games on youtube. They all looked really good and a I encourage any prospective buyers to at least do the same if they have not played any of the Assassin's Creed games. I certainly plan on investing in past and future Assassin's Creed games.

I played the first couple ACs and enjoyed them but got a little bored with some of the game aspects. Haven't played any until this one (at least 4 years). Here's my take aways:Positives-Graphics are great! Story is pretty damn good...what's not to like about pirates!!! Battling numerous boats at once or a fort with rogue waves coming in is highly entertaining!!! They really captured the feel and environments with this game.Negatives-There aren't to many negatives but the few in the game are REALLY annoying!!! The tendency for your character to grab on to the most useless ledges, ropes, edges, etc. can get really old. I think this is a function of having the run button also be the grab button (because you run a lot in this game). If they were separate buttons it might work better. You'll be running down an alleyway and if to close to something you'll grab it or climb up it. Same with roof tops, pillars, trees, etc. I think by now they could come up with some smarter interaction AI. Then when you do need to grab something specific he'll either grab the wrong thing or do nothing at all. Perfect example...when finding a treasure chest if you run up to it he'll jump on top and squat down. Completely useless!!!! Things like this shouldn't be in the game. Don't let it be an option to have happen. I know it adds to the "realism" but come on, I want to open the chest, not sit on it.  There are lots of these moments in this game. Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag is another solid installment in the series.  4 to 4.5 star is where I put this game. The slicing of the sword and diving off a roof to assassinate a guard are great, especially when the camera slows down just a little.  Or hitting a guard with a berserk arrow and watch as they attack each other.  One of my favorite ways to take care of guards when you are surrounded is to drop that smoke bomb.  You quickly slice them up and move on.  The hunting is also a nice change of pace from walking here and there.  But I do have some negatives.  Getting used to maneuvering the ship can be very frustrating.  You turn or accidentally run into a tiny island.  You can't back up, obviously, but it does get frustrating.  Once you get more comfortable with the ship it does become more fun.  I also hate the way he jumps on everything or can't jump up to a short ledge when he can scale a wall in two seconds.  On the other hand it is fun when he lands where you want him too.  Another negative is when you have to ease drop on some guards and you get caught and have to do it all over again.  You sit, walk, sit again and walk closer and you just happen to flinch in the wrong direction, start all over.  But overall the pros out weigh the cons.  This is a fun game.  Taking out a large ship or destroying a large base are great.  The graphics look great, the water looks actually like water, the ship has a lot of detail and even the rain looks good.  Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag is a great start to the PS4 and gives you a taste of things to come.

AC IV is not by any means the greatest Assassins Creed to date but it is a huge improvement over AC3 and for PS4 owners, it is arguably the richest gaming experience of all the available launch titles.Pros:The ship-to-ship combat is very fun, offering upgrade incentives and varying degrees of challenge to the player.  Kenway's ship is upgradable by looting resources from enemy ships and upgrades are necessary to fight larger ships with more armor and firepower.  Upgrading the ship takes a significant amount of looting and treasure hunting, but it is fun and never felt like work even though it's quite repetitive.Game-play in AC IV is very smooth and the graphics look excellent for an open world game with basically no load times.  I had almost no issues climbing, jumping, running, or swimming throughout the game, although the controls while swimming underwater take a bit of getting used to.The multiplayer content is great.  I have played every other AC title and never played multiplayer on any of them, so I was very pleasantly surprised at how enjoyable multiplayer is in AC IV.  So far (early 2014) this multiplayer experience has provided me with more replay value than any other game for PS4.The scavenger hunts are always one of my favorite parts of any AC title and AC IV has added some new treasures to find across the pirate infested Caribbean.  My favorite things to chase down are the sea shanty's which attempt to fly away as you approach and once captured, they provide your crew with a new song to sing as you sail the open sea.The portion of the gameplay outside of the animus is unique, without giving away any spoilers I will say that you are coerced by a mysterious man to steal data from the Abstergo office and deliver it to some familiar allies from previous games.The weapons and combat great, offering you killing power and mobility that you're used to from AC titles but in a new environment.Cons:The story follows Edward Kenway, a pirate who finds himself mixed-up with assassins and templars in the Caribbean Sea.  Edward's loyalty is really only as good as the gold it provides at first, but throughout the game that changes as he get's more involved with the power struggle between the two secret societies.  Edward does not develop any lasting relationships with other characters which leaves me as a player quite indifferent to who he is or who the other characters throughout the game are.  The story will not be anybody's favorite part of this game, and would have docked some stars if the open world environment didn't pick up the slack.  Also Kenway is not really an Assassin, which doesn't affect the gaming experience but it does cause some detachment from the over-arching conflict that is present in other AC titles.Climbing back onto the ship gets to be a little tedious as Kenway will find many reasons to stop the ship throughout the gameplay and unless your near a dingy on the the beach you have to swim out and climb up the side of the ship many many times.  This didn't really bother me much, but it would be ideal if there were a sort of lift (like you might find in the cities to propel you to the top of a building) to assist you out of the water and onto the deck of the Jackdaw.The multiplayer is in need of patching, I have been playing on a consistently for about three months following the release of the PS4 and loading the multiplayer menu for AC IV still causes the game to freeze on a regular basis.  Matches will also sometimes get a bit buggy as players come and go during the character selection, but this is more due to connectivity issues than the game itself.  I have posted on Ubisofts forums about these issues and am still awaiting a fix.As with all Assassins Creed titles, there is very little danger to your character.  I wish it weren't quite so easy to stay alive during the fighting in Assassins Creed, but it's also fun to be nearly invulnerable when surrounded by enemies.If you own a PS4 and you want to have some lasting content on your new console, I recommend this game over all the other launch titles for the PS4.  My 5 stars would have been a 4 stars if this game hadn't come at a time when the PS4 was desperately starving for more content.

"AC IV: Black Flag" is more a pirate game with "AC" gameplay than an "AC" game with a pirate theme. This is good, because the main "AC" storyline is so convoluted and confusing at this point that a departure feels like a breath of fresh air. There's still weird story moments that are hard to piece together and follow, but "Black Flag" is very much about putting you in the shoes of a pirate named Edward, and seeing what kind of trouble he can get into. As Edward, you gain command of a ship fairly early on, allowing you to sail the open seas and engage in some very exciting naval battles. Some enemy ships are tough though, and require an equally tough upgraded ship to overcome. The gorgeous tropical open-world of "Black Flag" is gigantic, with tons of large and small islands to explore, each with an insane number of collectibles and side-content. It can be very satisfying to slowly conquer one piece of the map at a time, progressively upgrading your equipment and your ship to becoming the ultimate pirate. It's also a little too slow at times, with so much to do that the game can feel extremely repetitive toward the end. Having too much can also be considered a good thing, and I might also consider this my favorite game in the series.--- 4.5 STARS ---
