First of all, I don't understand why people give a game a 1 star review because it requires Uplay.  That has nothing to do with whether or not the game is good.  And make no mistake, this game is good.The world:In my opinion, this is the single most important aspect to nail down in games like this, and Watch Dogs does a good job.  Obviously there will be plenty of comparisons to GTA5.  And while Watch Dogs ultimately falls short of GTA5's glory, it's still a darn good game in it's own right.  I think I would have been really impressed with the game's rendition of Chicago if GTA5 hadn't set the bar so high already in it's depiction of SoCal.  This is easily the 2nd best "world" in games of it's type.  Many have complained that it lacks soul, but it actually did begin to grow on me as I progressed through the game.  No, it's not over the top and zany like Saints Row or GTA, but it's not a flat, bland world of cookie cutter buildings either, and the underground hacker vibe starts to take on a life of it's own.  Additionally, being able to learn information, albeit limited information, about nearly any citizen you see lends it's citizens a certain human aspect that's not apparent in other games.  Hacking into people's laptop cameras to spy on their private lives has a guilty pleasure about it, and many of the things you'll witness are funny, tragic, sexy, etc.Story/Characters:The story line is pretty decent, but nothing earth shattering.  I found myself less interested in Aiden getting revenge for his niece's death than I did for the other story lines in the game such as the human trafficking ring, and DedSec's (a hacker group eerily similar to the real life hacker group Anonymous) desire to take down ctOS, which is the Orwellian company that has monopolized all things digital in the name of safety and convenience.  Aiden Pearce, the game's protagonist, is fairly cliche although not an unlikable character.  Jordi is a sadistic and ruthless Asian man who helps Aiden from time to time.  Claire is an emo hacker chick with questionable motives.  Most of the game's other characters are believable except for one, Raymond Kenney.  Kenney's supposed to be a legendary hacker that's gone completely off the radar, but when you finally meet him he feels more like a dumb hillbilly than a legendary hacker.  I think they were trying to avoid a stereotypical nerd with glasses and a pocket protector as being the best hacker, but they went too far the other direction and Kenney just isn't believable as someone smart enough to do what he's done.  He'd feel more at home cracking open a beer can in a trailer park than being the best hacker in Chicago.Graphics:The graphics are pretty good on high settings.  I can't say that the game looks a great deal better than GTA5 did on Playstation 3 though, even with settings on high.  Rain effects look realistic and the character models look nice, with the exception of Aiden's sister who looks a little bland.Driving:Many have complained about the game's driving physics, but I had no problem.  It's not quite as "fun and easy" as GTA5 but not quite as realistic as GTA4.  Probably somewhere in between.  Aside from buildings, cars and trees, pretty much everything is destructible so you won't spend a bunch of time crashing into things that slow your momentum, you can just plow right through and keep on going.  The boats in the game feel similar to GTA although they seem to be much faster.Hacking/Puzzles:Even if this game had no driving or shooting, it could nearly stand alone as a puzzle platforming game.  Unlike in other Ubi titles such as Assassin's Creed, solving the "climbing/platforming" puzzles is actually fun in this game, especially when combined with accessing different security cameras to give you viewpoints otherwise unobtainable, which are then used to solve parts of the puzzle.  Some puzzles require equal parts platforming and hacking of cameras, and each puzzle seemed fresh and not overly challenging, but still rewarding when completed.  The hacking mini-game was one I wasn't too fond of, you basically rotate T or L shaped joints to allow the "info" to carry on through the lines to it's destination.  Most of them aren't too difficult but they're not exactly fun either, so I find myself grumbling when another one would pop up.Shooting:Shooting works as well as most other 3rd person shooters.  You can choose to go in guns blazing or try to take a more measured, stealthy approach and each side feels equally as balanced and challenging in most situations.  Leveling up grants you points you can spend in skill trees to upgrade your abilities in hacking, combat, driving, etc.Side missions:There are plenty of side missions available.  Some require you to steal and deliver vehicles to a specific location before a clock expires, some require you to lure the cops' attention and then lose them so that your buddies can pull off a crime elsewhere, there are missions that require you to take down a convoy of enemies before they reach their destination, and there are missions that have you infiltrating a stronghold of enemies and eliminating them.  There are also mini games such as chess, drinking games, poker, etc.  Digital trips offer a break from reality and have you terrorizing the city in a mechanical spider tank, mowing down demons in an armored muscle car, shooting aliens with laser guns, and sneaking through a dystopian city while hiding from killer robots.  None of them compared to the campaign missions, but many of them are worthwhile and I found myself completing all of the optional missions, which is rare for me.Final verdict:I have a feeling that if this game had released before GTA5 did and hadn't come with a slew of technical issues right out of the gate, it would be a unanimously well-received game.  I enjoyed it much more than Saints Row 4 and GTA4, but GTA5 set the bar ridiculously high and Watch Dogs falls just short of that mark.  Don't let that dissuade you from playing it though, I had a blast with the game and probably played for at least 40-50 hours, and will eagerly await any DLC that comes.  Don't let the Negative Nancy's out there skew your opinion of this game before you play it, it's a really good game and if you enjoy games in this genre at all, you'll love it like I did.

But unless the game throws me an unexpected curve ball, I don't see that happening much.*UPDATE - After playing for a few more hours and playing some more of the various mini-missions I can definitely say this game is a solid 4 star game.  It sort of holds itself as a game with lots of complicated gameplay and depth...but kind of feels more like a normal game with lots of gimmicks. Just way more hyped than necessary.I would also like to make very clear that I am running this game on high with very few issues on a GTX 760.  I see a few frame skips now and again and some screen tearing, but nothing game ruining.  AMD users may have a worse experience.  Uplay also sucks, but for the most part the service has only had a few slow moments or issues with me saving my games.  Usually works when I try again to connect, etc.  I agree that this shouldn't happen at all, but it is what it is.**UPDATE - I've not been experiencing the same graphics and crash issues as others here.  My system seems to run the game fine on high setting all around.  That said, after about 20 hours of gameplay I'm knocking off 2 stars.  Honestly, I don't really see too many bugs...per se.  I would actually consider the issues that most people, including myself, are having are actually design choices.  Here's the list:-Hit zones on pedestrians, they are non-existant.  You get into a gun fight with bad guys in the streets and any stray shot from any gun that hits any pedestrian on ANY part of their body kills them instantly.  You lose good guy points for every pedestrian injured and more for every pedestrian killed.  So this is a bad thing for people like me trying to be the good guy.-Law enforcement is dumb, dumb, dumb.  Why is it that there are no boat cops?  You want to get away from the cops.  Drive your car off a bridge and then swim to a bridge support, then wait for the cooldown.  The helicopter can't even combat this amazing new hiding technique called "hiding under a bridge".  Secondly, why is it that there are no free roaming cops to randomly catch me in the act of committing one of the many crimes I commit on a single play through.  They don't exist.  You will never be busted for pulling a gun, ramming other cars with your car, stealing a car, hacking an atm, etc., unless a randon pedestrian calls the cops at which point you have the ctOS scan for you.  If you fail to escape the yellow scan areas, then the cops finally come for you.  But guess what?  If you escape the yellow areas, you're off scott free!  This city has an amazing crime detection technology with cameras everywhere and the ability to see EVERYTHING...and yet escaping the cops is as easy as jumping into the water under a bridge.-That last bullet leads in to my next issue.  The cops don't come unless a pedestrian calls them.  But wait...you don't want the cops to come even then, scare off or kill the caller before the call charge completes.  That's RIGHT!  An amazing crime prevention system all over the city and no way to trace a dropped cell phone to send the cops.  the ctOS doesn't even try to scan the area in the event that you shoot and kill the caller.  So the lesson UBI is trying to teach us here is that if someone catches you committing a crime and tries to call the cops...kill everyone in the area?-This next issue is my favorite because I take advantage of it all the time.  Say you're chasing a criminal trying to bring them down after they just committed a crime.  You're running through the streets for a couple of blocks.  Boring eh?  Not so, because while you're running after this criminal you can have your profiler out and hack peoples' bank accounts the entire time.  That's right!  You're chasing a guy at full sprint, but you can hack peoples' calls and bank accounts while running past them on a crowded street.  WHAAAAAAAAAAAAAT?!-But wait you say, you can't hip fire in this game?  Nope, you can't.  You can hack people's bank accounts while running at a full sprint after a gang member who's probably shooting at you, but you can't pull you gun out and shoot at him without looking down your sight.-Repetitive...that's all for that one.I'd like to finish off with the "coup de grace" to sum up most of these issues with one fantastic experience...I hacked a Blume affiliate, which, if you allow it, puts a contracted hit out on you online.  Within a few minutes someone online will usually enter your game and begin to hack your phone.  You need to not only find this person and identify them, but then the game tells you to kill them before they get away.  So, this last time I played I found the person that was hacking me.  They instantly jumped into a car right next to me.  I ran up to pull them out but the game didn't let me, even though the car hadn't begun to move.  So I turned around and grabbed a small hatchback. So here I am in a car, sitting in the cockpit of a boat being driven into the bay at full speed.  I say to myself, "cool I'll get out and shoot this guy in the back while he drives the boat.  They're stuck in the boat anyway."  I open the door and the game dumps me right off the deck of the boat and into the water in the middle of the bay.  They reached the land on the other side and somehow magically got out of the boat and got away.  The end...to me playing this game anymore.***Final UPDATE - I'm on the verge of a one star rating.  After doing just about everything the game has to offer and completing most side missions, this is my final assessment...-UBI still hasn't even attemptd to actually optimize the game.  But why would they, it's the same engine that's been giving them issues with the later Assassin's Creeds-The online is terrible. So if they don't kill the you before you make it to the water, you've won.-The missions are all the same. But I'm sure the game has lots of appeal to those out there that love seeing lots of poorly drawn, half naked digital women in games and hearing the F word yelled at them every other second. It's perhaps inevitable that with Watch Dogs, there are some who would compare it to the other big open-world game based relatively closely on the real world:  GTA.  For those of you who think it's GTA vs Watch Dogs -- let me stop you right there.  These games are fundamentally different, and so I would say "Why not both??"  Yes, they're both based in an open world, and both basically allow you to do practically whatever you want.  But in GTA, for the most part, there aren't many consequences for your actions.  Run down a ton of people on the street, get some stars, and then lead the cops on a hilarious and explosive chase.  If you die - no worries, you'll respawn at home (hospital - whichever version of GTA you're talking about), with various amounts of dollars missing from your wallet.  Go back outside -- do the same stuff over again.  And honestly - that's what makes GTA the great game it is.  Knowing that you can do what you wish, and the game won't hold it against you.  With Watch Dogs, this concept no longer applies.  Now your choices start to matter.  Now the consequences matter.  As McFly would say, "This is Heavy, Doc...."For those of you who have been under a rock the past couple of years - Watch Dogs has been a highly expected game from Ubisoft, who went so far as to delay the release of this game by around 6 months, just to try and perfect it.  In Watch Dogs, you're in the city of Chicago, who's infrastructure and crime prevention system is run by a supercomputer named ctOS.  In all actuality, this reality isn't that farfetched.  Driverless transit systems are common (London, Seoul, Tokyo, DC, San Francisco, among others) and we all know the ever-prevalent security camera systems in many cities.  The only difference here is in the game, everyone's information is also tied into the system.  Characteristics, bank accounts, credit cards, school and criminal records - you name it, it exists in the system.  So the question arises, "What if someone hacks the system?"  And it's with this premise that Watch Dogs has you play in...I won't lie - I downloaded the game a tad early, thanks to some various websites (I'm sorry, after getting burned on the last 3 preorders I've done for PC - Command and Conquer 4, Mass Effect 3, and SimCity 5, I don't intend on any game getting the best of me again), and I can really say that the game lives mostly up to its hype, although it still needs some work on the PC.The environment of Chicago looks fantastic, and from the dry run I played, the main storyline is actually quite good.  My main beef with the PC version is the driving handling is awful, and it's especially a pain when there's a chase going on, and you're trying to avoid hitting pedestrians, (trust me, watch what happens the first time you hit a street walker - go on, I dare you!) and your car just refuses to make that turn you need it to make.I gotta give props to the Ubisoft guys - the NPCs in this game are some of the best I've seen yet.  I remember walking towards an intersection, and just then an accident occurred, and everyone starts pulling out their phones and recording/taking pictures.  Also, depending on what kind of reputation you get later in the game, people will start to recognize you, and either call the cops or try and take a picture of you, based on whether you choose to be good or bad.  Pay attention to the banter and dialogue of the NPCs, and it becomes clear Ubisoft really worked hard on this aspect of the game.The game specs recommend quite a beefy computer - but I was able to play it quite smoothly on my Lenovo W530 laptop (2.3 GHz Core i7, nVidia K1000, 256 GB SSD, 16 GB RAM), although I did have to turn off some of the reflections and ambient occlusion and all that.  Only choppiness I got was from some cutscene videos that stuttered, though the audio came through no problem.Online play is somewhat optional - the game early on forces a mission on you to at least attempt the online scene, so at least you can get a feel for the play, but fortunately, that's it - storyline wise at least.  Online Decryption is actually a lot more interesting than I thought it would be - having a team vs team, with everyone throwing their hacks around, is tons of fun.All in all, Ubisoft did an awesome job on the game, which in retrospect they better have, since they took an extra 6 months to finish up.  The game gets a solid 4.5 stars, but the originality of the concept bumps it up in my book to 5.

The 5 stars is for gameplay.Yes, the PC version stutters even on a core i5 rig with SSD, 12 GB of RAM and the latest nvidia gtx graphics card, that's true. I have mine turned down to lowest settings and the fps still stutters. Also, the graphics are nice but not mind blowing. The daytime looks ok, night time looks better. The cars (especially the american muscle cars) drift like crazy and you feel like you're driving on ice. The single player missions are fun but, once you get good at driving and shooting, it's not too challenging. The main character, Aiden, is pretty two-dimensional and boring. The storyline is nothing to write home about.So after all that, why the 5 stars? Because online hacking is, for me, awesome as hell. There have been so many brilliant, holy cow, moments. Think of it as an amazing hide and seek game where hiding takes a lot more skill than seeking. To hide and win, you have to quickly figure out where all the good hiding spots are and be extremely strategic about using your whole 1 minute to initiate. You do get losers who disconnect when you're about to beat them, but despite that, I've still been able to get past 10,000 notoriety, which gets you lots of amped up skills. I don't even mind being profiled by my target because it means I can jump into a car and have a great time getting chased and trying to get away. I can't remember the last time I had this much fun online. I seriously can't.Give the online hacking a chance. You will get your butt kicked many many times until you figure it out, but once you do, it is such a blast. To get good, do a search on Youtube for "watch dogs online" and watch people like DPJSC08 to see what they do.UPDATEI'm now at 14,000 notoriety and climbing. Still love the online hacking and play it every day. Also, be sure to watch FRYINGHARD on twitch.tv. He is ranked 36th in the world for online hacking and has 37,000 notoriety. That guy is amazing. I've learned tons of tricks by watching him play.

I've been a big Total War fan since Rome 1, so naturally I was more than excited for this reboot of my old favorite.  The game is far more ambitious in scale than just about anything else Creative Assembly has attempted in the past and in many ways I think that they took off more than they could chew.Features that added flair and immersion to the game have been cut, largely due to the time required to implement them for the host of civilizations you can play as.  For example, cut scenes that would show your agents and spies at work or a family tree of your ruling dynasty are gone.  Many aspects of the game seem to lack the polish that CA's earlier, more focused titles seemed to revel in and this significantly impacts your ability to get immersed in your empire.The strategy in the game (both on the battlefield and on the campaign map) are simpler and less interesting than they could be.  There is oftentimes an obvious and clearly best choice for all of the moves that you make, which significantly reduces the fun factor.  As others have lamented, the AI on the battlefield is not the best and is particularly spotty in naval and siege battles.  Additionally, once you reach a certain point in your campaign your victory becomes all but assured and therefore boring.  Other games in the series have attempted to combat this tendency by introducing large, world-changing events like a Hunnic or Mongolian invasion in Europe or political maneuvering in Japan.  Rome's way of dealing with this is the introduction of a civil war system, but this isn't fleshed out and merely spawns a group of uninteresting units at your capital to quickly dispatch of.Total War: Rome 2 lacks the polish, focus, and intrigue of past Total War games.  It is not a BAD game, to be sure; there is still a lot of fun to be had conquering Africa as Egypt or Germany as the Gauls.  However, what is most frustrating about Rome 2 is that it could have been so much more.

I've been a fan of saints row almost from the beginning. I missed the first game, butSaints Row 2 - Xbox 360still ranks among my absolute favorite games of all time. It was fast, fun, funny, violent, but had a tense, engaging story with likeable characters, rounding out the experience. It is that last element that was missing from the third iteration. WhileSaint's Row: The Third - Xbox 360was still fast, fun, and violent, it was missing a lot of the funny. Worse yet, the vibrant engaging characters from the second seemed muted and generic. I am beyond happy to say that has been addressed with Saints Row 4.Right off the bat, the over the top feel of the game hits you hard and never lets up. You are the president of the United States and it is your job to stop evil aliens from taking over the world. You fail; spectacularly at that. You and all of your friends are imprisoned in a virtual prison, and this is where the fun begins. Because the world is virtual, you now have access to super powers, the two most prevalent among them being super speed and hulk jumping, for lack of a better term. This, unfortunately, is also where the games biggest problem comes in.Saints Row 4 is a big, ambitious game, and I respect what they were trying to do. The super powers are cool and well implemented, but the overall structure of the game remains unchanged from past iterations. Sections of the virtual city are still called "Hoods", your friends, now politicians, celebrities, and secret agents, are still referred to as your "homies". You still have access to your "gang", despite the fact that they become all but useless against most enemies in the game half way through. Despite having super speed and, thanks to the glide ability, practically being able to fly, too many missions find reasons for you to be in vehicles, which are not nearly as enjoyable to use as your powers are. Unfortunately, at least with my copy, lag was a huge issue when jumping, because the game autosaved every five seconds, making platforming far more difficult that it needed to be, and marring the overall immersion of the game.Worse yet, the game is still littered with mini games, many of them hit or miss. Racing through cramped side streets, terribly unenjoyable platforming sections, insurance fraud (ugh), mayhem sections (UGH), and terrifyingly enough vehicle mayhem sections (WHY!?), are among the many mini games that dangle valuable upgrades in front of you, that are only unlockable after getting difficult to earn gold medals. To add insult to injury all of these mini games are saddled with an arbitrary time limit, ensuring that, if by some miracle, you actually enjoy any of these diversions, the extra stress of having to do it quickly will sap that enjoyment right out.This game could have been great but Volition wasn't willing to shake conventional staples to the genre. Thankfully however, the rest of the game is fantastic. The story related missions are all quite engaging and the story is absolutely crazy, made all the better by the triumphant of the characters that you knew and loved from the first two games. Volition even went as far as to address issues such as "Why did Shandi go from fun to frumpy between games 2 &3?" and "What's Pierce's problem?". Incredible dialogue, tons of character development, and a metric ton of call backs, inside jokes, and awesome sing a longs of the radio remind you why you fell in love with these characters in the first place.By now, you'll have noticed that the positive points of my review revolve around knowing about the past games. To fully enjoy this game, it is best to have played the games that came before. If you've at least played through, and beaten, the second game though, that should suffice. This final game in the series is an excellent cap to a strange series, loaded with generous heaps of fan service for long time players. While it is totally possible to enjoy it without having played what came before, you will be lacking valuable context, and the lions share of the jokes and in game dialogue will go totally over your head. My favorite moment in the game was when the playa and Pierce are driving along and begin to sing along with one of their favorite songs. A certain person does something that doesn't sit well with them, and it was one of the funniest moments in any game I've ever played, mostly because I recognized the callback from the second game.Saints Row is a fun game, with great ideas, serviceable execution, and brilliant story and dialogue. While having played the past three games aren't required, I would strongly suggest completing the second game for the much needed context, and also because it is the best game in the series. All in all, Saints Row 4 is an enjoyable, if technically flawed, gem of a game that is fun for most, but sensational for fans. If you like the series, this is a must buy.

A lot of noise has been levied at SAINTS ROW IV as being more of an add-on adventure to SAINTS ROW THE THIRD, and while there may be some nuggets of truth to that, it's still a complete gaming experience. Also, a lot of noise has been levied at many video game sequels lately that they've done nothing to enhance the experience of the previous games, and in many cases are just using all the same things we've seen in the previous games, even graphics-wise. This is a criticism I've been seeing a lot on this game, and especially BATMAN: ARKHAM ORIGINS. And while the whole concept of the SAINTS ROW games aren't exactly new, I would rather play any of the SAINTS ROW games than any of the GTA games any day of the week and twice on Sunday.Why? It's simple: There's nothing about SAINTS ROW that takes itself seriously (that is particularly true of this game), and that's kind of beautiful as opposed to some of the gameplay in the GTA games. I would go further to say that the more recent SAINTS ROW games are satirizing the GTA games, but that's a discussion for another time. Let's take some time to focus on this game here.Basically, through a series of absurd scenarios, the leader of The Saints has become President of the United States. All of your Saints (Pierce, Shaundi, Kinzie, etc.) are with you, and you even have Keith David as your Vice-President. Not the video game voice acting of Keith David; it's really Keith David. But an alien race attacks Earth, and you are trapped inside... well, we don't want to call it The Matrix EXACTLY because that would be copyright infringement, but between you and me, it's The Matrix version of Steelport. So now, you're gaining superhuman abilities (super-speed, freezing powers, fire powers, extrasensory abilities, etc.), and you're bumping off aliens left and right until the time comes to fight the big boss. And along the way, you act like a complete and total psychopath.Despite that this feels kind of similar to the previous games, particularly THE THIRD, it's still a fresh and hilarious expansion of this universe. The new rides, the new missions, the NEW POWERS!!! The powerset you obtain as you go through the game is gleefully destructive; sometimes it's like PROTOTYPE but without the self-seriousness that goes with that game.I never felt that I was being cheated by lagtimes, or that the graphics were ever spotty, unless that's the intention (which does happen often in this computerized version of Steelport). There's even an eight-bit side-scroller you get to play alongside NyteBlayde!! The only thing that is a bit less for me (merely on a personal note) is that the music isn't quite as good. And there's a little too much dubstep for my tastes. But that is where my only real gripe is.SAINTS ROW IV might look and sound like THE THIRD, but it feels very different thanks to the superhero-on-crank inspired lunacy that Deep Silver created for this game.

Instead of killing you you kidnaps you and drops you into a simulation of Steelport that is suppose to be based on your worst nightmares. And in the beginning it is. You are in 1950's America until you shoot your way out of the illusion. After that, it's missions to bring down Zinyak and rescue other players or go on missions to disrupt the simulation. I personally think that both aliens and zombies are overdone, but the humor in this story, plus the intelligence of Zinyak is enough to get past that. Also the super powers which basically make the cars and planes pointless and guns kind f secondary.In the past, we relied on cars to take us across town to missions. Now, probably prematurely, we get super speed running right away, and it upgrades into never running out. So you can literally speed across town at high speeds instead of driving and never stop. And why would you drive when it takes longer? It's kind of a shame because the streets and cars are so detailed, as in the last game. Around that time, you gain the power to super jump which lets you leap up tall buildings and jump across them. After that you get Glide which may be my favorite. This allows you to jump off that high rise tower and glide across the city to each destination. Like flying. Shortly after you get the ability to run straight up a building instead of jumping and bouncing up bit by bit. Hitting the ground does not hurt you because this is a simulation. The super powers you use to fight include in order, freeze, fire, telekinesis (mind lift people and throw them), stomp, and telekinesis energy drain. You also can upgrade guns to alien type which means it has a laser that needs to recharge instead of bullets. Other weapons include the dub step gun that kills with music, the black hole gun that sucks people into a black hole, and a floppy adult toy bat. The side mission that you need to unlock these powers (that and scattered power orbs you collect like currency) are the Fraud missions, tank missions, Genki missions that are much like the ones from SR3, but with new ones like alien ships and other alien themes. You also fight waves of enemies to take over the town just like in 3, but with super powers you can jump to the top of a building and aim from there. Unless you have flying enemies they can't get up that high. You also hack stores with a pipe/lazer puzzle that can be challenging and impossible alternately. I think I preferred when you could buy them.The downside is sometimes odd and unfun missions where for example, you are a 2-bit tank that upgrades into a modern tank, you fly a ship through crevices, or you drive a bike. The bikes in simulation are terrible to control, and the ship scene in the beginning is tedious and not fun.Lastly I wanted to mention that in the beginning the game was plagued with bugs and glitches.Now, in 2014, I have picked the game back up and started over, and in 5 days, it has frozen randomly three times. It freezes the entire PS3 and you need to get up and restart it. It also has glitched in a tower and refused to let me out via invisible walls more than once. If you look on Youtube you can find all kind of glitches recorded. I actually e-mailed the company, and their response was that they already released patches, and that I should try the game on a friend's PS3 to see if it was my PS3 or the disc. Okay. So who is going to let me borrow their Ps3 for a few days OR let me come over and sit on their couch for 6 hours a few days in a row to see if it glitches eventually? Oh, I'm just going to be in your living room shooting aliens, don't mind me...They said that it is not normal to for it to glitch or freeze that many times, but look on the internet and you will see that it happen to numerous people. I mentioned that which they ignored. The problem here is that i like this game, but at this point, with it glitching and freezing, I may not get to finish it. The only times this has ever happened was with Assasin's Creed 3 and 4 (3 was plagued with glitches and freezes and although I hated it, I finished it and took it right back to Redbox), and one boss in Lego Lord of the Rings. And I own over 40 games. So apparently their patch did not fix everything. Think about that before you buy this game, because some freezing experiences I have read have been worse than mine.

Let's get the bad out of the way first. Yes, Saints Row 4 reuses the maps, character models, art assets, vehicles, weapons, and progression system from 3. It was built from an unfinished expansion while Volition hung in a hoary nightmare limbo between the folding of THQ and their purchase by Deep Silver. As such, SR4 seems rather stale, as though it doesn't bring much freshness to the table in terms of gameplay.But under all that samey rust, there's some gleaming steel of awesome.The plot sees The Boss, now president of the United States, trapped in an alien virtual reality prison. Escaping, you must return to the prison to wreck havoc, which allows Kinsey (your hacker friend from the first game) to slowly undermine the alien regime. Periodically you must also venture aboard the alien ship in the "real" world, missions which have a less cartoony, more cautious feel. Within the simulation you develop an arsenal of superpowers, complete a variety of familiar minigames to achieve territory control, and generally just mess stuff up.Missions in the simulator are frankly rather lackluster. Most optional missions are just strings of minigames you would play anyway (I could turn half of them in upon getting them) and the campaign missions are all pretty easy. But studded into this are gems, such as the inside of an accomplice's head rendered as a 16-bit fighting game (which itself could carry a full length title) or a spaceship escape set to Haddaway's What is Love? The problem is that these slivers of awesome are mostly stacked toward the game's end, and you have to wade through a few hours of Saints-Row-3-Over-Again to see them. There are other oddities- vehicles become useless fairly quickly due to your powers, and the new guns (Dubstep gun!) so hugely outclass the regular pistols and shotguns you'll never use your whole arsenal. A number of environments that were interactive in SR3 are just left in and sit around being eerily empty as well.For me, the good and fresh outweighed the bad and stale (especially a fantastic 80s cartoon reference at the end that I won't spoil) but I can't in good conscience say that will be true for everyone. Part of what made Saints Row 3 so awesome was that it was all new and all that craziness came as a surprise; here most of it won't. It's still a better crime adventure than GTA and a better superhero game than Prototype, but is it a better Saints Row than 3? Not really.

The Disney Infinity Cars play set is one of the first play sets to be released separately from the game itself. Unlike the other play sets, the Cars play set focuses primarily on driving ('cause, you know... they're cars). The experience is very fun and currently one of my favorite play sets.The package comes with the Cars play set and two figures, Lightning McQueen (the main character of the series) and Holley Shiftwell (an agent who appeared in Cars 2). The figures themselves are very nice and features sticker-like decorations rather than paint. The only thing I don't like about them is that, in gameplay, they play exactly the same.Gameplay, as stated earlier, is different from the other play sets. Instead of fighting enemies and solving puzzles, you drive around Radiator Springs and do things such as race and tow other cars. This unusually simple concept is done very well, mostly due to the extra things you can do in the play set. I especially love collecting toy box pieces and destroying things in the town. This play set, while short, is to me significantly more fun than the Cars 2 game (also developed by Avalanche).Overall, this is one of my favorite play sets. Though I would have appreciated it if they made the cars play differently, the gameplay maintains the greatness of the other play sets without being unoriginal. I would highly recommend this to anyone who plays Disney Infinity.Final Score: 8.5/10

If you read my review for Disney Infinity, you would see that I am quite a fan. From the start I knew that I had to get the play set for my favorite movie franchise, and it has finally arrived: the Toy Story in Space play set!The figures: Once again, I am very impressed with these Disney Infinity figures. The cartoonier-than-usual look translates well into the figures as usual. My one problem: no Woody. He's my favorite character, and if I hadn't already bought him previously I'd have to go through the entire campaign as Buzz or Jessie (which isn't bad, but I still prefer Woody).Gameplay: Fun, but when you start, it's pretty slow. I found myself more bored in this play set than any other one that I have played. The little green men from the movies keep giving you these missions that are pretty much the same kind of missions just with slight differences (i.e. "Make me look like Lotso" or "Make me look like Jessie"). Not to mention Buzz, Jessie, and Woody have the exact same gameplay, and I am not really fond of that style of gameplay (you throw pixar balls that don't hurt bad guys hardly at all or ram your shoulder into them). Now, things DO pick up once you purchase a jet pack from the toy store. After I bought that, I was able to fly (no pun intended) through these normally slow missions with ease. Plus, it makes playing in the Toy Box more fun as well.Graphics: Like the previous play sets, this game boasts some very nice visuals. The overall sci-fi look is very pleasing to me (being as I am a part-time Trekkie and a major Star Wars fan), and it is definitely better than the rather underwhelming graphics of the Monsters University play set (they weren't bad graphics, just not as good as the other play sets').Despite some minor flaws, I do really like this set. Considering that these characters are so beloved and that the things you unlock really help the gameplay in the Toy Box, I think that this is definitely a worthy purchase. The play set was a little disappointing, but, in the end, still very fun. The biggest draw-back is the $35 price tag. If you have that kind of money to spare, than I would recommend buying this.Overall: 8.0 out of 10.

Metro Last Light absolutely blew me away.Part of it may have been because I went into the game with somewhat limited expectations. Metro 2033, the previous game in the series, was a game that was thick with incredible atmosphere, but struggled to keep my attention due to clunky controls and a handful of very annoying game mechanics. Metro Last Light brings back that incredible, post-nuclear war subterranean environment that is the Russian metro network, only this time they deliver a game that is not only much more streamlined in its interface, but has gameplay controls that can easily hang with the best first person shooters out there. Add in smarter, non-bullet spongy AI and a revamped stealth system, and Metro Last Light is a winner all around. It has become one of my absolute favorite first person shooters of the entire seventh generation, sitting comfortably alongside Far Cry 3, Borderlands and Bioshock on that hallowed pedestal.Playing through Metro Last Light stirred feelings that were very reminiscent of those that I felt the first time I played one of my favorite games of all time, Half Life 2. The two games are similar in many ways. Aside from both featuring silent protagonists and having a perfectly potent mix of hard hitting humanity and science fiction, they both are focused, somewhat linear first person shooters that have mastered the art of storytelling through environment. Through Metro Last Light, we are treated to one of the moodiest, most alive game environments the genre has ever seen. The bleakness of the irradiated Moscow city square, the dankness of the tunnels swarming with horrifying creatures, the devastated-yet-still-optimistic human settlements living in the metro stations - Metro Last Light has some of the most impressionable, unforgettable locales you've ever seen in a video game. The developers, 4A Games, really stepped it up in this dept., which is saying a lot considering the fact that Metro 2033 was already quite the achievement in this regard to begin with.Being able to navigate the world of the post-apocalyptic metro with the improved controls, gameplay, and mechanics was exactly what was needed, and is exactly what the game delivers. Metro Last Light is filled with tense, exciting gameplay that is interspersed with just enough down time in the stations (aka underground settlements) to give the game a perfectly paced feel. The story was surprisingly excellent as well, showing how the ugliness of man can still stand out even in a devastated world, and how the human spirit can overcome this darkness. An incredible final battle and one of the most memorable, haunting ending sequences I've ever seen perfectly round out this superb game that was unfairly overlooked in 2013. This is a thinking man's first person shooter, one that I'd easily recommend to anyone who appreciates atmosphere in games, a quality that when done right,  is hard to come by.One of the best games of 2013.

This game hasn't received the attention I feel it deserves, maybe because it doesn't have an EA logo flash up or a Ken Levine to give interviews about it on IGN.This was a comparatively low budget game. Google "Jason Rubin: Metro: Last Light is the "triumph of an underdog"" for more on that, but it doesn't feel like a low budget game.I love this post-apocalyptic genre, and one of my favorite games of all time is Fallout 3 (and the prior two). That said, this game has a more believable, dark, gritty atmosphere. There is a weight to the environments that never leaves. Even last year's The Last of Us had a beautiful forest at some point. This never has that. It's all dark, all dead or dying. As you move through the metro you can pick up chatter by non-player characters just engaging with their environment. A child playing with a boat in a squalid underwater lake, another being calmed (and lied to) by their father that she'll see mommy soon. There's a constant air of despondency, like in McCarthy's The Road.So, how is the game play? It's solid. It's not perfect. The human enemies are regrettably easy to kill. Hiding in the dark and head-shoting them works a treat. The monsters are tougher and less predictable, and you can't hide from them.One of the better questions a player should ask at the end of a game is: "Will I look out for the sequel?" and for me the answer is "Yes.".

This sequel takes everything from the predacessor and makes it more polished, more visceral, and far far more entertaining to those who may have felt taken aback by the borderline lackluster affair in 2033(I liked it)Metro Last Light picks up after the events of the first game and tells more of the aftermath of Artyome's actions in 2033. The threat of the Dark Ones still lingers, and larger than life events are on the horizen for the peoples of the Metro. Its up to the newest Ranger of the Order to save everyone from complete obliteration.... last bullet... last hope... last light.....The gameplay is largely unchanged, you can still do a multitude of actions typically done for you in other games, like charge your flashlight, observe your objective(in real time on a notepad) and even whipe debris and blood from your gasmask(which you also have to manually equip) there hasnt been any dreaded "streamlining" in this regard. Where slight changes have been made(for the better) is in regards to combat, a simple melee button has been added, and the gunplay is much more responsive and tighter than before, ensuring you aren't flailing about when a mutant is trying to take a chunk out of you.The game's previous issue of weapon level progression has also changed, ditching the system of buying a gun with preset upgrades in exchange for an actual customization system allowing you to choose different attachements(such as scopes, silencers, and stocks) sadly the bayonette for the Shambler(assault shotgun) is absent this time around >_< The game progresses through a number of levels, ranging from the dark dank depths of the Metro to the surface world above, both being infested with enemies, both human... and otherwise.Needless to say, you should enjoy this game, its a wonderful addition to your gaming library, and you should have no regrets picking this title up*NOTE, the one issue I had with this game was the nudity in one particular level, and the themes of rape in another... these additions seemed both juvenile(boobs) and offensive(rape) and I didnt much care for them, nevertheless, still an amazing game*

Should be withdrawn from Sale - but the real fault is my own.  There are ample reviews of this game on the internet that roundly disclaim it as an unmitigated disaster on the PC platform and barely playable on gaming platforms.  It's so bad in terms of playability that JJ Abrams, the producer of the film on which the game as based, publicly discredited it after it was released.  If it weren't for the fact that I should have researched this more, I'd be asking for my money back - but seeing how well-known the problems with the PC version of the game are, I have to sheepishly admit that I failed to do sufficient research to know what I was getting.This is so bad on the PC that I can't get past the first real clever bit in the Helios-1 first adventure.  There's a door you're supposed to hack open using the tricorder and holding either the E key to do the hack yourself, or the Q key to have the other player perform the hack.  There's an onscreen panel telling you what to do since the Helios-1 mission is more of a gamplay tutorial.  And the instructions don't work - the door never gets "hacked" to open - I've spent an hour on just trying various combinations of sequences of operations and nothing works.  When I look at gameplay videos from the same game played on an XBOX 360 you see the specific instructions on the screen followed using the designated keys from the controller and the door opens - but not on my PC version.So I start looking around the internet and I find that Digital Extremes, the developer of the game, doesn't even acknowledge its existence as their product.  Their only acknowledgement consists of an interview on another website in which they express wonderment at why JJ Abrams condemned their product.So - if you're on any platform but the PC, at $15 (which should drop to free for the PC shortly as long as you waive liability to Amazon), the game might be playable.  I certainly see lots of video of people going thru the levels on other platforms on youtube - but so far I've seen nothing on the PC.  But even on other platforms like the XBOX 360 I see lots of complaints about the gameplay.Although somewhat pretty to look at for the introductory cinematics and the use of authentic-sounding voice-overs for the main characters, it's pretty obvious that this was rushed into production and that Digital Extremes never intends to do anything to fix the unplayable version for the PC.Now if anyone happens to know how to get the door open when running on a Windows 7 PC I'd like to hear about it.  But for now I'm stuck in the tutorial.  And if I ever do get past the door and find the rest of the game remotely playable I might up the review to 2 stars - but based on the research to-date this game needs be withdrawn!-----  Update  ------As promised, if I found a way to open the door I'd upgrade this rating to 2 stars.  I did find a way.  The default key mappings for using the tricorder are to use the L-Shift key to select the tricorder and the E key to use the tricorder according to the on-screen prompts - and when doing so you get the feedback that the tricorder is working but holding the E key has no effect although there is some visual feedback that something is going on.  I eventually decided to try remapping the keys to have them more closely resemble other games I have played. The default key mapping in the game overloads the LShift key and the E giving them context-sensitive differences in behavior - meaning the game interprets them differently depending on what you're doing - and I think that's where the flawed performance starts - however they're doing key processing they aren't doing it well.  In any case I remapped the tricorder to work from the X key and the Use Tricorder to the F key and then adjusted several others to compensate for the fact the X and F keys were used for other functions.  Lo and Behold, the next time I tried using the tricorder on the door it worked exactly as it was supposed to.  I also noticed that my new key selections were displayed from that point on when the tutorial continued training me - which is actually a plus.But all that really did was let me find numerous other flaws, both visual and procedural.  As I should have expected it's very linear, you have to do what they want you to do in the order they want you to do it in and from the position they want you to do it in or you will fail.  I watched Spock walk right through a set of Zombie vulcans who were whooting right through him.  So I'll stick with my assessment that this isn't a very good game but since it's now playable if you remap the keyboard. I'd raise my value estimate to $5 tentatively assuming that I don't run into more serious glitches.  If you remap the keys to prevent the overloading of keys (giving the same key multiple functions) you can play the game but it's a very predictable linear third person shooter with numerous bugs.

But we did it in coop, fully complete.  Some waypoints are glitchy, so restarting was needed, and we learned not to quit until we knew there was a save point.  But it's no wonder JJ Abrams wants his name removed from anything to do with this game.  It's that bad.

Graphics mean quite a bit in this generation of games.The actual game-play has been made easier also. Getting stuck on invisible barriers has not been a problem anymore like it was in the original "Borderlands". Shooting things and collecting items has been made easier to do. As far as game-play goes however, it was already spectacular in the original so improvement was nearly impossible.The big improvement that I noticed, was the actual story itself. In the original game, there was only text besides introducing new characters which brought about a 10 second cut-scene. The story in this sequel is brought on by actual dialogue, explaining things much more clearly. This makes the game a lot easier to play for hours and hours without getting bored.Navigating menus is also improved, by being more colorful and having more information displayed at once.My only gripe is that loot is pushed more than it should be. The original had a lot of loot, so much that it was nearly impossible to have seen it all, and this sequel has much, much more than that. But the developers also have different names for the guns that are memorable, so my one gripe is actually fixed.This product also comes with the Season Pass, which is also great, and adds hours and hours of more play-time. All-In-All, this bundle is definitely worth adding to your (Steam) library!

Hello. This is a horrible remake/remaster(whatever) for an 'ok' game, here's why:1.) Input lag (THIS is the single biggest problem) on LCD TVs. In which case, hey, what is the POINT of HD Remastering IF you can't play it on an HD display without Input lag? This of course makes Wakka's Overdrive, Tidus's Overdrive, and the Lightning Strike challenge almost impossible on most LCD displays. I've personally fixed this for my own TV because I can but you might not be that lucky. So consider that.2.) Not all models are HD. In cutscenes you'll notice the your characters having nice round races and remastered bodies. However, the characters they talk to along their journey have flat, pixelated faces. I'll even go as far as to say that Tidus's model is sloppy, and the little tag on his 'HD' hoodie is a blurred up, rushed mess. There is now a yellow filter with static over Tidus's childhood memories. (It's pretty awful)3.) No skippable cutscenes, you can't turn in-battle/post-battle voices off, you can't switch to Jap vocals, the save screen has been removed and the ugly PS3 XMB save screen has replaced it, you can't turn voices off in general, you can't turn the music off, some, but not all, of the rearranged music is awful. The metal in the in-battle bgm gets very repetitive-- pretty much forcing me to mute the TV to enjoy the game. The rearranged tracks, for the most part, are a huge disservice to the game as it feels like the synthy/orchestra arrange is just way too drawn out, plus, a few chords in the music have been axed and replaced with softer ones. (Like the chase bgm that occurs right after Macalania Temple, what is up with that? I like the old percussive beats waaay more.)4.) Soft reset takes you back to the game selection part of the disc, rather than the starting screen of the game you're playing.5.) Unfortunately, it's not Final Fantasy 9 HD. Why they remastered 10 first? Probably because 10 doesn't emulate all that well on Fat ps3s so they could never release the game for PSN's Classic store. If you want to play 9, 8, or 7- You can do it on any PS3 because they all read the discs. (Although, 8 has a few glitches when emulated on the PS3)'6.) Audio issues, game crashes, and various graphic bugs. (Specifically in the Calm Lands) Every so often, the game crashes. Most of the time it's during a Chimera Brain fight and during the monster casting Megiddo Flame. Sometimes when loading your save from the Monster Arena the game loads with no bgm at all, which would be cool IF the first battle you got into didn't completely freeze your game at the black screen. There are bugs where if you have dead party members, when Yuna goes to summon you actually see their dead bodies float out of the camera view. There are graphic bugs all throughout the game if you pay attention to the details. On top of this, the Calm Lands background IS NOT HD. You can see the edges on the 'tiles' that were not blended or 'remastered' at all.You can call FFXHDRemaster a remaster/remake/redesign-- they had to take the save screen out and completely redesign the background to make it work on the PS3 for HD displays. They went as far as to change the music, improve the spell animations, and redesign the models. I guess you could also call it a redesign of the game-- they had the budget to make any changes/improvements and they did take liberties on changing some things and not others.IF you want video proof of the constant crashes, I'll gladly upload one when I buy my PVR.(It's happened several times in Calm Lands, and no, my disc is not scratched at all)--Because of the input lag, this is a broken -HD- remake/remaster, as it is intended for HD displays.-- I cannot give this any more than 1 star until a patch arrives -for everyone-. My TV is the E3D420VX and after tuning it down a few settings, I'm now able to play with no input lag. I know there are quite a few TVs that don't have this setting, and so I'm pretty much informing you all of how bad the input lag is (because even with Input lag, I had no problems in other games--this is the first game on PS3 that I've had to change my TV settings for to get it to work right). Check your TVs settings before you buy this.

...this is a good title. However, a newcomer to the series should stay away. This game has aged incredibly poorly. Really, only FF veterans should apply++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++I'll be reviewing the product here. It will obviously include a portion reviewing each game, but if you want a review that is based solely on the game, build yourself a time machine and return to circa 2003.The HD collection looks beautiful. Seriously, FFX and FFX-2 are some of the most beautiful JRPGs on the PS3, which is amazing (and sad), since they are over a decade old. I'm not nearly as in love with the music. They've remixed it, and somehow, the bass has really been lessened. After an hour of playing with the controls on my own system, I still can't re-create the sound of the original. That's too bad, too - I think this remix has actually enhanced the flaws of the soundtrack. I miss the driving beat behind the opening (and, in fact, the driving beat behind pretty much anything).Square has made the choice to remove the instruction book, but at least has given us an insert. I wish the insert was a hard card, though, as the cases are clearly designed to hold something to dampen pressure placed on the middle. It's not a huge deal, though, and it's certainly better than the cheap-looking nothing given by Namco-Bandai these days.The load times are atrocious. The music skips at time. The latter is hardly game-breaking, but the former really makes the proceedings drag.(PROTIP: in FFX, be sure to allow every member of your party to perform some non-trivial action in every battle - this will really cut down on grinding, and lessen the load-time problem).FFX:This game looks absolutely beautiful in HD. Although I've already mentioned it above, it bears repeating - this is the best-looking JRPG from a company not named Square or FROM, at least among the ones I've played (which is a pretty large selection).Unfortunately, this title really hasn't aged well. The story and its delivery, in particular, are abysmally bad. Perhaps in 2003, this was OK, but the RPG has grown up. In fact, were I to trace the downfall of the JRPG, it would probably stem from here. Characters move from point A to point B, engaging in pointless dialogue, and acting in the only fashion that might drive this stinker of a plot. In fact, I don't think the developers even cared about plot, except as a way to deliver mind-blowing, but utterly nonsensical, cutscenes. Watch as Yuna performs a sending, which turns into a rock concert, complete with a rising stage of water. Behold as our summoner, who supposedly trusts her companions with her very life, continues to withhold vital information from them (and vice versa). Why? Because that's the only way the plot is going to move forward. It even appears in the most trivial of times: why does Tidus leave the blitzball tourney final for Wakka, instead of, say, Botta, or Datto, or one of the other also-rans who wondered if they would be warming the bench? After all, by that point, my Tidus has usually scored two goals.Sure, it's a trivial thing, but it sticks in the mind, leaving the player to wonder, "Why do they always act so stupidly?"Battle is OK. It's a simple system - faster players move/attack more quickly and more often, slower players move/attack more slowly and less often. You know the order of the characters from the beginning, and are allowed to switch out on the fly. I always thought they looked stupid switching out, though (particularly since you can just switch a character over and over, and apparently, the enemies don't care). In the original version, each character had a role to play in the main game (black mage, white mage, blue mage, fighter, thief, etc.). However, apparently the International Version added something called an "expert grid", which allows characters to be whatever they want early. Don't use it - it makes an already-easy game absolutely trivial.(PROTIP: When asked, take the "standard grid".)The sphere grid is arguably the worst leveling system I've ever seen. It's a disaster. It's painfully slow and tedious, and there is no auto-level option (and really, for most of the main game, that's actually what you'll be doing - moving along a linear path, taking whatever is in front of you). I hated it then, and I hate it more now.For nostalgia's sake, I give this game 4 stars. If I was playing it fresh today, I might give it only 2, but I remember its greatness at the time. But it's a much weaker title today.FFX-2:This game was deplored by many, but it's not bad. Yes, the plot is even dumber than FFX (to the point of being foolish), but the game only takes itself seriously a few times. The gameplay is significantly better - the beloved job class system of Final Fantasy V (and Final Fantasy III, although I only played that game later, and it sucked)returns in the guise of "dressspheres". Wear different clothes, and have different powers. My main complaint is that later dresses are vastly more powerful and better than early ones, so really, the early ones are just to learn a few abilities and pave the way for the endgame dresses.Don't get me wrong: this story is abysmally bad as well. But it just doesn't have the stink of FFX (or other FF titles). It knows what it is, and works in those parameters. No one would ever confuse this slop with Hemingway, but it understands that. Compare this, e.g., to FFX, which seems to think it has so much to say on so many issues (religion, parent-child relationships, war, etc.). At 39, I find this significantly more palatable.FFX-2 had a satisfying NG+ system, and the international version adds a few nice touches as well. Battle works nicely - enemies can now attack in more real time, which makes the proceedings more frantic. However, again this game is very easy. My biggest problem with this game is that often, you don't know what items do. The descriptions are remarkably vague. Also, it's very easy to miss things in this game, and I just hate games that require guides.Again, this game looks gorgeous. I personally like FFX better (the color palette is brighter and more remarkable). Also, this game is far more non-linear than its prequel, and while it doesn't do as well as the majesty of FFXII, more control for the player means more fun for the player.But again, nostalgia rules here. I just don't think either of these games give a good idea of the awesomeness that once was Final Fantasy. But if you played them before, they are worth the re-buy, if only for the great HD support. Have fun!oh, by the way, in both games, I think the trophies are like Square-Enix itself: lazy and unimaginative.

By this point, you likely know if you like Final Fantasy X and its sequel, the somewhat confusingly titled X-2 (no one seems to agree: "ten two?" "ex-two?"). For my part, I liked FFX, but it was never among my favorites of the series. As I've been playing, I've noted with some irony how many similarities the game has to the much-maligned Final Fantasy XIII, far more than the unfavorable comparisons abounding online would suggest. Still, despite the less-than-stellar dialogue and sometimes wooden and irksome characters (I'm looking at Yuna and Tidus, respectively), Final Fantasy X is undoubtedly a great entry into the series. X-2 is less well remembered, but the worst one can say about it is that it's a fun distraction without the weight of the original.For this review, I'm focusing largely on the HD port, and I'm pleased to say that it was handled very well. The underlying game is showing its age, and a shiny coat of HD paint isn't going to change that, but it does make everything look sharper and flow much better. It's easy to see why this game made such a visual splash when it first came out.This HD remix, however, does more than simply upscale the resolution of the older titles. Rather, there are a wealth of added features that make it worth the price of admission. Probably the biggest draw is the addition of the "international edition" content, which includes extra challenges and allows for greater customization and flexibility. Some of the music has been redone, and while I didn't find it noticeable during gameplay, a hardcore fan could probably tell the difference. There's also a new story content, some which, it has been suggested, hint at a possible return to Spira in a future Square Enix game. I grew up with the Final Fantasy series and have been a fan until recently.  I count Final Fantasy X among the best - some might criticize the story, others critique the less 'ATB' focused battles - but I think it was an entry with a winning formula.  I will discuss the differences and some pros and cons comparing this to the PS2 version.  Oh, Final Fantasy X-2 was a lot of fun also - very different at the time, but I'll post a bit about that as well.Cons:- Remastered soundtrack.  Look, I love the remastered version!  But many of the songs vary quite a bit from the originals.  Most noticeably is the battle music.  It's great, but it's much more intense and a bit louder than before.  It's quite jarring.  Luca's theme for example is also a bit odd - some weird sound effects which sound out of place.  But other tracks, such as Zanarkand, Yuna's theme, the Shine themes, and especially the boss themes - are great improvements.  So pro and con I guess.- Loading times.  Yes, Final Fantasy X on the PS2 had nearly unnoticeable loading times.  No loading screen.  HD graphics in this game for sure, but the loading times are a bit much, especially when it's a long load for a six second flashback to Tidus as a kid.- NPCs.  Yes, they are rough.  The graphics were tweaked, but the non players are very rough and it shows.  The other problem is that they left the sprite glitching.  So when a character puts his/her hand on another's shoulder, the glitchy gap still appears.  I would have hoped they would have fixed some of these minor interaction issues.- Character dubbing / mouths.  Yes the dub is great.  But I would have loved a Japanese audio.  Mainly because the higher resolution graphics REALLY demonstrate the disparity in the speech and the mouth movements.  It's borderline comical at times.  Reminds me of Bruce Lee films!Okay, so that sounds really nitpicky - and it is!  But let me tell you what you get that makes this a solid FIVE star re-release.+ Widescreen baby!  All I really wanted was a true widescreen version of this game and Square Enix delivered!+ Gorgeous graphics.  Just think about this - it's still basically a PS2 game but with updated textures and 3D rendering.  So there is a lot of the PS2 edging, but much has been smoothed out.  You really notice the smoothing vs edging on Tidus' hood.  That is the most common thing I noticed.  But the background textures pop vividly.  Again - this isn't a true PS3 game - so it isn't going to have Final Fantasy 13's level of graphics.+ Two and a half games in one!  And an interactive novel of sorts...  But it does leave us wondering if there might be one more sequel to this series.  The main treats are Final Fantasy X and X-2 of course.  Also added in some interesting extra challenges into the games - secret bosses and such!  =)+ $39.99 release price for Special Edition and subsequent standard edition.  A great value.  Especially since this is a solid, main line game from SE.  Consider: many remakes of Dragon Quest, for example, were the same release price for DS.  Granted - those are full overhauls - but still, the point can be made - amazing content for the price.+ And finally - what I consider among the best Final Fantasy games.  The additional challenges in the monster arena, for example,  were some of the great joys.  It's not a hard Final Fantasy game - the Aeons are incredibly overpowered - but it's an engrossing game.  Everyone will have their particular favorites of course, but I count X among the better of the more recent systems Final Fantasy titles - and much better than a LOT of the PS2 RPGs out there (with some exceptions of course!)If you haven't played it, this is a solid RPG that deserves a run through.  It's an amazing experience.  And the addition of X-2, which is great fun, but kind of a wonky, fan service type of story, is a great bonus.  Both games are highly recommended.  And bonus story and content never hurts!

I do not know how much of my appreciation of Final Fantasy X is pure nostalgia, but this is one amazing port. As soon as the opening theme started, all old feelings rushed back to me like a tidal wave. I immediately felt emotionally attached. I knew I was in for a treat, and this title would dominate my gaming time for a big while. But trying to put reminiscence aside, I will place this game in a contemporary context.First, presentation: Square-Enix actually put some effort into this two games, unlike other mobile offerings (here's looking at you iOS ports). The up-rezing, texture clean up, and the character model tweaks, along with the beautiful bright OLED on the VITA, makes for a very, very pretty game. I do not remember this game looking as lively before. Some character models could have been better, but it did not distract me much.Second, sound: While there were some musical liberties changed, some more for an updated score, I enjoyed the audio. I never felt like I should turn down the music at any time. The voice acting was descent, however, some points were cringe-inducing (don’t you agree, Tidus?).Gameplay: For the most part, it remains faithful to the mechanics of the PS2 version. It remains a turn-based system, in RPG old-school fashion. I liked this formula in this more modern presentation. I forgotten how engaging the leveling system could be. Swapping party members in mid-fight makes it seem like you’re in control of a larger group, not just three characters. And the summoning system is awe inspiring. I didn’t mind grinding at all, even though I usually dislike random encounters. I will say however, that moving the character with the VITA’s controls proved to be challenging, and not very responsive.Third, Story: This is the main reason why I like RPG’s. FFX’s story still holds up very well to this day. It contains all the elements I look for in a long story: Humor, sorrow, melancholy, anger, fear and action. The character development is really well done for most of the characters, from the unique protagonists, to the complicated villains. They are quite interesting and make the player connect with them. However, there is one major blemish here. Tidus was and still remains one of the most annoying, awkward characters in the game. His reactions and interactions with the others made me wish Yuna would look somewhere else. But as a whole, they are all memorable.I strongly recommend it. Go get it and get submerged in the wonderful world of Spira.

When I first heard about this remastery, I was skeptical. Anyone can see that I have bought several collections and remasteries in my purchasing history, and I have enjoyed each of them for what they are and because I no longer own each of those games for my PS2 (that and trophy support = plus!). Never the less, most of them feel like they just took a Blu-ray disc, plugged three games onto it, gave them an HD boost in graphics and sound (which isn't a ton of a boost but still), and release the game for gamers like me who might not own the games or never played them. Don't get me wrong, I am glad they do it most times, but some companies overdo it (Konami, in my opinion) or do a shoddy job (Silent Hill collection). Which is why I was worried with this "collection"; I loved FFX, it is my personal favorite FF besides 8 and 9 (7 is a given really anymore). I was scared that Square Enix would just take the PS2 versions of each, make them HD'ed, and sell the games as they were. But to my surprise, they did so much more, and that is why this is not just a collection, but a full blown remastery of the two games. Square Enix went back in time almost, and not only made the games look new, fresh, and overall better, but they remade the music, added new themes or revamped them, new textures, ect. ect. In short = they rebuilt both games from the original blueprints, and made them look, feel, and sound fresh and great once more. The cinematics still look great, so there was no need to make them new again really (and they didn't). Really the one downside to the remastery in terms of looks is the lip sync to the dialogue; somehow, they neglected to rework the dialogue to the mouth movements, for they still look awkward at times. Overall, the graphics, sound, and presentation, as well as cinematics all are fantastic and great. Gameplay wise, it remains the same as before with some upgrades in terms of the presentation of the battles and whatnot, but in general the game plays and operates in the same outline as the original PS2 version did. For those who didn't play the original, the battles operate in a turn based system, with attacks, abilities, items, magic, and so on available to be used, and even the ability to switch characters in and out with a couple button presses (which is vital at times, and can also be extremely helpful when wanting to get the entire party some experience). It is a simple battle system, but it's deeper than it seems, and is a system that you learn new things with harder and harder battles (appropriate uses and importance of Yuna, when Auron is vital versus Titus versus Wakka, and so on). This game is rewarding, encourages grinding with nudges at times, and is a game that is focused and linear in many ways, yet has much to do on the side as well (which is what FF-13 lacked). If you loved RPG's, especially turn based RPG's, then get this!
