With Sonic Colors and Sonic Generations, it’s safe to say that over the past few years the Blue Blur has been doing pretty good for himself. Now he seeks to make a new hit with his latest game, Sonic Lost World. As part of a partnership with Nintendo, SEGA has released Lost World exclusively on the Wii U and 3DS. Though I haven’t played the 3DS version, I can say that the Wii U version is another one of Sonic’s great ones.The story starts with a sky battle between Sonic, in a plane accompanied by his trusty sidekick Tails, and Eggman, who has a bunch of creatures called flickies captured in a capsule. Sonic seeks to free the flickies, but Eggman decides to drop them. Sonic saves them, but the plane they’re on breaks down. They crash land on a planet known as the Lost Hex, where they meet enemies known as the Deadly Six. It’s up to Sonic and Tails to stop Eggman and the Deadly Six from accomplishing their unknown goal.In terms of story, Sonic Lost World has sort of a mixed bag. On one hand, you have six new villains who just aren’t that interesting. On the other hand, they make the story feel fresher, and lead into an interesting twist in the plot. Like the past two Sonic games, the tone is fairly goofy, with characters cracking puns every now and then. Unlike the other two games, this one is more adventurous with some actual serious moments taking place. Though I appreciate the slightly more serious tone, it does make the goofy moments seem more out of place.Sonic Lost World’s gameplay is very fun. The game follows the same basics of most Sonic games. You run through a level at high speed while collecting rings and jumping on robots heads with a lock-on move called the Homing Attack. However, this game offers plenty of new things to make the experience new. First, the levels are designed to be spherical, like Super Mario Galaxy. Every round platform has its own gravitational system. This allows you to beat the levels in a variety of different ways.Second, this game adds a new attack. In pretty much every 3D Sonic game before this one, you would attack enemies with a Homing Attack. In this game, the Homing Attack returns, but a new move is added, which is a kick. The kick makes things more interesting and allows you to do things like take out multiple enemies at once by kicking one into the others.And third, this game allows you to choose when to run fast. Sonic now runs fast when you hold down the ZR button. Otherwise, he runs like most platformer characters. This takes away most of the frustrations of being out of control and is a welcome addition to the series. What I also like about the run button is that it creates what the game calls a parkour system. Simply put, it allows you to run on walls and things of that nature. This adds another level of depth to the gameplay.There are some things that I’m sure that people will find annoying. You’re probably wondering:  Are there cheap deaths? A few. But what Sonic game doesn’t feature a cheap death or two? All this game does is reduce the number of deaths thanks to the run button. Is Sonic slower (as IGN pointed out)? Yes. But he still has a great amount of speed and is still a lot faster than the average platformer character. As a Sonic fan, who has had a lot of experience with the frustrations of previous games, these things were easily overlooked.The only thing I really dislike about the gameplay is the boss battles. Most are overly simple and can be beaten in the first try. This in it of itself is rather disappointing. Then one of the final bosses is overly difficult. It required me to do something that I never had to do earlier, which, as a result, had me forget how to do it.The graphics are absolutely beautiful and excellently showcase what the Wii U can do. All of the characters, levels, and items feature a great amount of color that few games have been able to match. The game runs at an impressive 60fps, with virtually no frame rate drops. Edginess is kept to a minimum, with the only visible edginess being on a big screen when characters are close to the camera. Though the graphics aren’t over-the-top realistic, the artistic style shows very few flaws and is a very good fit for our favorite hedgehog.The level design is also great. Despite using some cliché themes (such as desert, forest, etc.), this game makes what should be quite bland look very good. As I said earlier, the game uses a gravitational feature that allows extra exploration. Not very many Sonic games have as good of level design as this.The voice acting is… good. When compared to that of Sonic Generations, it’s getting better. Characters like Amy Rose who had horrible voices are now at least bearable. Mike Pollock’s Eggman is as usual great, and Roger Craig Smith and Kate Higgins do a good Sonic and Tails. Still, it’s times like these where I miss the previous voices, considering how well they fit the characters.Fortunately, when it comes to music, Sonic once again delivers. Lost World’s music is much more orchestrated than the previous games and features one of the best themes in a Sonic game. This game has a soundtrack where the main theme will play over and over again, but because it’s so good you really don’t care.Sonic Lost World has become one of my favorite Sonic games and currently my favorite Wii U game. When compared to Colors or Generations, I honestly couldn’t say which is best. Wherever I would put it, it would definitely be up there with them. The gameplay is fun and exciting, the graphics are practically perfect, and the soundtrack is great. SEGA really did a good job making Super Mario Galaxy for Sonic. As I said, there are some frustrations, but being as those are common in Sonic games, I’m not too upset about them. But with those frustrations in mind, I can only truly recommend this game to those with previous Sonic experience.Final Score: 9.3/10

This is an EXCELLENT installment in the 3D Sonic Era, now let me tell you why:If you were to jump back to the old-school 2D Sonic the Hedgehog, you'l notice almost immediately how incredibly important precision is. Speed is essential, but it's more the illusion of speed instead of the actual use of incredibly fast movement. Simply holding right on your D-Pad will not earn you victory, but there is some "auto-pilot" involved in every Sonic installment. In this newest Sonic, you'll feel the speed you always have, but this time you'll have that insane timing and precision required in order to beat the level in time. With a slight overworld and powerups shared throughout the community, this game brings in Sonic Generations and Sonic Colors fused with a bit of Sonic Adventure. You can have one of the best Sonic experiences you ever have with this game. While the boss fights leave you wanting more, the only Sonic game with intricate boss fights is Sonic Adventure (1 & 2) while others really just involve Mario-esque timing and jumping patterns.Gameplay being solid, let's look at other aspects. The music is amazingly scored and more similar to classic Sonic versus the Punk-Rock newer Sonic. The graphics are beautiful and Sonic (and his world/friends) has never looked better. The controls are great; while they boast a learning curve, once mastered they are seamless and implemented very well with the Parkour mixed with the RUNRUNRUN of it all.  The one downside is, playing as other characters had become an incredible little pallet cleanser, but it's not terribly missed since this gameplay is so fresh and pristine.Sonic fans will want to give this game a try, because it truly reinvents Sonic with the most attentive respect for its roots. Slightly childish, but intentionally so. Lazy translations and not always perfect mouth animation sync'd with audible speech, but we're used to that!

It has absolutely nothing to do with "think fast," but it genuinely emphasizes "take your time to think it through" which I've only hated in any game.Don't get me wrong, it's not a horrible game, especially for people who are under the age of 4 (not meant as an insult, I mean it. It's good for newbies), but if ever there was a disgraceful title to any video game series, this is it. It summarizes Mario, Donkey Kong Country, and Skylanders, and it's a shining example when you're helping someone young understand the word "downfall."Best game on the wiiu, though.

This game does have some flaws but I'm still giving it 5 stars overall because it is a great new direction for the sonic franchise in my opinion. I also feel that this game is highly misunderstood by the game reviews and players alike. If you play this game treating it like a whole new game with new controls its excellent but if you play this expecting a fast paced sonic game you might be disappointed.Yes sonic is slowed down in this game, yes the controls take a little getting used to(sonic has a kick/homing attack/spin dash/climbing), yes some cheap deaths can be expected, yes some parts are difficult and might frustrate you, and yes the boss battles could have been better. STILL this is a great game and I had a great time playing it.I might be in the minority but I felt that the slowing down of sonic just made him that much more precise. Sonic controls wonderfully in this game once you've got all the moves down. He isn't all that slow either, if you want to speed run through the levels you just need to master the spin dash and double jump to blaze your way through if you really wanted to(check some youtube videos of players who are good at speed runs).Sonic has some new moves as well like the ability climb up trees and wall run across walls, it takes some practice but soon enough you'll run across walls collecting rings and climbing up walls to different areas. I really enjoyed all of sonic's moves and felt the controls were spot on.I really enjoyed many of the levels as well and even though some parts in some levels were difficult I surprisingly enjoyed the challenge, others may get frustrated but it depends on the player. There are some cheap deaths throughout the game but nothing that's unavoidable. The boss fights could have been better but I still enjoyed some of them since they had some cool concepts involved even though they were easy. The color powers are okay but nothing special though I did like the drill and a few others.I basically played this game like a platformer, I took my time in some levels and blazed through others depending on the level design. I really liked this game and with the update that gives you a life for every 100 rings and more lives when you get a game over, it is even more enjoyable. I played the game after this update maybe that's why I did not mind the difficult parts. Also the yoshi island dlc is free and was quite cool.I can recommend this game to platforming fans and sonic fans if they treat this game like a new one which it actually is. I liked this new direction for sonic but I understand that some people may not. At the price it is going for nowadays I say it's worth it. Happy gaming.PS-it is one of the games worth playing on Wii U and can serve as a holdover for people waiting for the bigger releases coming this year.

For months now, I've owned theNintendo 3DS version of Sonic's latest outing(If you'd like, you can see my review on that - I gave it a 4). Ever since I've been a newly proud owner of the Wii U, though, things seemed to be looking bright for the console edition, as that was one game I eyed. Now that I finally got the game, picked it up and put it down numerous times, I can't help but feel that this is one unstable game. Whenever I wanted to really relish its atmosphere, it decides to throw me off in various ways instead.When you first get into the game, it plays like a winner. The first couple worlds of the game offer splendid level design that cooks up multiple pathways as you run, jump, Spin Dash, and use the signature Homing Attack on classic-era enemies. However, no longer is there any Boosting a laSonic GenerationsorColors. Instead, we can actually move Sonic around the place smoothly, and he can run up walls via the new parkour play mechanic.Sonic is surrounded by scenic environments (With the game being at 60 frames-per-second, no less!), and the music is outright awesome and diverse!As great as the game sounds so far, it slowly becomes worse until you hit the fourth world, Frozen Factory, in which the title's flaws really thrive by then. Initially, the only worries are that the parkour isn't easy to control when running on sides of walls, and that the Wisp power-ups have no reason or explanation of being in the game. They aren't as fun to use, if not worthy to play with (and you have to press A to resume the game after using one). Oh, and there's the briefcase for whenever you want to use items.Why can't we just find the item capsules in the actual level? It's not convenient to tap the briefcase on the Wii U's GamePad to get one! Same goes for hints (?s)! Plus, why does Sonic have to pop a truckload of animal capsules to progress on to certain points in the game? Not only does it force you to backtrack, but the numbers required are excessive, regardless of whether or not you use circus tents to play bonus games to earn animals.And I didn't even mention the later problems.Enter the bosses, which are disappointments compared to how they were in previous installments in the series. The Deadly Six are one-dimensional beings who are there just to be this game's group of baddies, featuring the most generic cartoon tropes ever for each one. And they put up no fight....until deep into the game. Normally, they only take 4 hits (2 if you charge your Homing Attack each time), and their attacks are uninteresting.Then as Desert Ruins hits the scene, that's when you come across changes in gameplay....a LOT. Not too badly here, though, as there's just one level where Sonic runs automatically. When Tropical Coast comes in, it forces you to guide moving fruit into blenders in one level. And then as Frozen Factory arrives, each level becomes its own thing. Sonic will have to try and deal with the stupidly slippery ice physics, and also turn into a snowball and behave like the marble inMarble Madness. There's so many levels that change up the entirety of the gameplay often that it never feels consistent.When there are levels that stay with the 3D/2D platforming formula, though, the game decides to throw in surprisingly difficult pieces of enemy layout and level design at you. Unfortunately, the game handles these parts as well as its overall structure. The game feels rushed, as there are portions of levels that don't allow for freedom in how the level is played. They are overly precise and rely a lot on trial-and-error. Lava Mountain, the final world, is appropriately DEMONIC for containing all of these troubles in design in every frickin' corner!More particularly, Lava Mountain Act 2 (Which has aquatic scenery - Because lack of consistency), where Sonic uses grind rails the entire time. He also has to avoid INSTANT-DEATH MINE CART BOMBS (Yes, even Super Sonic can't survive them) placed in the worst possible positions while also needing to jump precisely to grind rails spread sporadically or else he'll fall into the bottomless pit below. This stage sums up this entire game in one level.So...Why does this game get a 3 instead of a 2 or 1-star rating? Because the game still has the potential to be fun. There really are levels that are a joy to play through. Not every bit of my experience in the game was miserable. However, the game floods itself with disappointment, and considering that Sonic Colors and Sonic Generations were great titles, it's a shame they are followed up by this.If you ask me if you should get this or the 3DS version, I say definitely go for the latter. The handheld counterpart not only features one gameplay style (The 3D/2D formula, albeit with a few level-specific gimmicks that don't change the gameplay drastically), has no backtracking involved, but the control is SO much better and more reliable (especially with parkour mechanics - I was able to parkour like a pro!), and the challenge is very well fairer (there are numerous opportunities for extra lives, and there's a lot less trial-and-error/other annoyances). I'm not saying the game doesn't have its own flaws, but it still provides a better experience than this console version.Or if you didn't already play them, you could just buy Sonic Colors or Sonic Generations instead.

The mechanic of flipping back and forth between the future warfare (2030 or something) and flashbacks to the Cold War in the 60s-80s was fantastic.  They really put a lot of effort into that campaign and the game in general.The hype before the COD Ghosts launch talked about the "totally redesigned engine" and all this stuff, but it's very dated, graphically.  It's the same old small iteration on the id tech engine.  Nothing was thrilling, nothing was immersive, it was total crap.Multiplayer is obviously where they put their money, but it was boring.  It was pretty much identical to the previous games, but somehow, more dull, less gadgets, less technology.  Lots of cheaters using lag switches, etc, especially on the 360 version, which is a very hackable console.Overall, a terrible flop of a game.  Widely considered the death of the series. Probably why it's on sale now at a budget.On a side note, I played Battlefield 3 back in the day, and wasn't too impressed.  It was graphically poor.  Too much chaos.On the other hand, Battlefield 4 on the PS4 (the definitive) version is killer.  Epic.  The campaign was at least 10-20 times longer than Ghosts, and more thrilling and immersive.In multiplayer, the maps are enormous, and on PS4 and PC, it's 64 players!  You have 5-6 player squads, so team play is paramount,  All kinds of vehicles, Jets, Helos, Tanks, Trucks, etc, and you can spawn on a player in a vehicle, say a Helicopter, and your teammate flying the vehicle, while you can switch between stations (machine gunner seats, etc).  Spawn in a tank and a teammate will either drive or operate the secondary gun,  You capture areas and can spawn from them.  You can parachute from planes and helos and capture points.  It's like COD times 5 or 6,  A truly epic game,As squad leader you can give orderers, and anyone can use a quick menu to make quick questions/commands/etc.And one of the coolest parts, is if you sign in on the EA website, you cannot only further customize your soldier, but you can go into battlemode and see, in realtime, the map, and everything that's going on, in your browser (I recommend Chrome).  They did some top-notch HTML5 work here.  You san see strongholds, characters (including you), a all in real time, it's a real, working, second screen that runs in the browser, and there's a full-screen button.  So you can have your laptop/PC/MAC next to you and see all of the action tom the minimap, but in full screen, and if you're a commander, you can target objects, etc.  It's pretty amazing how they got all of this to work.Last note, if you're going console, get the PS4 version, as it is the definitive version, running at 1080P without a hiccup (the review sites, like GameTrailers, noted that MS wouldn't allow them to show footage from their versions prior to launch…  questionable?  They also said the PS4 version's graphics were on par with the PC version with graphics set to HIGH).  It's one crazy, but again, epic game!  Reminds me a bit of Tribes 2; steep learning curve, but once you've got it, it's a masterpiece.  If you're deciding on which one to get between this and COD Ghosts, definitely get Battlefield 4; it has taken the crown, COD is DOA.

First of all, I have to say that this game gets a lot of unfair bias. It is a decent and solid Call of Duty game, and I'll explain why below. Sure, it's fast and you die quickly and you can definitely get frustrated with it. However, it's a Call of Duty game. What did you expect? All the CoD games have low health and very short gun fights, be it Black Ops 2, MW3, BO1 or MW2, you name it.Pros of Call of Duty Ghosts for PS4:1) Hit Detection - This obviously depends a lot on your internet speed, but in my experience, currently playing this game on college internet (with NAT type 3, or the worst nat type) with over 300 hours clocked in, I can say that the hit detection in this game is very reliable and good. When you shoot at someone, you at least get hit markers - WHICH is a sign that at least your shots registered. Also, because hit detection is good in this game (and your shots hit the body when you point at an enemy) Sniping is really fun in this game. You get a lot of 1 hit kills, which makes it rewarding. You hate being sniped? Well you should learn how to snipe for yourself then. It can be very fun and rewarding to master sniping in this game.2) Weapon Variety - Assault rifles have been separated into 2 categories now: a) "Assault Rifles" (automatic and burst fire rifles) and "Marksman Rifles" (semi-auto). This is, of course, in addition to all the other weapon categories like SMGs, LMGs, Shotguns, Snipers, Riot Shield, and Knife. Basically, this means that there are more automatic weapons to choose from in this game. I like this a lot, compared to say Black Ops 2, where the automatic and semi-auto assault rifles were smashed together into one category, so it felt like there was lees variety there. In general, Infinity Ward has been very consistent with offering a huge amount of weapon variety in their games. (I mean, despite MW3's controversial "copy and paste" feel, it had the most weapon variety and prestige levels out of any CoD game.)3) Good Selection of Perks - In this game, not only is there a wide variety of all the perks we love plus more, but perks feel a lot more important to understand in this game than past Call of Duties. For example, as I played through my 300+ hours of Ghosts, I learned a few tricks about perks: Blast Shield is an absolute necessity to this game, and works very effectively against all explosives, notably the irritating new IED (throwable claymore); Quickdraw is very necessary for sniping; Focus (a perk that gives you less flinch) also reduces ADS idle sway, and is very helpful when using an automatic weapon, since the guns recoil with each bullet, so spraying with an automatic weapon kicks a lot. Etc.4) New Squad System (prestiges) is AWESOME - Basically, you unlock 10 soldiers, and these 10 soldiers represent your 10 prestiges. Once you "prestige," you move onto the next soldier but you are now able to go back to your previous soldier (prestige) and use all your previously unlocked weapons! Did you get home today and feel tired of grinding XP with the junk starting assault rifles and SMGs? Do you wish you could just "play for fun" and use all your powerful and fun weapons from the past? Just go back to the previous soldier! Simple as that. Also, this means that you have more custom classes to choose from. Each soldier has 6 custom classes X 10 soldiers = 60 custom classes to switch between by the end of the game! WOW!Cons:1) Server Lobbies aren't very reliable - What I mean is that while I DON'T lost connection to a match during the match, I usually lose connection during the pre-game lobby. This is irritating, especially when I meet some cool players and then get "kicked" out of the lobby due to a connection error.2) Camping - As you might have heard already, there is a lot of camping in this game, and this is largely due to map design. It's almost as if Infinity Ward encourages you to camp in this game. Maps are huge with lots of middle battlefield area to get killed by campers on the sides. Secondly, there are a lot of camping spots in this game - at least way more than MW3. I remember in MW3, infected used to be so difficult to survive in because there was no where to camp - you just had to run around and hope for luck. In Ghosts, there are so many camping spots that people survive in Infected for a long time, which is proof of this. Finally (the most frustrating of them all) Third, the gold camo challenge requires you to camp and lean kill. That's right. If you want gold guns, you need to get about 100 kills by camping. This is probably the most disgraceful part of Ghosts. Camping should be a side effect of the game - not a challenge!!! Instead, they force you to camp. Or you can resist....then no gold guns for you!!!3) Extinction - This mode is not only a knock-off of zombies, but it's very limited compared to zombies. Basically, for those who don't know, Extinction is an alien "minigame" in Ghosts similar to the Black Ops series' zombies mode. What you get in the box is 1 (I repeat, one) game mode for extinction. No survival mode. No grief mode. Just 1 mode. And if you buy the DLC, you'll end up having.....2 modes. Yes. Honestly, I feel that extinction is a total joke, and I'm wondering if they should have included it at all. It's kindof deceptive, since they advertised it heavily before the launch of the game and in every DLC video. However, it is such an insignificant part of the game that I wonder if it's that honest to market that feature that heavily.4) Squads - Basically bots mode. Not very replayable because it's just not very fun or addicting.So basically, all you get when you buy Ghosts is a solid multiplayer and campaign. I actually enjoyed the campaign, and I'm not sure why it got so much hate as well. I think it's worth it, and I think that if you want a solid Call of Duty multiplayer with a decent campaign, you should get this game. It's on discount now - even better for you!

I own the first Modern Warfare, Black Ops 2 and Ghosts. I also own Battlefield Bad Company 2 and Battlefield 4. I've played them all though at some point and love them all. Who picks sides? What Ghosts is is pretty much a different game altogether. If I feel like playing the best Battlefield, I'll play BF4 (even though it takes time finding a decent server sometimes) and I'll love it. If I feel like playing the best CoD game, I'll play Black Ops 2. But Ghosts is a combination of the two to me. It feels like Battlefield at times yet doesn't stop feeling like a CoD game. The maps are bigger and there are places for campers.. But that's the thing, I like that challenge in these maps. Black Ops 2 was smaller and didn't quite make you feel like camping. It made you constantly on the move and that's pretty much the feel of the series that was lacking in this game which in turn enraged many gamers that wanted to 'replace their old copy' so to speak. Battlefield 4 is huge but sometimes you'll run for a whole minute and get pegged by a sniper or deal with campy flag holders. In CoD Ghosts you get campy flag holders as well but it never feels like a huge setup for nothing. The maps are bigger but not VAST and you can react quickly or accordingly without wasting your whole match figuring out the snipers strategy. You have time to change your approach through trial and error without spending too much time doing so. Same goes for Free4All. This doesn't feel completely like a CoD or Battlefield game. It's a whole new game. And I like that. It felt like the first time I played Blacklight Retribution on PS4. I don't feel like I was replacing an old best title like I did with the jump from Bad Company 2 to BF4 when I got into Ghosts. I'll still play BO2 from time to time because it's the best CoD game in my opinion. But Ghosts is new and it almost feels like a hybrid of Battlefield's BC2 and CoD's BO2. Right in the middle size-wise and a seemingly combined gameplay aspect. A mix of everything I like about both titles. I wonder if the company had released this as a different title while mentioning that it is a CoD clone or something... Would this have taken so much heat? Who knows. This as a game, I'd easily give a 9/10. If you were expecting to play the same game again, you'll be surprised...

Before I start the review, let me say one thing -- I love Call of Duty. Some of you may want to crucify me for that, but I still love Call of Duty, and I have been a big fan since I first popped Call of Duty 4 into my PS3 a few years ago. It has the same fast-paced multiplayer action in every installment, with a cinematic campaign and fun co-op modes thrown on top for an overall fantastic package. Ghosts is Infinity Ward's latest Call of Duty installment. It was hyped to have a dramatic story in its campaign, a unique new Squads mode, and the familiar Call of Duty multiplayer mode with the usual improvements made to keep it fresh. But how good is it?CAMPAIGNThe story has you playing as Logan Walker, a soldier fighting for a country that is under attack from the Federation, a power-hungry South American superpower. In the first minutes of the game, a Federation squad hijack ODIN, an American controlled space station that has the ability to shoot devastating lasers at Earth, and immediately begin firing on the United States. A nation that was once a powerful and influential power in the world is reduced to nothing more than a barren wasteland.The story starts off strong, with an initial focus on you and your brother defending San Diego from the foreign invaders. However, without spoiling anything, the story eventually becomes unfocused, and loses the desperate feel that was present early in the game. Instead of defending America from the Federation, you start globe-trotting to places like Venezuela and Antarctica, making it feel just like the Modern Warfare games. You go from one explosive set-piece to the next, with little cohesion between the events. For example, you go from flying a helicopter through an enemy infested base, to blowing up an oil rig in Antarctica, to swimming and shooting underwater, to shooting in space. Yes, space. It feels like the developers came up with cool set-pieces that they could put in the game, then tried to come up with a story to tie them all together. While it was like this in the Modern Warfare games, at least you genuinely cared for your teammate's lives, like Soap and Captain Price. In Ghosts, that feeling is gone. In the end, I didn't really care what happened to my teammates. I just wanted to see what the next epic set-piece was.In terms of gameplay, it is pretty much what you'd expect. Actually, it is exactly what you'd expect. You run, shoot, run, shoot, reload, watch the obligatory explosion that causes your character to fall back, run, shoot -- you get the idea. It's the same cinematic formula that has been used in other Call of Duty games, and it works -- at least, to me it does.Overall, Ghost's campaign features the same cinematic gameplay that has been present in all Call of Duty games. However, without a good story to back it up, this campaign felt noticeably more average than any previous Call of Duty campaign. It isn't quite up to par with the Modern Warfare games, and it certainly isn't up to par with the Black Ops campaigns, which I believe are the best campaigns in the FPS genre. If you are going to get this game just for the campaign, then I strongly recommend renting it, as it is not worth full price for the campaign alone.MULTIPLAYERNow it's time for what any true Call of Duty fan wants to hear -- the multiplayer. Anybody that has played Call of Duty multiplayer knows what to expect -- fluid and fast-paced gunplay that isn't too hard to pick up and play. Unlike, say, Battlefield, where you need to play for a few hours to familiarize yourself with all of the vehicles and classes, Call of Duty is as easy as picking up a controller and playing.So what's new? The create a class system has been retooled, allowing for more freedom in how you want to play. It is basically Black Ops 2's Pick 10 system, but only perks count, instead of everything from weapons to attachments. The better the perk, the more points it takes to equip it. For example, Sleight of Hand, which allows faster reloading, costs two points, while Deadeye, which slightly increases your weapon's power after every kill, costs five points. You can also customize your soldier -- a first for the series. Completing specific assignments award you gear, such as helmets, armor, and masks. The customization is a cool new feature, but it doesn't matter that much, considering you never see your character during gameplay.There are a few new game modes. In Cranked, whenever you get a kill, you have thirty seconds to get another kill, or you explode. During the thirty seconds you gain faster mobility, and faster reload speed, which can help you get the next kill. In Blitz, players must run through the enemy's portal in their spawn to score. Once you score, you get teleported back to your side. Grind is basically Kill-Confirmed, but instead of simply picking up dog-tags, you must take them to one of two banks in the map to score. In Hunted, you spawn with nothing but a pistol with a clip of ammo. To get better equipment, you must take weapons that drop into the map from care packages. In Search and Rescue, you only have one life, but if your teammate picks up your dog-tag after you die, you get to respawn.That's about it. While I still had a great time playing the multiplayer, I felt that it wasn't new enough. The back of the box states that the game features "redefined multiplayer." I'm sorry, but I didn't really see what was redefined about it. It was basically the exact same thing we have played before, only with a few new modes and a slightly revised create-a-class system. However, while it may not be completely new, it is still really fun. It seems more balanced than previous Call of Duty games. With a few exceptions (the MSBS is a ridiculously overpowered one-burst, one-kill death cannon), the weapons seem to all be balanced. In Black Ops 2, SMG's seemed overpowered compared to the other weapons. In Ghosts, all of the weapons are around the same power level, and there is a weapon for every player. For example, I am a big LMG fan in this game, while in previous Call of Duty games I never really liked them that much.Besides multiplayer, there is also Squads mode. In this mode, you customize a ten person squad, and take a selection of them into a match, versus either another player and their squad, or all AI opponents. While it can be entertaining to take a squad of snipers into a match on a big map and dominate another player's shotgun-equipped squad, I found that Squads is mostly just glorified bot matches. Since the Squads matches are played exactly the same as a standard multiplayer match, I found myself wishing I was in an actual multiplayer match against more unpredictable opponents. While the AI for the squads is really good, I found that they never really switched tactics. They just run around and shoot, save for the occasional objective capture.The one mode that I absolutely loved in Squads was Safeguard, which is basically Survival from MW3, but with a few tweaks. For example, instead of buying weapons, perks, and equipment from pre-determined points around the map, they drop from the sky as care packages in random locations. It is also four player co-op, instead of two players. Safeguard is an absolute blast, especially if you're playing with friends.There is also Extinction, which is Infinity Ward's take on the popular Zombies mode in the Treyarch Call of Duty games, trading out the mindless zombies for quick and intelligent aliens. Instead of simply surviving wave after wave of zombies, Extinction has players drilling into alien hives with a drill that they must carry with them. There are 14 hives to destroy, with an escape from a nuclear bomb to end the game, which takes around an hour to play through. If you're playing with three other people that know what they are doing, then Extinction can be a blast. However, since there is only one level, it gets old after a few games. Infinity Ward is going to support Extinction with DLC, so that should increase replay value for Extinction if you have purchased the Season Pass.The graphics in Call of Duty are basically the same graphics that you have seen in any Call of Duty game since MW2 in 2009. For a next-gen game, Ghosts looks outdated compared to, say, Battlefield 4. While the PS4 version looks better than the current-gen versions, you can only tell the difference if you are playing the two versions side by side. If you have already bought Ghosts for the PS3, there isn't much of a reason to upgrade - even if you are taking advantage of the $10 upgrade deal for PS3 to PS4.The audio is pretty much what you would expect - tons of gunfire and explosions, and an epic soundtrack. The voice acting, while good at times, can seem pretty forced and dull, especially from Hesh, your brother in the campaign. His voice actor sounds like he's constantly waiting for the next lunch break. Other characters, like Merrick and Keegan, sound so generic that you can hardly remember their voices. Other than the voice acting, everything else is up to par with other Call of Duty games.Overall, I am a bit disappointed with Ghosts. For the first next-gen Call of Duty, I was expecting just a bit more. However, with that said, I still had a blast playing it, and there was never a moment of boredom in its campaign and multiplayer options. While some additions are lackluster, like Squads, I can still see myself playing this game for quite some time. However, for Infinity Ward's next game, I expect a bit more innovation. Just adding some new modes and killstreaks doesn't make the game next-gen.---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Overall Score: 8.0 out of 10Story: 7.0Graphics: 7.5Audio: 7.0Gameplay: 8.5Replay Value: 9.0

The concept of swap-able characters seemed interesting to me, which is kind of why I ended up buying this despite my reluctance after the monumental disappointment that was Skylanders Giants. Still, I only ended up paying about $40 for this game (bought it during the Black Friday deals) so I guess I can live with it even if just for the sake of a multiplayer game.Anywho, on to the game. I give the game a low rating for 3 main reasons: the levels, the intro, and the bosses.The problem with the levels is that they're unnecessarily long. It's kind of like the creators wanted to hush those that complained of Giants' shortness by making this game longer, but didn't think it through. Rather than make them interesting, or add a greater variety of levels with more diversity, they essentially just dragged levels out far longer than they should be. It actually got rather boring and left me considering using a fast character like Ghost Roaster to speed through the decidedly mind-numbing levels.As for the intro, that's where they got truly ridiculous. Each time you start the game, or even just go back to the main area (Woodburrow), you have to listen to the guy near the front give you some options for what to do. This, of course, comes after watching the last bits of the level you previously beat if you haven't yet beat the game. Now, feel free to correct me if you have found a way around this as nothing I have tried worked (not pressing Y, X, start, select, anything).Oh, and lets not forget the bosses. Why is it the final two bosses combined are easier than the boss that came before them? Don't get me wrong, the whole game was extremely easy regardless of your difficulty, but at least the puppeteer boss actually put up something of a fight.Putting that aside, I rate the game 2 stars instead of 0 stars because some of the new figures were at least entertaining and fun to use. I bought a full set of new characters (all 16 swaps and 16 core), and they were relatively good. I also give them some credit for actually putting out 32 new figures rather than the 16 Giants had, and for not raising the prices again as they did with Giants (which saw a $5 increase from adventure to battle packs and $1 increase on core figures). However, they lose points for once again making all the triple packs involve 2 remade characters and 1 new, which essentially forces those of us that only want the new core figures to buy all of them as single packs.

This review is more about determining which characters to buy to get through 100% of the game so you're not spending a ton on needless characters.  The series already has substantial popularity with a ton of reviews written.Concerning the portals.  Swap-Force characters can only operate on the swap-force portal.  They will not function on the Spyro or Giants game portals.  However, The Spyro and Giants charcters will work normally on the Swap-Force portal.As you travel through the maps of the game you'll come across various "turn-offs" (caves, doorways, etc...).  There are things to be earned/won/collected in each of these areas.  These areas require a character with either a certain ABILITY (i.e. spin, bounce, dig, sneak, teleport, etc...)  or of a certain ELEMENT (fire, water, earth, etc...)The elemental characters need not be a swap-force character.  They can be from either of the other series (Spyro, Giants). You have to have a character from each of the elements.There are also areas you must have a swap-force character with a specific ability to enter.  As an example, Wash Buckler is a water element character with a climb ability.  He can open water areas and climb areas. You must have swap-force characters that cover all the abilities.The only other type of character that is needed is a GIANT. There are certain boxes that only a giant can open.It's a fun game.  Kids are really into it and can't wait to get the next series.  After you complete the story There are still ton's and ton's of other activities to complete within the game.If you don't start off with all the necessary characters you can still select areas of the story to go back to and find items you are missing.Hope this helps.

Specifics: it's infuriating that, at least on my PS3, if you forget to plug the cable into the guitar until you've already started the program, the program refuses to recognize it -- you must actually turn off the PS3 and turn it back on to get the guitar usable.  Sure, maybe this is a PS3 limitation, but why in Hendrix's name didn't they discover this during their testing and give you a clear message like "No guitar detected -- you need to plug it in, or turn your PS3 off and on to get it working".But that's not all.  Many irritating quirks.  Why can't I skip the Ubi login screen?  Why can't I skip the confirmation when I exit a song in Learning Mode?  Why does it force me to check my tuning before every single song?  I was hoping to get 100% on that Ramones song: why did it award me 108.3% instead?  Why is the Tone Creation a haphazard, embarassing, audibly-ineffective trainwreck? Having played guitar on and off for over 20 years, I didn't expect much from this "game". I have hardly picked up my guitar in the past year and originally bought this for my nephew who wanted to learn how to play guitar. After all the research I did, I decided to pick it up for myself. Install on the PC went well, but I do occasionally get issues where it will conflict with my Astro mixamp, which usually involves me plugging and unplugging the usb cables into different usb ports on my computer until they both decide to play nice with each other.The first issue with this game is that the neck display is upside down. If you have ever looked at guitar tab the High string is on top and the low string is on the bottom as if you laid your guitar on your lap and looked down at it. Luckily you can change this in the settings, but it should really be this way by default. Anyone who learns to play guitar from this game will have a lot of problems trying to read normal guitar tabs.I was skeptical of the guitar hero style interface at first, but it seemed to work well at first. When things are slow it's easy enough to figure out which note you need to hit. The real issue comes when you are trying to learn a song like The Spirit Of Radio by Rush. There are so many notes in the first part of the song that it is completely impossible to figure them all out even at extremely slow speeds using the Riff Repeater. I know that playing the song in the normal mode will only give you a few notes, but this also has huge problems. It seems to just throw notes out randomly and gives you indication of which fingers you should be using to finger the notes, which means that every time it throws out another note you may have to completely change how you are fingering the notes.The same issues happen on songs like Peace of Mind by Boston. It starts you out playing single notes, then changes to two strings and then three or more string. For the beginner this can be extremely frustrating, because it doesn't show that what you are actually playing are parts of a chord, so beginners will try to finger each group of strings individually instead of only adding or removing a single finger from a chord. This one of the many placed where this makes learning songs much more difficult than it should be.Another issue is that it just throws out symbols in the songs without any explanation of what they are. I was able to figure out slides and vibrato easy enough, but things like bends are not obvious at all. I just read in another review that there is an explanation somewhere in the interface, but I have not seen it even though I looked for it. This leads to the next issue I have with the game. The manual is completely worthless. Other than a few overly simplified troubleshooting tips, there is really nothing in it. This is the place where all the symbols you would need to know to learn to play the songs correctly should be. When playing the games, there is little on no explanation of what you are supposed to be doing. For some inexplicable reason they take the fret board view out of these and expect you to remember what the string colors are supposed to be when playing the games.The other problems this game has are the tuner, which will tell you your strings are out of tune, then after you tune them individually it will check them again, but completely miss that they are still out of tune because you have a floating tremolo. It's like it doesn't really check the strings the second time you go through them. When you have a floating tremolo (like a Floyd rose) every time you tune one string it will pull the others out of tune. depending on how out of tune your guitar is you may need to go through several times to get the strings in tune. I guess they just expect everyone to use the crappy Epiphone guitars pictured on the box.Finally, there is some severe problems with accuracy when you are playing faster parts of songs like the intro of Desolate Motion by Karawan. I have had it give me a 100% accuracy on the beginning part when played at full speed in the riff repeater several times even when I made some rather sever mistakes.So, this game can be fun to an extent and help get kids interested in playing guitar, but it will only take you so far. Without assistance from someone who knows how to play guitar this game will teach you all kinds of bad habits which will cause all kinds of frustration when you try to play more advanced songs. The way the game throws out random notes while you are learning the songs can be a little hard on the ears, so if you are buying this for someone, you should include a set of headphones with it.

I thought it would be a cool learning tool disguised as a game.  I wanted to get the latest version in hopes of an increased number of supported video drivers for the PC version; an issue mentioned in other reviews.INSTALLATIONMuch to my delight, it Rocksmitth 2014 installed perfectly on a HP 2000 laptop with an Intel Core 3i processor, 8GB of ram with a proprietary HP integrated video card - not listed as supported by the Rocksmith folks.  (I purchased the game knowing this - checking the maker's website first.)  I knew that I had a desktop that does have the supported set-up, so I figured if it came down to it, it was still usable for us.Prior to installation I had her get a Steam account.  The software installs with a DVD (one is included for PC and another for Mac), but uses Steam so it uses less of your system resources.  Despite this, some systems may run into issues with installation.  **Read all the reviews and ask questions prior to your purchase.  I recommend checking out the manufacturer's support area too.PLAYS LIKE A GAMEProbably because it is!  But it's a game that I think would appeal to ages 12 and up who also want to learn to play.  Rocksmith is very similar to Guitar Hero, but you use your own guitar and you're actually learning while you play the game.  The game also grows with you, so you continue to build on your skills.  The software adjusts and shows you things like how to tune your instrument.My daughter loved this software immediately.  She'd been looking up YouTube videos and had a book, but this software immersed and engaged her.I'm not sure if you can buy more songs to add to it (I think you can for XBox...), but that was one of her first questions to me.  It comes with about 70 songs, but enough to get you started and challenging enough to keep you going for awhile.CONCLUSIONUBI Soft has a winner in Rocksmith 2014.  They've put a lot of thought and innovation into this package, and it's a stellar way for beginning electric guitar and bass players to have fun while they learn.I purchased this for fifty dollars, which considering the price of the game and the cable sold separately, made this quite a nice deal.I highly recommend this software, but warn potential buyers that for the PC/Mac version, you'll want to have a supported system or be prepared to say your prayers and roll the dice on compatibility.For me at least, this version does work for Windows 8.1, with video graphics not mentioned as supported by UBI Soft, so I'm thrilled and so is my daughter. I am a bit torn here, but I've decided to go with a full five stars for the following reason:This product has managed to achieve what several decades of guitar lessons by video/DVD/web have not. It has actually made me a better player. Gradually, with lots of encouragement, and a very forgiving learning curve. (Unlike Ubisoft's war games, which are unforgiving, merciless and tedious!)Here's the fatal flaw:When your game system is connected to your TV via an HDMI cable, there WILL BE A NOTICEABLE LAG between when you play a note, and when you hear it back. This makes Rocksmith all but worthless as you fumble around trying to play notes ahead of time, out of sync with the music. It's a miserable experience and you'll hate it. Ubisoft is aware of this and has made users aware of the flaw in the startup screens of the game. There's a warning that says you should connect your audio directly via analog cables. DO NOT IGNORE THIS. HDMI will yield an entirely unsatisfactory experience due to latency in the round trip that the audio has to take from your guitar back to your ears. However, if you're willing to do a bit of hacking and reconfiguring, you will be rewarded with a teaching tool far beyond anything I've ever experienced.The cheapest solution I've found, for users who have the original Xbox 360 RGB+Red/White audio cable, is to crack open the gray plastic housing around the connector and throw it away. This is the cable that you stopped using when you upgraded to HDMI. Then plug the now-much-slimmer-but-still-sturdy metal connector into your Xbox right next to your HDMI cable, this may be a tight fit if your HDMI cable has a lot of fat plastic around it's ends. Ignore the RGB cables, just plug the red/white cables into an old bookshelf stereo, or ipod dock, or anything you have that will take this very common audio input. Listen through that and mute your TV while you play. You will now experience very little latency and you can get on with learning.Other users have said plenty about how well this "game" executes against it's stated purpose of teaching you guitar, so I'll leave those reviewers to dive into the details. I just wanted to chime in to say that this game is absolutely worth the technical hassle if your goal is to move beyond "aspiring guitar player" to "actual guitar player". After all, if you're a guitar player, you'd better get used to the idea of troubleshooting some cable issues. It's gonna be part of your life.

In looking through the reviews here, I have to agree that there seems to be some fake reviews and padding.  How many grandparents/parents could possibly be reviewing this and how can they give a review for something they haven't played?!  So, here's a real review.  I am a total beginner and I've played the game almost every day (except when my fingers hurt) for about four weeks.But first a tip:  turn off voice commands (under options).  For those people that are finding this game glitchy...me, too -- until I realized the game was picking up random sounds and interpreting them as commands and switching screens on me.The GoodFor the cost of a couple of guitar lessons you get a pretty cool game that resembles Guitar Hero.  There's a boat load of songs and tons of instructional lessons on technique.  For the price, that's worth it right there.Starting out, it's really fun.  The strings each have a different color and you can successfully play along and feel pretty good about learning and about your ability to be a potentially good guitar player.The Riff Repeater is awesome.  You can take a part of the song and adjust the speed and difficulty and it will loop over and over to help you really get good.  Love this feature.The BadProgression - I would say that there are no songs on here that you can master as a beginner.  I suppose that's OK but kinda discouraging.  In the beginning, you start out having a song where you have to play a single string every ten seconds - which is a bit too easy for even the worst beginner.  And then out of nowhere, a chord will appear.  But that's usually OK - you can figure it out.  But then, it goes from too easy to too hard in a heart beat.Buggy Programming -  Even if I factor in that I am pretty bad, there is still 10% of the time that the program doesn't pick up that I played the right string.  It seems to get worse the more complicated the chord.  I even stop the song and make sure I have the string or chord right, start it again so I know I have it right and yet still.  What's bad is not having it scored properly means the song won't progress in difficulty for you.The song list.I guess this is why I doubt the reviews from "grandma who bought this for the kids and they love it".  Who knew grandmas were such big metal fans.  The lack of musical variety is pretty pathetic and ultimately will limit my interest in the game.  I can't really find that many songs I'm interested in learning to mastery.  And I wouldn't even mind the metal and hard rock if the songs were all iconic hits and granted there is Walk this Way. Poison's Pour some sugar on me, BlitzKrieg Bop, Kink's You Really Got Me and The Trooper.  But I can't understand why there are so many songs I've never heard of and seem to have no appeal.  They could have added really cool songs that are fun to play.  How about including a Chuck Berry song as a tip of the hat to the past -- some Hendricks -- Lynyrd Skynyrd-- or some funk or blues?  And where is AC/DC, Van Halen or Led Zeplin??!!!  And while I'm at it -- female rockers get no respect on here.  No Heart (Barracuda would have been AMAZING to learn), Joan Jett, Pat Benatar, Evanescence...no anything.  Jeez -- three songs by female groups I've never heard of -- and lame songs at that.The Announcer -  I'd like to meet the person at Rocksmith who wrote the responses to give after you finish the song -- I'd curse him out.  Example.  Last night I cranked the difficulty up to 100% on a song just to try it.  I was going to do the best I could even if I only hit 1 out of every 5 or 6 notes.  At the end of the song the game says in a really snotty voice, "Poor performance!".  Nice.  If that were a human guitar teacher, he'd be fired.  The game also says "Bad performance" or "Needs more work" in a nasty tone.  Who talks to people trying to learn like that?  I guess some jerk at Rocksmith, that's who.ConclusionI'm not sorry I bought the game.  I like it OK.  I would recommend it but only with the caveats I just gave.  I'll use the riff repeater and learn the few songs I like.  I looked on the DLC songs coming out and even those don't expand the variety.  I wish this game was so much better because the concept is a good one.

They should include one in the box-- it is needed that badly.Once that is resolved, you end up with something amazing. This CAN really teach you how to play a guitar or bass or if you already know how to play, can really help you polish up on your skills.It's an absolute blast. First of all I bought this to LEARN guitar as I live in a very rural area, I played it consistently for two weeks for a total of 100-110 hours then shelved it and here is why.I just couldn't get it to click for me and there was some audio lag which caused me to miss notes and I tested this with riff repeater. After playing an absolutely ridiculous amount of Diablo 2 with friends and family, I skipped out on Diablo on the PC because of the infamous auction house. Diablo's wrath is back, and our button-mashing heroes must defeat him and his "endless" army yet again. While the story does reference the previous titles (Deckard returns!), Diablo 3 shines with it's simple yet incredibly addictive gameplay. You pick one of several classes that range from the Witch Doctor (summoner of pets and uses poison spells) to the Monk (the Chuck Norris class who punches and kicks baddies). Diablo's system begs for you to play the game several times through with each class, as you won't see every skill each class has to offer without multiple play throughs. And the thing is, you'll WANT to play multiple times. Every play through is different thanks to Blizzard's algorithm of making every player's world a new and random one. The game is also is very impressive in the graphics department, looking ahead of it's time with gory visuals and excellent lighting.If you're a fan of this franchise, I'm pretty sure you've already bought this game and beaten it on "Hell mode". For anyone who is on the fence, take the risk and try it.

Blizzard is well known for making good games and Diablo III is another quality game.  First off,  buy this game used. The only thing that comes in the box is the disc and a one page manual so any extra money spent on a new copy is only for plastic wrap and that annoying sticker that makes the game really hard to get in to. The mechanics of Diablo are solid. The controls are easy to learn and customizable to your liking. The game pad makes combat really fun and easy by making the left stick move and the right stick dodge with left trigger to lock on. The buttons are all basically for attacks and spells/skills so there really isn't a lot to learn beyond remembering which button is equipped with which attack or skill.  The story is good and has that Blizzard humor throughout. The graphics are high quality considering it is a console game with limited rendering power. With the new expansion out and coming soon to consoles this is a great time to pick this game up. The expansion ushered in a lot of changes on the PC which fixed a lot of the known problems and has brought back many who gave up and also inspired new explorers to join in the fray. The changes should be reflected in the console versions especially the Xbox One and PS4 versions which will have the expansion included. Diablo III has a lot going for it with multiple characters each with many different styles, appearances, and attacks which gives players the ability to replay the game and have different experiences with each play through. The co-op aspect is another of this game's awesome features. Get together with friends at home or far away and play a four player game in which working together is rewarded. Too many games are about player versus player so a game that is about working together is nice to see, at least on consoles. The leveling, skills, and gear are acquired through grinding so it can be very unappealing to some players but the old school RPG dungeon crawling fans will love it. The game is a top down third person isometric style game which is also very familiar to old school RPG fans but may be unappealing to some players. Diablo III really is about friends, gear and story so prepare for some good times and lots of loot.

The 1 star rating describes it as 'hating it,' which I didn't so I opted for the 2 stars, 'I didn't like it.'  I'm not comparing this to the PC version, but this being a game on the market, I do have to compare it to something.I actually began playing with high hopes, which is always a bad idea to start a game or begin a movie, it usually never works out that way.  I went in thinking of World of Warcraft; why wouldn't I?  Blizzard developed both games and its really the same genre and play style.  I expected a fun factor but only found grinding.  I don't want to grind a console game, I wan't options, interaction if not choices.  Many people complain about linear game play, this was pretty much that.  I completely compare the grinding with Warcraft, but Diablo III took out the character customization, the choice of playing as different races, no control over the camera angle, great, but tiny art.  I actually played Warcraft for a few years and had multiple characters, this game actually felt nothing like that, just grinding (you wouldn't think that since Warcraft was so freakin' popular, why go to a lesser version of a great formula?).  I was up there at level 25 or so and still looked ragged, with cheesy dialogue, and nothing to look forward to.  I felt this game took itself too seriously, it just had no fun factor.  The intro story was also very dull, where's the new and exciting?This would have been fun a decade or more ago,but after playing it, there is just no evolution.  I don't want to say this is for hard core gamers, I'd say this is a farming game and there is more out there so I put this down and picked up another title.  Honestly, the game could have included fighting combos and spectacular weapons/armor from the beginning, why wait?  I'd have to compare this to DMC, Bayonetta, God of War...and why not?  They are fighting games, hack and slash, and how does this differ?  Why couldn't this game have that type of interaction?  Some of the character models were pretty good, but they were so small as to barely be visible, then you get bombarded with attacks and lack of character development on the villain side that it's not enjoyable.  There's only so much you can say about the graphics as well.  Compare this to Ratchet and Clank; All 4 One... those graphics and that game play I feel put this title to shame.  I know they're different, but even a dungeon crawler should offer more today than 10-15 years ago.A simple,predictable plot, mediocre characters, no options or choice in character customization besides putting on some barely visible brown gloves or barely visible tan gloves, linear game play, farming at center stage, no camera control, zooming in or out freedom taken away, hordes of enemies which leads to superficial fighting, exaggerated setting (how much of a cellar can a cathedral have for crying out loud?), poor environments, repetitive game play to the extreme made me resell my copy pretty quickly.I would say this is strictly for Diablo fans, which I was not, and apparently will not be any time soon.

...but small things keep it from perfection. Nostalgia and Tales fans will gobble this up. If you are a fan of JRPGs that has been disappointed this generation (and who hasn't?), but haven't played these titles, I recommend them highly. If you are new to RPGs, this might not be the best start point, though.++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++I remember frantically searching for Tales of Symphonia 10 years ago when it was first released to the Gamecube. It was a good selling title (in Madison, WI, many stores were sold out on day 1, something you NEVER see with games this generation). I found it, purchased it, and loved it. Years later, I also bought Tales of Symphonia: Dawn of the New World for the Wii. It was not nearly as hard to find, it was not nearly reviewed as highly, and yet I found it, I bought it, and loved it. I still own both games.It therefore might seem strange to re-purchase my old games for the PS3. However, the lure of HD is strong, and the extras from the PS2 version of Symphonia were enough to lure me in. Plus, although I'm not the avid trophy hunter I once was (since the birth of my daughter), I still like hearing the ping.First things first: this game's packaging makes it feel cheap. In fact, it feels like a used game. Namco has made the decision to go paperless with this game, so there is no physical instruction manual. That's too bad, as I've always enjoyed manuals for RPGs. But what really makes this annoying is the fact that the case still has clips to hold the manual. That makes the product feel like a used game (even more so, since this is previously-released material), which is a turnoff. At the very least, they could have put in an insert, like EA does.Onto the games. Tales of Symphonia is a fine JRPG. While it suffers from many of the problems that have plagued JRPGs this generation (such as cliched characters, long and pointless dialogue, interminable cut scenes), it is redeemed by a story that is far greater than the dreck we've come to know and loathe this generation. Religion, racism, blind and fanatical nationalism - all are expertly woven together in a concept that still remains surprisingly effective. Further, the art concept of the game really enhances the experience. To this day, I remember the staircase with corpses floating ethereally about the party. It was a great image that really helped along a more-than-perfunctory story. Yes, as I said before, the delivery can be tiresome, but if you can see around that, you will really enjoy the ride.Combat is a strength in all Tales games, and this is no different. It's not the best, by any stretch (in fact, I found combat in the sequel to be better, e.g.), but any Tales game is a step above what you find in any other JRPG, with the sole exception of the Valkyrie Profile titles. As always, you have active roam, with numerous artes and attacks with which to pummel the forces of evil that stand before you. Good stuff.Perhaps it's a nostalgia bias, but I find that this game runs more stiffly than the Gamecube version. While the graphics are pleasing enough (with their HD cleanup), I feel more stutters in this game than I did on the original version. It's not game-breaking, though, and in any case, the game has not frozen up on me. But it does detract from the experience.Tales has a world, and enemies are always present on the screen. Moreover, the many sidequests make an already-meaty game even more involved (although I seem to remember missable quests - a constant detraction from Tales games).Dawn of the New World doesn't have the story of the original Symphonia, and the characters are more annoying (I particularly hate the early banter between the main characters, even more so after battle). But like any Tales title, it has a great battle system, and DotNW has a thoroughly enjoyable monster training mechanism. It's a weaker title overall, but still quite fun.In both games, prepare for difficulty spikes. They are particularly bad in DotNW. Of course titles, grade and the like are found here. Strong as always.The game includes a Japanese language track. Personally, unless you're trying to show off your chops, I would suggest you stick to the functional English-language track. It's certainly not the best, but it's not horrible...usually. It still beats the unintelligible (to most) squeaks and squeals of the Japanese girls, though. Localization of Tales games has never been a strength IMHO (certainly not on the level of Square), but again, it's functional. Some of the grammar really offends, though (I particularly like when the translators use "whom" when they really mean "who" - that one REALLY grinds my gears). But my only real gripe is that people take too long to say too little.These are solid games, and should be played by any JRPG fan. Be prepared to dedicate some time to the proceedings, however (and possibly slavishly follow a guide if you want everything in the game).

I am really disappointed to see this version of ToS is based not on the Gamecube version (which ran at 60fps everywhere but the overworld), but the technically inferior PS2 version (which only ran around 30fps). For some reason, the makers of the HD version left it at 30fps (plus or minus here and there, with odd judder occurring where you wouldn't expect it), which is a bizarre decision as the PS3 obviously has more than enough power to handle it at 60fps, even with the higher res graphics. The ideal solution would have been to base it on the PS2 version, yes, but bump the frame rate up to 60fps so it at least looks as good as the GC version frame rate wise. Speaking of the HD update, there are a lot of very jaggy lines (especially hair) and blurry textures that most HD updates I've played have just plain done a better job updating. Also, to me Lloyd's movement doesn't feel as crisp/precise as it did on Gamecube, maybe because of the slower frame rate.I understand frame rate isn't important to some people, and some people can't even tell the difference between 30 and 60fps, but to me, frame rate is the most important thing when it comes to graphics (for example, on PC I will turn all settings down in order to get 60fps). So to me, it's a big disappointment that ToS isn't running at 60fps.So with this review, I am calling attention to this HD conversion and this technical issue specifically, and my dissatisfaction with it, hence the 2 stars. Content-wise, ToS is a 5 star game and one of my favorite RPGs of all time, and I definitely do recommend it if you haven't played it before, but the issues have to be called out.Note: I didn't mention Dawn of the New World simply because it's not really worth mentioning, though at least it runs at 60fps. Also note- if you want, you can buy these games individually on PSN for $20 each, currently.
