This mouse has a great feel, both for gaming and for everyday use. It's designed to be used right- or left-handed and is quite comfortable -- as long as your hands aren't too big. It's pretty narrow for a gaming mouse, so if your hands are on the large side, your thumb and pinky may rest on the table. Not exactly ideal. I have average adult male hands, and the mouse is *just* wide enough to be comfortable without having to squeeze too much with my thumb and pinky. The textured, rubbery sides do feel great and the wire is fabric, not plastic.The side buttons take a little getting used to. They are thin and placed high on the sides, which prevents accidental clicking but requires a vertical movement to line up your finger. It's fine once you get the hang of it.This mouse suffers from one strange flaw -- there are five levels of sensitivity, controlled by a center button (pretty standard), but there is no visual indication of the current level (not so standard). The only way to know is to remember or to click the button and see what happens. This makes no sense, especially considering that there are plenty of lights on the unit, which are apparently just for show.

This is a really attractive mouse that looks great sitting on your desk. The plug and play performance is great but I'm not playing any twitchy FPS games to judge its DPI performance or input lag. However, the key factor I look for in a mouse is comfort and this one just couldn't do it for me. It's very rounded...and doesn't really work for me the way other more elongated mice do. I saw one reviewed say this makes the mouse ambidextrous but neither I nor my left handed test subjects found the mouse to be comfortable.However, for the price, you get a premium package from the box all the way down through the nice cloth-enclosed USB cable. But, for all the extras, it really came down to comfort and I went back to a cheapo e-blue mouse within days.

UPDATE 5/11/14: I may have judged this game too soon, as I'm finding that the more missions I complete, the better I have learned the nuances of stealth, panther, and assault modes. Plus, now having tons of cash to unlock different loadouts and weapons it has made it much easier to get through these missions, even on rookie mode.So based on continuing to push through and learn as much as I can about the game and the unique gameplay, I'm upgrading my review to 4 stars!=======Let me start off by saying this is my first Tom Clancy game. Generally I'm an RPG player, but this game looked so beautiful I wanted to try it. From an artistic standpoint, I wasn't disappointed. From the environments, to the character designs it's really quite well done. Lots of eye candy, especially on ultra graphics settings if your GPU can handle it. The fluid movement of the character and the ability to interact with the environment is top notch.One of the major issues I'm having is being forced into certain play styles. I'm terrible at stealth, and many of the missions require it which means I've found myself making one tiny little mistake and having to start over again...and again...and again. After the 8th or 9th attempt it just isn't fun anymore. Even on rookie mode I've found several of the missions impossible to complete and have aborted the mission to try something else. I love the different loadout options for weapons and gadgets, and have tried pretty much every permutation of stealth tactics, but all it takes it one little misstep and the whole mission is done for - even if I've made significant progress (many of the side missions do not have checkpoints - so once you mess it up, you have to start from the beginning).I've also become disappointed at being in a mission and going past a door that I can't do anything about unless I play co-op. Well that's all well and good if you have a friend who has the game and you can schedule gaming time with, but since the majority of the mission is single player, why prevent me from experiencing everything in the game just because I can't coordinate time on someone's calendar to help me out?And then there are the bugs. So many of them. I've been in the middle of a mission and the keyboard just suddenly stops working (some players have reported a regular 30 minute lock-up in the game). The mouse actions work just fine, but I can't get the game to recognize any key I'm pressing on the keyboard. So I just get to sit there and let myself get killed and have to cntrl-alt-delete to kill the game. Over and over this has happened - and it just adds to the frustration of finally making progress on my 10th attempt only to have the game crash.Beautiful game and with so much potential - but the forums are full of issues with buggy gameplay (and I should probably mention that awful bug with full screen and windowed mode - don't touch ANY keys when the game is starting if you want to stay in full screen - what the heck is that about).I want to keep trying to get through the game - but I fear I'm missing out on half the game because it's simply too hard or too buggy to complete a simple mission. Even the AI suggestions cause problems - in many of the stealth missions it's recommended that you shoot out the lights to create shadows, but if you shoot out too many the guards get suspicious and the mission fails anyway.It seems like there is a really interesting storyline in this game, and I want to play it out, but finding myself bored after multiple attempts to do basic tasks. I welcome any and all comments that could help me and other players work their way through this beautiful game.

This is a review for the downloadable Burst DLC only, not the full retail disc version. The original Naruto Shippuden Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 game is a masterpiece for the most part... but this DLC? not so much... The DLC adds a new boss battle,new playable character, 100 battle challenge mode, some enhanced visuals and some unlockable images.. and that's it.. not really worth it and i'll tell you why..the Challenge missions are fun, and what you'll spend most of your time with since it's the only new content that takes time to beat.The "New Chapter" is misleading.. it's not a new chapter it's just an impossible to win, complete unfair, frustraing boss battle with you playing as Itachi and Sasuke against the Sage Mode form of Kabuto. Kabuto has 2 battles.. the first one is winnable but the second  he has  5, yes 5 health bars! that take little damage which drags the battle out for a while. If you fail, and you will fail.. every time.. you can have to restart the battle at the second part of the battle where he gains his 5 health bars, but the difficulty remains the same, instead of of being lowered so you can win it like in the other boss battles from the original Naruto Shippuden UNS 3 game did... essentially, not matter how good you get.. the boss battle isn't winnable and is extremely frustrating..The "HD Visuals" that were supposedly enhanced for the Burst DLC  aren't a mixture of visuals that only look slightly better, some blurry ones that actually look worse the the original's graphics, and ones that looks the same and were untouched.The only other good thing about the DLC besides the Challenge missions is the "new" character Sage Mode Kabuto ( i say "new" because he could have had sage mode as an awakened form (and probably did at some point in the game's production before it was presumably was put on hold in order to make more money and release it as DLC) he is a good new character.. but $10 for one character and some quick challenge missions isn't really worth it.. even if you get the retail version which includes the all the DLC costumes it still isn't worth it since the costumes are just cosmetic.So to recap.. one new character. an impossible, frustrating boss battle. partially enhanced ( and partially worse) visuals, new challenge mode for $10 is a rip off big time.. don't bother getting the DLC unless you just want Sage Mode Kabuto are willing to pay $10 for one character..

Vivid, detailed visualsA celebration of everything MarvelFun in co-opCons:Predictable, repetitive designOccasionally cumbersome controlsNo real challengeDetailed Review:Developer TT Games has Lego games down to a science. It should have; it's now been almost nine years since the studio first reconstructed the Star Wars universe in endearing virtual Lego bricks. In video game terms, that's light years.Fast forward across the entire lifespan of PS3, and Lego Marvel Super Heroes is about to put to bed the console generation it helped welcome, and you can tell TT Games has made an effort to give a proper send-off.If you're any kind of serious Marvel fan you'll probably have already Googled this game's character list. It's simply immense - there are no fewer than 155, and that excludes DLC. Bursting at the seams, it has more Marvel characters than the original Pokemon Red and Blue games had critters. Merely unlocking them all is half the fun, because you are collecting characters from entire universes - The Avengers, X-Men, The Fantastic Four, Spider-Man and loads more.Despite the complications in dealing with multiple star franchises, the game's single-player campaign manages to pull it all together with an amusing plot. At the outset, it launches into chaotic Lego brick-exploding battles, rapid-firing super heroes at the player as if they came free with packs of Cheerios. Spider-Man, The Hulk and Iron Man kick off proceedings with a fight against Sandman and Abomination at Central Station. Then Mr. Fantastic and Captain America join the fray. Then Human Torch, Thor, Jean Grey, Cyclops, Wolverine - they just keep coming.As the campaign unfolds, you head from one iconic Marvel landmark to another, from Stark Towers to Asgard - tackling super villains at every step. You'll take on Doctor Doom and his mighty 'Doom Ray of Doom', before showdowns with Doctor Octopus, Loki, Magneto, M.O.D.O.K and even the Statue of Liberty. Yes, the actual statue.Clearly, the series hasn't forgotten its sense of humour. Slapstick cut scenes and a script full of consistently charming wit are amusing enough to make even the most hardened cynic crack a teethy grin. Younger gamers are bound to find it hilarious.All of this is grounded within an open-world hub in the form of bustling Manhattan island. Before each mission starts, you're let off the leash to explore, skydiving dramatically from the SHIELD Helicarrier to the streets below. From there you can commandeer vehicles from helpful citizens, compete in timed races, take on sub-missions offered by numerous NPCs or just explore the open city seeking out tokens (which can be spent to unlock more characters).It's fun to burst around the city as Human Torch or Iron Man, but this is where some small niggling issues arise. Flight in the open-world setting is given increased speed to compensate for the distances you're required to cover, but the controls can be touchy. Car handling is also twitchy and imprecise. Navigation through the town can be cumbersome because of this.The main missions are triggered by entering the building, or area indicated on your HUD, and it isn't long before the game settles into its fixed gameplay patterns. Players enter a building, moving from one room to another, activating a series of character-specific switches while constructing and operating Rube Goldberg-like Lego machines as your angular heroes chase a villain towards a major showdown. Each set-piece is beautifully realised, and the waves of enemies and giant bosses ensure the action remains intense throughout. As always, drop-in-drop-out co-op also serves to enhance the fun.Lego Marvel Super Heroes certainly starts with a bang, but the campaign begins to show a lack of imagination. Repetition quickly sets in, and will inevitably begin to take its toll on core gamers who won't see many deep nuances in the experience. At it's heart, when you strip away all the superhero-themed fat and fanfare, this is essentially a 12-hour conveyor belt of switches, packaged with a bundle of clearly labelled keys shaped as Marvel characters. It's the same level design formula you've come to know and expect from TT's Lego games, but now feels like it's at an evolutionary dead-end.Signposting is comprehensive and persistent, so getting through its intricate array of mechanical Lego levels requires little strategy or skill. Winning is simply a matter of identifying the next switch (be it a Shield switch, a claw terminal, a breakable wall, a buildable contraption or a blockade of ice), selecting the character required to bypass it and pressing 'B'. To that extent, the shiny, Marvel-branded outer shell is merely a vehicle for churning out this rather basic and repetitive gameplay mechanic over and over again.Don't expect the formula to change. Simple, lighthearted and approachable fun has been the mantra of the Lego games series since the critically-acclaimed Star Wars trilogy, and Marvel Super Heroes is no different.The lack of challenge makes it perfect for younger players, while the Marvel characters will only broaden its appeal. It's destined for success.But for everyone else, it's a shame that a game based on one of the world's most creative toys and set in one of the wackiest collections of fictional characters ends up being so predictable.

I purchased Lego Marvel Super Heroes together with an Xbox One as a gift for my nieces. We've had fun with it, but it's far from perfect.Lego Marvel comes on the heels of the recent surge in popularity of both Lego video games (thanks mostly to Lego Star Wars) and the Marvel superhero brand. This game certainly uses this popularity to its advantage. The graphics aren't spectacular. The story struggles to engage. 4-player co-op is glaringly missing.The gameplay is particularly peeving. This is a game clearly intended for kids. I was surprised, then, to find that even I had to search online how to pass certain areas. Completing certain parts of the game can be annoyingly confusing and unclear. And when not struggling to move on, you spend a good portion of the time simply collecting lego pieces or holding a single button to assemble things. In other words, the gameplay is imbalanced, bouncing back and forth between too hard and too simple.All that being said, it's important to put this game into perspective. First, for a game licensing popular brands marketed at kids, it's actually put together pretty well. Those types of games are usually mediocre at best. When you remember that, Lego Marvel suddenly stands out at the top of the pack. It's unfair to expect award winning gameplayAlso, when you take into account that the selection of games available for Xbox One is currently limited, Lego gains even more points. If they can forgive the frustratingly confusing parts, I think the kids will enjoy this one.

I just can't. Yes, this game is not without its flaws: it is a short game; the weapon arsenal this time out is limited and pretty uninteresting; and there are none of these inter-space dogfights and missions that we saw in TOD and CIT.All of that said, this little game is an absolute charmer. The graphics are GORGEOUS, even more impressive than TOD and CIT  (I especially loved the settings for the various missions -- jungle planets, desert planets, swamp planets, all wonderfully crafted and graphically convincing). I would highly recommended it.

Let's address the elephant in the room. Clank is a tool (both literally and figuratively). I've now played three Ratchet & Clank games, and he adds little to no value to the franchise. I put up with the pointless Clank mini-games in Crack in Time and Tools of Destruction, but the buck stops here. I'm putting Insomniac on notice - stop with pointless mini-games or you will lose a customer (as if they give a damn, lol). I just needed to get that off my chest, now on to the review.Combat - As usual, this is primarily a third person shooter with a tiny bit of melee sprinkled in. I elected to turn off the auto aim which resulted in tougher combat. I liked the tougher combat because previous R&C; games were a bit on the easy side. It would have been nice to maybe see a different melee attack. It's been the same wrench throwing/swinging attack for the past few games, and it's starting to get boring. I understand the wrench is a staple in the franchise, but couldn't we get another melee attack in addition to that? Maybe Clank could be used in a melee attack, being that he's not doing any damn thing else...Weaponry - Out of all the R&C; games that I've played, this is my favorite group of weapons. There's too many for me to discuss, so I'll just touch on a few of them. Once you collect the full catalog of weapons; you'll be able to turn enemies into snowmen, unleash lethal demons, throw sticky grenades, use a rocket launcher, target enemies from a distance with a sniper rifle, and make use of a `jack in the box' that can literally scare bad guys to death (one of my personal favorites). But the fun doesn't stop there. If you collect 9 missing `blue prints', you'll be granted with the mother of all super weapons. It's called the RYNO VII, and it's nothing short of spectacular. It has more than 1,000 bullets, which is unusual for a R&C; weapon. To put this in perspective, the next closest weapon holds under 100. Here's a little tip: Unlock this as early as possible. I didn't get my hands on it until very late in the game, so I had very limited use with it.Enemies - Unfortunately, this is the weakest area of the game (besides Clank, of course). There are only 4 or 5 planets, so I'd expect to see a different enemy type on each planet. The same few enemies were recycled on all of the planets, for the most part. I'll go out on a limb and say the same 4 or 5 enemy types were reused over and over. The boss battles were fun, but nothing too special. While playing the game, I felt like the enemies never quite measured up to the awesome weapon choices.Miscellaneous - There are several side-missions to do (only offered on one of the planets). Also, I didn't think the game was as short as some of the reviewers made it out to be. If you take your time and explore the planets, plus do some of the side-missions, I think you can probably eke out about 10 hours of gameplay. For those die-hard R&C; fans, you'll be happy to know the arena battles are alive and well.I deducted a star because Clank's little missions were beyond frustrating, and you'll be forced to do them. I'll put it this way: If I were ever to meet Clank in person, I'd buy him a pair of lungs, then I'd probably lead him to a lake, and hold his head under water until he drowned (or rusted to death, whichever the hell comes first). Now you have an idea how frustrated I was while playing as him. If they feel the need to include such nonsense in the game, it'll be good idea to make them optional side-missions, just saying. Also, the enemy variety wasn't great, and that contributed to my overall score. Into the Nexus is a pretty good game, just not a great one. God of War I, you're up next!!!

DaganRonpa is a wonderfully bizarre combination of Pheonix Wright, Corpse Party, and And Then There Were None. Summoned to a prestigous academy by a lottery, you are suddenly trapped within the complex by a homicidal mastermind, who tasks you and 14 other students to murder one another to escape the school. After the murders, you then have to endure a trial in which you try to prove the culprit, lest everyone but the murderer be killed. Along the way, you can develop relationships with your fellow inmates, all of whom have interesting and often very murky backstories. The body count rachets up really quickly, so theres very little complacency, with a very shadowy subplot in the background.Gameplay is fairly straightforward, especially with the exploration portion, in which you can quickly teleport around the school to interact with others, which is a very nice feature. The class trials are a lot more involved, and they twist up the Pheonix Wright formula artfully. While you have a laundry list of evidence and statements, you only have to deal with a handful of items during every "argument." There are a few frustrations with this, as the contradiction can be rather thinly sliced between two similar statements or items. Theres also "white noise," random text lines that appear to literally block your attempt to point out a contradiction, which does little except to draw out the segment only to use a feature of the Vita. In addition to the arguments, theres multiple choice questions and identification of suspects to mix it up. Finally theres a rhythm game thats rather tacked on and overdone in which you "slay" your opponent.Graphics and audio are novel. Other characters have 2D like cutouts. The audio is mostly voiced, though only the trials and cutscenes are fully voiced, and the cutscenes, while disturbing at times, are well put together.Overall, this is superb. Novel gameplay, interesting characters and story, and a clever use of dialogue and story development make this the lone 5 star Vita game I've played thus far.

Before I get into specifics of the game, I'll lay some ground work as to the story (spoiler free of course).You are Makoto, a very average teen-age boy chosen to join the elite "Ultimate" students at Hope's Peak Academy. The school is the institution of many ultimate students, who are the best at what they do. Only the best and brightest get into Hope's Peak. However, quickly the students find themselves in a deadly game lead by a sinister mastermind, Monokuma.In short, Monokuma tells the students that they are all trapped inside the school with no way to escape EXCEPT to kill another student without anyone else finding out "whodunnit". If that happens, the student will be set free, and the rest of the student body will be punished. However, if the murderer is found out, then the murderer will be punished, and the game will continue.The game has very interesting and relatable characters (minus 1 or 2 annoying ones), each having a very unique personality. Some characters, despite the situation, actually seem to be enjoying themselves. Some are downright pushy, and demanding. Others... mysterious, you never know what's going on in their head. Which makes it all the more difficult to decide who to believe, and who not to believe.-Gameplay-At certain points during the game, you're allowed free roam of the school (which is done by allowing you to freely walk the school, in 3D). Once entering a smaller room where you can explore, the navigation will become point-and-click. Using triangle will allow you to see what items/characters can be interacted with, and simply clicking 'X' on those characters/items will perform the interaction. Interacting with students will allow you to spend time with them, learn some of their background, and build a relationship; in turn, increasing your Stat Points (SP), and possibly gaining a new ability to use during the trials. Interacting with objects can sometimes net you a Monokuma coin, which can be used in a coin slot machine in the shop to gain items. These items can be given as gifts to other students, which (depending on the item and character) may improve or hurt your relationship with them.Upon the discovery of a body, the game will enter "Investigation Mode". You'll be able to examine items in greater detail, taking note of important clues (which will be added to your "Truth Bullet" notes). Speaking to other students during this time may give some insight to what they think happened, and could lead to some discoveries of your own. Investigation Mode will continue until all Truth Bullets are found.Then begins the Class Trial. The class trial consists of 4 main sections: Endless Debate, Hangman's Gambit, another section consisting of destroying false statements in time with music, and the Review.Endless Debate - you are given certain truth bullets (between 1 and 6) to use against weak statements made by other characters. Weak statements are shown as text in a different color (yellow if I remember correctly). Just sit and listen. Once a weak statement appears that you believe you have a truth bullet that contradicts it, select that particular truth bullet (by pressing 'L') and fire it at the statement (using triangle). If it's correct, the trial will progress, if it's not... you'll lose health. Losing all of your health will cause everyone to believe you're the culprit and you'll lose (this goes the same for all main trial sections).Hangman's Gambit - a simple game of hangman, but I hope you were paying attention just before this section started... otherwise you'll be lost. Sure, you're given a few letters, but without knowing the previous accusations.... you'll be lost. Knowing what letters to select to fill the puzzle, just shoot the letters one by one and fill in the puzzle. Pretty simple.Rhythm Section (1v1 Debate) - this part begins when you have someone backed into a corner. They are spouting random statements to refute your proof. Simply press 'X' to lock on to the statements, and triangle to fire. You only have so many bullets though, so you'll have to press square from time to time to reload your truth bullets. Pressing 'R' will slow down the tempo a bit, and also give you unlimited truth bullets. Each time you destroy a statement, their health is chipped away.... vice versa if you miss statements, you lose health. Reduce their health to zero and you'll have the opportunity to land the final blow and prove them wrong.Finally, we have the Case Review. This portion, in my opinion, is extremely well done. You pretty much have a comic book laid out in front of you, which just so happens to have some missing panels. The comic book illustrates the events that happened during the murder, and gives you a bank of panels at the bottom of the screen to fill in the missing pieces (note that clicking an empty panel will give you a hint as to what goes there). Once you're done, the murder will be played out in comic book fashion (and it's very well done, btw).After all is said and done, the student body will vote as to who the guilty party is. Which leads to one of my few disappointments of the game. A cutscene showing the results of the vote has not been updated, it appears very blurry as if it was directly ported from the PSP version (this also is the case for another scene where Monokuma activates the punishment button). The guilty party is chosen, and then "punished" in front of everyone, in many unique yet bizarre ways.The trials and punishments are easily the best portions of the game, followed by the investigation. There are multiple trials, and each trial is increasingly more difficult to figure out.... leading to the trial becoming much more interesting. In the early portions, you can kind of have an idea of who committed the crime before you walk into the trial.... but later on, I didn't have a clue.I also want to note that you are granted an SP meter to use during segments of the trial. It acts differently depending on what segment you are in and it will refill quickly after use.- End gameplay-The presentation is beautifully done, with bright colors, very detailed environments, special effects, etc. This thing got a major overhaul from the pics I've seen of the PS2 version. I only noticed one or two instances where the devs cut corners on the port.The story, like other games of this nature (999, Virtue's Last Reward, Phoenix Wright, ect) will draw you in and have you hooked from beginning to end. You grow to care about the characters, especially one in particular (won't give it away though).The music is very fitting to the scenarios, and its very well done. Some seem to rave over the music, which is fine... I think the music is indeed great, but I don't necessarily need the soundtrack.I feel like I'm beginning to dig pretty deep on what to say, so I'll let the review end here.All I have left to say is.... when DanganRonpa 2 hits later this year, I'll be picking it up on day 1. This is a truly excellent experience, and I highly recommend it for anyone who enjoys this type of game.9/10The game also includes an NG+ mode called School Mode, which I haven't played... so I really can't comment on it.

I've been dubious about "Danganronpa." The fandom hypes it up to be one of the greatest things since sliced bread, and I've been suckered into playing or watching too many bad things with those promises. Still, though, the concept intrigued me, and new titles on the Vita are always a sight for sore eyes, so I had to pick this up on launch day. I still had apprehensions, of course, what with the characters coming across as cookie-cutter stereotypes and the art style initially striking me as trying too hard to be "quirky." But with confidence in Spike-Chunsoft, developers of the fantastic "999: Nine Hours, Nine Persons, Nine Doors," I jumped into the game and hoped for the best. It was a good call on my part, as "DanganRonpa," in spite of its flaws, is on the way to becoming one of my personal favorites of this year.The novel concept involves a completely ordinary high school student who is accepted into a prestigious academy due to a lottery drawing. But upon his arrival, he blacks out and wakes up in a sterile room, which turns out to be his new dorm. Turns out, the protagonist and a group of elite prodigies have been kidnapped and locked inside of a school cut from the rest of the world, all while being taunted by a maniacal teddy beard (I'm not kidding.) The only way to get out is to "graduate," which involves murdering another student and getting away with it. All of these new acquaintances are instantly turned against one another, and as you make friends throughout the entire experience, it may be very likely that your new best buddy is, in fact, the guilty party. And if you don't play your cards right in the class trials, everybody but the murderer will be executed. High stakes, indeed.It's hard to describe this game, as it's kind of amalgamation of various genres, all mish-mashed into one frantic but ultimately rewarding experience. Primarily, players will progress through things as a visual novel, scrolling through a lot of dialogue (and I do mean a lot; even while scrolling at a brisk pace, it took me three-plus hours until my first trial) to progress the plot, build the world, and understand the characters. In a way, it's a lot like the "Persona" series, minus the demon-fighting; you talk, build relationships, and see how those relationships shape the overall experience. While some might find this dull, I'm finding the characters to be incredibly fascinating and diverse. Furthermore, the element of any given person being the murderer adds a pressure-cooker atmosphere underneath even the most harmless of exchanges, as even the most harmless person could be the murderer. Plus, you don't know who's going to live and who's going to die, which makes every exchange seem infinitely more urgent.Aside from scrolling through dialogue, players will engage in the investigation of crime scenes when somebody finally does kick the proverbial bucket, gathering evidence in the form of "Truth Bullets." As that name might suggest, this is nothing like "Ace Attorney," despite some basic similarities in their investigation mechanics. Once you've collected enough ammo, so to speak, the trial begins, and here's where things get interesting. In order to find contradictions in different statements (these come out during "Non-Stop Debates," which are back-and-forth exchanges between all of the characters,) players use a targeting reticle to shoot their evidence at conflicting statements. On top of that, players have to do a hangman-style game to find letters to construct key words for evidence, and engage in a rhythm game segment to argue with the accused party. Sounds hectic, yes, and at first, it is. But once you get into the flow, things begin to make sense in a crazy sort of way. When all is said in done, the murderer is executed in an incredibly elaborate way that can only be described as "Looney Tunes" meets "Saw." Ah, yes, and did I mention that this is all timed? Yep.This is all tied into a neat little package by some excellent visuals. The character designs are blissfully unique, and despite the fact that some characters are a bit archetypal, they make up for it by being very visually appealing. Furthermore, the overall visual aesthetic, which reminds me of a darker "The World Ends With You," is seductive in the way that it pulls you into the sadistically cartoonish world. Everything is hyper stylized, from exaggerated facial expressions to copious amounts of neon pink blood. While it's silly at times, that's almost what makes it so endearing; such dark and gritty subject matter, offset by the stylish and silly tone, makes for a game quite unlike anything else on the marketplace. Topped off with some very punchy and well-translated dialogue, that has a distinctive sarcasm and wit to it, along with a hypnotic soundtrack and you've got a winner.While it's true that some elements of this game might be grating on the nerves to some, such as excessive amounts of dialogue and some pacing issues, I've found myself entranced with this unique little gem. Perhaps it's not perfect, but most games aren't, but what "Danganronpa" has going for it is pure, unadulterated style. It oozes out of every exchange with characters, out of the murders themselves, and just about every other thing you can imagine. Visual novels very rarely manage to maintain a consistently interesting tone, let along blend humor and horror effectively, but somehow, Spike-Chunsoft has done it.For those willing to put a bit of time into scrolling through dialogue, "Danganronpa" is a fun and creepy little thrill ride that's unlike anything else out there, especially on the Vita.Score: 9

Game Information:- # of player(s): 1- Memory Required for saves: 834 KB- Touchscreen, Rear Touch Pad supportRated "M" for the following content:- Blood- Intense Violence- Strong Language- Suggestive Themes" All Rise! The only escape from this shocking killing game... is murder!"Danganropa: Trigger Happy Havoc, is a visual novel made by Spike Chunsoft, and published by NIS America for the PlayStation Vita.The story revolves around fifteen students who awaken trapped in a high school, Hope's Peak Academy, and are told by the headmaster of the school, a black and white bear named Monokuma, that they must live there forever; unless someone kills a fellow student to earn their freedom. Each student is the best in their particular field and are referred to as an Ultimate, such as the Ultimate Pop Idol or the Ultimate Baseball Star; the story is told through the perspective of the main character, Makoto Naegi as he interact with his fellow classmates to uncover the truth of their imprisonment.The game is broken into two parts: the investigation/daily life and the class trial.The investigation/daily life features are:- Interacting with objects/evidence- Speaking with other classmates- Spending time with other classmates to learn more of their back story- General progression of the storyFor the most part the investigation/daily life has little game play and instead serves to further the story for the player.The class trial is game play orientated and involves player heavily. The features are:- Nonstop Debates, the player must aim the cursor on lies/contradictions and shoot a "truth bullet" to raise an objection; select evidence to either affirm or disprove a claim- Hangman's Gambit, The player must aim the cursor to select glowing letters and spell the hidden word that is on the lower half of the screen.- Closing Argument, the player must piece together the case events in comic book style to prove who is the culprit- Bullet Time Battle, the player must press buttons in rhythm to the beat of the music, to shoot, reload, and aim "truth bullets"This game is recommended to people who like visual novels, or like games similar to the Zero Escape/Phoenix Wright series.

When I first read that this was mostly a text-based game, I cringed.  The Vita is still an underdeveloped powerhouse that was well utilized in titles like LittleBigPlanet, Tearaway, Persona 4, and Uncharted, so I experienced a little dismay that the most recent entry was text-based.Boy, was I wrong.  Yes, this game is text-based, but what a twisted and demented premise and story behind it!There is a sick psychopathic bear named Monokuma who has tricked many of the nation's best students ("ultimates", such as the Ultimate Swimmer, the Ultimate Pop Star, etc.) into coming to an elite, private school academy (Hope) which has been highly regarded as a school that produces students who are guaranteed success for life.  Your character?  Well, you're the average Joe who is in the school because you were drawn by lottery...you're the Ultimate "Lucky" Student.However, not all is what it seems.  The school is a veritable prison with no apparent way out.  Worse still, the bear makes its appearance and offers the students 2 choices:  live there forever in peace and harmony OR kill someone and--if the student gets away with it--they can "graduate" and the other students are summarily executed.  While in practice, you couldn't imagine why anyone would entertain the thought to begin with...but then Monokuma fuels each of the student's motives for doing so in a way that I won't spoil here.  Suffice it to say that it's quite clever and comparisons to the movie SAW are easily made.What follows is a beautifully twisted tale of mystery and paranoia with your free time spent developing your skills through social interactions until a murder occurs.  Once a murder occurs, you need to gather evidence for the inevitable trial that takes place.  And that's where the game truly shines.  You use your evidence in the form of "truth bullets" to shoot down phrases of your fellow classmates when the evidence/arguments that they provide either are contradictions/lies.  The trick, however, is picking the WEAKEST argument that occurs since some of their statements may have a weak basis, but only a certain part of the evidence can be shot down effectively; it's pretty well done.  There are also moments of hangman-like minigames where you have to pick letters to form the word of a piece of evidence that is relevant to the case.  When you finally make your accusation, a rhythm-based game will have you defending yourself against a torrent of denial.In description, it seems weird, but it's immensely fun.  The text-based aspect of the game is full of dialog that's engaging and will also have you learning more about all 15 inhabitants of the school.  Doing so (and giving students presents) will unlock certain "powers" to aid you in trial.All in all, I never would have thought myself to be engaged in a mostly text-based game, but man, this game has changed my outlook on such a thing.  The story is cool and the background music is amazing.I highly recommend this!For those of you who are wondering about the "Mature" title, yes, there is violence although the blood in the game is a hot pink.  However, how the students die is quite varied and disturbing at times and the game doesn't hold back on the language with certain characters (including the Ultimate Biker Gang Leader) and there are the occasional double-entendres (that made me laugh), so while the attraction to the game as a mystery-solver may be enticing to a younger audience, please keep in mind that the "Mature" rating is deserved here so choose accordingly.

Who is this game NOT for? Anyone under 18. The official website requires you to enter your birthdate.Why? It's stuffed full of extreme violence in the form of  torture style executions and regular murders, blood, suicide, extremely perverse adult humor, explicit language (every swear word in the books), and what games call "adult situations". The violence is often mixed in with the humor, and at least one of the torture scenes is so over the top brutal that it is hard to watch. The creator admits the game was inspired by "Saw".Who else is this game NOT for? Anyone who does not like to read. The game consists of NO battling, NO fighting. It's all walking around and exploring, talking to other students, looking for clues, and then finally figuring out the mysteries with those clues in a court room dungeon. Hours of reading dialogue. If you didn't like 999 or Virtue's Last Reward, you probably won't like this.The game has the horror, mystery, and visual novel aspects of 999 & Virtue's Last Reward, the trial based mysteries of Phoenix Wright (and these comparisons have already been made by at least 2 separate game review sites), and the unsettling, disturbing feel of Corpse Party.That said...What's the game about? You start the game as Makoto, a very plain, average, boring Japanese high school student. That point is emphasized over and over.He, along with a number of other students, has been selected to attend a prestigious boarding school for highly skilled "Ultimate" students that guarantees success upon graduation. This may be due to the fact that the students selected to attend are already pretty much set for life. For example, there is an Ultimate Affluent Progengy (aka the rich heir to a fortune born to one of the most powerful families in Japan), the Ultimate Programmer, Ultimate Gambler, Ultimate Baseball Star, Ultimate Swimming Pro, Ultimate Writing Prodigy...and so on. Makoto is the Ultimate Lucky student. Not because he is lucky, but because he is so ordinary that he is lucky to have been chosen. There are also a few that don't make much sense to be attending such as the Ultimate Fan-fic Writer and the Ultimate Biker Gang Leader...You go to your first day of school and the school is empty. The next thing you know, you are waking up in a secure building with metal sheets over the windows and a bunch of other students who have no idea what's going on.That's when a little homicidal bear -Monokuma- walks in and tells you that you are trapped in the school forever. Unless...you murder another student and get away with it. There are cameras everywhere and a set of rules, and of course a trial. If you murder someone and are caught, you are executed. If you are not caught, you go free and everyone else is executed.The game consists of NO fighting, no battling, no leveling up. Just walking around the school, exploring with point and click, finding clues, and solving murders. During "free time" you have the option to get to know other students and give them gifts to max out your friendship and earn skills. Kind of like Persona social links, but less involved.Once you start the game, every day you will wake up, explore, and talk to other students. Occasionally Monokuma pops up to threaten you, make jokes, give you clues, or try to push you into murdering each other. Once a murder occurs, you collect clues and go to trial.The regular gameplay is very similar to 999 or Virtue's Last Reward minus the escape the room puzzles meets Phoenix Wright. The trial gameplay only mirrors Phoenix in the way that you need to find the evidence in your file of clues that proves why certain statements are false. The difference is that words stream across the screen and once you elide which are false, you need to shoot them down with the correct clue or statement. It can get confusing to know what exactly the game wants you to combine, and when. The rest of the trial consists of a rhythm game of shooting down statements to a beat, and a fill in the scene graphic novel. The last game comparison is Corpse Party that also has a similar unsettling horror and dread that builds in inside you and can't quite believe you are seeing during the executions.The entire game switches from extreme violence to strange humor in the blink of an eye. It is very heavy on Japanese culture, and the humor reflects this. There is constant sexual innuendo due to characters constantly mistaking innocent statements for dirty ones, and some of it gets pretty explicit. Monokuma at one point talks about his white stuffing exploding out.Overall, if you love to read, love mysteries, love Japanese games, and can get past some of the grotesque over the top execution murders, you should love this game as much as I do. 6 days in, I am at the final chapter, but in 6 to 7 months, the seconds game will release.My only complaint is that the controls are not always responsive. There seems to be glitches where no matter how many times you press the correct statement, it does not register. This can result in time running out 12 minutes later, and failing the case. It has happened to me on more than 3 occasions, with it taking as many as 15-20 tries to get it to respond. Which means playing the same thing over and over 15-20 times or more. EDIT: I would suggest setting the difficulty on average or easy, ask it isn't really "gamer skill", but instead it gives you more chances to make mistakes in the trial. Mistakes are easy to make when you have to tap words that are semi-responsive while there are other words criss-crossing across them that you need to avoid tapping, and also when you just aren't sure what the game is asking. You know WHY the stement is false, but not exactly what words they want you to use and in what order to PROVE that.

The mystery-solving aspect of this game is way overhyped. This is an interactive novel first, a carnival game second, and is just barely a logic puzzle game at all. I played on "Kind", or the middle difficulty, and found that the characters would more or less rub evidence in your face. I gave that a pass and continued to play, curious about the story and how it would play out, but two major problems stuck out for me.First, the titular "refutation bullets" that you use to refute false statements aren't used consistently. In some parts of the game, you are meant to use refutation bullets to support true statements. This could have been avoided with some simple rewording so that refutation bullets actually refute things. The way the system is currently designed turns the trials into word association games or "guess the best match" games instead of actually using logic to find contradictions as they relate to the case.Second, the timeline segments of trials is not fun and pointless. Basically, once the game has told you for the 1,000th time what happened because you are an idiot, it asks you to put these little pictures in the correct frames in a manga to show for the 1,0001st time what happened. Most of the time that wasn't so bad, but there was at least one timeline where two of the pictures had no discernible order. Like in the trial segment of the game, you are reduced to guessing.If you can't trust the system in a logical puzzle game, it's not a logical puzzle game.Playing on the harder difficulties only changes the amount of hints you get and increases the difficulty of the carnival minigames. It doesn't change the fact that refutation bullets are illogical (1/4 of the time you use them to support things, not refute things) or that putting clipart in order is lame after you have already reached the conclusion of the trial.

Yes, this is one of those "Visual Novel" games that Japan has in abundance.  We get very few of them translated directly, but as soon as I found out about this and what it was kinda about, I just had to get it.And I loved it.The gameplay during any free time is easy, you can go wherever you have available and check things to collect the coins; during the free time you can talk to people and give them gifts to raise their friendship.  You don't have to worry about getting the relationships up in the main story 'cause you have the 2nd game mode that makes that super easy after you beat that main story.The investigations are pretty much straightforward; you can't miss anything.  The trials in the game become easier once you figure out the controls.  I admit that I didn't comprehend the controls AT ALL when the in-game text tutorial was trying to explain it.  It's much easier to use the touch controls during the trail than attempt to use the old PSP version style controls.it's more interesting and fun if you try your best not to spoil the story for yourself;  Figuring out what all happened and laying it out is thrilling and cool than knowing where everything goes and stuff before you get started.There are a few "glitched" trophies, for trophy hunters.  Or perhaps just typo-ed.  There are several trophies that say "every" trial, but really you just have to do the task with one.Now, the 2nd mode of the game.  Oh, I'm really loving the 2nd mode of the game. xD  School mode is really really fun.  It's like a mini-game thing where you assign people jobs and collect stuff in the school to build versions of one demented bear. If you, like myself, watched the anime before the game was even announced, then, well, all I can say is that it follows it pretty closely. No... extremely closely. But play it anyway, because it's a great remake of a classic.When explaining DanRon to a major gamer friend who had never heard of it, I told her it was "a little bit like Persona". But only a little. Like Persona, it has a visual novel (VN) navigation and flow, but during free periods, you take control of your character and do what you wish. Another way is that the day is divided into segments: DanRon starts with breakfast in the dining hall, then either a group activity or free time, followed (usually) by free time again, and then night time. During these free periods, you can--and should--strengthen your bonds with the other characters by having some one-on-one time with them, also like Persona.Each chapter is divided into three phases: exploration, investigation, and class trial. The free time and group events I just described all occur during the exploration phase. Sometimes you may get bored of having so much free time, but it is necessary for you to gain more skills to be used later. At the end of the exploration phase, someone is guaranteed to discover a dead body. Then, the chapter moves into investigation, where you must gather clues--"Truth Bullets" as they are called. "Dangan" in the title translates as "bullet"; "ronpa" means "defeating in an argument", so the main focus of the game is to win arguments in the class trials by using these Truth Bullets. The class trial is where your deductive reasoning, aiming and shooting, and even rhythm skills are put to the test by the rest of the class.When you have soundly won every argument in all the class trials and defeated the game, a post-game extra opens up, which will be completely new even to those who have seen the anime, and I had as much fun playing it as I did the main game. I won't say more about it, at the risk of spoiling it.Finally, if you want to avoid ear cancer, listen to the Japanese original audio. I usually do when it is available, but I tried the English dub. (I always give it a chance before switching back to Japanese.) If you've ever wondered why it is that some people are adamant about original Japanese audio, then play the Prologue in Japanese to get used to the original character voices, then switch to English on Chapter 1 or 2. I have come to expect English dubs, mostly, to feature brassy-voiced, overly dramatic delivery that's more caricature than character, but this was a new low: not only the names but even English words (like "dissociative") were mispronounced, and Monokuma... poor Monokuma sounded like the Wicked Witch of the West as performed by William Shatner.Long and short: Great game, with three different difficulty settings, different difficulty adjustments for logic and action (you want "mean" logic but "gentle" action? That's OK!), characters that are memorable from the beginning (even the ones who die right off the bat), and KILLER music. But I have to deduct a star for the English dub and the limited replay potential. Final rating: 4.

I love graphic novels and adventure games. I burned through 999 and Zero Escape: Virtue's Last Reward. They were excellent horror/mystery hybrids that gave the player an investment in the characters. I really wanted everyone to survive (well, almost everyone, but I won't spoil anything here). Nippon Ichi's localisation is excellent. Similar to Phoenix Wright, there are copious cultural and anime references thrown in (especially for uber-otaku Hifumi Yamada). This adds a touch of humour and lightens the bleak mood of suspense, horror and ceaseless trepidation.DanganRonpa takes a similar vein with high school students. Not yet ready for independent life and for the most part naive and inexperienced, they are thrust in a situation very similar to the premises in the Saw films - they must do unspeakably awful things to survive (or escape, in this case) - murder a fellow student and get away with it. As very few of the students know each other (the protagonist only knows the pop star), the apparition of murder looms close behind at every step.With spine-chilling music, a brilliant premise and courtroom scenes reminiscent of Phoenix Wright (albeit with a dark, macabre and ghoulish twist), the multiple paths, relationship-building and collectibles provide replay value far beyond that of 999 or Zero Escape. There is a considerable amount of text to slog through, but it's never dull or repetitive. I always find it hard to turn off and go to bed at night. Anyone who likes being scared out of their wits will love this game.

These days with many game titles it has all become about the graphics and how realistic it can be. This game turns that notion on its head instead and with beautiful artwork, a fantastic music score, and great storytelling it becomes all about how immersive its world is.Its style of gameplay is nothing new in fact it’s reminiscent of early PC games that many of the younger generation will not know so it will be new to them.The dungeon crawling is fun and maze-like with hidden passageways and treasure to be found, and a similar experience to Metroid in which some areas are unaccusable until later abilities and items are gained. The auto-traverse system is great for getting across the map to areas already explored so going back through an area is never dull.Seals are something unique to this game that is the major goals of each dungeon. With some having as many as 16. At these seals you can utilize gems to summon monsters which when you defeat them you then have control over the seal allowing you to change up which demons are in your party or save your game. Gems are not all the same some will encourage item drops for specific types of weapons or armor others increase the quality of those drops. Gems are dropped by monsters or purchased from the store (for a hefty sum). Encouraging you to battle in order to get better weapons.The Battle System is fantastic simple to understand but complex to master. You have the ability to create a party of your choosing with multiple classes to choose from never locking you into characters with classes you don't like or want. This also means that if you don’t have a good balance the game will be even more difficult for you. With all that is the ability to summon a demon to aid you while you can’t control them they are crucial to many of the more difficult battles. However summon them too often or for too long and they will turn against you making it an even more difficult battle.The music score is great in that it is beautifully written, and easily fits into the background acting as a compliment to the game rather than imposing its presence on the players.Characters are varied and quirky with a lot of choices when it comes to interacting with them. Each with a voice over that fits its character design.The story is interesting and provides enough early on to get you hooked for when the narrative really begins to move.The Economy system is different in that it is not easy at first to make a lot of money and if you leave the difficulty high each time you leave the Inn you must make it count to make a profit. You never really need to purchase items from the shops except for maybe gems and some of the better albeit much more expensive healing items.There is so much to this game that this overview is very brief and limited. It is one of the best and most well balanced games I have come across. This game is money well spent.

The other day, I had a conversation with an acquaintance about the Japanese game industry while putting some money down on my preorder for this game. I asked if he had played the rebooted Devil May Cry, and he replied that, no, he hadn't played any of them. In fact, according to him, he didn't really like playing Japanese games, as they weren't very innovative, and that any innovations found in current ones were already in American games twenty years ago. Of course, I didn't want to cause a scene and debate the guy in the middle of a store, but to me, it's this kind of gamer entitlement that is caustic towards the industry at large. Games don't always need to be incredibly innovative in order to be truly great experiences. As long as the experiences themselves are enthralling, and aren't complete rip-offs of other games in the same vein, them being radically different is not necessary to me, by any stretch of the imagination.And it's because of this personal standard that, to me, "Demon Gaze" is not only a stellar example of its genre, but a fantastic game in its own right. Yes, we've all seen grid-based dungeon crawlers before, that type of RPG is nothing new. But when it's done this well, with characters this endearing, a plot this utterly bizarre and lovable, and gameplay so airtight that I can't help but want to sink every waking minute into it, the fact that this is a formula invented by games in the 80's tends to not matter. Because, as a complete package, it's excellent.Players start out by customizing a protagonist out of a vast selection of portraits and naming them, before setting them loose in the world. Unfortunately, regardless of what gender you choose, the protagonist will always be identified as a human male, which is kind of a bummer for both those who like playing as their own gender or who like switching it up when playing a game. Regardless, your character is a Gazer, somebody with the ability to battle demons, then capture them and wield them in battle. This ability is seen as something to be used and exploited by Fran, the charming cheapskate manager of Dragon Princess Inn, who immediately houses you and slaps you with a debt to pay off. You pay off this debt by exploring dungeons in the world of Misrid, killing demons, getting loot, and eventually, finding the boss demon of each dungeon and capturing them for use in battle. But while the plot seems to be moving at a predictable clip in the early hours, a significant twist reframes the narrative and gives you new motivation to push onward."Demon Gaze"'s is a plot that works on two entirely different levels. Framing everything is the idea of being a Gazer, and all of the trials and tribulations that come with that designation. At the same time, a large focus of the game is on interacting with the characters of the Inn, all of whom have pretty distinct personalities and are a joy to talk to. With these two contrasting focuses, the entire experience is one whose tone is inconsistent in the best way possible. At one point, a giant monster might besiege the inn and attempt to lay ruin to it, threatening the lives of all the inhabitants. Then, shortly thereafter, your character might barge in on a maid creepily purveying the manager's undergarments, and then be given the option to outright punch her. Do you want to fight a demonic beast with chainsaws on their arms, or grope the manager's breasts to prove that she's human? Share an intensely homoerotic bathing moment with a naked pretty boy, or summon demons from the underworld to pillage their corpses? You can do all of this, and much more, in "Demon Gaze," and the result is a charmingly bizarre chimera of a game, one part bizarre comedy laden with flagrant sexuality and slapstick humor, one part poe-faced demon hunting tale. For some reason, it works on both levels, and the writers should be commended for pulling it off so well.On the same token, the developers deserve praise for managing to take first-person dungeon crawling and turning it into a fun, fast-paced experience. Players basically enter a dungeon, then have to explore tile by tile in order to map out the entirety of it. All the while, they will encounter both random encounters and predesignated ones, varying wildly in difficulty. If you win one battle without very much effort, there's a good chance that the next set of enemies will mop the floor with you, and then some. Difficulty spikes here are huge, and can be immensely discouraging at first. Luckily, the game's loading times are incredibly brief, and as each dungeon progresses, your party will activate seals that beget enemies with certain items, depending on what gem you activate them with, and then turn into save points. Insofar, each dungeon has around eight of these, so the more you play, the more save points you'll gain access to. That means that you can die, go to the title screen, then hop right back in within under thirty seconds or so. Couple this with the fact that at around level six or seven, the main character learns a spell that warps the party back to the inn, and the experience is made a lot more accessible. You just have to work a little for the luxury.On top of the core mechanics, the economic system in place here is one of the most fascinating I've experienced. Seeing as your characters are taking residence in an inn, you'll need to pay rent upon returning from a dungeon. This rent goes up according to your party's level and head count. Not only that, but you'll have to rent extra rooms for each member of your party (which you create and customize,) which raises in cost each time. If you can't front the rent, you'll go into debt. If you consistently pay it on time, you'll get both refunds and bonuses. Speaking of money, prepare to be shocked at the ridiculous prices the two shopkeepers charge for items, weapons and armor. That's because you really don't need to buy their wares in order to progress, except for perhaps in the beginning. Once you start acquiring gems that hand out specific types of items, you'll get better gear in dungeons than what the store tends to offer, and you'll sell what you don't need to the stores, along with miscellaneous items, in order to keep getting money, paying rent, buying gems, and renting extra party rooms. It's one of the only in-game RPG economies that I've seen work in a cyclical, cause-and-effect style, and it's impressive in its consistency.I feel it's also important to talk about the usage of demons a little bit. After breaking the seals in a dungeon, players will track down and fight that dungeon's boss, then give its soul to Fran, who then gives it to you as a "key" that you can use in battle. This key lets you summon the demon and have it do various things, like buff your party, attack the enemies, and heal you. Not only that, but having certain demons equipped lets you do things outside of battle, as well. For example, Chronos lets you walk on hazardous surfaces like lava and poison, and Comet lets you find hidden doors to break down. The thing, though, is that in battle, your demons will turn against you if a certain meter depletes, and the game will charge you MP to put it back in the key. Because of this, gaining affinity with each demon and keeping that meter high by landing attacks and doing other things becomes a crucial strategy.When you look at the gameplay, and how many different hats it tries to wear, it becomes incredibly difficult to not admire "Demon Gaze" for its pluck and tenacity. As a visual novel, it works exceedingly well, with a relatively diverse cast of likable characters, and dialogue that ranges from engaging to abstractly hilarious. And as a role-playing game, it fills its boots quite nicely, with plenty of noticeable upgrades, a nice range of classes, and an overall encouraging tone of trial-and-error. Easier (and harder) difficulties even become available shortly after you've been introduced to all the basic mechanics of the game, making it accessible to almost anyone. Perhaps the quest objectives are occasionally a bit vague, and perhaps the game should make it more clear that you'll probably need certain classes sooner than later (pro tip: get a healer pronto,) but for me, the occasionally ambiguous, open-ended nature of the game made it more fun to sink my teeth into."Fun" would be a key word to describe the rest of the game. All of the character designs are bright and adorably goofy, from an dwarf whose green afro that has plastic ducks and sharks in it, to a morose mortician who sleeps in a coffin and has a propensity to wander around the inn in her undergarments. The music is generally pretty chipper and infectious, even in some of the more serious moments, and the liberal usage of Vocaloids make it stand out from everything else on the marketplace. Topping it off is an English localization that stands head-and-shoulders with the excellent efforts put forth by NIS earlier this year with the stellar "Dangan Ronpa," complete with an excellent English vocal cast.My acquaintance argued that Japanese games, as a whole, don't "innovate" nearly as much as ones made in America. Putting aside the fact that lumping a whole country's games together is incredibly problematic and unfair, think about the AAA games that make it big here. "Bioshock Infinite," for instance, was certainly a wonderful and fresh game, but was its gameplay particularly novel or innovative, save for the skyhook? No, not really, it was just a well-executed shooter with a stellar narrative and a memorable cast. Same goes for most games that get showered with praise, in America, Europe, Japan, or anywhere else for that matter. In my opinion, very few things are truly innovative, especially in the increasingly bloated game industry, and to expect every game to offer some type of innovation is beyond silly, at least to me.With that said, "Demon Gaze" is a fantastic game, and one of the shining examples of how you can take an established genre and do it exceptionally well. Yes, we've seen dungeon crawlers with the earlier MegaTen games and the "Etrian Odyssey" series (which is actually a bit outclassed here, in my opinion,) but NIS has given us one with a memorable cast, a novel hook, engaging gameplay, and snazzy presentation that sets it apart from competitors. No, this isn't a particularly new type of game, but if it's this engaging, does it really need to be? I would argue not, and I would also argue that "Demon Gaze" is one of the best games on the market.Score: 9.5

I'm going to keep this on the shorter side. I have been awaiting this games release since e3 2012 when it was announced. I was so stoked when I found out it was to be released on November 19th (4 days after the PS4 launch date) but then October 15th of 2013 it was delayed to Spring 2014, which is a broad window. To finally get it on May 27th, I knew the days leading up to it would be LONG (thank goodness I had Wolfenstein to tide me over). I bought the Limited Edition PS4 edition, the Collector's Edition Strategy Guide (Which is a must have, its very well written) as well as the season pass.As soon as the fedex man delivered my package at 10:30 am, I tore (well opened carefully) the package to check out all that I had bought. I was kinda of worried that the Aiden statue wasn't going to be a very good figure and that it would feel cheap and plastic-y. But I was wrong and it was a very nice sturdy heavier statue (felt like it was made of resin, with the base the only plastic part). Next came Aiden's Mask which was wearable (which was a +), it was very well constructed *Note* - The design the mask is pretty dark grey, unlike the picture where it stands out, it isn't as noticeable and light in real life*. The art book came after this, it was very well crafted, the pictures were gorgeous and it was printed on the high glossy photo paper. Next, was the steel book, which is a slick black book with logos and pictures on the front, back and side (The inside is blue, with the left side being a picture of a mans legs with a camera torso/head, and the right side was a monkey) Inside the steel book was the soundtrack and the main attraction the GAME! As far as the value of this product, in my opinion it was worth the $130.00I am only 3 missions into the game, but I have been exploring the city of Chicago (beautiful graphics). And I have not found one single thing I haven't liked with the game. When I first started, I kinda spaced about the whole hacking concept and I couldn't get past the first 2 cops, until I realized that I should be hacking items to get the cops distracted. I am having a blast running around stopping crimes, doing quests, and playing as Aiden in this beautiful crafted world. So far everything is tight (Gameplay Mechanics, Voice Acting, Story, Dialogue, etc.) This is definitely a game that will take you a very long time to complete. Don't rush through, and give the developers what they wanted. A play through of the entire game, start to finish, 100% completion. I would say you won't be sorry, for I know for my 4 hours so far in this game, I have not.

Alright: The actual Limited Edition stuff included a Steelbook for the game which is really nice, Aiden's facemask, whcih is comfortable and fits any sized head (lol)...plus it looks cool and is actually kind of warm (if you live in a winter state, this may apply), an Aiden statue which also looks cool (gun in one hand, smart phone in the other) and an art book which isnt super long but is still quite nice. The included soundtrack is meh in my opinion. So, as far as Limited Edition stuff goes, this one is pretty nice.As far as the game itself, I really ejoyed it a lot.  The side mission varieties do get a little boring after a while, but actually, the game itself is really cool. That said, some of the side missions, like tracking down a serial killer or assaulting gang hideouts were super cool. The ctOS scans on all the citizens really help to make this version of Chicago a living and breathing city. Plus, the NPC's are generally engaged in day to day activities and conversations, adding a surprisingly deep element to the city itself.Aiden himself isnt the most likeable main character. You will probably not think too much about him after you finish the game, and the story is also decent but not necessarily memorable. However, the supporting cast is amazing, especially Al Jourgensen (oops...I mean T-Bone). In fact, there is a mission where you have to save TBone that was maybe one of the best missions I have played in any game ever. The main missions in general were quite good though. Some were lacking and some were amazing, but the greater percentage of them were at least good and a lot of fun.The stealth aspects of this game really shine as does the ability to manipulate your environemt and hack enemy stuff to affect the outcome of missions and battles. The gunplay was actually quite a bit of fun as well. The driving was floaty at first until I realized that each type of vehicle absolutely handled differently and got used to them individually...after that, driving became a lot of fun.Online play: this was particularly brilliant in my estimation. The Online hacking missions were awesome whether you are the hacker or the hackee as it were. The online decryption is just awesome MP madness. It was easy to lose 2-3 hours at a time simply playing that. The Online racing was cool, and the Online missions where a player using the phone app uses the city aganst you as you try to get through multiple checkpoints in a vehicle was also fun as hell and a brilliant way to tie in the phone app with the game.Overall, this game defintiely had its flaws, and was probably way overhyped, but I still gladly surrendered 60+ hours of my life to this game and will look forward to future instalments to this series. This is definitely UbiSofts new Assassins Creed in that you can probably expect yearly releases in this IP.Cheers.

This is the first and so far only game I played in this series. First off this isn't a typical RPG at all, so don't expect an over world, towns to walk around and don't even expect to ever see the actual characters on screen besides in illustrated drawings during cut scenes. Think "tales" series skits. Anyway that aside, THIS GAME IS FUN! I was about to put it down after about an hour or so, however I let myself get into the game as I wanted to like it and boy was I happy I did. First off the battle system is very good and stays true to most turn based RPG's. Graphically it seems like Dragon Quest, you see the fully 3d enemies in front of you in a line with 1 or 2 rows. Your characters are in rows as well even though they are not visible. The rows play out like Lost Odyssey, where position matters. There is also an auto option which is great. There is a story and it seems good so far but really the object of the game is to dive deeper and deeper into whatever area you are playing in. You will end up going back to town, which is basically just a menu with options on where you wanna go, and stock up on health, new items etc and go back out. There are side quests and of course main quests. Sides are mostly finding items for townspeople or killing certain monsters. Yes they are sides but you get rewards and most of all much more exp points than any battles, so you'll do as much of them as you can. Bottom line, it gets very repetitive, but while staying so fresh as the enemies get tougher and tougher. The farther in you go, you get warps so you can easily get around. Getting around is the best part because of the maps in which you can customize. This game is 5 Star as long as you know what your getting into.

This game starts the player off with 2 choices. Play through a story mode with precreated characters or let you imagination go to work in the classic mode where you determine your characters. Story mode was very satisfying, sure some of characters were a bit cliche-ish but each of them had depth as you came to realize through not only the story but through a couple sidequests as well. Gameplay mechanics can punish you if you don't know what you're doing(as with most of atlus' rpgs). Not looking a world map enemies(F.O.Es) can get you killed especially if you have no understanding of their weaknesses. Interesting subclassing mechanics can be found in items known as grimore stones that add a bit more strategy to the combat system(even allowing for some almost game breaking combos).This is also the first game I've ever played where I was responsible for the map I used to get around. This feature adds a bit of difficulty in the sense that if you mess up your map, you could very well get yourself into bad situations with enemies(I've done it plenty of times in later dungeons) Artwork and the soundtrack are typical superb quality I've come to expect from Atlus, many a time have I just found myself sitting there listening to the background music will strolling through dungeons. The classic mode is pretty much the same thing but without predetermined characters and dialogue outside npc conversations, there's even an option to enjoy the ds soundtrack to the game in the options menu. All in all, if map drawing and dungeon crawling are your ideas of fun then this game comes highly recommended. Hoping Atlus does a remake to the other games in the series as well.

What we have here is a simple racer;  as others have mentioned, reminiscent of the old Sega rally games.  The graphics are pretty decent and hold up well on the Fire TV HD screen.  Six iconic rally cars such as the Subaru WRX and Lancia Stratos can be driven, although aside from horsepower there’s apparently nothing else to differentiate them.  The track selection is woefully thin.The controls are where a lot of players take issue with this game.  I’ve only played it on Fire TV.  I do agree that the steering is on the twitchy side although it’s hard to know how much to attribute to the Fire controller dead zone, with no option to adjust the sensitivity.  For that matter, the controls are minimal. You get gas & brake, change view and that’s it.  No manual gear shifting option and no handbrake.  As you would expect, the physics are on the arcade side but pleasing enough.  The brakes in this game are like throwing out an anchor, meaning anything more than lightly tapping the brakes is to be avoided if you want a decent time.  Ditto, stay off the grass which will slow your car like a glue mousetrap.The other source of complaint is the punishing time limits in the Challenge mode.  While the races against the AI cars are easy enough, there’s no question that some of the time trials are very tough to beat, requiring absolutely mistake free driving over multiple laps.  And what is your reward for grinding through these 30 events ?  Unlocking a nice career mode perhaps or at least more cars & tracks ? No, absolutely nothing follows.That’s the issue with Pocket Rally in a nutshell.  If feels like a demo for some deeper, better game.  Even for the modest outlay of 99 cents, there’s just not enough content here.

The game is good in that there are minimal permissions.It took me back to my days playing Colin McRae Rally and also that annoying thing that Codemasters do that you have to meet a minimum requirement to continue. I shouldn't be forced to have to meet a requirement.I played the first stage 5 times before getting through and even then I only got there by 0.21 of a second. Especially for level 1, it seems a bit too hard. Who knows what the last level would be like.The game itself though has really nice graphics and the physics and handling was very good. Would have loved some vibration when touching down after a jump.In the end though, I uninstalled. It's ok, but not great.
