Edit - I knocked my review down from three starts to two stars after a recent discovery.  The split screen multiplayer does not work well at all for a party situation.  They WAY OVER ENGINEERED IT.  Every time someone else picks up a controller the game freaks outs and claims to have lost connection to the controller.  what is happening is Forza tries to keep track of which player is holding which controller and when someone passes a controller to someone else you have go through this very un-intuitive process of re-registering that new person or setting them up as guest.  It simply does not work well.  Imagine a room of four or five 10 year olds taking turns at racing two at a time.  After each race they swap out one kid at a time ("I play winner") and Froza says "connection lost with controller".  The only way to get the next kid in is to go through several annoying steps that are not logical nor intuitive.  So I hear "Daaaad it's doing it again".  The idea is that Forza would recognize every player and every player ideally would have a microsoft live account.  And if you were ever at someone eleses house forza is supposed to recognize you there.  The problem is the kids just want to take turns playing a video game.  So for that I give ti two stars.Original review ---I bought Forza motorsport for the express purpose of having a next gen game to show of the next gen graphics.  This game delivers on that front.  I love the interface, the show rooms and the Top Gear narrations.  This game was made for fans of the automobile.  The driving is superb and I don't even like driving games.  The controls are easy to learn but driving well is difficult to master (the right amount of difficult to provide a fun challenge).Where this game falls short is no surprise, everyone is talking about it. The number of tracks is too limited and they push you to purchase (with real money) car packs on you all the time.  It feels like a free-to-play game, yet it's not free.A big part of the game is racing to earn credits so you can buy more expensive cars which open up more racing opportunities.  Here is a huge grind.  Luckily I discovered if you log into the Forza website you will find reward credits which help early on (several 100,000's credits to be had).  Of course you can buy credits for real money but that's kins of lame.  The cost of the additional cars seem to be a bit outside the scope of what you would earn with normal play so it tempts you to buy credits with real money.It's as if the makers of the game couldn't decide on the right revenue model, charge premium price or go free-to-play.  They decided to do both at the same time for this game and it just doesn't work.  Maybe they should make this a free game and give tons of credit to those of us who bought the title at full price.

I have played a lot of these games over the years, and my favorites were Gran Turismo 2 and Gran Turismo 4. They had the same thing going for them - a well-done career mode and tons of content. While I didn't play Forza 4, I did get Forza 3 and while I really did not like that game's career mode, I had a great time in the hot lap mode, working on my times and tweaking my cars. So it is with Forza 5. The staid career mode is more than made up by the hot lap mode, called Rivals. If you are into beating times and improving, it's great.The career mode, while a bit dry, is better than most. I will say the game benefits a lot from the Drivatar system. Normally the AI in these games is just awful. In Gran Turismo they are scripted and stick to the line. In Forza they go from being terrible in one difficulty to perfect speed demons in the next. Here there is a large amount of granularity in difficulty and they drive dynamically and keep you guessing. It works.Forza 5 is a launch game, as we all know, and to its credit it still feels like a fully-formed game with a lot of content. There is a lot to do in this game. It suffers, though, compared to games on last-ten platforms. Forza 5 has far less content than Forza 4 and still lacks some things in GT5/6. UtechSmart's Venus which I received as a 'for review' item, is the mouse a gamer would love especially if the gamer was into anything that would benefit from numerous stored macros. Its 12 macros buttons plus the ability to store several profiles could eliminate the need for a gaming keyboard. It will work well 'as is' bu simply plugging it into a USB port but, when configured through the included setup program it can be made to be and do just about anything you would expect from a gamer's mouse.Let me begin with features that would make some not to want a Venus with the understanding that many gamers would not be bothered by these or even view some as positives.- WIRED only - The wire is braided which makes tangles less likely but it's a wire nevertheless. Gaming mice as a class tend to require more power than regular ones and you don't want your mouse to give up on you while playing but it would have been nice if the Venus was configured as wired/wireless.- RIGHT-HANDED ONLY - The side buttons are meant to use with your thumb so there's no way you can use it efficiently if you are left-handed. I don't know if they make a left-handed version.And, now, for the good things:+ BUTTONS GALORE - 12 thumb buttons, plus another small button for the index finger plus the regular 2 mouse buttons, 2 Function +/- buttons , the clickable scrolling wheel and a profile select switch at the bottom. And all of the above are properly placed within easy and comfortable reach.+ THUMB REST - This is very important because the 12 side buttons take all the space on the left side. But the Venus has a nicely shaped rest ledge on the left where your thumb can rest when not active.+ WEIGHTS - Yes, indeed. If you feel that the mouse is too light, you can add as many as 8 little weights into a special compartment and make it heavier.+ CUSTOMIZE EVERYTHING - The software allows you to assign just about any function or macro to any of the buttons.+ CREATE YOUR OWN PROFILES - Not surprisingly, you can create you own with specific button assignments for functions and macros, light colors, sensitivity and so forth.+ 16000 DPI sensitivity - of course you can set it lower but it's good it's there.+ ADJUSTABLE mouse point speed, scroll speed, double-click speed and polling rate.+ 18-MONTH WARRANTYNot on the list above, I would like to note that I was very please with the mouse's overall shape, balance (remember, adjustable weight) and responsiveness. It's been ergonomically sculpted to make my hand feel very comfortable while operating it and the thumb rest makes all the difference in the world.In the end, no matter how well a product performs, the questions anyone is probably asking are: 'do I need it?' and 'is it worth it'? For anyone who is not a dedicated gamer, the answer should be... maybe. Casual PC gamers like myself are likely to find that the Venus is the ideal pick because it can perform awesomely as a gaming mouse and it's one of the best mice overall. If you ARE a gamer and are willing to spend some time getting used to it then the Venus could very much be 'it' unless you are willing to spend a lot more.

This mouse is best suited to two groups: gamers and people who do a lot of repetitive tasks on computers.  I will try to illustrate the benefits to each, comparing the functionality with more traditional gaming mice.BUILDFor the price, the Venus is surprisingly solid.  It does not quite feel comparable to high end mice in terms of durability or ergonomics, but it does not feel like a cheap knockoff either.  The wire is the braided sort and the connector, albeit chunky, is heavy duty.  The surface has a matte feel that prevents slipping.  Some optional weights are included, but for long gaming/work sessions, it might be best to forgo them.The appearance is... well, it's nerdy.  This mouse knows who it is for (me!).  The glowing lights and alien design fit right in with case mods and gaming keyboards.  Still, it is not so flashy that it would be an issue for an office or living room.BUTTONSOnce of the most critical factors for a mouse is how responsive the buttons are.  Thankfully, the Venus has very nice, clicky primary buttons.  The side programmable buttons are not as nice, with a bit mushier feel.  If you know what a Wacom tablet's buttons feel like, you have an idea.  They are very usable, regardless.The ergonomics of the mouse seem designed around an average hand.  I also have a G9x, which has two sizes of shells, and this one is closer to the larger size.  I generally like smaller mice, but the shape works well for me.The side buttons are contoured, making finding the right button without looking reliable.SCROLL WHEELScrolling is smooth, with soft clicks between scroll notches.  There is sadly no hyper scrolling (free spinning) mode similar to Logitech mouses, but that may be proprietary.  The click works well and is easy to accomplish without accidentally scrolling.TRACKINGThat high DPI is no joke!  With the slightest hand movement, you can control the game or move the cursor across the screen.  This is good for competitive gaming, but also important for reducing repetitive stress to the hand for office workers doing the same thing over and over.  The DPI is higher in the Venus than my much more expensive gaming mouse.SOFTWAREFirst, I want to mention that the software on the website was in .rar format, so I needed to download a free utility to unpack it.  This seems fitting with the nerdy aesthetic, but hopefully something they will change soon.Installing the software was painless in Windows 7 and the mouse was immediately recognized.  As with other mice, all of the buttons can be programmed, along with scroll speed, LED color, DPI, etc.  Profiles can be saved and loaded to make switching settings for different programs fast.  Overall, very similar to Logitech or SteelSeries software.With all these buttons, this is an ideal mouse for use with macros, such as those written in autohotkey.  If you do a lot of the same tasks over and over for work, I recommend looking into it.  By using this mouse, a lot of wrist and hand pain can be avoided, plus things can be sped up in some cases.  This is a major benefit over standard gaming mice.SUMMARYThe Venus is a substantial, precise mouse with a lot of buttons to work with.  It is worth considering their other mice, among other brands, if you do not need them, but for the intended audience and price it is great.Thank you to UtechSmart for providing a review unit.

I'm only a few chapters in, but I wanted to get my first impressions down.I bought this directly through Steam because they were having a sale. It took me about 4 days to download the whole thing, which is probably still faster and cheaper than getting it through the mail on a DVD (after I adjusted my PC to not sleep, the downloading went much faster).Second, I am a fan of the original Thief: The Dark Project, Thief II: The Metal Age and Thief (III): Deadly Shadows. I have vivid memories of crawling along cobbled stone corridors with my beady eyes affixed to the light gem, hoping I'd timed the guards' routines correctly. I have a vivid of memory of the moment it dawned on me that this was not a first person shooter game, but a first person stealth game and how that changed everything for my gameplay.The first Thief game is the classic and the standard by which all others are compared. I was a little disappointed by Thief II because of the steampunk robots, but I got used to them and there was enough creep factor that it made still highly enjoyable. There was also an open city that you could explore at your own pace and whim, searching for every jewel and gold nugget, hoping to hit 100% on your stats. The third Thief was the leat enjoyable for me, because it seemed very small and linear. They had done away with the rope arrows and given you a pair of climbing gloves and as much as I fought sometimes with getting a good hold on the ropes, I loved them. I missed the pagans and the religious zealots (Hammers).I've been waiting for Thief 4 for a long time (as I'm sure many have), and when you wait that long and hope that much with only teases and hints to sustain you, it's unlikely any company can adequately satisfy every desire and dream you have.Square-Enix has come close, much closer than I'd hoped.Graphics:Strangely, I'm experiencing some lag and low framerates more on the cut scenes rather than in gameplay. I haven't spent a lot of time adjusting the graphics options because it's tolerable.It's a beautiful game. The lighting is perfect, better perhaps than the first Thief. The first Thief game had me adjusting the shadows both up and down. I liked the dark shadows, but I also spent a lot of time starting at absolute blackness trying to discern what was there. I don't have that issue with this game. The characters look good, and after so long for them to not be dramatically improved over the original game would be unforgiveable. They move good. The city is beautifully lit, both from afar and up close. It's dark enough for the right Thief ambience, but bright enough so you can tell what you're doing.Gameplay:This is a combination of the original Thief games, but you can also see some Dishonored influence (which was obviously itself influenced by Thief). For example, the new "swoop" is similar, though not identical to Dishonored's "blink". It's not a bad addition. The lay out of paths are (so far) more linear like Thief III. Even Dishonored would have at least 2-3 different paths you could take. This for me is its greatest weakness so far. The openness of games like Arkham City/Origins and Far Cry, etc., the ability of Valve games to get you where you need to go while keeping the illusion you can go anywhere makes this game seem a little closed in, which is a shame because you can see the possibilities of the little nooks and crannies that could have been something interesting. One thing great about the original Thief was you learned to dive into the water, to explore every tunnel because you might find a corridor that led to an underwater cavern where there were spiders and a treasure chest. So far, those little extras are missing.The AI of the Guards is much better here. I've spotted a few clues here and there about treasure which are fun to remember and follow up on. This has been mentioned in other reviews, but one of the frustrating things is getting somewhere and not being able to jump. I agree. If it looks like a place you can jump, you should be able to. As opposed to the original, when you've been spotted, there is a sound effect to alert you, a sort of quiet rush/roar. That's not bad and I like the graphics of the Eye with the red dots that let you know how in danger of being discovered you really are.So far (and I'm still early in the game), I miss the zombies, the hammer spirits with the sounds of chains. I even miss the skull that used to appear when you were dead. Here, in many situations, if you're discovered you simply fail, not necessarily die. In later chapters, it appears you can fight your way out and run.I don't have a problem with Garret's voice. I have vivid memories of the original. I can hear it as I type this, but the "new guy" is a good actor and it's working pretty well for me.Once I've finished the game, I'll update this, but so far I'm pretty happy with the purchase. It's definitely better than Thief III. It does some things better than the original Thief, but overall I'm afraid I'm still finding the original slightly more interesting from a play perspective.Updated 6/24/14:So I'm still playing and like the first thief, I've ended up running between two regions because I caused a ruckus, and it's fun to watch the characters react to that.One thing I forgot in the orignal review was the inclusion of a sort of "alternate sight". Batman gets "detective vision". Here it's called "Focus" and it highlights all the items you can interact with, including widows, etc.Another thing I noticed is that the rope arrows wouldn't work. I shoot them into wood and nothing happens. It turns out you can only use the rope arrows in certain places, which is a little counter intuitive. You can see them in focus, and mostly I've been using them to get to rooms that are otherwise inaccessible. There is some of the discovery of the earlier games. For example, I steal a plaque from some place and suddenly there's a switch behind it. But what does it do? There are lots of places designed for you to discover.

Thief is not just a game, its an experience of the dark and there have been none more darker themes for a Thief game than this one. A city in terror, penetrated with a disease, greedy merchants, sinister politics, scared guards and a traumatized Garrett, there are only questions and so few answers.GamePlay - 4/5Thief plays like any other Thief game, a true stealth experience (and it is intended to be played that way). There are shadows and enough of them to get past guards, pick pockets, complete goals without getting spotted. It's in this gameplay that Thief fans and stealth players will find maximum satisfaction. At time, you will need to knock them out or kill them but it is not necessary since Garrett is not a killer. There are multiple ways to approach the goals and Garrett is free to choose the path he wants. It highly satisfying when you stumble upon a secret path to your goal. Upgrades and weapons are available from dealers around the town.The best feature I like is lockpicking. Just turn off the damn assist and you will know how thievy you will feel picking locks. Its one of the best lock picking I have seen in games. (The fingers move ever so slightly letting you know when to click, its a satisfying experience)Jumping, climbing is context sensitive and Garrett cannot climb places which the devs do not allow. In my gameplay this was not a big issue but might not provide the freedom which certain players want to enjoy.Garrett has the ability to "Swoosh" for a short distance which is a quick dash through the shadows. The feature has been cleverly implemented and swooshing over noisy surfaces will get you heard/spotted. Players will definitely use this a lot.The problem for a few people will arise from the map and navigating the city since it is very confusing at first (If Waypoints are OFF). I had a hard time figuring it out for the first 2 chapters, now I have a hang of it and I know The City, all exits, entries and secret paths to tranverse between various parts. Once I figured out The city, I felt that the devs did this in order to provide the player a sense of being lost and discovering the city by themselves, but still the map is not implemented well (no reference points to orient the players).Graphics - 5/5This game is eye candy. I have played it on PC with Very High Settings and it has top notch graphics. The dark shadows, lighting of lamps, night sky, Garrett's clothes, in-game textures are all well done. However, it is a dark game and most colors seen are grey and black, it just adds to how dark themed this game is.Story - 2.5/5The story (without spoilers) is mostly about a disease ridden city, an exploitative authority, some supernatural elements and Garrett's confusion. The game has a decent start sequence to throw Garrett in a confused state. There is no clue why things happened the way they are and Garrett is supposed to figure it out. There are foes and friends and the game makes them clear early on. I havent played the entire game, so lets wait for the ending sequence.Environments/Discovery - 4/5The environments are superb. There are hidden passages, underground tombs, rooftops (sort of) etc. The game shines when you find these secrets. The experience is exhilarating, Thief is about discovery. It is game for the patient so take time to look at the environments, they are your friend.Try to find the side missions, they are extremely satisfying and provide great additional gameplay besides the main story. Also, the more gold you earn, it is good for getting upgrades.One thing where I believe Thief misses out is populating the city. You will hardly run into people in the city. I understand its a diseased place but the city should have more people. It just feels that something has been stolen from the Thief :)Music/Sound/Voice Acting - 4/5Sounds are an integral part of any modern day game and Thief does a great job at this. The music stays low and slow as Garrett sneaks through the shadows but as tension mounts, guards discover and chase Garrett. the music picks up and adds on to that excitement superbly. You run through the streets, climb ladders and try to evade them, its an intense feeling. As you discover secrets, a satisfying chime adds to your accomplishment. In the dark corridors of tombs, the sounds are murkier and deathly. Voice acting in this game is just fine, I would have liked better voice acting specially for Garrett. The villain in the game does a far better job. NPC dialogues are best ignored, they can be absurd as well as astonishing at times.Overall, it is a superb Thief game and I am loving every moment of playing it. There are moments where the AI is not upto the mark, but it does a decent job of keeping you on your toes. I would advise to play this game on Master difficulty with Lockpicking and waypoints OFF. I bought this game on Steam for $14.41 on sale, its worth much more than that.Note: The game can be approached with a lethal way of killing everyone but it is not recommended since Garrett is neither very agile nor skillful at wielding blades, also it spoils the experience of the darkness.EDIT-----After finishing the game I would say that it has a very weak ending which spoils the entire premise. I am taking down my rating from 4 to 3 now. This game is certainly not worth the full price, this is one of the weakest endings I have seen in a game for a long time.

This charming little game was off my radar for a while, but when it appeared as a Playstation Plus freebie, I was curious and picked it up. I found myself pleasantly surprised by Brothers' creativity, even if the puzzles are a little too easy.The story is fantastic- it is not told through words but I found myself truly caring about what happens to these characters and I wanted them to succeed on their journey. The story feeds directly into the gameplay- the two brothers must work in tandem to make it past many environmental obstacles and creatures in order to save their father by getting healing water from the Tree of Life. The less I say about what happens the better, but I was drawn into this beautiful world with subtle but effective music quickly and was enthralled all the way through the game's brief three hours. The older brother has the ability to pull levers and swim, while the younger one can squeeze through tight spaces and reach higher platforms by being boosted up. Most of the puzzles had the brothers separated while helping each other through an area. My favorite part was one where they are scaling a castle while tied together by a rope, since it was cool how each one helps the other reach the next handhold.Much of the challenge comes from controlling the two characters at once. Each one is controlled with an analog stick, and each one also has an all-purpose action button. Once I got the hang of controlling both brothers with ease and precision (after maybe 30 minutes), I found the puzzles not challenging at all. Although the puzzles are well-implemented, I doubt most will have trouble figuring out how to get past each obstacle for very long.I didn't really mind the lack of challenge because the story was so well-crafted and there are some truly beautiful moments. This is a short game, but I think it would be worth the $15 and I recommend it. Just be aware that you're not in for a big challenge, but a simple but well-told story and a beautifully crafted world.

Brothers is a short game- a few hours- but defines itself by its unique approach to character controls and puzzles.  At first the thought of controlling two characters at the same time seems daunting, but the formula is simple enough.  This game requires the use of a controller (I used a 360 controller), and each thumb stick controls the movement of each brother.  Besides the movement, the triggers acts as the action button that is used to grab hold of objects, hang on ledges, and distract enemies.  In most cases, puzzles require the team work of both brothers- the oldest brother utilizing his height and strength and the youngest brother utilizing his small frame and speed.Visually, the game meets expectations matching the color palette of games like Bastion.  The story is carried through visual cues and has no real dialogue.  The plot revolves around the life lessons of love, loss, regret, and blame.  Given the mechanics of the game and lack of dialog, the game works well to present a simple adventure story.  I did feel that the game’s climax was hindered by the stories original easy-going nature.  It lacked the proper build up to hit the ball out of the park.  The ending felt rushed and important visual cues were easily overlooked.  Overall, the game made its point that a tired storyline can be reinvigorated by approaching controls and puzzles differently.

At it's core, Brothers is a simple puzzle game where you control each brother with a stick and a button.  The puzzles are easy to figure out, but simultaneously controlling both brothers is like patting your head and rubbing your stomach.  It takes a bit of practice.Story:  10/10When their father becomes ill, two brothers must venture into the unknown to find a healing spring and bring back a cure.  Along their journey, the brothers will face ravenous wolves, trolls, giants, griffins, traps, and other majestic beasts.  Even though, the brothers speak in a fantasy language, their gestures communicate everything you need to know.  You get a strong sense of their personalities through their actions.  The mischievous younger brother is afraid of water and can't swim, but he has an affinity for animals.  The more focused older brother protects him and he does most of the physical labor.  The puzzles complete many side quests with strong themes of family, love, sacrifice, and loss.Gameplay:  8/10The only real gameplay here are the puzzles.  Once you see them, it's fairly easy to figure out what you need to do.  But simultaneously controlling both brothers takes a bit of practice.  The gameplay is 100% linked to the story.  So, you are constantly learning about the characters and the world they live in, as you are solving the puzzles.Atmosphere:  9/10The graphics are pretty good and the music sets the mood.  All of the creatures, characters, architecture, magic, really blend together to create a memorable experience.Replay Value: 1/10The game is only about 5 hours long and there's no reason to replay it.Maturity:  Young TeensThere's no swearing in the game and the fantasy violence is on par with many of the recent adventure movies.  The story has a few scary moments and a few sad ones.Overall:  9/10This is a great game that you won't forget.  It's original, has an interesting atmosphere and it's full of emotion throughout the adventure.  At times, this game goes on sale for as low as $5 and if you can get it cheap, it's a must buy.Buy it if you love emotional stories.Buy it if you love adventure.Buy it if you love puzzle games, although these puzzles are more about coordination, than solving complex riddles.Avoid it if you want combat, battles, or destructive magic.If you enjoyed this game, you should like Limbo, Bastion, and for older systems, Ico and Shadow of the Colossus.

The Good: Wonderful art, heart wrenching ending, unique control and gameplay, fun boss fightsThe Bad: Short length, controls are hard to get used to, story has no depth, too easyBrothers is about two boys who travel across their land to find a magic sap from a very special tree. They need this sap to heal their father who has come down with a life threatening illness. That's pretty much all their is to the story. However, that's not the touching part. Brothers doesn't really start hitting your feelings until the end. Brothers has a unique gameplay mechanic where you control each brother with an analog stick. It's takes some getting used to, and you never completely get used to it, but using both brothers at the same time is a unique way to play a game.The game consists of simple puzzles. They aren't anything complicated and don't take much thinking to figure out. Some puzzles only certain brothers can solve. There may be a gate that the smaller brother can squeeze through so he can lower a bridge for the bigger brother. Some times they have to work side by side such as in water. The smaller brother can't swim so he needs to hold onto the older brother. The only other buttons you use are the triggers. One assigned to each brother for grabbing stuff.There are some boss fights in the game which are a lot of fun. One early on consists of fighting a troll. The little brother needs to lure him into a cage while the older brother closes it with a lever nearby. There's only one way in so the little brother has to slip through bars to escape. It's moments like this that make Brothers shine and make you smile. Later on in the game it gets darker and more grim. Puzzles involve dismembering dead corpses of giants. The gameplay ideas change throughout the game like when they have a rope tied to each other and you use it to swing each other around cliffs. The game feels like a grand adventure, but it's short lived. You can beat it in 4 short hours wanting so much more.The game looks really good, while not technically impressive the art style is great and the game has many beautiful vistas. The story is lacking any depth, but it's the adventure that counts here. If you have a free evening for gaming, Brothers is one of the best indie games you can buy this year.

If you ever hear anyone say how much they love the Amazing Spider-Man 2 Game, you can be sure they're saying they love the amazing "Spider-Man 2" game and not "The Amazing Spider-Man 2" game.  Confusing?  Let's go back in history for a bit.The Sony Playstation was blessed with two incredibly fun Spider-Man games.  They were some of the best superhero games on a console, and they were pretty popular.  The Playstation 2 got, in time for the release of the first Spider-Man film a game that was basically a visually upgraded version of those two.  It played the same, it just looked better.  Then Spider-Man 2, the film, was released, and a game came alongside it for the three major consoles.  While the film was making history as one of the greatest superhero movies, the game was doing the same for superhero games.  It was just the right combination of every good idea a Spider-Man game ever had, and practically none of the bad ones.The major differences between that game and all the previous ones were that the game was open world, so you could travel around the city all you wanted, and that web-swinging was impossibly fun.  For the first time in a Spider-Man game, swinging was realistic, as it had your webs attaching to buildings, and the physics engine did the rest.  Most Spider-Man games after that one had used the same formula, with varying degrees of success, but to this day, Spider-Man 2 is still the game all other Spider-Man games are measured against.With the release of the Amazing Spider-Man film, Beenox (who have made the last Spider-Man games, which were not open world) released a game based on it (technically, it was a sequel).  I have not played that game, but I know two things about it: it is open world, and it doesn't have realistic web swinging.Now, with the release of the last film's sequel, there's this, the last game's sequel.  This one is also open world and has realistic swinging again, which they nailed.  Swinging is incredibly fun, just as it was before, but sadly, that's one of the very few things the game has going for it.The most obvious problem, though not the worst one by any means, is the graphics.  They are Playstation 2 quality.  Before I played the game I thought people were exaggerating when they said that, but they weren't.  No other open world game I've played on the PS3 has graphics this poor, even the oldest ones.  Saints Row looks better.  The first one.  And that game had you on the street all the time, where there's more detail, they would have had an excuse to look simpler.  Spider-Man is easily the most detailed model in the entire game.Low-res textures will make you think the game is still loading them, but after you've spent half a minute staring at a building's surface you'll sadly realize it won't start to look better.  Low polygon count means there's a lot of jagged edges, as if the resolution is really small and the screen is getting stretched (which is probably what's happening).  Ligthing will make shadows stutter around as if a guy holding a lamp behind you was having a seizure.  Then the animations are just weird.  Spider-Man exaggerates his gesticulations when he speaks, to the point that it looks as if the game is glitching.Then there's the sound.  The music sounds a lot like the one from previous-franchise Spider-Man games, so they're not being particularly original.  Voice acting is surprisingly mediocre.  For reference, here's a list of the movie's cast members who've lent their voice and likeness to be used in the game:- Stan Lee.That's it.  Yeah.  No one else returned, which, again, is a surefire sign that this game was made CHEAP.  Stan Lee, bless him, doesn't ask for much for his roles, as he does it for love to his characters, so it's not surprising he's here.  But the problem becomes really striking for Spider-Man, who's the one character you have to listen all the time.  His voice is quite annoying, specially because he just won't shut up while playing.  Plus, again, he doesn't look or sound AT ALL like Andrew Garfield.  If you're not a fan, you might think that's a plus, but the sad truth is that he doesn't look or sound like Peter Parker either.The game's story is an even bigger mess than the movie.  There's no plot, just a collection of subplots laid out one after another, as if that's enough to form a cohesive story.  The game is a sequel to the first game but also a retelling of the movie's story, which can and will get confusing.  As I said before, I didn't play the first game on the PS3, but I did play the 3DS version, which has basically the same story, so trust me, things will get annoying.Another problem with the gameplay is that you are many times forced to play as Peter Parker in some areas.  And I don't mean it as a skin/suit change.  You are Peter Parker, photographer, and that's all you do.  You can't jump, you can't swing, you can't fight.  They take away all the fun parts of the game.  You will also have to take pictures as Spider-Man, and it's not any more fun.  You have to move the zoom on the camera until one exact point (when the meter turns green, good luck noticing that the first few times) or the picture won't be accepted, even if you take a better one than the one the game wants.  They could have added a focus option to make this more realistic, but no, they cheapened it again.Yet another impossibly annoying part are the random events.  Those are, in spirit, par for the course in an open-world Spider-Man game.  You have random crimes or people in distress showing up and you can choose to tackle the problem for extra XP, for more gameplay or just to feel more like a hero.  But see, in the old games, those were a CHOICE.  Now you have a good/bad meter and you're forced to do them if you want to keep being considered a hero by the people.  And I mean that in the most literal way.  This is not like, say, Red Dead Redemption, in which your good/bad meter goes up if you help people and it goes down if you attack them.  Here, the meter will go down simply by inaction.  And I don't mean by going to a mission and failing.  Missions show up ALL THE TIME on the map, but they go away a couple of minutes later and if you don't reach them in time or decide not to do them your meter will go down, and if it reaches the bad area you will be ATTACKED AS A CRIMINAL by a task force.  For not going to the other side of the map to stop a random crime.  I can't even begin to explain how mind-numblingy stupid that is.Another annoying part about those missions is that every single time after you finish one there will be a newscast scene talking about how people love Spider-Man.  Every. Single. Time.  When you finished your side missions in previous games, you got a congratulating message on screen but Spider-Man was instantly controllable again, and you could keep playing even while the message was still fading.  Now you have to wait until the newscast ends, then until the camera fixes back behind Spidey again and then until the congratulatory message goes away.  Every time.But see, combat is fun.  It's not fantastic or anything, but it's serviceable.  The side missions can be fun too, so you can just reach for the close ones and your meter will stay mostly in shape.  And swinging is really, good actual fun, so there's always a good incentive to go from here to there.  There are a bunch of collectibles and upgrades to be found, such as comic books which you can read, action figures which give the characters' backstories, new suits to wear or minigames to play.  I could have forgiven all the bad if at least the game's good parts exceeded the bad ones.But then there are the bugs.  Oh, my God, the bugs.  And I mean game-breaking bugs.  Yeah, there are graphic glitches once in a while, but those are merely annoying.  These bugs, though, will ruin your fun.  Spider-Man will get stuck on walls sometimes while swinging, so if you're in a hurry to reach a side-mission before it goes away, you will be out of luck until you can get him to jump off.  Enemies will get stuck on walls, which can instantly knock them out, which will take away the fun of combat, or render them invincible, which will halt your progress.  Sometimes missions just won't appear, so you will be stuck in open mode with nothing to do but swinging.  Those last two will require you to exit the game and reload a save in order to continue playing, and, of course, there'll always be a section you have to replay.I want to make this very clear: very little care was put into this game.  Spider-Man 2 on the GC/PS2/Xbox was the game that proved that movie-licensed video games could be great and didn't need to be haphazardly made because people would buy them just for the franchise.  This one is the exact opposite.  This game was definitely made in hopes people would buy it because of the movie.  Don't be one of those people.  I was one because, well, there was precedent.  Unfortunately, instead of keeping with the tradition, they ruined it.  I was fooled, but there's no reason you have to be too.  There's value in this game, there's fun to be had, but not at the price they ask for it.  Get this game when it's $20 or less.  It's barely worth that, much less anything more.

Video games based on comic book character didn't used to get respect because, to be quite frank, they didn't used to deserve it. Many of the old games based on comic book characters were either cheap adaptations or really sloppily made games (ie. Superman 64). Yet, in the past few years, like the comic book movie genre, comic book characters have slowly gained more respect in the video game universe. With games such as Batman: Arkham City reaching a level of mastery that few games can reach, it is unsurprising that gamers have expected more from the genre than previously. Generally, the less successful comic book games have been adaptations, and the more successful ones have been original stories.The Amazing Spider-Man 2 is a mixture of both. While the game is based around the universe of the film released with the same name, Beenox has taken the route of creating a completely original story that is separate from the film entirely. Additionally, Spider-Man also has the strength of past Spider-Man movie adaptations such as Spider-Man 2, which many consider the best movie licensed game to date. With Beenox returning to manual web swinging and promising to expand upon the first game, is The Amazing Spider-Man 2 The Game truly amazing? Seriously though, I am so sick of that pun... way overused.Whereas most movie games take the route of directly following the plot of the film, The Amazing Spider-Man 2 has decided to take the route of an original story, which coexists with the film universe, but with the story being entirely separate. With this, not only does the game not spoil any of the events of the film, but it manages to completely drift from many of the events of the film, minus a few key characters and scenarios. The story in the game revolves around the ol' web head searching for his Uncle Ben's killer, but this path soon leads him to an even greater threat. This threat is Cledus Kassidy, an insane psychopath who brutally murders criminals. To take him down, Spider-Man must also use Peter Parker to personally interact with characters, and even team up with Kraven the Hunter, a well known villain in Spidey's universe.The story here is a bit of a mixed bag. Unlike the first game, the story does tend to be more personal, which ultimately enhances the connection that we have to the character of Peter Parker. However, at the same time, it feels underdeveloped. The game opens with a really cool reenactment of Uncle Ben's death from the perspective of Peter Parker, but ultimately, the strong emotional toll falls flat after about the first hour of play time. After the first hour, Peter Parker is essentially shoehorned into the story just so the developers could say that he had more of an active role in the game, and while the roster of villains is impressive (ranging from Electro and Green Goblin, to others such as Kraven, Carnage, and Shocker), they all feel like they are just thrown into the story just because. At least in the film, the villains are all given an essential role and have a purpose for existing in this universe. The game doesn't give these characters the same justification for existing other than giving the players someone new to fight.That being said, there are some cool bright spots to the story. Despite the fact that some of it feels underdeveloped and rushed, the game does add a dialogue system. These dialogue options are available during key missions throughout the story, generally when in confrontation with a key villain.  It has absolutely no impact on the way the game plays out, but it does help flesh out the story, universe, and characters at hand. One sequence in particular has you talking to Aunt May towards the beginning of the game, and seeing Peter having a genuine conversation with Aunt May is something that was lacking in the previous titles, so seeing this side of Peter's life was welcome. The other ones ultimately help build up the story in interesting ways, and in some cases, make you wonder why they weren't just included as the regular dialogue in the game.However, unlike the first game, the problem with the narrative this time around is that it just didn't feel like a lot of fun. There are a few standout moments, but there were few surprises or moments of humor that genuinely stick out in my mind, unlike the first game. The game tried to focus more on Peter Parker, but by rejecting every other character in the universe, it failed to get a ton of emotion out of me, unlike the first game, where the interactions with Gwen and Doctor Connors provided the story with some genuine thrills. Whereas the film managed to develop the most essential characters in meaningful ways (including Peter Parker), the game seems more interested in spectacle than emotion, and even then it fails.The story isn't bad, but it feels far too short and inconsistent to really enhance the game. Even in terms of trying to build a relevant Spidey universe, the game fails, unlike other successful titles like Batman: Arkham City.When the story fails, however, the voice acting is pretty good. All of the voice actors do an excellent at portraying their characters from the source material, giving the sometimes stale dialogue a true sense of life and meaning. In particular, Sam Riegel is a fantastic Spider-Man, capturing the humor and conflict of the character quite well. Fortunately, Spidey is also given more quips this time around than in the first game, and the delivery of these quips makes for some of the most thrilling moments in the game.In terms of gameplay, The Amazing Spider-Man 2 feels very similar to its predecessor, but with some changes added that both enhance and hurt the experience simultaneously. For starters, the web swinging mechanics have been completely reworked. Whereas the first game's swinging mechanics felt automatic, never requiring you to attach webs to buildings or do much more than hold a single button, The Amazing Spider-Man 2 brings the web swinging closer to the feeling of Spider-Man 2 on the Playstation 2, while making it look every bit as impressive and effortless as its predecessor. Webs now attach to buildings unlike the first game, and depending on the environment around you, you will have to alternate between the left and right triggers in order for Spidey to attach to things to swing from.The mechanic also includes a few extra additions, such as a swing boost, catapults, and the ability to incorporate the "Web-Rush" mechanic from the first game. For people who haven't played the first game, know that with a click of a button you are able to direct Spider-Man to a specific point on screen and he will get to it in the most efficient way possible. This may mean jumping off the side of a wall and running across a building or web zipping to a flagpole. Fortunately, players don't need to rely on the mechanic as heavily as they did in the first game, so it is well incorporated with the sense of momentum that is offered in the open world.The Amazing Spider-Man 2 also returns old features from previous titles, such as the "spider-sense" feature from Spider-Man 3, where players are allowed to look through walls and enemies and points of interest will be highlighter. For players of the Batman Arkham games, think of it as Spidey's version of "Detective Mode" and you'll have an idea of what to expect. This new mechanic works well with the new stealth mechanics, which include a far less frustrating camera and some cool new takedowns that make for both a challenging, yet rewarding stealth experience. It's miles ahead of the first title.Manhattan as a whole seems expanded upon from the first game. While the map is claimed to be as big as the first Amazing Spider-Man (though it seems bigger), the scope of it is much greater. Buildings are taller, there is more noise as you swing above cars, and there are many more things to do. Spidey can now compete in races, combat tours, Russian hideouts that unlock new costumes, and so much more. Suffice to say, there is far more replay value in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 than there was in the first game. These additions are welcome, and will keep fans of the character coming back for more.Despite the improvements to the city and exploration, there are many elements of the gameplay that remain heavily flawed. For starters, the combat remains similar to the first game, and while some things are improved, there are new additions that make it less satisfying. Like the first game, the combat does echo "Batman: Arkham City" with its focus on the offensive, with a countering system implemented to keep the player on their toes. The system worked well in the first game mainly because of the enemy types, but shockingly, The Amazing Spider-Man 2 appears to have less enemy types than even the first game did. This, in turn, makes the combat get repetitive quickly, and furthermore, there is a serious lack of challenge in the combat. Throughout my play through of the game, I only died twice and neither of them were from direct confrontation with an enemy. The combat is responsive, and it works fine, but the repetition and lack of variety makes it nowhere near as fresh as the Batman Arkham games, or even other Spidey titles.Main story missions seem to have been improved from the first game. Whereas the first title mainly enclosed the player to dull indoor levels throughout the story, The Amazing Spider-Man 2 makes the level design much open. This allows the player with freedom to tackle a mission how they please, whether they want to take a stealthy approach or take the enemies on head on. Fortunately, the game provides you with enough options both in terms of combat maneuver and level design to make either one possible and satisfying. This makes the story missions quite a lot of fun to play through, even when the story itself isn't quite up to par.Yet, the game sometimes tends to punish your heroic actions. This comes in the form of a new "Hero or Menace" system that has been implimented into the game, which essentially acts as a karma system. Whereas in some games like Mass Effect or inFamous the system is impacted by dialogue choices throughout the game, the karma system in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 is impacted by how often you complete the random crimes occurring throughout the city. These crimes will appear on your map, and you as Spidey will have to complete some of them. As time ticks on, some of them will start to disappear, with new ones reappearing in their place. Essentially, as you complete crimes, your karma becomes closer to "Hero" status, but if you fail to complete them, then your karma will decline towards more of a "menace" status.If your karma gets low enough, OsCorp will send robots and other threats after Spidey to act as an annoyance. Ultimately, this encourages you to do the random crimes sprinkled around the city. The concept, on paper, sounds like a good idea, but the game never gives you enough time to complete a lot of these crimes. Even if you are trying to actively do all of them that you can, there are so many going on at once that it is difficult to do them all, and inevitably, your karma will keep on dropping, no matter how responsibly you use your great power.The other big problem with these random crimes is that they don't feel seamless. One of the best parts about Spider-Man 2 on the Playstation 2 is that you were able to swing through New York and stop a bunch of crimes without interruption. Once a crime ended, you may have a screen pop up on screen to tell you how you did, but this could be skipped with a click of a button. Even in the first Amazing Spider-Man title, once a crime was over, players were able to jump right back into web swinging without delay. However, The Amazing Spider-Man 2 breaks this sense of immersion by including a cut scene at the start and end of EVERY SINGLE CRIME that you complete in New York. This not only acts as a cheap way to lengthen what is a REALLY short story and game, but it also makes the crimes feel less random and more scripted, which breaks the sense of immersion of being Spider-Man.Still, if you can get past this flaw, there are some fun crimes for Spidey to tackle. Whereas the first game in the series included only a few forms of random crimes, The Amazing Spider-Man 2 has added several more. In addition to stopping car chases and beating up some bad guys, there are also civilians to save from burning buildings, huge shootouts on rooftops and construction sites, and much more. The increase in the amount of random crime is welcome, especially because you will be doing a lot more of it than you had previously. However, even these events can become repetitive, as you will be doing the same things repeatedly. However, even with the repetition, there is still always something satisfying about pulling that last civilian out of a burning building or pulling the hostage out of a getaway car. It's in these moments that you really feel like Spidey cleaning up the streets of New York.Speaking of the streets of New York, they don't look too bad. I played the game both on the Playstation 4 and the Playstation 3, and while it is clear that the graphics were built with the last generation of consoles in mind, the graphics are not bad whichever one you do play them on. On the Playstation 4 version, textures are noticeably better, as is the framerate, but either way you will get a game with some awesome Spidey animations and a good looking city, but a lack of detail in other characters that can sometimes bring you out of the immersion. Still, keeping in mind that the graphics were made with last generation in mind, they aren't too bad. The rest of the production is about up to par with the graphics, with the sound design being solid, yet with an original score that is largely forgettable. Of course, the production is not up to par with most triple A titles due to the fact that the budget and time was limited to the film's release and Activision, so some of these cut corners are forgivable as long as you are able to look past them.The Amazing Spider-Man 2 is an incredibly mixed bag. It includes a ton of good ideas, and tons of great execution. Yet, for every good change in the game, there is another bad one to counter it. Touring New York and swinging through the streets hasn't been this good in a decade, and there is tons of cool fan service for Spidey fans. Yet, the execution of some ideas such as the story and the "Hero or Menace" system hurt the game as a whole. There also seems to be a great sense of familiarity, as the game doesn't change a heck of a ton from its predecessor (although the good changes made really enhance the experience). The Amazing Spider-Man 2 was this close to being a great Spider-Man game, and if some of the annoying flaws were worked out, it could have been. Still, if you can look past these flaws, you may have a fun time with The Amazing Spider-Man 2. It may not be amazing, incredible, or spectacular, but it saves the day anyways.The Amazing Spider-Man 2 The Game Verdict:Pros:+The swinging mechanics are easily the best since Spider-Man 2+The web rush mechanic only enhances exploration further+Improved stealth mechanics are a blast+New York is expanded upon since the first game, making for more replay value.+Tons of awesome unlockables for Spider-Man fans.+Interesting story idea+Level design is significantly better than in the first game+Great animations for Spidey, and the graphics overall are serviceableCons:-The story feels rushed, never developing it enough for the audience to care-TOO SHORT-The "Hero or Menace" system is frustrating and breaks the immersion of being Spider-Man-Ugly character models-Repetitive combat-Forgettable musicFinal Score: 7.5/10

While not perfect, The Amazing Spider-Man 2 on PS4 is a very good, freedom to choose your path and explore styled super hero game that is fun to play; imagining you're Spider Man with good controls.Controls:L2 WebSwing Left Hand, Wall Run when close, Boost swing holdL1; Web PullR2 Opposite of L2. Tapping either R2 or L2 swings faster.R1: Web Rush Target mode, FPV, Tap is quick rushPad: Pause, Cellphone Menu hold.Right Analog: Camera. R3: Photo mode to take picturesLeft Analog: Move where you want, L3 descend/perch like Batman from Arkham Games.X Jump, Propel Upwards while in air.Circle: Web Shoot, Seismic Blast (hold)Square: Attack moves and combos/timing.Triangle: Interact with objects, or dodge/roll.Pros of the game include:+Open City free to explore that nicely recreates most of Manhattan Island, NYC. Reach the tallest skyscraper and hop off any time you want as a super hero, Spider Man.+Controls are responsive and most of the time, easy to get the hang of.+Lots of Classic Villains to battle.+Fun fighting gameplay similar to Arkham's multi enemy fights.+The new Left or Right webslinging is more realistic and believable compared to ASM1.+Cool new abilities for SpiderMan including the cool web slingshot and new fight moves like the Seismic Blast. Upgrade from the weak character you start off with to create a super Spider Man later on.+The City's details have improved a lot, and the city feels more like NYC, having visited there myself a number of times. Even the Museum of Natural History is present this time. Very colorful game and the time of day variations are really nicely done this time.+The great camera set up of the first game returns, making you feel more like you're in the game and playing as Spiderman thanks to the closer, over the shoulder view, which backs off a bit while webslinging.+More comics to collect through the city, to unlock actual comics to read in Stan Lee's Comic Shop. His shop also includes collectible figurines of characters, a Spider Man arcade that lets you brush up on your fighting moves, a poster gallery, bonuses, etc. 14 comics to unlock and read in all of actual Spiderman Comics.+Stan Lee appears in the game and does voice acting which is a nice addition considering the great history of characters and stories he has originated with Marvel way back when.+Explore freely on foot your apartment and the comic store, among other interiors.+Great ambient sounds of the city that captures the sense of being there.+Time of day varies based on the missions for the first playthrough so far.+Graphic sharpness looks great on the PS4. 1080p.+auto save system.+The awesome webrush move returns, allowing you to target your next place to sling to for more precise controls through the city.+Lots to see and do in the city, and more interesting with the Hero Meter, which depends on whether you want to fight bad guys committing crimes in the city or not. If you help the city, you get more rewards. If not, some minor penalties begin.+Great soundtrack and good voice acting most times.+Nice animations most of the time.+15 or so suits to unlock and wear each with unique bonuses.Negatives that could use refinement include:-First off, the game begins on the title screen with literally a PS3 movie playing of scenes in the city, which had me very nervous at first. Thankfully, that was only a movie and the actually PS4 game looks much better than the PS3 version shown there. But...-This game was clearly made with the PS3 as the foundation. Textures are sometimes pixelated and polygons are often squared off at the edges. Not a big deal most of the time, but with the PS4, I was hoping they'd increase the quality as with other games, but they may have been pressed for time.-The first Shocker boss was a bit frustrating, since the game suggest doing certain moves, but you're better off just jumping away from him instead of trying to pull off the suggested moves, which more often than not get you hurt from my first playthrough.-Some of the fights lose sight of the enemies, resulting in cheap hits offscreen from bullets. Targeting enemies takes more getting used to this time than the first game's set up.-+While the webslinging update is nice with more control of the left and right swing, it's also more realistic and takes a learning curve to adapt to, compared to the ease and fun of the first game's web slinging. Some may enjoy this, but I keep looking for places to attach my webs while falling, and if there isn't a building close by, find one before you lose momentum. I think I will appreciate it more after a few more days of play.-+ When you hit a building, you don't automatically stick to it this time, so be sure to press the triangle button quickly, which can be a bit cumbersome when both fingers are on the analogs controlling SpiderMan. Not a big deal though, and offers more control, so that's good.I was expecting PS4 textures as Ghost Games accomplished with Need For Speed Rivals compared to the PS3 version, but other than that, the game does look like a super high res and much more detailed PS3 game running on a PS4. Good, but they really could have done more with the graphical power of the PS4.Even so, I do recommend any fan of super hero games to play The Amazing Spider Man 2 for some classic game play and open city action.Gameplay: 9/10Controls: 8/10. Not always easy to adapt to, but very good.Graphics: 7/10. Nice detail but PS3 textures on PS4.Story: 8/10. Interesting.Action: 9/10. Lots of action.Freedom: 9/10. Choose to explore or play missions.Sound: 9/10. Great music and sound.Fun: 9/10. Mostly fun.Replay Value: 9/10. With an open city, lots to do and see.

Many gamers (at least those who are old enough) long for a Spider-Man video game that generates the same unadulterated joy from web-slinging around NYC as the original Spider-Man 2 video game, which was released for the sixth generation consoles (Xbox, PS2, Gamecube). A few games have done a pretty good job of recreating that feeling (Web of Shadows & Shattered Dimensions have my vote). However, even after all these years there has yet to be a Spider-Man video game that achieves the perfect harmony of superlative exploratory mechanics, combat, and graphics/sound. Many people will likely purchase The Amazing Spider-Man 2 in a continuation of this chasing of a dream, as I did. However, I must urge you not to fall for this trap. Not only does this game fall far short of the mark, history may eventually mark it down as one of the worst Spider-Man games ever made.For most, the game mechanics pertaining to environment traversal - think web-swinging, web zipping, wall crawling, etc. - are the most important part of what makes a Spider-Man game great. Admittedly, they aren't terrible in this game, they're...mediocre. They implemented an unusual web-swinging approach that ties your left and right arms to the left and right triggers, so if you want to swing from your left web-launcher you pull the left trigger. It works well enough in that you gain more control over which direction you wish to angle, but there is a trade-off of simplicity. However, swinging overall just doesn't *feel right.* Spidey doesn't always grab onto buildings at higher altitudes when I feel like he should. There seems to be a minimum period between swings that is a bit too long. Even utilizing the game's mechanics for increasing your swing speed (or using the slingshot move) you still can't go all that fast. Spidey seems to get baffled when he gets too close to buildings. It seems that in general web-swinging seems to have received too little attention as an expense of a more polished web-zipping (called web rush in this game) system. While cool to watch and perhaps more efficient, this mode is much more boring and largely automated. Finally, it's been a long time since I've seen a game that had worse mechanics for actual running around, as both Peter Parker and his alter-ego seem largely incapable of doing so in a human-like manner.If we were to look at this category alone (and it is almost fair to, given that swinging around New York is largely what most people buy these games for) it might get a 3.5 star rating. However, where the game falls farther from grace is with respect to just about everything else. I'll skim through these pretty quickly.Graphics: This is a game coming out during the transitional period between the end of seventh generation (Xbox 360) and the beginning of the eighth (Xbox One). Graphically, it looks like it belongs somewhere closer to the last transitional period between the Xbox and the 360. Honestly, they barely tried here. New York itself looks okay, but most of the character models are s*** compared to the standard set by recent 360 games, much less Xbox One games.Sound: Meh, nothing to write home about. Voice acting is a bit below par, and occasionally characters will speak over one another in a manner that seems accidental, but other than that nothing to speak of.Side-missions: Most of them are fun the first time, and the game adds new varieties periodically. However, they aren't just repetitive; they are cookie cutter duplicates. It's hard to care, much less have fun, rescuing the 57th person from a burning building or a weird electrical field. What's worse is that these missions seem to crop up continually, but also expire if you don't complete them in time, netting you a bit more of a reputation as a menace rather than your friendly neighborhood Spider-Man. If you're something of a compulsive completionist like me this is enough to drive you mad.Main story: I haven't completed enough of this yet to comment, will update review once I have.Combat: The Batman Arkham series has definitely set the bar for superhero combat, but for a time the Spider-Man games reigned supreme. Some of the past ones had a wide variety of unlockable moves based on certain button combinations that were both fun to and effective. Sadly this game has been reduced to a dumbed-down button mashing affair consisting of X to attack with the occasional Y to dodge or B to temporarily immobilize an enemy. The few unlockable combat moves alternate between boring and useless. Even more odd, you can execute a special Spidey finishing move after building up a good combo, but the amount you need seems to be both too high and very variable, so that you can rarely use it effectively.Other: The load times are intolerable for the size and detail of areas being loaded. I own every single Spider-Man game to date. I'm a Spider-Man nut and the moment any of these games hit the market they hit my system for some swing time. This is one of the better Spider-Man games on the market and certainly the best Beenox made Spider-Man game. There have been some big changes this time around. For example you actually have to think about which hand to use while web slinging since you can shoot webbing with your right and left hand using the right and left triggers. And attempting to shoot a webline from the wrong hand can make you fall. It also helps while turning corners to shoot with the corresponding hand. The web rush is back from the previous game which is a plus. Although I have noticed it doesn't work as well as it did in the first game. I put the first game back in my system to make sure and as it turns out the web rush system worked much better in the first Amazing Spider-Man game. Every time you'd push the web rush button in the first game it worked. It seems like half the time you push the web rush button in this new game it doesn't work. I'm glad the web rush is back, I just wish they took the time to make it work as well as it did in the first game. So what about the improvements?Unlimited crime! Better swing mechanics! Smoother combat! A better story line! More classic villains! More than a dozen different costumes that actually effect gameplay! Stealth gameplay has been vastly improved! A nice variety in side missions! And Peter Parker missions this time! Oh, and let's not forget the fact Stan Lee makes more than just a quick cameo in this game. He plays a big role this time around and it's great! I won't spoil it for you but let me just say it is all very clever and adds lots of replay to this game.I am thoroughly enjoying this game. I have run into a few minor bugs but nothing game breaking (which will probably get patched anyway). The ability to choose dialogue ala "Mass Effect" was a nice touch as well. If you are a Spider-Man fan there is no way you will not enjoy this game.*updateI'm much further into this game and I have to say the story line is great! What they do with Kraven and Spider-Man is just fantastic. The debate they get into over whether or not they should ever take a life, and if it is ever justified is just flawless. I was not expecting this caliber of writing for a video game movie tie in. I also really enjoyed what they did with a certain serial killer in the Spider-Man universe. Normally I don't care for changes to story lines and characters from the comics but what they do with this character was very inspired. I don't want to ruin who and what they did, but let me just say the writing for this game is top notch. Best Spider-Man game story since the Ultimate Spider-Man game which was written by the great Brian M. Bendis. So that's saying a lot. You know Beenox has done this game right when, more than once, I actually thought to myself the story line in this game improved upon the story line from the movie. That's all, I just wanted to give an update.*update 2I've finished the game and put a lot of hours into the game after having complete it. I love swinging around New York (and replaying missions) but what is starting to drive me crazy is before every random crime it has to load. Which is weird because you can see the guys you are about to fight in real time before it loads. But any way it loads to show you a small cut scene when you arrive and then cuts to another small cut scene when you win and then has to reload the city. When in ALL other free roam Spider-Man game there is no loading to fight the random crimes and loading when you finish the random crimes. It's time consuming and annoying. It also pulls you out of the game. But worst of all is the Daily Bugle news spots they play OVER AND OVER AND OVER AND OVER...and over after each crime resolved. There really should be a way to turn those off. Or at least skip them the moment they start. Instead you have to watch at least half or sometimes more of each of them before the game lets you skip it. And for someone like me who plays this game non-stop for hours and hours it can get pretty annoying to have to watch those Daily Bugle news reports 1000 times.So over all this is a great Spider-Man game (possibly the best Spider-Man game yet right along side "Web of Shadows") and unlike the Amazing Spider-Man game before it, this one lends itself to being played non-stop like most of the other free roam Spider-Man games because of the unlimited crime. I just wish they didn't have to load every time I wanted to do a random crime. And every time after you complete a random crime.*update 3Ok, last update. I've put a ton of hours into this game even after finishing it. There is lots to do after beating the game. And the swing mechanics are actually much more dynamic than how they first appear. I find myself looking for the tallest buildings to shot a web onto so I can swing around it giving me 360 degrees of movement from that one web line. The web slinging only seems shallow to those who haven't mastered them. Beenox made them easy to use but complex to master. I can now do all kinds of neat tricks while web swinging around the city that I had no idea I could do when I first started this game. Any way, I just wanted to say if you enjoyed this game you have to play "Spider-Man: Web of Shadows."*update 4Ok, seriously for real last update. After putting about a hundred hours into The Amazing Spider-Man 2 and hundreds of hours into Spider-Man:Web of Shadows, I can finally say that The Amazing Spider-Man 2 is THE BEST Spider-Man game I've ever played followed closely by Web of Shadows.

I got a DS Lite yeeeeaaars ago, and loved it. But I have since grown more fond of traditional gaming consoles where I can connect them to my 55" LED HDTV. Being a pretty big Zelda fan, I finally decided to try out the newest line in the DS family where it came with the free Zelda game and awesome Triforce-themed shell.First of all, it's beautiful. I love how even the bottom of the DS has a glossy black Triforce design to mirror the gold one on the top. The paint seems very high quality and can withstand a lot more wear and tear without leaving visible scratches compared to most consumer electronics. I only wish the Zelda game included was the actual game cartridge instead of the download code (I will always prefer a hard copy of something where ownership rights are vastly better, but another topic for another day).I love the 3D effect, and use it more often than not, but I also like that they give you control over it so you can turn it down or off when necessary. You have to be looking directly at the screen from a perfect centered angle to get the 3D effect, so sometimes when you're playing somewhere that you don't have as much mobility or a good lighting environment (like outside in direct sunlight), games are better enjoyed with 3D off. Whenever possible though, I have it turned on max because it really is cool and adds to the immersion.Before buying it, I've played around with 3DS demo units in stores briefly, but never knew about cool features like StreetPass and SpotPass. Now, after having bought one, StreetPass is by far my favorite feature. It allows you to connect with other nearby 3DS consoles, and depending on the game, will reward you or present new challenges depending on your StreetPass activity. The included StreetPass Mii Plaza game is quite addictive once you get started. I have purchased a few games solely based on their integrated StreetPass integration because it is just that fun.I still prefer watching things on a huge screen in 1080p, but they pack a lot of fun into this small thing. The only real negatives I have for it are the low resolution (after being used to even my 5" phone screen being 1080p, the lower 3DS resolution is quite noticeable), and I wish the battery life was a little better. But I'm never too far from somewhere I can charge, so not a big deal.I am also completely sold on the XL version being a must. It doesn't even seem that big to me, honestly. So after becoming accustomed to the XL, I can't even imagine using the non-XL units with about 40% less screen area. Definitely get the XL. And definitely don't get the 2DS! No 3D, smaller screens, no flip screen (for better portability and screen protection), and it just plain looks ugly. The 3DS XL is the most fun gadget I've bought in a long time. I even was able to get my wife to enjoy it enough to get her one as well (the Disney-themed Mickey ears version). It's a lot of fun closing out the day with some Download Play-compatible (wireless multi-console multiplayer using only one cartridge) games like Mario Kart, Mario Party, and Star Fox. Super easy 5 stars here.

Since purchasing the DS I've acquired a few other handhelds: the Game Boy Advance SP (with super backlight action), a knock-off Game Boy Color that has backlighting, and the PSP. I love them all, but not as much as I love my new 3DS, which I got on release day.All those handhelds have their own unique titles, and have provided me and many others countless numbers of playtime. But I never had the GBA and GBC on release day when the games were huge, so I'm using them as back-ups for the games I want to play. And my DS Lite already had GBA functionality, so I got many GBA hours in through that.The PSP is great, but I have as many games for that as I do fingers on one hand, and I use it mostly for PSN games.But the 3DS I got on release, and I feel that in order to get the most out of a machine it's best to get it during its heyday. This way you can play with others who have the same system. There are retro enthusiasts, like me, and those who don't let consoles die just because they're "last gen"--like me--but this review isn't about those.This review is about the 3DS XL Zelda edition and all its glory.I always wait a couple years before buying a new system. The same goes for any electronic item I plan on having for a while, and, now that DLC is prevalent, individual video games. I knew that Nintendo would update their 3DS eventually, if not before my two-year deadline was up, as evidenced by all their handhelds. Every single Game Boy and DS have been updated and upgraded, and the 3DS is no exception.The XL was announced, but to my dismay it kept the same graphics ratio as the 3DS, just larger, and didn't have an extra circle pad. I told myself I'd wait till they added another circle pad to the mix, but then the Zelda edition of the XL/LL was announced.And I wanted it. I wanted it badly. This was the moment I'd finally jump into the current generation of Nintendo handheld bliss.After carefully reviewing the list of games that support a second circle pad (which isn't many), I convinced myself that I'd just get the Circle Pad Pro from Nintendo's online store (which I did, and which still isn't being used).I loved the design of the 3DS from the beginning, but there were some things I wanted to change, like having a black circle pad and black bezel. I felt the gold bezel would contrast from the screen, so I ordered a black matte decal from DecalGirl, then got the Cyber Gadget circle pad (or "slide" in Japan) cover set, both of which you can find reviewed in my profile.So on to the machine.I won't go into reviewing too much, because there are so many reviews of the hardware itself. I will say the Triforce design on this one is amazing and simple. I'm not a fan of consoles or handhelds which have characters in your face or are designed with tacky symbols. While many like the Pikachu and Yoshi 3DS XLs, I'm not a fan of them at all because I feel they take away from the design and seem like eyesores.My favorite limited edition designs so far are the Zelda regular 3DS, the Monster Hunter designs, and the Fire Emblem 3DS. I like the Japanese Charizard one as well, but that's because Charizard is one of my top 5 favorite Pokémon.This edition is the most simplistic while still evoking the Zelda franchise with full force. What can be more symbolic of all the Zelda titles other than the legendary Triforce? The black and gold mesh extremely well, and does a fantastic job of combining A Link between Worlds and the previous Zelda titles in one.Like I mentioned, I wished the bezel was black, but I can live with just applying a decal. But why, oh why, they decide to leave the Circle Pad gray on all the handhelds is beyond my understanding. It's an ugly color which clashes with all 3DSs. In any case, I use my Cyber Gadget covers most of the time anyway.I freakin' love my 3DS. I take it everywhere with me to StreetPass; I live in Chicago, so my days can vary from 1 to 9.I'm so glad I bought one, and I can't wait for the day I get a Wii U. I don't have many 3DS titles, and I actually ended up selling the code for the ALbW download since I prefer physical formats, but for the titles I do have I manage to get many hours of playtime, even with a busy life with work and family and personal projects.I use the 3D slider about halfway to three-quarters, and anywhere between those are my sweet spots. While the XL is pretty easy on the hands, I have a Cyber Gadget grip and it makes gaming so much more comfortable. I have grips for all my handhelds, and will continue to do so for any future ones.If you're a Zelda fan, this is the 3DS to get. While the aspect ratio may not be as sharp as a regular 3DS, the XL provides a better experience for aging eyes. The black and gold XL looks great closed or opened, and my wife has commented on how much time I spend on the machine. Not sure if that's a good thing or bad thing, but I'll leave that here to show just how much time I spend on Nintendo's latest golden handheld experience.
